With the pretence that a spectator has failed to understand instructions, thereby giving the magician a pretext to take an already intended action. [obsolete after 1896, formerly very rare] Originally French theatrical lingo denoting an actor's remarks directed off-stage. REF: Hoffmann in Robert-Houdin (1877 tr), 111n. Thence French conjurors jargon by 1868 Robert-Houdin. Thence English-speaking magicians jargon, there being no precise equivalent English phrase or word, by 1877 Hoffmann, 204, 214, as "à la cantonade"; 1896 Roterberg as "parlant à la cantonnade".

(See also: Side Issue, A.) n. Spiritualistic materialization effect where a spirit emerges horizontally from the magician's side in a cloud of vapor, turns upright, steps forward, and speaks to the audience. [archaic since 1907]

n. The role of the evil magician in the traditional English Christmas "pantomine" of Aladdin. [rare] Abanazar in this Arabian Night's playlet is a choice part for "real" magicians, most prominently Albert Chevalier (1888), Charles T. Aldrich (1914 in USA in Chin-Chin), Fred Culpitt, Donald Stuart (1920s-30s), Claude Chandler, Edward Victor (1937 on), Les Levante (1937 & 1942), Terry Seabrooke (1970s), and Granville "Faust" Taylor (1984). REF: Waller (1948/1980), 219; Sharpe (1976), 66; Ogden (1997), 145; Price (1985), 307.
See: Mene Tekel Board. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Mene Tekel Board".)
n. An egg bag disguised as a North African fez; the Fez Egg Bag. [fairly common] 37
a. In the mainstream of magical knowledge. Opposite of underground. [very rare, probably nonce]

1.n. A magic word, that is, a command-word spoken ostensibly to trigger an effect. [obsolescent among magicians and then usually tongue-in-cheek] Abracadabra was originally a spell to ward off ills. Used as early as the 2nd Century AD in Rome. And in Britain as late as during the Great London Plague of 1665, as noted by Daniel Defoe in his novel, A Journal of the Plague Year (1723). Modern research traces this remarkably durable word back to around 2000 B.C. to the ancient Sumerian AB-BA-TAB-BA-RI- GI ("O my/our father who art in heaven!"). This potent plea to catch the ear of the god eventually became the Greek abrasadabra, a Gnostic Christian term of around 150 A.D. used to invoke divine aid. This interpretation seriously undermines the earlier scholarly guesses that it was coined from either the name Abrasax, a Gnostic leader, or from the three Hebrew words Ab (the Father) + Ben (the Son) + Acadeh (the Holy Spirit). The modern spelling first appeared in a 2nd century Latin poem by Q. Severus Sammonicus. REF: J. Allegro, The Sacred Mushroom and the Cross (London: Hodder and Stoughton, 1970), 160-162; OED/2. For the earlier views see the OED/1 and Morris (1977). The RHD/2nd, in a careless guess, dismisses the word as "perhaps reflecting recitation of the initial letters of the alphabet." Thence magicians jargon patter-word by 1886 Holden as "Abracadabra Arabi Pasha Pass"; 1900 Stanyon in Magic, 4, as obsolete; 1903 Hoffmann, 441; 1922 Branson; 1937 J.G. Alexander; 1939 Barbara Stanwyck in Jinx; 1947 Braue in HMM; 1947 Hugard in HMM; 1948 Easley; 1948 Elliott; 1950 Jonson; 1953 Branson; 1956 Dexter; 1957 Leroy in HMM; 1969 Nelms; 1978 Gross; 1979 Fisher; 1981 Ray-Mond; 1982 Ginn; 1983 Desfor; 1984 Bamman in LR as obsolete; 1988 Waters as obsolescent; 1988 Gavilondo in Magigram; 1988 Albrecht cartoon; 1994 Rohde & Schröder in Almanach; 1997 Lee cat #11; 2002 J. London in MagiCurrents as “wave your wand and say Abracadabra”. 2.a. Magical. [rare, and then usually somewhat facetiously] 38 "All the gimmicks and gizmos of the abracadabra business were new and mysterious to most of our company." — Marion Nicola in F. Marshall, Those Beautiful Dames (1984), 9

n. A concealed assistant—unsuspected by the audience—who works the tricks by pulling threads while in the wings, operating traps from under the stage, or working mechanisms from inside large apparatus. Compare thread puller. [rare]
n. The Four Ace Trick (see) being the most usual synonym. [fairly common]
n. The Four Ace Trick (see) being the full and most usual title. [fairly common] Famous versions are the Collins' Aces and the McDonald Aces.

n. Any movement used to show a hand apparently empty (clean) when an object (such as a ball or coin) is palmed in it; a handwash. [fairly common] "I'd like to point out that Leipzig, along with most top manipulators in his field, took a dim view of acquitments as a matter of course, especially those involving motions like ‘washing the hands'." — Roy Benson in The New Phoenix #326 (1955), 112 Usually an obviously unnatural gesture, hence often unconvincing. The most effective and therefore most commonly used method is the changeover palm. Another is the pincette. Acquitments were featured by Theo "Okito" Bamberg. 39 This word, from the Old French "aquitement" (meaning "releasing"), entered Standard English in 1643 (Milton) in the same sense. REF: OED/2. Thence adapted (or even coined independently) by magician Burling Hull shortly before 1910 to designate "sleights designed to acquit the hands of any suspicion of concealing an article." REF: Hull (1910), 23. Thus magicians jargon from 1910 Hull; 1929 Deveen; 1935 Hugard; 1938 Hilliard; 1944 Thayer cat #9/5; 1947 Zovello in HMM; 1948 Norman; 1949 Farelli in HMM; 1949 LePaul; 1949 Hay; 1953 Elliott; 1956 Dexter; 1967 Baron; 1972 Griffin; 1976 Tarr; 1980 J. Marshall; 1981 Lees/MacMillan; 1982 Beam; 1987 Johnsson in LR as "aquitment" [sic]; 1992 Burt ad in Genii as "aquitment" [sic]; 1993 Riser in MUM; 1998 L&L cat NOTE: Interestingly, this word is now obsolete in English except among magicians, although with them sometimes—
n. Effect where a matchbox placed on the back of the magicians hand gyrates and opens. [fairly common]

n. A full (52-card) pack of marked playing cards with a baseball-themed design on the back. [archaic, formerly fairly common] Designed in the late 1910s by the S.S. Adams Company of New Jersey. The round baseballs are marked using DeLand's clock system.
n. The Add-on being the most usual synonym.
n. Apparatus that permits the magician-mentalist to switch the numbers selected by the volunteers for a set that gives the predicted total. [rare]

a. Said of anything that gives unfair advantage. [rare although widely understood] "Almost every card worker uses an advantage or key card of some sort to allow out of the ordinary effects impossible otherwise, so I have no qualms about using a short card for this." — Ted Annemann in The Jinx (1938), 331 This charming term—more a descriptive in-joke than a euphemism—was originally the argot of card sharps by 1591 Robert Greene as "Dice of advantage"; 1843 Crambrook cat; 1865 Evans as the "advantage player" & "advantage cards"; 1866 Barnum as “advantage-cards”; 1877 Grandin pricelist as "advantage and marked back playing cards"; 42 1902 Erdnase as the "advantage player"; 1905 Ritter as "advantage card playing"; 1922 Downs letter to McGuire as “advantage playing at cards”; 1933 Cameron as an "advantage player". Thence magicians jargon by 1923 Elliott as "advantage playing devices"; 1938 Annemann in Jinx #47; 1990 Grismer letter to Busby as "advantage card play"; 1991 Weber in Inside Magic as "advantage card play".
See: Rising Cards. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Rising Cards".)
n. Effect where fish are caught in mid-air by rod-and-reel; fish-catching. [fairly common]
See: Flower Darts. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Flower Darts".)

n. The Miser's Dream (see) being the later and now more usual synonym. [obsolescent after 1957] Performed under this title by Charles Bertram who introduced it in his act on 15 March 1885 at St. James's Hall, London. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 93. 43
n. The Miser's Dream being the later and now more usual synonym. [obsolescent]

n. Effect in topological magic where long loops of paper (or cloth) are cut (or torn) lengthwise to produce typically, first the expected two separate loops, then, surprisingly, two interlocked loops, and finally a single double-length loop. [common] "’You have seen the puzzle of the Paper Ring?' Mein Herr said.... ‘Yes, I know that Puzzle,' said Lady Muriel. ‘The ring has only one surface and only one edge. It's very mysterious!'" — Lewis Carroll, Sylvie and Bruno Concluded (1893) This curious and appealing trick is based on the mathematical topologists’ Möbius Strip, the three-dimensional yet one-sided surface discovered in 1858 by German mathematician- astronomer August Möbius and published by him in 1865 (although independently discovered and published in 1861 by Johann Listing). It became a popular parlor-magic trick after 1882 when first published for parlor-magic enthusiasts in Gaston Tissandier's Popular Scientific Recreations, which was the enlarged English translation of his Les récréations scientifiques (1881). First included in a professional magic act toward the end of the late 1800s by French magician-shadowist-chapeaugraphist Félicien Trewey who used it as a pet effect. Thence emerged by 1900 as the professional conjurers "Mystic Afgan [sic] Bands" in a version commercially marketed in Britain by Ellis Stanyon. Originally (and sometimes still) used with paper strips until 1920 when Carl Brema substituted cloth to save time by quick hand-tearing rather than slow scissors-cutting. In Jan 1922 Brema, on the suggestion of his associate, Philadelphia lawyer James C. Wobensmith, added the now-standard multiple-pasted twists and marketed it as "The Red Muslin Bands". This version was a pet effect of Blackstone (by 1924) and Downs (by 1926). In 1930 Stanyon published his Remarkable Evolution of the ‘Afghan Bands', his original variation that produces 2 to 5 untwisted but linked bands. By 1945 Fred Rickard introduced a further minor modification in the Wobensmith design. And Winston Freer created a rather bizarre handling. In 1977 Ed Eckl popularized (but admittedly didn't invent) the zippered cloth that he marketed as "Möby-Zip", which was later pirated by several other dealers. REF: Stanyon #4 (1900), 21; Stanyon in Magic (Nov 1903), 21; Hilliard (1938), 860; Gardner (1956), 70-77; Gibson (1927); Ed Eckl, Gardyloo (1977), 30-31; Gary Ward, "The Story of the Afghan Bands", Linking Ring (Apr 1994), 60-61. NOTE: Clarke in Magic Wand (Oct 1924), 138, wrongly claims that this trick is explained in H. Dean's book of the 1720s.

n. The Vanity Fair illusion (see). [obsolete after 1907, formerly rare] From the title of the then popular song that Alexander Herrmann used as the theme music in presenting his "Vanity Fair" illusion. REF: Gibson (1968), 78.

1.n. Popular early version of the Levitation Illusion. Operated by a free-standing hoist concealed behind the back cloth. Compare Asrah. [obsolescent, once common] Reportedly invented in Germany by Albert "Venturini" Winkler (who sold British rights to Gamages in 1910). First (?) performed in Europe in 1902 by Otto Heinemann as "The Mysterious Aga," Heinemann also claiming its invention. Featured by Devant (1906), Goldin (1907), etc. Created an instant sensation but was so widely and frequently shown in vaudeville and carnivals—including both deliberate exposures and poor performances that virtually assured self-exposure—that its audience appeal was saturated by 1905. Still, this remained the main type of levitation until Servais Le Roy introduced his superior version, Asrah, in 1914. However, because the Aga apparatus is much simpler and compact, it has continued to the present as the preferred alternative for small-stage and carnival work. REF: Magical World, I (1910), 25; Hilliar in Sphinx (1906); Boston & Parrish (1947), 94; McKinven (1980), 35; Stanyon in Magic (Nov 1904), 11-13, (Jul 1906), 73-74. The origin of this odd word is uncertain. It may well be, as Bruce Armstrong speculates, the Turkish title Agh or Aga (as in the "Aga Khan"), meaning a master, great lord, or commander-in-chief and that the magician who adopted it was, in effect, dubbing the illusion "chief of them all." REF: Armstrong (1976), 73; Warlock (1986), 9.

n. Initials for Associate of the Inner Magic Circle, meaning the 3rd most advanced degree of membership granted by The Magic Circle, the premier London-based magic society (founded 1905). This intermediate degree was added in 1907 to the two original ones (M.M.C. & M.I.M.C.). [rare]

n. Traditional British Christmas-season pantomime that often features stage magic by the character of the evil wizard, Abanazar. The original (with scenario by John O'Keefe) premiered in 1788 at The Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, London. Later revisions were by Charles Farley (1813), H.J. Byron (1861), etc., and most recently (1959) with music by American composer Cole Porter and book by Peter Cooke. The Scottish Ballet premiered a ballet version with score by Carl Davies at Xmas 2000. The role of Abanazar in this Arabian Night's playlet (but set in China) is a choice part for "real" magicians. REF: Raymond Mander & Joe Mitchenson, Pantomime (New York: Taplinger, 1973), 17, 22, 23, 30, 31, 45, 46, 48, 50; Ogden (1997), 4, 10, 144, 145; J. Maskelyne (1949), 25-26, 27, 170;
n. Card effect where spectator thinks of any card and removes it, magus writes name of that card 46 on another, which proves correct. [rare]

n. The effect where the face-cards in a deck or packet are replaced by their backs. [rare] First marketed in Linking Ring in Aug 1930 by Jean Hugard who claimed its invention on that occasion. In 1933 Ralph Hull marketed his gaffed N.R.A. Deck, one of whose sequences produced an All Backs effect. The first all-sleights version was the famous Dai Vernon one, which he first published in Hugard's Magic Monthy in Jun 1949 and again, in more detailed form, in Hugard & Braue’s Expert Card Technique (3rd ed, 1950). REF: Busby FAX to Whaley, 28 Oct 1993; Hugard note in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jun 1949), 552; Racherbaumer in Linking Ring (Aug 1997), 105.
n. A coin box with a small hole through which coins seemingly can be made to penetrate under cover of a handkerchief. [rare] Popularized by Al Baker and Nate Leipzig. REF: Bobo (1966 edition), 489.
n. Effect where spectator examines & shuffles an Alphabet Deck and forms a 5-letter word face down yet the mentalist devines the word. [rare]
n. Effect where the mid-part of a volunteer's fore-arm is seen to have vanished after after being placed in a horizontal box and cut through by two steel blades. [rare]

n. The arcs of visibility and invisibility inside and outside the lines of sight between audience and trick. All visual effects are worked inside that angle; all methods remain hidden outside it. Hiding is provided by cover. Compare angleproof. [common] "Angles forever remind us that we conjurers live in a half world, divided into out front (which is magical) and backstage (where the wires are)." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 36 52 "Angles are tricky with coins, bothersome with cards; with billiard balls they are almost an insuperable obstacle." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 180 Referred to as the "angle of visibility" in 1909 by J.N. Hilliard; 1927 Tarbell. Thence jargon simply as the angle by 1927 Tarbell; 1934 E.G. Brown; 1936 Thayer cat #8; 1941 Vernon as "the ‘angles' are very good"; 1947 Hay; 1956 Dexter, 28-29; 1961 Andrus as the "angles of vulnerability"; 1976 Tarr as "be sure to get your angles right"; 1976 Cervon as "bad angles"; 1983 Ammar; 1985 Kaufman as "good angles"; 1996 Busby in Thauma #31 as "no angle problems". a. Adjectivally as in angle-proof. [fairly common] "Even the Imp Bottle has angle problems." — Rick Johnsson, Practical Impossibilities (1976), 3
n. A card (or packet of cards) protruding (jogged) at an angle from the deck's side or end.

n. Hypnotism; Mesmerism. [obsolescent, formerly rare] Originally, by 1782, the lingo of Mesmerists (having been coined by Anton Mesmer), meaning the pseudo-scientific concept that all humans are immersed in an invisible all-pervading natural fluid force similar to the physicist's magnetism. Gradually replaced by the term "Mesmerism" beginning in 1802. REF: OED/2; Alan Gauld, A History of Hypnotism (Cambridge: Cambridge UP, 1992), 1-270.
n. Effect where a coin jumps about by itself in a glass tumbler. [obsolete, formerly fairly common]

n. Effect where a cigarette emerges from a pack, floats to the magician's lips; the cigarette pack changes into a matchbox, which opens and a match floats out, strikes itself, and floats up to light the cigarette. [rare]

n. Type of method where the hidden move has already occurred before the audience supposes it has. A major form of misdirection, specifically the one that deceives about timing; the one- ahead principle. Opposite of premature conclusion and premature consummation. [rare]

n. Trick where an ordinary liquid-filled bottle can be inverted and at the magician's whim either pour or, in apparent defiance of gravity, not pour. [common] "Wanna know what the biggest selling pocket trick of all time is? It's Isley's Anti- Gravico." — Karrell Fox in The Linking Ring (Mar 1987), 39 Depends on a clear-plastic stopper-gimmick. Invented in the early 1940s by Bob Andre, a Cleveland amateur magician, business executive, and commercial inventor ("Snap-on Blocks," etc.). Calling it Anti-Gravico, he demonstrated it privately to friends, including magicians Stuart Cramer, Robert Nelson, and John Isley. Isley, a demonstrator at a magic-and-joke shop, recognized its commercial potential and in 1943 bought the rights for $24 and the promise that it be advertised as "Andre's Anti-Gravico". Going into home-industry business for himself as The Mystic Isely (note spelling change), Isley manufactured and marketed it. His first ads, in Jan 1944, in Genii, Linking Ring and Sphinx credited it as "a ‘Bob Andre' creation"; but, beginning next month, he changed the ad to read "Isely's Anti-Gravico" and dropping any mention of Andre. The trick was an instant success, widely pirated by April, and proclaimed "best pocket trick of the year" by William Larsen Sr. Because of Isley's shoddy marketing ethics, the trick became generally miscredited to him. REF: Stuart Cramer, "Bob Andre's Anti-Gravico," The Linking Ring (Apr 1985), 40-42.

a. Said of effects that defy the law of gravity. [fairly common] Early examples are the floating wand and the hydrostatic glass. More recent ones are Anti- Gravity Glasses, Anti-Gravico, and Wa-Ter-Lu.

n. Effect where two tumblers placed on a cloth-covered book or board with the magician's thumb between them will remain there when the magician turns the platform upside-down; the Japanese Glass Levitation (obsolete); the Mesmerized Glasses (obsolete). [rare] An authentic Japanese trick first published by Ishii Black in The Magician (1914 or 1915) using either a paper covered fan or book. First demonstrated in the West in 1936 by Japanese magician Tenkai to the staff (William Larsen Sr, Gerald Kosky, and William Taylor) of Genii magazine, which promptly published it as the "Japanese Glass Levitation". A pet effect of Jack Gwynne since 1940 and Harry Riser in 1940s &50s. REF: Genii (Nov 1936), 11-12; Charvet (1986), 218-221.

n. Comedy effect where the end of a stick placed horizontally on the edge of a surface will leave the rest of the stick suspended in space regardless of which end is so placed. Not to be confused with the Floating Wand. [very rare but not nonce]

n. A magician specializing in the exposure of fraudulent spiritualistic mediums. [obsolete after 1910] The word "spiritualist" entered Standard English in 1852. The term anti-spiritualist was coined in 1855 by English- Jewish magician Joseph Jacobs (playbill) but did not catch on until 1873 when British magicians John Nevil Maskelyne and George Alfred Cooke took the term to advertise the spiritualistic exposé part of their popular act. Still used as jargon as late as 1910 (Leroy's catalog).
a. Adjectival form of anti-spiritualist. [obsolescent after 1932]
(See also: Diavolo Antonio.) n. Automaton trapeze artist that performs several amazing feats under the magician's direction; Antonio Diavolo. [rare]
n. Effect where the magician produces from his pockets any single card or card-hand requested by a spectator; Cards from the Pockets. [rare]

n. Effect where the magician pours from a single vessel a succession of different drinks requested by the audience; the Magic Bar. [fairly common] Progenitor of this effect was Blaise Manfre who in the early 1600s introduced the art of the Water-Spouter, swallowing plain water and spewing forth streams of "wine" or "beer" on demand. Apparatus versions—better suited to squeemish audiences—followed, leading first to the Inexhaustible Bottle, the Magic Kettle, and then, since the mid-1920s, to the modern Magic Bar created by French magician Ryss.

1.n. Generally, any visible piece of equipment, whether faked or not; props; paraphernalia. [obsolescent] 57 "The ideal conjuring performance is a happy combination of apparatus and sleight of hand." — T. Nelson Downs & J. Northern Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909), Introductory "There's enough apparatus in the magic shops for all the magicians in the country, but are there enough magicians in the country for all the apparatus?" — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1946), 278

(See also: apparatus trick.) n. A specific example of apparatus magic, that is, an effect whose method is a self-working device. [rare] ABRIL LAMARQUE: "Someday I'd like to see you do an apparatus trick." DOC DALEY: "Someday you'll see me do the fish-bowl production." — Conversation of 17 Feb 1954 as quoted in The New Phoenix #302 (1954), 5

n. Conjuring with self-working devices. A single specific instance is termed an apparatus trick. [rare] "Many magicians seem to believe that it is easier to do apparatus magic than much of the sleight-of-hand variety. I think that it is easier to do apparatus magic poorly, but it takes just as much thought and routining and handling practice to do apparatus magic well as any other type." — Phil Willmarth in The Linking Ring (Mar 1986), 73
See: apparatus conjurer. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "apparatus conjurer".)

n. A specific example of apparatus magic, that is, an effect whose method is a self-working device. [rare] ABRIL LAMARQUE: "Someday I'd like to see you do an apparatus trick." DOC DALEY: "Someday you'll see me do the fish-bowl production." — Conversation of 17 Feb 1954 as quoted in The New Phoenix #302 (1954), 5
v. To produce. Opposite of to vanish or to disappear. [very rare]
n. A production being the much more usual synonym. Opposite of a disappearance. [fairly common]
n. A collapsed spring-loaded vinyl production item that when triggered instantly expands to simulate a soda or beer can. [rare]
n. A candle (lit or not) that is produced in the magicians hands. [rare]
n. A walking-stick that can be produced out of thin air. Compare the Vanishing Cane. [common]

n. Stage illusion whose effect is the production of a pachyderm. Opposite of the Vanishing Elephant. [very rare] A suitable production box was first devised by Gustave Fasola who built a minature working model sometime in the late 1920s. He sold this to Howard Thurston who had it built full-scale and premiered the illusion in Fall 1928. Shown only one week by Thurston because his 700- pound Indian elephant, Delhi, died. This apparatus was bought by Will Rock from Jane 60 Thurston sometime between 1938 and 1940. Doug Henning presented the effect in his 1976 TV special. REF: Thurston, 8 Jul 1928 letter to Dante; Gibson in Phoenix #5 (1942), 20; Gibson & Young (1961), 141; Christopher (1973), 234.
(See also: Appearing Can.) n. A collapsed spring-loaded vinyl production item that when triggered instantly expands to simulate a soda or beer can. [rare]

n. Any object ostensibly brought from a distant place by the spirits. [rare] Originated with spiritualistic mediums. Recently a specialty of Uri Geller and Sai Baba. The word entered Standard English in 1894. REF: OED/2; Keene (1976), 10. Thence magicians jargon by 1946 Hugard in HMM, 266; 1948 Rawson in Ellery Queen’s Mystery Magazine; 1988 Waters; 1996 Silverman; 1997 Waldman; 1998 Barry Cooper in LR as trick title.

term: Arabian Bead Mystery, The; Arabian Beads
definition: n. The Beads of Prussia being the most usual American synonym and the Carmo Beads the usual British one. [rare]

n. The secret knowledge of facts that enable certain tricks to work without sleights, prearrangement, or apparatus; secret knowledge.. [very rare, possibly nonce, despite its usefulness] Examples: — Cutting a deck does not disrupt the rotated sequence of the playing cards. — Tearing a folded piece of paper both ways leaves the center intact. The center-tear principle. — The number of spots on the two opposite faces of every honest die totals seven. This is the so-called seven principle. — The English names for every card in a deck contain either 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, or 15 letters. This fact is the basis for the mnemonic system by which all spelling tricks work. — The one-way deck principle. — The mirror principle. — The black-art principle. — The hydrostatic glass. — All examples of bio-magic. — All examples of mathematical magic, including topological magic. Originally Standard English since 1547 in the general sense of deeply hidden secrets. "Arcana" is the plural, "arcanum" is singular", and "arcane" is the adjectival form. REF: OED/2. Adopted as magicians jargon in this sense in 1969 by Henning Nelms, noting (p.128) that, while many magical effects and methods depend on this category, "conjurers have never developed a technical name for it."
n. A chopper that threatens to cut off the volunteer's arm. [fairly common]
v. To watch the tell-tale movements of a drawer's arm; arm-reading. [very rare]

n. Pretentious early synonym for the art of magic. [obsolescent after 1937, formerly rare] "The literature on conjuring can hardly be said to be replete with histories of l'Art Magique." — H. Adrian Smith, "Magical Histories", Tops (Jul 1937)
n. Codename for the sub-stage elevator used by members of the various Thurston illusion shows. [obsolete, formerly very rare]
n. Stage illusion where a woman steps out of a picture painted by the magician. [obsolescent; once fairly common]
n. The Ascanio Spread (see). [very rare]
1.n. The famous levitation illusion, widely conceded to be the most effective one used, where the assistant is first levitated and then vanished in mid-air. [common]
n. Official title of each of the chartered local branches of the Society of American Magicians (SAM). It is the equivalent of a Ring in the International Brotherhood of Magicians (IBM). [rare]

n. Any person who helps the magician perform a trick. [very common] There are two general types of assistant: overt and covert, the former called a volunteer, the latter a confederate, plant (1.n.), or stooge. REF: Bob Haskell, "The Lady Assistant", M-U-M (Aug 1951); Jan Jones, The Magician's Assistant (1982). "As a performer who most of his life has worked alone, I have always envied the magicians who have one or two trained assistants. So many wonderful effects are possible, so many smooth transitions can be made." — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1952), 1016 "The assistant is the most visual 'prop' the magician has...." — Pamela Toliver in M. Chavez, Prestidigitation and Showmanship (1968), 29 "Marian may have been billed as an assistant but in this and many other effects in the Murray show, she was really the magician. The unsuspected hidden-aide who performed the necessary." — Val Andrews in F. Marshall, Those Beautiful Dames (1984), 17
n. Stage illusion where the assistant, bound to an upright board, switches place with the magician under cover of a curtain. 66 [rare]

n. The unconscious psychological process by which the brain categorizes its perceptions. [rare] Exploited by the magician to achieve misdirection. "You, the magician, make a movement or show an object that produces, by association, a familiar image. You contrive in fact to bring about a result contrary to the normal association. Result: surprise — a conjuring trick." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 2

n. Stage effect where a female assistant levitates and then turns somersaults. Pronounced a- STAR-tee. [archaic after 1906] Used a lifting and rotating pole (masked by black art) projected through the rear curtain.

n. Apparatus that covers the effect where a ball and a wineglass are placed side-by-side in a small cabinet, the door closed, and the ball has jumped into the glass. [rare] Pirated version in mid-1960s by Jim Simon (Worth Magic Company) giving one of the effects in Stewart James's multi-part Sefalaljia routine. As James wryly commented: "I expect the originality in that version was the use of a cocktail glass." REF: Busby interviews of 30 Dec 1987 and 3 Jul 1988; Busby (1995).

n. Effect where, as three cards are taken one-by-one from a deck in one houlette and placed in a second, the spectators call "stop" and the card in transit at that moment is the chosen card. [fairly common] This apparatus version of the Stop Trick was invented by British magician-mechanician Jack Hughes in the late 1930s. First marketed in the USA in 1946 by Abbott's. REF: Lever (1981), 8, 41-45; Elliott in Phoenix (1946), 460.

n. The magician's calculated manipulation of the audience's interest to keep its attention focused on the essential parts of the effect as the trick unfolds to the exclusion of the secret method or methods employed. [rare] "Effective attention control is never recognized as such." — Dariel Fitzkee, Magic by Misdirection (1945), 47 The general techniques of attention control are misdirection and pointing. Specific misdirective techniques are sudden or suspicious movement, making a loud noise, appearance of a bright color, etc.
a. A magic trick or routine that has often played successfully before lay spectators. [common]
See: Down and Under Deal. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Down and Under Deal".)
n. Stage effect where an assistant is put inside a tall stack of automobile tires and, when the tires are removed one-by-one, she is seen to have vanished. [very rare]
a. Said of any trick or apparatus whose method of operation requires no sleight of hand; self- working being the more usual synonym. [fairly common]
n. A specially set-up pack of playing cards. [very rare]

n. Words appearing on a surface by seemingly supernatural means. [rare] Originally the argot of spirit mediums since 1883 when it referred to the medium's hand being directed by a spirit. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1921 C. Alexander; 1931 Mussey & Oursler; 1935 Annemann; 1941 Larsen; 1945 Thompson; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1950 Jonson; 1987 Coleman; 1993 Hollywood Magic cat #18; 1997 Waldman.

n. Any seemingly self-operated, robot-like mechanism. [obsolescent among magicians; once common] "A relationship between magic and automata has been credited with the moving of magic from the streets and marketplaces to barns, vacant stores, and finally to the theatrical stage itself." — David Price, Magic: A Pictorial History of Conjurers in the Theater (1985), 11 Automata were a popular adjunct to magic shows from the early 1700s until the late 1800s. The most famous was Von Kempelen's Automaton Chess Player of 1769. Another was Clarke & Maskelyne's Psycho, which was conceived in 1873 and premiered in 1875. REF: Mary Hillier, Automata & Mechanical Toys (London: Jupiter, 1976); Annette Beyer, Faszinierende Welt der Automaten (Germany: Callwey, 1983); A. Chapuis & E. Droz, Les Automates (Neuchâtel: 1949); A. Chapuis & E. Gelis, Monde des Automates (Paris: 1928); Eliane Maingot, Les Automates (Paris: 1959); Sharpe (1983), 119-158, 191; Conrad William Cooke, Automata (London: 1893). Standard English since 1611 Coryat as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1742 English translation of Vaucanson; 1784 Philip Thicknesse pamphlet. Thence magicians jargon by 1777 Droz, London ad as "autamata"; 1796 Haddock ad; 1805 Pinchbeck; 1811 Philipstal & Maillardet, Bridgewater poster; 1820 Maelzel handbill; 1829 Boy’s Own Book; 1857 Magician's Own Book; 1878 Cummings handbill; 1897 Hopkins; 1907 Houdini in CMM; 1912 Goldston; 1950 Young; 1956 Dexter; 1979 Lamb; 1988
n. A pack of 52 irregular playing cards faked with sanded pairs placed back-to-back. 71 [archaic, formerly very rare]
a. Adjectival acronym for Black Art (3). [rare]

term: back-and-front palm; back and front palm
definition: n. Any sleight, specifically an acquitment, that covertly transfers one or more cards (or a coin or thimble) back and forth from the front to the back of the hand, thereby permitting the entire hand to be shown apparently empty; the Continuous Front and Back Hand Palm (obsolete). [fairly common]
n. The back palm being the usual synonym; the backhand palm (obsolete). [obsolete after 1931, formerly very rare]

n. A sleight that conceals an object (usually a card or coin) at the back of the hand; back palming; back hand clip (obsolete); backhand palm (obsolete); reverse palm (1) (obsolete). 73 [common] "As an exhibition of dexterity this is probably unsurpassed in card manipulation, but it is of little aid in the performance of tricks. However, everything may be put to some use, and the back palm once helped us out of a difficult situation—’but that is another story'." — S. W. Erdnase, Artifice Ruse and Subterfuge at the Card Table (1902), 147 "If anybody tries to tell me that Cardini does a superb back-palm I shall sock him in the jaw. He does not have to do a back-palm. He just picks the cards out of the air." — Rhadamanthus Jr in The Jinx (1941), 789 Anatomically a misnomer (as pointed out by Sachs, Erdnase, Hilliard, Gaultier, Hugard, Zovello, Page, and Busby) because it uses the hand's back and not its palm. However, as seen under the entry for palm, that word became conventionally extended to any hiding-place in or around the hand and not just literally in its palm. Described as a common sleight with a coin (as the "Reverse Palm") as early as 1877 by Sachs (p.7). Mastered with coins in 1884 by T. Nelson Downs in his back-and-front palm acquitment. As used with a card, this sleight was seemingly invented by card gamblers, although presumably only as a flourish because it is inappropriate in card play. In any case, the sleight was introduced to card magic when in 1887 a Spanish gambler from Mexico taught it to Otto Maurer, a prominent German-American magical apparatus manufacturer-dealer in New York City. [Selbit miscredits Maurer with its invention.] Maurer later taught it privately to several American magicians including Dr. James W. Elliott and Harry Houdini. [According to Houdini, he and Elliott got their instruction from Maurer at the same time, although in separate private sessions. Roterberg miscredits the invention to Elliott but confirms that Houdini taught it to Howard Thurston who taught it to Augustus Rapp around 1898.] Elliott taught it to his partner, Barney Ives, and the two passed it along to William E. Robinson, Alexander Herrmann, Servais Le Roy, Nelson Downs, and Lawrence Crane. Performed publicly in America in 1895 by Downs and in France around 1895 by Harmington ("Fanque") at the Théâtre Robert-Houdin. Between 1895 and 1897 it became a pet effect of Downs, Imro Fox, Houdini, Robinson, Ziska, and Thurston. From 1898 on it was done to death by legions of cardmen. REF: Thurston in Selbit (1901), 119-120; Houdini in Elliott (1923), 15, 323; Roterberg (1897); Rapp (1959), 122; Clarke in Magic Wand (1928), 34-35; Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1943), 29-32.

n. The area—usually literally a room at the back—in some magic shops reserved for advanced magicians. [fairly common] "When I was a kid I always wanted to see a magic dealer's back room; it was sort of like going backstage." — Jay Marshall in The New Phoenix #320 (1954), 87 The more famous were in Vernello's in Chicago (ca1901-ca1907), Martinka's in New York City (ca1900-ca1911), Carl Brema's Magic Shop in Philadelphia (1920s), U.F. Grant's shop on 42nd Street in New York (1937), Harry Smith's in Toronto (since 1939), Al Flosso's in New York (1940s-50s), Gene Gordon's in Buffalo (1945-69), and Lou Tannen's in New York.

n. The unpublicized inventors (or designers) and builders of the cunning stage illusions and props presented as if they were the magician's own creations. When the back-room boy builds only stage illusions, he is called specifically an illusion builder. [rare] Among the more important have been: Opré ( -1846), Dutch prop maker for David Leendert Bamberg & De Grisy (?) Legrand (fl.1840s), French prop & automata maker for Robert-Houdin N.E. Chase (fl.1850s), American prop maker in New England Hermann Liebholz (1832-1875), German wood-turner in Hamburg Thomas Howell (fl.1870s-80s), British mechanic for J.N. Maskelyne & A. Herrmann William E. Robinson (1861-1918), American illusion designer to A. Herrmann Henry Bates (fl. 1st decade of 1900s), English mechanician for David Devant James "Jim" Collins (ca1882-1942), British mechanician and carpenter to Houdini Guy Jarrett (1881-1972), American illusion inventor Cyril "Yetty" Yettmah (ca1883-1949), British illusion designer John Martin (1882-1968), Lithuanian-born British mechanician Herman Hanson (1882-1973), Swedish-born carpenter-magician David J. Lustig (1893-1977), American developer of many of Dunninger's "brain-busters" Edmund Spreer (1902-1983), German-born mechanician Jack Hughes (1906-1981), British dealer-inventor Eric C. Lewis (1908-1993), British dealer-inventor Harry "Devano" Mitchell (1918-1996), British amateur mechanician Ken Brooke (1920-1983), British dealer-improver of routines Gil Leaney (1921-1993), British illusion builder Alan Wakeling (1926- ), American illusion designer Charles Reynolds (1932- ), American illusion designer John Gaughan (1940- ), American illusion designer/builder Don Wayne (1948- ), American illusion designer Bill Smith (1955- ), American illusion builder Jim Steinmeyer (1958- ), American illusion designer Franz Harary (ca1962- ), American illusion designer Originally British slang since 1941, referring to the anonymous scientists and engineers who made their quiet contributions toward winning World War II. REF: OED/2; Partridge, 8th ed. 75 Thence magicians jargon (reinforced by the fact that they often worked in the back rooms of the magic shops that employed them) by 1956 Dexter, 98; 1971 Harbin tape; 1985 Sharpe; 1986 Dawes & Setterington, 41; 1988 Waters;
See: Sack Escape. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Sack Escape".)
n. A sack attached to a table (or the magician's clothing) to serve as a servante. [obsolescent]

term: Baking a Cake in a Hat
definition: (See also: Cake Baked in a Hat.) n. Effect where the magician pours the messy ingredients for a pudding or cake into a borrowed hat, produces the cooked solid, and returns the hat unsoiled; the Pudding in Hat (obsolescent). [common] A popular comedy effect among magi from as early as 1749 when French sleight-of-hand man Delisle magically cooked an omelette in a hat. Hyman "The Incomparable Young Dutchman" Saunders produced pancakes in this manner during his tour of Jamaica in 1775. Performed by Ingleby Sr in England in 1822, again with pancakes; and by Anderson by 1841 with a pudding. Marketed by 1843 by Crambrook in London. Writing in 1853, French magician J.N. Ponsin therefore rightly called this trick "well known". A pet effect of Al Baker (1941). Since the 1950s a popular TV-magic kid-show trick. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand, XIV (1925), 34.
n. A gimmick-free self-levitation of a few inches (2 to 5) from standing position. [rare]
n. Pocket magic effect where a ball passes through a solid brass bolt threaded through a brass cube. [fairly common]
n. The Ball Vase, particularly the earliest model with telltale grooves around its top. [rare]
n. Conjuring with balls; ball tricks. [rare]
n. Sleight-of-hand with balls, particular billiard ball manipulation. [rare]

n. A flourish in billiard-ball manipulation that transfers a ball across the back of the spread fingers, one finger at a time. [rare] Although only an ornamental sleight, the ball roll can serve to convince the audience that the hand is otherwise empty when in fact it can simultaneously have a second ball palmed. 79
n. A dropper made of cloth to hold several billiard balls and deliver them successivly by squeezing a flexible ring at the bottom end. [rare]

n. Effect where a steel ball slowly sinks into a brass or glass tube for the magician but not when a volunteer handles it. [fairly common] The method requires a second tube that slides unnoticed within the visible outer tube. Can be operated from a distance by a thread. Evidently first marketed (and thus probably invented) by Carl Brema in 1926 as "The Mysterious Ball-Bearing Trick"; although reportedly in Bartl or Willmann catalogs around that same time.
n. The Ball Vase (see) being the most usual synonym. [fairly common]

n. Apparatus to vanish and/or produce a ball; the Ball and Vase; the Ball Box (Brit.); the Egg- Box (obsolete). [fairly common] Described as early as the 1763 edition of Dean's The Whole Art of Legerdemain (pp. 64-65) as the "Egg-Box" because of it's ovoid shape. A standby of toy shops and children's magic by 1860. A major variant is the Morison Pill Box. REF: Stanyon in Magic (Feb 1912), 38.

n. The effect where a small flat object (usually a coin, sometimes a wedding ring or key) is vanished and later discovered inside a tightly wound ball of wool; the Coin in Ball of Wool. [obsolescent, formerly common] The method involves loading the center of the wool ball through a coin slide as in the Nest of Boxes trick. First mentioned in 1843 in Crambrook's catalog where it is called "The Worsted Trick." First 80 explained by Wyman in 1857 in The Magician's Own Book where it is called "The Dime in the Ball of Cotton" and next in 1859 by The Secret Out, which called it the "Ball of Worsted." A pet effect of Chung Ling Soo (Robinson).
(See also: balloon worker.) n. A performer of balloon sculpture or balloon magic; a balloon twister; balloonologist; a balloon artist. [fairly common]
n. Any shapes produced by balloon sculpture. [rare]

n. In general, conjuring with balloons; specifically, by means of balloon sculpture. [rare] While most balloon workers are content with producing clever figures, a few also integrate them with magic in effects such as the Linking Balloons and the Color Changing Balloons. These truly magical performers include Mal Robbins, Jim Sommers, Richard Cawolsky, Richard Osterlind (since 1984), and Norm Barnhart.
See: Needle through Balloon. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Needle through Balloon".)

n. Type of balloon magic where figures (usually animal) are formed by blowing up and twist-tying long, slender rubber ("pencil") balloons; balloon modeling. [fairly common] Seldom deceptive but a clever and increasingly popular allied art act by magicians. The rapid creation of the figures is a delight to both children and (when obscene) to adult club audiences. Reportedly innovated in the mid-1930s by a French magician as a complete nightclub act. Independently reinvented by Herman J. "Balloons" Bonnert, a Scranton, Pa., novelty wholesaler who, while idly toying with some stock balloons, accidentally discovered the twist-tie principle and recognized its potential for creating figures. Calling these "balloon tricks", Bonnert presented them at magicians conventions as early as 1939 (when Jay Marshall was present) and as recently as 1945 (as Tommy Windsor recalled). Other pioneer balloon-sculpture acts were by Windy Blow (by 1945 in Britain), Wally Boag (by 1947), Don Alan (by 1952), Tommy Windsor (beginning in 1953), Bev Bergeron (late 1950s), Mal Robbins (late 1950s), and John Shirley (late 1950s). REF: Joe La Monica, Balloon Sculpture (1976), 3, citing Charles Mardo and Lou Tannen; Marshall in Don Alan, The Rubber Circus (1958), 15; E. Warlock in Linking Ring (Sep 1986), 103-104.
n. A performer of balloon sculpture or balloon magic; a balloon twister; balloonologist; a balloon artist. [fairly common]
n. A balloon worker being the most usual synonym. [rare]

n. The billet test (see) being the current synonym. [obsolete] Originally the argot of American spiritualistic mediums by 1866 Barnum. Thence 1901 Sylvestre cat as "Ballot Reading Test"; 1904 Stanyon in Magic as "The Ballot Test"; 1922 Houdini as a "Ballot Test". Thence magicians jargon by 1903 Stanyon ad in Magic, 43.

n. A free entertainment to draw customers. [rare] "Harry and Frances [Usher] ... booked a circuit of five-and-ten-cent stores to perform the second-sight trick as a 'bally' for selling horoscopes." — David Price, Magic (1985), 467. Originally American carnival cant well before 1928 meaning the stunt or the "barker's" spiel used to draw a crowd. From "ballyhoo", which had entered Standard English in 1901. REF: RHHDAS; Webster's 10th Collegiate; OED/2; Gresham (1953); Sorrows (1985); Ogden (1993). Thence magicians usage by 1925 in title of magazine Thayer's Magical Ballygram #1; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1958 Kanter cat #10 as "outdoor ballys"; 1964 Taylor; 1985 Price; 1988 Waters; 1998 T. Robbins in MUM. a. [adjectivally] [rare]

n. Name given the Talking Skull by Joseffy, David P. Abbott, Floyd Thayer, and Thomas H. Chislett. [rare] Named after Giuseppe Balsamo, an Italian common thief and forger who was widely but mistakenly believed to have disguised himself as Count Alessandro di Cagliostro (1743-1794), the celebrated occultist. REF: D. Abbott (1908), 6-9; Berg (1983), 43-44.
n. A large woolen egg bag faked with a secret pocket running up one side, entered from the inside bottom. Compare Albini Egg Bag. [very rare]
n. A type of thumb writer where the lead is set in a metal band that clamps around (usually) the thumb. [rare]

n. A toy pistol that when triggered deploys from its barrel a flag with the word "BANG!"; a Comedy Gun being the original but now less usual synonym. [common] “As for the 'Bang Gun’, it is so unlike any real weapon ever seen on land or sea that its use is only justified before an audience composed of children who are just able to read words of four letters.” — Jean Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jun 1945), 124 "Any member caught using a Bang Gun in public for any purpose will be expelled forthwith." — Clayton Rawson, "The Witchdoctors Club By-Laws," 1961 "[A] Bang Gun ... is not funny unless you can read." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (4th ed, 1982), 327 Marketed in Britain by Harry Leat in 1932 and perhaps invented by him. Marketed in the USA by Holden's by 1936, by Kanter's (as the "Silent Gun with a Big 'Bang'"), and by Abbott's (as the "Comedy Gun") by 1940. Rereleased in 1956 by Harold Sterling. A pet prop of Carl Ballantine. In 1943 Orson Welles conceived of and premiered the Bang Rifle. REF: Leat in Leat's Leaflets #27 (1932); Holden's Catalog #5 (1936); F. Marshall in New Phoenix (1957), 178; Tommy Hanlon Jr interview with Whaley, 12 Dec 1991, re Welles.

n. A special tool in the form of a small brass ring used to separate locking coins. [rare] Probably invented by Bill Brema who was using this tool for his modified Nickels and Dimes trick sometime between 1943 and 1945 during his employment by Kanter's. This is, I believe, the only tool (as opposed to a gaff) unique to magicians and only coinmen at that. REF: Buffum (1981), 91, 93.

n. Stage effect where an assistant alternately appears and vanishes from a raised and curtained platform containing a small doll-house; the magician explaining that the assistant is in the doll- house, which is then easily carried off stage by an assistant. Then, when the spectators complain about a suspicious bulge in the curtained platform, the magician pulls the curtains off, revealing only a bare skeleton frame. [rare] This very rare application of a sucker gag to a full-stage illusion was invented by Guy Jarrett in 1908. The method used — the counter-weight principle to give the illusion of a light and hence empty — "bungalow" had been invented in 1879 by Nevil Maskelyne for his Cleopatra's Needle illusion, contrary to Jarrett's attempt to claim it for himself. Bangkok Bungalow was featured by Thurston since 1916. REF: Jarrett (1936/1981 ed), 11, 62-70; Boston & Parrish (1947), 61-62; Busby (1995), 11.

n. Effect where spectators freely take all but one of several envelopes, one of which contains paper money; the remaining one—the magician's—is always found to be the one with the money; Just Chance (Brit.). [fairly common]

1.n. Close-up magic performed at a bar, specifically a magic bar (2), by either a bartender- magician or a bar magician. [fairly common] “Bar magic is like New York, if you can do it there, you can do it anywhere.” — Doc Eason in L&L Catalog of Magic (1998), 47 85

n. A magician who works tables in a saloon; a Pub Magician (Brit.). Compare bartender- magician. [rare] Among the better known are Al James of Schulien's in Chicago and Allan Hayden formerly of The Forks in Buffalo.

n. Production apparatus that allows a long rod to be pulled out of a shallow container such as a hat or mouth. [archaic, formerly fairly common] Inspired by the so-called Pudding effect and apparatus of tin first described in 1634 by Hocus Pocus Junior. In the more recent version the "pole" is, in fact, a coil of flexible material (originally cardboard) that, when pulled, spirals out into a stiff rod of some 5 feet in length and 2½ inches diameter, its structure disguised by spiral barber-pole colored bands. Marketed as early as 1843 by Crambrook in London. A 15-inch version was sold by Bland by 1890. As a production from his mouth, a pet effect of "Chung Ling Soo" (William E. Robinson) in 1900. REF: Dean (1763); Hoffmann (1890), 302; McArdle (1963).
n. Nickname of The Barnstormer, newsletter (published since 1938) of the Boston Assembly (Herman Hanson Assembly #9) of the Society of American Magicians (S.A.M.). [very rare but not nonce]
n. The effect where the performer frees himself from a sealed wooden barrel filled with water. 86 [rare]

n. Bottom(s) being the more usual synonym. [very rare but emerging] Originally the argot of card sharps decades before the 1980s. REF: Busby inteview, 11 Jul 1988. Thence magicians jargon by 1988 Busby orally as "I dealt some basements".
n. Effect where the center card (a Queen) of a three-card fan turns its back on the spectators 87 when the packet is fanned again. [very rare]

n. Stage effect where an over-sized dummy general's head is carried by two toy soldiers on-stage on a stretcher, placed on a tripod formed by three rifles, and a cloak wrapped around the structure; the general comes to life while the magician vanishes in a cloud of smoke; and when the general removes his false head he is revealed as the magician. [rare] Joe Karston's presentation by 1936 of the Todd brother's original Vampire illusion. The toy- soldier theme was, I presume, inspired by Laurel & Hardy's then recent popular movie, Babes in Toyland (1934).
n. The Beads of Prussia (see) being the most usual current American synonym. [very rare]

n. Effect where a handful of beads and a piece of string are swallowed and brought out strung; the Carmo Beads (Brit.); the Arabian Bead Mystery; the bead trick. 88 [rare] Originally an authentic Indian trick. First reported as introduced to the West by "Those Superior Indian Jugglers from Seringapatam" in or soon after their arrival in London in late 1815. Ramo Samee, a former member of that Indian Moslem troupe, was performing it in England on his own after 1818 and introduced it to the USA in 1819. (Soon afterwards another ex-member of the troupe, Kia Khan Khruse, substituted sewing needles to create the Needle Trick, subsequently made famous by Houdini, which in turn inspired the Razor Blade Trick.) In Jun 1827 an otherwise unknown British magus, Mr. Usher, performed the bead version in Worcester as part of his "representation of the Indian and Chinese Jugglers." REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (Dec 1928), 178; Moulton (1983), 10; Usher, Worcester poster in Magic Circular (Sep 1966). After having been long replaced by the Needle Trick and the Razor Blade Trick, Carmo reintroduced the bead version in his act in Britain in 1932. Soon after, Scottish amateur magician John Ramsay, unaware of the historical background and seeking a fresh version of the popular Needle Trick, chose to use a bead necklace. He published this reportedly flawed reinvention in the Magic Wand. In the USA, Albenice, also unaware of Carmo's work, read Ramsay's article, evolved a much improved method, premiered it at the Arabian Night Club on Broadway in New York City, and arranged to have it marketed in 1939 by U. F. Grant as "The Arabian Bead Mystery". It was a pet effect of Jay Marshall in 1940. However, John Fedko's retitled "Beads of Prussia" has become the current term in the USA, while the "Carmo Beads" remains its most usual British synonym. REF: Annemann in Jinx (1939), 433, 476, and (1940), 506, 580; Art Leroy in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jan 1958), 88; Davenport in Demon Telegraph #53 (1940); Abbott's Catalog No.6 (1940), 201.
n. Effect where a flashlight in a bag or handkerchief lights when the spectator holds it over the only pile of cards whose top card is the previously selected card; Laser Beam. [rare]
n. A special type of up-the-sleeve holdout machine. [rare]

term: behind the back force; behind-the-back force
definition: n. The force of a single card while the magician turns his back to the volunteer. [rare]
n. The spectator or spectators or, less literally, audience being the modern synonyms. [obsolete after the mid-1800s]

n. A magician's table fitted with an accordion-like false top that could fall surreptitiously to create a shallow container. [obsolescent after c.1855] This apparatus was the secret of the trick best known as the Great Escamotage that vanished an assistant from under a cone placed upon the table. It may have been used for this effect as early as 1790 by Conus. It was so used by 1828 by Jules de Rovère, then in 1838 by Sutton, and in 1846 by Robert-Houdin. Ponsin referred to it as still current in 1854. Soon thereafter Robert-Houdin himself drove the device out of fashion. Smaller versions to vanish small animals were still in use as late as 1876 when described by Hoffmann and even by Conradi- Horster around 1920. Revived for human illusions by Chung Ling Soo and, in his 1925 full- evening show, by Houdini for his "Radio 1925" illusion. REF: Sharpe (1983), 25; Hoffmann (1876), 449; Gibson & Young (1961), 150-151. The original French term was Tables à soufflet by 1854 Ponsin.
n. Strippers trimmed along the sides to bulge at the center; side strippers being the usual synonym. [rare]
n. Flexible Glass being the American synonym, which see. 90 [fairly common in Britain]
n. Effect where a square of see-through netting is folded up into a bag; livestock placed within; and, when net falls open, the livestock visibly vanish. [fairly common]

n. A corner of a playing card that has been slightly curled; the corner crimp. [fairly common] Used either as a Key Card or as a phase during a Three-Card Monte routine where the corners of two of the cards are successively bent and unbent to give the effect of one card turning into another.

term: SEE UNDER: Knock Out Card Trick
definition: n. Any challenge stunt, particularly a bar bet, even vaguely magical, that can be so phrased as to sound enough like a sure-thing to elicit a wager from a sucker. [common] Most betchas are mere stunts of minimal skill, several rely on secret information, but a few do depend on a simple sleight or on covertly prepared materials. From the common American colloquial expression "betcha [bet you] I can/you can't do this." Thence magicians jargon by 1942 Dan Morris & Doc Hurwitz in Phoenix #16, 68; 1947 Lorraine; 1949 Gardner; 1952 T. Bamberg as "a mere betcha"; 1953 Walsh & Mishell; 1954 Gardner in HMM; 1961 Ganson as "a mere ‘betcha'"; 1962 Houghton in HMM; 1969 Stover in Chaos; 1975 Wilson & Gibson; 1976 Blackstone Jr; 1986 Johnsson in LR as a "bar- betcha"; 1988 Waters; 1996 Goodsell in MUM; 2000 L&L cat #13 as “Bar Btchas”.

n. Effect where three differently colored (or four differently numbered) solid wood or plastic blocks dropped one-after-the-other into a tube (cardboard or metal, square or round) emerge in another color sequence; Wiz Blocs; Wonder Blocks. [rare] 91 T. A. Waters, at separate points, attributes the invention of this classic pocket trick to Conradi (later modified by Selbit) and Will Blyth. Gerald Heaney attributes it to Professor Hoffmann. REF: Waters (1988), 30, 38; Heaney (1924), 33.
See: Breakaway Fan for the modern and most usual synonym.. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Breakaway Fan for the modern and most usual synonym.".)
a. Adjectivally as in Biddle Grip, etc. [fairly common]

n. The hold taken on a deck of playing cards as a get-ready for the Biddle Move. [fairly common] Introduced in Elmer Biddle's trick, "Transcendent", in Genii (Apr 1947, p.241); and then in Hungard's Magic Monthly (Jun 1948, p.434).
n. Pun implying excessive use of the Biddle Grip. [very rare]

n. The sleight, specifically a utility move, that returns a previously slipped-off card to the top of the deck under cover of taking the next card. [fairly common] "Personally, I think this is the greatest card sleight to appear in the last ten years." — William W. Larsen [Sr] in Genii (Apr 1947), 241 92 “When I moved to Biddle St. a few years ago witty friends allowed as how I had done the Biddle move.” —Edgar Heyl in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Nov 1962), 22
n. The original version of the Vanishing Motorcycle premiered by David Devant in Dec 1913 when he vanished a Royal Enfield complete with its rider from a packing case. [archaic]
n. The Asrah levitation. [very rare but not nonce]

n. Effect where a marked piece of paper currency vanishes and is discovered rolled up in a cigarette; Cig-O-Bill. [fairly common] Inspired by the Card in Cigarette effect and method. This trick was being performed by British magician Oswald Rae in New York in 1930.
n. The Himber Wallet (see) being the later and now most usual current synonym. [obsolete by 1980, formerly rare]

term: Bill in Lemon; Bill and Lemon (Trick), (The) [U.S.]
definition: n. Effect where a borrowed and marked banknote is vanished and then produced from inside a lemon; the Lemon Trick; the Lemon and Bank Note (Brit.). [common] A pet effect of Emil Jarrow and claimed by his editor (Jarrow [1941], 3) as Jarrow's invention. 93 Herman Hanson (1974, 25) recalls Jarrow performing it as early as 1916 at the Hippodrome in Chicago. Ganson-Vernon (1963, 33) state that it "probably originated" with Jarrow. This is likely, as Jarrow had become a professional magician around the turn of the century, nearly a decade before Hilliard (1909, 315-317) first reported and explained the trick. The 1919 Thayer catalog hedged, reporting only that: "This well known trick was made popular by Jarrow." Also a pet effect of Paul Rosini, Lee Grabel (by 1956), Doug Henning (in 1981) and several performers who have discovered it is a good trick for getting tips from customers who prefer to let them keep the lemon-soaked bill. The effect and method was presumably inspired by the earlier Card in Lemon trick. REF: Busby in Arcane #12 (1984), 153-154; Thayer cat #4 (1919), 60. See also Jay (1986), 87, who claims it was a joint invention of Jarrow and Malini.
n. The sleight that exchanges one piece of paper money for another. [fairly common]
n. Effect where a piece of borrowed or marked paper currency is torn and restored. [rare] One common method is a bill switch plus tearing of a dummy bill. A pet effect of Johnny Paul (by 1950).

n. A small metal or plastic cannister with a screw-on or lockable cap. After being shown empty and sealed, this device can then produce a previously borrowed piece of paper money, a playing card, small handkerchief, etc. [common] First marketed in 1924 by Carl Brema and perhaps invented by him. The Double Bill Tube was invented by Walter Gibson (by 1928) and first published by him in Seven Circles magazine in 1931. Named after its original use with paper money. Although "bill" was strictly Standard American usage ("banknote" being the British), British magicians adopted bill tube without question.
n. A pocket index specifically designed to store billets. [obsolescent, formerly rare]

n. A knife whose blade is faked to hold a concealed billet that the mentalist-magician can then secretly insert into an envelope or other container for later revelation. [rare] This device was originated by magicians to introduce a borrowed-and-vanished finger ring into an orange while ostensibly cutting it open. It was being marketed by around 1858 in London by Henry Novra as the "Fruit Knife".

n. A mentalist magician who simulates the billet effects of a psychic billet reader. [rare] Originally the argot of psychic readers. Thence magicians jargon by 1936 Annemann in Jinx #22; 1947 Boardé; 1995 Busby in Thauma #29, referring to Bert Reese; 1996 Silverman re Reese; 1996 Booth in LR re spiritualist T. John Kelly in 1940.

n. The sleight that exchanges a piece of folded paper (a billet) supplied by a volunteer for a dummy provided by the magician; billet switching being the less usual synonym. Compare pellet switch. [fairly common] "The point that should be remembered with a Billet Switch as opposed to a Center Tear is this: A good Billet Switch will give you access to a lot of information regardless of the position of the writing on the paper." — Richard Osterlind, The Surrounded Slow-Motion Center Tear (1986), 18. This technique was invented by spiritualistic mediums in the late 1800s.
See: billet reading. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "billet reading".)

n. Any medium-sized (1¼"-2" diameter) ball used by magicians for so-called billiard-ball manipulation. [common] "Billiard ball is just a conjurer's pet name for the little spheres he manipulates. Although Maskelyne and Devant in Our Magic [actually only Devant] advocate real ivory balls because they sound more convincing, I have never met a performer who took their advice." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 179 In the above quotation, Hay correctly suggests that almost no ball manipulators use ivory; but, in fact, both Silent Mora and Edward Victor did so in addition to Devant. In any case, the so- called billiard balls favored by most magi are of wood or plastic and range in diameter from 1¼" to 2". Regulation balls used in the game of table billiards are slightly over 2" in diameter and were originally of elephant ivory but now plastic. In 1925 Cardini invented rhinestone-studded billiard balls in Australia. He was inspired by a full-sized version used by the popular American jugglers, the Littlejohns, all of whose juggling 96 props were covered with rhinestones and who shared the bill on the Tivoli vaudeville circuit. At Cardini's request, the they made him a set of miniature balls. Paul Fox designed and used rhinestone-studded aluminum balls, a version of which is now (1987) manufactured in Paris by Monsieur Décamp. REF: Price (1985), 342, for the Cardini-Littlejohn connection; Waller (1948/1980), 197-198, who places the Littlejohns in Melbourne in 1916, 1925, 1930, and 1943.
n. Apparatus that substitutes a ball for the cube in the original Sliding Die Box. [rare]
n. A holder specifically designed to hold billiard balls. [rare]

n. The sleight-of-hand routine using billiard balls; ball manipulation. [obsolescent, once fairly common] First performed by Joseph Buatier (de Kolta) in 1875 when he introduced his Multiplying Billiard Balls routine. Later famous performers were John Henricks (1898), Martin Chapender (1904), Clément de Lion (1901), Carl Rosini (1905), T. Nelson Downs, Burling Hull (by 1910), Arnold de Biere, David Devant, Lewis Davenport, Cardini (by 1923), Dante, Rooklyn, Edward Victor, Roy Benson (by 1967), and Zum Pocco (by 1970).

n. The branch of magic whose methods involve less well known capabilities of human body structure and physiology. [very rare, probably nonce despite its usefulness] Examples are fire eating, fire walking, glass eating, pulse control, and other such carnival, 97 fakiristic, or yogic feats.

1.a. Pertaining to dove magic or magic with other birds such as parakeets or parrots. [rare, usually colloquial and often pejorative] “Most Magicians are content to use bird tricks they have seen others do. Yet endless possibilities are open for the thinking wizard.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jul 1959), 23
n. A magician who works with birds, usually doves or parakeets; a dove worker. [rare, colloquial and usually facetious]
n. The Vanishing Birdcage (see) being the usual synonym. [rare]
n. The Growth of Flowers being the more usual synonym. [obsolete, formerly fairly common]

a. Beveled, as applied only to a stripper deck. [obsolescent] From the Standard French word biseauté meaning beveled. Thence French jargon because of the shaved tapering of the cards in the deck. French magicians jargon by 1799 Guyot; 1973 Alain. Thence English-speaking magicians jargon by 1874 Hoffmann in Every Boy's Paper as "biseautè pack"; 1906 Stanyon ad in Magic as "Besaute [sic] Cards"; 1923 E.F.B. [Bagshawe] in Magical Monthly as article title "A Biseaute Hint"; 1923 Elliott, 101, as "cut biseaute, ‘extra strong'"; 1956 Dexter; 1979 Lamb as "biseauté cards".

n. The stripper deck (see) being the American synonym. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common] British magicians jargon by 1874 Hoffmann in Every Boy's Paper; 1882 Hamley cat; 1897 Hercat; 1905 Keene; 1908 Stanyon ad in Magic as a "Besaute [sic] Pack"; 1910 Magical World; 1913 Roterberg cat #15; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1933 Davenport cat; 1933 Walker; 1935 Goldston; 1947 Histed; 1948 Norman; 1969 Gibson, calling it French jargon; 1973 Alain; 1980 J. Marshall; 1988 Waters as "biseaute deck".
n. Contraction of a bit of business, which is the more usual synonym; a hunk being the emerging synonym. [rare]

n. By-play (verbal or physical) on the part of the magician; also as simply business and bit; more recently as a hunk of business; and most recently as simply a hunk. [common] "Amateurs and dilettantes in magic ... forget that a novel bit of ‘business' or a witty quirk in patter will rejuvenate even a weak old trick." — Karl Germain, 1932 notes, quoted in The Linking Ring (Apr 1987), 48-49. "New tricks, at best, are but old plots in new guises. However, a twist or bit of business that gives an old plot a new lease on life for present day audiences, is very valuable." — Fred Lowe, 1969 lecture notes Originally vaudeville cant by 1920. REF: Lustig (1920). Thence magicians jargon by 1920 Lustig; 1923 Elliott as "this bit of ’business'"; 1937 Hugard; 1939 Ross Jan 17th letter to Miller; 1939 Kanter cat; 1941 Booth; 1943 Larsen in Genii; 1946 F. Ireland; 1948 Hugard & Braue; 1953 Crimmins in 99 HMM; 1956 Vernon Jan 12th letter to Ross; 1956 Gardner in HMM as "an amusing bit of business"; 1956 Dexter; 1968 Severn as "bits of funny business"; 1969 Nelms; 1970 Boles; 1972 Griffin; 1973 Brooke; 1974 Guaranteed cat; 1975 G. Davies in Abra; 1975 Pierre; 1976 Dalal in Mantra; 1976 Gill; 1978 Bergeron; 1981 Abbott cat #22 as "One of the funniest bits of business in Magic"; 1983 Lewis in Berg; 1984 Kornwinder; 1986 Magicians' World Newsletter; 1990 Booth; 1997 Lee cat #11; 1997 Abbott cat #25; 1998 Collectors’ Workshop ad in MUM; 2005 L&L Presents.
n. Comedy effect where magus takes a large bite out of a ceramic dinner plate and then restores the plate. [rare]

n. Slangy contraction of business. [rare] Originally American theatrical slang by 1861. REF: RHHDAS. Compare RHD/2nd. Thence magicians jargon by 1944 R.B. Edwards in Phoenix #65; 1972 Griffin as "a bit of biz"; 1982 Ginn as book title
n. A performer or devotee of bizarre magick; a goeticist; a mage (2). [rare]

3.n. The method of achieving invisibility based on the principle of camouflage that adjacent objects of same color and tone are, in the absence of shadow, perceived by the human eye as a single object. Thus a black object against a black background (or red against red) is invisible. 101 Compare Black Magic(2). [common] "The most astonishing magical effects, not possible in any other form of Conjuring, are produced by what is known as Black Art." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (Feb 1904), 53 "Though almost any conceivable effect can be produced with the aid of Black Art, magicians the world over have done little else but copy those introduced in the beginning." — Charles Waller, Magical Nights at the Theatre (1948/1980), 79 This method was first applied to conjuring by German theatrical manager Max Auzinger when on 28 Jun 1885 he premiered a full stage act at the Passage-Panoptikum in Berlin. Performing initially as "Maxistan A. Uzinger" and later as "Ben Ali Bey," he called it the "Schwarze Kabinett" (Black Cabinet). Auzinger's partner, Charles Arbre, got the secret and separately exhibited it in Germany in 1886 as "Ben Azra El Muz". Soon thereafter, two German (or Dutch) performers appeared, fresh from Germany, in Canada, where they attempted unsuccessfully to get funding (from, among others, Harry Rouclere) to put on this act. However, billed as "Ben Ali Bey" they premiered it in the USA in 1886 at the Miners Bowery Theater in New York City. The method was introduced in Britain on 23 Dec 1886 when Buatier De Kolta patented, advertised, and performed his "Modern Black Magic" act at the Egyptian Hall in London. De Kolta had independently reinvented the method in Fall 1886 from reports of Auzinger's effect. William Ellsworth Robinson had seen the pseudo-Ben Ali Bey show at the Miner's Bowery, figured out the method, and decided to pirate the piracy. Robinson, billing his act for the first time as "Black Art" and performing as "Achmed Ben Ali" opened in 1887 on the new Keith-Albee vaudeville circuit, which he played for seven months. Soon after, Harry Rouclere also pirated the pseudo-Ben Ali Bey show on the basis of having seen it when a momentary stage blunder tipped the method. Meanwhile, back in England, Charles Bertram (who had presumably seen De Kolta's act in 1886) added it to his show at the Alhambra in London in 1887, billing it as "Black Magic." REF: Stanyon in Magic (1904), 53, 61-62, 69; Fischer (1929), 182-183; Rouclere in Sphinx (1930), 242; J.N. Maskelyne letter in Magic Circular (1908), 220-221; Jenness (1967), 59; Gibson (1966), 105-107; Waller (1948/1980), 78-79; Bertram (1896), 82, 135-138; Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 98, (1928, 41; Gloye in LR (Feb 1986), 63-65. NOTE: Charles De Vere in a letter in The Magic Wand (1915, p.97) claimed he was present and still had the program for the performance of a black art act ("Black Art") by "Ben Ali Bey" (Max Auzinger) in Antwerp way back in 1873. This date is almost certainly too early. The term Black Art was first married to the method as jargon in 1887 by W.E. Robinson. Thence 1888 Maurer cat; 1891 Burlingame; 1897 Hopkins; 1901 Selbit; 1905 Atlas Trick ad in Sphinx; 1907 Keene; 1909 Bamberg cat; 1921 Thayer cat #5; 1950 Hay; 1953 Christopher in HMM; 1956 Ireland Publications as booklet title;1957 Furst; 1977 Schindler; 1980 J. Marshall; 1988 Waters; 1990 Reynolds in Fisher poster; 1991 Steinmeyer; 1991 Wakeling orally; 1992 Dickson orally; 1993 Charvet in Magic; 1993 Abbott cat #24; 2001 Drake in MUM. a. Adjectivally as the black art act, black art principle, black art table, black art well, etc. [very common]

2.n. Figuratively, from the above literal meaning, a sudden and unexpected climax that could be marked by the dowsing of stage lights. [rare] "Then her G-string flew to his beard—blackout!" — Dai Vernon, orally, 1985, recalling one stage magician's accident.
See: double-blank. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "double-blank".)
n. A blank-faced card (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare] 105

n. Effect where a selected coin, placed on a metal tray and covered with an inverted champagne glass, penetrates the cover, joining a second coin underneath. The later U.S. version is titled Blasted Jr. [rare]

n. The American variant of the British Blasted trick, substituting U.S. coins (a nickel and a one cent piece) for the British coins (a half crown and penny) and a clear Petrie-type laboratory dish for the champagne glass. [rare]

n. Effect where the magus slices deeply across his thumb, drawing a line of blood, and then instantly heals the gruesome wound. [very rare, possibly nonce] First exposed in 1880 by Arprey Vere. A pet effect of Stuart Cramer (in 1939). REF: Cramer in Jinx (1949), 713. 106

n. Any method of handling or sleight-of-hand that secretly manipulates objects while appearing "fair." [rare] "Whether the procedure is true or 'blind' the same apparent action is maintained throughout." — S. W. Erdnase, Artifice Ruse and Subterfuge at the Card Table (1902), 22 Common examples are the false shuffle, false cut, and cull, which retain or arrange playing cards in a set order. Originally the argot of British criminals in the sense of a "feint" by 1811 (Lexicon Balatronicum). Thence the argot of American card sharps by 1865 Evans, 29; 1902 Erdnase, 21. Thence magicians jargon since 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 164, as "a very barefaced blind"; 1913 Elbiquet; 1920 Stanyon in Magic; 1923 J.W. Elliott, 118, as "done as a 'blind'"; 1944 Hugard in HMM; 1949 Hay; 1959 Marlo; 1984 Vernon as "whether executing the true or the blind"; 1988 Waters. a. False, as in blind cut or blind shuffle. [common] Originally the argot of American card sharps by 1902 Erdnase, 39, as "The blind process of riffling". Thence introduced to magicians jargon in 1902 by Erdnase/Harto, 127; 1910 Hoffmann in Magic Wand; 1928 Leat & Jonson; 1946 Buckley as a "blind riffle shuffle"; 1948 Norman; 1984 Vernon; 1991 Busby in Whaley as "a Blind Riffle".

n. A false cut (of a deck of cards) being the more usual synonym. [fairly common] The term originated among American card sharps by 1902 Erdnase, 21; 1957 Radner; 1973 Livingston. Thence magicians jargon since 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 127; 1909 Hilliard; 1911 Hoffmann; 1921 Buckley; 1931 Mussey & Oursler; 1938 Ross Sep 6th letter to Miller; 1940 Hugard & Braue; 1958 Ganson/Endfield; 1969 Gibson; 1978 Müller; 1984 Vernon; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Govan in Australian Magic Monthly; 1991 Busby in Whaley. v. To false cut (a deck of cards). 107 [rare] The verb form was American card sharps argot by 1902 Erdnase, 20. Thence magicians jargon by 1938 Stuart Judah pamphlet; 1938 Searles; 1948 Fitzkee/Buckley.

n. A false shuffle being the more usual synonym. [rare] Originally American card sharps argot by 1902 Erdnase, 20; 1957 Radner. Thence magicians jargon since 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 126; 1946 Buckley; 1948 Norman; 1955 Woda in HMM as "I use the ‘Erdnase Blind Riffle Shuffle'"; 1956 Dexter; 1975 Barnhart; 1978 Müller; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Govan in Australian Magic Monthly; 1991 Busby in Whaley, 178; 1991 Ortiz. v. To false shuffle being the more usual synonym. [very rare] Used as verb by American card sharps by 1902 Erdnase. Thence magicians jargon since 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 176; 1946 Clive. NOTE: Also as gerund "blind-shuffling" in 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 141; and as "by blind shuffling" in 1991 Ortiz.

n. A bandage or other seemingly opaque device to cover the eyes, ostensibly to prevent seeing. [common] "It is a fact that the gag of seeing along the nose with a common blindfold is very little known, and with the addition of cotton wads, you stump even those who do know it." — Theo. J. Anneman [sic] in The Sphinx, 15 Jul 1924 “The best way of concealing that you’re looking at something is to wear a blindfold.” — Paul Fox orally to Dai Vernon as quoted in Busby, The Secret of the Palmettos (1998), 10 Conjurers were using blindfolds by 1740 when Guyot exposed the original method of defeating a blindfold by the downward glimpse in the card stabbing trick. In 1816 British psychic charlatan Margaret M'Avoy pretended while masked to "see" words and colors with her fingers. The Blindfold Walk was first performed sometime before 1821 by English stonemason Dennis Hendrick on a wager. And French clairvoyant-magician Alexis Didier used a fake blindfold in 1847. The Blindfold Drive was introduced in 1885 by Washington Irving Bishop. REF: Busby & Osterlind, The Blindfold Book (1987). Standard English as noun only since 1880, long preceeded by the verb form. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1895 Burlingame #1; 1912 Goldston as "a genuine ‘blindfold'"; 1920 Lustig; 1931 Douglas cat #16; 1936 Thayer cat #8; 1939 Kanter cat; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1942 Ireland cat #10; 1944 Hugard in HMM; 1945 Sterling cat #2; 1946 B. Hull; 1949 Hay; 1954 Tarbell; 1956 Christopher in HMM; 1956 Dexter; 1966 Inzani-Henley cat #1; 1980 Tannen cat #13; 1981 Waters; 1982 Avadon in Berg; 1983 Cassidy; 1997 Abbott cat #25.

n. The trick of driving a vehicle while blindfolded. [common] Usually performed as a publicity effect. Invented and first performed by American mentalist Washington Irving Bishop in 1885 in New York City using horses and carriage. Also performed by Raymond on the West Coast (1904-07), Blackstone (1911-13), and C. A. George Newmann. First to use the automobile was Joseph Dunninger in 1917. Thence by Paul Fox (late 1930s), Harlan Tarbell (1940), Kalanag (1956 in Brazil & 1957 in Portland, Maine), David Berglas (1950s), John Calvert (1960s-1970, 1992), Uri Geller (1970s), James Randi (1970s), Dr. Eldoonie (early 1980s, coast-to-coast), Jon Marshall (early 1980s), and Richard Osterlind (mid- 1980s). On 17 May 1931 Rajah Raboid made the first "sealed eye blindfold flight" at the Curtiss-Wright Airport in Baltimore, a feat that became a stock publicity stunt of John Calvert since the 1960s. The world record non-stop drive (69.7 kilometers) was set in 1984 by Swedish magician Tom Miller.

n. Effect where a blindfolded magician strolls, avoiding avoiding obstacles. [very rare but not nonce] First performed sometime before 1821 by English stonemason Dennis Hendrick on a wager. Used as a publicity stunt by Ted Annemann. REF: Christopher (1975), 81.
n. Effect where a magus raises a blister on his thumb or finger tip (complete with his own prints) and then makes it visibly and slowly disappear. [rare]
n. Effect where a solid square wooden block drops through two square tubes separated by a glass or plastic plate. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]

n. The controlled movement of an entire packet of playing cards (a block) during cuts and shuffles. [rare] Developed mainly by Dr. Jacob Daley. A pet of Dai Vernon. First described by L. L. Ireland in 1935 in his Year Book.

n. A marked card where tiny portions of the printed back design are inked out to either emphasize or diminish selected parts of the design. [very rare] Originally card sharps argot as in 1902 Erdnase, 17, as "blockouts"; 1927 Gibson, Bunco Book, 86, as “block out” &
n. Effect where a cord is threaded through the hole in a block; with volunteers holding both ends of 111 the cord, the magus removes the block. [fairly common]

n. Effect where a ball rolls back and forth on top of a cord stretched between the hands of the magus.
