[rare] Originally a trick of jugglers, it is named for world-famous 19th Century French tightrope-walker "Charles Blondin" (Émile Gravelet, 1824-1897) who in 1859 became the first person to walk across the Niagara Falls. The magic trick version was reportedly invented by British magician Tom Sellers. The secret is an invisible thread parallel to the cord, the ball rolling between them. REF: Waters (1988), 37.
n. Stage illusion where an assistant or volunteer receives an apparently mortal wound, yet survives untouched. One example is tongue cutting. [rare]

n. Effect where magi holds a bouquet of flowers (feather or real), plucks off all the blossoms, and new ones (of a different color) quickly bud and flower; Blooming Rose Bush. [fairly common] Entirely mechanical. A featured effect of Kellar, Germain, Dante, and Dell O'Dell. Made for decades by Horace Marshall, then by Hughes Magic (1985-2000), and again by H. Marshall and Company (after 2000).

(See also: Blooming Bouquet.) n. Effect where magi holds a bouquet of flowers (feather or real), plucks off all the blossoms, and new ones (of a different color) quickly bud and flower; Blooming Rose Bush. [fairly common] Entirely mechanical. A featured effect of Kellar, Germain, Dante, and Dell O'Dell. Made for decades by Horace Marshall, then by Hughes Magic (1985-2000), and again by H. Marshall and Company (after 2000).
n. Flick book (see) being the modern synonym. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]
n. Apparatus (a gaffed tube) that vanishes a silk when the magician or volunteer blows through it. [rare]
n. An emptied hen's egg-shell with hole for loading. [obsolescent] Formerly used for tricks mainly with silks. Now largely, perhaps entirely, replaced by sturdier hollow wood or plastic eggs.
n. Effect where a stack of different colored wooden checkers impaled on a rod change position under cover of a tube. [rare]
n. Stage effect where one person in a cabinet slowly and visibly changes into another. [rare]

n. A sleight for controlling a playing card replaced in the deck, bringing it second from the top in most handlings. [fairly common] First explained in Ellis Stanyon's New Card Tricks, 2nd Series (1902), 5. Later by Dr. Elliott (ca1915 and 1923) and by Frederick Montague, M.P., in his Westminster Wizardry (1928), 75, where he brought the card to the top. Victor Farelli modified this by 1932. Tommy Tucker then became the first cardman to bring the card in second, which is now the most usual handling and meaning. Tucker’s version became a pet sleight of Paul LePaul. REF: Farelli in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Feb 1953), 1046, and (May 1955), 285; Farelli (1933), 29; Busby in Epoptica #1 (1982), 39.

n. The sleight that exchanges a coin openly displayed at the fingertips for a finger-palmed coin by tossing the latter into the free hand instead of the first coin, which is now retained palmed between the thumb and first finger. [fairly common]
v. To place objects in various predetermined pockets as coded locations, rather like using the magician's entire costume as a pocket index. [very rare]

n. Object(s) concealed on or under the magician's clothing. Compare pick-up load and body loading. [fairly common] "Body loads can make for effective magic." — Will Ayling, Oriental Conjuring and Magic (1981), 261 Masters of this technique have included Servais Le Roy, Leon the Great, and David Devant, as well as all magi who specialized in the Goldfish Bowl production such as Phillippe, Robert- Houdin, Chung Ling Soo, Okito, and Fu-Manchú. The use of body loads has declined as magi have abandoned their commodious old-fashioned costumes. 115
n. A load produced from the magician's clothing. Done by means of a body steal. [rare]
n. The steal of a body load. [rare]
n. General term for sleeving, lapping, vesting, cuffing, and pocketing. [fairly common] 116

n. A metal cylinder (a variant of the drumhead tube) open at one end that can be shown empty and placed upon a cylindrical stand for a production. [rare] First marketed by Petrie-Lewis, crediting its invention to a "Mr. Bogert". REF: Petrie-Lewis catalog (1939).
n. A specific type of Key-Bender. [rare]

n. Alternate word for patter. [obsolete in English after 1933] “The ‘boniment’ or ‘patter’ is the story told by the performer. It is the verbal clothing, in fact the ‘mise en scene’ by which an illusion is given an appearance of reality.” —Norman Triplett, The Psychology of Conjuring Deceptions (1900), 42 "A running accompaniment of talk should be indulged in, each Pass [in the Cups & Balls] having its own boniment or ‘patter' carefully rehearsed." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (Feb 1912), 34 Originally adopted as jargon by French magicians by 1858 (Robert-Houdin; 1974 Poulleau in Dif #3) from the Standard French word meaning "the seductive words of a charlatan." Thence borrowed as occasional jargon among English-speaking magicians by 1876 Hoffmann; 1896 Bertram as "bonnement; 1897 Stanyon; 1902 Hilliar; 1902 Neil; 1918 Hoffmann; 1933 Farelli as part of article title; 1964 Christopher

n. Effect where the mentalist reveals unseen entries chosen by a spectator from the page of a book (or, generally, any publication). The major sub-categories are the Dictionary Trick, the Magazine Test, and the Newspaper Test. [common] “There are hundreds of book tests available for the modern mentalist, but only a few meet the requirements of the discriminating performer.” 119 — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Nov 1960), 66

n. The person who makes bookings, a booking agent. [rare] "The bookers have a fetish about youthful looks and dark tresses. Changing one's hair coloring is one of the simplest ways to pacify a booker." — David Price, Magic (1985), 469 "Once you know what your prospective booker is thinking and planning, you can work to their [sic] goals and get the job." — Jeff Busby in Thaumaturgist, No.33 (Feb 1997), 2 Magicians usage by 1935 Frazee in Sphinx; 1946 Braue in HMM; 1947 Boston & Parrish; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1984 A. Dawes in F. Marshall; 1986 Dawes & Setterington; 1996 R. Miller in LR as a "booker of trade show magicians".

n. A formally contracted date. [common, particularly among pros] "Give the audience what it wants and you will get your booking and be a success." — Jack Merlin, ... and a Pack of Cards, Pt. III (1927) "Why, if you have only one booking in a month, is that the date that everyone wants to book you for?" — Terry Seabrooke in M-U-M (Oct 1997), 13 Originally British (later American) theatrical jargon since 1884. REF: OED/2; Fay (1930). Thence magicians jargon by 1923 Leat as "bookings"; 1923 Thurston, Oct 10th letter to Dante; 1950 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1974 Hanson as "steady bookings"; 1985 Price as "six months of solid bookings"; 1987 Huffman in LR as "a few bookings"; 1987 Albrecht cartoon on Busby Magic Inc. Xmas card as "I haven't had a booking in 3 years."; 1988 Klein as "show bookings"; 1992 Garrett in MUM as "that second booking"; 1996 Booth in LR as "my

n. A small disc with a stub of pencil lead in its center that, when glued to the pad of the magician's thumb, acts as a thumb writer. [fairly common] 121 This extraordinarily cheap and effective secret writing device was invented in the mid-1940s by Eric Mason, British graphic artist and semi-pro mentalist, and marketed by him as "Boon" by 1958. He sold thousands of these disposable items by 1980 despite its piracy by some dealers. REF: Mason & Richardson (1982), 1-2; Corinda (1958), 5-6, 16; Lees (1984), 134.

n. Stage name adopted by many magicians from the mid-1800s to 1930. [obsolete] "Bosco", the true surname of two popular Italian magicians of the 1800s, first became cast as a buffoon-magician in 1904 when star vaudeville illusionist Servais Le Roy created the team of "Le Roy-Talma-Bosco" together with his wife, Mercedes "Queen of Coins" Talma, and comedian Leon Bosco. The 8 successive comedian "Boscos" with the "Le Roy-Talma-Bosco" troupe from 1904 to 1930 when Le Roy retired. The special interest of this term here is that it is one of the few in magic that have been adopted by American slang where its first meaning was a geek: "’Bosco! Bosco! Eat-’em-alive Bosco. You can't afford to miss this marvel. Bosco! Bosco!' ... Of the twentieth- century Boscos there are, alas, many. You will find them all over the world, in street carnivals, side-shows, fair- booths, and museums, and why the public supports such debasing exhibitions I have never yet been able to understand. ... [N]ever has my soul so risen in revolt as at the sight of this bestial exhibition with which the name of Bosco, a nobleman and a conjurer of merit, has been linked." — Harry Houdini, The Unmasking of Robert-Houdin (1909), 307-308. Finally "bosco" reemerged without the initial capital with the broad meaning of fool by 1925 in the American Legion Weekly as "Any Broadway bosco will tell you." It was obsolete by 1973 except as a dictionary entry. Lexigographer J.E. Leighter's suggestion that the word may have come from the British slang "bosky" (meaning tipsy) can be ruled out. REF: RHHDAS, 249. Magician James Randi (1992), 95, writes: "I have wondered whether there is any possibility that 'Bozo' is a variation of ‘Bosco.'" This is quite possible given that "bozo" (meaning a foolish or clownish fellow) has been American slang

n. The type of coin box that is comprised of a German Box with a lid or, equally, an Okito Box with a bottom recess. [fairly common] Since 1952 when Bobo assumed the inventor was the widely known George L. Boston, American professional stage magician, most writers have given this false credit. In the first edition of this book I erred in attributing the invention to the other (but less well known) magician of the same surname, Dr. Arnold "Doc" Boston, a New Jersey dentist and amateur sleight-of- hand artist associated in the 1940s and 50s with the New York inner circle. In a subsequent telephone interview Arnold Boston assured me he did not invent the trick and said he didn't 122 have any idea where the name came from. In 1988 Don Albrecht suggested in jest that it originated in the city of Boston and it now seems he was probably right. REF: Bobby Reynolds, interview of 16 Apr 1988 with BW, said that George Boston (not one to hide his light under a bushel) never claimed its invention; Arnold Boston, interview with BW; J.B. Bobo interview with BW admitting his attribution to George Boston was pure assumption.

n. The self-contained version of the old Growth of Flowers (1), in its primary sense of the instantaneous production of a bouquet from underneath a cone. [common] The felicitous term "Botania" was evidently coined by Willmann's of Hamburg, Germany, by 1920 as title for their self- contained cone-and-pot version of the trick using feather flowers. Being a more convenient synonym, it is not surprising that it soon became generally applied to all versions. Thence ca1920 Heaney cat #24 re Willmann's prop; 1923 Leat, 14, as L. Davenport's title for their version; 1947 Abbott cat #9; 1947 Holden ad in HMM; 1950 Max Andrews ad in Abra; 1979 Lamb; 1983 Tannen cat #14; 1983 Tricks Co. cat #2; 1984 W. Wilson in New Tops; 1988 Waters; 1991 Hughes Magic ad in LR; 1993 Hollywood Magic cat #18; 1997 Lee cat #11; 2000 Abbott flyer.
n. The Passe Passe Bottle being the most usual synonym. [rare]
1.n. British synonym for the Imp Bottle, which is the modern and more more usual synonym. [obsolescent]

n. The bottom deal being the more usual synonym; basement(s). 123 [fairly common] Originally (?) American card sharps argot by 1930 McGuire as "dealing bottoms"; 1977 Sharper in Prus as "dealing seconds or bottoms"; 1982 Hayano;1984 Shields orally as "he dealt a nice bottom". Thence (?) magicians jargon by 1927 Merlin; 1932 Baker in Broadway Magic News; 1948 B. Elliott in Phoenix #146, as "unlike any bottom seen on land or sea"; 1960 Marlo; 1969 Racherbaumer in Hierophant #1 noting it as a vogue-word among the cardmen of the Chicago inner circle; 1981 P. Harris; 1984 M. Nash orally; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1991 Ortiz;

n. The false deal that deals the bottom card of a deck while seemingly dealing the legal top one; bottom dealing. [common] This deal is not only notoriously difficult but usually produces a tell-tale "click" sound called talk. Originally a card sharp's sleight. Girolamo Cardano, in an obscure passage written around 1530, implies the use of this technique among Italian card sharps. According to John Morris (writing in 1873) this sleight was perfected in the USA in 1834 by a skilled card sharp named Wilson. In any case, it was used at the gaming tables of America by 1843 (Green, p.72). The term originated as the argot of card sharps by 1890 (Quinn; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne; 1902 Erdnase). However the sharps soon abandoned this term in favor of a succession of such more colorful and better disguised synonyms as "base dealing" (by 1890 Quinn), "subway deal" (by 1944 MacDougall), "cellar dealing" (by 1962 Garcia), and now simply "basements" (by 1987 Busby orally). Borrowing from card sharps, J.N. Maskelyne introduced the term and technique to magicians in 1894. Thence magicians jargon by 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 127; 1911 Hoffmann; 1933 Annemann; 1940 Hugard & Braue; 1946 Jonson; 1948 Fitzkee; 1950 Rawson in HMM; 1960 Marlo; 1979 Lamb; 1983 Cassidy; 1983 P.H. Lyons in Arcane; 1987 Bannon in LR; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1991 Ortiz; 1998 Ammar in L&L flyer; 2002 Econ in LR. v. To make the bottom deal; to deal bottoms. [rare]

n. A sleight that palms off the card at the bottom of the deck. Less often used than the top palm, its antonym. [fairly common] The bottom palm was in use among magicians as early as 1853 by Viennese magician J. N. Hofzinser, but otherwise was very rare. After publication in 1902 of Erdnase's fine book on card sharpers sleights, a few more magicians adopted it. Popularity came only with the appearance of Hugard & Braue's Expert Card Technique in 1940. REF: Hatch (1985), 204n; Green (1961), 27. This term originated as American card sharps argot by 1902 Erdnase, 86. Thence magicians jargon in 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 142; 1910 Hatton & Plate; 1911 Hoffmann in Magic Wand; 1921 Buckley; 1927 Merlin; 1947 Rawson in HMM; 1950 Hay; 1958 Ganson/Endfield; 1976 Tarr; 1984 Koornwinder; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1997 A-1 flyer; 2000 Owen in LR.

n. A stack (that is, stock) of playing cards at the bottom of a deck. Opposite of a top stock. [rare] Originally American card sharps argot by 1865 Evans; 1892 Quinn; 1894 Maskelyne; 1902 Erdnase. Thence magicians jargon by 1920 Stanyon in Magic; 1984 Vernon; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1991 Ortiz. a. [adjectivally]

n. A small box without a bottom. [obsolete after 1936] Used as a utility device for vanishing objects. First mentioned in 1693 by Ozanam for vanishing coins. Used in the mid-1800s by Robert-Houdin in the nest-of-boxes for his Le Desséchement Cabalistique trick.

n. Stage illusion where when a roller shade is pulled down in front of a large cabinet (decorated to look like a dressing-room but otherwise empty) a woman's shadow is seen to dance but when the shade is raised she has disappeared. Almost opposite to the effect of the Bridal Chamber. [rare]
n. Effect where a bowl is filled with confetti that after being covered with a cloth and uncovered has turned to water. [rare]

n. An apparatus conjurer, derisively. [rare] "Despite the props, Jack [Gwynne] was not what is sometimes referred to as 'a box magician.' There are no clever boxes but a very clever magician who used some props to make magic happen." — David Price, Magic (1985), 345
v. To box (2) the cards, making a faced deck; facing the deck (U.S.). Opposite of backing the deck. [very rare but not nonce]
See: Brassiere Trick. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Brassiere Trick".)
n. The Gray code being the earlier and most usual synonym. 129 [rare]
n. Marking cards by adding long lines to those playing card decks that already feature such lines in their printed back patterns. Similar to line marks. [very rare, possibly nonce]
See: Secret Addition. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Secret Addition".)
n. A sleight that reverses a card in a deck during the cut. [rare]

term: v. [See take a break and hold a break.]
definition: n. The Breakaway Fan (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare]
n. An oblong container whose top, bottom, and four sides detach to show that the contents (usually a rabbit) have vanished. [rare]

n. Those playing cards most likely to be called by a spectator when asked to freely name any card. [very rare] "The choice usually goes Red, Hearts, Picture and Female." — Herman L. Weber in Thompson (1945), 120 "When a woman thinks of a card it is usually a red one. A big percentage there." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Nov 1947), 370 "Over the years many such lists have been compiled; none of them agree completely, and there seems to be an interesting variance depending on the particular nation or geographical area in which the request is made." — T. A. Waters, The Encyclopedia of Magic and Magicians (1988), 44 This is the application to playing cards of the psychological force. By playing the percentages, the performer relies on getting "a lucky break". The classic example of the use of break cards is Ralph W. Hull's Name-O-Card, which he published in 1932 in his Eye Openers.
n. A card setup that enables the magician to derive the value and suit of the chosen card from the previous card by a simple double mnemonic. [rare]

n. Stage illusion where a large empty cabinet reveals a fully furnished bedroom complete with serving maid and blushing bride. Compare Boudoir of a Dancing Girl. [rare] A pet effect of Goldin (by 1907), Thurston (from 1908), Gustave Fasola (from 1910 when he introduced this illusion in Australia), Blackstone (from 1913 when he bought it from the estate of Herbert Albini), Amadeo Majeroni (by 1930), and David "Fu-Manchú" Bamberg (in 1937). REF: Price (1985), 294, 506, 507; Christopher (1973), 229; Blackstone Jr (1985), 45, 106-107; Waller (1948/1980), 168; Bamberg (1988), 155.

n. A slight bend or arch in a playing card (or block of cards or entire deck) that runs either lengthwise or crosswise, bowing it; a crimp. British usage prefers bridge, American crimp. [fairly common] This bend creates a key card. Invented by card sharps and was in common use by British sharpers as early as 1552 (Walker; 1635 Hocus Pocus Junior; 1674 Cotton). Also with French sharpers by 1853 (Ponsin) and American by 1857 (Green). Thence adopted by magicians by 1876 (Hoffmann). Originally the argot of British (later American) card sharps by 1843 Crambrook cat; 1844 Anderson; 1855 Wyman; 1859 Lever as earliest citation in the OED/1; 1868 Green; 1875 Hartz; 1896 Bertram). Also known among British sharps by its French equivalent, "the 'pont'" by 1896 (Bertram). Thence magicians jargon in Britain by 1876 (Hoffmann, 39; 1909 Hilliard; 1912 Stanyon in Magic; 1928 Leat & Jonson; 1931 Douglas cat #16; 1934 Farelli; 1946 Jonson; 1979 Lamb) and borrowed in the USA by 1896 (Roterberg; 1903 Carter; 1937 Hugard; 1983 Racherbaumer; 1988 Waters; 1996 ["1997"] L&L cat). NOTE: Also borrowed in German by 1990 (Wedler). v. To put a bend in a card; to crimp; bridging. [rare]

n. Apparatus that straddles the magician's or volunteer's nose, allowing the effect of a string being pulled through the side of the nose; later called the Nose Trick. [obsolete after 1843, formerly rare] First reported and explained in 1584 by both J. Prevost and Reginald Scot. Still marketed as the Nose Trick as late as 1882. It was a pet effect of Lewis Carroll. Although the original apparatus has not been made for nearly a century, its method has inspired the original Pillars of Solomon trick and the current ones of Piercing a Woman and Sword Thru Neck.

n. A finely jogged card. Compare brief card. [very rare] Originally the argot of American card sharps by 1894 Koschitz. Thence, but only in its above defined sense, magicians jargon in 1984 Vernon, 213, 222; 1991 Ortiz, 69.

n. Obsolete and always rare synonym for a long card, specifically one that is, however incongruous the word, in fact longer rather than wider. [obsolete] Curiously, the argot of British card cheats had used "the Breef" to mean a card that was wider than the others in its pack back in 1674 (Cotton). And contrariwise they also used "Breef" to designate a card trimmed on its side edge to make it narrower in 1714 (Lucas). However, by 1815 (Ingleby) their argot was using "brief card" to mean a longer card. In the same period, Ingleby (1815) called a longer card "The old Gentleman" in cautious reference to the Devil, while Anderson (1844) called a thicker card "the Old Gentleman." American card sharps used "briefs" for both a wider or 135 narrower card by 1894 (Koschitz; 1912 Quinn). In 1973 (Livingston) "a brief" meant a single stripper card introduced in the deck.
n. Stage illusion where a woman assistant in a simulated TV cabinet slowly fades from view to immediately reappear in a similar box. [rare]

n. Effect where a borrowed pocket-watch is smashed into pieces and later restored. [rare] The original device often used for this effect is the Watch Mortar. The effect was first (?) exposed in 1784 by Decremps, and again in 1785 by Astley, and yet again in 1800 by Gale (3rd ed.) as "The Watch pounded in a Mortar". A pet effect of Pinetti (in 1784), and John Rannie (in 1804, Salem ad). The prop was being marketed in London as early as 1843 by Crambrook who stated that the mortar was of French manufacture. A later version of this effect invented by British magician Devono in the 1850s substituted the Watch Bag for the mortar. A pet effect of Dante.
See: Breakaway Fan. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Breakaway Fan".)
n. A disrupted Mexican Turnover change. [very rare, possibly nonce]

n. Conclusion of a magician's funeral when a wand is snapped in two to signify the end of his career and life. [fairly common] This is the only funeral rite peculiar to magicians. First performed on 4 Nov 1926 in the Elks 136 Club ballroom in New York City when Francis Werner, a past-president of the Society of American Magicians (S.A.M.) broke a wand over the casket at the end of the funeral service for Houdini. This ceremony with its accompanying few words written for this occasion were later, in modified form, made a formal ritual of the S.A.M. charter (where it is formally called the “S.A.M. Funeral Ceremony”). Later adopted by the International Brotherhood of Magicians (I.B.M.). REF: Christopher (1969), 248; Silverman (1996), 415.

n. The Box Trick escape performed with addition of a canvas cover. [rare] "The Brooks Trunk is by far the most reliable of the ‘secret release' box tricks, and almost defies detection." — Sam Sharpe, The Magic Play (1976), 84 Devised by English magician Herbert Brooks by early 1912, changing it from a wooden trunk to one of steel in 1915. REF: Price (1985), 268-269.

n. The modern version of Robert-Houdin's Aerial Suspension, substituting a simulated broomstick. [common] Seemingly originated as a carnival exhibit before 1924 and long before 1945 when Bruce Elliott characterized it as "a hoary old timer." A pet effect of Richiardi Jr (by 1949), Orson Welles (1956), George Goebel (1982), Mark Wilson (1980s), and Marco the Magi (1980s).

n. The sleight that switches tabled playing cards by pushing one with another. [rare] Originally a card sharps sleight. The advertised exposé by Darwin Ortiz (1984, pp.28-29) of what he calls "the Brush" is, in fact, only "the Spread". Originally the argot of American card sharps by 1982 Busby; 1984 Ortiz. Thence magicians jargon in 1982 Busby in Epoptica #1, 19, as "a still-secret gambler's move"; 1985 Larry Jennings; 1996 ["1997"] L&L cat.

n. Highly commercial conjuring geared to adolescent taste. [rare and usually colloquial, now obsolete] Originally the derogatory American popular slang noun and adjective "bubblegum" applied since 1963 to the simpler type of rock music of such groups as The Archies, the Partridge Family, and the Monkees that appealed to pre-teen audiences. REF: RHHDAS; Wentworth & Flexner (2nd ed, 1975); Barnhart dict, 1980 Supplement. Thence magicians jargon reportedly in the early 1970s (Busby 1984 orally). a. [adjectivally] [very rare but not nonce] "Paul Harris, self-confessed guru of the bubble-gum magic set seems to be well aware of the make up of his audience and writes strictly to please them."
n. The false count that keeps one or more playing cards curled up out of sight under the deck while counting the visible cards. [fairly common]
See: Double Box Illusion. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Double Box Illusion".)

n. The classic double-sided paper-fold used to produce, vanish, or exchange flat objects such as coins by a simple turnover sleight. [fairly common] "Like that other old war horse, 'Out to Lunch,' effects with The Buddha Papers are endless and limited only by your imagination." — Brother Shadow [Carl Herron], The Papers of Gautama Siddhartha (1997) First described in 1584 by Reginald Scot (then 1634 Hocus Pocus Junior, 1668 John White, and 1763 H. Dean) to exchange one coin for another preloaded one. Called "The Witched Paper" in 1843 Crambrook cat. Also described in 1857 in The Magician's Own Book, 44, as "To Change a Dime to a Quarter."

n. A spring-steel clip that attaches with a prong to the bottom edge of a wooden table and serves as a hold-out for playing cards. [rare] "A great deal of machinery is used by expert players in holding out, ... but none are so practical and so easily worked as the ‘bug'." — Gerritt M. Evans, How Gamblers Win (1865), 37 A lowly name for the simplest of all card hold-out devices, the bug was invented by card sharps (evidently in America) well before 1865 when Yankee card sharp Gerritt M. Evans first reported having been "playing it a long time". Thence adopted by magicians by 1931 (Mussey & Oursler, as the "card clip") primarily in demonstrations of the methods of card cheats but also for holding bundles of handkerchiefs. Originally, as the "bug", the argot of American card sharps by 1865 Evans, 36; 1877 Grandin pricelist; 1883 as earliest citation in the RHHDAS; 1884 Will & Finck cat; 1891 Quinn; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne; 1894 Koschitz; 1896 Bertram in Britain; 1911 Meyer; 1917 Lipman cat; 1917 Magic Novelty Co. cat; 1921 Herrmann Magical Co. cat; 1931 Smith; 1936 Don F. E. Fox in newspaper; 1961 Scarne; 1973 Lampkin; 1984 Ortiz. Thence magicians jargon by 1941 Horowitz in Jinx; 1955 P.H. Lyons in Ibidem; 1988 Waters, 170; 1993 Brookshear in
n. Early slang term for a session. [obsolete]

n. Classic stage effect where the magician catches a bullet fired at him from a pistol or rifle; the Bullet Catch; the Gun Trick being the original but now obsolescent synonym. The main variant is Russian Roulette. [common] "Don't try the d__n Bullet Catching Trick no matter how sure you are of its success. There is always the biggest kind of risk that some dog will ‘job' you." — Kellar, letter to Houdini, 1918, quoted in Christopher (1969) First known report in 1597 (in Theatre of God's Judgements, a translation by Rev. Thomas Beard of an unidentified French book) as having been performed shortly before by a French magician named Coulen [sic]. Canadian Algonquin Indians were using the bullet catch by 1723 to demonstrate their invulnerability to the newfangled guns of the white men. Thus Philip Astley's claim (1785) of having invented the trick in 1762 may well represent an independent act of invention but not a precedent. Katterfelto was doing it in 1781. In 1787 the "English Hussar" (probably Astley himself) was performing "The Art of Gunnery" in Ireland while that same year the Irishman, John Brenon, was catching bullets in a handkerchief in New York. Later notable performers (with dates of performance and notice of all woundings and killings) have included: --Maginnis, British conjurer, caught bullets on his sword-point in Boston, 1800-1801. REF: Moulton (1919/1983), 4. --John Rannie, a Scot, was catching bullets on a dagger's point in New England by 1805, claiming the "power of magnetism." REF: Pinchbeck (1805), 38-39. --Comus, French conjurer, in Bordeaux in 1805, using his wife as target. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1925), 96. --Khia Khan Khruse, pseudo-Indian conjurer, in Dublin in 1818 when he was not, as rumored, killed. REF: Dawes (1979), 170. --Louis de Linski, Polish magician who on 10 Nov 1820 mortally wounded his target (his wife) onstage in Arnstadt. REF: Frost (1881), 194; Clarke in Magic Wand (1925), 97. --DeGrisy-Torrini [a possibly fictitious French magician invented by Robert-Houdin] who killed his possibly equally fictitious son Giovanni in 1825 at Strasbourg. REF: Sharpe (1983), 188. --Olivier senior, English magician, in Strasbourg, France, in 1828. REF: Sharpe (1983), 188. --Signor Antonio Blitz, English magician, by 1830 to around 1835 when in New York City was wounded in the hand. REF: Christopher (1962), 58. --Big Scott, in England in 1820s when half of one cheek shot off. REF: Dexter (1955); Dawes (1979), 173. --Sieur Parizet, France, 1829. --John Henry Anderson, from 1 Apr 1837 to 1856. REF: Price (1985), 61; Dawes (1979), 171-175. --George Sutton, in England by 1838. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1925), 41. --David Prince Miller, in England in 1839. REF: Lamb (1976), 22. --Cunningham, English, c.1840. REF: Frost (1876), 264. --Arnold Buck, London, 1840, seriously wounded in face. REF: Robinson (1989), 6; Clarke in Magic Wand (1926), 41. --Hall, at London fairs, early 1840s. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1926), 38. --Andrew Macallister, ex-assistant to Anderson, around 1850. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1926), 86. --John W. Wyman Jr after 1851 when he bought the trick from Anderson. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 207. --anonymous Frenchman (?), killed sometime before 1854 by a soldier in the firing squad. REF: Ponsin, II (1854). --Robert-Houdin, twice only, in Algiers on 28 Oct 1856 and at an Algerian Arab camp that November. --Eugene Bosco, Italian, in 1857 when at Weimar his pistol blew up, injuring his hand. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1925), 143. --Annie Vernone, in England in 1857. REF: Dawes (1979), 171, 173. --Antonio Poletti, Italian, in London in 1859. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 39. --Col. Stodare, by 1865. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1926), 207. --Dr. Adam Salomon Epstein, 25 Apr 1869 when slightly wounded at the Cirque Napoléon (later Cirque d'Hiver) in Paris. REF: Dif #1 (1971), 283-284; Christopher (1962), 171. --Cramped Hand, American Ponca Indian, around 1875 in a tribal ceremony. REF: Christopher (1973), 71. --Charles Andress, around 1879 when nearly shot by a Western miner. REF: Price (1985), 109. --Hartwig Seeman, Swedish magician, around 1880. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 42. --E. Cooper Taylor, 1881 in Western USA. REF: M-U-M (Apr 1990) 29, 31. --Louis Duprez, a Franco-Briton, in England in 1883. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 39. --De Line, a French magician, in 1890 when he killed the target, his son. REF: Gresham (1953), 287; Dexter (1955). 142 --Alexander Herrmann, seven performances until 1896. REF: Christopher (1973), 193-195. --Adelaide Herrmann, once only, on 5 Sep 1897. REF: Dawes (1979), 172-173. --Michael Hatal, on 28 Oct 1899 when killed at the Hungarian Odd Fellows Hall in New York City. REF: Mahatma (Nov 1899). --Robinson Barnett, around 1900 when wounded in Hawaii. REF: Dexter (1955). --Jean Hugard, numerous times from early 1900 to at at least as late as 1908. Sometime, when on the opening night of his second tour of New Zealand, he was slightly wounded in the chest. REF: Dexter (1955); Waller (1948/1980), photo. --Prof. Blumenfeld ("Herr Bosco"), killed onstage at the Cigogne Hotel, Basel (Bâle), Switzerland, 24 Jan 1906. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1925), 144. --Charles Albert Nicol ("Von Arx"), in 1914 when wounded in the jaw. REF: Gresham (1953), 287; Price (1985), 235. --William E. Robinson ("Chung Ling Soo"), from 1904 to 1918 when mortally wounded onstage at the Wood Green Empire Theatre in London. REF: Dexter (1955). --The Black Wizard of the West, killed in Deadwood, South Dakota. REF: Christopher (1962), 171. --H.T. Sartell, killed onstage in Lynn, Massachusetts. REF: Dexter (1955); Christopher (1962), 171. --Orville Meyer, 1933. REF: Linking Ring (Aug 1984), 48. --Theodore Annemann, 1933, when taught by Meyer, to 1938. --Maurice Rooklyn, 1934 when wounded on two occasions in Australia. REF: Rooklyn (1973). --Horace Goldin, 1939, in London. REF: Roy & Andrews (1985),58. --Rouclere Jr, 1939 in New York City. REF: Jinx (1939), 469. --Maurice Fogel, from 1941 to 1960 with the standard Bullet Catch, and then since 1970 with his Russian Roulette invention with rifles. In 1970 Fogel was shot in the shoulder by a 22-bullet while doing this version. REF: Robinson (1986), 161-164; Hyla M. Clark (1976), 153-155; Lenier in Talisman (1970), 58. --Peter Warlock, in World War II. REF: Dexter (1955), 134. --Orson Welles, Aug 1943, in Hollywood in his Mercury Wonder Show. --David "Fu-Manchú" Bamberg, 1943, in Mexico. REF: Olson (1986), 157, 204. --Milbourne Christopher, May 1957, as a TV first on NBC-TV's "Festival of Magic". Repeated in Oct 1957 in London for BBC-TV. REF: Christopher (1973), 429. --Robert Nedbalski, taught by Meyer, 1970. REF: Linking Ring (Aug 1984), 48. --A South African performer, 1974, shot in stomach while doing a Russian Roulette version. REF: Lamb (1979), 127. --Doc Harad, an American magician, 1974, when killed during rehearsal of the Russian Roulette version. REF: Lamb (1979), 127. --Robert Cassidy, 1976-80s with the Russian Roulette version with revolvers. REF: Cassidy (1984), 80-85. --Carl Skenes, 26 May 1980 on “That’s Incredible!” ABC-TV. REF: Linking Ring (Nov 2000), 62-64. --Paul Daniels, in 1982 on TV. REF: Frank (1987). --Ben Robinson, 5 times 1985-1993, when slightly wounded in a hand. --Roland Khan, in 1986. REF: Linking Ring (Sep 1986), 32. --Fernando "Marvo" Tejada, in Columbia, 1988, when shot dead on stage by a spectator. REF: Magic Circular (Feb 1988), 29; Ian Adair in Trixigram (Apr 1988), 17, 29. --Nellie Fell, 48, in Napier, New Zealand, 3 Sep 1991, when shot in the temple by her partner during a Whirling Brothers Circus show. She survived. REF: Genii (Nov 1991), 60; Linking Ring (Nov 1991), 98. GENERAL REFERENCES: Ben Robinson, Twelve Have Died: Bullet Catching--The Story & Secrets (Watertown, MA: Magic Art Book Co., 1986); Ben Robinson, "More History of Bullet Catching", Magicol (May 1989), 2-6; Dawes (1979), 169-183; Jay Marshall in New Phoenix #346 (1957), 207-209; Orville Meyer in Genii (Dec 1942); Christopher (1962), 171-172; Christopher (1973), 70-71, for Amerindians; Gresham (1953), 279-301; Dexter (1955), 134-153. Kellar's repeated urgings to Houdini that he eschew the gun trick was heeded. Houdini was fearless but simply avoided any tricks that could fail. Although the few magicians who risk the bullet catch often ballyhoo that it has killed 12 performers, they do this only to imply that their audience has a grand opportunity to witness the fateful 13th. In fact, as seen above, the trick has killed at least 10 performers (8 magicians and 2 assistants—3, if we count De Grisy's son) and wounded eleven. Small wonder it is so seldom performed.

n. The version of Shooting thru a Woman where the magician fires a pistol at her middle and the bullet punctures a playing card held by the assistant, passing through her to smash a suspended pane of glass in front of the target on a waist-high table. [rare] 143

n. Effect where a small model masted boat floating in a large bowl of water alternately tips over on its side and then rights itself. [rare] Originally (and still almost exclusively) an Indian trick. First exposed in 1922 by Branson. It is a self-contained device worked automatically by a hydrostatic mast. This is the principle behind the popular modern novelty shop item, the bobbing Gigaloo Bird. The word was Anglo-Indian by 1825, meaning a harbor ("bunder", from the Persian bandar) boat. REF: Yule & Burnell, Hobson-Jobson (1886); OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1922 Branson as "bunder-boat"; 1925 Okito in Sphinx; 1947 Histed, 94; 1981 Ayling as "The Bunder Boat"; 1984 S. H. Sharpe in LR.
See: Buried Alive. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Buried Alive".)
a. Said of a playing card that is lost in its deck. [fairly common]

n. Effect where the magician is interred underground for a prolonged period (up to 40 days) yet emerges in good health; burial alive. [rare] First reported by E.W. Lane in 1836 as practiced by Egyptian conjurers. Next reported as used in 1837 by Indian fakir Haridas at Lahore, India. A pet effect of Houdini (in 1915, 1916, and 1926), Blacaman (1920s-30s), and Swami Brahma (in 1939). The performance of this trick has been outlawed in India since 1955. In 1990 American escapist Joe Burris died in an unrehearsed attempt to escape. REF: Sharpe in Ayling (1981), 18; Seigel (1991), 168-170; Annemann in Jinx (1940), 494.
n. A performance that spoofs mindreading or mentalism. [rare]
n. An elaborate transposition illusion where three assistants change places between a box and a cage each time the magician strikes a gong. [archaic, formerly rare]

n. Effect where a handkerchief is borrowed and burned yet recovered intact from the flaming bowl. [archaic after 1939] "Do you have one of the old fashioned Burning Globes? This was once a popular piece of 146 apparatus, but it is seldom seen today except in the repertoire of old-timers or collectors." — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Oct 1956), 488

term: SEE UNDER: Cut And Restored Turban
definition: n. Effect where the upside-down escape artist must make his escape before the suspended rope burns through, dropping him to an untimely demise. [very rare but not nonce]
v. To lose a playing card in its deck. [rare]

n. By-play (verbal or visual) on the part of the performer; a bit of business; biz; a hunk of business; a hunk. [common] Originally theatrical cant by 1671 Villiers as cited in the OED/2; 1833 Lamb in OED/2 as "stage business"; 1930 Fay; 1934 Betts glossary; 1940 Sobel dictionary; 1949 Dolman as "stage business"; 1953 Laurie as "piece of business" in oldtime vaudeville; 1961 Bowman & Ball dictionary, as "business" and "stage business". Thence magicians jargon by 1902 Stanyon in Magic, 59, as "comedy business"; 1903 Hoffmann, 450, as "very old ‘business'"; 1923 Elliott as "this bit of ‘business'"; 1923 Thurston, Sep 12th letter to Blackstone; 1928 Culpitt as "diverting ‘business'"; 1933 Vernon Jan 5th ms letter to P. Fuchs [Fox] as "then ’business' of holding up the light and so forth"; 1936 Thomas in Devant; 1936 Ross Aug 4th letter to Miller as "the usual business"; 1940 Abbott cat #6, 235; 1944 Parrish citing its theatrical origin; 1944 Hugard in HMM as "some amusing business"; 1969 Nelms, 278-294; 1970 Boles; 1972 Griffin; 1981 Abbott cat #22 as "stage business"; 1983 Sharpe as "stage 'business'"; 1991 Edwin cat #1 as
n. The faro shuffle being the more usual synonym. Some cardmen define the butt shuffle as an uncontrolled faro. [rare]

n. Effect where two or more simulated (paper) butterflies are kept hovering together by fanning. [obsolescent, once fairly common] Originally the invention of Japanese conjurers who called it Ukare no Ch [literally, the Fluttering of Butterflies]. Invented (or at least introduced) by Itchosai Yanagawa. Seen in Japan in 1863 by British magician Hugh Simmons (later famous as "Dr. H. S. Lynn") who introduced it to the West where he performed it at least as early as 18 Apr 1864 at the Tremont Temple in Boston. Later that year, J. H. Anderson, or rather his daughter-assistant Lizzie, became the second of many occidental magicians to adopt this trick and the first to perform it in Europe, doing so at St. James's Hall in London. Again staged in London in 1867 by Asi-Kitch-San (or Minnmo), a member of the first Japanese magic troupe to tour Europe, imported by British juggler-magician D'Alvini. Also performed by Itchosai Yanagawa himself in Paris in 1867, J.N. Hofzinser (d.1875) in Vienna, J.N. Maskelyne early in his career in London, Ishii Black in Japan in 1914, Haakon Edeling in mid-20th century in Finland, and Charles & Mignon in Canada in 1946. Now rarely seen. REF: Stenman (1952-53), 52; Clarke in Magic Wand (1926), 37, (1928), 181; Moulton (1919/1983), 60; Waller (1948/1980), 36-37; Lynn (1873); Dif #1 (1971), 288; Fischer/Hatch (1985), 192n; Ayling (1981), 158-161; Taylor (1964), 26.
n. The version of Sawing through a Woman that uses a carpenter's circular saw. [fairly common]

n. Effect where a steel ball slowly passes through a solid sheet of glass that has been placed in a box with holes at top and bottom. [rare] Originally marketed by John Snyder Jr (through Kanter's) by 1939 as "De Luxe Ball Through Glass" and by 1940 by Davenport's as "The 'Miracle' Steel Ball thro' Glass". The Davenport effect and method inspired such later popular tricks as Coin of the Realm where a coin penetrates the glass plate.

a. Magical being the modern synonym. [obsolescent after 1890] Originally Standard English by 1624 (spelled "cabbalistic") from cabbala or kabbala, referring to the 13th Century belief in a particular mystical interpretation of the Old Testament. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1826 Testot program (in Houdini [1909], 254) as "the Cabalistic Art"; 1828 Rovere, London program as "Cabalistic Voyage"; 1831 Marriott program as "The Cabalistic Art"; 1837 Buck, British program as "Cabalistic Experiments"; 1840 Anderson, London playbill as "Cabalistic Phenomena"; 1842 F. Andoe, British playbill as "Cabalistic Phenomena"; 1848 as the Cabalistic Clock; 1857 Magician's Own Book as "mutter some cabalistic words"; 1877 Heller program as "Cabalistic Cookery"; 1888 as the Cabalistic Star; 1907 Roy in Magic as "after pronouncing some cabalistic words"; 1912 Stanyon in Magic as "to simulate a cabalistic power"; 1940 Abbott cat #6 as S. James's trick title "Cabalistic Chronology"; 1992 Randi as "cabalistic symbols".

(See also: Card Star (1).) 1.n. Mechanical apparatus that automatically produces five chosen playing cards at the tips of five points of a large metal star mounted on a stand; the Cabalistic Star (obsolete); the Fairy Star (obsolete). [obsolescent, once common]

n. The terms cabaret and nightclub are essentially synonymous, both referring to an evening dining-drinking place that provides live entertainment on a small stage. However "cabaret" usually implies a smaller, more intimate setting. The world's first cabaret was the Chat Noir [Black Cat], which opened in Paris in 1881. Cabarets then spread to Holland (in 1895), Spain (1897), Germany (1901), Austria (1901), Russia (1908), Prague (1911), Norway (1912), England (1912), and Switzerland (1916). The term "nightclub" was coined in 1894 but the French word "cabaret" did not enter Standard English in this sense until 1912 (OED/2). With the decline of vaudeville, variety, and the music-hall around 1930 in the USA, Britain, and the Continent, cabarets and nightclubs provided a refuge for many professional magicians who could make the transition from the big stage. Since the late 1930s they have been a major venue for magic. REF: Lisa Appignanesi, The Cabaret (New York: Universe Books, 1976); Harold B. Siegel, Turn-of-the-Century Cabaret (New York: Columbia University Press, 1987).
n. An act of club magic performed in a cabaret-type nightclub; cabaret magic. [rare] 150
n. Club magic performed in a cabaret-type nightclub; a cabaret act. [rare]
n. Short for the Silk Cabby (see). [fairly common]

n. Stage illusion where one person changes into another inside a large wooden cabinet. Self- contained, it could be worked surrounded by a committee of spectators and afterwards examined by them inside and out without revealing the secret; the Proteus Cabinet. [rare] Using the same V-mirror principle that mechanician Thomas W. Tobin had invented and sold to Col. Stodare in 1865 for the latter's Sphinx illusion, Prof. John Henry Pepper enlarged the effect and premiered it later that year at the Royal Polytechnic Institution hall, London. A later, elaborated cabinet-within-a-cabinet version is known as the Morritt Cage. Originally called simply "Proteus" (from the man in Greek myth who could take different forms) in 1865 by Pepper who himself soon renamed it The Cabinet of Proteus. Thence 1927 Gibson; 1985 Sharpe as historical; 1988 Waters as historical.
n. The Rope Gimmick (see) being the original and more usual term. [obsolescent, formerly rare]

term: Cake Baked in a Hat; Cake in Hat
definition: n. Effect where the magician pours the messy ingredients for a pudding or cake into a borrowed hat, produces the cooked solid, and returns the hat unsoiled; the Pudding in Hat (obsolescent). [common] A popular comedy effect among magi from as early as 1749 when French sleight-of-hand man Delisle magically cooked an omelette in a hat. Hyman "The Incomparable Young Dutchman" Saunders produced pancakes in this manner during his tour of Jamaica in 1775. Performed by Ingleby Sr in England in 1822, again with pancakes; and by Anderson by 1841 with a pudding. Marketed by 1843 by Crambrook in London. Writing in 1853, French magician J.N. Ponsin therefore rightly called this trick "well known". A pet effect of Al Baker (1941). Since the 1950s a popular TV-magic kid-show trick. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand, XIV (1925), 34.
n. Stage effect where a canary bird is loaded into a pistol, which when fired at a lit table lamp, reappears inside the incandescent bulb. [rare]

n. Effect where a lit candle penetrates the magician's arm that is covered by an empty metal sleeve. [fairly common] A U.F. Grant copyright, first marketed by him by 1968. Possibly invented by Bill Foust.
n. Effect where a candle flame is carried at the finger tips from one candle to another or to light a cigarette. [fairly common]

term: Cane to Silk; Vanishing Cane to Silk
definition: n. Effect where a a cane held between the magician's outstretched hands instantly transforms on command to a large handkerchief. Compare Silk to Cane for nearly opposite effect. [fairly common]
n. Two silks, one in each hand, appear when a cane vanishes as in the above effect. [fairly common] Invention is credited to G. [George or Gus?] Davenport by Gary Darwin (1988), 8.

n. Apparatus in the shape of a walking stick whose upper portion springs open at a touch to form a tripod-supported stand that the magician then makes into a table by fitting his hat (faked with a built-in socket) onto the pole. [rare] “Since I first saw the Cane to Table or Table to Cane listed in a magic catalogue, I have been fascinated with the feat. I have, or have had, almost a half dozen different models.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Mar 1952), 909
n. A stock reading (see) being the most usual synonym. 154 [very rare, used only by mentalists]

n. A playing-card effect where a succession of cards disappear when sandwiched between other cards, apparently "eaten" by the "cannibal" cards, or so the accompanying patter story would have you believe. [fairly common] "The Cannibal Card plot, since its conception by Lyn [sic] Searles, has been a favorite among magicians and laymen alike. And, why not, when one considers the delightful combination of snappy card magic and the consumption of raw, human flesh." — Dan Huffman in The Linking Ring (Nov 1987), 72 Both concept and original method were invented by Lin Searles and marketed by the Owen Brothers in the late 1950s. Searles' method used special cards. In the late 1960s Alexander Elmsley invented a method that replaced Searles' trick cards with a Buckle Count. Elmsley's version was first published (with minor variation) by Matt Corin in 1971 (in Kabbala #1). This latter version was published as a complete routine by Walt Lees in 1981. A pet effect of Juan Tamariz. REF: Busby in Busby-Corin cat (May 1981), 25.

term: cannon-ball trick, the; The Cannon Ball Trick
definition: n. Effect where a solid cannon-ball (of wood) or a hollow metal ball (that permits an extra load) is produced from an empty hat. [archaic after 1924] A pet effect of Adalbert Frikell. Using bowling balls, a pet effect today of Don Alan and John "The Great Tomsoni" Thompson. REF: Stanyon in Magic (Mar 1912), 45-46, for various methods.

v. To secretly add one or more palmed playing cards to the top of a deck; capping the deck; to palm on. [rare] "Most magicians do not know how to ‘cap' a deck properly. Perhaps it's because they have spent so much time learning how to palm cards that they believe replacement is a trivial point." — John Murray, Inside (1984), 56 Originally the argot of American card sharps by 1931 Smith as "cap the deck". Thence magicians jargon by 1984 Murray; 1985 Johnny Thompson orally as "cop one and cap the deck"; 1991 Ortiz. n. The secret addition of a palmed card to a deck. [very rare]
n. A utility business-card case gaffed so mentalist can view a written message closed inside. [rare]

n. The climax of a routine; kicker (1) being the more usual synonym. [rare] Originally general slang meaning a climax (from "to cap" = to crown) by 1790. REF: OED/2; Wentworth & Flexner (1975 ed). Thence magicians jargon by 1941 Charles Bertram Jr in Jinx #140, 793; 1973 William Wizard in The Magician's Magazine as "add a capper"; 1975 Kosky; 1978 Gross; 1982 Busby in Epoptica #1 as the "capper to the routine"; 1986

n. A playing card gaffed with leaves of carbon paper and white paper to receive an impression. [very rare] Despite many later claimants, this card device was invented by James Maxwell and first described in print in the Magic Wand for March 1920. REF: Hugard (1937), 303. This principle was embodied in the Mental Masterpiece impression deck that gives a carbon-wax impression of the volunteer's writing. REF: Annemann in The Sphinx (Nov 1929).

n. A complete performance of card magic. [rare] "As an ornamental sleight or flourish the backhand palm with cards is an exquisite thing; but it is a frail foundation on which to build a card act, as many vaudeville performers have done." — T. Nelson Downs & J. Northern Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909), Introductory

n. The cardboard box in which a deck of playing cards comes used as a prop (faked or unfaked) in tricks. Compare card box and houlette. [fairly common] First used as a magic prop in 1904 by Clinton Burgess by cutting open a tiny window in the lower right corner to reveal the suit and value of each card before it is withdrawn, one-by-one. Then in 1915 by Stanley Collins in his Penetrating Card trick. The Vanishing Card Case was invented by Milbourne Christopher, with later versions by Allan Lambie and Tommy Wonder. The Card via Cardcase to the Ceiling was invented and marketed by Al Stevenson in 1958. The Shrinking Card Case effect was pioneered by Peter Kane and John Cornelius. REF: Burgess in Magic (Feb 1904), 55; Reinhard Müller, Card Cases (1987).

n. Effect where playing cards gradually form themselves into a multi-tiered tower-like structure; a Castle of Cards and house of cards being the less usual synonyms. [fairly common] "Though it can be visually appealing, the card castle is so obviously flimsy and collapsible that the mystery value of its appearance is negligible." — T. A. Waters, The Encyclopedia of Magic and Magicians (1988), 57 Based on the children's pastime that had been popular since at least as early as 1641 when English poet Milton wrote of a "House of Court Cards". German philosopher Lichtenberg referred to them as a Card House (Kartenhauser) in the late 1770s. Invented as a magical effect by 1882 when marketed by Hamley Bros. Devant implies the inventor was G.W. Hunter, which is at least chronologically possible, as Hunter had turned to magic in 1878 at age 28. An improved model was developed by Louis Nikola and performed by him in 1931. A further improved version was developed by Eric Lewis after World War II. And in 1945 Lu Brent published the plans of his invention of a build-it-yourself model, commercially marketed since 1983 by John Fedko. REF: Maskelyne & Devant (1911), 278-279; Lewis, I (1980), 79; L.P. Guest in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1945), 181, 186; Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Feb 1946), 192.

term: Card on Ceiling; The Card on the/a Ceiling (Trick)
definition: n. Classic effect of a chosen card sticking to the ceiling when either the entire deck is thrown or apparently fired from a pistol. Compare Card on the Wall and Stamp on Ceiling. [fairly common] "The Card on Ceiling has proven to be one of the most impressive and talked about card effects 158 in the entire realm of card magic." — L&L Publishing, Catalog of Magic (1996 ["1997"]), 21 Usually done as a publicity stunt because the effect is so astonishing that the host will often leave the card in place for years, pointing it out as a trick of the magician who did it. The earliest description and exposé of the chosen-card-to-ceiling version (using soap as the adherant) is in Richard Neve's book of 1716. Performed in Jan 1802 in Boston by Scottish magician John Rannie (Jan 1st ad). The method was being sold in London in 1843 by Crambrook. Later a pet effect of Leon Herrmann (by 1899), Milton Franklin Andrews (by 1902), Max Malini, Orla Moody, Bert Allerton (1940s), Eddie Fields, Jay Marshall, and Michael Ammar. Modern magi use Magician's Wax. REF: Busby in Whaley (1991), 153-156; Clarke (1924), 139; Moulton (1919/1983), 4.

term: Card in Cigarette; Card in the Cigarette
definition: n. Effect where a playing card is vanished and later discovered inside a cigarette. [fairly common] This trick was featured (including the torn corner) by famous Italian manipulator Yank Hoe as early as 1883 in London and by 1896 in the USA. A pet effect of A.J. Cantu (late 1920s), Fred Keating (early 1930s), and Paul Rosini (1930s). The Bill in Cigarette is a later version. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (Mar 1928), 43; Burlingame, II (1896), 24.

n. The methods (sleights, locator cards, etc.) by which the magician keeps a deck of playing cards in a desired order while seemingly mixing them. [fairly common] "Few conjurors will disagree that the Kelly Replacement, when well executed, is one of the cleanest forms of card control that can be found." — Peter Warlock in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Aug 1956), 465

n. Type of dropper or holdout, pinned under the jacket, that delivers one or more playing cards to the magician's hand from a metal clip. [rare] Originally a card cheaters device. Introduced to magicians by American gambling expert and magician Audley Walsh. REF: Tannen cat #4 (1963), 313.

term: Card in Egg; Card in the Egg, The
definition: n. Effect where a volunteer tears and keeps corner from a playing card that the magician vanishes and then finds inside an unbroken hen's egg when he taps it open. [rare] The magus loads the vanished card when he breaks the egg with a gaffed card-producing card wand (described by 1829 and marketed by Henry Novra by around 1858), fountain pen (by 1924), or pencil (by 1932).
n. A rack (easel) with a ledge or compartments to display an array of playing cards upright to the spectators; a card stand. May be gaffed or not. [rare]

term: Card on Forehead; card on the forehead
definition: n. Effect where the spectator's chosen card is discovered stuck to the magician's forehead. [rare] First published in the Jan 1941 issue of Tops as "The Stuck Card Trick". A pet effect of bartender-magician Frank Shields (by 1974), Derek Dingle (by 1976), and Michael Finney (in 160 1980s-90s). REF: Gloye in The Linking Ring (Sep 1996), 85.

n. Effect where a playing card is chosen, returned to the deck, wrapped in a handkerchief, and shaken to make it slowly emerge into view. A later variant that additionally encloses the deck in its card-case is the Penetrating Card. [rare] "The Card Through the Handkerchief is one of the classics of card magic. Performed correctly, it is as strong an effect as you could wish for." — Blackstone Jr & Reynolds, The Blackstone Book of Magic & Illusion (1985), 185

n. A compact, compartmented file that separates several (up to 52) playing cards in prearranged order to be selected by touch from the magician's pocket; a pocket index specifically designed to store playing cards. [fairly common] First described in early French magic texts. Reportedly used by Hofzinser in the mid-1800s. Certainly used by J.M. Hartz in the late 1800s. An inferior variant using multiple holders distinguishable by differences in shape was invented, probably independently, by Simon in 1882. Described in 1897 by Roterberg (pp.63-67) who unimaginatively called it "The Card Receptacle". Described in 1908 by Clinton Burgess for an “Any Card Called For” routine. Used by 1915 by Herbert Brooks to work his own Any Card Called For routine. Adapted to billets by Al Baker as the general utility pocket index shortly before 1925 when exposed by Annemann. REF: C. Burgess in Conjurers’ Monthly Magazine (Jul 1908), 337-338; Hoffmann (1911), 185- 186, calling it merely "a card-case of peculiar construction"; Miller and Wilson, Charlie Miller on the Card Index (1979?); Annemann (1935), 15; Abrams (1992), 8n, attributing the innovation of adapting it to billets to Annemann in the Sep 1924 Sphinx. 161

n. Apparatus that reveals selected cards. [archaic] Inspired by the coin ladder but only by the appearance of that apparatus and not its mechanism. REF: Barbi Walker & Robert Seaver (editors), The P&L Book (1992), 241-250.
(See also: changing ladle.) n. A large trough-shaped serving spoon gaffed with a secret compartment to permit the exchange of small, flat objects such as cards or billets; a Card Ladle. [archaic]

n. Effect where a playing card is vanished and discovered rolled up inside an orange or lemon when the latter is cut open. [rare] First published in 1853 by Ponsin using a lemon, thereby predating the claim by Ernest Thorn who used an orange. Inspired the famous Bill in Lemon trick.

n. Conjuring with playing cards; card tricks being the more usual synonym. Compare card manipulation. [very common] "Clearly, to travel the royal road to card magic, you must begin with the fundamental principles and learn these well, as you would in learning any other art." — Hugard & Braue, The Royal Road to Card Magic (1948), xvi "Probably the most popular branch of magic is card magic, at least more has been written about 162 card conjuring than anything else." — John J. Crimmins Jr in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Apr 1952), 920 "Card magic has been constantly improved until our present-day card men have reached a peak of perfection never dreamed of." — Bill Simon in The Linking Ring (Mar 1954) "One must, after all, remember that card magic has progressed rapidly since the cut-off date of the Potter index of 1964." — Jeff Busby, Short Sheet (May 1986), 2 "[T]he modern style of close-up card magic is in part the result of incorporating card cheating methods into magic—something that required moving to the card table as a performing arena." — Darwin Ortiz, The Annotated Erdnase (1991), 19

(See also: Zens' Card Miracle.) n. Effect where spectators select five cards from a 25-card packet, shuffle them back in, display the whole packet on a card easel, whereupon the magus picks out the chosen cards. [rare]
(See also: Cards to Pocket.) n. The Cards up the Sleeve (see) being the most usual synonym. [fairly common].
n. The original version (using a confederate) of the Card to Wallet trick. [obsolete after 1932]
See: Rising Cards. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Rising Cards".)

(See also: card throwing.) n. The flourish that sails a playing card from the hand out to any chosen part of the audience; card scaling. If it returns to the thrower, it is termed a Boomerang Card. [rare] "Mere ornamental displays, such as card-throwing or springing the cards from hand to hand, are permissible, inasmuch as they do not tend to give away the secret of any trick, but it is doubtful whether even these do not lessen the magical effect of a performance." — Louis Hoffmann, letter in Magic (Feb 1901), 38 "This is one of the oldest of the ornamental sleights ...." — T. N. Downs, The Art of Magic (1909) "Many, many years ago I made it a practice to ask one and all laymen with whom I might be talking about magic, what trick had impressed them the most. Invariably it was Thurston's card throwing." — Stuart Cramer in The New Phoenix #373 (1962), 320 Magicians can routinely project cards 60 to 120 feet, depending on their skill. The still-current "official" world-record distance shot of 185 feet, 1 inch, was made on 12 Jun 1979 by Kevin St. Onge (Guiness Book of World Records, 1984 edition, p.402). On 4 Nov 1976 at the BBC Centre in London, American magician Ricky Jay made an official 135-foot throw, as his bid to establish himself in the Guiness Book. According to Waters in 1988, Jay's personal best is now an unofficial 190'6". Commonly performed by magicians by 1868 when first explained by Robert-Houdin. Scaling was featured by Alexander Herrmann (from 1861), Mehây (1870s), Carl Hertz (by 1896), Félicien Trewey (by 1898), Ellis Stanyon (by 1898), F.E. Powell, Howard Thurston (by 1901 to 1935), Leon Herrmann (by 1902), Sidney Lee, Houdini, Ferraris (by 1914), J. Warren Keene (by 1914), Nightingale, Raymond (by 1926), Stuart Cramer, Harry Thurston (by 1931), Will Rock, Ben Franklin IV (by 1962), Finn Jon, and Ricky Jay (by 1976). REF: Ricky Jay, Cards as Weapons (1977); Pabular (Dec 1976), 345; Waters (1988), 61; Stanyon in Magic (May 1920), 60-61. This flourish, while quite common, has been slow to acquire a jargon term. Originally merely described, clumsily, as "To Throw a Card" in 1876 (Hoffmann; 1902 Hilliar), "throwing a card" in 1877 (Sachs), or "throwing cards" in 1909 (Hilliard), or "Throwing a Card" in 1913 (Stanyon in Magic; 1954 Hugard in HMM). Later called "scaling the cards" in 1945 (Hugard), and "scaling cards" in 1923 (J.W. Elliott; 1961 Gibson & Young; 1977 Jay; 1982 Hay 4th ed).
n. A small servante specifically designed to hold a deck of playing cards behind a chair or table. [obsolete after 1958, formerly fairly common] Originally attached to the back of a chair.
(See also: Spider Web Card.) n. Stage effect where a selected playing card is vanished and reappears at the center of a mechanical spider's web when the web is spun. [rare]
n. The Boomerang Card (see) being the most usual synonym. [very rare] 164
1.n. The Stabbed Deck (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare]

n. Type of effect where a blindfolded magician discovers the spectator's chosen card by sticking a dagger or sword into a scattered pile of cards and impaling the correct one; the Card Stab (2). Compare the Stabbed Deck. [fairly common] Exposed first in 1740 by Guyot (also 1800 by Gale). A pet effect of Hyman "The Incomparable Young Dutchman" Saunders (in 1784 in Jamaica), Charles Bertram (by 1896), Nate Leipzig, Karl Germain, Max Malini, Maurice, and John Kennedy (in 1980s-90s). A fine version ("Psychic Hat Pins") using hat pins was invented by Dick Zimmerman in the late 1970s.

1.n. Mechanical apparatus that automatically produces five chosen playing cards at the tips of five points of a large metal star mounted on a stand; the Cabalistic Star (obsolete); the Fairy Star (obsolete). [obsolescent, once common]

n. Apparatus permitting the effect of a chosen playing card being caught (that is, appearing impaled) at the tip of a sword. [common] Used in stage performance as early as 1842 by Viennese magician Ludwig Döbler in London and around 1853 by Robert-Houdin. Used by London street conjurors by 1861 (and probably in the 1840s). Exposed in 1876 by Hoffmann (p.121). REF: Sharpe (1983), 32; "Confessions of a Street Conjurer" (1861). “I’ll meet you at the dueling grounds with Milton Chase card swords or nothing. As for seconds, I chose Charlie Miller’s.” — Bill Larsen’s reply to Joglar’s challenge in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Apr 1951), 778

n. The flourish that sails a playing card from the hand out to any chosen part of the audience; card scaling. If it returns to the thrower, it is termed a Boomerang Card. [rare] "Mere ornamental displays, such as card-throwing or springing the cards from hand to hand, are permissible, inasmuch as they do not tend to give away the secret of any trick, but it is doubtful whether even these do not lessen the magical effect of a performance." — Louis Hoffmann, letter in Magic (Feb 1901), 38 "This is one of the oldest of the ornamental sleights ...." — T. N. Downs, The Art of Magic (1909) "Many, many years ago I made it a practice to ask one and all laymen with whom I might be talking about magic, what trick had impressed them the most. Invariably it was Thurston's card throwing." — Stuart Cramer in The New Phoenix #373 (1962), 320 Magicians can routinely project cards 60 to 120 feet, depending on their skill. The still-current "official" world-record distance shot of 185 feet, 1 inch, was made on 12 Jun 1979 by Kevin St. Onge (Guiness Book of World Records, 1984 edition, p.402). On 4 Nov 1976 at the BBC Centre in London, American magician Ricky Jay made an official 135-foot throw, as his bid to establish himself in the Guiness Book. According to Waters in 1988, Jay's personal best is now an unofficial 190'6". Commonly performed by magicians by 1868 when first explained by Robert-Houdin. Scaling was featured by Alexander Herrmann (from 1861), Mehây (1870s), Carl Hertz (by 1896), Félicien Trewey (by 1898), Ellis Stanyon (by 1898), F.E. Powell, Howard Thurston (by 1901 to 1935), Leon Herrmann (by 1902), Sidney Lee, Houdini, Ferraris (by 1914), J. Warren Keene (by 1914), Nightingale, Raymond (by 1926), Stuart Cramer, Harry Thurston (by 1931), Will Rock, Ben Franklin IV (by 1962), Finn Jon, and Ricky Jay (by 1976). REF: Ricky Jay, Cards as Weapons (1977); Pabular (Dec 1976), 345; Waters (1988), 61; Stanyon in Magic (May 1920), 60-61. This flourish, while quite common, has been slow to acquire a jargon term. Originally merely described, clumsily, as "To Throw a Card" in 1876 (Hoffmann; 1902 Hilliar), "throwing a card" in 1877 (Sachs), or "throwing cards" in 1909 (Hilliard), or "Throwing a Card" in 1913 (Stanyon in Magic; 1954 Hugard in HMM). Later called "scaling the cards" in 1945 (Hugard), and "scaling cards" in 1923 (J.W. Elliott; 1961 Gibson & Young; 1977 Jay; 1982 Hay 4th ed).

n. Classic effect where the spectator's chosen card is discovered as the one in the deck that sticks to the wall. Compare Card on the Ceiling. [fairly common] First performed by Pinetti in London in 1784 by firing a pistol, as described and exposed later that year by Decremps and next year by Astley. This version was marketed by 1843 by Crambrook in London. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1925), 91. Another, improved method simply throws the real deck at the wall where the chosen card 168 adheres. That version (using a small tack) was published, but probably not for the first time, in 1829 in The Boy’s Own Book (p.201, as “The Drawn Card Nailed to the Wall”) and then in 1857 in The Magician's Own Book (p.63, as “the Nailed Card”). A pet effect of American saloon keeper Matt Schulien in the 1950s and 1960s.

n. A magic wand gaffed to receive a rolled-up playing card so it can be surreptitiously introduced into an egg or other container. [rare] First mentioned in 1740 by Guyot who describes a wand loaded with a rolled-up playing card. Again in 1829 in The Boy’s Own Book (pp.202-203) as a hollow stick with a spring-loaded rolled-up card for the Card in Egg trick. Marketed in London around 1858 by Henry Novra "to pass a card into an egg." Theodore DeLand Jr designed a card wand that produced a printed silk bag that spread out to simulate a previously forced playing card. In DeLand's version, a different card face was printed on each side so that a card discovery could be repeated once with forced cards. REF: Christopher in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Mar 1955), 263. 169

n. Effect where a folded playing card, visibly sliding back-and-forth within another folded card, turns inside out. [common] Developed by British cardman Roy Walton in 1974 as a commercialized modification of Busby's Into the 4th Dimension and Beyond (1973), Walton acknowledging Busby's "principle". Popularized by British cardman Derek Dingle on American TV, specifically the Barbara Walters "Not for Women Only" show.

n. n. Nickname of the Magic Castle in Hollywood. [fairly common] Opened on 2 Jan 1963 by William Jr and Milton Larsen in a turreted Gothic Victorian mansion in the Hollywood Hills. Serves as a lavish private club for its (in 1988) nearly 5,500 members, including over 2,500 magicians. 175

(See also: Card Castle.) n. Effect where playing cards gradually form themselves into a multi-tiered tower-like structure; a Castle of Cards and house of cards being the less usual synonyms. [fairly common] "Though it can be visually appealing, the card castle is so obviously flimsy and collapsible that the mystery value of its appearance is negligible." — T. A. Waters, The Encyclopedia of Magic and Magicians (1988), 57 Based on the children's pastime that had been popular since at least as early as 1641 when English poet Milton wrote of a "House of Court Cards". German philosopher Lichtenberg referred to them as a Card House (Kartenhauser) in the late 1770s. Invented as a magical effect by 1882 when marketed by Hamley Bros. Devant implies the inventor was G.W. Hunter, which is at least chronologically possible, as Hunter had turned to magic in 1878 at age 28. An improved model was developed by Louis Nikola and performed by him in 1931. A further improved version was developed by Eric Lewis after World War II. And in 1945 Lu Brent published the plans of his invention of a build-it-yourself model, commercially marketed since 1983 by John Fedko. REF: Maskelyne & Devant (1911), 278-279; Lewis, I (1980), 79; L.P. Guest in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1945), 181, 186; Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Feb 1946), 192.

n. The false deal that deals playing cards from the middle of a deck while seemingly dealing the regulation top one; centers; a middle deal; a middle. [fairly common] "Ironically, the number of center dealing techniques in print far exceeds the number of people who can actually perform a deceptive center deal." — Darwin Ortiz, The Annotated Erdnase (1991), 125 An almost legendary sleight. Extremely difficult to perform—the hardest of all according to Bruce Elliott (1952) and Frank Garcia (1962). Hence seldom mentioned much less used. Of great value to its few practitioners because it nullifies the defensive value of an honest cut. The few magicians who use it do so only for exposé demonstrations of card sharping, except for Gene Maze who does apply it to card tricks. Originally the invention of some American card sharp, possibly the old Mississippi riverboat gambler from whom Allen [not "Bill"] Kennedy [not "Thompson"] reportedly learned it around 1920. In any case, Kennedy worked the sleight profitably for some ten years, holding it such a closely guarded secret that few of the brethren knew the move even existed. Then, in 1932, magician Dai Vernon, having heard rumor of Kennedy's feat, tracked him to his home in Pleasant Hill, Missouri; and, posing as a "card hustler" working trans-Atlantic liners, was taught this "awe-inspiring" sleight. Later mastered by Charlie Miller, John Scarne, Luis Zingone, Fred Robinson, and Gene Maze. REF: Dai Vernon, ms letter to Paul Fox, 22 Apr 1932; Faucett W. Ross, letter to Roger Klaus, 3 Jan 1961 [sic] naming "Allen Kennedy"; Pueblo Star-Journal, 7 Aug 1938, with AP story on Vernon; Bertram (1978), 80-82; Vernon tape (1977); Bruce Elliott & James Tuck, "The Search for the Middle Deal" in Saga magazine (1952), 51-53 & 61; Busby in Whaley (1991), 240; Ortiz (1991), 124-125.

n. The sleight that enables the mentalist to obtain a torn center. [common] "From the profusion of methods in print, it's beginning to look as if the Center Tear is receiving the sort of attention in mentalism that the Double Lift has received from card men!" — Richard Osterlind, The Surrounded Slow-Motion Center Tear (1986), 1 178 Judged by Hilliard (1938, p.899) "one of the best impromptu tricks ever devised." The method is that the volunteer is induced to write a secret word or brief question in the center of a square of paper that he then folds twice. This puts the writing at the billet's corner fold. The mentalist tears up the billet, palming the torn center, which may then be glimpsed covertly. This brilliant subterfuge was evidently the invention of some anonymous psychic reader among whose colleagues it remained a closely held secret until disclosed to a mentalist magician from whom it gradually diffused among magic and mentalism circles. The documented record begins in the winter of 1928 with British-born Canadian magician Sid Lorraine during his visit to Cambridge, England. There he met J[oseph] T[aylor] Garrus, an American student who was a mentalist and magician. He taught Lorraine the center tear, saying he had learned it from a medium who had admitted it was not original with him. Later that year, Lorraine described the secret in letters to Tom Bowyer, Ted Annemann, and Joe Ovette. Annemann replied by postcard that the notion was new to him but that "it has possibiities". American mentalist-magician Joseph Dunninger had somehow also learned the trick. He taught it in 1930 or 1931 to Martin Sunshine, professional mentalist and then partner in Al Baker's magic shop on Broadway. By 1931, Sunshine was using it in private psychic readings and that year taught it to his friend Theodore H. Arnold, a wealthy New York amateur mentalist. Arnold demonstrated it to his friend, Annemann, who—with this added input—finally decided it was a money maker and submitted it to Thayer's Trick of the Month Club. However, appropriately, Ovette was first in print, selling it himself in 1931 in a narrowly distributed manuscript titled "What Is It?". Annemann was only second when in August 1932 Thayer's Trick of the Month brochure published the "Ne Plus Ultra Reading Method". Annemann, with ill-informed generosity, mis-credited his most recent tipster, Ted Arnold, as the inventor. In any case, this version, as publicly performed in New York by mentalist Mogul, effectively popularized the method. Next, in 1935 in Jinx #6 (p.24), editor Annemann published a modified version where a word in a newspaper is circled. Five years later, in 1940, Dunninger himself finally went to Annemann with what he said was the original method, claiming that he had worked it out all by himself way back around 1915. Annemann, taking Dunninger's belated word, "corrected" (that is, further garbled) the historical record that he himself had been editorially responsible for, in writing the introductory note to Dunninger, "The Secret", in The Jinx #74 (1940). The only way Dunninger's claim can be supported is if some connection, even indirect, can be established between him and Sid Lorraine's Yank at Cambridge. Subsequent variations in handling are Al Koran's "One-Handed Center Tear", Al Baker's "Umbrella Move" (published in 1949), and Richard Osterlind's radically new fold and method, the "Surrounded Slow-Motion Center Fold", invented in 1984. REF: Sid Lorraine, 2 Nov 1964 letter to Bill Madsen; several papers by Al Mann including, most importantly, The Tesseract (1978); Annemann in Jinx #74 (1940), 495; J.G. Thompson, Jr, Centermental (n.p.: Ed Mellon Releases, [1965]) 1, 3; Baker (1949), 10; B. Bernstein (1980); Busby, interviews, 1984 & 1988; Lorraine 24th Jun interview; Abrams (1992), 123; North in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (May 1961), 100.

n. A blackboard cartoon-sketching entertainment with patter. An allied art of magic. [fairly common] Although non-magician chalk-talk artists often worked their own act, a few trouped with magicians, like Frank Caveny with Karl Germain (in 1900). Expert magician chalk-talkers have included J. Stuart Blackton (in 1894), Selbit (1910s), Harlan Tarbell (1920s), Buddy O'Day (since mid-1930s), Ted Salter (1940s), and Ed Harris. Seldom seen today, although the late O'Day was still performing as late as 1987; and a few contemporary magicians, including Al Ellis, have taken it up. Cartoonist Roger Price's famous "droodles" of the 1950s are simply a modernized version. Originally American English since around 1830-40. REF: RHD/2nd. But OED/2 gives earliest citation only as 1881. Thence magicians jargon by 1911 Selbit as "Chalk-Talk"; 1924 Tarbell; 1931 Welles in Variety & Billboard want ads; 1939 Kanter cat; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1941 Chicago Magic cat #18; 1967 Graham; 1970 Boles; 1982 Albrecht cartoon in Epoptica #1; 1984 Ed Harris ad in New Tops; 1986 Magic Shop Hot Sheet as "Gospel cartoon chalk talks"; 1988 Waters; 1990 Booth; 1991 Salter in letter to Whaley. NOTE: "chalk talking" in 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1940 Abbott cat #6. And a "chalk talker" in 1941 Chicago Magic cat

n. A dare accepted by the magician to perform some specific trick, usually either some very difficult or dangerous feat or a conventional trick under special constraints or test conditions. 180 Compare betcha. [common, particularly with escapologists and mentalists] "When a magician issues a challenge, he immediately changes his offering from a conjuring trick to a sporting proposition. He should therefore be prepared to face whatever comes along." — Charles Waller, Magical Nights at the Theatre (1964/1980), 184 "Real challenges will seldom be forthcoming. Therefore, challenges must be prearranged." — William Larsen, "The Great Handcuff Escape Act" (1944) Usually solicited as a publicity stunt. The first magician to issue a public challenge, and using that word, was evidently Dr. James W. Elliott, the famous American card manipulator, by Dec 1896 and also in the announcement issued by his manager in the Sep 1898 issue of Mahatma. This triggered a flurry of imitators. That same year John Henricks put forward his challenge as champion billiard-ball manipulator. Welsh Miller followed with his challenge as champion coin manipulator. Then, in 1899 Houdini introduced his challenge handcuff act. REF: Elliott letter in Magic (Oct 1907), 6; Price (1985), 159-160, 190-191. See Moulton (1983), 19-20, for W. C. Houghton's 1832 "challenge" to Chabert for a fire-oven and poison-eating contest.

1.n. Type of effect where one object or characteristic is seemingly transformed into another by an undetected substitution or switch; a transformation (1). See also color change. [obsolescent, formerly common] "The fundamental principles of a sleight of hand trick, practically any trick or stage illusion for that matter, are Three Only in number, viz., Production, Disappearance and Change." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (Jun 1912), 67 This word, originally Standard French as le change, was used by French magicians in this sense by 1868 (Robert-Houdin). Thence borrowed as jargon by their English confrères by 1876 Hoffmann; 1877 Sachs; 1902 Erdnase/Harto; 1931 Mussey & Oursler; 1981 Ray-Mond; 1984 Vernon; 1987 Huffman in LR as a "card change". v.t. To exchange; to make a transformation (1); to make the change; to ring. [obsolete after 1931, formerly fairly common]
