n. A playing card faked either by omitting or mixing spots (pips) at one end or by mechanism as with the flap card. [fairly common] A card with detachable spots was described in 1693 (Ozanam, using white wax) and again in 1740 (Guyot, using soap).
n. A large trough-shaped serving spoon gaffed with a secret compartment to permit the exchange of small, flat objects such as cards or billets; a Card Ladle. [archaic]

n. A billfold faked to permit the exchange of flat objects such as cards; a switch wallet. [rare] The first changing wallet, based on a cunning hinging principle, was the so-called Himber Wallet invented by 1924 and popularized in 1963 by Richard Himber. A modified version is the Horwitz Wallet. Others include the Miracle Wallet that has an easily stolen pocket and the Dalal Wallet that does the switch at its transparent "window".

(See also: Devil of a Hat.) n. Title of the Inexhaustible Hat routine as carried to its limit by J. M. Hartz. [rare] Joseph Michael Hartz, a Liverpuddlian Briton, began developing this act in New York around 1877 and had it fully perfected when he returned to England in 1883. Later a pet routine of Carl Hertz. REF: Hoffmann (1911); E. Dawes, “Michael Hartz and Le Chapeau Du Diable”, The Magic Circular, V.71 (1977), 131-135.. “An act similar to Hartz’s Devil of a Hat would be greeted as a novelty today.” — The Looker-On in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Feb 1948), 397

n. The amusing art of creating multiple characters by refolding a single hat. An allied art of magic. [fairly common] 185 Practiced and probably invented as early as around 1590 by popular French comedian "Tabarin" (Jean Salomon) who created some 10 characters. In France this art is called Le chapeau de Tabarin. Revived in 1870 by another French comedian, Mons. Fusier with some 15 characters; and adopted by Félicien Trewey in 1875 with, eventually, 35 characters. Thence in Britain by R. A. Roberts (around 1903), Mr. Willis, Robertson Keene, Owen Clark, Arnold Crowther (1920s-30s), Oswald Rae (by 1928), and Fred Culpitt (in the 1930s). In the USA by Percy Abbott, Stuart Cramer, John Booth (since ca1930), Frances Ireland (since 1940s), Francisco (1940s), Milbourne Christopher (by 1952), Tommy Windsor (in 1962), Seymour Davis (by 1986), and Harry Anderson. And in Germany by Cha'Peau (by 1988). REF: Neil (1903), 331-332; Clarke in Magic Wand (1924), 40; Stanyon in Magic, III (1903), 29.

n. A performance of manipulative magic in the style of the Chavez school course in magic. [very rare but not nonce] The Chavez Studio (now College) of Magic was founded in 1941 in Los Angeles by Benito and Marian Chavez, giving private instruction to aspiring conjurors. Its post-war accreditation in 1946 under the GI Bill led to a small-scale flood of students. Consequently, between 1960 and 1962, the widow Chavez added a 17-lesson, 600-page correspondence course. While the more famous Tarbell Course taught a multitude of tricks covering the full range of magic, the Chavez Course focused pragmatically on teaching complete routines (limited to card, coin, cigarette, and dove manipulation) to prepare their students to give a commercial stage act. Giving value for money, it produced such successful graduates as Richard Aimes, Don Alan, Gene Brandt, Mel Brown, Vivian Cosby, Walter E. Cummings, Dicky Dean, John Fedko, Neil Foster, Phillip Graham, Bob Gurtler, Dennis Haney, Chuck Kirkham, Gerrie Larsen, Dino Mazza, Arie McChesney, Mark Miller, Nardini & Nadyne, Norm Nielsen, Channing Pollock, Paul Svengari, and Irv Weiner (1947). Following the death of Marian Chavez in 1978, Neil Foster continued the school in Colon, Michigan, from 1979 until his death in 1988, while Dale Salwak handles the correspondence course out of Los Angeles. REF: Booth in Linking Ring (Dec 1986), 57-60.

Six

1.n. The performance of authentic Chinese conjuring, usually by Chinese themselves. [rare] "Speaking of the Chinese, it is a most noticeable thing that their methods of vanishing and concealing articles are the same as those practiced by ourselves, which fully demonstrates the fact that there is only one proper way...." — Edwin Sachs, Sleight of Hand (1885 ed), 75-76 Few authentic Chinese tricks have become part of the standard repertory of Western magic. These are the Goldfish Bowls (introduced in 1837), the Color Changing Coins (by 1890), the Torn and Restored Paper (in 1898 by Ching Ling FOO), the Human Volcano routine (in 1898 193 by Ching Ling FOO), the Stack of Fishbowls (in 1909 by HAN Ping Chien), the so-called Kuma Tubes (in 1915 by Japanese magus K.T. KUMA), and possibly the Linking Rings. The only Chinese props adopted in the West are the Kuma Tubes and the Foo Can. REF: Robert van Gulik, “The Mango Trick in China: An Essay on Taoist Magic”, Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japan, 3rd Series, Vol.3 (1954), 117-175. The few authentic Chinese magicians who have performed their traditional art successfully in the West (with the dates and places of their performance there) have been: "The Chinese Jugglers", ca1830 (London). Sometime in the mid-1830s a troupe of three Chinese magicians (perhaps the same as above) performed unsuccessfully in Paris. Breaking up, one went on to Dublin where in 1837 he taught Phillippe both the Linking Rings and the Goldfish Bowl. "The Chinese Magicians" (with magi TUCK Quy and WAN Sing), 1853 (USA), 1854 (England). The Chinese Artists, 1869 (Australia). Ching Ling FOO, 1898-1900 (USA), 1904 (South Africa), 1904-05 (England), 1909-12 (Europe), 1912-15 (USA). Tan Kwai Troupe, 1905 (Europe). HAN P'ing Chien, 1909 (USA), 1912-14 (London), 1912 (Paris), 1914-16 (USA), 1922-23 (USA). LONG Tack Sam, ca1912-14 (Europe), 1914-1921 (USA), 1922 (England), 1923 (USA), 1923 (Australia/New Zealand), 1925 (Australia), 1925-27 (USA), 1928-29 (Australia), 1929 (USA), 1929 (Europe), 1930 (Argentina), 1931 (Australia), 1932 (USA), 1933 (Australia), 1934 (USA), 1935 (Australia). KWONG Sing Wah Troupe, 1927 (Australia). JUNG Kor Moi & Co., from Shanghai, 1935 (Vancouver, Canada) LU Chang Fu, 1930s (Europe). Choriki, 1930s (USA). Among the few first-hand descriptions of magic and magicians in China by travelling Western magi are those of H.S. Lynn (1863), Charles Bertram (1901), Howard Thurston (1906), L.H. Branson (early 1900s), and John Mulholland (c1926). Other early Western magicians in China include Arnould (1876).
n. Original but now obsolete term for the famous black-art Square Circle (see). [obsolete after 1947, formerly rare]
n. The Linking Rings (see) being the more usual synonym. [fairly common]
See: Ombres Chinoise. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Ombres Chinoise".)

(See also: Snowstorm in China.) n. Effect where torn bits of paper in water are formed into a sodden mass yet, when fanned, become instantly dry and flutter from the fingers like snow-flakes; Wintertime in China. [fairly common] First reported in Japanese conjuring books of the 1700s according to Christopher (1962, p.121). Performed in London in 1885 by Italian magician Yank Hoe (Clarke in Magic Wand [Mar 1928], 43). First exposed in 1910 by both Devant (pp.36-38, as "A New Drying Machine") and Hatton & Plate (p.223). Presented in Australia in 1913 by the magicienne with the "Japanese Village" troupe. Again exposed in 1914-15 by Ishi Black and in 1927 by Tarbell (Lesson 4, p.8), the latter calling it "Wintertime in China". Writing in 1922, Branson (pp.7-8) mentions having seen Chinese conjurors doing it. Used by Dai Vernon in his "Harlequin Act" in New York City in 1938 and carried over to his "Dai Yen" and "Dr. Chung" Chinese acts of the early 1940s. Later a pet trick of Fred Keating (in 1952), Stewart Judah (by 1955), Abb Dickson (by 1982), Peter Samelson (in 1984), and Sitta (1980s).

n. Effect where a cord or tassle connecting two (or lately three) wands is cut, yet when one end is pulled its severed half also rises; the Chinese Wands; the Mora Wands. [common] This very old trick is, despite its name, of European origin and is, in fact, not in the repertory of traditional Chinese conjurors. Originally called the Pillars of Solomon and later also the Hindu Wands. In its original version the faked sticks could not be fully separated; in its later modifications they can. The original method was first exposed in 1693 (by Ozanam; also 1740 Guyot; 1785 Decremps). This trick was also performed with bamboo sticks (with beads on the string instead of tassels) by Indian street magicians by 1917 (Elbiquet; also 1922 Branson). It was a pet trick of Silent Mora (by 1925), Fred Keating, John Booth (early 1930s), Roy Benson, and Fred Kaps.

(See also: Temple Screen.) n. A four-panelled screen (each panel 9x12-inches) cleverly hinged so they can always be convincingly shown as three. Used to produce small items. [common] "All those who can't do a decent Half Pass by March 30 will be sentenced to perform Grant's Temple Screen between strippers in a filthy nightclub in Oklahoma City for the rest of eternity." — Richard Kaufman in Genii (Dec 1987), 398

(See also: Chinese Sticks, The.) n. Effect where a cord or tassle connecting two (or lately three) wands is cut, yet when one end is pulled its severed half also rises; the Chinese Wands; the Mora Wands. [common] This very old trick is, despite its name, of European origin and is, in fact, not in the repertory of traditional Chinese conjurors. Originally called the Pillars of Solomon and later also the Hindu Wands. In its original version the faked sticks could not be fully separated; in its later modifications they can. The original method was first exposed in 1693 (by Ozanam; also 1740 Guyot; 1785 Decremps). This trick was also performed with bamboo sticks (with beads on the string instead of tassels) by Indian street magicians by 1917 (Elbiquet; also 1922 Branson). It was a pet trick of Silent Mora (by 1925), Fred Keating, John Booth (early 1930s), Roy Benson, and Fred Kaps.
See: Water Torture Cell. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Water Torture Cell".)

term: Ching Ling Foo Water Can; Ching Ling Foo Can
definition: n. The Foo Can (see) being the current synonym. [obsolete after 1982, formerly fairly common]

n. Effect where three or four cubes (dice, dominoes, or sugar cubes) travel mysteriously from place-to-place and hand-to-hand. [fairly common] Although the invention of this effect is generally credited to Max Malini, Holden claims that it had been published long before in an (unspecified) magic book. Holden is correct. The trick is fully described by Stanyon in Magic in 1912 as "The Travelling Sugar", using 4 lumps of sugar. Stanyon mentions that Lewis Davenport suggested to him the substitution of 4 dice. REF: Holden in Sphinx (1927), 90; Stanyon in Magic (May 1912), 61. Malini, using a 3-cube format, made it famous by 1927 when it was first marketed (without authorization) and under that title by Modern Magic. S. Leo Horowitz, on seeing Malini do it, reinvented the method and routined it in 4-cube format but promised to keep it secret during Malini's lifetime. First published by Horowitz in 1947. A pet effect of Al Goshman (using bottle caps) and Doug Henning (using small sea shells). REF: Horowitz (1947).
n. The variant of the Rice Bowls (see) that uses cylindrical jars. [rare]

n. A metal cup, magnetically faked, to use in a one-cup one-ball version of the Cups-and-Balls routine; a Chop Chop Cup, being the less usual synonym. [common] "Perhaps the primary reason for its continuing popularity is that the Chop Cup has a unique advantage over most other magic props: it combines the ability to utilize a mechanical principle with sleight of hand." — Mark Wilson (ghosted by Earl Wilson & Alan Wakeling), The Chop Cup Book (1979), v
n. The playing card selected from a deck by a volunteer; the selected card. [common]
n. A particular card force that takes place in the volunteer's hands; the 203rd Force. [rare]
n. Original title of Fred, which see. [rare]
See: Potsherd Trick. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Potsherd Trick".)
n. Acronym for "clubs, hearts, spades, diamonds" to indicate this specific sequence of the suits in a deck setup; CHaSeD being its mnemonic synonym. [very rare]
n. Conjuring with cigars. [rare to obsolete to reviving]
n. A metal cigarette case where the cigarettes act as a secret flap. [rare] The principal models are by Bert Allerton (using loose cigarettes) and Pat Conway (using a dummy row).

n. Popular pocket-magic effect where a cigarette is pushed through the center of a borrowed coin and smoked. [common] Requires a precision-made fake coin, which is switched for the borrowed one. Based on Dr Eugene Bulson's Pencil Thru a Nickle gimmick coin, which was made and first marketed by Brema in 1930. The cigarette version was introduced by American manufacturer-dealer Pressley Guitar, according to Waters (1988, p.158). A pet effect of Don Alan (in 1978) and David Copperfield (in mid-1980s).

n. A concealed mechanical device (dropper) specifically designed to gravity-feed cigarettes covertly into the magician's hand. It is a thin, metal box . [fairly common] 199 The first dropper for cigarettes was invented and built in 1902 by Frank Ducrot at the suggestion of Otto Hornmann. It was marketed in the USA as the "Hornmann Dropper" by 1910 and introduced into France in 1913. REF: Clark (1937).

n. Effect where a lit cigarette can be snuffed out in a handkerchief held in the fist after which the cigarette has vanished and the hank is undamaged.. [fairly common] The is the classic effect that uses the thumb tip.
See: Enchanted Cigarette Holder. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Enchanted Cigarette Holder".)

n. Conjuring with cigarettes. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common] The cigarette was invented by American Indians by wrapping tobacco in corn leaf, as noted in 1492 by Columbus. Pipe smoking—also an Amerindian invention—was introduced into England in 1585 and the modern cigarette (tobacco rolled in paper) was first made in Europe on the Continent in the 1700s on a roll-your-own basis and called "sigaritos" and "cigarritos". The word "cigarette" (literally little cigar) was coined in France and borrowed by Standard English in 1835 (Webster's 10th Collegiate). Commercially made cigarettes were first produced in France in 1843, in England in 1865, and in the USA in 1866. Commercial production quickly changed the cigarette from a luxury item to a mass-market one and hence the basis for cigarette tricks. Cigarette tricks were originated in the 1800s by sailors, circus clowns, and street jugglers. The first recorded stage routine was by a popular assistant clown in 1885 in Paris at the Nouveau Cirque. Another pioneer performer around the same time was the famous Parisian street juggler known as the "Zouave, Roi des Fumeurs". The earliest known magician to perform with cigarettes was Zirka, "Queen of the Cigarettes", who performed in France by 1905. She was the wife of Peruvian magician L'Homme Masqué (José Antenor de Gayo). The first all-cigarette act was introduced by the Spaniard, José Florences Gili ("Señor Florenze" and "Florence"), in Europe, South America, and the United States where he arrived in 1914 (according to Christopher [1973] although Hilliard [1938] makes it in 1918). Another Spaniard, "Frakson" (José Jiminez Seville), introduced his act in South America before 1914, toured Western Europe during World War I, and New York City in 1926. The Spaniard, Fran-Klint, took his spectacular act to France (in 1916), England (1922, 1925), and Australia (1924, 1926). The Welshman, "Cardini" (Richard Valentine Pitchford), brought his act to New York City in 1926, simultaneously with Frakson. Japanese sleight-of-hand man Tenkai, during an extended stay in America, developed his fine cigarette production act in 1929. A pet effect of Frenchman Keith Clark (from 1931), Russian-American Paul Duke (from 1935), the German Fredo Marvelli (by 1937), American Art Lyle, American Sam Berland, and Briton David Berglas (1960s). A full cigarette- manipulation routine was a standard part of the post-WW II Chavez Course in magic. Regrettably fallen in popular favor due to the current wide-spread aversion to cigarettes, although used through the 1980s by Lance Burton, Haruo Shimada, Tom Mullica, and Rocco. REF: Clark (1937).
n. A magician who specializes in cigarette manipulation. [obsolete, formerly rare]

n. Effect where the magician mimes rolling a cigarette and placing it at his lips, yet when he takes a match from a matchbox and lights it, a real and smoking cigarette appears; the Phantom Cigarette. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]
n. A cigarette vanisher (see) being the more usual synonym. [fairly common]
n. An elastic-activated pull specifically designed to vanish cigarettes; cigarette pull. [common]
See: Bill in Cigarette. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Bill in Cigarette".)

n. Abbreviation of The Magic Circle, the most prestigious British magic club. [fairly common] The Magic Circle was founded in 1905 in London by Neil Weaver, Herbert J. Collings, and Ernest K. Adams with 23 magicians including David Devant as its first president. Its membership, which grew to 250 by 1907 and 1,500 by 1979, and was limited to males over 18 until 1991 when women were admitted. Since it began publication in 1906, the official members-only journal has been The Magic Circular. REF: Dexter (1956), 51-62; Dif #2 (1971- 74), 407-410; Lamb (1979), 96; Severn (1979), 151-152, 231-233. "In recent years the Circle has been the object of some controversy due to its refusal to admit women as members—a policy which has been a source of embarrassment to many people both within the Circle and in the larger British magic community." — T. A. Waters, The Encyclopedia of Magic and Magicians (1988), 215 201 "As Paul [Daniels] told me face to face: ‘List me six real potential T.V. star magicians within The Circle and I'll listen to you.' I am afraid I had to be silent." — Ian Adair in Trixigram (Nov 1988), 23

(See also: Squaring the Circle (1).) 1.n. Effect where a metal hoop held at the magician's fingertips instantly becomes square; the Circle to Square. Not to be confused with the Square Circle production box. [fairly common]

n. The magicians simulation of supernatural hearing. [very rare] Originally the argot of psychics by 1864 Brevoir as cited in the OED/2; 1891 A. Medium; 1921 Alexander. Literally means "clear hearing". Thence magicians jargon by 1946 S.H. Sharpe; 1959 Corinda.

n. The magicians simulation of second sight. [fairly common] Originally a French word, clairvoyance, meaning literally "clear vision". Borrowed and adapted to mean having occult vision as the argot of English-speaking psychics by 1847 as cited in the OED/2; 1891 A. Medium; 1901 Sylvestre cat; 1921 Alexander; 1976 Keene. Thence (?) adapted as magicians jargon as early as 1846 Eagle, Ashby playbill; 1848 Compars Herrmann, Aug 21st London program; 1854 Anderson, Leeds playbill; 1855 Wyman; 1876 Hoffmann; 1877 Lynn; 1880 Vere; 1886 Peck & Snyder cat; 1898 Houdini cat; 1905 Bodie; 1909 Hilliard; 1928 Clarke in Magic Wand; 1935 Annemann; 1948 Kaplan; 1950 Boardé; 1972 Tan Hock Chuan in Swami; 1976 Goldstein; 1979 Lamb; 1980 Tannen cat #13; 1983 Cassidy; 1984 Albrecht cartoon in Epoptica YB; 1988 Waters; 1989 Müller card file; 1990 Wedler; 1992 Randi; 1994 Earle in MUM.;1997 Waldman. NOTE: Parapsychologists now term clairvoyance "remote viewing" by 1984 (Booth).
n. A magician or his assistant who simulates second sight. [rare]
See: classic palm. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "classic palm".)
n. The two-handed pass (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare]

a. Classic being the more recent and more usual adjectival synonym, although some nitpicking linguistic purists would insist on preserving the older form, "classical". [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]
n. The cut force (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare]
n. A type of break-away box. [fairly common]

(See also: Smoke Trick (3).) 1.n. The effect where smoke is generated inside an upside-down tumbler (or other sealed container) or two tumblers placed rim-to-rim. [rare] The method of this standard effect of chemical magic involves secretly mixing ammonia with hydrochloric ("muriatic") acid. Described in a magic book as early as 1872 in Cremer's Hanky Panky under the title "How to Introduce Cigar Smoke into an Air-tight Vase". A pet effect of 847 Chung Ling Soo.
n. Stage effect where a large but very light-weight replica of London's famous Egyptian monument disgorges two heavy assistants. [archaic]

n. A coin sleight that retains coins in one hand while seeming to drop them into the open palm of the other; the Downs click pass and the Clink Pass being less usual synonyms. [fairly common] This sleight was invented by T. Nelson Downs and first described by him in 1900 (Hilliar/Downs). The deception is caused by the loud clinking sound made, as if the coins had really fallen into the other hand. Used in working several coin-passe tricks including Coins to Glass and Coins through the Table.

n. A regular plaid egg bag with a built-in fabric chicken for the final ("climax") production; the Comedy Egg Bag being the less usual synonym. [fairly common] First marketed by 1944 by U.F. Grant as "Menge's Climax Egg Bag", which implies that the inventor was R.N. Menge, Grant's partner in their magic shop in Columbus, Ohio, during World War II. However Grant may have played a contributing part in its invention, as by 1931 he had already made a chicken-shaped standard egg bag for Eddie Welch to use in his kid shows.
n. Effect where a borrowed finger-ring encircling the base of a vertically-held rod (wand or pencil) 206 slowly rises and pops off. [rare]

n. A workshop of instruction and criticism, particularly at magic conventions. [rare] Founded as the Open House in 1939 by the New York Assembly of the Society of American Magicians (S.A.M.). The title was soon changed to The Clinic and the concept spread in the early 1940s, the term becoming generic. REF: Elliott in Phoenix (1944), 271; Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (1944), 50, and (1953), 68.
1.n. A wire-metal holder that pinch-grasps a coin, card, or other small object. One specific type is the Excelsior clip, another is the ball clip. [common]
n. Later alternate commercial name for Clippo (see), which is the most usual synonym. [rare]
n. Effect where two (or more) paper clips link when clipped to a lengthways-folded slip of paper that is then pulled open. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]
n. Later alternate commercial name for Clippo (see). [rare]

n. Effect where the dial moves on a clock-face without apparent mechanism, stopping at a pre- selected number; the Cabalistic Clock (obsolete); Obedient Clock (obsolete). [rare] This effect was performed as early as 1777 by Breslaw when he called it the "Magic Clock". Also performed in 1806 by De Philipsthal (program) and in 1816 by Gyngell Sr (poster). These original models were animated by concealed thread pulled from offstage, as exposed as early as 1791 by Eckartshausen. On 3 Jul 1845 French clockmaker-magician Robert-Houdin premiered his "La Pendule Cabalistique". As we now know from an original in the possession of French magic dealer Jean Caroly, this model (or, at least, a later modification by Robert- Houdin) was activated by electricity. Hofzinser invented a version controlled by a movable weight. Later a pet effect of Robert Heller (1851), De Biere, Fred Keating (1930), and Cecil Lyle. Seldom performed today. REF: Sharpe (1983), 159, 166-172; Frost (1876), 130; Houdini (1908); Sardina (1950), 57-58; Fischer (1942/1985 tr), 165-166.
n. Method for reading marked cards printed with a circular pattern marked on its circumference to be read clock-wise. [rare]
n. Any card trick with a layout corresponding to a 12-hour clock-face. [rare]

a. Said of magic performed close-up. 209 [fairly common in Britain] Originally a military term since 1809 meaning in immediate proximity. Thence magicians jargon by 1903 Stanyon ad in Magic, 14, as "deceptive at close quarters"; 1906 Selbit, 4, as "close- quarter work"; 1907 Keene as "at close quarters"; 1912 Goldston as "to perform ... at very close quarters"; 1920 Waller as a "close quarter program"; 1925 G. Johnson as "close quarter work"; 1932 Thayer cat #7S as "practical for close quarters"; 1939 J. Ramsay in Jinx as "performed at close quarters"; 1944 Parrish as "a very close-quarter trick"; 1945 J. Brearley as a "close-quarter trick"; 1950 Hugard in HMM as “standing around at close quarters”; 1952 G. Armstrong as a "close-quarter card trick"; 1976 Gill as "close-quarter magic" and "items for close-quarters"; 1987 Griffiths in Supreme cat as "close-quarter magic".

a. Adjectivally usually hyphenated or as one word, closeup, as in close-up case, close-up magic, close-up pad, etc., all suggesting the intimacy of the setting. [very common] "A close-up show should always appear impromptu." — Ian Adair, Conjuring as a Craft (1970)
n. A complete act of close-up magic. [fairly common]

n. Any hand-held box (such as an attaché case or small valise) fitted with compartments in which the peripatetic close-up magician can carry all his apparatus; a prop case. [fairly common] The earliest reported example was Scottish magician Victor Farelli’s “’Body-Load’ Box”, which he’d invented and used for many years before retiring from the stage in 1939. His hinged-top 16"x10"x5" attaché case was fitted with 9 compartments holding enough props for 30 effects plus a make-up box and some toilet articles. REF: Farelli in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jul 1952), 957. The invention (probably an independent reinvention) of this convenience is attributed to Dai 210 Vernon, the much travelled Canadian close-up worker, by British magician Lewis Ganson, who recalled six years later that when Vernon first visited England in 1955, the local magi were almost as impressed to see such a handy device as they were by the magic the legendary Canadian produced from it. REF: Ganson (1961), 21. May have had its origin in the Suitcase Table, which had at least three makers by 1928. REF: Thayer cat #7 (1928), 237. "I find that a Gag Bag makes an excellent close-up case. It will hold cards, coins, etc. very nicely. There is something about having the bag you carried your props in magically changing into five different colors at the end of your act that really impresses an audience." — Rick Ross in The Linking Ring (May 1987), 72

n. A conjuror who specializes in performing close-up magic; a close-up worker; a close-upper (2). [fairly common] "Few close-up magicians in the world have not at one time or another made use of the magic that [Dai] Vernon created." — Bill Severn, Guide to Magic as a Hobby (1979), 139
n. A close-up pad (see) being the original and still more usual synonym. [fairly common]

n. A looking-glass (usually and ideally of the 3-panel folding type) used by a close-up magician to practice moves in front of. [rare] "The best mode of judging one's success in this particular [palming] is to practice before a looking-glass." — Robert-Houdin, The Secrets of Conjuring and Magic (1868/1877 tr by Hoffmann), 48 "The only proper way to practice [sleights] is to be seated in the usual manner at a card table with a looking glass opposite; and much time and labor are saved by this plan. The correct positions and movements can be accurately secured, and the performer becomes his own critic." — S. W. Erdnase, Artifice Ruse and Subterfuge at the Card Table (1902), 24 "A few trials before the looking-glass will determine the exact amount of speed to use in riffling the cards." — J. Northern Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909), Chapter III "The beginner should practice in front of a mirror, first actually placing the card in the left hand, then imitating the natural action as near as possible ... while retaining the card in the right hand." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (Oct 1919), 4 "Practice before a mirror is a good way to learn sleight-of-hand." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Mar 1955), 260 The idea of using a mirror to practice sleight-of-hand was, as Busby pointed out, first published by French master Robert-Houdin in 1868, specifically for palming. He was followed in English 212 by Sachs (1877), 74, for the Fan Force; Hoffmann (1889), 99-100; and Stanyon (1898), 2. Erdnase's advice of 1902 was directed to both card sharps and sleight-of-hand magicians. Two years after Erdnase, American card sharp Frank Bonville also recommended the use of a mirror for practice in his The Little Secrets (1904). REF: Busby in Whaley (1991), 162-163, 402n42; Ortiz (1991), 48

n. A mat used by performers of close-up magic to give a proper surface for working cards, coins, etc.; a close-up mat being the later and still less usual synonym. [common] Made of thick cloth or felt approximately 12x16 inches oblong and usually rubber-backed to prevent sliding on the table. The forerunner was a simple carpet placed on a table, as first recommended in 1634 by Hocus Pocus Junior in his The Anatomie of Legerdemain for working the Cups-and-Balls thusly: "He that is to play must sit on the farther side of a Table, which must be covered with a carpet: partly to keepe the [cork] balls from rolling away, and partly to keepe them from ratling ...." The earliest known specifically designed model was the travelling tray covered in green baize with a low rim used by American card sharp and amateur magician "Erdnase" (Milton Franklin Andrews) in his travels and illustrated in his Artifice Ruse and Subterfuge at the Card Table (1902). American close-up magician Dr Sidney Ross was reported to have been using a close-up pad in the 1930s and early 1940s. Dr Stanley Jaks used a jewelers velveteen display mat. Both Don Alan and Ross Bertram were using soft cloth mats in the early 1950s. In 1963 Laurie Ireland's magic shop was the first to market one. But it was Lewis Ganson's published recommendation in 1966 of using a portable felt pad that made it popular. REF: Busby in Whaley (1991), 162; Bertram (1983); Ganson, I [1966], 23.
n. Any small table used for close-up magic. [fairly common]
See: close-up effect.. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "close-up effect.".)
n. Close-up magic; close work (obsolete). [common]

n. A magician specializing in close-up magic. 213 [fairly common] "The good close-up worker will always be versatile and be able to perform under almost any conditions." — John Mendoza, Close-Up Presentation (1979), 53
1.n. A close-up effect. [rare]
n. Now called close-up work (see). [obsolete since 1959, formerly fairly common]

n. The concluding trick in an act; the close; the closing. Opposite of the opener. Pronounced CLO-zer. [fairly common] “The most important trick in a vaudeville performer’s routine is his closer. ... The second most important feat is the opener.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Oct 1953), 50 214
n. A closer being the most usual synonym. [rare]
n. Comedy conjuring as performed by a magic clown. [very rare]

(See also: magic clown.) n. A clown-magician; a clown whose act includes conjuring. [fairly common] Among the better known magic clowns in the USA have been "Zovello" (Sam Wishner, since 556 1940s), Hal Griffin (in 1950s), "Paolo" (Paul Klingler), Ernie Kerns, and "Rebo" (Bev Bergeron, 1958-65).
n. Conjuring performed in a cabaret or club; club magic; club show; cabaret act [Brit.]; cabaret magic [mainly Brit.]. [fairly common]

n. A booking for a single performance at a club, banquet, lodge meeting, etc. [fairly common] "Club date is an all-encompassing term. On a club date you can entertain fifty women at a banquest, a thousand bankers assembled in convention, an insurance company's Christmas celebration, or a dozen people in a private apartment." — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Aug 1953), 29
(See also: club worker.) n. A magician who performs in a cabaret or public nightclub; a club magician. [rare]
n. Club magic (see) being the more usual modern synonym. [rare]
n. A magician who performs in a cabaret or public nightclub; a club magician. [rare]

n. A specific magic word. [obsolescent since around 1808] This was the magic word favored by British poet and amateur magician Dr. Oliver Goldsmith in 1767. Also used by the British conjuror, Ray, in performing before King George III and Queen Charlotte (married 1761) until sometime soon after 1808 when a comedian gave "cocolorum" as one of Ingleby's magic words. REF: Dawes (1979), 136; Frost (1881); Clarke in Magic Wand (1925), 135. Used in patter as recently as 1950 by Jean Hugard who, however, as a magic history buff, was probably only honoring the term. "Then he utterred the magic words 'HOCUS POCUS, HI COCKALORUM CROKUS' and there was the rope all in one piece and free from knots." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jun 1950), 669 Two sources for this strange word have been suggested. It may be from the Flemish kockeloeren meaning to crow or cockcadoodaloo. Or, more likely, from Cock Lorel, the name of the fictitious British sailor-vagabond in the time of Henry VIII (reigned 1491-1547). In either case, the proper name first appeared in print around 1515 in the poem Cocke Lorelles Bote [Cock Lorel's Boat]; and "cockalorum" entered Standard English by around 1715 in the sense of a self- important or boastful person. REF: OED/2; Arthur F. Kinney, Rogues, Vagabonds, & Sturdy Beggars (1973), 312n36; Thombury, Shakespeare's England (1856).

n. The deliberate comic failure or exposé of a trick or tricks by the magician; burlesque magic (U.S.). [fairly common in Britain] Originally British circus cant by the 1940s, from the British slang term "cod" meaning (by 1873) a fool. REF: Andrews (1971); OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1971 Andrews; 1988 Adair in Supreme Newsletter; 1988 Waters as "primarily" British; 1988 Ogden in Genii; 1989 Kennaugh in Magigram. NOTE: Also "cod props" in 1907 Stout ad in Magic, 80. And as "’cod' apparatus" in 1936 K. Thomas in Devant; a "cod magician" in 1971 Andrews; 1997 Hudd; "’cod' effects" in 1983 P.Warlock in Magic Circular; "the cod rabbit routine" in 1987 E. Warlock in LR; a "cod act" in 1988 Adair in Trixigram; "cod magic acts" in 1997 E. Warlock in LR; and “‘cod’

n. Effect where two (or three) large metal containers (goblets or cocktail shakers) are shown empty, filled with brown and white (or blue) paper shavings respectively, and then proven to be hot coffee and milk (and sugar) respectively. [archaic, once fairly common] Introduced (and reportedly invented) by Kellar before 1876 as one of his pet effects. Used a switch of duplicate set of containers. The apparatus was called the Coffee Vase. Thence widely copied for awhile, particularly by Robert Heller (by 1878, billing the trick as "Mocha"), Imro Fox (by 1902), Chung Ling Soo, and Amasis (by 1910). REF: Gibson (1966), 94-96; Waller (1964/1980), 59; Moulton (1919/1983), 90; 1909 Stanyon in Magic, 41.
n. The apparatus used to do the Coffee and Milk trick. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]

n. A rolled-up band of narrow paper (or mylar). Comes in three sizes ranging from the small mouth coil through the hat coil to the large tambourine coil. If cast as a streamer into the audience it is called a throw-out coil. [common]
n. A complete performance of coin magic. [fairly common]

n. Effect where a coin is vanished to later reappear inside a narrow-necked bottle. [fairly common] First described and marketed in 1873 in the Hartz catalog (p.72). That original and still usual method uses a folding coin. Later, gaffed bottles were also used to baffle the know-all.

n. A small round metal container to exchange (change) coins. [common] The major types, all commercially available, are the Boston Box, German Box, Okito Box, and O-Korto Box. A rarer variant is the Brema Box. First described in 1634 in Hocus Pocus Junior's The Anatomie of Legerdemain.
1.n. A coin pail being the more usual synonym.
n. A hand gimmick (catcher) that brings coins to the fingertips without using sleights. [fairly common]

n. A concealed mechanical device (dropper) specifically designed to gravity-feed coins covertly into the magician's hand (or directly into a hat or pail). One type is the Kellar Coin Catcher. [fairly common]

n. A method of folding a coin up in a square piece of paper in such a way that it falls secretly into the palm. Compare handkerchief fold, which uses a silk. [fairly common] "If you do not know how to make a coin fold, you should not be reading this book." — Eric C. Lewis, A Continuation of Miracles (1980), 209

n. A kerchief faked with a coin sewn into one corner. [very rare] This gimmick was first exposed in 1584 by both Prevost and Scot. Then in 1585 Napolitana, 1612 Rid, 1634 Hocus Pocus Junior, and 1668 White.
n. A holder for one or more coins that permits them to be released one at a time. [rare]
n. A tall stand that enables the coins to fall (tumble?) slowly and noisily. 220 [fairly common]
n. Effect where a marked coin appears inside a transparent cigarette lighter. [rare]

n. Conjuring with metal coins; numismagic. [common] Coins first entered circulation in the eighth century BC in both West and East. And while it is likely that they were manipulated by cheats and conjurors from early time, the first documented use of sleights with coins is in 1584 in Reginald Scot's Discouerie of Witchcraft. "It seems like every coin worker has at least one version of 'Coins Across,' a classic of coin magic." — Peg Shickler in M-U-M (Oct 1997), 34

n. A magician who specializes in close-up coin magic. Compare coin manipulator. [fairly common] Notable examples are Nelson Downs, Mercedes Talma, Nate Leipzig, Allan Shaw, Welsh Miller, Nate Leipzig, Milt Kort, J.B. Bobo, and David Roth.

n. A sleight-of-hand performance with metal coins; coin work. 221 [fairly common] “Zalma [Talma], very beautiful and charming, did coin manipulations which I couldn’t see in the third row!” — Charles Miller, letter to Goshman in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Apr 1956), 417
n. A magician who specializes in coin manipulation. Compare coin man. [fairly common] Notable examples include Nelson Downs, Mercedes Talma, Houdini, Allan Shaw, Manuel, Al Flosso, and Ross Bertram.
n. A metal "champagne" bucket (usually but not necessarily gaffed) to noisily receive coins produced during a Miser's Dream routine; a coin bucket (1). [common]
n. The Cabala effect and method but with a coin rather than a steel ball. [rare]
n. The flourish that rotates a coin edge-over-edge across the upturned knuckles of a hand and, then, back again; the Steeplechase. [fairly common]

1.n. A flat tube-like coin dropper through which a coin can be gravity-fed into the magician's hand or into an apparently impenetrable object (such as a Nest of Boxes or the Ball of Wool). A money slide (obsolete). [fairly common] Exposed in 1876 Hoffmann, 198, 207; 1877 Sachs.

n. A rack (easel) to display coins to the spectators; a coin easel (obsolete). Usually gaffed. [rare] “Magicians who use tables should have their tricks built in the table top. ... Built in coin stands would have no suspiciously thick bases.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jul 1947), 332

n. A wand mechanically faked to produce a folding coin from its tip by activation of a stud; a money wand (obsolete).. [common] Used in performance as early as 12 Mar 1872 by American magicienne Madame Cora de Lamond at the Masonic Hall, Dunedin, New Zealand. First described and marketed in 1873 in the Hartz catalog (p.70). First exposed in 1876 by Hoffmann (p.203) when called the "Half- crown Wand" (also 1885 Sachs 2nd ed). Later models can be loaded with as many as five folding coins. REF: F. Marshall (1984), 12-13.
n. Magic with coins, particularly by sleight-of-hand. [fairly common]

n. Classic effect where four coins pass invisibly from hand to hand; Flying Eagles (obsolete). [fairly common] "Perhaps the most popular of all coin routines to perform on the street is the classic Coins Across." — Michael Rubinstein, Inside Street Magic (1985), 11 "It seems like every coin worker has at least one version of 'Coins Across,' a classic of coin magic." — Peg Shickler in M-U-M (Oct 1997), 34

term: Coins to Glass; Coins into the Glass
definition: n. The effect where several coins held in one hand visibly and noisily arrive in a transparent tumbler held in the other hand. Compare Visible Coins in Glass for a later apparatus version of this effect. [very rare] This effect was invented by T. Nelson Downs (using his click pass sleight) and first exposed by him in 1909.
n. Effect where several coins successively vanish from one hand, seemingly pass up the sleeve (or so the audience is told), to audibly drop, one by one, into the opposite trouser pocket. [rare]

n. A prepared deck or mechanical deck that is secretly substituted for a genuine deck of playing cards during a performance; a cooler. [fairly common] "The 'Cold Deck' is a pre-arranged pack that is introduced at an opportune moment. ... The name is probably derived from the fact that the deck must await its opportunity long enough to contract a chill in the interim." — S. W. Erdnase, Artifice Ruse and Subterfuge at the Card Table (1902), 18 Originally and until recently the argot of American card sharps by 1857(San Francisco Call of Apr 3rd as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1857 Green; 1865 Evans; 1887 Devol; 1890 Quinn; 1894 Koschitz; 1902 Erdnase; 1904 Bonville; 1915 Innis; 1924 Henderson; 1927 Gibson; 1931 Smith; 1933 Cameron; 1949 Scarne; 1950 Moss; 1962 Garcia; 1970 L. Miller; 1973 Lampkin; 1976 F. Thompson; 1984 Ortiz. More recently also called by sharpers a "cooler" (by 1915 to the present). Both terms reflect the fact that such a freshly introduced deck will feel perceptibly colder, at least according to Merlin (1927), Scarne (1961), Garcia (1962), and Lampkin (1973). The most recent sharpers term is a "package" by 1984 (Ortiz). Thence magicians jargon as cold deck by 1927 Merlin; 1936 G. Johnson in Devant; 1943 Hugard in letter to Braue; 1946 Buckley; 1949 Turner; 1950 Fabian in Abra; 1952 Fries in HMM as "exchanging the pack in use for the set-up or 'cold' deck'"; 1975 Pierre; 1978 Müller; 1980 Gardner; 1987 Lyons annotation; 1990 Wedler; 1992 Randi (with a

n. The act of introducing a secretly stacked deck into the trick; switching in a cold deck. [rare] Originally the argot of American card sharps by 1894 Koschitz; 1909 Irwin; 1915 Innis; 1921 Herrmann Magical Co cat; 1931 Smith; 1933 Cameron as "cold-decking";; 1973 Lampkin. They also called it "coming the change" in 1876 (Cremer, 99). Thence magicians jargon by 1935 Annemann in Jinx #6; 1953 Elliott in Phoenix #294; 1957 Rusduck; 1981 Busby in Arcane #3; 1984 Martin Nash orally; 1985 Welles on Merv Griffin Show; 1991 Vicki Busby orally.
v. To give a cold reading. [rare]
n. A cold reading. 226 [very rare but not nonce]
n. A mentalist or pseudo-psychic who performs cold readings. [rare]

n. Giving accurate details of a spectator's past, present, or future solely on the basis of visual observation. Compare fishing, pumping, which can be used as supplementary techniques. [fairly common] "At first I used what are called 'cold readings' .... A typical cold reading is to say that you have a scar on your knee. Everybody has a scar on their knee, because everybody fell down as a child. Another one is to say that a big change took place in your attitude between the ages of 12 and 14." — Orson Welles, 1966 interview in Playboy (May 1967), 58 "Cold reading is the purest form of mentalism." — Jeff Busby in Thaumaturgist, No.31 (May/Jul 1996), 6 This notably effective technique originated with fraudulent mediums, although it was in a very real sense tipped to the lay public by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle in his accounts of the instant face- to-face deductions of Sherlock Holmes, which Doyle began publishing in 1887. REF: Ray Hyman, "'Cold Reading': How to Convince Strangers That You Know All About Them', The Zetetic, Vol.1, No.2 (Spring/Summer 1977),18-37. Originally the argot of psychic mediums by 1924 (Houdini; 1946 Welles in Variety; 1953 Gresham; 1977 Hyman) from the fact that the client walks in "cold" — previously unknown to the medium or fortune-teller. Thence borrowed as jargon among mentalist-magicians by 1947 Boardé; 1950 Plato in Coven; 1951 Nelson; 1952 Zolotow; 1956 P. Marcus in Mental-Wise; 1959 Corinda; 1971 Nelson; 1974 Minch; 1975 Dalal in Mantra; 1976 Goldstein; 1976 Shiels; 1979 Fulves; 1981 Ray-Mond; 1983 Ruthchild in New Invocation; 1984 Saville & Dewey; 1985 Webster; 1986 Albrecht cartoon in Busby Magic Inc. Xmas card; 1992 Randi; 1993 Abbott cat #24; 1995 Earle in MUM; 2001 Brad Henderson letter to Whaley; 2004 Hyman orally.

n. A hobbyist who systematically accumulates magicana, that is magical artifacts or memorabilia such as books, posters, props, bookplates, or autographs. [fairly common] "Savren was the first great English collector of magicana and magicians are quite in his debt for saving the historical mementos and passing them down to the present generation." — Price (1985), 194, referring to James Savren (ca1824-1891), an English barber and part- time magician "Until a very few years ago, the collectors of magical literature could be counted on the fingers of one hand. ... Today, collectors are becoming legion ...." — H. Adrian Smith in Tops (Aug 1936). The collecting of magic began with such performers as Robert-Houdin (died 1871) and Hofzinser (died 1875) who accumulated much apparatus during the course of their careers, items that were passed along to others after their death or retirement. The first major collector of magicians posters and playbills was James Savren (died 1891). His collection passed to Henry Evanion. 227 The earliest major book collector of was Hardin J. Burlingame. His strong collection of magic books & scrapbooks (begun in 1872 & seriously since 1895) passed to Dr A.M. Wilson in 1918. Now in the Byron Walker Collection, making this latter the world's oldest, largest, and best private collection. The next major book collection was begun by William E. Robinson (until he sold to Dr. Saram R. Ellison). Then Ellison (with 600 titles in 1902 and 2,000 in 1908 when he sold to Dr. Samuel C. Hooker). In 1936 Hooker gave his augmented collection to the New York Public Library where it remains. The largest collection of conjuring periodicals (exclusively English-language ones) is that of George L. Daily. Begun in 1972, it has been the world's largest magic magazine collection since 1978. By 1989 it comprised over 1,100 titles with some 45,000 issues. GEN REF: Severn (1979), 173-196.

n. Effect where spectators cut deck three times to select cards, magician sets aside four Kings, places the three chosen cards in the deck, yet discovers them sandwiched in the separate packet of Kings. [fairly common] This sandwich effect was invented by Roy Walton and first published by him in 1969 in Abracadabra. Ed Marlow helped popularize it after 1969 when he published his first of many variants in Heirophant #2. REF: Racherbaumer in Linking Ring (Nov 1994), 95.

n. The effect of visibly transforming one small hand-held object (such as a card, silk, ball, or thimble) into another; a transformation (1). [common] The method used is called a switch. The term color change, which began by describing a literal change of color, has evolved into a partial misnomer because it became extended to include changes of suit or value of cards as well as of their color. This term was inspired (but not coined) as jargon by David Devant with his pretty effect (premiered in 1893) of passing a colored handkerchief through a large dye tube to have it emerge a different color.
n. A walking stick that visibly changes color in the magicians hands. [rare] A multiple award-winner invented by Fantasio.

term: Color Changing Shoelaces; Color Changing Shoe Lace
definition: n. Effect where a shoelace changes color in the magician's hands. [fairly common]
n. The Color Changing Handkerchief (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare]
n. A Three-Card Monte routine using specially printed playing cards (2 red diamonds, blue 231 diamond, and a "$14" gag card. [fairly common]
n. Effect where the magician divines which of six colors has been selected by a volunteer placing one colored side of a cube upright in a sealed square box. [common]
See: Sands of the Desert. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Sands of the Desert".)

n. Apparatus based on the old Flick Book principle where a bound volume can be flipped through to show its pages successively blank, in black-&-white, in full color, and, finally, blank again. Compare the Stamp Album. [rare]
(See also: Scrawny Chicken.) n. Comedy prop in the form of an emaciated rubber (or sometimes cloth) chicken, usually used as a production item. [rare]

(See also: Climax Egg Bag.) n. A regular plaid egg bag with a built-in fabric chicken for the final ("climax") production; the Comedy Egg Bag being the less usual synonym. [fairly common] First marketed by 1944 by U.F. Grant as "Menge's Climax Egg Bag", which implies that the inventor was R.N. Menge, Grant's partner in their magic shop in Columbus, Ohio, during World War II. However Grant may have played a contributing part in its invention, as by 1931 he had already made a chicken-shaped standard egg bag for Eddie Welch to use in his kid shows.

n. Conjuring performed with a comedic plot or patter; magicomedy. Compare burlesque magic. [common] "Most comedy magic is a spoof of the art, doing a trick badly or exposing it at the end." 232 — John Carney in The Linking Ring (Sep 1986), 61 "Comedy born of bewilderment is the only comedy that should be in magic." — Dai Vernon as quoted in D. Bamberg (1988), 253 "If you do comedy magic, remember that you must still have some real foolers to gain the respect of the audience." — Bev Bergeron in Severn (1979), 48
n. This apparatus is an electric lightbulb faked with built-in battery to enable it to light up in the magician's hand. [rare]
n. That more-or-less brief period during a trick when the magician is clean, that is, free of incriminating evidence. 233 [rare]
a. Said of magical effects, tricks, routines, or acts that appeal to paying spectators. Never used in its common Standard English pejorative sense. [common]

n. Two or more volunteers who, acting as a surrogate for the entire audience, join the magician on stage to check the apparatus for trickery, observe the magus at close quarters, and/or assist him in a trick. [fairly common]

1.n. The audience. [obsolescent after 1885, formerly common] Originally theatrical lingo meaning the audience. Thence magicians jargon from as early as 1721 Neve; 1763 Dean; 1763 Palatine herald; 1787 English Hussar program; 1795 Boaz poster; 1800 Gale; 1801 Magony program; 1805 Pinchbeck; 1809 Arbuckle, Vauxhall playbill; 1815 Ingleby; 1829 Boy’s Own Book; 1838 Parlour Magic; 1842 Charles Dickens Dec 3rd letter to Prof. Felton as "conjuring the company's watches into impossible tea caddies"; 1843 Crambrook; 1857 Magician's Own Book; 1861 Novra cat as "the laughter of the entire company"; 1876 Hoffmann; 1876 Cremer as "puzzle the company"; until 1885 (Sachs) around which time it was generally superseded by audience. Subsequent rare citations of company are 1902 Erdnase/Harto; 1909 Hilliard; 1919 Jordan as "to the company's wonder"; 1920 Stanyon in Magic as "Pack may be examined and shuffled by company."; 1949 Turner; 1950 Jonson;
n. Title of address of any member of the Society of American Magicians (S.A.M.). [rare]

n. Use of a confederate. [obsolescent after 1875, formerly common] "Reader, I Have promised you to write something of Confederacy, that when you see or hear some Fancy done you shall be no Stranger to it, but know how to do it as well as any Jugler in England, for by Confederacy mighty Wonders are wrought, which seem incredible and impossible." — H. Dean, The whole Art of Legerdemain (6th ed, 1763), 60 Roger Bacon applied the word in the early 1300s to conjuring. Also Reginald Scot in 1584 as "confederacie", Rid in 1612, Hocus Pocus Junior in 1634 as "Confederacie" & "Confederacy", and Neve in 1721. Mr. Highman Palatine, a major conjuror in England, advertised in 1763 that he "does not exhibit by the Help of Confederacy, as a late Performer in this City did." Later citations are 1763 (Dean), 1800 (Gale 3rd ed), 1829 (Boy’s Own Book), and 1857 (Magician's Own Book). Continued in common usage until 1875 (Hoffmann). Thence increasingly rare, as in 1897 (Hercat), 1903 (Stanyon in Magic), 1928 (Blyth), 1932 (Thayer cat #7S), 1940 (Hugard), 1944 (W. Larsen), 1944 (Fitzkee), 1945 (Nicholson in Thompson), 1945 (Hugard in HMM), 1959 (Elliott), 1956 (Dexter), 1981 (Fulves), and 1988 (Waters, 84).

n. A magician's secret assistant who poses as an audience volunteer; a stooge; a plant (2); a horse (in a hypnotic act). [common] "I do not unreservedly condemn the use of confederates when one is essential to put in action certain mechanism which the conjurer is unable to operate himself and which is indispensable to the execution of the trick, as, for example, to pull a thread when the occasion arises, to turn a handle, or to pass an object secretly into the conjurer's hands." — J. N. Ponsin, Ponsin on Conjuring (1853/1937 tr), 33 "I cannot suppose that any conjurer would for one moment dream of employing confederates among the audience. This sort of joint hoax has now gone quite out of fashion." — Robert-Houdin, The Secrets of Conjuring and Magic (1868/1877 tr), 35 "It is unfortunately true that even to this day some performers still stoop to the use of confederates, and this is especially true with regard to so-called mind-readers and escape artists." — Jean Hugard, Houdini's "Unmasking": Fact vs. Fiction (1957), 19 "Any Union General of the Civil War called for by the audience. No Confederates." — Al Baker describing his Spirit Pictures, as quoted in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1948), 452 “Don’t use confederates unless you want to run the risk of getting caught later with your plants down.” — Jim Thompson in The Linking Ring (Jan 1951) "The show [Kalanag's] is loaded with stooges. There were so many of them—I counted seven I was sure of—that I was beginning to believe maybe the guy does carry a company of eighty— sixty of them confederates." — Robert Lund in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Sep 1957), 65 Originally Standard English by 1548. REF: OED/2. First applied to conjuring as jargon in 1584 by Reginald Scot. Thence 1612 Rid; 1655 Ady; 1668 White; 1721 Neve; 1763 Dean 6th ed; 1800 Gale 3rd ed; 1815 Ingleby; 1829 Boy’s Own Book; 1857 Magician's Own Book; 1897 Hercat; 1906 Houdini in CMM; 1913 Stanyon in Magic; 1924 Heaney cat #25; 1929 Gibson; 1934 Read; 1944 W. Larsen; 1945 236 Hugard in HMM; 1957 Maréchal; 1976 Goldstein; 1979 Lamb; 1979 Fulves; 1980 J. Marshall; 1981 Ray-Mond; 1988

n. The goal of bewildering, dazzling, or otherwise distracting the attention of the audience so that it does not notice the secret method being used during a trick. A minor and inelegant form of misdirection. [rare] "The essence of conjuring is to make people confuse what they thought they saw with what they actually saw...." — John Wade, The Trade of the Tricks (1974), 14

term: SEE UNDER: Flags of All Nations
definition: 1.n. Magic words. [obsolete since 1855] "What conjuration and what mighty magic." — Shakespeare, Othello (1604), Act I, Scene 3 Originally Standard English by 1375 in the sense of a spell or magic words to call upon supernatural forces. REF: OED/2.

term: dazzling us with his wonderful conjurations."
definition: v. To do magic in its non-supernatural sense. [fairly common] "The two dimes are heard to fall into the hat, and every one is persuaded that you have conjured one of the dimes out of a person's hand, and sent it into the hat." — John Wyman Jr. in The Magician's Own Book (1857), 4 "The ball is at the outset conjured away, i.e., made to disappear by palming." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (Mar 1912), 42
n. A handgun faked to produce a loud but harmless noise. [rare]
n. A female magician; a magicienne being the most usual synonym. [very rare, possibly nonce]
1.a. Pertaining to the country of Conjuria, a fictitious-spoof land of magicians conceived by Bruce Dunn. [obsolete, formerly very rare]
n. Magicana being the more usual synonym. [very rare]

n. Magic being the most usual synonym. Loosely, legerdemain. [common] “On Thursday and Friday Mr. Robin gave his astonishing performances of legerdemain, or to use the good old English name, which is now fast going out date, if it is not already gone, conjuring.” — Soulby’s Ulverston Advertiser, 21 Jul 1853 "Conjuring is the only absolutely honest profession—a conjuror promises to deceive and does." — Karl Germain, quoted in Cramer (1966), 107 "The essence of conjuring is to make people confuse what they thought they saw with what they actually saw...." — John Wade, The Trade of the Tricks (1974), 14 "Lying and conjuring are two arts that must be carried out successfully to be of any use." — The Great Levante in Eric Lewis, The Magic of 1936 (1936) "Conjuring and the occult seldom constitute a happy marriage." — John Booth, Psychic Paradoxes (1984), 44

n. Doing (inventing and/or performing) magic for other magicians, that is, magic designed to puzzle fellow magi by the deviousness of the method rather than the dramatic entertainment of the effect and presentation; magic for magicians; magician's magic; hobby magic; intrigue tricks. Always used in a perjorative sense. A specific instance is called a magician fooler. Opposite of commercial magic. [fairly common, particularly in Britain] "Conjuring to Conjurers is a fool's game and a waste of time. I have spent many hours watching that kind of thing, and only a fraction of it would be of any use in front of a general audience." — Harry Leat, Thoughtful Magic (1923), 49 "That futile thing, 'conjuring for conjurers'." — Charles Waller, quoted in Farelli (1934), 30 "Conjuring for conjurers is my passion and my besetting weakness." — Louis Histed, The Magic of Louis Histed (1947), 38 "'Conjuring for conjurers' is a vice in a professional. In an amateur it is a vice only if he hopes to turn professional." — Henry Hay, Cyclopedia of Magic (1949), 10
(See also: conjurer's pistol.) n. A handgun faked to produce a loud but harmless noise. [rare]

n. Alternate spelling of conjurer. [obsolescent except in Britain] Preferred spelling variant in The Conjuror's Magazine (1792); The Conjuror Unmasked (1795), The Conjuror's Repository (1803); Crambrook cat (1843); Logrenia playbill (1857); The Magician's Own Book (1857); Frost, The Lives of the Conjurors (1976); Hoffmann (1876); Hamley cat (1882); Goldston (1905 but not in his later works); Carrington (1909); Noakes (1920); Carlton (1920); Waller (1920 also 1929); Culpitt (1928); Blyth (1934); Tarr (1976); Gill (1976); Blackstone Jr & Reynolds (1985), Supreme cat (1986); Randi (1992, xi, referring to British usage).
n. A magician who specializes in contact mindreading; a muscle-reader being the most usual synonym; a thought-reader (2, obsolete). [very rare, possibly nonce]

term: Continuous Front and Back Hand Palm
definition: n. The back-and-front palm being the usual synonym. 241 [obsolete since 1901, formerly very rare]

n. Effect where, after the four aces are shown and covered by a handkerchief and three indifferent cards covered by another and a volunteer removes one of the aces and places it with the indifferent cards, the two packets are shown to have tranposed. [very rare]
n. Any sleight (such as a false count, false cut, or false shuffle) that keeps selected playing cards in or moves them to a desired position in the packet, thereby establishing card control. [common]

n. A cold deck being the more usual synonym. [rare but widely understood by card magicians] Originally (from "cold deck") the argot of card sharps by 1915 Innis; also 1933 Cameron; 1935 Pollock as earliest citation in the RHHDAS; 1961 Scarne; 1962 Garcia; 1977 Prus & Sharper; 1981 Ortiz in Casino & Sports Magazine. Thence magicians jargon by 1988 Waters, 85; 1991 Ortiz, 207, as "switch in the cooler"; 1998 Busby as “So Al Baker
n. A popular trick where several coins are made to vanish and then appear within an upside-down glass on a specially gimmicked display stand; Visible Coins in Glass. [fairly common]
n. The copper-silver effect being the more usual synonym. [rare]
n. The type of crimp where only one corner of a playing card is bent; the bent corner; a cornered card (2, obsolete).
1.n. A corner short (see) being the usual synonym.

n. Stage effect where trays of clothing are stacked in an empty trunk, a spectator choses a costume, and a (female) assistant emerges dressed in that costume while the others have vanished. [fairly common]

n. A minor sleight that palms a (large) coin by using the thumb to slide it up near the tips of the middle and ring fingers. [obsolete after 1887, formerly very rare, possibly nonce] Originally French magicians jargon as la coulée by 1876. REF: Hoffmann (1876). Thence British magicians jargon from 1876 (Hoffmann) to 1887 (Hoffmann).
1.n. A false count of playing cards, as in the Buckle Count, Collins Count, Elmsley Count, Hamman Count, Jordan Count, etc. [common]

n. The act of counting down. [rare] Originally the argot of American card sharps by 1894 Koschitz; 1931 Smith. Thence magicians jargon by 1935 Stebbins; 1940 Gardner; 1948 Braue in HMM; 1969 Gibson. a. [adjectivally] [fairly common]

n. The method that uses a balance-beam to make heavy objects seemingly weightless. [very rare but not nonce] First applied to magic in 1879 (and premiered in 1880) by J.N. Maskelyne in his Cleopatra's Needle illusion. This inspired De Kolta's Cocoon (1885) and was the basis of Owen Clark’s production of cannon balls, Jarrett's Bangkok Bungalow (1908), and Copperfield in an illusion that he introduced in 1991.

n. Memorization of the initial position of certain playing cards in the deck to assure control over them during subsequent handling; a countdown. [very rare] 248 Originally the argot of American (?) card sharps by 1894 Koschitz; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne. Thence magicians jargon by 1911 N. Maskelyne; 1935 Stebbins.

1.n. Literally, a physical screen created by interposing an object (the magician's hands or body, or an assistant or prop) between the secret action and the spectator's angles of vision. [common] “Two covers are used in the standard routine of the trick generally known as 'The Ace Assembly.’” — Albert Goshman in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Sep 1955), 325
n. Effect where two glasses of milk are produced from two thin plaques, one painted with a cow, the other a pasture. [rare]

n. Effect where the magi divines the uppermost number on a die placed inside two boxes; Dice Wonder. [rare] A classic slum-magic pocket trick made magical in the hands of Dutch magician Flip in the 1980s.

1.n. Stage illusion where the entire body of an assistant placed in a coffin-like box, which is raised above the stage, is consumed by flame and later restored whole and alive. [obsolescent, once fairly common]
n. The Vampire (see) being the modern synonym for this stage illusion. [obsolescent]

n. Stage illusion where the performer escapes under cover of a curtain or screen after being securely bound to a large wooden cross by ropes around the arms, waist, and legs, the rope ends being held by two spectators. [rare]

n. The set-up or lay-out of a deck or part of a deck of playing cards in such a way that the parts mathematically cross-reference to each other; the intersecting sets principle. [rare] Used to produce apparent mindreading or divination effects. The earliest example is the very old Pairs Repaired trick, first mentioned in 1740 by Guyot. Modern and usually better disguised applications have been invented by Jack Merlin (Telepathy Card Trick in 1927), Louis Histed (The Miracle Divination), S. Leo Horowitz (The Twenty-Five Card Trick by 1938), Al Baker (his Vocalepathy gimmick by 1941), Paul Fox (Five- Card Mental Selection and his Miracle Gimmick by 1947), Orville Meyer (Multi-Mentality), Al Koran (The Princess Card Trick Plus), Ross Johnson, Irv Weiner, Stuart Judah, Stewart James, Orville Meyer, Phil Goldstein, Ray Grismer (Foxy in 1974 and then Foxiest), Tony Griffith (1975), Simon Aronson (1978), Jeff Busby, T.A. Waters, and Terry Nosek. REF: Peter Tappan, The Impostress Princess (1986).
n. The cut force (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare]
v. To do the Downs Palm.

n. Cruise ships provide regular employment for many magicians. The first may well have been Egyptian magician Gali-Gali who was working liners in the Mediterranean back in the early 1920s. Amedeo became the first American in 1938 when he worked the Canadian Pacific Line. Dai Vernon, Francis Carlyle, and S. Leo Horowitz followed in the late 1930s to early 1950s. Lady Frances worked cruise ships around 1950. Siegfried Fishbacher began his career working German liners as a bartender-magician in 1960, adding Roy Horn later that same year to form the now spectacular team of Siegfried & Roy. They left the cruise-ship circuit in 1965 for bigger things. Frank Garcia worked cruise ships 1961-67. June Merlin also worked this circuit around that time. For a list of more recent magicians who have worked cruise liners see my Who's Who in Magic under "Cruise Ships".. REF: The Jinx #45 (Jun 1938), 307; and Doug Anderson, Straight Talk about Cruise Ship Magic

n. The effect of supernormal perception, whether telepathic or clairvoyant. [very rare, possibly nonce] Originally coined by the French physiologist and psychic researcher, Charles Richet, and first published by him in his Thirty Years of Psychical Research (Engl. tr. in 1923). REF: OED/2. Thence mentalist-magicians jargon in 1935 Annemann in Jinx #4.

n. The glass or rock crystal sphere (faked or unfaked) used by mentalists for crystal gazing. [fairly common] "A crystal ball is an 8-ball. Those who believe in the fakirs are not in front of it, but behind it." — Sam Grossman in New York Daily Mirror, 19 Dec 1939, as quoted in The Jinx #74 "Crystal gazers are seldom seen these days but the crystal ball is still an interesting object to use when you present mental magic." — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jan 1955), 231 Originally Standard English since 1855 as given by the OED/2; 1935 Magnuson. Anderson; 1949 Tannen cat #1 as "Crystal Gazing Ball"; 1952 Abbott cat 254 #13 as "Crystal Gazing Balls"; 1954 Davenport’s ad as “Crystal Gazing Balls”; 1963 Stevenson in HMM; 1972 Dalal in Swami; 1976 Owen cat #9 as "Crystal Gazing Ball"; 1979 Lamb; 1980 Gibson; 1984 Magic Inc ad in New Tops; 1985 Tilford ad in LR as "Crystal Gazing Ball"; 1987 Magic Shop Hot Sheet; 1988 Waters; 1995 Tannen cat #18 as "Crystal Gazing Ball"; 1997 Lee cat #11; 2004 Robbins ad in LR.
n. The Crystal Casket being the more usual synonym. [obsolete since 1911, formerly rare]

n. A magician who uses a glass crystal globe as a prop in a mentalist trick, routine, or complete act. [rare] “Crystal gazers are seldom seen these days but the crystal ball is still an interesting object to use when you present mental magic.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jan 1955), 231 Originally either Standard English or the cant of psychic researchers by 1898. n. The act of simulating the fortuneteller's art of scrying with a crystal ball; scrying. [fairly common] Particularly popular among mentalists of around 1920, usually using a gaffed crystal ball. Originally the cant of psychic researchers by 1889 (Proceedings of the Society of Psychical Research, V.5, p.507, as cited in the OED/2). Thence that of fortunetellers by 1921 (Alexander). n. Crystal gazing being the more usual synonym. 255 [rare] "In earlier (and leaner) times, my father worked a crystal-gazing act in carnivals and small towns, but said he decided to give it up when he discovered that people were taking it seriously." — Harry Blackstone Jr, The Blackstone Book of Magic & Illusion (1985), 82 Prominent magicians who worked this included Claude Conlin (1907-25), Ralph Richards (1910 to mid-30s), Mystic Clayton (1922), Nicola (1922), Houdini (in 1925-26 but as an exposé), "Chandra" (James S. Harto, by 1928), Dr. Korda RaMayne (Robert A. Nelson, 1930s), and "Rajah Raboid" (Maurice P. Kitchen, by 1931).

n. Effect where three silks placed in a 12" high clear tube change into three real oranges (or similar objects) when covered and uncovered by an empty metal canister. [fairly common] Its invention is credited to both Ellis Stanyon and U.F. Grant by Darwin (1988), 9; and to Grant by Holden's.
n. Abbreviation for the Copper-Silver Coin. [rare]

n. A shuffle that removes (culls) cards from known positions in the deck and brings them to the top or bottom. [rare] Originally the argot of card sharps in 1902 (Erdnase, 78, who possibly coined the term). Thence magicians jargon by 1931 Sharpe; 1936 T. Tucker; 1937 Hugard; 1942 Marlo; 1949 Tannen cat #1; 1976 Gill; 1977 Barnhart in Genii; 1978 Müller; 1981 Scalbert; 1984 Vernon; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1991 Ortiz. v. To do a cull shuffle.

term: Curry Turnover Change; Curry Change Turnover
definition: n. A sleight that exchanges one playing card for another while turning it from a face-up to a face- down position; the Turnover Change. [fairly common] "Paul Curry's Turnover Change ... is one of the finest and most deceptive of all good card changes and not too hard to master." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Feb 1946), 196

n. The trick or entire routine where a piece of rope or string is apparently cut yet then shown whole again. [very common] "If you give a magician enough rope, he'll cut and restore it." — old saying, quoted in Pecor (1979), 99 "Death came to see thy tricks, and cut in twaine Thy thread, why dids't not make it whole againe?" — Anon., "Epitaph on a juggler" (1641) “Probably the trick most often done by magicians at the present time is the cut and restored rope ....” — Jean Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Aug 1945), 140 This still-popular effect was described and with detailed instructions in four of the earliest books on conjuring. First, as applied to a string, by J. Prevost in 1584. Second, with "a lace", by Reginald Scot also in 1584. Third, next year, using a string, by the Italian, Horatio Napolitana. Fourth, using "a piece of Tape", by Hocus Pocus Junior in 1634. Also exposed in 1693 by Ozanam. The effect was described in 1843 by Crambrook who called it "The Tape Trick". Harlan Tarbell was (by 1926) the first to substitute rope for string in this effect. REF: Hilliard (1938), 785-787; Holden in Sphinx (1926), 253.

term: cut-and-restored string; Cut and Restored String
definition: n. Earlier version of the Cut and Restored Rope (see); the Cut String Restored (obsolete). [fairly common]

term: Cut and Restored Turban; cut and restored turban
definition: n. The effect where any long strip of cloth (such as muslin or cheesecloth) is cut (and sometimes also burned) yet then shown whole; the Hindu Turban; the Turban Trick. [rare] 260 Based in effect and method on the old cut-and-restored string. Originally in its cut-burnt-&- restored cloth version an authentic Eastern effect. First reported by English traveller E.W. Lane in 1836 in recalling an Egyptian street conjurer (Háwee) in Cairo who had sometimes cut and sometimes burned a muslin shawl in the middle and then restored it whole. Then first performed in Europe at the Albert Palace in Battersea Park, London, in 1886 by Indian moslem conjuror Sayad Hussan from Hyderabad. Next staged in 1910 by Western-trained Hindu magician "Ram Bhuj" (A.N. Dutt) at the Croyden Empire, London. Later became a standard trick in the Western world. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (Dec 1928), 135, 179; Price (1985), 510.

term: Cut String Restored, The; the cut string restored
definition: (See also: cut-and-restored string.) n. Earlier version of the Cut and Restored Rope (see); the Cut String Restored (obsolete). [fairly common]

n. Card effect where the 4 Aces are lost in the deck, yet the magician reveals each one by a series of cuts. [fairly common] “We have used ... 'Cutting the Aces’ for about five years and the cardman who doesn’t gain a reputation doing the trick is most inept.” — Fred Braue in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Oct 1946), 260

term: Cutting a Cigarette in Half; Cutting a Camel in Half
definition: n. Effect where a cigarette is shoved into a slotted metal tube, cut through with a safety razor blade, and restored. [fairly common]

n. Effect where an assistant steps into a tall cabinet, her neck strapped with leather that has chains leading horizontally through holes on either side to padlocks on the outside; the cabinet door is closed and 5 solid metal blades, each as wide as the cabinet, are shoved thru slots at 10-inch intervals, each visibly penetrating to thru to the back of the cabinet; the door is opened to reveal the assistant both intact and still shackled by her neck. [rare] "Cutting a Girl in Sixths is not as spectacular as many illusions but it has entertainment value and a definite advantage in that it can be worked completely surrounded and close to an 261 audience." — Ken Griffin, Illusion Show Know-How (1972), 36

n. Effect where a small box is placed over assistant's head and long daggers thrust through from many directions, yet, when box is removed, assistant's head is unharmed. In later version the front may be opened to show the head vanished but the daggers in place; Sword Box (1). [fairly common] Both effects and methods are simply smaller versions of the Sword Cabinet. The method for the later, visible version, is either the V-mirror or Black Art. The second version was invented in the early-1930s by U.F. Grant as "The Invulnerable Lady". REF: Abbott's Catalog, No.6 (1940), 453.

n. Card effect where the two red Aces transpose with the black ones. Not to be confused with either Cavorting Aces or Jacob Daley's version of Vernon's Travellers. [rare] So-called because this was the final card problem that Dr Daley was developing during the weeks before his death and not, as some assume, the last trick he performed. To clarify this point of confusion, the following points are in order: On 17 February 1954 the noted New York plastic surgeon and superb amateur sleight-of-hand artist, 51-year old Dr. Jacob Daley, did two card tricks during lunch on the stage of the Art Directors Club at 115 East 40th Street. The first was the Cavorting Aces. The second—which was also his last because Daley died of a massive coronary upon returning to his table—was an original version of Vernon's Travellers, the theme having been suggested to him a few weeks earlier by Bill Simon. The other magicians at this otherwise lay meeting were Abril Lamarque, Francis Carlyle, Roy Benson, and Ben Dalgin. The above eye-wittness account is evidently Abril Lamarque's. Some later magicians have wrongly assumed the last trick was Cavorting Aces. And even some of those who correctly identify Daley's version of Vernon's Travellers as the last trick ever performed by Daley, mistake it for the very different trick that Vernon termed "The Last Trick of Dr. Jacob Daley". REF: Ganson/Vernon (1957), 210-211; The New Phoenix #302 (5 Mar 1954), 5.
n. A sleight that shows 3 playing cards as 2 by drawing the top card back with the thumb while pushing the two lower ones forward as one. [rare]

n. Stage effect where the barefoot magus prances upon shards of glass without injury. [rare] Originally a circus side-show act by 1896 when first exposed by W.H.J. n. A colored paste used to secretly mark a playing card by giving it a shiny or tinted smudge, thereby making it a key card. [common] Ordinary silver-colored eye-shadow makes an effective daub and, indeed, as fancily repackaged and greatly overpriced is what is often sold by gambling-supply houses. Originally the invention of card sharps to mark cards during play. French sharpers were using a black-lead impregnated rag by 1861 when exposed by Robert-Houdin. American sharps 266 were using daub by 1894 when exposed by J.N. Maskelyne. A gambler taught the technique to American magician Dr. James W. Elliott who first adapted it to magic by creating a key card for card tricks. Before his death in 1920, Elliott tipped it to only one or two intimates in magic. Until 1932 it was used regularly as a closely-held secret by Al Baker, Paul Rosini, John Scarne, and Dai Vernon, and very few, if any, other magicians. REF: Robert-Houdin (1861), Ch.15; J.N. Maskelyne (1894), 53-55; Hilliard (1938), 66-76. First published to magicians by Dai Vernon in 1932 in his "The Vernon Card Location" but still not widely known until 1938, judging from the following evidence. First marketed to magicians in 1935 through Abbott's Catalog #3 as "Caroselli's Magic Dauber" but seemingly overlooked. In 1936 Gravatt referred to "gambler's daub" (plagiarized in 1937 by Hugard). In the Jun 1938 issue of The Jinx, editor Ted Annemann remarked that: "Only a few magi to date have used daub, and it has been kept quite exclusive." Again commercially marketed to magicians sometime around early 1938 by magician Caryl Fleming as Golden Glow (a brand already familiar to sharps by 1933 when described as "new" by Judson Cameron). Then, in The Jinx Summer 1938 issue, Annemann noted that: "Daub, which is an apt name for the substance used by gamblers and card artists..., has become rather popular in the past few months and several of the dealers are stocking it. However, no one has yet revealed a truly inside secret of the brethren...." Originally (and still) the argot of American card sharps by 1917 Lipman cat; 1931 Smith; 1932 Evans Secret Blue Book; 1933 J. J. Cameron; 1933 Walsh/Scarne; 1961 K.C. Card Blue Book; 1962 Garcia; 1968 Weiner in New Jinx #70; 1973 Lampkin; 1977 Prus & Sharper; 1981 R.M. Cameron; 1984 Ortiz; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Munari. Thence magicians jargon by 1932 Vernon; 1933 Walsh & Scarne; 1937 Hugard, giving 2 tricks by Vernon; 1938 Litzau; 1938 Hilliard; 1938 Annemann in Jinx; 1939 Kanter cat; 1940 Hopkins; 1941 Holden cat #8; 1947 Abbott cat #9 as "Silversheen Daub"; 1948 Kaplan; 1949 Tannen cat #1; 1950 Boardé; 1951 Weiner; 1956 Dexter; 1959 Christopher in HMM; 1968 Racherbaumer/Fields; 1976 Tarr; 1978 Müller; 1980 Adair; 1981 Grippo; 1987 Stevens ad in Genii; 1988 Waters; 1988 Grismer; 2001 Magic Methods cat. v. To apply daub to a playing card. [very rare] Originally card sharps argot by 1911 Meyer; 1981 R.M. Cameron. Thence magicians jargon by 1948 Norman; 1969 Gibson. a. [adjectivally] [rare] Originally card sharps argot by 1933 Cameroc as "daub work". Thence magicians jargon by 1983 Cassidy as "the daubed page"; 1987 Albrecht cartoon in Epoptica #8 as "daubed"; 1987 Stevens ad in Genii as a "daub kit".

n. Daub. [very rare] Originally the argot of card sharps by 1939 MacDougall; 1981 R. Martin Allen. Thence magicians jargon by 1945 Wheeler cat referring to the daub itself; 1952 Crimmins in HMM as a "manuscript ...
