a. Said of a prop that, having been used, is no longer needed. [very rare but not nonce] Probably originally American carnival usage. Thence (?) magicians jargon by 1972 Griffin.

n. Card effect and patter story of the legendary Poker hand of "Aces and Eights" held by James "Wild Bill" Hickock when in 1876 he was shot in the back and killed in the Mann & Lewis Saloon in Deadwood, Dakota Territory. The actual cards Hickock held are disputed. [rare] "Henry Christ's Dead Man's Hand and Arthur Monroe's Voodoo are good examples of what a dramatic or weird build-up, cleverly woven about these two excellent tricks, can do to make magic good theatre." — David Bamberg, Illusion Show (1965/1988), 301
n. The display and demonstrations by magic dealers of their wares at booths or tables at magicians conventions. [rare]

n. Honorary position awarded since Jul 1907 by vote of the Society of American Magicians (SAM) National Council. It is the highest elective honorary office in the SAM and is a lifetime appointment. The eight SAM Deans so far (with years held) are Harry Kellar (1907-22), Frederick Eugene Powell (1922-38), Al Baker (1938-51), Jean Hugard (1951-59), Herman Hanson (1959-73), Werner Dornfeld (1973-82), H. Adrian Smith (1983-92), and Jay Marshall

n. A Gray Code (see) being the most usual, although less appropriate, synonym. [rare] "By the way, these digital rings are more accurately called 'de Bruijn Sequences', I have found by reading [computer expert Donald] Knuth." — P. Howard Lyons 20 Nov 1978 letter to Jeff Busby
n. Stage effect where a living woman's head rests disembodied upon a sword placed across the arms of a throne. [rare]

1.n. Stage effect where an obviously live human head is shown in tableaux to be detached from its body; originally called the decollation of John Baptist (obsolete). [rare] Uses a double, as first exposed in 1584 by Scot.

n. Stage illusion where one or two birds (usually ducks) have their heads cut off and then restored. If two birds are used, one is black, the other white, and their heads get put back on the bird of the opposite color. [very rare but not nonce] This fine old effect had been first performed for Egyptian Pharoah Cheops by magician Dedi who successively severed and restored the heads of a goose, a duck, and and ox (he balked at doing it to a man). REF: Christopher (1973), 8-9. Revived by 1801 in the West when British magician Magony included a decapitated & restored rooster in his act. By 1807 Thomas Ingleby was using a version in his act in London. His chief competitor, Moritz, quickly copied Ingleby's bird trick. Then in 1815 Ingleby explained his method for "The cutting off of a Cock's Head and exhibiting the bird alive again" — the method requiring the sacrifice of a duplicate fowl. It was already a common trick in Burma and China. REF: Magony program in Magic (Nov 1909), 11; George Johnson in Magic (Dec 1906), 17-18; Sidney Clarke in Magic Wand (Oct 1925), 133, 135. A more advanced version of this trick was first reported (and probably invented) by Italian magician Bartolomeo Bosco in 1838. He used two pigeons (one black, one white), decapitated both, placed their heads on blocks and their bodies in false-bottomed boxes, "restoring" them with apparently switched (artificially colored) heads on two live duplicate birds. REF: Robert-Houdin (1858/1859 tr), 125-127. Gustav Frikell did the black-white pigeon heads exchange sometime before 1875. His method was probably the modern humane one. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand, V.15 (1926), 133. By early 1903 Imro Fox had included Frikell's two-bird/two-box version in his act in London. Later that year "Bosco" (as part of the Le Roy, Talma, & Bosco "Triple Alliance" show) was regularly decapitating two ducks (one white, one black) and restoring them with heads switched. Featured by Henry Hilton in England sometime before 1937 and Orson Welles in his 1943 Hollywood tent show. REF: Magic (Jul 1903), 85, (May 1904), 80, (Apr 1906), 53; Waller (1980), 129; Holden (1937), 23.

1.n. Specifically, a trick, which is the modern synonym. See also the deceitful phrase “no deception”. [obsolescent after 1882, formerly common] "It is not altogether the inventor of a deception, but the performer, who claims the principal merit." — W. F. Pinchbeck, The Expositor (1805), 58-59 "'It's done with mirrors' applies to only a tiny fraction of modern deceptions." 272 — Milbourne Christopher, The Illustrated History of Magic (1973), 2
(See also: Illusion Steps.) n. An enclosed step-ladder with two or more steps faked to hide an assistant before an appearance or after a vanish; Deceptive Steps. [rare]

n. A full set of playing cards; a pack being the principal British usage. [very common in U.S. but only fairly common in Britain] "But whiles he thought to steale the single Ten, The King was slyly finger'd from the Deck." — Shakespeare, Henry VI (ca1592), Pt.III, v, i, 44 273 "[As] this article has been written for an American magazine, I have used, throughout, the term ‘deck' instead of ‘pack', its English equivalent. To be perfectly candid I think the former is the better of the two, as no confusion can possibly arise between it and the word packet." — Victor Farelli in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Aug 1946), 245 “Handling most standard decks feels like shuffling a stack of blotters.” — Jeff Busby, flyer, 1988 Originally the lingo of British card players in the 1500s, passing into Standard English at the end of that century as confirmed by Shakespeare. Thence adopted by American card players but dropped by the British in favor of "pack". REF: OED/2; Hugard in HMM (1945), 121; Dexter (1956), 126; Lamb (1979), 51. Thence American magicians jargon by 1902 Erdnase/Harto; 1909 Hilliard, who also uses "pack"; 1914 Stanyon in Magic, 80, explaining to his British readers that "’Deck' is an American term for ‘Pack.'"; 1923 Burgess in Elliott; 1978 Müller re its American usage; 1979 Lamb re its American usage; 1986 Hades cat #2; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Ortiz.

n. Any action (usually a sleight, sometimes mechanical) that substitutes surreptitiously one pack of playing cards for another. Used to switch in or switch out any type of prepared deck such as a stacked deck or a marked deck. See cold decking. [fairly common] "There are a number of very subtle and deceptive sleight-of-hand deck switches for use at the card table, but very few of them have ever found their way into print." — Darwin Ortiz, The Annotated Erdnase (1991), 41-42

n. Earliest known title of the original version of the human decapitation trick; Decapitation (1). [obsolete after 1668, formerly fairly common] This trick was being performed on the Italian peninsula in the mid-1500s when first reported by the baffled Girolamo Cardano. It was performed in England as early as 1582 by Kingsfield of London at Bartholomew Fair. First exposed in print in 1584 by Scot. The trick was evidently still being presented in England as late as 1763 as a sideshow. REF: Cardano; Scot (1584); Dean (1763), 98-101. The term originated by 1387 as the Feast of the Decollation of St. John the Baptist, celebrated on August 29th in the Roman and other Christian churches. From the Latin meaning the act of beheading. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1584 Scot; 1612 Rid; 1634 Hocus Pocus Junior; 1668 White. NOTE: This effect shares (with the Bridle) the earliest trick-titles known to have been used by English-speaking magicians themselves, as revealed by Reginald Scot in writing in 1584 of it as one "which the jugglers call the
n. The gambler's cop (see) being the most usual synonym. [very rare but not nonce]
1.n. The Vanishing Lady illusion. [rare] "The DeKolta Chair Vanish is one of today's most popular illusions."

n. Various trick cards and decks printed for and marketed by Theodore DeLand Jr. [very rare] DeLand began privately making gaffed cards as early as 1905 when he printed for Henry Hardin the latter's Monte Cristo Deck. DeLand later marketed his own special cards, including the Phantom Card (1907), X-Ray Deck (1907), Pickitout (Jun 1908), Knock Out (Jul 1908), Fadeaway Card (1908), Papel Blanco (1908), Nox-em-all (late 1908), Two Card Monte (c1909), Sphinx Card Trick (mid-1909), DeLand's Dollar Deck (1910), Million Dollar Mystery (1) (1910), and Fly-a-way (early 1911). In 1918 he sold all rights on his entire line to S.S. Adams, whose company still sells DeLand’s Dollar Deck.

n. Slang abbreviation of demonstration (3); a demo (U.S.). [fairly common] "Sales are never really the object of a dealer's Dem., which is more to see and be seen." — Dennis H. Vickery in Supreme Newsletter (Feb 1988), 10 Originally the lingo of British salesmen by 1968. REF: OED/2. Thence British magicians jargon by 1983 Lees as "a long dem"; 1988 De Courcy in Magigram as "a dealer-dem"; 1988 Adair in Trixigram as "after the stage dem". v. To demonstrate. [rare]

Thence magicians jargon by 1984 Busby in Epoptica #6 as "during demos in the dealer's booth"; 1988 Fletcher in Genii; 1988 Grismer as a "bridge demo"; 1992 White in MUM as a "dealer demo"; 2001 Lee ad in MUM as "video demos". Plural also as "demoes" in 1984 (Warlock in LR as "close-up dealer's demoes"; 1986 Bamman in LR as "various

n. A magician employed by a magic shop as a salesman showing (demonstrating) tricks to customers. Compare pitchman. [fairly common] "As any visitor to Colon knowns, Percy Abbott is a great demonstrator. His long experience as a professional magician enables him to add showmanly touches to the tricks he presents." — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Apr 1957), 557 Outstanding demonstrators have included Percy Abbott, Al Cohen, Bunny Collins (since mid- 1980s with Tannen's), Paul Diamond (1980s-90s), Art Emerson, Jimmy Herpick (1940s-50s with Tannens), Norm Jensen, Milt Kort, Bob Little, John Mueller (with Tannen's until retired early 1980s), George Sands (1930s with Tannen's), Duke Stern, Daisy White (1920-30s with Ducrot's), Lex Zaleta, and Joe Zering. Many subsequently famous magicians apprenticed as demonstrators, including Cardini (with Gamage's in 1918), Alan Wakeling, Shimada (with Tenyo 1953-58), and Ken Brooke (with Harry Stanley in 1960s). Former magic demonstrators who found fame elsewhere include comic Steve Martin.
n. Clear-glass prop shaped like an old-fashioned milk bottle filled with milk that slowly empties itself. [obsolete, formerly rare]

term: SEE UNDER: magic depot & magical depot
definition: n. The sleight that seems to place a playing card mid-deck while really placing it beneath the top (or second) card; Tilt (2). [rare]

n. One particular mechanically-operated deck of playing cards used for the Rising Cards effect. Compare Martin Pack. [rare] Operated by a gravity-driven elevator concealed in a hollow deck. This method was first conceived by American magician Dr. L. Vosburgh Lyons and shown in 1936 in his home-made model to an enthusiastic Ted Annemann. The first production model was made for Lyons by Herman Hanson. Learning that a pirated model was being made, Lyons licensed U.F. Grant who made and marketed it in mid-1937. Bob Sherman advertised it in his magic catalog as the "Lyons Card Rise". Another pirated version was also made in Germany in the late 1940s. Note that in Lyon's model the deck cannot be fanned to "prove" it is ungimmicked. REF: Annemann in Jinx #32 (1937), 204; Elliott in Phoenix #175 (1949), 703; Albo, III (1977), 5- 10; Lewis #3 (1983), 175. In June 1948, British amateur magician Harry "Devano" Mitchell used the same basic mechanism in a mechanical deck that could, however, be fanned. Devano's superbly crafted version was based on a pendulum-driven rising cards device invented by Louis Histed. This substantially improved version was popularized by Don Alan on the Ed Sullivan TV show. It was also a pet effect of Johnny Paul (1950s) and Albert Goshman (1970s). REF: Dexter (1956), 100; Rogers in Linking Ring (Nov 1985), 76-78.
n. The Rising Cards effect worked by the Devano pack. [fairly common]

n. Title of the Inexhaustible Hat routine as carried to its limit by J. M. Hartz. [rare] Joseph Michael Hartz, a Liverpuddlian Briton, began developing this act in New York around 1877 and had it fully perfected when he returned to England in 1883. Later a pet routine of Carl Hertz. REF: Hoffmann (1911); E. Dawes, “Michael Hartz and Le Chapeau Du Diable”, The Magic Circular, V.71 (1977), 131-135.. “An act similar to Hartz’s Devil of a Hat would be greeted as a novelty today.” — The Looker-On in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Feb 1948), 397
n. The Devil's Handkerchief being the original and still most usual synonym. [fairly common]
n. The Devil's Handkerchief being the original and still most usual synonym. [rare]
n. A newspaper faked with a secret pocket. [very rare]

n. Stage illusion where the assistant stands in an upright cabinet topped by a square rack with many short spikes. The cabinet door is closed and the spike-rack is forced down through the assistant to the floor by outside handles running through slots, yet the assistant emerges unharmed. [rare]

n. Sleight of hand being the modern synonym. [obsolescent after the mid-1800s; previously common] 281 This fine antique phrase began as pre-jargon as early as 1612 in Rid as "right dexteritie of the hand". It finally emerged as jargon in 1724 when apparently coined by the then most popular British conjuror, Isaac Fawkes, for use in his advertisements. He probably chose this wording to make clear that he did not rely on supernatural aid in an age when the Witchcraft Acts of James I and Mary of Scotland were still (and until 1736) on the books, although prosecution had long been in abeyance.
a. Said of a double-faced card or double-faced coin. [rare]
n. Automaton trapeze artist that performs several amazing feats under the magician's direction; Antonio Diavolo. [rare]

1.n. The small cubes used in the several gambling games of the same name and marked with 1-to-6 spots on each face. [common] "DIE, n. The singular of 'dice'. We seldom hear the word, because there is a prohibitory proverb, 'Never say die.'" — Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911) Dice and dice games date from ancient times and many cultures. Crooked dice soon followed: loaded dice (including tap dice), misspotted dice (including tops and bottoms), etc. REF: John Scarne with Clayton Rawson, Scarne on Dice (1945). The word dice has been Standard English since the 1300s. Gaffed dice of any kind were originally called, in Standard English, simply "false dice" by 1552 Walker; 1577 Northbrooke; 1591 Greene; 1612 Rid; 1674 Cotton. Thence magicians jargon by 1873 as loaded dice; 1910 Stanyon ad in Magic as “trick dice”; 1949 as misspotted dice; 1960 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM as “gaffed dice”; 1988 as tap dice; 1998 Draun video. 2.n. Large cubes decorated like gaming dice used in various tricks such as the Die thru Hat and the Sliding Die Box. [rare]

1.n. Hyphenated as dice-box, the British term for what the Americans now call a dice cup. [rare] This simple cup-like device to assure a fair roll of the dice was in use by 1552 when it was called a "Dice boxe". By 1636 dice sharps had already developed a gaffed version, which was termed a "Cogging-box" to cast out only those dice wanted by the sharper. REF: OED/2 citations under "dice-box" and "cogging". Originally British gamblers lingo by 1552 Huloet as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1843 Crambrook cat; 1865 Evans;

n. A smooth-insided opaque container in which dice are shaken yet controlled; a dice-box (1) (British). [rare] The regulation cup used in dice games is horizontally ribbed on the inside to insure turning of the dice when shaken. The smooth-sided dice cup, used strictly for cheating, is called in American dice sharps' argot a "slick cup" by 1950 Maurer; 1961 Scarne; 1962 Garcia; 1984 Ortiz; and a "whip cup" by 1984 Ortiz. Originally American gamblers cant, as either "dice cup" or simply "cup", referring to both the fair and foul apparatus, by 1877 Grandin pricelist; 1945 Scarne. Thence magicians jargon by 1943 Marlo; 1953 Walsh & Mishell; 1963 McAllister; 1973 Alain; 1976 Busby cat #2A; 1977 Johnson; 1981 Abbott cat #22; 2003 Marucci in LR..

n. Conjuring with dice. [rare] "Dice magic is seldom seen and is a welcome change to add to your repertoire." — Guaranteed Magic, Bob Little's Catalog of Magic #1 (1974), 83 Hofzinser introduced misspotted dice into his magic act in 1842 to force a number by switching in the misspots with a changing box. REF: Hofzinser, 16 Mar 1847 letter to Pospischil, in Hatch (1985), 204. The earliest reported use of loaded dice in a public performance of magic was by French magician Eugéne Verbeck in London in Feb 1885. REF: G.W. Hunter in Magic Wand (1915), 83. Many dice divination tricks work on the simple fact that each fair die is made so that its opposite pairs of faces total seven points (the seven principle).

n. An effect of mathematical magic where a volunteer puts out in a column a set of five cubes each of whose sides bears a 2 or 3 figure number and the magus instantly gives the total, thereby simulating a lightning calculator. [fairly common]
n. Most usual British synonym for the American Card Duck, which see. [very rare, except in Britain]

(See also: Dictionary Trick.) n. The type of book test that uses a prepared bound glossary; a dictionary test. [fairly common] This sub-category of Hofzinser's book test was invented by J. N. Maskelyne and premiered by him sometime before 1882 at the Egyptian Hall in London using Nuttall's The Standard Pronouncing Dictionary of the English Language (1863). First explained in 1885 by Sachs. REF: W. & F. Hamley, Catalogue (1882), 94; Hoffmann (1903), 490.

n. The type of book test that uses a prepared bound glossary; a dictionary test. [fairly common] This sub-category of Hofzinser's book test was invented by J. N. Maskelyne and premiered by him sometime before 1882 at the Egyptian Hall in London using Nuttall's The Standard Pronouncing Dictionary of the English Language (1863). First explained in 1885 by Sachs. REF: W. & F. Hamley, Catalogue (1882), 94; Hoffmann (1903), 490.

1.n. Faked oblong container with four flap openings to give the impression that a large die slides from one end to the other; the Sucker Die Box; the Sliding Die Box. Not to be confused with either the dye box or the dice box. 285 [common] A primitive 2-door, non-sucker version was described in 1854 by Ponsin (Vol. II). Invented in its 4-door sucker version by English magician-ventriloquist Alexander Davis and premiered by him in the USA in 1886. Davis sold the manufacturing rights to Otto Maurer who first marketed it in 1887 as the "Most Wonderful Dice Trick". Davis' visiting nephew, Prof. Davison, bought one and brought it back to England where he premiered it in 1889. Consequently we may dismiss the later claims to invention by Sidney Lee (c.1896) and British impresario-magician Julian Wylie (c.1899). The die box was a pet effect of "Carlton" (Arthur Philps) who by 1907 created its still current form of sucker presentation. REF: Sharpe/Ponsin (1937), 146; Ed Vyson, Wizardry (1906), 13; Maurer cat (1888), 103; Waller (1948/1980), 138-139; Dif #2 [c.1972], 103.

(See also: Di-Ciphering.) n. An effect of mathematical magic where a volunteer puts out in a column a set of five cubes each of whose sides bears a 2 or 3 figure number and the magus instantly gives the total, thereby simulating a lightning calculator. [fairly common]

term: Die thru Hat; Die through (the) Hat
definition: n. Effect where a large die-like cube sinks thru the top of a borrowed bowler hat and is found underneath it. The Dissolving Die (obsolescent); the Hat Die (obsolete). [rare] Premiered (and possibly invented) by John Henry Anderson in the 1840s. First (?) exposed in 1857 in The Magician's Own Book (p.27) using one real and one shell die. Modern versions have the die pass through a tube.

n. A small-time showplace in the USA, popular from the 1870s to the 1910s, that offered cheap admission. Equivalent of the British "penny gaff" of the 1800s. [archaic] So-called because admission was typically a mere dime (10¢). Several subsequently famous magicians, including Houdini and The Great Leon, worked their way up through dime museums; others, like Ziska, declined to that level; but most who started their professional careers in dime museums just stayed there. Being too cheap to afford elaborate stage effects, dime museums, like carnival and circus sideshows, featured static illusions of the Headless Woman and Living Head types.
1.n. Effect where a silver dime becomes a copper one-cent piece. [archaic]
a. Having the quality of becoming smaller, as with the Diminishing Cards and Diminishing Glove. [very common]

n. Effect where a single playing card grows smaller. [rare] 287 "The single Diminishing Card is one of those novelty tricks that comes in a package of 'Ten Great Card Tricks for $1.00' is used twice in the parlor and promptly forgotten." — Al Baker in The Phoenix #54 (1944), 221 Variant methods were invented by Ed Massey (and introduced by him in 1922 in his New and Original Magic) and McQuade (by 1936).

n. A gaffed deck of playing cards consisting of 40 cards (omitting the court cards), 20 of which are regulation and 20 have regulation backs but the fronts are half-cards with one end regular and the other with the back design. Additionally they were readers, their backs being marked. [very rare]

a. Straightforward or uncluttered in method and/or effect. [fairly common] "Bolder and more direct methods seem to be the rule of the day and in this case the rule seems to be a good one." — Ted Annemann in The Jinx #7 (1935), 28

n. Anything (gesture, movement, patter, etc.) that draws the spectator's attention to the effect. Opposite of misdirection. [rare] "Misdirection might better be defined as controlled direction because what is actually happening is that the magician is controlling, or directing, the attention of the audience." — Charles Pecor, The Craft of Magic (1979), 234

a. Said of any step (but usually the ending) during a trick where the magician is burdened with tell- tale fakes or gimmicks. Opposite of clean (2.a.). [very rare but not nonce] Originally police & criminal slang meaning possessing incriminating evidence by 1927 (D. Hammett as earliest citation in 289 the RHHDAS). Thence magicians jargon by 1984 Kaufman in Richard's Almanac as "left you 'dirty'".

n. The secret moves or gaffs in a trick. [common] "I suffered stage fright and shook so bad I couldn't do the dirty work." — Robert Orben in Severn (1979), 159 "It was a perfect example of doing the dirty work when the audience least expected it." — Mike Caveney, The Great Leon (1987), 46 “Flosso seemed to have let himself learn ... which jokes and actions would just naturally cover the dirty work.” — Teller in Genii (Oct 1995),891
v. To vanish. Opposite of to produce or to appear. [very rare]
a. Having the attribute of a disappearance; vanishing being the much more usual synonym. Opposite of appearing. [fairly common]
See: Vanishing Knot(s). (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Vanishing Knot(s)".)
v. To disclose a hidden object; to perform a discovery; discovering. [rare]
v. Making a discovery; to discover. [rare]

n. The incongruity or anomaly that is inevitably present in any method used to produce an effect. The period (or periods) during each trick in which discrepancy occurs is called that trick's weak point (or weak points). [fairly common] "Every good trick must have a discrepancy." — Dr. Jacob Daley "Every good trick should have one discrepancy." — Dr. Daley, as misunderstood and therefore misquoted by Zavis (1973), 18 "Even the most trivial discrepancy may provide a clue that reveals a device and destroys the illusion." — Henning Nelms, Magic and Showmanship (1969), 133 "Unfortunately, few conjurers adopt any systematic procedure for detecting and eliminating discrepancies." — Henning Nelms, Magic and Showmanship (1969), 142 Jeff Busby judges Daley's notion of discrepancy to be the central concept in the special theory of magic. I deem it the central concept in the general theory of deception (including its detection) and Busby concurs. Jimmy Grippo was a master of hiding the discrepancy in certain card tricks by setting it up in the preceeding card trick.
n. An impossible-to-reconstruct effect where a spectator's chosen card instantly reverses itself in the deck. [rare]

n. Tradename of a small chopper marketed by Abbott's. [common] The basic concept was invented by American magus Lester "Marvello" Lake and sold as an exclusive to Abbott's where "all details and application of the principles involved were worked out by [Percy Abbott's partner] Recil Bordner." First marketed by Abbott's around 1941. It was an immediate best-seller and has continued so to the present. A pet effect of Jewel Aich in 292 1988 in his own giant head-chopper version. REF: Abbott's Catalog #18 (1969), 261.
n. The process in magical deception used to hide the method of a trick. Opposite of simulation (1) in the latter's primary sense. [very rare]

n. Effect where a metal coin covered by a cloth disappears when dropped into a glass of water; the Melting Coin. [rare] Uses a glass or clear plastic disc that is switched for the coin. A pet effect of Alfred C. Gilbert (by 1920).
n. A drastic or violent type of diversion. Compare confusion. [rare]

v. To get rid of an object secretly after the effect of a vanish; to make a get-away; to go south. Compare pass off and vanish. Opposite of to load or to steal. [common] For example, a coin vanished by concealing it in the hand can then be deposited (ditched) in a pocket on some pretext—too often the unconvincing ones of reaching for a handkerchief or some woofledust. Originally, by 1900 (as earliest citation in the RHHDAS; 1909 Tillotson; 1924 Henderson), one of those popular slang words (meaning to abandon) that linguist H. L. Mencken proudly dubbed a "saucy Americanism". NOTE: The earliest citation in the OED/2 is only 1921. Thence magicians jargon. First in America by 1937 F. Ross, Jun 11th letter to C. Miller; 1944 Annemann; 1945 H.D. Wise in Thompson; 1979 Lamb; 1979 Severn; 1983 Lewis in Berg; 1983 Osterlind; 1984 J. Thompson orally; 1987 Acer in Genii; 1997 M. Gallo in MUM as "ditch the shell"; 1997 Lee cat #11 as “ditch it in your Topit”. Then in Britain by 1956 Dexter; 1967 Baron; 1970 Adair; 1977 Delvin. n. A get-away being the more usual synonym. Opposite of a steal. [very rare]

n. Stage illusion where the assistant is manacled while standing in a cabinet, the doors closed, wide blades pushed through on either side to divide the two parts of the cabinet and the lady, which are then separated; then the process is reversed until the assistant is revealed in her original position. [rare]

n. The effect where the magician mysteriously discovers which one or in what order several seemingly identical objects have been moved or otherwise selected by a volunteer. [fairly common] “The magician then looked at the faces of the cards in each pile and made a quadruple divination. He announced which pile the card had been found in, which pile it was in now, named the card, and, finally, found it” — Clayton Rawson in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Sep 1950), 697

n. Effect where a small wooden duck bobs about at command in a water-filled bowl; the dancing duck. [rare] Originally a trick of East Indian conjurors. First reported in India in 1877 by Harry Kellar who, in 1886, was the first to publish it. Also seen in India in 1899 by Charles Bertram. First performed in the West in 1896 by The Elite Hindoo Fakeers troupe from India. Karl Germain saw their show and added this trick to his act, becoming the first occidental magician to perform it. REF: Kellar (1886), 119-120; Cramer (1962), 36-37; Bertram (1911), 113-114; Sharpe (1983), 137.
v. To divine; to make a divination. [rare]
n. Illusion where an assistant, suspended folded-up in an African cargo net, instantly vanishes when one side of the net is dropped; the Cargo Net. [rare]

n. Delaying-patter used by a stage magician or magical master of ceremonies to gain time while the next act is being set up. [very rare, but not nonce] Originally (by 1865 as earliest citation in the OED/2) and still criminal argot meaning to serve time in prison. Thence carnival cant by 1970 meaning delaying-patter. REF: Boles (1970), 23. Thence magicians jargon by 1970 Boles. NOTE: Also as verb to "do time" in 1980 J. Marshall meaning to lengthen an act with business.

term: Doll House, The; Doll's House Illusion
definition: n. The stage illusion where a large dollhouse, shown empty, disgorges the magician's female assistant. [common]
v. To treat one or both surfaces of a playing card with a foreign substance; doping. [very rare, possibly nonce]
n. Effect where the spectator, given a free choice among six face-down tabled playing cards, always choses the one with a red circle on the front, all others always having a black circle. [rare]

1.n. A magician's or assistant's look-alike. Used to substitute for them in a transformation (2). Compare disguised assistant. [fairly common] Partial doubles (to provide a living head detached from a seemingly decapitated body) were used by European conjurors as early as 1582. East Indian jugglers were the first to use complete human doubles, doing so by 1832 in connection with the Indian Basket Trick. Thence first documented in Europe by Col. Stodare for his version of the basket trick in 1865 when he used twin sisters. However it is suspected that Robert-Houdin used look-alikes in his 298 famous trick in Algiers in 1856 in which he vanished an Arab from under a cone. The use of doubles became almost universal among stage illusionists during the two decades straddling 1900, particularly with Morritt (Fly-To by 1893), Le Roy (The Flying Visit in 1894), Devant (The New Page in 1906), De Biere, Hertz, Lafayette (The Lion's Bride in 1911), and Blackstone. Seldom used after World War II and then only with the few surviving large troupes, notably the Soviet Kios.

n. An act with two magicians or magician and assistant, performing together. Not to be confused with an act employing a double (1). Compare single act. [fairly common] Many early magicians performed with assistants, and a few performed as part of a troupe that may have included one or more other magicians, each performing separately. The first magic act that used two magicians working together was that of Maskelyne & Cooke who premiered on 19 Jun 1865 with their Box Trick. They had been inspired to create this act as an exposé of the American spiritualists, the Davenport Brothers. Later famous teams include the Houdinis (Harry and Bess), the Boutons (Harry and Pete), Siegfried & Roy (since 1960), Sheets & Spill (early 1980s), and Penn & Teller (1980s), as well as most two-person mindreading acts. Originally vaudeville cant by 1905. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1954 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM as "busy on the coast in a double act with his wife"; 1955 Dexter, 39, as "they worked a double act"; 1974 D. Wallace in Swami; 1976 Gill; 1984 F. Marshall as "a professional double act"; 1986 E. Warlock in LR as "she did a double act with her mother"; 1988 Sleight in Magigram;
n. A bill tube within another tube. [rare]
n. A false bottom (see).
1.n. Two playing cards handled as one; a double (2) being the less usual synonym. [fairly common] REF: Ascanio, About the Handling of Double Cards (1982 tr).
(See also: Double Undercut.) n. The undercut sleight done twice in succession; a double cut. [fairly common]
n. The dove production where the magus produces simultaneously two doves, one from each bare hand; twin dove production. [rare]
n. A letter envelope (or pay packet) faked with a secret compartment either inside one or at its back. [rare] This device was first exposed in 1584 by Reginald Scot.
n. A transformation (2nd type) between the magician and an assistant acting as a double. [rare]
n. A double-faced card (see) being the most usual synonym; a double card (3). [fairly common]

n. A trick coin with a different face on each side (such as the faces of an American silver dollar and an English copper penny). [rare] 303 Made from coins of identical diameter that have been halved and the two faces soldered back- to-back. Invented by 1584 when first described by Reginald Scot in telling of "A notable tricke to transforme a counter into a groat." Also mentioned in Guyot in his Nouvelle remembrances. Long unused by coinmen (as opposed to gambling cheats), the double-faced coin enjoyed a revival in the 1940s and 50s.
a. Said of a chafing dish (chick pan, dove pan, phantom tube, etc) whose commodious lid or other part is fitted with two separate load chambers. [fairly common]

(See also: back-and-front palm.) n. Any sleight, specifically an acquitment, that covertly transfers one or more cards (or a coin or thimble) back and forth from the front to the back of the hand, thereby permitting the entire hand to be shown apparently empty; the Continuous Front and Back Hand Palm (obsolete). [fairly common]
n. A false extra trouser pocket sharing the same vent, which can be shown empty. Compare top- of-pocket dodge. [rare]
n. A coin faked with either two heads or two tails. [very rare but not nonce] 305
n. The undercut sleight done twice in succession; a double cut. [fairly common]

n. Principle in apparatus design that places a fake partition in front of the real back wall to provide a place of concealment; false wall. [rare] This is the hidden method that works such apparatus as the Doll House, Jap Box, Milk Pitcher, and Modern Cabinet.
n. Effect of the vanish of a live dove between two 12x12x1/8 inch hinged boards. [rare]

n. A routine or complete act using dove magic. [rare] "I wanted to be like Channing [Pollock]. And I did well with the doves in the cabarets of Japan. There weren't many dove acts there." — Shimada interview in Clark (1976), 102
n. Effect where a rubber balloon is inflated and placed on a tray; and, when the balloon bursts, a live dove instantly emerges. [fairly common]

n. A fake bottle with an upper compartment to contain and pour liquid and a lower one, which when opened or, if of glass, broken, releases its load—a dove, usually with a previously borrowed and vanished ring, threaded on a ribbon tied around the dove's neck. [obsolescent] This trick was being performed as early as 27 Aug 1849 by J.H. Anderson at Balmoral Castle before Queen Victoria, when two doves were released. Explained in 1877 by Sachs, calling it "Bacchus' Dovecot".
n. A restraint that leaves the bird's wings free and, being camouflaged, can be left on after the bird is produced. Compare dove bag. [fairly common]

n. Conjuring with doves. [fairly common] "You cannot practice dove magic outdoors unless you have an unlimited supply of doves." — Gary Ouellet in Genii (Mar 1992), 358 308 Doves have been used by magicians at least as early as 1733, judging from Hogarth's illustration of Isaac Fawkes' performance at Southwark Fair that year when he advertised his "India birds". The first full dove routine was devised and presented by 1909 by Karl Germain. Developed as a complete act privately by Paul Fox. When popular Mexican magician Abe J. Cantu came to the USA seeking new material, Fox suggested a dove act and gave Cantu some of his innovations. Cantu publicly introduced the dove act by 1947. It was an instant sensation, quickly copied by several others including, most importantly, Jimmy Ravell, Tony Kardyro (in his "Señor Torino" guise adopted in 1950), Jimmy Rogers (by 1950s), Channing Pollock (1950s), Al "Chop Chop" Wheatley (1950s), Jimmy Reneaux (1950s), Ian Adair (since 1950s), General Grant (since 1950s), Ron Urban (late1950s-60s), Shimada (since 1960s), Kazuo Hatta (1960s), Goldfinger (since 1960s), Thomas Hylton, Lance Burton, Johnny Thompson, Joseph, Amos Levkovitch, James Dimmare (since c1982), and Tony Clark (since 1988). REF: Wade (1974); Cramer (1962), 26-31; Goodliffe (1946); Vernon in Genii (1966), 508; Kardyro (1955); Christopher (1973), 426.

n. A smaller (2½ to 5 inch deep and 8 to 10 inch diameter) version of the Duck Pan; the Chafing Dish (obsolescent). [common] Used to produce a live dove or similarly sized object from the load chamber in its suspiciously commodious lid. If fitted with only one load chamber, it may be termed a Single-load Dove Pan; if with two, a Double-load Dove Pan. Marketed by 1888 by Otto Maurer who called it a "Pigeon Pan".
(See also: Rabbit Trap.) n. A trap-table with an oval spring-hinged double-flap opening to vanish a bunny or bird; a Dove Trap (archaic). [archaic after 1924, formerly rare]
n. An injog where a playing card in a fanned deck is held perpendicular to the floor. Opposite of an upjog in position, although the latter move is usually done openly. [rare]

n. The deal-plus-shuffle that removes playing cards from a packet until only a single card remains by successively dealing the top card and moving the second card to the packet's bottom (or vise-versa) until only one card is left. [rare]
n. Sleight that switches a playing card in the process of dealing it onto the table. [rare]
n. The nose peek being the modern synonym. [rare]

n. A fictitious mentalist created in 1917 jointly by Claude Conlin ("Alexander"), Floyd Thayer, and Carl Owen to push Thayer's line of apparatus and tricks in mentalism. Conlin was later replaced by Bill Larsen. [rare]
n. The double-locking flap slate that automatically locks and is released by pressure on a secret latch. [rare]

n. The yellowish flash powder made from the pulverized spores of the lycopodium moss that ignites with a sparkler-type effect. [rare] Lycopodium powder was used as a flash powder by Hofzinser (died 1875). (Previously—by 1829—it had been used for the Dry Hand effect.) REF: Fischer/Hatch (1942/1985), 53.

n. Conjuring suitable for performing in the intimacy of a drawing-room; formerly parlor magic. [obsolescent due to the obsolescence of the word "drawing room"] From Standard English "drawing-room" since 1642. REF: OED/2.

a. Said of the stage scenery and costuming of an act. [rare] "The show [Kalanag's] is well dressed, generally speaking." — Robert Lund in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Nov 1957), 64 Originally theatrical cant since 1741. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1937 Annemann in Jinx #31 as David Bamberg's "is the most beautifully dressed show to hit these shores"; 1945 Dorny in Jean Hugard Testimonial as "a magnificently dressed show"; 1985 Roy & Andrews as "a wonderful act, superbly dressed and rich in fine magic"; 1986 Bamman in LR as "The illusions, all beautifully
v. To set-design and costume an act. [very rare but not nonce]
n. Novelty practical-joke faceted glass goblet that leaks on the dupe when he tries to drink from it. [fairly common]
n. A false count used with the Linking Rings trick. [rare]

n. A concealed mechanical gimmick that automatically delivers a succession of objects ready for production; an automatic holder; a loader (obsolete). [common] Depending on the specific object to be delivered, droppers may be variously distinguished as a ball dropper, card dropper, cigarette dropper, or coin dropper.
(See also: Indian Prayer Chain.) n. Effect where the top ring in a foot-long chain of interlocked metal rings repeatedly tumbles to the bottom ring on command. [rare]

term: Drum That Can(no)'t Be Beat(en), The
definition: n. The Drum Illusion (see) being the modern synonym. [obsolete]

n. Effect where innumerable items (silks, flags, ribbons, and finally a female assistant) are pulled from the paper covering of a large hoop; the Girl in the Drum; the Drum That Can't be Beat (obsolete). [rare] This is a larger version of the Tambourine trick. Probably invented, according to Ellis Stanyon, by William "Chung Ling Soo" Robinson, although not premiered by him. A pet effect of Professor Field (sometime in the period 1880-1895), Valadon (1903), Chung Ling Soo (Jan 1908), Chefalo (1913-37), S.S. Henry (around 1918-1933), Blackstone; and John Calvert (1939). REF: Stanyon in Magic (Mar 1904), 65, (Dec 1908), 20; Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 38; Waters (1988), 114; D.Bamberg (1965/1988), 212, where the invention is miscredited to Chefalo who did not even début until 1899.

n. A large wooden half-barrel (hexagonal or round) with double-hinged lids used to produce a duck or exchange objects. [fairly common] Worked by the mirror principle, its metal strap-bound wooden staves being doubly reflected. Pet apparatus of David Copperfield.

n. A shallow metal container (about 4½ inch deep and 14 inch diameter) with a long handle and a fitted lid of the same dimensions. A smaller version is termed a Dove Pan and a miniature one a Chick Pan. [fairly common] "From the very nature of the lid of the duck pan, deep as it is without apparent practical reason, it could be suspected." — Dariel Fitzkee, The Trick Brain (1944), 64 Used originally to produce a live duck and later any other object (such as a rabbit or small dog) that can be loaded into the capacious lid. Invented sometime between 1900 and 1905 by Belgian magician Servais Le Roy, although the same but smaller mechanism had been used earlier by other magi to produce smaller birds. Le Roy sold one to Carl Rosini who premiered it 316 in the U.S. around 1914. REF: Christopher (1973), 303; Olson (1966), 36, who mistakenly calls Le Roy's model a "Dove Pan".

n. Stage sucker effect where several ducks vanish from a wooden box on a draped table (perhaps protruding some feathers which prove to be a feather duster) and the table too can be taken apart to show only a skeleton frame; Where Did the Ducks Go? [rare]

n. A silent act being the more usual synonym. [obsolescent, formerly rare] A complete act performed in mime is a dumb act or silent act. In an otherwise talking act, a segment that is mimed is said to be performed in dumb show. In this context the adjective "dumb" carries no connotation of "stupid", merely that of "speechless", as in "struck dumb" or in "deaf, dumb, and blind". Originally vaudeville/variety lingo by 1907. REF: Marvello ad in Magic (Feb 1907), 40; White (1926); Carrington (1939). Thence magicians jargon by 1907 Marvello ad in Magic, 40, as "wanted ... showy tricks for dumb act"; 1943 Tarbell; 1986 Charvet, 30, re vaude.

1.n. Any object that mimics another, such as an imitation bottle, cigar, lit cigarette, water glass, human head, or billet; a fake being the more usual synonym. [rare] One common type is the shell; another is the Asrah.
n. A pasteboard carton faked with a load chamber. Used for color-changing silks. Not to be confused with the Die Box, which uses dice. [fairly common]

n. A cylinder (large or small) faked with a load chamber; a dyeing tube (obsolete); a changing tube (obsolete). Major variants are the large Phantom Tube = Ghost Tube and the Genii Tube. [common] Used for color-changing silks. Invented in 1892 or 1893 by David Devant on the suggestion of fellow magician G.W. Hunter. Premiered by Devant at the Royal Music Hall in Holborn, London. Devant's was the full-sized, visible tube and the forerunner of the concealed hand dye tube. REF: Hoffmann (1903), 241-242, 247-251, 303; Devant (1931), 61. Compare Goldston (1931), 151.
n. The Color Changing Handkerchief being the most usual synonym; silk dyeing. [fairly common] 319
n. A dye tube (see) being the later and now current synonym. [obsolete, formerly fairly common]

n. Topological method that permits a single playing card to appear to turn inside out. [very rare] This was the first application of mathematical topology to cards. Invented by Jeff Busby and first published by him in 1973 in his Into the Fourth Dimension. It was adopted the following year as both the method and effect of Roy Walton’s Cardwarp.
n. A display stand or rack. May be faked or unfaked. If for cards, it is usually called a card easel or card stand; if for coins, a coin easel or coin stand. [rare]

n. A magicians simulated evidence of psychic materialization from a ghostly figure. [rare] Originally a trick of spiritualists. First presented as a conjurors effect on 1 Oct 1906 at St. George's Hall, London, by J. N. Maskelyne as "A Side Issue" in an effort to win the £1,000 prize offered by Archdeacon Colley for reproducing the spiritualistic effect of ectoplasm coming from and returning to the side of the medium's body. Because Maskelyne performed only the first part of the effect, Colley declined to pay. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 151. Originally the cant of spiritualists by 1901 from its earlier (1883) coinage in biology. REF: OED/2; Keene (1976). Thence magicians jargon by 1929 Doc Nixon; 1939 Douglas cat; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1959 Corinda; 1967 Shiels in New Jinx #65; 1975 Woody Allen; 1987 Coleman; 1996 Silverman; 1997 Busby in Thauma; 1997 Waldman.
n. A playing card marked on a side. [rare] 321
n. A coin-palming position where the coin (or stack of coins or a finger-ring) is held obliquely between the base of the thumb and the palm of the hand. [fairly common]

n. Marked cards (readers) with tiny markings along the outer borders of the backs or along one side of the deck. Compare edge marking. [rare] First made commercially available to magicians by 1914 by Theodore DeLand in his "Four 322 Dollar Deck", which was simultaneously advertised to card sharps. Originally the argot of card sharps by 1927 Gibson, Bunco Book, 90; 1937 Radner. Also called by them "edge work" in 1932 Evans Secret Blue Book; 1933 J.H. Johnson; 1984 Ortiz; 1991 Munari; 1998 Busby. Thence magicians jargon as edge readers by 1942 B. Elliott in Phoenix #19; 1945 Gibson in Conjurors’ Magazine; 1947 Histed; 1958 Dexter, 136; 1984 Lyons orally; 1998 Busby.
See: Mene Tekel Board Educated Pencil. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Mene Tekel Board Educated Pencil".)

n. The part of a trick that the spectators are meant to perceive—not what really happens; a trick (2). In every trick (in that word's primary sense), the effect is shown while the method is hidden. Abbreviated as F/X and FX in the plural. [very common] Every effect can, in theory, be accomplished by at least two methods. In outlining how a specific trick is done, the plurality of conjuring how-to textbooks present it in two consecutive paragraphs, the first titled "EFFECT", the second "METHOD". Among the more influential authors who follow this practice are: Hilliard/Downs (1909), Proskauer (1936), Gibson (1942), Elliott (1943), Turner (1949), Ganson (1950), Bobo (1952), Corinda (1958), and Fulves (1981). "It is the effect which is all important as it is that which registers upon an audience immediately. The method should remain a mystery or the illusion is destroyed." — Lewis Ganson, Routined Manipulation, Part I (1950), 5 “The effect is all that counts, not the method.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jan 1952), 890 "In Magic, today as always, the effect is what counts. The method or methods used are always purely secondary." — Dai Vernon, 5 Aug 1954, in conversation with Jean Hugard "Get a good effect, and you have a good trick." — Bill Turner, The Card Wizard (1949), 94 "The number of magical effects is strictly limited, but the number of tricks is infinite." — Louis Histed, The Magic of Louis Histed (1947), 22 "While to a magician a modern method of doing an old trick will convert it into a new trick, to the layman it remains simply the same old effect." — Jean Hugard, Encyclopedia of Card Tricks (1937), 318 "Some day, I'm going to use an ‘electric deck' in my act just to prove the folly of spending months practicing effects that could be achieved by simpler methods." — Cardini in The Sphinx (Mar 1934), 4 "Although many of the effects are old, the methods used by the modern magicians are much 323 more sophisticated." — David Price, Magic (1985), 29
n. The version of Three-Card Monte for children where the three cards picture an elephant, a hunter, and a peanut. [rare]

n. A Ball Box shaped to hold and vanish a hen's egg. Now called the Egg Vase. [obsolete after 1924, formerly fairly common] This version of the venerable Ball Box was, in fact, the original model, having been in use as early as 1693 when first described by Ozanam.

term: Egg on Fan; Egg and Fan (Trick) [U.S.]
definition: n. The Sterling Egg Trick (see), being the original British synonym. [common]
n. Conjuring with hen's eggs. [rare]

(See also: Eggs from Mouth.) n. Effect where several hen's eggs are produced one-after-another from an assistant's mouth; the Human Hen. [rare] "The trick is not one suited for indiscriminate performance, but it is one highly appreciated by juvenile or bucolic spectators ...." — Professor Hoffmann, Later Magic (1903), 399 325 The original method used 3 or more real eggs and a sleight to make successive loads. By this method, a pet effect first of Bellachini/Berlach (around 1870), the reported inventor. Thence Hellis, the Herrmanns, and Hertz (by 1904), as well as several lesser magi. Later, collapsible egg-skins were adopted to permit a single load of 6 or more "eggs". A pet effect of Benito Chavez (1939). REF: Hoffmann (1903), 401; Hilliard (1909).
n. Modern synonym for the Egg Box (see). [rare]

n. Effect where several hen's eggs are produced one-after-another from an assistant's mouth; the Human Hen. [rare] "The trick is not one suited for indiscriminate performance, but it is one highly appreciated by juvenile or bucolic spectators ...." — Professor Hoffmann, Later Magic (1903), 399 325 The original method used 3 or more real eggs and a sleight to make successive loads. By this method, a pet effect first of Bellachini/Berlach (around 1870), the reported inventor. Thence Hellis, the Herrmanns, and Hertz (by 1904), as well as several lesser magi. Later, collapsible egg-skins were adopted to permit a single load of 6 or more "eggs". A pet effect of Benito Chavez (1939). REF: Hoffmann (1903), 401; Hilliard (1909).

n. Conjuring as originated and/or practiced in Egypt--ancient and modern. [very rare but not nonce] The world's earliest magician known by name was Dedi from southern Egypt around 2600 BC who performed for Pharoah Cheops. The most famous modern Egyptian magician was Luxor Gali-Gali who performed throughout the world 1910s-70s. REF: Edward William Lane, An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (London: 1836, 2 vols, 402+419pp); Clarke in Magic Wand; Paul Brunton, A Search in Secret India (1936; repr 1979, 288pp); Keel (1957).

n. Stage illusion—an elongation effect—where the head, feet, and hands of an assistant placed in a cabinet are stretched apart to unnatural distances; Stretching a Woman; the Stretching(2). [fairly common]
n. A magician's table secretly wired to work various tricks requiring electricity. [archaic]
n. Stage effect where an assistant in an electric chair vanishes when the electrical switch is closed. [archaic]

n. Effects worked by secret electronic devices. Compare computer magic. [rare] Pioneers were William B. Dobson who began designing electronic props for Bob Nelson in 1946 and in the 1960s the East Germans Herbert Paufler and Widano, the Dutchman Tony Anverdi, and the American Bud Morris. In the 1970s they were joined by David Howarth and Derek Lever.
n. Effect where playing cards in three or more separate stacks move up and down in their respective stacks, rather like a multiple version of the Ambitious Cards. [fairly common]
n. A concealed trap set into a stage, which moves up and down. [rare]
n. Effect where 11 playing cards dealt by a volunteer into the magicians hand repeatedly change in quantity. [rare]

(See also: Jardine Ellis ring.) n. A small metal hoop with a faked shell. [common] Used originally in a semi-sleight-of-hand version of the Ring-on-Stick trick, it has been adapted for a few other effects. It is a shell-ring switched for a genuine ring. A modern coin-like variant is the Hong Kong half.
n. Abbreviation of the Elmsley Count (see), which is the more usual synonym. [rare]

n. The 4-as-4 false count that conceals the third card down from the face in a 4-card packet; the Ghost Count being the original but now less usual synonym; contracted as an Elmsley; acronymed as an EC. Compare Jordan Count. [common]
1.n. Stage illusion where a female assistant is revealed behind different giant playing cards as they are moved about as in a Monte effect; Find the Lady (2). [rare]

n. An MC, which is the more usual spelling. [fairly common] Originally Standard English since 1933, as alternate abbreviation of "master of ceremonies". REF: OED/2. 330 Thence adopted by magicians by 1939 SAM Who's Who; 1946 Braue in HMM; 1949 Gardner in HMM; 1959 Joglar {Christopher] in HMM; 1969 Magicland cat #38; 1988 Waters; 1989 G. Anderson note to Whaley; 1992 Weldon in LR; 1992 Weill in Genii; 1993 Seabrooke; 1997 Salwak in LR. v. [as verb] [rare] Adopted by magicians by 1946 Braue in HMM as “Dorny ... emceed”; 1955 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM as to "emcee the affair"; 1993 McComb in Seabrooke as to "emcee a show"; 1998 Sandy in LR as “Todd Robbins emceed”. a. [adjectivally] [rare] Adopted by magicians by 1945 Thompson as "emsee [sic] work"; 1954 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM as “shared emcee duties”; 1997 Racherbaumer in LR as "good for emcee work". *emceeing [U.S.] g. To work as an MC. [rare]
n. Regal title appropriated as advertising puffery by a few early magi to imply they were more than mere Kings of conjuring. [obsolete after 1903, formerly rare]

n. Strippers trimmed to taper along the ends. Opposite of side strippers. [rare] End strippers are harder to detect than side strippers, which taper along the sides. All effects done with side strippers are possible with end strippers—and more. Originally the argot of American card sharps by 1884 Will & Finck cat; 1891 Quinn; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne; 1962 Garcia; 1973 Livingston. Thence magicians jargon by 1936 Holden cat #5; 1937 Hugard; 1939 Kanter cat; 1940 Annemann in Jinx #105; 1949 Hay; 1952 Farelli in HMM; 1960 Haines cat; 1969 Gibson; 1983 Racherbaumer; 1990 Wedler; 1990 Albrecht cartoon in Busby Xmas card; 1994 Munari ad in LR.

n. Refers among American magi to the old Half-dollar-sized British "copper" (actually bronze) penny, even after 1971 when Britain changed its coinage in size and to the decimal system. Britons then called it the "Old Penny" as opposed to the smaller "New Penny". [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]

n. Acronym of Entertainments National Service Association, the British equivalent of the American U.S.O. Established in 1939 at the beginning of WW II, it provided a venue for entertainers, including many magicians, to entertain British military personnel at home and abroad. The standard joke was that the initials stood for "Every Night Something Awful". Succeeded in 1945 by the Combined Services Entertainments (C.S.E.) [rare]

n. An evanishment being the more usual synonym; the act of a vanish. [rare] With this spelling, this word is most curious. It is not recognized by any of the standard English dictionaries. Moreover, it is etymologically incorrect, the Latin and Old French roots being, respectively, evanescere and evanir meaning to disappear from sight and cognate with the Standard English words "evanesce" and "evanescent". That those few who use it are among the more literate of magic writers tends to rule out mere illiteracy or typographical error. To them the word probably looks and sounds correct, although lexicographers would class it as a "spurious word" because of its mistaken etymology. In any case, "envanishment" is evidently an original coinage of magicians. REF: Bill Palmer, "Is Magic an Evanishing Art?", Occasionally from CMSJr, No.11 (Spring 1992), 105-107.
n. A playing card faked with a pocket (at one end or side or in the middle); a pocket card. [rare] 332
n. The sleight that secretly substitutes one envelope (and its contents) for another. [rare]

(See also: sealed message reading.) n. Effect in mentalism where performer reads messages in closed envelopes; the envelope test. [rare] "One of the standard tests in the field of 'mental magic' has long been the reading of messages placed in sealed envelopes." — George G. Kaplan, The Fine Art of Magic (1948), 211. Done by the one-ahead method, the first envelope to be read being either that of a stooge or made transparent with alcohol.
n. The Professor's Nightmare (see) being the most usual synonym. [fairly common]

n. A magician specialized in an acrobatic or balancing act. [obsolete] Originally Standard English by 1760 from the French équilibriste. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1816 Gyngell, London playbill; 1861 Kirbye; 1871 Satsuma Troupe, Boston playbill; 1888 Maurer cat; 1900 Mahatma; 1900 Everette ad in Magic; 1904 Stanyon in Magic.

n. A method of forcing that depends on intentional ambiguity in the magician's instructions to the spectator; a verbal "Hobson's choice". Less often called conjurer's choice or magician's choice. [common] This method was first exposed and published in 1785 (Decremps) as used by French magicians. "Equivoque is one of the most valuable tools to the mentalist, if it is used properly. If it is handled poorly, it is embarrassingly transparent to the audience. If it is worked successfully, it is straightforward mindreading—without gimmicks or props." — Phil Goldstein, Verbal Control (1976), 2 Standard but rare English in its minor sense of words used with double meaning in an attempt to deceive from 1616 (Ben Jonson) to 1877 (J. Morley). REF: OED/2. Thence (with spelling variants noted) common jargon among English-speaking magicians since at least as early as 1877 Hoffmann; 1909 Hilliard as "the familiar ‘your right or my left' equivoque"; 1937 Hugard; 1937 Sharpe as "equivoke"; 1948 Fitzkee/Buckley; 1950 Hay; 1980 Anderson; 1980 J. Marshall as "equivoces"; 1983 Cassidy; 1988 Waters; 1989 G. Nielsen audio; 1991 Flora flyer; 1991 Ortiz; 1992 Webster in Genii; 1993 Krenzel in LR; 1993 Earle in MUM; 2003 Eldridge in MagiCurrents. 333

n. Old word for magic. [obsolete] Originally Standard French and from the French word escamot (ultimately of Arabic origin) meaning a cork ball and referring to the Cups-and-Balls trick. Borrowed by Standard English. Began to be replaced in both French and English by prestidigitation after 1815 but still current in English as late as 1855. REF: Robert-Houdin (1868/1877 tr), 42.

n. Old word for magician. [obsolete after 1891] Originally Standard French and meaning one who works with cork balls. Borrowed by Standard English as early as 1749. Gradually replaced (after 1815 in French and after 1832 in English) by the newly minted prestidigitateur and, later (in English), prestidigitator, although still used in English as late as 1855. English-speaking magicians jargon by 1864 Simmons, Boston newspaper ad; 1891 Cazman, London program; 1992 335 Randi as French term; 1997 Bluemle in LR; 1997 Waldman. NOTE: The very rare variant "escamotos" was used (coined?) in 1855 by James Savren (Maidstone playbill).

1.n. Any effect where an escape artist frees himself from a restraint such as a knot, handcuff, thumb cuff, strait jacket, sealed container, or jail cell. The method used is called a release. [very common] "Escapes have been one of the most intrigueing phases of magic ever, probably because they more closely approach the supernatural than other types of trickery." — Annemann in The Jinx (1939), 396
n. A magic act involving escapes. [fairly common]

n. A magician who specializes in escapes; an escapologist; an escapist; an Escape King (obsolete) [common] "Don't insult me by calling me a magician. I am an escape artist. In America if you shake any tree a dozen magicians will fall out." — Houdini, 1910 Australian press interview as quoted by Gresham (1959), Ch.23 Houdini was the most celebrated and possibly the best of all escape artists; although, as he himself reported with uncharacteristic modesty, handcuff releases had been performed (by La Tude in France) as early as 1700. The late 1800s saw the work of the Davenport Brothers (posing as spiritualists), Maskelyne & Cooke, and Dr. Redmond. Houdini's bitterly resented leading contemporaries at the turn of the century were "Brindemour" (George W. Brown), Cirnoc, The Great Raymond, Nicola, W.M. Melmore, and "Cunning" (Robert Cunningham), and, later, Blackstone (in 1922). His main successors have been Hardeen (his brother), Murray, Mardoni, Sidney Radner (since 1941), Docweiss (1940s-60s), Alan Alan (since 1948), James Randi (c1950-1989), Howard Peters (1970s-90s), Hans Moretti (1970s-90s), Karl Bartoni (until 1980s when switched to mentalism), Shahid Malik (1970s-90s), Jason Randal (1970s-90s), Norman Bigelow (since 1972), Nick Janson (1980s-90s), Paul Mathews, David De-Val (1980s-90s), Steve Baker, John Novak, and Dean Gunnarson (since 1982). 336
n. An escape artist. [obsolete, formerly rare]

n. Escapology being the more usual synonym. [rare] "Most types of escapism, as with conjuring deception, must protect their secret methods: hidden keys, faked construction, or clandestine assistance." — John Booth in The Linking Ring (Aug 1997), 81
See: escape artist. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "escape artist".)

n. An escape artist being the most usual synonym. [fairly common] “For sheer enterprise Randi tops the current crop of escapologists.” — Frank Joglar [Milbourne Christopher] in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (May 1958), 134

n. The branch of magic specialized in escapes; escapism. Opposite of enterology. [fairly common] 337 "To me, Escapology has always seemed one of the most boresome forms of stage entertainment." — Charles Waller, Magical Nights at the Theatre (1948/1980), 157

n. Nickname of the Jornadas Cartomágicas [Cardmagic Journeys], since 1974 the annual international two-day workshop of card magicians held in the Spanish town of Escorial. Sponsored by the Escuela Mágica de Madrid. [rare]

n. A deck of 25 cards whose faces alternate the five standard ESP symbols: circle, cross, three vertical wavy lines, square, and star; Rhine Deck. Compare Zener cards. [common] "Long before ESP cards were invented, mentalists were presenting a twenty-five-card test utilizing ordinary playing cards, chosen at random from a fifty-two-card pack." — Dunninger, Dunninger's Secrets (1974), 183 Originally devised in 1930 by Dr. Karl E. Zener (1903-1961) of Duke University's Psychology Department for use in Dr. J.B. Rhine's early tests for telepathic ability. Copyrighted by Rhine and first marketed by him in 1937 as "ESP Cards", substituting a square for Zener's original rectangle. Thence introduced to magic in 1938 by Ted Annemann for mental effects and other tricks. Originally dubbed "Zener cards" in 1930 by Dr. Rhine who by 1936, after Dr. Zener left his research program, renamed them "ESP cards". Rhine's fellow parapsychologists adopted both terms but soon came to prefer the latter. REF: Abrams (1992), 281n-282n, gives a brief history of variant ESP decks used by magicians. Thence magicians jargon (with variant noted) in 1938 Annemann; 1941 Rickard in Genii; 1948 Holden cat #15; 1949 G. Anderson; 1951 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1955 Mellon in Mental-Wise; 1959 Corinda; 1959 Nelson cat #26; 1959 338 Owen cat #5; 1960 Haines cat; 1965 Mulholland; 1966 Inzani-Henley cat #1; 1971 Cox; 1972 L. May in Swami as "E.S.P. Cards"; 1973 Dalal as "E.S.P. Deck"; 1974 Dexter; 1978 Müller as "E.S.P. Deck"; 1978 Becker; 1979 Lamb as "ESP cards"; 1981 Cassidy in Vibrations; 1987 Hollywood Magic cat #16; 1987 Supreme cat as "E.S.P. cards"; 1988 Waters; 1989 Leveridge price list; 1989 Tannen cat #16; 1990 Select Magic price list; 1995 Tannen cat #18 as "E.S.P. Deck"; 1997 Lee cat #11 as “E.S.P. Cards”; 1997 Abbott cat #25; 1999 Busby & Osterlind.

n. Any method of card location that attempts to find the volunteer's chosen card by approximation. If done visually, the method is called Natural Estimation; if by touch, Mechanical Estimation. [rare] "One of the most talked about and least used 'sleights' in the armory of the card man is Estimation." — William P. Miesel (1986), 29 Probably invented by German-American dealer A. Roterberg and first published by him (1897, pp.71-72) as the method for his "The Lost Found" effect. Reappeared in T. Nelson Downs (1909, pp.137-138) as the otherwise unnamed "Fourth Method" for "locating a chosen card". A pet sleight of Downs (by 1909), Morris "Moe" Seidenstein (since 1930), John Steranko (by 1962), Edward Marlo (since 1962), Frank Thompson (by 1964), Jeff Busby (by 1980), and Bill Miesel (by 1980) REF: Busby in Miesel (1986), 51-54; Larsen Jr, Genii (Nov 1962), 112; Müller, Estimación (1986).
n. A pack of playing cards faked to be simultaneously readers and strippers. [fairly common]

n. An embellished variant of vanish, which is the much more usual synonym; envanishment [spurious?]. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common] Originally Standard English throughout the 1800s but since obsolescent. REF: OED/2; Merriam-Webster 3rd International. Thence preserved like a "dragon in amber" in magicians jargon by 1900 Stanyon; 1901 Selbit; 1914 B. Hull; 1927 Orrin; 1932 Deveen; 1932 Vernon/Ross; 1940 Annemann in Jinx #76 as "the evanishment of knives"; 1940 Hugard & Braue; 1943 Welles playbill; 1944 Fitzkee; 1946 Farelli; 1947 Boston & Parrish; 1947 T. Elliott in Gen; 1952 Okito/Parrish; 1953 B. Elliott; 1954 Joseph as the "evanishment of a elephant"; 1956 Warlock; 1959 Owen cat #5; 1976 Gill; 1985 Lewis; 1990 Dawes; 1992 Bill Palmer in Occasionally from CMSJr; 1994 Parrish; 1997 Busby in Thauma #35 as “obsolete”. 339 NOTE also adjectivally as "the evanished lady" in 1966 Cramer, 39; and "an evanishing art" in 1992 Palmer in

n. A small spring-metal stationery clip (also popularly known as a "bulldog clip") fitted with a hook. [rare] Used as a utility holder, particularly for cards or a coin (making it an improvised hooked coin).
See: Expanding Cube. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Expanding Cube".)
n. Effect in coin magic where one coin joins another wrapped in a handkerchief held by a volunteer. [rare]

n. A magician who discloses trade secrets to the lay public. [rare] "I am strongly opposed to ‘exposers' whether on the stage or in magazines addressed to the general public." — Prof. Hoffmann in The Sphinx (Dec 1914) "Strange that exposers do not realize that they are killing the game that is bringing them their daily bread." — Houdini in M.U.M. (Dec 1918), 4 "It is needless to remark that he does not expose any of his own program tricks. Exposers never do." — Annemann in The Jinx #23 (1936), 146 "Even the first exposer, Reginald Scot, apologized for giving the game away, and only did so to prove how easily men's minds can be beguiled." — S. H. Sharpe in Devant, Secrets of My Magic (1936), 15 343

n. Disclosure to the lay public of the method behind a trick; exposé being the less usual synonym. [common] “It is a fact that in the so-called Golden Age of Magic of a generation ago exposure was more rampant than it had ever been. All the ‘greats’ — Maskelyne, Devant, Servais LeRoy, Goldin, Houdini and many others, divulged treasured secrets in the pages of popular magazines and newspapers.” — Jean Hugard in Hugard’d Magic Monthly (Dec 1944), 86 "All magicians...denounce the exposure of conjuring secrets to the general public; but there is no general agreement whatever about what constitutes exposure." — Henry Hay, Cyclopedia of Magic (1949), 212 "The yellow thread of exposure seems to be inextricably woven into all fabrics whose strength is secrecy, and experience proves that it is much easier to become fire proof than to become exposure proof. It is still an open question, however, as to what extent exposure really injures a performer." — Houdini, Miracle Mongers and Their Methods (1920), 98 "It has been my experience that more secrets have been revealed by the poor performance of amateurs, who squawk at exposures." — Fulton Oursler in The Linking Ring (Jan 1941), 830 "As a general rule, any exposure should be reserved exclusively for instances where pretenders to the supernatural are involved; not those who stop with claims of only the supernormal." — Dunninger, Dunninger's Secrets (1974), 235 "Magic suffers more from lethargy and stagnation than from exposure." — A. M. Wilson in The Sphinx (Jan 1927)
n. A false count of three cards that handles two as one, replacing the pair beneath the single card. [rare]
v. To bring the two halves of a deck of playing cards face-to-face; facing the deck. [very rare but not nonce]
n. A pack of playing cards where the bottom packet is face-to-face with the top packet. [rare]
n. A gaffed card version of the false palm adapted to a playing card printed with a back pattern in color and pattern to match a human hand to allow the shown genuine card-face to be vanished. [rare]
a. Genuine; real; true; ordinary. Opposite of false or blind. [rare]

(See also: Card Star (1).) 1.n. Mechanical apparatus that automatically produces five chosen playing cards at the tips of five points of a large metal star mounted on a stand; the Cabalistic Star (obsolete); the Fairy Star (obsolete). [obsolescent, once common]

n. Any of several false knots (in rope, string, or a silk) that simulate real ones; false knot being the less usual synonym. [fairly common] First described for a magic trick in 1584 by Reginald Scot in explaining how to convert a square knot into a slip knot (under cover of a handkerchief).

See: trick card faking g. Making a fake; generally, gimmicking; specifically, marking, etc. [rare]. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "trick card faking g. Making a fake; generally, gimmicking; specifically, marking, etc. [rare]".)

n. A commercially marketed set of 52 variously faked playing cards—blanks, double-backers, double-facers, misspots, etcetera, one or more of which to substitute for real cards in a regulation deck. Hence the occasional usage "Fa-Ko Deck" is, technically, a misnomer. [fairly common] Conceived by Syl W. Reilly, copyrighted in 1927, and first marketed by Nelson Enterprises in 1928. Later (by 1936) marketed by Reilly himself and (since 1960) by Haines House of Cards.

n. The secret compartment at the base of certain apparatus; a double bottom (obsolete) Compare false wall. [fairly common] "There be divers juggling boxes with false bottoms, wherein manie false feates are wrought." — Reginald Scot, The discouerie of witchcraft (1584), Bk.XIII, Ch.31 This is an ancient principle in magic. For example, Albertus Magnus (1193-1280), the great 13th-century philosopher, scientist, theologian, Dominican priest, and teacher of Thomas Aquinas, was not above practicing some natural magic. His goblet, used for dispensing potions to his patients and now in the Historical Museum in Cologne, has a false bottom to conceal an emetic. And the above quote from Scot proves that the false bottom was a standard device by 1584. It continued in vogue until the early 1800s after which it declined in popularity. 349 REF: Dawes (1979), 21; Robert-Houdin (1868/1877 tr), 24.
n. A trick card (see) being the modern synonym. [obsolete]
n. Method by which the number of objects (such as cards, coins, or pieces of paper money) seems more or less than its real total; also simply a count (1). [common]

n. Any sleight where a deck of playing cards seems to be fairly cut when, in fact, its original order remains undisturbed; less usually called a blind cut. [common] "Now I give the cards another false cut." — Penn Jillette in The New Yorker (15 May 1989), 62 This sleight was invented by card sharps and first recorded as used by British cheats at Whist in 1674 (Cotton). The term originated in the argot of card sharps as early as 1865 Evans, 20; 1915 Innis; 1924 Henderson. 350
n. Any dealing of a deck of playing cards that appears fair but is not. Major examples are the bottom deal, second deal, and center deal. [rare]

(See also: Sixth Finger.) n. A simulated human digit, hollow and flesh-colored, added to the magician's hand as an inconspicuous extra middle finger; false finger (fairly common); extra finger (obsolescent); hollow finger (obsolete); Slik Silk. [common] Being hollow, it is used for the production of silks. This device was first described in 1896 for this purpose by both Charles Bertram and August Roterberg. Maurice Garland was using it by 1903 when reported in Hoffmann’s Later Magic. Gary Darwin attributes its invention to Charles Morritt. REF: Magic Wand (1934), 149; Bertram (1896), 238-239: Darwin (1988), 19. "The customer at one of our display stands at a convention trying to insert the 'Sixth Finger' onto his middle finger — "It's rubbish" he stated, "It couldn't possibly fit anyone's finger". When I showed him that it was supposed to fit in-between the fingers and not to be worn, he didn't believe this." — Ian Adair in Trixigram (May 1988), 16 "After the handerkerchief is produced, false finger and handkerchief can both be handed out for examination." — Al Baker in The Sphinx (1930), 272

n. A simulated human hand used secretly to substitute for one of the magician's own hands, leaving the other free for surreptitious manipulation, particularly in the Full-Light Séance; the Third Hand. [rare] First described (using a false third hand on a telescoping rod) anonymously in the Oct 1898 issue of Mahatma. REF: Busby (1995).

n. A flesh-colored pad that can be held invisibly in the palm of the hand used to vanish a silk. Compare Fadeaway Card which hides the face of a playing card. [rare] First described in 1896 by Charles Bertram as a painted metal pad clipped to the sides of the hand to cover a load of two silks in the palm. In 1904 Stanyon described "The Palm Shield". Theodore DeLand invented and in 1908 marketed the Fadeaway Card, a playing card that could be invisibly palmed because its back was printed flesh-colored complete with lines and whorls. Al Baker developed his "Finger-Palm Fake", a flesh-colored cardboard pad, which when palmed would hide any small flat object such as a billet. This may have been an independent reinvention of the old device mentioned by Bertram. In any case Baker did not publish his version until 1951. In 1951 Frank J. Rigney invented one using flesh-colored 351 adhesive tape to form a pocket in the palm. REF: Bertram (1896), 239-240; Stanyon in Magic (Jun 1904), 86; DeLand catalog (1914); Baker (1951), 70; Rigney in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Apr 1951), 773.

n. Any sleight that simulates a fair shuffle of a deck of playing cards but serves another purpose such as retention of the deck's order, a transfer of a block or blocks of cards, or the placement of the deck into a controlled order; a blind shuffle. [very common] "False shuffles ... must simulate genuine shuffles." — Walter B. Gibson, Modern Card Tricks (1932) “What well-known cardman, working close-up, absent-mindedly began talking to himself: ‘All right. First I give the pack a good false shuffle, then a false cut!’ — and didn’t understand why the customers chuckled?” — Fred Braue in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Mar 1948), 403 This card-control sleight was first described being used by British conjurors in 1584 by Reginald Scot (also 1612 Rid; 1721 Neve; 1763 Dean; and 1800 Gale). This first false shuffle merely retained the top stock (of one or a few cards) by letting it fall last. Later both card sharps and magicians developed various versions including the Zarrow Shuffle, Push Through Shuffle, Pull Through Shuffle, and the Triumph Shuffle, all of which give full-deck control. Marginal examples are the Slop Shuffle and the Faro Shuffle. The noun form originated among card sharps by 1857 Green; 1865 Evans. Thence borrowed as magicians jargon by 1859 Secret Out; 1863 Parlor Tricks with Cards; 1876 Hoffmann; 1896 Bertram; 1905 Hilliard in Magic; 1907 Chung Ling Soo [Robinson] in Magic; 1911 Stanyon in Magic; 1926 Gibson; 1928 Merlin; 1946 Zovello in HMM; 1948 Norman; 1982 Okal; 1988 Waters; 1989 Maven in LR; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Busby in
n. The thumb tip (see) being the later synonym. [obsolete after 1905]

(See also: double wall.) n. Principle in apparatus design that places a fake partition in front of the real back wall to provide a place of concealment; false wall. [rare] This is the hidden method that works such apparatus as the Doll House, Jap Box, Milk Pitcher, and Modern Cabinet.
n. An arc of hand-held playing cards; a card fan. [common]
See: fanning deck. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "fanning deck".)

n. The first tradename for fanning powder. [obsolete since 1969, formerly rare] Introduced to magicians in the early or mid 1930s by ex-cop and gambling dealer-magician Audley Walsh using a then secret formula and marketed by him as "Fan-Ez". Later pirated by others using the same name or under thinly disguised variants such as Ireland's "Card Prep"

1.n. The method that induces a volunteer to choose a pre-selected card by feeding it into his fingers from a fanned deck; the classic force; the Hofzinser force; the force(2). [fairly common] This bold method for forcing a playing card was apparently used by conjurors as early as 1582, as implied by a baffled Girolamo Cardano's description of the performance of Neapolitan amateur Francisco Soma. The basic method was first exposed in 1584 by Scot (also 1785 Decremps; 1876 Hoffmann). Modern masters of this ruse have included Al Flosso, John Mulholland, and Dai Vernon.
n. A card manipulator who specializes in card fanning. [rare]

n. Zinc stearate, finely powdered, for dusting on playing cards to insure an even slickness when 354 fanned or otherwise manipulated; marketed under the tradename Fan-Ez. Also used in the Dry Hand trick. [common] Introduced to magicians in the early or mid 1930s by American ex-cop and gambling dealer- magician Audley Walsh using what was then a secret formula and marketed by him as "Fan-Ez". See Soo-Zee for the special box invented by Ken Allen in the 1950s to apply fanning powder quickly and evenly. REF: Art Johnston in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Sep 1955), 315.
n. A performer who creates visual fantasias or fantasies in the allied arts of magic, particularly with shadowgraphy and chapeaugraphy. [obsolete after 1897, formerly rare]
n. A small cabinet used to reappear silks tied onto a cross-bar from which they had been previously untied and removed. [rare]

n. A puppet show with string-operated marionettes. [obsolete, formerly fairly common] Standard English since 1771, from the Italian fantoccini, meaning little puppets. REF: OED/2; 1772 Carlo Perrico ad in Apr 1st The Gazetteer and New Daily Advertiser (London). Thence (with spelling variant noted) magicians jargon by c.1780 Flockton, British playbill; 1839 J.R. Smith ad in Rochester, NY, Daily Democrat as "Italian Fantocini"; 1855 Cremer ad; 1948 Waller, 143.
n. Stage effect where a boy masked and dressed as a farmer and a girl masked and dressed as a witch are transformed into each other in a double exchange. [rare]
n. A faro shuffle. [rare]

n. Apparatus used by mind-readers to get secret information on small cards. Compare Roller Box, which delivers on one long scroll. [rare] Used as early as 1922 (Dr. X) as a prompt in the question reading act. After a batch of the spectators' written questions have been stolen by confederates they copy them onto several small index cards and place in the upper section of the Faro Box. The mind-reader now gets the loaded box hidden in the lectern or under cover of a handkerchief holding the crystal ball or simply palmed under the ball.
