The mind-reader sees the question on the top card, announces it, gives an answer, and then pushes off that card with the fingers, dropping it into the lower section of the box and bringing the next question into view. Originally the cant of American card players by 1877 (E.M. Grandin pricelist; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne; 1896 How in Strand Magazine; 1941 Horowitz in Jinx), referring to the metal case (fair or gaffed) used for dealing cards one-by-one in the game of Faro. Similar in appearance to the box used today in Black Jack. This gaming device was invented, patented, and made in 1812 by Robert Bailey, an American gamester for use in his Faro banks. Known as "Bailey's patent box", it dealt fair; but, as Bailey himself noted, it was soon gaffed by others. REF: Robert Bailey, The Life and Adventures of Robert Bailey (Richmond, Virginia: 1822), 138-141. Thence (as adapted to a different device for mind-reading) magicians jargon by 1928 Thayer cat #7; 1936 Holden cat #5; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1945 Nelson in Thompson; 1952 Keller & Fetsch in Phoenix #261; 1954 Andrews cat #4; 1976 Owen cat #9; 1988 Busby annotation; 1992 Minch.

n. The visual verification of the equal division of a full deck or packet of playing cards after the start of the Faro interweave but before it is completed. [rare] In 1958 American cardman Ed Marlo claimed that "years ago" he had discovered this technique, which two other Faro cardmen have told me is too obvious to mention. Anyway, Marlo gets full credit as the first to publish and give a name to the "obvious". REF: Edward Marlo, The Faro Shuffle (1958).

n. The false shuffle where the cards interleave in a fully controlled manner; a Faro; the butt shuffle; the Weave (obsolete); the Wedge (obsolete). Compare In Faro and Out Faro. [common] Originally a popular card game around 1650 in France where it was called "Pharaoh" or 356 "Pharoo". The special shuffle was adopted by 1726 when it was first reported for cheating (by running up a split) by the anonymous The Whole Art and Mystery of Modern Gaming Fully Expos'd and Detected (pp.91-93). In 1843, J.H. Green in his An Exposure of the Acts and Miseries of Gambling (p.195) noted this shuffle's use in the game in the USA and calls it a recent innovation for "running in the cards". In 1894 J.N. Maskelyne described the shuffle in detail. In 1902 Erdnase mentioned perfect riffle shuffling but dismisses it as unnecessary for gambling cheating. In 1915 S.V. Innis mentioned tabled Faro Riffle Shuffles used for running up complex Poker stacks, Riffle Stacking, and the Reverse Faro. Perfect Faro Shuffles were being performed by C.T. Jordan in 1919, by T.N. Downs & Fred Black in the 1920s, and in the 1930s by Jacob Daley, Charlie Miller, Dai Vernon, and only a very few others. In 1940 Hugard & Braue publicized the shuffle as applied to magic and included Black's mathematical tables. Popularized by Edward Marlo in 1947. In 1956 Jerry Andrus contributed to this body of work. In 1957 Rusduck published the Stay Stack in his Cardiste. In 1957-58 Alex Elmsley did the first systematic analysis of the Faro Shuffle's mathematical properties and in his series of articles revolutionized magicians thinking on the subject of the Faro, defining new terminology. Later in 1958 Edward Marlo added many routines to this now standard sleight. REF: Diaconis in Science (30 Apr 1982); Busby in Epoptica #1 (May 1982), 40-43; S. Brent Morris, "On the Faro Shuffle", Linking Ring (Nov 1997), 77-81, & (Dec 1997), 59-64. Originally the cant of American card players by 1894 J.N. Maskelyne loosely as "the faro dealer's shuffle". “One of the oldest and prettiest of coin flourishes, though better known to the gambling fraternity than to magicians, is a one-handed faro shuffle of a stack of half dollars or poker chips.” — Martin Gardner in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jan 1951), 739 Thence magicians jargon by 1940 Hugard & Braue; 1946 Hamilton in Phoenix #111; 1947 Marlo; 1949 Bill Woodfield May 7th letter to A. Walsh; 1951 Gardner in HMM; 1958 Marlo; 1962 Lorayne; 1969 Gibson; 1969 Racherbaumer in Hierophant #1; 1978 Müller; 1979 Lamb; 1984 Close in Epoptica YB; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1994 Econ in LR; 1998 L&L cat; 2003 Beam in LR. v. To do a faro shuffle; to faro. [rare]
n. Effect where a flowerpot with feather flowers visibly and instantly vanishes from an undraped table at the magician's command. [rare]

n. Effect where numerous lighted paper lanterns are successively produced from a bowl of water or a box. [rare] First exposed using a Jap Box in 1876 (by Hoffmann, 395). The trick may be of Japanese origin, being described and explained in 1914-15 by Ishii Black in his articles on traditional Japanese magic where the production is from a bowl of water. However, Branson, writing in 1922 (p.6), gives an eyewitness account of this effect by Chinese conjurors. Originally the Europeans' term for the traditional Japanese Buddhist Bon festival that welcomes ancestral spirits to household altars. Thence magicians jargon by 1876 Hoffmann; 1934 Nikola; 1981 Ayling.

n. An effect; the overt part of a trick (2). [once very common, now just fairly common] "There be divers juggling boxes with false bottoms, wherein manie false feates are wrought." — Reginald Scot, The discouerie of witchcraft (1584), Bk.XIII, Ch.31 "If TV is your goal, you'll need an ever-expanding bag of tricks. To date, I've done more than 1,100 feats." — Milbourne Christopher in J. Marshall (1955), 18

n. Compressible imitation blossoms composed of dyed goose feathers. A standard production item. Compare Spring Flowers and Flower Dart. [fairly common] Used exclusively by magicians. As feather flowers were already in existence in Britain by 1911, they could not have been invented by American prop maker Horace Marshall (b.1902), as claimed by Gene Gordon. However Marshall was the leading producer by 1953. REF: Gordon (1980), 23, 362.
1.v. In general, to simulate an action. [obsolete, formerly rare]

n. An empty gesture that simulates the transfer of a small object from one hand to the other or to another place such as to make a feint of throwing or in apparently grabbing it; a sucker move; a type of throw-off. [fairly common] "The Feint is one of the most effective aids to the performance of magic. It is a basic principle. ... The true nature of the feint in magic is the perfect imitation of some act which is designed to mislead the minds or the attention of the spectator. Being executed with extreme dexterity the feint is taken for a genuine act." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Nov 1949), 598 "... the trick is embellished throughout with many ingenious and novel 'feints,' the object of which is to throw the expert magician completely off the scent." — Victor Farelli, John Ramsay's Cylinder and Balls (1948), 5 "And, as there is not a single 'feint' employed from start to finish, it cannot be classified as ‘conjuring for conjurers'." — Victor Farelli, John Ramsay's Triple Restoration (1949), 6 Originally French magicians jargon spelled feinte, from the Standard French feminine noun, by 1853 (Ponsin, I, 21; 1868 Robert-Houdin). Thence British magicians jargon by 1875 (Hartz, with French spelling "feinte"). 359 Thence Englished as feint in 1876 Hoffmann, 174, as "introduce a feint"; 1877 Sachs as "make a feint of throwing it away"; 1901 Garland in Selbit; 1912 Stanyon in Magic as "the sleights and 'feints' of Cup and Ball conjuring"; 1920 Teale; 1931 Farelli; 1938 Hilliard; 1952 Lorayne in HMM, 943; 1977 Galloway; 1979 Lamb; 1981 Grippo; 1985 Kaufman; 1988 Waters; 1995 Racherbaumer in LR; 1997 Ed Brown. v. To feign. [very rare, possibly nonce]
n. A card force that uses the Hindu Shuffle. [very rare]
(See also: Abdul's Fez.) n. An egg bag disguised as a North African fez; the Fez Egg Bag. [fairly common] 37

n. Effect where the magus produces flames from either or both palms of his hands, or mouth, or pockets, or elsewhere on his body. [rare] The pyrotechnic gimmick is made but not invented by Japanese pro magician-dealer Yutaka Kikuchi.
n. Effect where a 5¢ piece taken from his pocket vanishes when the magi closes his fist and then opens it. [rare]
See: Zen’s Cards and Envelopes. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Zen’s Cards and Envelopes".)

n. A ventriloquist's life-like alter ego; a vent figure; a dummy (3). Compare hand puppet. [fairly common, particularly among ventriloquists] "You will note that we never use the term dummy to describe any of the characters in this book. The word is not descriptive of the lifelike characters we want to create." — George Schindler, Ventriloquism: Magic with Your Voice (1979), 6 Among the more famous that have been operated by magicians (with their dates of performance and the names of their magician-vent operators) are: "Little Bobby" (1840s-70s, Antonio Blitz) "Sailor Jim" (Arthur Prince) "George Byron, Jr" (around 1904, Harry "The Great" Lester) "Marmaduke" (by 1906, John Warren) "Dennis" (by 1911, Al Baker) "Charlie McCarthy" (1922-78, Edgar Bergen) "Elmer" (since 1930s, Max Terhune) "Don Roque" (since 1930s, Paco Miller) "Lefty" (since 1946, Jay Marshall) "Windy Higgins" (Paul Stadelman) "Matilda" (since 1942, George Schindler) "Junior" (1940s, Loring Campbell) "Jennie" (by 1944, Gerrie Larsen) "Eddie" (since 1946, Johnny Carson) "Lamb Chop" (since 1957, Shari Lewis) "Melville" (Marvin Kaye) "Blas" (Mago Frank) "Shorty Harris" (by 1979, Terri Rogers)

n. Stage illusion where the magician interacts with the image of a female assistant on a movie 361 screen until, when the lights go up, she steps out of the screen in the flesh. Compare Movies to Life. [archaic] "The cost of producing the film, the necessity of always having the same girl, and the need of the services of a motion-picture operator, plus the fact that the illusion is suitable only for a regular theater stage—all were reasons why ‘Film to Life' belonged strictly to a large vaudeville act or a full evening magic show". — Walter Gibson, Magic Explained (1958), 169

1.n. The version of Three-Card Monte that uses a Queen (usually the Spade Queen) as the target card. [fairly common] Originally the argot of Three-Card Monte card sharps by 1920 S. Collins, in England; 1920 Hertz; 1932 Mulholland. Thence magicians jargon by 1931 Cannell; 1933 Davenport cat; 1935 Grant; 1947 Fleischman & Gunther; 1950 Hay; 1955 T. Cooper in Magic Wand; 1956 Dexter; 1956 Ganson/Endfield; 1972 Sanderson; 1979 Lamb; 1982 Müller; 1986 Supreme cat; 1986 Dawes & Setterington; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1992 Randi; 1996 ["1997"] L&L cat; 1997 Abbott cat #25.
n. A small chopper that threatens to cut off a volunteer's finger; Finger Guillotine. [common]
n. A finger-flinger being the more usual synonym. [rare]

(See also: finger-flinging.) n. Performing sleight-of-hand; finger flicking. [common] "In these unfortunate days, when mere finger-flinging is regarded as ideal conjuring, the fact that all unnatural moves are bad, seems never to enter into the minds of the misguided." — J. B. Bobo, Modern Coin Magic (1952), 340

n. Magicians slang for a sleight-of-hand artist; a finger-flicker; a finger flipper. This is a mildly derogatory term when used by apparatus conjurers and mentalists. [common] "This word was originated by the late J. N. Hilliard to denote adepts in sleight of hand. I do not know if Mr. Hilliard intended the term to have a derogatory meaning, but that is the way it is now used." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1951), 816

n. Performing sleight-of-hand; finger flicking. [common] "In these unfortunate days, when mere finger-flinging is regarded as ideal conjuring, the fact that all unnatural moves are bad, seems never to enter into the minds of the misguided." — J. B. Bobo, Modern Coin Magic (1952), 340
(See also: Finger Chopper.) n. A small chopper that threatens to cut off a volunteer's finger; Finger Guillotine. [common]

n. Effect where the magician's finger penetrates a hat (usually borrowed). [obsolescent, formerly rare] Marketed to magicians as early as 1873 by J.M. Hartz in his catalog as "The Phantom Finger". The method became the basis for the later Knife through Hat and, thence, the Knife through Coat tricks.
n. The cigarette manipulation sleight that clamps a cigarette by its two ends between the tip and root of any finger. [obsolete since 1937, formerly rare]
n. The card discovery where the magician pretends to find the spectator's fingerprint on his chosen card. [very rare]
n. A sleight used to exchange billets. [obsolescent, formerly rare]
n. Method of holding a deck of playing cards at the fingertips of one hand in order to control the card that the volunteer has selected by a peek. 365 [rare]

n. A small tube holding a short piece of crayon and attached to an adjustable metal band to fit a finger or thumb. [rare] Useful in stage versions of mentalism where thick writing is desired for visibility. Invented by Don Tanner.

n. The knack of swallowing fire or other very hot liquids and objects. An allied art of magic. [fairly common] "Although not considered by the public as being equal to the wares of the magician, fire-eating is definitely a branch of the magic arts, depending on secret methods for its accomplishment." — David Price, Magic (1985), 24 An ancient and ever-popular art practiced by Greek jugglers as early as the 3rd Century BC. A specialty of Chinese magician Yan Yow in Philadelphia in 1853 and of Ching Ling FOO in the USA in 1898 with his Human Volcano routine. Among the proportionately few modern professional magicians who incorporated fire-eating into their acts have been Joseph Ovette (around 1900), William Robinson (by 1909), Edgar Benyon (from 1909 to 1968), Jean Hugard (by 1937 until 1945), Lenz (by 1939), Johnny Platt 366 (1940s), Ricki Dunn (1940s-50s), Amedeo, Donna Delbert (by 1949), Robert "Torchy" Towner, Howard Peters (1970s), Bob Sheets (in the 1980s), and Katlyn Miller (1980s). The Guinness Book of Records fire-eating record held by Reg Morris of England was broken on 14 Feb 1986 when Phenious Top of the Pop Top Cabaret Show in Orlando, Florida, extinguished 8,393 flaming torches in his mouth in two hours. REF: Dawes (1979), 54-60; Gresham (1953), 195-201; Linking Ring (May 1986), 60; Ogden (1993), 150-152.
n. A fire-eater (see), particularly as a publicity title to imply mastery of the art. [obsolete, formerly fairly common]
n. Conjuring with flames and inflamables. [rare]

n. A performer who strolls barefoot across a bed of hot coals. [rare] "The fire must be well burned, the ground surrounding it must be cool and loose. If any of my readers will do this, they can become fire-walkers overnight." 367 — Levante in The Sphinx (Oct 1932). Most notable of the very few fire-walking magicians was the Kashmiri, Kuda Bux, who, at the invitation of Harry Price, introduced fire-walking to England on 8 Sep 1935. An instant publicity sensation, Bux kept it in his repertoire until 1938. REF: Harry Price, A Report on Two Experimental Fire-Walks (London: 1936); Randi (1992), 217-218; Christopher (1970), 243-246, 249. Standard English since 1895. REF: OED/2.

n. Strolling barefoot across a bed of hot coals; a fire-walk; Hi-Watari (Jap.). Occasionally, an allied art of magic. [fairly common] Practised as a religious-mystical rite in several old cultures around the world, including currently in India, Sri Lanka, the Philippines, Japan, Fiji, and Hawaii. This interesting natural human physical ability (under exacting but simple circumstances) was revived in the mid-1980s as yet another popular "psychic" mind-over-matter fad in the USA, particularly for the more than 15,000 suckers who paid $100 (unrefundable for any who chickened out) to take Tony Robbin's 4-hour "Fear into Power" firewalk motivational seminar. REF: Baker & Nickell (1992), 178-180; Christopher (1970), 236-250; Ayling (1981), 150-152; Waters (1988), 133; William Poundstone, Bigger Secrets (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1986), 182-185. Standard English since 1899. REF: OED/2.
n. A wallet that when opened throws out a burst of flame. [rare]
n. Stage illusion where the assistant on a raised platform is wrapped in paper and set afire, vanishing from the paper and appearing in a water-filled tank on the opposite side of the stage. [rare]
(See also: Aerial Fishing.) n. Effect where fish are caught in mid-air by rod-and-reel; fish-catching. [fairly common]

n. The all too frequent tell-tale stuck-out-thumb during execution of certain sleights in card handling. 368 [rare] Originally gamblers argot by 1941 Vernon, Select Secrets, 5, as "Gamblers when referring to this glaring fault call it ‘The Fish Hook'." Thence introduced to magicians jargon in 1941 by Dai Vernon, Select Secrets, 5. Thence 1984 Busby orally; 1988

n. Acronym of the Fédération Internationale des Sociétiés Magiques [International Federation of Magical Societies]. [fairly common] Formally founded 5 Sep 1948 by leading Dutch magician Henk Vermeyden together with a few European magic societies. The first President was distinguished French magus Jules Dhotel. Holds a prestigious convention-contest (rotated among European cities and expanded to Japan in 1993), which is now held every 3 years, culminating in the award of a Grand Prix for excellence in magical performance plus other prizes in various categories. REF: Dif #3 (1974), 23-63; Camacho Barriga (1978-81), 90-98, 331-333.
n. Electronic apparatus that emits a brilliant burst of light. [rare]

n. Effect where a shuffled deck is divided among five spectators who each mentally select one 369 card. Then when the packets are gathered together and shuffled, the magician identifies each selection. Sometimes erroneously identified with the Princess Card Trick. [rare] The underlying mathematical principle was first analyzed in sufficient detail in 1813 by French geometer-mathematician Joseph Diez Gergonne (1771-1859) to become known as "Gergonne's Pile Problem". Card-magic versions were developed at the end of the 1800s and, more recently, by Al Baker, S. Leo Horowitz, Orville Meyer, Louis Histed, Paul Fox, Al Koran, Mel Stover, and Simon Aronson. REF: Gardner (1956), 33-41; Peter Tappan, The Impostress Princess (1986), ii, 3-16.

n. The telescoping (or sometimes folding) metal pole that produces a flag for the Flags of All Nations trick. [rare] The probably invented (and in its telescoping version) by Viennese semi-pro magician J. N. Hofzinser (died 1875) who used a 3-segment pole. REF: Fischer/Hatch (1942/1985), 88; and see under Flags of All Nations entry.

(See also: Flags of All Nations.) n. Effect where bits of tissue paper visibly grow in the magician's hands into a large display of cloth flags on flag poles; the Flag Trick. [archaic, formerly fairly common] First performed at a conference of German princes by Compars Herrmann (died 1887) using the flag staff telescoping-pole principle. The fact that Herrmann's principal inventor, J. N. Hofzinser (died 1875), also used this trick, a single (3-segment telescoping pole) flag production, indicates Hofzinser was the probable inventor of this particular effect and method. Later a pet effect of Buatier de Kolta (in 1875 in London), Charles Bertram (by Mar 1885), Yank Hoe (in 1885 in London), Karl Germain (from 1896), Melot Hermann (by 1901?), David Devant (by 1902), Carl Hertz, Edwin Maro, and Fred Culpitt. REF: Cramer (1962), 56; Fischer/Hatch (1942/1985 tr), 88-89; Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 93, 97, 203; Cramer (1966), 17-18.

(See also: Flags of All Nations.) n. Effect where bits of tissue paper visibly grow in the magician's hands into a large display of cloth flags on flag poles; the Flag Trick. [archaic, formerly fairly common] First performed at a conference of German princes by Compars Herrmann (died 1887) using the flag staff telescoping-pole principle. The fact that Herrmann's principal inventor, J. N. Hofzinser (died 1875), also used this trick, a single (3-segment telescoping pole) flag production, indicates Hofzinser was the probable inventor of this particular effect and method. Later a pet effect of Buatier de Kolta (in 1875 in London), Charles Bertram (by Mar 1885), Yank Hoe (in 1885 in London), Karl Germain (from 1896), Melot Hermann (by 1901?), David Devant (by 1902), Carl Hertz, Edwin Maro, and Fred Culpitt. REF: Cramer (1962), 56; Fischer/Hatch (1942/1985 tr), 88-89; Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 93, 97, 203; Cramer (1966), 17-18.

n. Effect where bits of tissue paper visibly grow in the magician's hands into a large display of cloth flags on flag poles; the Flag Trick. [archaic, formerly fairly common] First performed at a conference of German princes by Compars Herrmann (died 1887) using the flag staff telescoping-pole principle. The fact that Herrmann's principal inventor, J. N. Hofzinser (died 1875), also used this trick, a single (3-segment telescoping pole) flag production, indicates Hofzinser was the probable inventor of this particular effect and method. Later a pet effect of Buatier de Kolta (in 1875 in London), Charles Bertram (by Mar 1885), Yank Hoe (in 1885 in London), Karl Germain (from 1896), Melot Hermann (by 1901?), David Devant (by 1902), Carl Hertz, Edwin Maro, and Fred Culpitt. REF: Cramer (1962), 56; Fischer/Hatch (1942/1985 tr), 88-89; Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 93, 97, 203; Cramer (1966), 17-18.
n. A changing card faked by attachment of a hinged second playing card. [rare] First described in 1693 by Ozanam. Reinvented by John Brown (c.1830-1910) of London. REF: Goldston (1935), 228.

n. A spirit slate. Compare Dr. Q Slates. [fairly common] "The production of spirit writing on a slate by means of a flap, for which we have to thank the fradulent spirit mediums, is still a startling effect, provided that the flap is so disposed that its presence has not been suspected." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jul 1943), 7 Truesdell (1883) implies that the flap-method was already being used as early as 1872 by the American pseudo-psychic Henry Slade, the most likely inventor. Slade performed his slate tricks in England in 1876; and, by next year, a version of his flap slate (complete with a Slade- type nail-writer) was being sold in British magic shops when Edwin Sachs gave the first published description in his classic Sleight of Hand (1877). REF: Jeff Busby in Dominique Duvivier's Einstein's Blackboards (1996), 4. Originally the argot of fradulent spirit mediums by 1907 D.P. Abbott; 1922 Dr. X. Thence the jargon of mentalist-magicians by 1922 Dr. X, 62; 1931 Grant & Smith; 1931 Sellers; 1942 Goldston; 1942 Warlock; 1943 Hugard in HMM; 1946 Welles in Variety as "flap-slate"; 1950 Boardé; 1956 Christopher in HMM; 1959 Corinda; 1974 Dexter; 1976 Goldstein as "a set of locking flap slates"; 1977 Buffum; 1981 Scalbert; 1988 Waters; 1996

n. A fast-paced and startling magic act, one with flash (2). [rare] "It was a fast, nimble, flash act of 'press the button' magic." — "Cagliostro Jr" [Bruce Elliott] in The Jinx #129 (1941), 743 Originally vaudeville cant by 1929 (Bangor, Maine, Daily News), as "about the finest flash act we have ever viewed", in writing about a performance by Herman Hanson. Thence magicians jargon by 1930 Mulholland in Sphinx as "in this day of flash acts"; 1950 Elliott in Phoenix #214; 1958 Leroy in HMM re Goldin; 1986 Charvet, 30, re vaude; 1990 J. Thompson in Jeffreys; 1992 Pitts in LR.

n. An oblong piece of flash paper printed to simulate paper currency. [fairly common] First described in 1910 by Hatton & Plate as handmade. First commercially marketed in the late 1930s. REF: Annemann in Jinx (1939), 418.
n. Cotton wool chemically converted to nitrocellulose to make it ignite. Used both for its own effect and as the primer for various pyrotechnical devices; flash wool (Brit.). [rare]
n. A sudden, startling, and highly visual effect—usually used to begin or end a trick or routine; flash magic; a flash (2.n.). [rare]
n. A cotton or linen fabric kerchief converted chemically into nitrocellulose (gun-cotton) so it can be ignited in a sudden burst, leaving no trace. [archaic, formerly rare]
n. Conjuring tricks (or a complete act of same) that have sudden, startling, and highly visual introductions or conclusions, that is, flash (2.n.); flash effect. [rare]

n. Tissue paper made of nitrocellulose to ignite in a sudden burst, leaving no trace. [very common] Used to cover the vanish or production of a small object. This device evolved from the flash handkerchief by 1882 when it was first described in Messrs. Hamley catalog. Old-time British magician S. Gibney recalled in 1908 (Magic Circular, 286) that Bland of London sold flash paper as "Lighting Paper" in the early 1860s—possibly a false memory of the date. The publication in 1937 of Stuart Robson's Tips on Flash Paper stimulated its subsequent wide-spread use. Flash paper and the Radio Cue Prompter are the only devices I know of that were borrowed from magicians by professional gamblers—a small return for all that the magi owe to the sharps. Flash paper is truly the bookie's friend because it permits instant evanishment of the evidence (betting slips) during a police raid. Also issued to American OSS agents in WWII to make destruct-at-will notes. REF: B. Elliott in Phoenix #177 (1949), 707.
n. A small bowl containing flash powder. Compare fire bowl. [fairly common] Used to produce a sudden large puff of smoke.

n. A powdered chemical used to produce fire and smoke. One type is dragon's breath. [rare] Originally the lingo of photographers by 1889. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1932 Gibson; 1971 Tannen cat #9; 1986 Allen & Cook saleslist; 1991 Butler orally; 1995 Kidwell in LR; 1997 Lee cat #11; 1997 Abbott cat #25.
n. Thin cord treated to vanish in a flash of fire. 374 [rare] A European (?) innovation first introduced commercially in the USA in 1954 by Bullseye. REF: Jay Marshall in New Phoenix (Sep 1954), 64.

n. A magician's wand that shoots a bright flame from one end. Compare the shooting wand, which fires blanks. [fairly common] Invention attributed to James "Jim" Collins (d.1942), formerly Houdini's British mechanician and assistant. REF: Tannen cat #1 (1949), 249.
n. Flash cotton (U.S.) [rare]
n. The first thin and horizontal version of the original thick and vertical Money Maker that seemingly prints paper money. [rare]
n. Comedy prop depicting a cloth cut-out bunny. [common]
n. A break between adjacent playing cards that is held by a small pinch of skin of a finger or heel of the hand; a flesh grip (obsolete). [rare]

a. Said of any gimmick painted to match the tint of the magician's hand or fingers. [common] "Too many magicians worry too much about getting the right shade of flesh color paint on their gimmicks. I remember when Max Malini was in Chicago, back in the twenties; he did the silk production from a handkerchief ball. ... It was the knob from a brass bed post—and he never painted it." — Stewart Judah in The New Phoenix #319 (1954), 83
n. Paint tinted flesh color. [fairly common] "To blend flesh color paint to your own hand coloring, add flesh-colored face powder." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Apr 1946), 210
n. The Jordan Count being the original and still more usual synonym. [rare]

n. Effect where a glass sheet or mirror wrapped in newspaper (or loosely-woven fabric) can be penetrated in several places by any sharp-pointed object and the whole piece folded over, yet when unwrapped the glass is restored; Bending Glass (Brit.). [fairly common]

n. Effect where successive wads of paper disappear before the volunteer's eyes while the audience sees the magician casually toss them over the volunteer's head; Paper Balls Over the Head being the less usual synonym, one that tips the method. [fairly common]
1.n. The Vanishing Alarm Clock (see) being the more usual synonym.

(See also: Floating Wand.) n. Effect where the magician's wand floats at his fingertips; Floating Cane. Not to be confused with the Anti-Gravity Wand. [fairly common] Invention of this simple but effective trick is almost universally attributed to the great Viennese magic innovator, J.N. Hofzinser. Unhappily, although this claim was initially propagated by both Prof. Hoffmann and Ottokar Fischer, neither bothered to document—much less date—their assertions. This quite possibly true legend was first challenged by Henry Hatton who noted that the effect was being publicly performed by Compars Herrmann by 1869 (probably using thread as did Hofzinser). However, as it is now known that Herrmann got many of his tricks from Hofzinser since they met way back in 1851, Hatton's evidence actually buttresses the claims that Hofzinser invented it. In any case, Alfred "The Fakir of Oolu" Sylvester saw Herrmann's perform the Floating Wand at the Academy of Music in New York City and immediately pirated it for his own repertoire, but inventing as method the needle-gaffed wand, even to the point of rather unpleasant pain. Sylvester was unquestionably the first to perform it in Britain, doing so in 1873 as "The Mesmeric Suspension Wand." Later a pet effect of Charles de Vere (in 1871- 73), J.M. Hartz (by 1873), Ottokar Fischer, Fredo Marvelli, Jeff Busby (around 1961), and Carl Wiesinger. REF: Fischer (1942), 294-296; Hatton in Sphinx (Aug 1906), 66; Fischer (1910); Sharpe (1931/1973); Clarke in Magic Wand (1926), 208-209, (1928), 35; Sachs (1877), 161.

n. Effect where a small cork freely moves and jiggles in front of the magician's body. [rare] "The greatest close-up trick I have ever seen in my life." — Ken Brooke, The Ken Brooke Series #5 (1981), 1
n. Generic term for any effect involving suspension or levitation of a female assistant. [fairly common]
n. Stage effect where a baby-grand or spinet piano levitates; Onaip. [rare]
n. Table Lifting (see) being the original and still more usual synonym. [rare]
n. Stage effect where a violin floats in mid-air. [rare]

Unhappily, although this claim was initially propagated by both Prof. Hoffmann and Ottokar Fischer, neither bothered to document—much less date—their assertions. This quite possibly true legend was first challenged by Henry Hatton who noted that the effect was being publicly performed by Compars Herrmann by 1869 (probably using thread as did Hofzinser). Sylvester was unquestionably the first to perform it in Britain, doing so in 1873 as "The Mesmeric Suspension Wand." Later a pet effect of Charles de Vere (in 1871- 73), J.M. Hartz (by 1873), Ottokar Fischer, Fredo Marvelli, Jeff Busby (around 1961), and Carl Wiesinger. n. Any display of manual dexterity (with cards, coins, balls, fans, etcetera) that involves no sleight- of-hand and no intent to deceive, only to astonish by its sheer skill; an ornamental sleight, in the evocative phrase of Robert-Houdin and Hoffmann (1877) or "the airs and graces of legerdemaine" in Hay's flowery wording (1950). Collectively, flourishes are called manipulative magic (2). [common] "A series of brilliant flourishes leaves only the impression of juggling skill on the minds of the onlookers, and the performer's feats are dismissed by them with the remark, ‘He's clever with his hands.'" — Hugard & Braue, The Royal Road to Card Magic (1948), 37 “One of the oldest and prettiest of coin flourishes, though better known to the gambling fraternity than to magicians, is a one-handed faro shuffle of a stack of half dollars or poker chips.” — Martin Gardner in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jan 1951), 739 "To me, one flashy new flourish is worth ten invisible sleights." — Paul Harris, orally, quoted in Epoptica, No.2 (1982), 105 Robert-Houdin claimed (in 1858) to have coined this word in this sense around 1830.
n. Effect where a flower instantly appears in the bottonhole of the magician's jacket. [rare]

n. A dart with a feather flower at its rear. [fairly common] 383 Used mainly as a comedy prop. In use by 1886 as described in the Peck & Snyder catalog of that year when they were called "Aerial Flowers".
n. Conjuring with flowers, usually artificial ones. [rare]
n. An hypnotic trance, in a facetious sense as contraction of "influence". [rare] Standard English and in precisely this sense by 1909 as "Put the fluence on". REF: OED/2.
n. The false count that apparently shows all the backs or faces of the cards in a small packet to be the alike when in fact they are not. Not to be confused with the Hamman Count. [rare]
n. Card effect where magician shows a 5-card fan (4 Queens & an Ace), puts them under a handkerchief, removes one and shows both sides, and the Queens have vanished. [very rare]

n. The effect of flying freely about in the air as opposed to a mere levitation. [new] 384 Introduced as a magic effect by French illusionist Georges Méliès at the end of the 1800s. The assistant in a concealed body harness was suspended by invisible wires from a trolley running along a monorail hidden in the flyloft. Flight was limited to one horizontal direction as well as raising and lowering. A mid-air walking all around and upside-down over the stage area was advertised in the 1920s as "Raffanell the Air Lady" in a Reinholt Pfalz Catalogue A ("Illusions"). REF: Alexander Adrion, Die Kunst zu Zaubern (1978) includes a sketch of the apparatus; Wittus Witt in ABC of Faxic, No.26 (22/23 Jun 1992), 1, and #53 (8 Dec 1993), 1. The simple shoulder-and-back-harness with a single wire method used in the flying scene in the stage productions of Peter Pan by Margaret Lockwood (1949, 1950) and Mary Martin (.....) were too obvious to count as serious illusions. A better waist-and-hip harness with two wires was used by Sheila MacRae in her early 1960s nightclub act with Gordon, permitting considerable manoeuverability but requiring lengthy rehearsal. Re-invented (using a different principle, at least from that of Méliès) by John Gaughan and David Copperfield in 1991. Gaughan had built the first prototype — the levitation part — in 1984 for Orson Welles who never performed it. Convincing David Copperfield to include this levitation in his act, Gaughan built ten further prototypes until he and Copperfield worked out the flying part. Copperfield premiered it in 1991 in his touring show and it appeared in his 31 Mar 1991 CBS annual magic special. Lee Pee Ville presented a pirated version at the Berlin Wintergarten during 1993. REF: Gary Ouellet, "Flying: Live the Dream", Genii (Jan 1992), 196- 197; Ouellet telephone conversation with Whaley, 12 Mar 1992; Wittus Witt in ABC of Faxic #30 (31 Jul 92), 1, #43 (11 Apr 1993), 1, and #53 (8 Dec 1993), 1; Sheila MacRae, Hollywood Mother of the Year (New York: Birch Lane, 1992), 134.
n. The Vanishing Birdcage being the later but now most usual synonym. [obsolete after 1928, formerly fairly common]
n. Cards Across (see) being the usual current synonym. [obsolescent, formerly rare]
n. Effect where the assistant sits on a carpet supported by two screens which, when removed, leaves the carpet and assistant suspended in mid-air, as proven by the passing of a hoop. [fairly common]

(See also: Coins Across.) n. Classic effect where four coins pass invisibly from hand to hand; Flying Eagles (obsolete). [fairly common] "Perhaps the most popular of all coin routines to perform on the street is the classic Coins Across." — Michael Rubinstein, Inside Street Magic (1985), 11 "It seems like every coin worker has at least one version of 'Coins Across,' a classic of coin magic." — Peg Shickler in M-U-M (Oct 1997), 34
n. Stage effect where a playing table-model phonograph vanishes from the magician's hands under cover of a cloth. [archaic]
n. Stage effect where the magician's assistant is transposed from one cage suspended above the stage to another. Pronounced FLY-TWO. Also The Flying Visit (obsolete). [fairly common]
n. Acronym for favorite method. [very rare, probably nonce]
n. The one center of interest at any given moment during performance of a trick; the point of focus. 386 [very rare]

n. A metal coin faked by sawing it into two or more strips and hinging them together. [common] Used mainly for the Coin in Bottle effect and as the essential gaff in the Coin Wand. First described in 1876 by Hoffmann (p.203). Since that time the segments have been held together either by a thin rubber band running in a groove cut around the coin's rim or by precision-made spring-steel hinges.
n. A folding coin made from a U.S. half-dollar piece. [fairly common]
n. Effect where 10 red and 10 black cards placed face down in two piles transpose when handled. [fairly common]

n. A metal canister used to produce or vanish loads (usually liquid); the Ching Ling Foo Water Can (obsolete). [very common] It is a fake, fitted with a secret load chamber, controlled by whichever side the magician choses to pour from. Introduced to Western magic in 1898 by "Ching Ling FOO" (Chee-ling QUA), the most famous Chinese magician to perform in the West. One Westernized adaptation is the Invisible Bovine (= Foo Milk Can).

Jones in Genii; 1986 Supreme cat; 1986 Hades cat #2; 1987 West in LR; 1991 Ouellet in Genii; 1994; 1997 Kennedy Enterprises ad in LR; 1997 Lee cat #11; 2003 Riser in MUM. 1.n. Generally, any one of several methods that gives the volunteer a false sense of free choice, while he picks the object, number, or color that the magician has induced him to select. [very common] A fan force method to force a playing card was seemingly being used by the Neapolitan conjuror, Francisco Soma, as early as 1582 (Cardano). Two years later a fan force was admirably described by Scot (1584). In his posthumously published Sylva Sylvarum: or, A Natural Historie (1626), Francis Bacon (died that year) analyses the process of forcing a card, which he characterizes as "a Juggler's trick". Other variants with cards are the cut force and the knife force. A useful distinction was made in 1950 by C.L. Boardé between what he termed a Strict Force where only one thing is offered and the Ranging Force where the choice is among an array of, in fact, identifiable objects.

n. A false count that enumerates a packet of four cards but hides one by counting another twice. [rare] The first version, the Jordan Count, was introduced by Charles T. Jordan in 1919. Second was the Elmsley Count published in 1959 by Alex Elmsley. REF: Brooke #4 (1981), 10.

Thence magicians jargon by 1921 Lustig as to "'frame' up an act"; 1921 Dornfeld [sic] as "frame up some illusion act"; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1969 Christopher as "they framed an act"; 1972 Griffin as "we first framed our show for one nighters"; 1976 Reynolds; 1985 Price as "he managed to frame a fifteen-minute show"; 1988 R.W. Scott in LR as "learning how to frame their own show"; 1988 Parrish in Genii as "frame the act"; 1996 Monti as "had framed his own platform show". framing g. Routining a magic act or show; to frame. n. The mathematical property that ensures that any deck with an even number of playing cards, if divided into two equal packets, randomly cut from the tops, counted, and replaced on the opposite bottoms and the two packets placed together, the enumerated cards will be separated by the same number of cards that were in one of the original packets. [rare] The underlying mathematical principle was discovered by American magician John P. Hamilton and published in mid-1948 in the instructions for his "Eyes of the Gods" card trick, which was marketed by Holden's. Subsequently elaborated by Gene Finnell in his book, The Free Cut Principle (1967). REF: Holden ad in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jun 1948), 436; Braue in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Aug 1948), 452.

n. The simplest pass used to vanish a small object by sleight of hand; the tourniquet (obsolescent). A minor variant is the pincette. [common] This sleight was first exposed in 1584 by Reginald Scot. Originally and still also called the tourniquet, but that French loan-word has been slowly passing out of fashion (except in France) since the term French drop came into use by 1876 Hoffmann; 1903 Carter; 1937 J.G. Alexander; 1941 Elliott in Jinx #146; 1942 Gibson in Phoenix #4; 1950 Ganson; 1951 Christopher in HMM; 1965/1988 Bamberg; 1973 Alain; 1976 Tarr; 1979 Lamb; 1980 J. Marshall; 1981 Ray-Mond; 1985 Eldin; 1987 Harkey in LR; 1988 Waters; 1989 Bob King in Q; 1990 Wedler; 1992 Weldon in LR; 1992 Burt ad in Genii; 1998 Ammar.
n. A medium-sized (6 feet high), light-weight (15 pounds) guillotine that resembles the larger, heavier versions, including the original decapitation device of the French Revolution. [fairly common]

n. The thumb palm (see). [obsolete after 1948] Named after the famous German magician, Wiljalba Frikell (1818-1903), who was presumably a user of this sleight although almost certainly not its inventor.

n. Cards marked by splitting them and pin-hole pricking the face side before reattaching the backs. [very rare but not nonce] These marked cards are "read" by feel. Originally invented and used by card sharps. Later adopted by magicians but only very rarely because of the difficulty of manufacture. REF: Dexter (1958). Thence (?) magicians jargon by 1958 Dexter. n. The switch where all cards are handled face up. [very rare]

n. A complete performance (usually but not necessarily in the evening) by one performer or his troupe and lasting around two hours. [obsolescent, formerly common] "Who among the magicos who boast of their ability to do a full evening show could do one at the North Pole where the nights are six months long?" — Larry Arcuri, letter to Frank Joglar, in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1951), 778 "Like so many others, before and after him, poor Ray [J. "Ralston" Fink] found that New York is the cementary [sic] in which full evening magic shows find peace and quiet." — Arthur Leroy in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Aug 1958), 28 The once very popular full-evening show of magic exemplified by Kellar, Thurston, Kassner (in Germany), Blackstone, and Dante almost disappeared with the onset of the Great Depression. Howard Thurston's last full-evening show was 20 Apr 1931 at the Tremont Theatre in Boston. Revivals of the full-evening format in the 1930s and 40s by a few others, notably Dante, Blackstone, David "Fu-Manchú" Bamberg, Jack Gwynne (1945-56), Ralston, Dariel Fitzkee, Lee Grabel, Kalanag (after WW II), and Sorcar enjoyed only mixed success. George Goebel started his in 1968. The current magic vogue does see a few full-evening shows but even such a successful trouper as Blackstone Jr was often forced to mix short acts in among his touring dates. Other current full-evening travelling shows are by David Copperfield, Paul Daniels, and Doug Henning. Siegfried & Roy ran their twice-a-night show on a repertory basis in the main theater of the Frontier casino in Las Vegas until 1988. Occasional full-evening specials are mounted by, among others, Ted Lesley in Germany. REF: Hanson & Zweers (1974), 51; Blackstone, lecture, 27 Jan 1985. Originally, I presume, American vaudeville cant. Thence (?) magicians jargon (variants noted) by 1923 J.W. Elliott as "a full evening Magic show"; 1931 Downs Oct 2nd letter to Violet; 1932 Namreh ad in Sphinx; 1939 Annemann in Jinx; 1947 Boston & Parrish; 1949 Rawson in Phoenix #170; 1949 Kemp in book title Emergency Full Evening Show; 1950 Christopher in HMM as a "full evening show"; 1955 Frazee in New Phoenix #323; 1963 McArdle; 1965 Curry; 1967 Lund in Abra as “a full evening programme”; 1972 Griffin; 1979 Lamb as "a full evening show"; 1985 Blackstone Jr; 1986 Charvet; 1988 Waters; 1990 C. Jones in Jeffreys; 1992 Randi; 1996 Wade in MUM.

n. Effect where the magician, stretching a large cloth in front of his body with both hands, proceeds to produce several spirit-like manifestations from behind the cloth; Spirit Séance in Full Light (obsolete); the spirit cloth. [fairly common] There is much uncertainty about the invention of this ingeniously simple trick, although it seems 397 to be that of magicians rather than of spirit mediums. Its invention is plausibly credited to Karl Germain by Cramer but with no date indicated. At any event, in May 1909, Germain gave Adrian Plate an absurdly complicated and rather obvious version for inclusion in the forthcoming Hatton & Plate book—a version that pinned one end of the cloth to the jacket shoulder, leaving that arm free, masked by a complete dummy sleeve-arm-hand. Sounds like a deliberate throw- off to protect Germain's real method, which was the Spirit Cloth with false hand on a rigid pole. Even Hatton & Plate note that a simpler method, using a lazy-tongs-operated false hand and preceeding Germain's contribution had been published in Mahatma. This was the article by American amateur Dr. Frank Emerson in the May 1900 issue that first described the Spirit Cloth and noted its possible application to the full-light séance-type effect. I note that a 1904 Conradi-Horster price-list illustrates and describes the effect as "Das Pythagoras-Wunder", with what must be either a lazy-tongs or a rigid pole. Became a pet effect of Karl Germain and Frank Van Hoven. A non-spiritualistic version using this method has been featured by David Copperfield (in 1981). REF: Busby (1995); McDuff (1984), 3; Cramer (1962), 17; Cramer (1966), 86; Hatton & Plate (1910), 244-245; Emerson in Mahatma (May 1900).

n. A finger ring gaffed to produce a shower of sparks. [rare] Originated as a practical joke-shop item. Thence adapted by 1983 to commercial magic. REF: Brad Reeder & Bill Robinson, Sparks: The Funkenring Book (1986, 48pp).

n. A metal funnel faked with a double-wall whose inner compartment can hold a secret load of liquid to be discharged at the magician's whim; the Magic Funnel being a later and still less usual synonym; the Comedy Funnel. One particular routine is called the Human Pump. [fairly common] First described and explained in 1584 by Prevost in France. Next in 1634 by Hocus Pocus Junior in England. Then in 1655 by Thomas Ady in his A Candle in the Dark, in 1740 by Guyot, and 1763 by Dean. Obviously a popular trick, it was also reported being performed in 1825 by an anonymous conjuror at Bartholomew Fair. REF: Prevost (1584/1998 tr), 161-166; Clarke in Magic Wand, Vol.13 (1924/25), 92, 94-95, 137; Frost (1876), 103-104. 398

n. Effect where magus draws a card from a shuffled deck, writes a prediction on it, and drops it into a hat; a spectator picks any card and adds it to the hat. The spectator removes the two cards to find the prediction matches the second card. [rare]

n. Abbreviation for effects. One type is trick photography. [new, rare but emerging] Originally the abbreviation in movie scripts for effects (special or sound). Thence magicians jargon by 1987 F/X News Journal #1; 1988 Steve Burton in Abracadata computer magazine; 1992 Harary poster; 1999 T. James ad in LR. 399

1.n. A gaff; a gimmick. [U.S.] [rare] Originally carnival cant as a contraction of "gaff" (or, perhaps, "gimmick", or both) by 1946 Dadswell as earliest citation in the RHHDAS; 1953 Gresham; 1961 Scarne; 1984 Ortiz; 1988 B. Reynolds orally as "the greatest G on the joint". Thence magicians jargon, reportedly introduced by Bruce Cervon. Then 1977 Ricky Jay as "the 'G' on the joint"; 1980 J. Marshall; 1983 Busby orally as "the G" and "the G on the joint"; 1985 Lyons in A Tribute to Sid Lorraine as "the 'g on the

n. A gimmick being the earlier but recently less usual synonym; a gaffus; the G (1); gazoocus. [common, increasingly so since 1970; formerly rare] As magical jargon, this fine-sounding word has two separate origins that have recently fused. First, "gaff" meant a hook in the lingo of British sailors by 1656 to the present. Thence, in the early 1800s—certainly by 1857 (Green)—it became card sharps argot referring specifically to the dealer's finger-ring with a concealed hook to punch-mark cards during play. Sharps also called this the "spur" by 1857 (Green). Subsequently they extended the word "gaff" to the hook-like device in a faked Faro dealing box by 1873 (Morris; 1961 Scarne). Second, by 1811 (Lexicon Balatronicum), the word was independently coined as British carnival lingo meaning a fair, with the verb form "to gaff" meaning to game. These two meanings fused in American carnival cant by 1931 (Milburn) referring to a crooked wheel-of-fortune fitted with a hook- like catch to control its spin. Note also 1934 Rose as the "gaff's on the joint"; 1935 Wolverton as "the gaff on the skillo joint"; 1953 Gresham; 1985 Sorrows. Thence the argot of gambling cheats meaning any gimmicked device by 1945 (Scarne; 1950 Maurer; 1953 Gresham; 1962 Garcia; 1984 Ortiz). Note that, contrary to Scarne (1945, p.220), this is not the origin of the two popular slang expressions "He couldn't stand the gaff" and to "blow the gaff" meaning to wise-up a sucker, both coming down to us through an entirely separate etymological route. n. Stage and sideshow illusion where a sculpted bust of a woman slowly changes into a live one (and vice versa). Pronounced gal-ah-TEE-ah. 402 [rare] The method is a scaled-down adaptation by Herbert Albini of the Blue Room sliding-mirror principle. First introduced in the early 1880s as "Galatea" by Albini in his sideshow at the Royal Aquarium in London. Premiered in Australia in 1889 by Robert Jensen. Exhibited by A.B. Carrington in 1895 at the prestigious Jordan-Marsh department store in Boston. Revived around 1915 by Australian magician Matt Northcote as "Creation" and in 1946 by Bill Neff. Revived most recently in the 1960s in the USA as a carnival sideshow exhibit with the theme changed to Girl to Gorilla. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 201; Waller (1980), 79; P. Abbott (1960), 60, who miscredits the invention to Northcote; Price (1985), 168; W.D. LeRoy in Mahatma (May 1895), 7. The title is from the famous Greek myth of the sculptor, Pygmalion, whose beloved statue is given life by Aphrodite and named Galatea. Thence magicians jargon trick-title coined in the early 1880s probably by Albini. Thence (with misspellings noted) 1891 Martinka cat; 1895 W.D. LeRoy in Mahatma; 1902 Magic, 51; 1948 Waller as historical; 1968 Furst as "The Galetia

n. You make a geek." — Clem Faraday, 1938, quoted in Gresham, Monster Midway (1953), 14 Before the carnival geek was the carnival Bosco (see), usually and perhaps always as a proper name. White, "More about the Language of the Lot", American Speech (Jun 1928), for "geek"; Maurer (1931), for "geek"; Rose, The Sources of Slang (1934), for "geek show"; Wolverton glossary (1935); Mulvey glossary (1942); Gresham (1946) for "geek" and "geek show"; 1985 Sorrows. n. A Gellerism (see). [rare] Originally a term of parapsychologists, coined in 1975 by British mathematician-physicist-parapsychologist Prof. John G. Taylor in his book Superminds, a monument to the author's gullible acceptance of the claimed psychokinetic effects of Israeli pseudo-psychic Uri Geller. There is no gimmicked apparatus involved: just pure showmanship that proves successful under nearly all conditions." — Ben Harris, Gellerism Revealed (1985), 5 Mentalist-magicians jargon by 1974 Dalal in Swami, 117; 1974 Tan Hock Chuan in Swami, 139; 1976 Shiels; 1985 B. Harris; 1987 Busby in Short Sheet #15. NOTE: Also called "a Gelleresque bit" in 1987 Johnsson in Oct LR, 94.

n. Type of routine where a deck of playing cards seems composed entirely of cards of the same suit and value; Everybody's Card being the less usual synonym. [fairly common] A fine and very old routine whose effect was first described by Girolamo Cardano in his Piazza Universale (1582) in reporting a trick he saw performed privately by the young Neapolitan 407 aristocrat, Francisco Soma. Early exposés of various methods were given by Guyot (1740?), Dean (1763, as "every Man's card"), Decremps (1786), Robert-Houdin (1868, p.245 of 1877 English tr as "The Metamorphoses"), and 1876 (Hoffmann, 87). French jargon as "La Carte Générale" by 1877 (Sachs). Thence Englished as jargon by 1897 Roterberg, 162; 1909 Hilliard; 1949 Hay; 1978 Müller, 6; 1982 Busby; 1988 Waters.

n. Effect (or, more precisely, a puzzle) when the pieces of one picture or design are reassembled they seemingly occupy the same space but with a visual discrepancy such as an empty space or a smaller number of pictured objects. [rare] "Most optical illusions fail to hold our attention for long because the secret of their trickery is generally transparent. But the remarkable constructions known as ‘geometrical vanishes' are so confounding that they continue to delight, amaze, and cause people to question their own sense of sight after the mechanics of the puzzles have been explained." — Mel Stover in Games #20 (Nov/Dec 1980), 14 This type of cunning and sometime-fad puzzle originated in Europe in the 1700s. It is described in William Hooper’s Rational Recreations (1794) as “The Geometric Money”. The most famous version, a circular vanish, "Get Off the Earth", was patented in 1896 by American puzzle-maker Sam Lloyd, who sold over 10 million copies before his death in 1911. American magician Winston Freer designed the first version where the vanish was into the third dimension by bevelling the edges of the pieces. Best known of the more recent horizontal versions is "The Vanishing Leprechaun" (copyright 1968) by Canadian Pat Patterson Lyons (Mrs P. Howard Lyons) and W.A. "Bill" Elliott. These puzzles work by what Martin Gardner calls the Principle of Concealed Distribution. REF: Gardner (1956), 114-155; Stover in Games #20 (Nov/Dec 1980), 14-18.

1.n. French word for the apron-like pouch that the early (1500s to 1850s) open-air conjurers wore at the waist to carry their props and from which to produce and vanish items. Pronounced ZHEEB-see-air. [rare, formerly archaic] “When these charlatans and imposters do this trick, they carry at their belts in front a large leather gibecière or a large money bag, which is very useful to them for hiding these sorts of tools emplyed in their art.” — J. Prevost, Subtiles et plaisantes inventions (1584/1998 tr), 141 The earliest description (in an Italian poem by Teofilo Folengo published in Venice in 1517) is of the one used by the contemporary Italian cups-&-balls worker Boccal. Described and named in French as early as 1584 (Prevost; then 1693 Ozanam). The word also meant a game-bag, but was accepted publicly as the badge of the conjurer, hence the popular expression, a bag of tricks. According to Ponsin (1853), French conjurer Comus (1731-1807) was the first magician to attach his bag of tricks to his table, thereby inventing the servante. Nevertheless, as Ponsin also observed, the gibecière was still in common use as late as 1853. By 1868, however, Robert-Houdin noted that it had recently and quickly become obsolete. Karl Germain, at the turn of the century, was almost alone in using it. After a century of disuse, the gibecière has recently somewhat revived—first by Stuart Cramer (from around World War II to the present) then by Bob Sheets (by 1982), and Ted Welsh (by 1985). REF: Christopher (1973), 17; Linking Ring (Oct 1984), 81-82; Sharpe (1983), 121. French jargon (from the word meaning literally "game-bag") by 1693 Ozanam; 1740 Guyot; 1759 Carlo Antonio; 1868 Robert-Houdin. Its equivalent in German was Gaukeltasche. Thence recently revived as English-speaking magicians jargon (without the accent-grave spelling) by 1984 Cramer in Oct LR, 81; 1984 Willmarth in Oct LR, 82; 1988 Waters; 1988 Tannen's The New York Trikune as "gibeciére"; 1992 Randi; 1995 Burton ad in LR as "The Gibeciére". *2.n. By extension, a Standard French word for conjurer. [obsolete]
n. A gimmick, as an anagram of the word magic. [obsolete spelling after 1966, formerly rare] "Some wit or cryptographist interchanged the letters of the word 'magic' and said, what's the gimac?"

1.n. In general, any secret device or method used for magical deception; a gaff; a gimac (obsolete). [very common] This curious word unquestionably originated in American slang. The only question is in whose slang? The possible candidates are the jargons of magicians, carnies, circus folk, pitchmen, gamblers, or even sailors. Let's try to trace its history through its earliest citations in each of these lingos, while remembering that earliest reports do not necessarily nor even likely prove earliest use. Commenting on "gimmick", magician John Mulholland wrote in 1963 that "originally the word was found only in the 413 vocabulary of magicians." He added that it was appropriated from them by advertising copywriters and thence successively by TV producers, the business world, and finally the general public. REF: Mulholland (1963), 323-324; also Christopher (1973), 7, and Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jul 1955), 308. Contrary to all dictionaries, Christopher (and Mulholland) may be right. The word "gimmick" may possibly have been coined by some magician; although, as we shall see, I suspect that magicians got it from carnival or circus lingo. I find it already used as established jargon among American magicians as early as 1925 when Al Baker in a Jan 1st manuscript letter to Paul Fuchs (Fox) (in Busby Collection) refers to a thumb tip as "that is the idea of the gimmick" for one-man mindreading. In another ms letter to Fuchs, undated but post-marked May 1926, Baker gives the alternate spelling "gimick". However, the fact that Al Baker was already a veteran of travelling medicine shows, suggests a possible very early coinage by carnival or circus folk, long preceeding any citations picked up by lexicographers. Houdini, in describing his underwater burial feat, wrote on 13 Aug 1926 to James S. Harto, veteran Indianapolis magician and old friend from circus days together, that: "There is a rumor going around that there is a gimmick in my latest stunt.... Rest assured there is no gimmick, no trick at all—simply lying on your back and breathing shallow breaths is all you do." (Quoted in Christopher [1969/1970 ed], 313). Again note the possible circus connection. I also find Tarbell in 1928 (Lesson 50, p.3) referring to his rope-attachment invention as the "Rope Gimmick." The word had become sufficiently familiar among American magicians that in March 1929 John Mulholland titled his new column in The Sphinx "Gossip and Gimmick." The word first appeared in print on 22 July 1922 — in Variety and seemingly in carnival context as "Lolita...tips the gimmick on the joint." (This is also the earliest dictionary citation, specifically in the RHHDAS.) In 1927 Gibson in his The Bunco Book, 23, wrote “Nearly every [carnival] game has its ‘gaff’, which is sometimes called the ‘gimmick.’” In June 1928 "gimmick" was again reported as carnival and circus cant and with the specific meaning of a secret brake on a gambling device (White). In 1930 "gimmick" was reported (Maurer) as carnival and circus jargon, with the more general meaning of any cheating device, as in "we had a slick gimmick on our set joint". Later carnival citations appear in 1939 (Liebling where "gimmick" = "gaff") and 1961 (Scarne, ditto). Interestingly, by 1930 the word had already evolved within circus and carnival its secondary meaning of any unnamed device as in "Where's the gimmick that turns on this fan?" (Maurer). The word was entrenched among gambling sharps by 1926 OED/2, quoting Maines & Grant's Wize-Crack Dictionary, as the OED's earliest citation and its 2nd earliest known use in print. Thence 1928 Mathews, Dictionary of Americanisms; and they have continued to do so (1939 MacDougall; 1945 Scarne; 1962 Garcia). American sailors were using this term by 1926 (OED/2, quoting American Speech magazine). In 1929 "Gimmick" was already long in use among travelling pitchmen as reported in the memoirs of retired pitchman "Nevada Ned" Oliver in the Saturday Evening Post (19 Oct 1929), which is its earliest appearance in the popular (non- entertainment) press. In any case, later (and post-dictionary) magical citations (with variant spellings noted) are: 1927 Baker in Jun Sphinx, 125, as "Gimicks", which is the word's first appearance in print in a work specifically on magic; 1927 Guest in Sphinx, 308, as "a ‘grimmick' for the Rope Trick"; 1927 Blackstone Magic Co. ad in Sphinx as "complete with gimmick"; 1929 Tablets of Osiris, 10, mentioning the marketed "Find the Gimmik Pencil"; 1931 Douglas cat #16; Mussey & Oursler; 1931 Ireland; 1931 Gimmick magazine; 1932 Vernon Apr 20th ms letter to P. Fuchs as "gimicks"; 1932 Thayer cat #7S as both "gimmick" & "gimmic"; 1935 Abbott cat #3; 1935 Goldston, 129, as unfamiliar to him; 1935 Annemann as "gimic"; 1936 Annemann as both "gimick" and "gimmick"; 1936 Gimmic magazine; 1936 Loyd; 1937 Chanin; 1937 Hugard; 1937 Plough; 1938 Gimic magazine; 1938 Hilliard; 1938 F.B. Sterling pamphlet as "gimmic"; 1939 Douglas cat as "gimmacks" and "gimmick"; 1939 Kanter cat as "gimmick"; 1940 Hopkins; 1940 Mahendra as "gimics"; 1940 Abbott cat #6 as “Gimmick”; 1941 Abbott as both "gimmic and "gimmick"; 1941 Holden cat #6; 1942 Joseph; 1942 Ireland cat #10 as "gimmick"; 1943 Leeming; 1944 Parrish as "gimmic"; 1944 O. Meyer in HMM; 1944 Braue in HMM; 1945 Wheeler cat as both "gimmic" and "gimmick". After this the spelling pretty much standardized to gimmick (with exceptions noted): 1947 Kanter cat #8; 1948 Nelson cat #22 as “gimic”; 1950 Young; 1952 T. Bamberg; 1950 Bobo; 1962 Chavez as a "gimmic"; 1953 Hugard in HMM, 78; 1964 Haines cat #3 as "gimmic cards"; 1973 Dalal in Swami as both "gimmic" & "gimmick"; 1975 Pierre as a "gimic"; 1976 Tarr; 1978 Hudson; 1978 Becker as a "gimmack"; 1979 Pecor; 1980 Tannen cat #13; 1980 Adair; 1983 Clower; 1988 Magic City price list as a "gimic"; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Magic Methods cat; 1992 Randi; 1993 Abbott cat #24; 1997 Lee cat #11; 1998 L&L cat; 2002 Kennedy ad in LR.; 2002 Steinmeyer in Studies in Intelligence. NOTE: First entered Standard English as a new word in the Merriam-Webster International Dictionary, Second Edition, which defined it as "any small device used secretly by a magician in performing a trick." Subsequently, American 414 advertisers borrowed "gimmick" to mean something that catches public attention by an unusual twist or new approach in

term: Girl in the Fishbowl; Girl in a Fishbowl
definition: n. Illusion where an obviously live female assistant only a few inches tall is seen inside a small (say, two gallon) fishbowl. Similar to the Girl's Head in Fishbowl. [rare] A popular carnival attraction. Also presented at Billy Rose’s Casino de Paree in New York City in the early 1930s and (as designed by Steve Shephard) at Bimbo's 365 club in San Francisco in the 1930s and 40s. Revived in 1989 at Lou Owen and Marshall Brodien's circus-themed club Toto's in Chicago's Schaumberg suburb.

term: Girl without a Middle, The [Brit. and U.S.]
definition: n. Stage illusion where an assistant loses her belly when placed in a cabinet; Seeing Through a Woman (rarer and only in the U.S.); the Disembodied Princess; No Guts (colloquialism). [fairly common] "If I keep wearing the girdle and stay on the diet, I'll be able to do the ‘girl without a middle' with no box." — George Johnstone in Magigram (Apr 1988), 525, as caption for picture of a tightly corseted Gibson Girl. Effect invented by British magician P.T. Selbit using total escape of the assistant through a stage trap, leaving behind a dummy head and dummy legs. Premiered by Selbit in 1924 in the USA as "Man Without a Middle". Also performed in this version by Nicola, Billy O'Connor, and Rooklyn. In his later version titled "See Through a Soldier", Selbit eliminated the stage trap and kept the assistant's real legs. Oblivious of the inventor's modified version, Carl Owen's workshop with help from Herman Hanson "improved" Selbit's original version by similarly eliminating the stage trap, keeping the real legs in place, and (for the first time) animating the dummy head. This Owen version was commissioned by Howard Thurston who premiered it in 1932 as "Seeing Through a Woman". Also a pet effect of Murray (by 1933), Blackstone (by 1935 to 1947), Dante (1936), Blackstone Jr. (from 1980), Aubrey, and Joe Labero. REF: Steinmeyer & Jarrett (1981), 146; Christopher (1973), 271; Hanson & Zweers (1974), 48; Lewis & Warlock (1989), 164-166.
n. Static illusion where the full-sized disembodied head of a living woman is inside a fish bowl. Similar to the Girl in the Fishbowl. [rare] Marketed by U. F. Grant by 1939.

n. Gimmick made of clear glass (or plastic) that simulates the shape of a coin. Used exclusively for the dissolving coin trick. [rare] Premiered as "Beau Brocade" (the title of a novel by the Baroness Orczy) in 1909 by David Devant at St. George's Hall, London. Featured by Gustave Fasola (by 1911) and Harry Willard.
