n. The glide; the slide. [obsolete after 1938, formerly rare] Originally French magicians jargon meaning "glide (or slide or slip) the card" by 1876 when Hoffmann introduced it to English-speaking magicians. However this somewhat cumbersome term was soon rendered into English by the simple process of literal translation, first as glide (by 1897, Roterberg) and then as slide (by 1902, Erdnase). Thenceforward the French term virtually disappeared until making a last gasp in 1938 (Stewart Judah pamphlet).

n. A type of Ball Box in which the nested ball changes color each time the round cover is lifted. [archaic] Uses several differently colored shells within the cover. First described in the 1763 edition of H. Dean's The whole Art of Legerdemain. Became a standard toy-shop item.

n. A gimmicked handkerchief that moves mysteriously on any flat surface under the magician's hands. [fairly common] Originally marketed in 1958 as "The Solid Ghost". Remarketed in the early 1960s as "Glorpy the Gurkulating Ghost" by Madblood Creations (in California). In 1968 Jon Racherbaumer combined Glorpy with an Acrobatic Card in his "Sprite Sleight or Glorpy Rides Again" trick. REF: Tannen ad in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1958), 84; Busby annotation, Feb 1988.

1.n. Effect where the magician's white glove (or pair of gloves) cast upon a tray transforms into a live dove (or two). [fairly common] Exposed as early as 1855 by Wyman (p.37) using a changing-box. A pet effect of Frederick Eugene Powell, Howard Thurston (by 1925), Bill Neff (by 1946), and Shimada (by 1988).

v. To secretly steal or ditch an object. [common] "He [Reginald Scot] explains how a coin is already sewn into the handkerchief, and this is the one that the spectator feels, after the performer has gone South with the original." — H. Adrian Smith, "Sleight of Hand in 1584", Tops (Jan 1939) This term originated in American criminal argot meaning to abscond with something of value. Later applied in this same sense by American gambling sharps by 1902 Erdnase, 115, as "to 'go south' with extra cards"; 1944 MacDougall; 1945 Scarne; 1962 Garcia as "he went south with a couple of aces"; 1982 Hayano; 1984 Ortiz. Thence magicians jargon by 1939 Smith in Tops; 1940 Charlie Miller May 18th letter to Faucett Ross as "gone south"; 1950 Hay; 1950 Rawson in HMM as “cop the blank again and go south with it”; 1953 Fitzgerald in Phoenix #281 as "gone south"; 1969 Abbott cat as "go south"; 1971 Ackerman as "the left hand goes south with the cards"; 1978 Becker as "you have gone south with the gimmack"; 1980 J. Marshall; 1982 S. James tape as "they go south under the mat"; 1983 Racherbaumer; 1983 Miesel in Precursor as "Go South with the pair of dice"; 1985 Lucky Lista orally as "go south"; 1988 Waters; 1992 Rogers in MUM.

(See also: Contrario; Contrario Aces Goblin Glass n A glass drinking goblet that allows the magician to pour a liquid into it and toss the contents toward the spectators without wetting anyone, yet the glass is now empty. [rare] In 1949 Norm Osborn & Gene Thomas's "O'Lantern Magic" made these in volume for dealer Sam Berland..) n. Effect where, after the four aces are shown and covered by a handkerchief and three indifferent cards covered by another and a volunteer removes one of the aces and places it with the indifferent cards, the two packets are shown to have tranposed. [very rare]

n. A small metal tube that after examination by spectators is sealed at both ends; a handkerchief is marked and vanished; then produced from the sealed tube. [rare] This device (similar to the Drumhead Tube plus a thumb tip) was invented by John A. Petrie and marketed by him as the Goblin Tube by 1926.

a. Pertaining to the pseudo-occult performances of goetic magick. [rare] "Goetic pertains to witchcraft or ... goety—the theurgical employment of demons, spirits, etc. to effect sorcery or magic." 422 — Masklyn ye Mage in New Invocation #15 (1983), 180 "There is something soul satisfying in knowing you've deceived someone through the goetic. It is more than doing magic tricks. You are on an ego trip." — Tony Andruzzi in The New Tops (Oct 1983), 12 "No one but Maskelyn [sic] ye Mage seems to know what ‘goetic' means, but he's got enough other people using it so that it may eventually become a real word." — The Linking Ring (Jan 1988), 104 Originally Standard English by 1610, the occasional spelling "geotic" being spurious. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon in 1812 Testot, Brighton playbill as "Geotic [sic] Power". Then effectively recoined in 1981 by Masklyn in Apr New Invocation, 105, as "the Gallic goetic ‘Doc' Shiels"; 1987 Willmarth in LR as "goetic types have funny ways of spelling"; 1987 Johnsson in LR; 1988 Busby in Epoptica #11 as a "conclave of goetic types".
n. Bizarre magick (see) being the original and still more usual synonym. [rare]

n. A bizarrist. [very rare] "There is a difference between a magician and a goeticist. A magician says let's suspend disbelief and play fantasy.... The goeticist ... works to develop a fear in magick, a respect for the unknown." — Tony Andruzzi in The New Tops (Oct 1983), 12

n. Stage effect where a large sphere moves up or down an incline, stopping and starting at the magician's command. [archaic, formerly rare] The basic effect was first reported as presented (and plausibly invented) by the French circus clown, Lepère, in 1889 in Rouen at the Folies-Bergère and next year in Paris in the circus in the Champs Élysées. His "The Mysterious Ball" was a 30-inch hollow sphere operated from inside by the 5-foot clown who, acting as contortionist, simply kept shifting the center-of-gravity toward the direction he meant to move the ball up and down a straight incline. Later in the 1890s the great Austrian acrobat, "LaRoche" (Leon Rauch), adapted the ball to a spiral track and made it an international sensation, producing several immitators down to the present. REF: Jay (1986), 204-211, 327-328; Hopkins (1897), 146-148. This effect was introduced to magic in 1902 or 1903 by Kellar who called it the "Demon Globe". It is not known whether Kellar was inspired by the earlier circus version, but his method 424 (magnets concealed in a suspiciously large frame) was new, although more likely invented for, rather than by, Kellar himself. When David Devant met Kellar in the States and saw this trick, he decided to duplicate the effect. For the next two weeks, he worked with the staff at Martinka's magic shop in New York City, building a thread-manipulated ball that ran on a simple frame. On seeing this much-improved version, Kellar "generously" agreed to adopt it himself in return for granting Devant exclusive European rights to the effect. Devant publicly premiered his "Golliwog Ball" on 24 Apr 1905 in London at St. George's Hall. Also a pet effect of Owen Clark (by 1908) and Cecil Lyle (by 1937). REF: Devant (1936), 79-81; Devant (1931), 91; Moulton (1919/1983), 127, 128; Waller (1980), 232; Gus Southall in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Apr 1962), 87, for Devant’s own presentation.
n. A stage effect where an assistant seated in a chair is hoisted into the air where, when the magus fires a pistol, the chair falls to the ground in pieces and the assistant has vanished. [archaic]
See: "Un tour de Maître Gonin". (No further definition found in this dictionary for ""Un tour de Maître Gonin"".)
n. Sleight where a coin is concealed behind the palm-up hand, clipped near the tips of the third and little fingers. [rare]
See: purse frame. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "purse frame".)

n. Conjuring performed by modern Christian ministers as part of their evangelical pitch. [fairly common] The earliest known gospel magician was Frank Bennett Lane, a Protestant minister in Vineland, New Jersey. Learned magic around 1888 so as to combine it with his preaching. Billed as "The Mystic Philosopher", he took his "Magic with a Meaning" show, which included some large illusions and ran about 1 and a half hours, to the Chautauqua and Lyceum circuits. As late as 1910 this wrinkle had failed to catch in either the USA or Britain. REF: Stanyon in Magic (Feb 1911), 35. Then, in the 1920s, a few American Protestant ministers of religion, recognizing that magic could be an attention-getter, began to interlard their sermons with simple tricks to illustrate Biblical texts. The pioneer was Rev. Ted Voorhees of Pittsburgh who privately circulated his mimeographed Magic for Ministers booklet in the late 1920s. It proved sufficiently popular to warrant commercial publication in 1930. The leading magical evangelists in the 1930s and 40s were Edwin Brush, Douglas Roe, Philip Foxwell, and Rev. L.A. McDonald. The Rev. J.B. Maxwell published three books on the subject in the 1940s and David Hoy published his Magic With a Message in 1956. More recent authors include Rev. Lawrence Burden, Rev. Don Bodley, and Rev. Jim Dracup. Today, in America, there are several thousand gospel magicians. The Fellowship of Christian Magicians conducts an annual summer camp at Lake Winona, Indiana, 1,227 attending the 1986 meet. Smaller annual meetings (about 140 in 1988) are held in Britain. REF: Holden in Sphinx (1930); F. Ireland (1946); Severn (1979), 122; Alan Kennaugh in Magigram (Sep 1988), 23-25.
n. A conjurer who specializes in gospel magic; a Magic Minister; a Magi-Minister. [fairly common]
a. Said of certain effects such as the Gozinta Box where two (or more) containers successively contain one another. [rare] From the common colloquial expression for "goes into".
n. The pseudo-topological trick where one open-ended box is removed from another open- 426 ended box which is then boxed by the first; the In-N-Outer Box; Lubor Die. [fairly common]

n. An opening trick intended as an attention-getter. [rare] Originally American slang (meaning anything that captures attention) by 1966 Hunter S. Thompson as earliest citation in the RHHDAS. Thence magicians jargon by 1973 Dietrich & Jarrow as "the trade show performer launches a small series of tricks starting with the `grabber'"; 1977 Lorayne as "attention grabbers"; 1980 J. Marshall.

n. A street magician who sells (pitches) slum. [rare] Originally British street slang meaning an itinerant pitchman. Thence British magicians jargon by 1981 Lees tape; 1983 J.H. Haviland; 1988 Davison in Lever as "the grafters would often use magic to draw a crowd". grafting [Brit.] g. Pitching. [very rare] Originally, by 1887, British street slang meaning working. REF: Hotten dict. Thence British magicians jargon by 1981 Lees tape as "grafting in magic"; 1984 Breese in Sorcerer #4.

n. Any performance featuring torture tricks, that is, simulated gruesome horrors. Pronounced gran-GEEN-yol. [very rare] "Bizarre Magick is the Grand Guignol of conjuring." — Tony Andruzzi in M-U-M (May 1983), 24 This term is from "Le Grand Guignol", the small theater in Montmartre, Paris, that specialized in blood-and-gore melodramas from 1898 until it closed in 1968. Its effects were worked by standard methods of stage magic. The word entered Standard English in the above derivative sense in 1908 (OED/2).
n. Any large-scale illusion (3). [rare but emerging] 427

n. Stage effect where an assistant or volunteer standing on a table is vanished under cover of a huge cone. [archaic] The earliest reported notice of this effect was of the French fairground conjurer, Bernard, at the Paris fairs in 1769. First exposed in 1854 by Ponsin. A pet effect of French magus Jules de Rovère (in 1828), British magician George Sutton (in 1838), Viennese magus Ludwig Döbler, and Frenchman Robert-Houdin (from Sep 1846 until his spectacular performance in Algiers on 28 Oct 1856). Revived by Houdini in 1925 for his full-evening show. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1925), 41; Sharpe (1983), 25; Christopher (1973), 149; Furst (1968). 428

a. Said of magical sleights known to have originated with gambling cheats. Because this term is clearly an ethnic slur, it will be judged "politically incorrect" usage by some; but others will abide by the injunction to "Beware of Greeks bearing gifts." [rare] From French underworld argot "Grec" [= a Greek] meaning a sharper by 1861 (Robert-Houdin) and British English by 1528 (Roy & Barlow as "greke", as earliest citation in the OED/2; and "Greek" by 1887 Hotten dict). Thence magicians jargon by 1938 as the Greek Shuffle; 1984 as Greek Deal; 1984 Martin Nash orally as "Greek dealing"; 1996 [1997"] L&L cat as "The Greek Shuffle" (meaning the "Weave").

n. The dealing of the second card up from the bottom of a deck while pretending to deal from the top. [rare] Originally an American card sharping sleight by 1894 (Koschitz) as a throw-off against any player who might suspect a bottom deal because the cheat can freely flash the bottom card to "prove" his innocence of that much more common method. Thence adapted as a magicians sleight by 1903 when first exposed by Neil (p.60) who, however, correctly remarks that it is "less frequently needed" than the second deal. Although mentioned in passing in 1914 (Hardison), it wasn't fully explained in print again until 1970 (Ackerman). Originally the argot of American card sharps by 1939 MacDougall as "the Greek-bottom"; 1950 Goldin dict as "Greek dealing"; 1984 Ortiz as "the Greek deal". Thence magicians jargon by 1984 Videonics ad in LR; 1988 Waters; 1991 Ortiz.
n. The false shuffle where the cards are held as if for an overhand shuffle with half the deck seemingly interwoven with the other while in fact only a fair cut is being made. [rare]

n. A magic book, that is, an instructional manual used in bizarre magick. [rare] Originally the esoteric cant of British occult magicians by 1849, meaning a manual of charms; and, I suppose, before them of French sorcerers of the Middle Ages. The word is simply altered from the French grammaire, meaning a grammar. REF: OED/2; H.R. Evans in Magic (Jan 1902), 30, as "a grimoire of black magic". Thence the jargon of bizarrist magicians by 1974 Raven; 1978 Masklyn; 1982 Busby in Epoptica #2.

1.n. The effect of an instantaneous production (via sleight-of-hand) of a bouquet from underneath a cup or cone. Compare Botania for the modern self-working version. [obsolete, formerly fairly common]

n. Stage illusion where the magus places a tiny box or trunk into a large open 4-post cabinet, closes the curtains, and immediately when they are opened the box has enlarged to the size of a large trunk from which an assistant steps out. [very rare] A featured illusion of Raymond, which he called "Boy Scout"; and later (around 1929) of Majeroni. REF: Bamberg (1988), 155. 430

n. A small round table, usually a pair that flanked the magician's center table in the typical stage furniture arrangement of the 1800s. [archaic] The guéridon was seldom faked but, when so, was fitted with a piston. Originally Standard French. Thence French magicians jargon by 1877 (Robert-Houdin). Thence English-speaking magicians jargon by 1873 Hartz cat; 1876 Hoffmann; 1882 Hamley cat; 1886 Garenne; 1923
n. Original term for the trick of bullet-catching (see). [obsolescent, formerly common]
n. Effect where a thin strand of cord is torn into pieces and then restored; the Hindu Thread. [fairly common] First exposed in 1584 by Prevost.

n. A combination of the Hamman Count and Hamman's Flushtration Count [= Back Count] that produces the apparent showing of all ten surfaces of a 5-card packet while, in fact, hiding five. [rare] This seldom-used false count was invented by American magician-mentalist Phil Goldstein and first published by him in Son of Bat Jr in Aug 1976. Soon applied to his "Classic Tackler" trick. REF: Goldstein in The Linking Ring (Oct 1989), 87-91.

n. A playing card printed diagonally or horizontally with different values on each half, such as a King and an Ace; now called split-faced cards. [obsolescent after 1912, formerly fairly common] "The Cards may be made halfe of one print, and halfe of another; so by the divers manners of holding them, severall things may be shewed by the same Cards." — Hocus Pocus Junior, The Anatomie of Legerdemain (1634), [47]

n. The sleight that reverses the part of a deck of playing cards below a break so that the two packets face each other, thereby facing the deck (in U.S. jargon) or boxing the cards (in British). [fairly common] "All those who can't do a decent Half Pass by March 30 will be sentenced to perform Grant's Temple Screen between strippers in a filthy nightclub in Oklahoma City for the rest of eternity." — Richard Kaufman in Genii (Dec 1987), 398
n. The false count that conceals a multiple-card packet in a larger packet of cards. Not to be confused with Hamman's Flushtration Count. [fairly common]
n. A dye tube small enough to be concealed in the magicians fist, using to for color-changing silks through the hand. [rare]
n. Sleight of hand, which is by far the most usual synonym. [rare]

n. A puppet fitted to the hand. One version is the glove puppet, the most famous of which in magic is Jay Marshall's Lefty. Compare talking hand. [fairly common] Jean Foley was using one in the 1920s when they were otherwise quite new; and Gene Gordon soon adopted one ("Fido") as his pet opener. Gerrie Larsen was using another ("Peterkin") by 1941, Zovello was assisted by “Laughy” in the early 1950s, and Shari Lewis has used "Lamb Chop" since 1957. REF: Gordon (1980), 109-110. Magicians jargon by 1939 Kanter ca; 1948 Crimmins in HMM; 1953 Gardner in HMM; 1962 Ireland cat #17; 1963 Lawston cat; 1980 Gordon; 1981 Supreme cat #30; 1982 Hay, 4th ed; 1983 Ghastly Gallimaufry cat #2; 1990 Goodsell in MUM; 1992 Wassilak in Barnstormer; 1993 Abbott cat #24; 1997 KT Magic cat; 1998 L&L cat. "hand is quicker than the eye, the" [U.S.] phr. Catch-phrase meant to be taken literally. British usage has the "quickness of the hand deceives the eye". [common] "But if your Eyes are not as quick as my Hands, I shall deceive you all." — H. Dean, The whole Art of Legerdemain (1763), 9 "The real fact upon which all prestidigitation or quick finger conjuring depends, is the fact that 435 human hands are quicker than human eyes." — The Leisure Hour, No.542 (1862), 319, as quoted in the OED/2 under "prestidigitation" "From the palm to the back of the hand the card is made to glide with lightning-like rapidity. The old saying, 'The hand is quicker than the eye,' was never more true." — Lawrence Crane in Metropolitan Magazine (New York: May 1898), 511-512 "It is a time-worn saying that the hand is quicker than the eye, but it is very wrong." — Frank W. Thomas, "The Confessions of a Conjurer", Saturday Evening Post (13 Oct 1900) "DeLand is quicker than the eye." — Theodore DeLand's punning slogan on advertising plate for his Phantom Cards, 1907 "No worse libel could ever have been invented and used against God's wondrous creation—the human eye—than the hackneyed expression, 'the hand is quicker than the eye'...." — J. W. Elliott, Elliott's Last Legacy (1923), 188 "[M]y personal experience teaches me that oft times the hand is quicker than the eye: personally, I make use of several sleights which justify such a statement...." — Houdini in Elliott's Last Legacy (1923), "Editorial Addendum" "You don't ever want to tell 'em that about being slow; let 'em think you're fast." — T. Nelson Downs, 1924, as recalled by Hay (1982 ed). "The hand is not quicker than the eye, but the eyes see a great many things of which the mind takes no notice." — John Mulholland, The Art of Illusion (1944), 5 “How often we hear baffled spectators say “It’s up your sleeve,” “The hand is quicker than the eye” or “It’s done with mirrors.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Mar 1948), 401 Pioneer Polish-born American psychologist Dr Joseph Jastrow (1863-1944) was the first to do a laboratory study of magicians in action, proving that the sleights by his 2 subjects, Alexander Herrmann & Harry Kellar, were not quicker than the eye. REF: Joseph Jastrow, "Psychological Notes upon Sleight of Hand Experts", Scientific American Supplement, V.42 (19 Dec 1896), 17, 488.

n. A figure on a wall or screen projected by shadowgraphy; a shadowgraph. [fairly common] "The introduction of a few laughable Hand Shadows in the course of an hour's show will break the monotony of too much magic, and leave the audience duly impressed with the performer's ability as an entertainer." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (Oct 1900), 5 "Tacking a bed sheet to the wall of my room, I would practice my handshadows by candlelight which gives an excellent, non-feathery shadow." — David Bamberg, Illusion Show (1965/1988), 81 Originally Standard English by 1859 (Henry Bursill). 436 Thence magicians jargon by 1895 Little in Mahatma; 1896 Devant/Robert Paul film title, "Devant's Hand Shadows"; 1898 Stanyon; 1900 Hilliar; 1905 Goldston; 1913 Nikola as book title; 1924 Clarke in Magic Wand as "Handshadows"; 1935 Holden; 1952 Gardner in HMM; 1966 Gibson; 1970 Dawes in Thistle as “Coloured Hand Shadows”; 1979 Severn; 1985 Unger in LR; 1988 Darwin; 1994 Witt in ABC of Faxic; 2000 Crowe. a. [adjectivally] [rare]

n. The effect of a release from manacles; the handcuff trick. The cuffs may be faked or not. [fairly common] "Perhaps other 'dressed-up' stunts that Houdini performed onstage stayed with his audiences longer. But the handcuff escape and the jail escape were the bread and butter of his act." — Randi & Sugar, Houdini: His Life and Art (1976), 168 The handcuff escape had been performed as early as 1700 by La Tude in France and by Samri "The White Mahatma" Baldwin in 1871 in New Orleans. However, it was not until development of formidable modern-type cuffs between the 1860s and 1880s that it became a regular act with escape artists. This began in the 1890s with Joe Godfrey (an Australian in the USA) who was soon followed by Louis Paul, Zamora, and Houdini (from 1899 to 1908). REF: Gibson & Young (1961), 8-23; Waller (1980), 159-160. 437

n. An escape artist specialized in the handcuff escape. [obsolete, formerly fairly common] "Perhaps you know that all England is full of handcuff kings, same as in Germany, but through this all there is but one Houdini ...." — Houdini, letter to W.D. Le Roy, 2 Nov 1902, quoted in Christopher (1969/1970 paperback edition only), 306.

n. A hollow holder (of flesh colored rubber, metal, or plastic) for silks; a hank ball; a Stillwell Ball. [fairly common] Used to produce or vanish silks, this device may be either held or attached by a thread or monofiliment loop to the thumb so that the loaded ball can be swung out of sight while both the front and back of the hand are successively shown empty. If it has two holes, usually called a Palmo Ball.

n. A move that apparently wraps up a coin in the middle of a square of fabric while actually keeping it outside where it can be seen either to "penetrate" the kerchief or simply vanish. Compare the coin fold, which uses paper. [rare]
n. The forcing of a playing card under cover of a kerchief. [rare] 438 First published in 1933 by Sam Durborow, according to the Potter Index.

n. A faked pistol that vanishes a silk draped over the barrel; a Silk Gun. [rare] These rather obvious gadgets were being marketed as early as 1903 by Stanyon's, first as a gaffed rifle and then since 1910 as a pistol. REF: Stanyon ads in Magic (1903), 36, as "New Rifle and Vanishing Handkerchief" and (1910), 62, as "Pistol to Vanish a Handkerchief".

(See also: Handkerchief Gun.) n. A faked pistol that vanishes a silk draped over the barrel; a Silk Gun. [rare] These rather obvious gadgets were being marketed as early as 1903 by Stanyon's, first as a gaffed rifle and then since 1910 as a pistol. REF: Stanyon ads in Magic (1903), 36, as "New Rifle and Vanishing Handkerchief" and (1910), 62, as "Pistol to Vanish a Handkerchief".
n. A pull designed specifically to vanish silks; a hank pull; a handkerchief vanisher (2); a hank vanisher. [fairly common]
1.n. A handkerchief ball (see) being the more usual synonym.

1.n. Generally, the specific moves in a sleight or other manipulation of props or apparatus; conveyance (obsolete). [common] "From various sources the method was worked out, but Karl's handling remained unknown." — Stuart Cramer, Germain the Wizard (1966), 73 440 "Erdnase describes the classic handling of the top change." — Darwin Ortiz, The Annotated Erdnase (1991), 171
n. An acquitment; a wash. [very rare]
(See also: handkerchief pull.) n. A pull designed specifically to vanish silks; a hank pull; a handkerchief vanisher (2); a hank vanisher. [fairly common]
(See also: handkerchief pull.) n. A pull designed specifically to vanish silks; a hank pull; a handkerchief vanisher (2); a hank vanisher. [fairly common]

n. A street magician in the slang of British buskers and street conjurors. [obsolete?] "I am known as a Hanky-omer, that means a Street Conjuror in the Posh phrase." — Dick "Twister" Turpin in Magic Info (1981), 343 Literally a "magic-man", from the two British slang terms "hanky-panky" (magic), which entered British slang in the early 1800s, and "omee" (variants: "omer" and "omey"), which entered around 1840 and became general theatrical cant by the late 1800s. The suffix "omee" is from the Italian uomo (man) via Lingua Franca. REF: Partridge, Dict. of Slang, 6th ed (1967), 587.

n. A coil intermediate between the mouth coil and the tambourine coil. [fairly common] So termed because originally designed to just fit the round and flat bottom of a gentleman's top hat. Marketed by 1900.
n. Device to provide the load for the headgear in a hat trick. [rare]

n. Any trick or routine where one or more objects are produced from a hat; a hat production; the Inexhaustible Hat (obsolete). [common] The earliest version reported was the Cake Baked in Hat as performed by French sleight-of- 443 hand man Delisle in 1749. The Rabbit from Hat trick was introduced by French magician Louis Comte in 1813 but did not become common until the 1840s. The Inexhaustible Hat was introduced by French magician Comus in the early 1800s (and pushed to the limit in the late 1800s by J. M. Hartz in his Devil of a Hat). The Cannon-Ball Trick (from hat) was introduced by 1857.
(See also: Paper Hat Trick.) n. Type of paper tearing where colored pieces of paper are torn to make a paper hat; the Paper Hat Tear; a hat tear. [fairly common] 679

n. A mechanically-operated pack of playing cards that automatically protrudes three successive cards matching ones previously forced on three volunteers. [common] Several methods apply: threads, a built-in reel, rubber bands, wire springs, and sponge balls. First marketed by Holden's in Mar 1933 as the "Haunted Pack". Invented by Judson Brown, according to Pierre (1975, p.123); or by Louis T. Tannen, according to both Holden's 1936 catalog and Tannen's own catalogs #1 (1949) through #16 (1989). Tannen's improved model (by 1983) requires no force. A pet effect of Finn Jon and Dick Williams. REF: Waters (1988), 164.

n. The in-the-hands shuffle that mixes the cards by dividing the pack between both hands, spreading them, and pushing the two packets sloppily into one another. The false-shuffle version is called the Charlier Shuffle. [rare] "The Haymow is the oldest form of shuffle." — [Fabian] in Abracadabra #235 (1950), 12 Writing in 1909, J.N. Hilliard mentioned "a peculiar and rather effective movement known as the 'haymow' shuffle, which used to be employed in rural districts before the riffle shuffle became generally known." Originally the cant of American cardmen by 1904 Bonville, 33-34; 1992 Giorgio in Genii. Thence magicians jargon by 1909 Hilliard, 115, as "the 'haymow' shuffle", 115; 1948 Norman; 1985 Saville orally; 1988
n. A chopper that threatens to cut off the volunteer's head; guillotine being the much more usual synonym. [rare]
(See also: Decapitated Princess.) n. Stage effect where a living woman's head rests disembodied upon a sword placed across the arms of a throne. [rare]

n. Stage illusion where a decapitated yet obviously live human body is shown, its neck surrounded by a see-through life-support system of tubes. [fairly common] Opposite in effect but the same method as the Sphinx (or Living Head) illusion. Edmund Spreer built one as a theater-lobby display for the David "Fu-Manchú" Bamberg show in Spain around 1936. First described and explained in 1938 in Hilliard's Greater Magic. Ideal as a carnival or circus sideshow exhibit because the effect is startling, the apparatus is fairly cheap, easy to transport, and the setting is static. Consequently, by 1939, over 300 were reportedly being shown throughout the United States. Of these, no less than four were simultaneously being exhibited in Greater New York City alone. The most publicized was "Olga, the Headless Girl, Alive" run by magician Carl Rosini at Ripley's Odditorium at the World's Fair midway in 1939-40. Despite this initial flurry of excitment and many exposures, it remains a popular sideshow attraction. 445 REF: Olson (1986), 105; Annemann in Jinx (1939), 426, 430, 462, (1940), 516, 536, 587; M-U- M (Feb 1998), 27-30;

n. The type of prediction where the mentalist-magician forecastes a future newspaper headline by means of a sealed envelope (supposedly containing the prediction), which is in the safe- keeping of some dignitary until the time for opening. [fairly common]

n. Close scrutiny of the magician's handling by spectators, which threatens to detect the secret moves. The verb form is to burn. [fairly common] "I like to use a climax that takes the 'heat' off of the set up pack." — Roy Johnson in Epoptica #6 (1984), 389 Originally by 1925 underworld slang meaning close police surveillance. REF: RHHDAS. Thence the argot of American card sharps meaning unwelcome scrutiny of their card handling by 1977 Prus & Sharper; 1984 Busby; 1984 Ortiz. The sharpers also called it "steam" in 1984 Ortiz. Thence magicians jargon by 1981 Waters as "there is a little 'heat' on this phase of the methodology"; 1983 Cassidy as "the 'heat' is taken off the blindfold"; 1984 Charles in Epoptica YB as "when the 'heat' was the most intense"; 1984 D. n. A card effect where the change of the expected card occurs in the spectator's hand. [rare] "This Hellist [sic] Change has been neglected by present-day magicians to their own loss, for the effect is surprisingly good." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1952), 927 One of the earliest tricks to use a double lift. Invented around 1870 by British professional drawing-room performer-teacher-dealer "Professor" Robert Hellis. First published in 1876 by Hoffmann who had studied with Hellis. n. Mindreading in its more literal sense; muscle-reading being the most usual synonym. Nelson, Hellstromism (1935), 2

n. A bronze horse whose neck could be cut through without severing the head. [rare] First described around the beginning of the Christian era by Alexandrian engineer Hero (or Heron). A slot through the neck conceals an ingeniously designed series of cogged wheels. These rotate with the passing through of a sword in such a manner as to give way before the sword while locking in behind it to keep the head attached to the body. 447 At the 1936 IBM convention Chicago magic dealer Jim Sherman exhibited a Mickey Mouse figure built to work by Hero's method. REF: Hopkins (1897), 244-246; H. Adrian Smith in Tops (Aug 1936). During WW II the German Navy developed a “shaft passer” that would enable the catching cables of British minesweepers to pass harmlessly through the cables holding the German mines at specific depths. These worked like a revolving door. REF: Richard P. Feynman, “Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman!” (New York: Norton, 1985), 101.
n. A practitioner of sacred mysteries. [rare] From the Greek hierophantés, meaning sacred + reveal.
n. Effect where the directional arrow on an 8-inch square highway sign changes direction each time the sign is turned over. 448 [fairly common]

n. A finger-sized key ring, precision-fitted with a hinged segment. [common] American amateur magician Persi Diaconis noticed in a shop window a hinged finger-ring designed for the comfort of persons suffering from rheumatoid arthritis and promptly adapted it as a magic prop, which he presented to Richard Himber, American big-band leader (Guy Lombardo-type schmaltz) and amateur magician. Made for Himber by Willie Schneider. The initial model, a signet ring called Staggering was first marketed by Himber in late 1961 in a limited edition of 25. The second version, a wedding band called Towering was marketed in January 1964. Adopted by Al Koran, Billy McComb, Nick Lewin (since 1970s), Richard Osterlind, and Ted Lesley. A simple open-gap ring was also marketed by U.F. Grant around 1963. REF: P. Diaconis 28 Mar 1962 letter to F. Ross; Busby in Osterlind (1983), 2.

n. A billfold gaffed to permit the exchange of flat objects such as cards; Bill-Fooled (obsolete). [common] First published and described in 1584 by J. Prevost as string-bound wooden boards. According to Eric Lewis (1985), also “published in Simon Witgeest's Book of Magic during 1695." Indeed, the cardboard version was described in 1897 in Hopkins where it is called "The Magic Portfolio" and was being advertised and illustrated in 1924 in Heaney's catalog as "The Magic Trick Billfold" but at only 15 cents each was obviously only cardboard. In the Nov 1928 issue of The Sphinx, T. Page Wright & William Larsen describe a card trick that used what "could only be called a ‘Himber Picture Frame'", as one magic historian recently wrote. In 1937 British- American prop maker Loyd (E. Loyd Enochs) copyrighted the patter for his "Screen of Bagdad", two small panels hinged on this principle to switch cards. REF: Lewis (1985), 143; Hopkins (1897), 127-128; Heaney Magic Co., Catalog No.25 (1924), 208; Wheeler 1945 cat, p.20, for Loyd's version. Thus recreated as a (but not “the first”, as often claimed) changing wallet by Richard Himber and first marketed in 1963 by him as "Bill-Fooled". Himber was inspired watching Sam Schwartz switch a dollar bill using cardboard panels hinged together so that they opened from either side (then being sold by Gene Gordon) and said, "Sam, an important lawyer like you shouldn't be seen using a card-board gimmick, you should be using a leather wallet." Widely copied since Himber's death in 1966. REF: Ed Levy (editor), Richard Himber: The Man and His Magic (1980), 72; Sam Schwartz telephone interview with Whaley, 2 Nov 1992; Busby in Short Sheet #13 (1987), p.[3].
n. The Indian Basket Trick (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare]
(See also: Gypsy Thread.) n. Effect where a thin strand of cord is torn into pieces and then restored; the Hindu Thread. [fairly common] First exposed in 1584 by Prevost.

term: Hindu Turban Mystery, The; Hindu Turban
definition: (See also: Cut and Restored Turban.) n. The effect where any long strip of cloth (such as muslin or cheesecloth) is cut (and sometimes also burned) yet then shown whole; the Hindu Turban; the Turban Trick. [rare] 260 Based in effect and method on the old cut-and-restored string. Originally in its cut-burnt-&- restored cloth version an authentic Eastern effect. First reported by English traveller E.W. Lane in 1836 in recalling an Egyptian street conjurer (Háwee) in Cairo who had sometimes cut and sometimes burned a muslin shawl in the middle and then restored it whole. Then first performed in Europe at the Albert Palace in Battersea Park, London, in 1886 by Indian moslem conjuror Sayad Hussan from Hyderabad. Next staged in 1910 by Western-trained Hindu magician "Ram Bhuj" (A.N. Dutt) at the Croyden Empire, London. Later became a standard trick in the Western world. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (Dec 1928), 135, 179; Price (1985), 510.

n. An amateur performer, student, or collector of magic. [fairly common] "If it weren't for the hobbyists every magical paper would fold and all magic depots would close." — Annemann in Jinx #76 (1940), 506 Originally (by 1871) Standard English meaning a person devoted to a hobby. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon (variant non-standard spellings as "hobbiest[s]" noted) by 1940 Annemann in Jinx; 1941 Mulholland in Sphinx as “hobbiests”; 1943 Fitzkee as "hobbiests"; 1948 Houghton in HMM; 1950 Young; 1950 Crimmins in HMM; 1957 Maréchal; 1965 Curry; 1967 Graham; 1968 Furst; 1973 Severn; 1976 Gill; 1984 Goshman, lecturing; 1986 Willmarth in LR as "hobbiest"; 1986 Salisse in Dawes & Setterington; 1987 Davis in LR as "hobbiests; 1989 Seabrooke in Budget; 1995 Klosterman in LR; 2000 L&L cat; 2002 Sankey in L&L Presents. hocus *n. A magician. [very rare, possibly nonce] "Thus Hocas he's here. and here he is not, While death plaid [played] the Hocas, and brought him to th' pot." — "Epitaph ... On Hocas Pocas", quoted in The Witts Recreations (1640) "Did you never see a little Hocus by sleight of hand pypping a piece [coin] several times, first out of one pocket and then out of another?"

1.n. Old term for a magician, always in its non-supernatural sense and often with reference to the British conjuror of the first quarter of the 1600s who had adopted that name. [rare] "I alwayes thought they had their rudiments from some iugling Hocas Pocas in a quart pot." — John Gee, The Foot out of the Snare (1624) "Iniquity came in like Hokos Pokos, in a Iugler's ierkin, with false skirts, like the Knave of Clubs." — Ben Jonson, The Staple of Newes (1625) "I would we have Hokos-pokos for 'em then, your people; or Travitanto Tudesco." "Who's that, boy?' "Another juggler with a long name." — Ben Jonson, The Magnetick Lady, or Humors Reconcild (1632) "by the vertue [power] of Hocus Pocus ha-Pas" — Hocus Pocus Junior, The Anatomie of Legerdemain (1634), frontispiece "Epitaph ... On Hocas Pocas: Here Hocas lyes with his tricks and his knocks, Whom death hath made secure as his Juglers box; Who many hath cozen'd by his leiger-demain, Is presto convey'd and here underlain. Thus Hocas he's here, and here he is not, While death plaid the Hocas, and brought him to th' pot." — quoted in The Witts Recreations (1640) "... on the other side, Hocus Pocus, with three yards of tape or ribbon in 's hand, shewing his art of Legerdemaine, to the admiration and astonishment of a company of cockoloaches." — Enormities and Misdemeanours seen and acted at Bartholomew Faire (1641) "I will speak of one man more excelling in that craft than others, that went about in King James his time, and long since, who called himself, The Kings Majesties most excellent Hocus Pocus, and so was called, because that at the playing of every Trick, he used to say, Hocus Pocus, tontus talontus, vade celeriter jubeo, a dark composure of words, to blinde the eyes of the beholders, to make the Trick pass the more currantly without discovery, because when the eye and the ear of the beholder are both earnestly busied, the Trick is not so easily discovered, nor the imposture discerned." — Thomas Ady, A Candle in the Dark (1655), 29 This odd term entered Standard English from magicians jargon, one of the very few words or terms to do so. However, its origins are obscure and somewhat controversial. Dutch writer Gisbertus Voetius in his De Magia (1636) traces it to a legendary wizard named "Ochus Bochus" whom he reported contemporary Italian conjurors ("Agyrtae") appealed to during their performances with the magic words "Ochus Bochus, carmina praesto". One German author of about that time reported hearing the incantation as "Hogges and Pogges". Another German writer in 1660 names "Ockes Bockes" as a magician performing in Amsterdam. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (Jun 1924), 88-89. The most famous British magician during the reign of James I (1603-25) was later reported by Ady (in 1655) to have called himself "The Kings Majesties most excellent Hocus Pocus"; and one of the early books on conjuring, published in 1634, was written by the pseudonymous Hocus Pocus Junior. Named "Hocas Pocas" ("Hocas" for short) in a popular anthology of witty quotes published in 1640 (see above quote). . Soon before his death in 1694 the very Protestant Archbishop of Canterbury, John Tillotson, would sermonize that: "In all probability these common juggling words hocus pocus are nothing else but a corruption of hoc est corpus, by way of ridiculous imitation of the priests of the Church of Rome in their trick of Transubstantiation." Tillotson's guess, namely that "hocus pocus" deliberately profaned the most sacred words in the Latin Mass, "Hoc est enim Corpus meum", was 456 widely accepted. However, it is not only unsubstantiated but unlikely, as conjurors of the early 1600s would hardly so publicly provoke renewed persecution by a Roman Catholic clergy that had dominated Britain as recently as 1558. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (Jun 1924), 88-89; OED/2. Magicians jargon by 1634 Hocus Pocus Junior (see above quote); 1641 Bartholomew Faire pamphlet (see quote); 1655 [sic] Ady as "By the virtue of Hocus, Pocus, hay passe, prestor, be gone; now open your hand."; 1979 Lamb. 2.n. As magic words. [rare and now usually in the context of comic patter] Directly derived from 1.n. above, as invoking the magical power of the British conjuror who called himself Hocus Pocus. "by the vertue of Hocus Pocus ha-Pas" — Hocus Pocus Junior, The Anatomie of Legerdemain (1634), frontispiece "By the virtue of Hocus, Pocus, hay passe, prestor, be gone" — Thomas Ady, A Candle in the Dark (1655) "Hay passe, presto vade, jubeo, by the virtue of hocus pocus, 'tis gone." — Ady, ditto "Then he utterred [sic] the magic words 'HOCUS POCUS, HI COCKALORUM CROKUS' and there was the rope all in one piece and free from knots." — Jean Hugard, pattering, in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jun 1950), 669

n. A magician. [rare] "[W]e are fortunate enough to have several contemporary accounts of the performances given by the Hocus Pocus men." — Sidney W. Clarke in The Magic Wand (Jun 1924), 92, re the 1600s "Unfortunately, it appears that the general public of today is more likely to accept the perpetrators of fraud than the normal hocus-pocus man." — David Price, Magic (1985), 440

n. A magician. [very rare, possibly nonce] "More than a 1,000 hocus pocusers journeyed to Chicago to make the combined SAM-IBM convention a tremendous success." — Frank Joglar [Milbourne Christopher] in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jun 1950), 667.

(See also: Sixth Finger.) n. A simulated human digit, hollow and flesh-colored, added to the magician's hand as an inconspicuous extra middle finger; false finger (fairly common); extra finger (obsolescent); hollow finger (obsolete); Slik Silk. [common] Being hollow, it is used for the production of silks. This device was first described in 1896 for this purpose by both Charles Bertram and August Roterberg. Maurice Garland was using it by 1903 when reported in Hoffmann’s Later Magic. Gary Darwin attributes its invention to Charles Morritt. REF: Magic Wand (1934), 149; Bertram (1896), 238-239: Darwin (1988), 19. "The customer at one of our display stands at a convention trying to insert the 'Sixth Finger' onto his middle finger — "It's rubbish" he stated, "It couldn't possibly fit anyone's finger". When I showed him that it was supposed to fit in-between the fingers and not to be worn, he didn't believe this." — Ian Adair in Trixigram (May 1988), 16 "After the handerkerchief is produced, false finger and handkerchief can both be handed out for examination." — Al Baker in The Sphinx (1930), 272

a. Said of effects where one or more transposed or vanished objects magically return to their original place, such as the Homing Bells, Homing Card, etc. [fairly common]

1.n. Generally, any effect where a playing card vanishes and returns whence it came. [rare]

[fairly common] "Nudist magicians shouldn't use the hooked coin." — Clarke Crandall in The Talisman (19 Jun 1970), 70 Used to steal or ditch the coin. First described in 1900 by Hilliar (p.174). n. The attachment of a prop by thread or wires. [fairly common]
n. Moving a large metal ring over the suspended assistant in the Aga-type illusion to "prove" the absence of supporting wires or rods. [very rare]

Russell in Magigram; 1991 Kaufman in A-B-C of Magic Sets; 1994 Tilford ad in MUM; 1997 Lee cat #11; 2002 Diamond’s Magic flyer. House of Cards

[rare] “”In October [1997] I was added to the staff at Houston’s Magic Island as the first female house magician.” — Trixie Bond in M-U-M (Jan 1998), 29

n. Effect where the magician shows a metal gas jet attached to a short length of flexible tubing and, by merely blowing into the tube can produce flame from the jet. [rare] A once popular trick in Britain, although recently performed only by one top-line magician, Alan Shaxon (from 1945 to as recently as 1988). Seldom seen outside the British Isles.

(See also: Eggs from Mouth.) n. Effect where several hen's eggs are produced one-after-another from an assistant's mouth; the Human Hen. [rare] "The trick is not one suited for indiscriminate performance, but it is one highly appreciated by juvenile or bucolic spectators ...." — Professor Hoffmann, Later Magic (1903), 399 325 The original method used 3 or more real eggs and a sleight to make successive loads. By this method, a pet effect first of Bellachini/Berlach (around 1870), the reported inventor. Thence Hellis, the Herrmanns, and Hertz (by 1904), as well as several lesser magi. Later, collapsible egg-skins were adopted to permit a single load of 6 or more "eggs". A pet effect of Benito Chavez (1939). REF: Hoffmann (1903), 401; Hilliard (1909).
n. The Spike Cabinet (see) being the modern synonym. [obsolete]
n. The comedy routine with the Funnel (see) where the volunteer's arm is pumped up-and-down to produce the flow of liquid from the gaffed Funnel. [very rare]

definition: n. A specific string knot. [fairly common]

a. Relating to the pressures exerted by fluids, as with the hydrostatic glass. [common] Magicians jargon by 1897 as hydrostatic tumbler; 1913 as hydrostatic glass; 1945 Wheeler cat as a "hydrostatic bottle effect"; 1951 Christopher in HMM as a "hydrostatic trick"; 1978 Delben Co in Feinman as the "Hydrostatic Milk
n. Abbreviation for hypnotism, which is the more usual synonym. Pronounced HIP. [rare]

v. To make the over-throw sleight in Three-Card Monte, that is, to surreptitiously release the upper card of the two held. Pronounced HIGHP. [rare] Originally meaning to cheat in the argot of American criminals by 1914. REF: RHHDAS; OED/2; 1933 Walsh & Scarne. Thence introduced into magicians jargon in 1933 by Walsh & Scarne as "to overthrow or hipe". Thence 1983 Hayden, as "the Monte ‘hype'"; 1993 Busby in Thauma.

n. Hypnotism being the more usual synonym. [rare] "As far as hypnosis is concerned, our advise is to take the attitude that it is too hot a subject to handle." — Jay Marshall, TV, Magic and You (1955), 63
a. With the simulated quality of hypnotism, as in an hypnotic act. [fairly common]

n. A mentalism-magic act using hypnotism as its method; a hyp act. [rare] Magicians who performed hypnotic acts as part of their magic shows included Charles Morritt (who reportedly was the first to do so, sometime in the very early 1900s), Benjamin R. Badley (who in 1927 did a hyp act on radio!), Harry Willard, Ormond McGill, Peter Reveen, and John Calvert. REF: D. Bamberg (1988), 18.

(See also: pulse control.) n. Effect where the magician slows or stops his pulse at will. [rare] 744 "[T]he simplest things, like X-Ray Eyes, and Pulse Stopping carry ten times the impact of the elaborate Vanishing Cabinets, and chrome and Plastic props that look tricky to start with!" — Sam Dalal in Swami (Dec 1972), 47 The method is a hard pad or ball secretly placed in an arm-pit, which by blocking the pressure- point there controls the flow of blood into and from that arm. A pet effect of Indian street magicians. Described as early as 1918 in The Magical Record and then by Goldston in his Tricks of the Masters (1942). REF: Ayling (1981), 39, 305.
n. A gesture, specifically a pass (3), to induce hypnotism. [rare]

n. Type of effect in which an assistant, volunteer, or confederate (a horse) is put in a simulated trance by a mentalist magician prior to performance of some trick; abbreviated as hyp; mesmerism; animal magnetism. Compare stage hypnotism [fairly common] “Stage Hypnotism is a combination of Suggestion and 90% trickery. And this trickery element has been closely guarded and is the least known of the many branches of the theatrical profession.” — Robert Nelson in Nelson Enterprises Catalog No.22 (1948), 59 "As one who dabbles in a bit of hypnotism myself, I can testify to what all stage hypnotists know, and most doctors acknowledge: it is much easier to get 'control' over a person's will in front of an audience than it is in private, and the magician with his air of mystery, however phoney it may be, is more successful in less time than the legitimate man of medicine." — Orson Welles, "Out of a Trance", The New York Times (17 Apr 1949), Pt.II, p.4 "I'm one of those who believes that hypnotism has no place on the stage. Most of us look foolish enough without being told to act stupid by a stage Svengali." — Frank Joglar [Milbourne Christopher] in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1951), 862 The technique was invented in the 1760s by the Marquis de Puységur, a disciple of Viennese physician Franz Anton Mesmer who, by 1782, devised and coined animal magnetism as the first popular pseudo-scientific theory to explain hypnotism. Hypnotism was first adapted to magic in 1845 by Robert-Houdin as the intentionally false explanation of the method used for 471 his Light-and-Heavy Casket illusion. REF: Robert A. Baker, They Call It Hypnosis (Buffalo, NY: Prometheus Books, 1990); Alan Gauld, A History of Hypnotism (Cambridge: Cambridge Univerisity Press, 1992); Theodore R. Sarbin & W.C. Coe, Hypnosis: A Social Psychological Analsys of Influence Communication (New York: Holt, Rinehart, & Winston, 1972); Jonathan Miller, "Going Unconscious", The New York Review of Books, Vol.42, No.7 (20 Apr 1995), 59-65; Konradi Leitner, Hypnotism for Professionals (1953, 127pp) on stage hyp; Professor Leonidas, Stage Hypnotism (Chicago: 1901); J.F. Burrows, Secrets of Stage Hypnotism, Stage Electricity, Bloodless Surgery (London: 1914). The word "hypnotism" was coined (from the Greek hypnos, meaning sleep) in 1842 by Scottish surgeon James Braid; and "hypnotist", also by Braid, followed next year. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1895 F. Baldwin in S. Baldwin; 1895 Hewes in Mahatma; 1897 Hopkins; 1901 Sylvestre cat; 1901 Stanyon in Magic; 1905 Walford Bodie; 1925 Zancig in Osirian; 1930 Lustig; 1937 Annemann; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1941 Johnson Smith cat; 1945 Robbins cat #10 as "comedy hypnotism"; 1946 Sharpe; 1951 Journal of Hypnotism, V.1, #1; 1953 Leitner; 1956 Dexter; 1959 Nelson cat #26; 1959 Corinda; 1966 Gibson; 1973 Dalal in Swami; 1980 Anderson; 1984 Weibel in Jun LR; 1988 Osterlind; 1997 Busby in Thauma #35 as “stage hypnotism”; 2004

v. To simulate placing an assistant or volunteer in a trance or to enchant an inanimate object. [rare] This word was coined in 1843 by Scottish surgeon Dr. James Braid on the basis of his previous coinage of "hypnotism". REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1895 Burlingame; 1943 Larsen in Genii; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1956 Dexter; 1969 Nelms; 1973 Dalal in Swami as "hypnotise him" & "the assistant ... is hypnotised standing up"; 1973 Kaye; 1974 Dunninger; 1985 Price; 1997 Abbott cat #25. NOTE: Also as gerund-verb "hypnotizing" in 1958 Joglar [Christopher] as "hypnotizing a rabbitt"; 1992 Calvert tape

n. Stage illusion where a female assistant is placed in a cage that is then covered with cloth and raised by pulleys to the theater's dome where it is shown empty. Alternatively (as in Vince Carmen's presentation), the assistant may appear in the empty raised cage. [rare] Based on the old Palanquin illusion where the assistant is concealed by a counterweighted double-bottom that rises to the roof of the cage. Built by Cyril Yettmah for Howard Thurston who premiered it in New York City in 1929 and kept it in his repertoire until retiring in 1935. Later a pet effect of John Calvert (1939) and Vince Carmen (since 1976). REF: Holden in The Sphinx (1929); Gibson (1966), 155-156; Price (1985), 221, 312; Olson (1986), ix, 148, 150-153.

n. An awl faked with a spring-loaded shaft that disappears into the hollow handle; the Magic Awl (obsolescent); the Magic Bradawl (obsolete); the Bradawl (obsolete). [rare] Used to seemingly poke a hole in a person or object. In 1566 Johann Wier in his De Praestigiis Daemonum mentioned the use of this penetration effect in Germany among jugglers who we, if not the credulous Wier, may assume used gaffed awls and daggers. First fully described and exposed in 1584 by Prevost in France. Also described, exposed, and illustrated as a faked "bodkin" in that same year by Reginald Scot in England. This "bodkin" trick was again exposed in England in 1612 by Rid, in 1634 by Hocus Pocus Junior, and in 1763 by Dean. It is the method later used in the theatrical and toy knives. REF: Prevost (1584/1998 tr), 163-164; Clarke in Magic Wand (Jun 1924), 84.
See: Depth Illusion. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Depth Illusion".)
n. A magic act of substantial length composed entirely or mainly of stage magic including illusions. [fairly common]
n. An enclosed step-ladder with two or more steps faked to hide an assistant before an appearance or after a vanish; Deceptive Steps. [rare]

1.n. Specifically, a magician specializing in highly visible or large-scale effects (illusions, 1 and 2). Compare close-up worker. [common] "The illusionist has many problems that the sleight-of-hand man never encounters." — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Oct 1953), 50

n. An unconscious perceptual process of the audience exploited by the magician to achieve misdirection. [rare] "You can use it [the principle of imitation] to set up an almost irresistable motor reflex.... Whereever you look fixidly, the audience will look also. Even an audience of magicians can hardly refrain." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 5

n. The below-the-table subtlety where one hand secretly places a flat object such as a card or coin into the other, which having been previously shown empty, now rests innocently at the edge of 476 the table. [rare]

n. Effect where a vertical spike suddenly and visibly penetrates the abdomen of the assistant when she balances prone and is spun on it. [rare] The effect was conceived (using sub-stage rigging) in 1939 by Les Levante and published but never made or performed by him. The modern above-stage method was invented by Ken Whittaker. A pet effect of Mark Kalin (who introduced it), The Pendragons, and David "Le Grand David" Bull. Also used by Mark Wilson on "The Magic Circus". REF: Armstrong (1983), 127-130; Waters (1988), 176-177.
a. Said of a prop (such as an impression pad) that is faked to secretly copy handwriting. [rare] The use of impression paper was reported used by pseudo-psychics as early as 1907 (Abbott).

n. A writing tablet that will secretly copy anything written on the top sheet, specifically by wax or carbon paper. [rare] Carbon paper (originally called "carbonic paper") was invented by English potter-inventor Josiah Wedgwood (died 1795) to make copies of hand-written text. Carbonless copy paper was developed in the 1950s. Carbon paper was probably first adapted to secret purposes by magicians. Described as a magic trick in 1857 in The Magician's Own Book (pp.30-31) as "The Restored Document" where an audience member's written message on a page from a memo book is secretly copied by a home-made sheet of paper coated with oiled lamp-black before the original document is burnt. This device was later adopted by spirit mediums (by at least as early as 1921). Innovations by magi include Ed Stoddard’s Mental Miracle (1951) and Chuck Smith’s M-T Pad (1955). A recent version is Richard Osterlind's Impad (1986) in the form of a standard 3"x5" spiral notepad—a virtual return after 12 decades to the original 1857 model.
a. Said of magic performed extemporaneously—on the spur of the moment—as in impromptu magic. [common] "A close-up show should always appear impromptu." — Ian Adair, Conjuring as a Craft (1970)

n. A trick or routine that can be performed on the spur of the moment because it requires only simple apparatus and little preparation; impromptu work. Compare improvisational magic. [fairly common] "Impromptu magic requires as much private practicing as other forms of entertainment. One must always think up outs and new climaxes." — Michael Weber interview in The Linking Ring (Oct 1987), 55 "If you had genuine magical powers, you could perform magic any time, any place, at a moment's notice. This is the allure of impromptu magic that requires very little preparation or preparedness." — Jon Racherbaumer in The Linking Ring (Feb 1997), 89
n. An example or instance of impromptu magic; an impromptu effect. [rare]

n. Improvisational magic (see). [very rare] The term “improv” as an abbreviation of “improvisation” and “improvisational” was originally a theatrical term, although the earliest citations are only to 1979 in the OED/2, Additions Series, Vol. 2, and to 1982 in the RHHDAS.
n. Any change in the method or presentation of a trick. [rare] "Many a trick has died of improvement." — Al Baker, quoted in The Jinx (1936), 82

n. A magician who improves the inventions of other magicians. [rare] "I confess I'm an incurable 'improver'. When I use a prop in my act, I analyze everything about it and do anything necessary to make it easier to use." — Nathan Phillips in Dominique Duvivier's Einstein's Blackboards (1996), 19
n. The extreme limit of impromptu magic that not only dispenses with prepared props but even with rehearsed routines; improv magic. Compare jazz magic. [rare]

n. Full stage (see) being the more usual synonym. [very rare] Originally theatrical cant, then by 1920 (Lustig) specifically vaudeville. Thence stage magicians jargon by 1920 Lustig; 1980 J. Marshall.
n. A Gozinta Box made of plastic. [rare]

n. Location on stage where the stage magician performs (usually but not necessarily alone) close to the footlights, specifically between the first (open) and second (closed) curtains. It does not mean working alone (single), although that is often the case. [common, particularly among stage magi] Originally, by 1907, US vaudeville cant. The number refers to the term given the curtain. Thus "in ‘two'" means between the second and third curtains and "in ‘three'" means full stage. REF: Mysticus [Evans] in Magic (1907), 29; Downs/Hilliard (1909), 12; Lustig (1920); P.W. White, "Stage Terms", American Speech (May 1926); Wentworth & Flexner dict (1960 ed). Thence stage magicians jargon by 1907 Mysticus [Evans] in Magic as "playing in ‘One'"; 1909 Downs & Hilliard as "He 'worked in one,' to employ the vernacular of the stage.... "; 1920 Lustig as "makes his entrance in ‘one'"; 1926 Thurston, Nov 24th letter to Dante as "Remember, I am always looking for a small trick in one."; 1937 Holden; 1943 Fitzkee; 1947 Boston & Parrish as "working ‘in one'"; 1943 Tarbell; 1950 LeRoy in Sphinx; 1950 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM as "Warren Keene’s neat act in one"; 1958 Leroy in HMM as "'in one' or on a night club floor"; 1959 Owen cat #5 as "Use it in 'One' on large shows."; 1963 McArdle; 1964 Nightingale; 1972 Griffin; 1974 Hanson & Zweers; 1980 J. Marshall; 1986 Olson; 1988 R.W. Scott in LR as "The Miser's Dream was on a list of small effects Willard performed in one."; 1989 Seebach in NT as "performed ‘in one'"; 1991 Emerson orally as "working in one"; 1991 MarcoM in LR; 1992 Randi; 1997 Wiley in LR; 1998 Riser in MUM.

n. Full stage being the more usual synonym [very rare] Originally vaudeville cant by 1920 (Lustig) and probably at least two decades earlier. Thence stage magicians jargon by 1920 Lustig as "worked in 'three'"; 1943 Fitzkee.

n. The stage location between the second and third curtains. 480 [rare] Originally vaudeville cant by 1920 (Lustig) and probably at least two decades earlier. Thence stage magicians jargon by 1920 Lustig; 1937 Holden; 1980 J. Marshall.
n. A Faro Shuffle where the cards are faroed but the deck not squared up. [rare]
n. A magnetically operated Boston-type coin box. Compare Magna Coin Box. [rare]

1.n. Effect where the assistant is placed in a round, shallow wicker basket, which is repeatedly run through with a sword yet the assistant emerges unscathed; the Basket Trick; Hindu Basket Trick; Sword Basket. [fairly common] Originated as an authentic East Indian trick. Described as early as around 1832 by the Rev. Hobart Cautner while travelling in India at a village near Madras. Also observed in India and fully explained by Samri S. Baldwin. In this original version the basket is unprepared. A standard trick, it was featured by Bill Neff (1955), Ormond McGill (1957), George Goebel, Tom Ogden, and most recently staged big-time by Siegfried & Roy (in 1986). REF: Kellar (1886), 116-119; Baldwin (1895), 39-41.

n. East Indian conjuring, authentically presented. [rare] "... apart from their skill as snake charmers, in the basket trick, and one or two other illusions, the ability of the entire fraternity of Indian jugglers is beneath contempt." — Harry Kellar, A Magician's Tour (1886), 114 "There is a tendency now [1899-1900] amongst the native jugglers of India to emulate European conjurers, and it is not at all unusual to see them using a pack of English playing cards, with which they attempt the simplest of illusions." — Charles Bertram, A Magician in Many Lands (1911) Several authentic Indian tricks (both effect and method) have enriched the standard repertory of Western magic: the Bead Trick (which inspired the Needle Trick), the Bowl of Rice, the Basket Trick, the Sand Trick, the Mango Tree Trick, and the scent trick. And the lota has become a common prop. The Cut-and-Restored Turban effect is of Indian or Egyptian origin. Indian effects that never caught on in the West include the Bunder Boat and the Jumping Egg. This is hardly such a discreditable record as implied in the above quotes by Kellar and Bertram, particularly as most Indian conjurors—then and now—are impoverished street performers with a narrowly limited repertoire. It is true that these performers tend to rely more on flagging attention than on sleight of hand, but not only Uri Geller but perhaps even John Ramsay would approve. The first documented Indian conjurors to appear in the West were a small troupe that performed in London from Nov 1813 until Fall 1815. Next came "The Four Surprising Indian Jugglers", first in London in Dec 1815 and then throughout England and Ireland until 1818 when they broke up. This troupe of Indian Moslems included the subsequently celebrated Ramo Samee who continued on as a single act until at least as late as 1838, with time off for a tour of the USA in 1819-20. The troupe also spawned the almost equally noted Khia Khan Khruse who continued in England as a single for about 10 years as well as Vera Breda. The first Indian jugglers to appear in the USA arrived in 1818 and consisted of a group of moslems, the conjurer being one Sheick Weithershaw. Later notable performers of authentic Indian magic have included Mooty Moodaya (in London in 1840), Dugwar (in London 1877-80), Madaree (in London 1880), Sayad Hussan (in London 1886), Belaya Nimmaya (in London 1886), a troupe of North Indian magi & acrobats (at the Crystal Palace, London, in Oct 1900), and (or same as previous) the Hoosanmia Gureva & Troup (in Glasgow in 1901). REF: Dawes (1979), 131, 170- 171; Clarke in Magic Wand, V.17 (1928), 69-78, 125-182; Maskelyne (1949), 160-167; Booth (1986), 127-142; Moulton (1983), 9-10. The popular notion of a "mystic India" created a demand for pseudo-Indian magic— performers in turbans and brocades doing Western magic with an occasional more-or-less authentic Indian Basket Trick or whatever. First to exploit this demand were Western magi in 482 Indian disguise such as Isaiah "The Fakir of Ava" Hughes (since 1857), Alfred "The Fakir of Oolu" Sylvester (since 1873), Samri "The White Mahatma" Baldwin, and Frank "The White Yogi" Hewes, all of whom performed in the late 1800s. They were followed by several genuine Indians who were wise enough showmen to perform mainly or entirely Western magic: Ram Bhuj/Linga Singh (A. N. Dutt), Kuda Bux (Khuda Bakhsh), Gogia Pasha, Sorcar (Pratul Chandra Sarcar), and Sorcar Junior (Prafulla Chandra Sarcar). The favor was returned by several Western magi. Those who both traveled to India and published first-hand accounts of the local magic and magicians are Vanek (1868-69 & 1875-76, but left no account), H.S. Lynn (1876-77), Harry Kellar (1877-78), Joseph Devono (ca1878, but left no account), Samri S. Baldwin (ca1890), Frederick Bancroft (mid-1890s), James Bertram (1899-1900), Howard Thurston (1906-07), Major L.H. Branson (ca1910-22), "Carlton" (1911), "Elbiquet" (Branson, ca1915), John Mulholland (ca1925), Lieut.-Colonel Robert Henry Elliot (by 1933); Major Jasper Maskelyne (1944-45), Major Will Ayling (1945), and John A. Keel (1955). On magic in modern India see Lee Siegel, Net of Magic: Wonders and Deceptions in India (1991); and Ayling (1981), 51-54.
n. Effect where the top ring in a foot-long chain of interlocked metal rings repeatedly tumbles to the bottom ring on command. [rare]

1.n. Legendary if not mythical illusion in its classical version whose effect has the following plot: 1) In the open, 2) the conjuror throws a rope high into the air where 3) it remains straight up, its upper end out of sight. 4) A small boy climbs the rope until he disappears at the top. 5) The conjuror pursues the boy with a knife until he also disappears at the top. 6) Dismembered parts of the boy's body fall back to earth. 7) The conjuror descends and 8) restores the boy to life.
n. Any playing card used openly as a marker during a card trick. [rare]

n. Any playing card other than those on which the card trick depends; an X-card being a recent synonym. [common] "Clarke ‘The Senator' Crandall claims an indifferent card is one that doesn't care a damn about the trick either." — J. Marshall in The New Phoenix (1956), 170 “An ‘indifferent card’ is one who couldn’t care less.” — Leslie May in The Budget (Oct 1963) as quoted in HMM (Sep 1963), 7 484 "You'd be indifferent too, if you were lying face down on a table." — Charlie Miller, as quoted by J. Busby in 1988 Originally (?) the cant of card players by 1902 Erdnase, 62; 1931 Smith. Thence (?) magicians jargon by 1876 Hoffmann, 93; 1900 Triplett, 20;1900 Reeves in Magic; 1901 DeVere in Mahatma; 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 172; 1902 Neil; 1905 Hilliard in Magic; 1913 Stanyon in Magic; 1917 Elbiquet; 1923 Elliott; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1924 Anneman [sic] in Sphinx; 1927 Tarbell; 1936 T. Tucker; 1939 Kanter cat; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1942 Gardner; 1943 Hugard in letter to Braue; 1946 Hall; 1946 Buckley; 1948 Holden cat #15; 1948 Kaplan; 1956 Dexter; 1956 Ganson/Endfield; 1977 Lorayne, 24; 1979 Lamb; 1980 Kaufman; 1983 Bennett; 1988 Waters; 1992 Fields; 1994 Charvet in MUM; 2002 Hand in MagiCurrents; 2003 Riser in MUM.
n. Indian (Hindi) word for magic. [rare]

n. An exhibition of the products of several manufacturers or dealers. They are of two types: Commercial shows are open to the public and seldom include entertainment. Trade shows are open only to the trade and almost always include magicians and other entertainers. [rare] A major and lucrative venue for magical performance on stage. Karrell Fox pioneered the first large-scale magical stage productions at industrial shows, beginning with "The Magic World of Ford" for the Ford Motor Company.

n. A fake bottle, made of tin but simulating opaque glass, gaffed with compartments (usually 3 or 5) controlled by finger-actuated air-holes to permit the successive production of several different liquids (usually alcoholic). [fairly common] The basic air-hydraulic mechanism to dispense various liquids from a single spiggot was known in classical antiquity. For example a Grecian pottery vase of the 4th Century BC in the Allard Pierson Museum in Amsterdam operated on this principle. This type of device was first exposed in the 1st Century AD by Greek scientist Hero of Alexandria. The same method was applied to barrels as early as 1578 when described by French engineer Jacques Besson. First described in a book devoted to magic in 1635 in the 2nd edition of Hocus Pocus Junior's The Anatomie of Legerdemain. Thence emerged the bottle version, first reported used in 1821 by a Herr Schmidt. Subsequently performed in 1837 in Dublin by Phillippe (using both the barrel and the bottle). Robin later claimed to have performed with the bottle in 1842 in Milan; Anderson was doing so in 1846 at Balmoral Castle; and Robert-Houdin added it to his repertoire on 1 Dec 1847. The bottle version was first exposed in 1832 in The Humorous Magician and again in 1858 by Septimus Piesse in his Chymical, Natural and Physical Magic. A pet effect of Blitz (by 1857), Wyman (by 1857), and Kratky-Baschik (by 1858). REF: S.H. Sharpe (1983), 8, 85-92; Dif #1 (1971), 42-44; Snijder, Eine Zaubervase im Allard Pierson im Amsterdam (1937); Houdini (1909), 176-199.

n. A wooden box with a secretly-hinged 90-degree V-shaped flap-bottom/side that rotates in-and- out, permitting introducing multiple surreptitious loads; a tip-over box. Compare Jap Box. [obsolescent; common until 1920] First described in 1854 by Ponsin.

n. Effect where many different objects are produced from a large flat portfolio; the Magic Portfolio (obsolete). [archaic after 1920, formerly fairly common] A pet trick of Antonio Blitz (in the 1820s), Anderson (in 1846 at Balmoral Castle), Robert-Houdin (1847-48 season), Compars Herrmann, and Lennot (in 1856). REF: Gibson (1966), 47.
n. The Faro Shuffle where the top card (of an equally divided deck) is weaved in at the 2nd card from top (and 2nd card from original top becomes the 4th, etc.). Opposite of an Out Faro. [rare]

n. An ink-well faked to switch billets. [obsolete, formerly rare] Originally the argot of spirit mediums by 1922 Dr. X. Thence magicians jargon by 1924 Heaney cat #25; 1928 Thayer cat #7; 1977 Buffum as historical.

term: ink and water; ink to water
definition: n. Effect where a bowl of black ink turns to one of clear water, often with swimming goldfish. [rare] First reported in 1846 in the act of British-Jewish magician-ventriloquist Joseph Jacobs, although probably not invented by him. REF: Frost (1876), 219.

n. A confederate (stooge) recruited and instructed on the spur of the moment; an impromptu stooge. [rare] “He [N. Schiffman] apparently means ‘impressment’ — a word itself so rarely used for the action of creating an instant stooge even most well-informed magicians wouldn’t know what it meant.” — Jeff Busby in Thaumaturgist, No.35 (Dec 1997), 4 A procedure used to good purpose by, among others, Tom Bowyer (in 1930s) and Orson Welles (in 1944).
n. Effect where a rope loop is cut and restored. [fairly common]

n. Effect where the magus claims he will pay a specific sum of money if he fails to name the chosen card and shows a simulated insurance policy to cover possible failure. He miscalls the card, apparently losing; but then wins when, upon opening the policy, a giant picture of the right card appears. [common]

n. The psychological principle that the strongest (fastest, loudest, brightest) signal tends to win the competition for attention. [very rare, possibly nonce] "My principle of intensity simply means that the entire universe is constantly competing for the attention of every human being.... Intensity will win this competition for you: given an even chance, the loudest noise, the fastest motion, the brightest color will always capture attention." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 5
n. The effect where the magician interlaces his fingers, shows backs and fronts of hands empty, yet cards then drop one-by-one from them. [rare]

n. Illusion where two performers blend into one as a woman passes through the chest of a man. [fairly common] 490 Conceived by Jim Steinmeyer (who called it "Permeability") and designed and built by John Gaughan specifically for The Pendragons who premiered it on John Fisher's "Best of Magic" TV show in 1990. The apparatus must be tailor-fit to the bodies of the intended performers. Featured (as "Soul Passage") in Copperfield's 1991-92 touring show, using Copperfield's own modified method. REF: Charlotte Pendragon, "Interlude, An Illusion Whose Time Has Come", Genii (Feb 1991), 237; Gary Ouellet, "The Making of The Magic of David Copperfield XIV", Genii (Aug 1992), 665- 666.

(See also: cross-reference principle.) n. The set-up or lay-out of a deck or part of a deck of playing cards in such a way that the parts mathematically cross-reference to each other; the intersecting sets principle. [rare] Used to produce apparent mindreading or divination effects. The earliest example is the very old Pairs Repaired trick, first mentioned in 1740 by Guyot. Modern and usually better disguised applications have been invented by Jack Merlin (Telepathy Card Trick in 1927), Louis Histed (The Miracle Divination), S. Leo Horowitz (The Twenty-Five Card Trick by 1938), Al Baker (his Vocalepathy gimmick by 1941), Paul Fox (Five- Card Mental Selection and his Miracle Gimmick by 1947), Orville Meyer (Multi-Mentality), Al Koran (The Princess Card Trick Plus), Ross Johnson, Irv Weiner, Stuart Judah, Stewart James, Orville Meyer, Phil Goldstein, Ray Grismer (Foxy in 1974 and then Foxiest), Tony Griffith (1975), Simon Aronson (1978), Jeff Busby, T.A. Waters, and Terry Nosek. REF: Peter Tappan, The Impostress Princess (1986).

n. Close-up magic being the more usual synonym; intimate work. [obsolescent, formerly rare] "His [Rolland Hamblen's] intimate magic seemed more satisfying to me than his regular theatre act." — Tony Taylor, Spotlight on 101 Great Magic Acts (1964), 44

(See also: intimate magic.) n. Close-up magic being the more usual synonym; intimate work. [obsolescent, formerly rare] "His [Rolland Hamblen's] intimate magic seemed more satisfying to me than his regular theatre act." — Tony Taylor, Spotlight on 101 Great Magic Acts (1964), 44
n. Conjuring for Conjurers being the most usual synonym. [very rare]

1.n. A magician who devises entirely new principles in magic. [rare] "Don't tell every one you meet that you are the inventor of the back hand palm—because you are not." — J. Northern Hilliard in Downs & Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909) "There are perhaps a dozen true magician-inventors in the world and all the others used these men's ideas and sometimes improved them." — David Bamberg, Illusion Show (1965/1988), 121 492 "The ingenious inventors were those who were able to dream of wonderful impossibilities, solve them with simplicities (it had to be practical), and wind up with something that had all the elements of theatre. Selbit, LeRoy, Fasola, DeKolta, Morritt, Maskelyne, Yettmah, and Jarrett were all people like that."

n. Comedy effect where an empty condensed-milk can is unconvincingly "filled" when the magician mimes "milking" a cow's udder simulated by a blown-up rubber glove but then, when the can is inverted, much milk pours out. [rare]
n. Effect where a volunteer thinks of a card in an imaginary deck; yet, when named by the volunteer, it is revealed as the only card already reversed in the magician's real deck. [fairly common]

n. A suspended figure or a globe with trumpets that whispers intelligent answers in a woman's voice. [archaic after 1851, formerly fairly common] An ancient trick of priests who, from a place of concealment, spoke though pipes connected to the supposed source of the voice. Speaking figures of various sorts were exhibited in France and England from 1784 to 1851. The physicist E. J. Ingennato in a pamphlet published in 1800 first exposed the current popular version being exhibited in Paris. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1924), 26, 209, (1925), 99-100, 135-136, 138; Hopkins (1897), 102-103; Woodcroft (1851).

term: invisible pass, the; Invisible Pass, The
definition: 1.n. That long-sought but ever-elusive ideal type of card pass, one that cannot be detected by the eye. [rare] "In our view the usefulness of the Pass has been over-emphasized in the literature, and there is no such thing as a truly undetectable handling for the sleight." — Robert Gill, Magic as a Performing Art (1976), 106 "T. Nelson Downs ... taught me the two-handed pass which in his hands was almost invisible." — Cliff Green, Professional Card Magic (1961), 24 "Professor Loewy once drove some of the old time card men nuts with his invisible pass. He fooled them because he did a top change and then faked a pass." — Jay Marshall in The New Phoenix (1956), 170

n. Magicians thread. [common] "Happiness is an invisible thread that doesn't snap!" — Sam Dalal in Swami (Feb 1974), 103 No thread is, of course, literally invisible. Only circumstances (distance to spectators or masking background or near darkness) contrived by the magician can make it appear so. However, since 1959 with DuPont's invention, monofiliments have been approaching this ideal, Kevlex, for example, having 20 times the tensile strength of steel.

(See also: red-black shuffle.) n. A shuffle that keeps blocks of red and black cards separated, such as the four Clubs, Hearts, Diamonds, and Spades. [rare] Probably invented by Laurie L. Ireland (using an overhand shuffle). In any case, first published anonymously in Seven Circles in Sep 1931 and then by Ireland in New Card and Coin Manipulation (1935). A classic example is Curry's "Out of this World" trick. Modern cardmen use a riffle shuffle. REF: Martin Gardner in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jun-Sep 1950).

n. The invisible ghost who plays audience-request music on the baby-grand piano in the at the Magic Castle in Hollywood, California. [rare] Incidentally, Irma's drinks during sets are catered by Owen Magic Supreme's "Talented Tumbler" highball glass.

n. A card sandwich separated from the deck, such as on the table, in a box or wallet. [very rare, but not nonce] An example, perhaps the earliest, is Alex Elmsley's trick, "Between Your Palms". REF: Busby, interview, 25 Jun 1987.

term: It's a Pip; It's A Pip
definition: n. The changing card-index ("pip") trick that uses black latex ink (Pip Liquid) that may be rubbed off to alter the indices on a playing card. [rare] The effect was first described in Aug 1791 in the first issue of The Conjuror's Magazine using a mixture of jet and pomatum. Reinvented in 1937 using liquid black latex by American amateur magi (both judges by profession) Caryl Fleming and Charles W. Fricke. First marketed by Fleming, then by Abbott's until discontinued after their 1976 catalog. A pet trick of Buddy O'Day since 1938. REF: Evans in Tops (Oct 1940); Annemann in Jinx (1937), 246; Buddy O'Day in Linking Ring (Sep 1986), 72, 86-87.

See: juggle / juggler / jugglery / juggling 496 JJJ Jacob’s Ladder c. A paper tear that looks like a ladder. [very rare but not nonce] A pet effect of English performer Harry Moore when he toured the USA with the Harry Lauder show in the 1921-22 season. He would place the full-scale “ladder” against the back drop and then proceed to climb it! REF: Houdini, Houdini’s Papar Magic (1922), 149.. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "juggle / juggler / jugglery / juggling 496 JJJ Jacob’s Ladder c. A paper tear that looks like a ladder. [very rare but not nonce] A pet effect of English performer Harry Moore when he toured the USA with the Harry Lauder show in the 1921-22 season.
