He would place the full-scale “ladder” against the back drop and then proceed to climb it! REF: Houdini, Houdini’s Papar Magic (1922), 149.".)

n. Hindi word for magic, originally in its supernatural and later also in its non-supernatural sense. [rare, except in India] This word, originally Hindi, entered Standard English through Anglo-Indian in 1886 by Rudyard Kipling (as earliest citation in the OED/2).
n. An escape artist who specializes in getting out of locked jail cells as a publicity stunt. 497 [rare]
n. The art of escaping from locked jail cells. [rare]

n. A square-frame container with a removable bottom and one or two false hinged sides; Japanese Handkerchief Box (obsolete); Japanese Inexhaustible Box (obsolete); a hank box (obsolete). If it has one false side, it is called a "Single Load Jap Box", if two, a "Double Load Jap Box". [fairly common] "Maybe I am getting cranky on account of my arthritis, but it annoyed me to see a great big Jap Box used to vanish a single handkerchief." — Rhadamanthus Jr in The Jinx (1941), 789 Used for productions, particularly of silks. Designed to simulate the traditional Japanese rice boxes. REF: Glenn Gravatt, Jap Box Tricks (1937). Originally termed the Japanese Inexhaustible Box by 1876 (Hoffmann; 1891 Burlingame; 1903 Stanyon ad in Magic). Then as the Japanese Handkerchief Box in 1913 (Roterberg cat #15; 1919 Thayer cat #4; 1920 Holmes; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1937 Gravatt; 1941 Chicago Magic cat #18). Also, bizarrely, as the "Egyptian Handkerchief Casket" in 1915 (B. Hull) and the "Egyptian handkerchief box" in 1937 (Gravatt). Finally, contracted as standardized jargon to Jap Box by 1911 H.A. Robinson ad in Magic, 19; 1913 Roterberg cat #15; 1919 Thayer cat #4; 1920 Holmes; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1937 Gravatt; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1949 Hay; 1952 Christopher in HMM; 1957 Furst; 1962 Rice #3; 1964 T. Garrett in Psycho-Gizmo; 1965 Lawston cat; 1969 T. Palmer; 1973 Tannen cat #10; 1977 Tricks Co cat #2; 1979 Lamb; 1982 Tenyo cat; 1988 Darwin; 1989 UST Magic cat; 1992 Willmarth in LR; 1994 Tilford ad in MUM; 1997 Abbott cat #25.

n. A performance of pseudo-Japanese magic. [rare] The first exponent was Julia "Okita" De Vere by 1877, followed by Theo "Okito" Bamberg until around 1903 when he switched to voluminous Chinese costume, although keeping his "Japanese" stage name. Herbert De Caston also did a Japanese Act in South Africa in 1902. 498
See: Obedient Ball. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Obedient Ball".)

(See also: Butterfly Trick.) n. Effect where two or more simulated (paper) butterflies are kept hovering together by fanning. [obsolescent, once fairly common] Originally the invention of Japanese conjurers who called it Ukare no Ch [literally, the Fluttering of Butterflies]. Invented (or at least introduced) by Itchosai Yanagawa. Seen in Japan in 1863 by British magician Hugh Simmons (later famous as "Dr. H. S. Lynn") who introduced it to the West where he performed it at least as early as 18 Apr 1864 at the Tremont Temple in Boston. Later that year, J. H. Anderson, or rather his daughter-assistant Lizzie, became the second of many occidental magicians to adopt this trick and the first to perform it in Europe, doing so at St. James's Hall in London. Again staged in London in 1867 by Asi-Kitch-San (or Minnmo), a member of the first Japanese magic troupe to tour Europe, imported by British juggler-magician D'Alvini. Also performed by Itchosai Yanagawa himself in Paris in 1867, J.N. Hofzinser (d.1875) in Vienna, J.N. Maskelyne early in his career in London, Ishii Black in Japan in 1914, Haakon Edeling in mid-20th century in Finland, and Charles & Mignon in Canada in 1946. Now rarely seen. REF: Stenman (1952-53), 52; Clarke in Magic Wand (1926), 37, (1928), 181; Moulton (1919/1983), 60; Waller (1948/1980), 36-37; Lynn (1873); Dif #1 (1971), 288; Fischer/Hatch (1985), 192n; Ayling (1981), 158-161; Taylor (1964), 26.

(See also: Anti-Gravity Glasses.) n. Effect where two tumblers placed on a cloth-covered book or board with the magician's thumb between them will remain there when the magician turns the platform upside-down; the Japanese Glass Levitation (obsolete); the Mesmerized Glasses (obsolete). [rare] An authentic Japanese trick first published by Ishii Black in The Magician (1914 or 1915) using either a paper covered fan or book. First demonstrated in the West in 1936 by Japanese magician Tenkai to the staff (William Larsen Sr, Gerald Kosky, and William Taylor) of Genii magazine, which promptly published it as the "Japanese Glass Levitation". A pet effect of Jack Gwynne since 1940 and Harry Riser in 1940s &50s. REF: Genii (Nov 1936), 11-12; Charvet (1986), 218-221.

n. The performance of authentic Japanese conjuring, as opposed to a so-called Japanese act. [rare] Although traditional Japanese magic employs much subtle misdirection and early on adapted itself to elaborately dressed stage magic using large troupes, few of its tricks have entered the standard repertory of Western magic. Those that have been imported from Japan are the Butterfly Trick (in 1864 by H.S. Lynn who had learned it in Japan the previous year), the Water Fountains (in 1867 in Australia by Gengero), the Obedient Ball (by 1873 in Britain), Snowstorm in China [sic] (by Yank Hoe in 1885 in Britain), and the Anti-Gravity Glasses (in 1936 by Tenkai). Possible candidates are the Feast of Lanterns (by 1876 in Britain), the thumb tie (in 1901 by TEN Ichi), and the Egg on Fan (in 1905). Although the Japanese paper- folding art of origami (by 1901 in Britain) was not magical in its original setting, a few Western magi have so made it. With apparatus, the Jap Box (by 1876 in Britain) may be a Japanese original. (NOTE: The so-called Kuma Tubes are, in fact, of Chinese origin.) The Mikados of Japan refused to permit Japanese nationals to travel abroad from 1637 until 1854 when, prodded by Admiral Perry, the current Mikado "opened" the country. The first Japanese magicians known to tour the West were with a troupe of jugglers and acrobats that opened in London on 9 Feb 1867 and closed that April. The "Japanese Jugglers" toured the USA in 1867 from at least as early as 4 March to at least as late as 29 June under the management of Thomas Maguire of San Francisco and Prof. Risley (Richard Risley Carlisle). Another group called the "Tycoon Troupe" opened in Australia on 11 Nov 1867. Lenton & Smith's Japanese "Dragon Troupe" opened in Australia on 26 Dec 1867. Around this time another "Royal Tycoon Troupe" (led by William "D'Alvini" Peppercorn and featuring Asi-Kitch- San) performed for three years in San Francisco (in 1867), London (in 1869), and in continental Europe. From then on, numerous Japanese performers virtually flooded the West. The more notable have been: Satsuma's Royal Japanese Troupe, 1870-71 (USA), 1871 (Australia). The Osaka Troupe (Sakutaroo as the magus), 1872 (Australia). The Yokohama Troupe, 1877 (Australia). Manjee, 1886 (Australia). Joe Kitchie, 1887 (Australia), c.1888 (USA). The Mikado Geinin Kumayai Troupe, 1890 (Australia). Godayou's Tokio Troupe, 1891 (Australia), 1894 (Australia). SOTO Sunitaro, 1893-95 (USA). TEN Ichi, 1901-03 (USA), 1903-04 (Europe), 1905 (USA), 1909-12 (Britain). T. K. KUMA, 1904-1963 (USA). Tomo ASHAI, 1909-1919 (USA). The Tenka troupe, 1914 (Australia). Ko Ten Ychi Troupe, 1915 (Europe). The Miyako Troupe, 1916 (London). The Kamakura Family, 1919-24 (London). TEN Katsu, 1924-25 (USA). 499 Tenkai, 1924-1930s (USA). Haruo SHIMADA, 1960s (Australia; Mexico; Europe), 1970-74 (USA), 1975-present (USA). Princess Tenko, 1988 (USA & Europe). REF: Stenman (1952-53), 81; Price (1985); Waller (1948/1980); Clarke in Magic Wand, V.16 (1927), 195-196, V.17 (Dec 1928), 181; Moulton (1983); Clark (1976), 102-109. For a repertoire of pure Japanese magic see Black in The Magician Monthly (1914-15). Among the few Western magi who travelled to Japan before WW II and published first-hand accounts of the magic and magicians seen there were H.S. Lynn (1863), Vanek (1874, but left no account), Max Berol (1899), Charles Bertram (c.1901), and John Mulholland (c.1926).

n. A small metal hoop with a faked shell. [common] Used originally in a semi-sleight-of-hand version of the Ring-on-Stick trick, it has been adapted for a few other effects. It is a shell-ring switched for a genuine ring. A modern coin-like variant is the Hong Kong half.
n. The version of the thumb tie that uses pipe cleaners instead of cord. [rare] In 1939 invented and marketed by James "Jay" Marshall whose less familiar nickname is "Jasper".

n. Conjuring tricks where the performer does not know the exact sequence of moves he will use during a routine, selecting as he goes. Compare Improv Magic. [rare] This type of magic, pioneered by Daryl Martinez in the late 1970s, is pre-programmed and not truely jazz-like improvisational.
n. A billfold with a secret slit opening into one of its compartments. [rare]

n. The card duck being the generic and most usual synonym. [fairly common] This “improved” version of Laurie Ireland’s famous card duck was invented and manufactured by American pro prop-maker Warren Hamilton in 1946.
n. The false shuffle that retains the order of part of the deck by means of a series of injogs. [rare]
n. The 4-as-4 false count that conceals the bottom card in a 4-card packet; the Flexible Count. Compare Elmsley Count. [rare]

n. Novelty practical joke item that gives the dupe a buzzing feeling when he shakes hands with the joker; a Hand Buzzer. [obsolescent] “I’m a working guy,” he said. “Mechanical maintenance. I build and service joy buzzers.” — Woody Allen, “The Whore of Mensa,” The New Yorker (16 Dec 1974).
1.v. To perform magic; to conjure. [obsolete after 1876]

1.n. Old word for magician or conjurer in their non-supernatural meanings. [obsolete since 1857, except in historical references or as applied to oriental magi] "Generally speaking, then, from Elizabethan to almost early Victorian times, a juggler was the description of a performer we now call a conjurer, to the absolute exclusion of the latter term." — Sidney W. Clarke in The Magic Wand, Vol.13, No.121 (Mar/May 1924), 18-19 No standard dictionaries do justice to this grand old word. All blurr the sharp distinction between its original meaning of a magician (in its sense as a practitioner of natural magic) and its later meaning of a performer of acrobatic tricks with objects. They also miss the significant fact that this change in meaning took place during an unusually brief period, namely the few years around 1860. Thus, after that time and with little overlap, the magical meaning became obsolete (except as a synonym for Oriental conjurors) and the new acrobatic meaning completely replaced it. Standard English in this conjuring sense as early as around 1100 and as late as 1857. From the Old French jougleur and ultimately the Latin joculator meaning one who jests. Thus the modern English words "juggler" and "jocular" have a common root. REF: OED/2. Specifically used by magicians as jargon (with early spelling variants noted) by 1584 Scot as "Iuggler"; 1612 Rid as "Jugler" and "Jugglers"; 1634 Hocus Pocus Junior as "a common Iugler"; 1655 Ady as a "jugler"; 1716 Neve as "Jugler"; 1716 Gay as "Juggler"; 1763 Dean as "Jugler"; 1800 Gale; 1826 Boaz as book title The Juggler's Oracle: or, The Whole Art of Legerdemain Laid Open; 1834 Leitensdorfer as "Juggler's Tricks or Legerdermaine"; 1857 The Magician's Own Book, 2, re both old-time Western natural magicians and contemporary Eastern ones. Thence only in historical context as in 1924 Clarke in Magic Wand; 1938 H.A. Smith in Tops re Reginald Scot. Or otherwise used only with reference to contemporary Oriental magicians as in 1861 Novra cat as "Chinese jugglers" re the Goldfish Bowl trick; 1871 Satsuma's Royal Japanese Troupe, Boston playbill, as "Acrobats, Jugglers & Equilibrists"; 1876 Frost as "Indian jugglers"; 1886 Kellar as "Indian jugglers"; 1900 Stanyon in Magic, 13, as "Indian jugglers and acrobats"; 1909 Carrington re Indian street magicians; 1911 Bertram as "native jugglers of India"; 1917 Elbiquet as "native jugglers" of India; 1922 Branson as "Indian jugglers"; 1928 Clarke in Magic Wand as "Indian jugglers"; 1941 Chicago Magic cat #18 as “Hindoo jugglers”; 1949 J. Maskelyne as “Indian street jugglers”; 1981 Ayling as an "Indian juggler", a "Hindu Juggler", & a "Japanese juggler". 504 *2.n. One who deftly but undeceptively (more-or-less) tosses and catches or balances objects. [common] In this strictly modern sense of the word, jugglers and their art have existed since antiquity— particularly in ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome. However, the early ones were limited in their repertoire to relatively simple maneuvers with balls, clubs, and knives. And their place of performance was limited to the public streets and fair grounds. In 1830 magician Antonio Blitz introduced his plate spinning as an interlude in his magic act. The first all-round juggler to appear on a theatrical stage in Australia did not do so until 1862 and he was a Continental European named Mons. Dehrang. REF: Waller (1980), 32. The first Japanese jugglers known to have toured the West were with a troupe of magicians, and acrobats that opened in London on 9 Feb 1867 and closed that April. The "Japanese Jugglers" toured the USA in 1867 from at least as early as 4 March to at least as late as 29 June under the management of Thomas Maguire of San Francisco and Prof. Risley (Richard Risley Carlisle). Another group called the "Tycoon Troupe" opened in Australia on 11 Nov 1867. Lenton & Smith's Japanese "Dragon Troupe" opened in Australia on 26 Dec 1867. Around this time another "Royal Tycoon Troupe" (led by English gymnast-magician William "D'Alvini" Peppercorn ) performed for three years in San Francisco (in 1867), London (in 1869), and in continental Europe. From then on, several Japanese troupes that included jugglers were booked into Western theaters. The next major boost to getting juggling recognized as suitable for theatrical presentation occurred in the late 1800s when French fantasist-magician Trewey brought his magic-cum- juggling act to Britain. This art was truly popularized in English-speaking countries toward the end of the century by the spectacular skill of Polish juggler Paul Cinquevalli. REF: Waller (1980), 32-33, 37, 102. Modern magician-jugglers include Ellis Stanyon (since early 1890s), Harry Leat (1890s), George McAthy (died 1971), and Topper Martyn. Conversely, some modern jugglers such as The Flying Karamazov Brothers have performed their zany juggling act as an adjunct to the conjuring acts at Ced Clute's Magic Cellar in San Francisco in the mid-1970s. REF: J. B. Findlay, Juggling through Four Reigns (Glasgow: 1945). While most modern jugglers rely solely on dexterity, many magicians who juggle do not disdain the use of gimmicks or fakes to assist or enhance their feats. REF: Goldston (1912), 401-402. A mathematical theory of juggling was developed by Claude Shannon, American mathematician, electrical engineer, creator of Information Theory (1948), amateur juggler, and inventor of juggling robots. REF: Peter J. Beek & Arthur Lewbel, “The Science of Juggling,” Scientific American, Vol.273, No.5 (Nov 1995), 92-97. "[T]he juggler employs various little 'helps' each so trifling in themselves that they are never dreamed about by an audience, yet without such helps the trick is, practically, impossible." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (May 1903), 67 "A performer who produces magical effects should be an actor playing the part of a magician, but, all too often, a performer who manipulates plays the part of a juggler." — Lewis Ganson, Routined Manipulation, Pt.I (1950), 5 "A good sleeve-worker has the uncanny skill of a juggler and the precision of a marksman." — Will Dexter, Famous Magic Secrets (1956), 130

n. Red or blue ink (and two other substances) in a dilute solution of alcohol used to mark playing cards to create a juice deck. [very rare] Originally the argot of card sharps by 1968 Time (Canadian edition) as "the cards had been 'juiced'"; 1984 Ortiz, 42; 1991 Busby in Whaley, 418, as "the 'juice'". Thence magician's jargon by 1988 Waters; 1995 Lee cat #10 as "The Juice".

n. A pack of marked cards that are faintly colored by juice in a code of wide dashes and dots that cover the entire back, indicating (usually) value only. [rare] "You know there was a guy there who accused me of juicing the deck." — Steve McQueen in The Cincinatti Kid (1965) movie. "Down at the lab, the Mounties decided that the cards had been 'juiced' — the latest, simplest and cheapest way of card-marking. All the cardsharp has to do is put a ball-pen refill upside down in a cup of rubbing alcohol. In a few minutes he has a mixture that to the casual glance is invisible when applied to the backs of the cards. But when the dealer blurs the image by looking at the cards with his eyes out of focus, the dime-sized markings are as obvious as a neon light." — Time, Canadian edition, 6 Sep 1968

a. Having the quality of bigness, as in jumbo cards, jumbo coin, etc. [common] Entered Standard English in 1823 meaning clumsy or unwieldy. Thence popularized after 1882 when P.T. Barnum bought the giant (11½-foot tall, 6½-ton) African elephant named "Jumbo", which came to mean the largest of its kind. REF: OED/2; Webster's 10th Collegiate; John Culhane, The American Circus (1990), 125-137.
n. Oversized simulated banknotes used for greater visibility. [rare]

n. Oversized (usually 5"x7") playing cards (as well as Tarot and ESP cards), about twice the height and width of the standard bridge card; giant cards being the original but now less usual synonym. A full set is called a jumbo deck. [common] "If a Jumbo card is inserted in a bridge deck, it makes a wonderful locator." — Al Baker in The Sphinx, Vol.31 (1932), 273 The earliest reported use was by Buatier [de Kolta] in May 1875 during his first appearance in London at the Egyptian Hall where he made cards grow very small and then very large. REF: Christopher (1973), 163; Findlay in Fourth Collectors Annual (1952), 25. First printed and commercially marketed, specifically for stage magicians, around 1900 in Spain as the "Baraja Española No.111 Gigante"; then in Germany in 1917 by Conradi-Horster as the "Conradi Riesenkartenspiel". REF: Müller (1982), 1-2. Jack Miller (who had begun using jumbos in 1920) created the first full jumbo-card routine in 1923 to become billed as "The Original Giant Card King". "Jumbo Playing Cards" were used by Houdini in 1925 in his Giant Card Star illusion. REF: Gibson & Young (1961), 152-156.
n. An oversized coin, 2 or 3 inches in diameter. [rare]
n. A pack of playing cards composed entirely of jumbo cards. [rare]

n. Effect where an egg leaps out of a bowl of water. [very rare] A trick of Indian origin. Sometimes performed as the climax of the Dry Sands trick. First observed in India and reported and exposed in 1895 (by Baldwin, 59-62; also 1909 Carrington, 31).

n. Effect where a feather leaps spontaneously from a container after water is poured in. [very rare] The gimmick is a spring held compressed by a soluble substance. This clever trick was first reported (by Decremps) being performed in Paris in 1784 by Pinetti (using pen knives) who was the likely inventor. At that time Decremps presumed the method was a pulled thread. The next year Pinetti published his real method to discredit Decremps. In 1854 Ponsin substituted a plume. An Indian conjuror used this same gimmick to propel a ceramic rabbit as observed by Bertram around 1899. Carrington reported its use by Indian magicians using both eggs and rabbits with sugar in 1909. In 1937 Sharpe mentions spoons as the propelled prop. REF: Gaultier (1914/1945 tr), 22, 27, 28; Ponsin, II (1854/1937 tr), 96; Carrington, Hindu Magic (1909), 31-32.

n. Effect where a spoon (or other object) resting at the bottom of a bowl of water suddenly jumps out. [rare] 510 The method is a prepositioned spring anchored with a crystal of sugar or salt, which, when it dissolves, triggers the spring. First exposed by Prevost in 1584 with a knife or coin. Later described by Ponsin in 1853-54 with plumes. REF: Prevost (1584/1998 tr), 21-23, 37-39; Ponsin (1853-54/1937 tr), 96-98.
n. An Hawaiian priest or sorceror. [very rare]
n. The Deep (Classic) Palm (see) being the more usual synonym. [new term, rare] "The Kaps Subtlety is a popular buzzword for the Deep Classic Palm." — Jeff Busby in Short Sheet #13 (1987), p.[7]

n. Effect where magician drives finger thru center of a metal coin, deforming it. [rare] First described and exposed by French amateur magician Ponsin in 1853 using a switch of a real for a gaffed coin. Marketed in that version in 1901 by Stanyon as the "Finger through Penny". By 1911 William "Chung Ling Soo" Robinson used a shell-coin to disguise the gaff. Re-invented and improved in the 1980's by American coinman David Roth. REF: Ponsin (1853/1937 tr), 55-57; Stanyon ad in Magic (Apr 1901), 64; Stanyon in Magic (Jan 1911), 25-26.

n. The cut-and-restored string where the key section is initially held together by wax- impregnated thinned-out and overlapping ends. [archaic] This was the best known of Harry Kellar's several tricks with string. Kellar traded the secret to "Frazee" (William Meyenberg) who used the trick but kept the secret. Kellar also disclosed the secret to a "well known performer" in Clyde Powers' magic shop, but that person broke his pledge of secrecy and sold it for $20 to Sam Bailey. Bailey then marketed it through his Bailey & Tripp magic shop in Cambridgeport, Massachusetts. REF: Frazee in New Phoenix #323 (1955), 102; Cramer (1962), 46.

term: Kelly Bottom Placement; Kelly Bottom Replacement
definition: n. The Ovette Master Move (see) being the more usual and more accurate synonym. [fairly common] "Few conjurors will disagree that the Kelly Replacement, when well executed, is one of the cleanest forms of card control that can be found." — Peter Warlock in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Aug 1956), 465 Named after Frank Kelly, a New York amateur magician, although he did not invent it.

n. A secret master-object hidden among seemingly identical objects (such as other cards, rings, safety-pins, coathangers, or symbols). Used as an abbreviation for key card, key ring, etc., but only when the context of a card trick, ring trick, etc., is understood. [rare]

n. Any gimmick that facilitates key-bending, namely the surreptitious bending of a latch-key. [rare] Contrary to widespread belief, Uri Geller, the originator and popularizer of key-bending, never uses a gimmicked device much less having invented one. He uses only the leverage of his fingers on these, let it be known, highly bendable pieces of metal. The first gimmick was the Bongo Bender invented by Ali Bongo in 1975. The most recent, the "B. H. Gimmick" was invented by Ben Harris. REF: B. Harris (1985), 27-39.
n. The effect where a latch-key (for house or automobile) bends. [rare] This effect was invented by Israeli pseudo-psychic Uri Geller.

n. The secret playing card (unknown to the audience) used to find another adjacent card (unknown to the magician) previously selected by the audience; a locator card. The key card may be either faked or not. [very common] “Many are the effective tricks which depend upon the use of a key card.” — Jean Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Mar 1946), 201 This device was first described as used by British conjurors in 1584 (Scot). The most common type of key card is a regular card that has been glimpsed. The earliest faked key cards were either longer or wider than the others in the deck so they could be indentified by feel during handling. The long card and the wide card were later (in the 1920s and 1930s) generally replaced by the short card. Any single card in a one-way deck can become a key card by simply reversing it.
n. The gaffed safety-pin in the gimmicked version of the Linking Pins. 514 [rare]

n. A metal hoop faked with a narrow gap, which may either be left open or fitted with a spring closure (in which case called a locking key ring). Used to join otherwise solid rings into a chain, as in the Linking Rings trick or the trick that links wedding bands supplied by the audience. [common] “Did I tell you that the key ring of my linking ring set has two gaps in it?” — Al Stevenson in Hugard’s Magic MonthlyI (Nov-Dec 1960), 69
n. A mechanically self-working version of the Seven Keys to Baldpate effect. [fairly common]

n. The sleight unique to the Shell Game that pops the ball into the fingers as the shell is pushed forward. 515 [rare] Possible only with a rubber ball ("pea"). Professional Shell Game operators call this the "kickout move" (Garcia, 1962). Magicians jargon by 1938 Read; 1950 Ganson, 66; 1976 Page, who was taught it by Jack Chanin.

n. An extra-surprise finish to a trick. [fairly common] "Both [Wyman & Jack Baker] really performed a good magic show, but the kicker was having the Frankenstein Monster walk out into the audience just before a black-out." — Bev Bergeron in The Linking Ring (Nov 1996), 130 Possibly from the American poker-players term (in use since 1892) for a card held in reserve as a bluff or in hope of improving one's hand. REF: OED/2; Mathews dict (1951). Emerged by 1941 as general American slang meaning any surprising twist REF: RHHDAS. Thence magicians jargon by 1942 B. Elliott in Phoenix #5; 1953 Marlo; 1959 Braue in HMM; 1960 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1969 Walton; 1970 Jennings in Genii; 1971 Racherbaumer in Kabbala; 1972 Anderson; 1976 E. Lewis in Abra; 1976 Johnsson as "a rather strong kicker"; 1976 Freer in Mantra; 1977 Garcia, as "a knockout 'kicker'"; 1977 Lorayne; 1982 Crosthwaite in Pabular; 1983 Tannen cat #14; 1983 Fulves; 1983 Ammar; 1984 Goldstein in Genii; 1986 Hades cat #2; 1987 Abbott flyer as "a surprise kicker"; 1991 Ortiz; 1992 Duschek in MUM; 1996 Bergeron in LR; 1997 Lee cat
See: children's magic. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "children's magic".)
See: allied arts. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "allied arts".)

n. Advertising title used by or applied to many early top-billing magicians, the male counterpart of the female Queen. [obsolescent, formerly common] "At the risk of offending some 'Great,' 'King,' or 'Emperor,' or the trio for that matter, we will not withhold any secret that we believe will interest and profit our readers." — Ellis Stanyon editorial in Magic (Dec 1903), 30 "This was an era of manipulative specialization. ... Kings of Coins and Cards, all uncrowned and some of them with anything but blue blood in their veins, were battling to establish their thrones in the theatres of the world. The thing became a blight." — Charles Waller, Magical Nights at the Theatre (1948/1980), 127

n. Effect where the magus can place a tiny plastic mummy-like figure in its case but, when a volunteer tries, it jumps out. [rare] The method for this popular pocket trick is magnetism. Variants of the King Tut-Ankh-Amun in his sarcophagus theme include the West German “Pedro”, a dog that won’t stay in its bed, a nude woman in her bathtub, etc., etc.
n. A pass where the top half of the deck is pulled over and around the lower half to face the deck. [very rare] First published in Robert-Houdin (1868/1877 tr), 168. 517

n. Effect where an egg in a drinking glass and a handkerchief in the magician's hand are transposed; the Egg and Handkerchief trick. [fairly common] This is one of the earliest sucker effects. The original version, evidently invented by and certainly made popular in London by Colonel Stodare in the mid-1860s, used a real egg, two handkerchiefs, and a metal fake egg (hollow with a hole for vanishing one of the handkerchiefs). Alexander Herrmann adopted this as a sucker effect by the mid-1870s. In 1878, Andrew G. Waring, disapproving generally of any exposé such as that inherent in sucker effects and specifically that used by Herrmann, invented the bottomless glass to eliminate the sucker element by vanishing the fake egg down trap. By 1903, German magician Hans Meckel had also adopted this bottomless glass and trap version. By 1909, T. N. Downs added a piston to his trap-table to make the trick virtually self-working. Later in decline, it was revived as a pet effect by Judson Cole in the early 1930s. REF: Hamley cat (1882); Teale (1920), 389.

n. Effect where a large butcher knife cuts deeply into the magicians forearm. [rare] This ancient geek-type effect, first published 1584 by both J. Prevost and Reginald Scot, uses a knife whose blade is gaffed with an oval cut-out edge. The modern device by Ricardo has a spring-retracting cut-out with self-contained blood squirter.

term: Knife thru Coat; Knife through the Coat
definition: n. Effect where the magician's blade penetrates a volunteer's jacket without slicing the fabric. [fairly common] Based on the late 1800s Finger through Hat trick. A pet effect of Jack Miller (in 1910s). And later by Al Wheatley who taught it in the mid-1930s to Tommy Tucker who, forgetting his knife at one performance, improvised his later famous "Scissors through Coat" trick. This old trick was re-popularized in 1948 when Vincent Harrison both marketed his Spear-it Knife method thru Tannen's and published it in Tarbell. Thence a favorite of Bob Read, Mike Caveney (by 1986), and Ken de Courcy. REF: ESP Inc ad in Linking Ring (May 1986), 29; Martin Gardner in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Oct 1948), 475.

n. The forcing of a playing card by the volunteer thrusting a knife blade into the pack in fair fashion and the magus negating this by either slipping the top force-card to the top of the lower half as he lifts off the upper half or, more recently (Cardini's method), by substituting a card for the knife and cutting to a break. [rare] The original method used a force deck (Stanyon in Magic [Jun 1914], 81). Invention of the modern method (using a card and a break) is credited to Richard Cardini by Charlie Miller (C. Miller, undated letter to F. Ross).
n. A magician who specializes in the allied art of knife throwing (see). [rare]

n. Stage effect where the magician pitches knives that successively outline his human target. [rare] This death-defying effect was first reported in ancient Rome where the throwers were called ventilatores. The art was reintroduced to the West in 1853 in Philadelphia by Chinese magician 519 Yan Yow and in 1854 in England by Tuck Quy. Both were on tour with the "Chinese Magicians" troupe, apparently accomplishing this feat by sheer dexterity. Subsequently became a standard carnival and circus attraction. Japanese also excelled in this in Western circus performance in the late 1800s. A totally safe method was devised by 1897 by Paris magic dealer Émile Voisin using a target-board mechanically gaffed with pop-out knives whose appearances were triggered to coincide with the magician's simulated throws of the real knives. In the early 1930s Rajah Raboid did blindfold knife throwing at his female assistant. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand, V.13 (1924), 27, & V.17 (1928), 178; Christopher (1962), posters on pp.123, 124; Hopkins (1897), 153-156; Gresham (1953), 81-93.

n. Effect where, after 5 playing cards are shown back-&-front and several wrapped in a handkerchief (or envelope), one of the remaining cards vanishes from the hand and reappears in the hank (or envelope). [rare]

n. Effect where a chosen card (or other object) is discovered by a toy automobile. [rare] The effect and gaffed car were invented by Dutch magician Dick Koornwinder Jr. It won first prize for Close-Up Magic at the National Dutch Convention in summer 1971. First marketed by Ken Brooke as "Koornwinder Kar". The first pirated version was "Wondercar", made in the USA 520 by J. & H. Magic Works (R. Good and J. Hill) for Hank Lee's Magic Factory, which marketed it by 1981. A later version is "Crystal Car", made by Seleciones Magicas for Queen of Hearts, which marketed it in 1987. A pet effect of Juan Tamariz. REF: Ken Brooke Series #10 (1984), i, 10-14; Busby in Epoptica #6 (1984), 353.
(See also: Magician's Dream, The.) n. A 48-card deck of playing cards faked with multiple banks of 12 cards repeated; the so-called Koran Deck. [rare]
n. A particular type of card exchange (switch). [rare]

n. The mathematical principle that enables playing cards to be counted down in such manner that the numerical value of the final card is the same as the first with a greater than 80% likelihood. [rare] Discovered by Martin Kruskal and first published in The Pallbearers Review, that is sometime between 1965 and 1975.

n. Multiple production effect using two large (12x18 inch) tubes (and the Organ Pipe method) that climaxes with the production of a jar of water, which is then shown to be larger than the tubes. [fairly common]

n. The chair suspension effect where a ladder replaces the board. [rare] Technically a suspension rather than a levitation. Invented by Walter "Zany" Blaney in 1954, premiered it in 1965, and has marketed it since 1986, the first model going to David Copperfield who first featured it in his 1986 China special and for the next three years. REF: Walter "Zany" Blaney, "The Anatomy of a Rip-off", The Linking Ring (Apr 1993), 62-65.

n. Effect where eight cards are chosen, shuffled back into the deck, and then produced from the top and bottom. [archaic] This card trick was possibly invented and certainly named by French magician Comte sometime in the early 1800s and was one of his favorites. First published by Ponsin in 1853. It immediately became a pet effect of Robert-Houdin who added it to his act that year. Also a pet effect of professors Hellis and Hoffmann (who had been taught it by Hellis by 1867). Republished by Robert-Houdin in 1868, Hoffmann in 1876 and 1878, and Kunard in 1888. Appears in Erdnase (1902) as "Top and Bottom Production". A pet effect of Charlie Miller. REF: Busby in Whaley (1991), 231-232; Robert-Houdin (1868/1877 tr), 221; P. Warlock in Linking Ring (Jul 1984), 45.
1.n. Stage effect where a woman in one cage changes places with a lion in another. Not to be confused with the Lion's Bride. [rare]

1.n. Generally, all non-magicians; laymen being the most usual synonym. [rare] "It is a curious fact ... that suspicion in the minds of the laity [about palming] never extends to the magician's left hand. It is only his right hand that they try to keep under close observation." — Audley Walsh in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Apr 1945), 115
See: Mene Tekel Deck. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Mene Tekel Deck".)
n. The sleight where a seated magician uses his lap as a servante; lapping being the more usual synonym. [rare]
n. An oversized ring used with standard ones in some Linking Ring routines. [very rare] 524
n. A utility sleight for reversing (1) one or more cards in a deck. Pronounced LARRY-VERSE. [fairly common]

n. Impossible seeming card locations done during late-evening card sessions. Usually so boring to the laity because of the number of contrived restrictions that they are only appropriate for other, equally interested, cardmen. [very rare but not nonce]
See: Chinese Laundry Ticket.. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Chinese Laundry Ticket.".)

n. A group of spectators composed entirely of non-magicians; laymen; the laity (1). [fairly common] "A lay audience can't always appreciate the art of magic. People think I have a trick deck or something. But there's no way I could do the things I do with a trick deck of cards." — Derek Dingle, interview in Clark (1976), 45 "The opening night must have seemed weird to the lay audience when the magicians would appear to applaud at the wrong time. They were applauding the technique and not the trick 525 itself." — David Bamberg, Illusion Show (1965/1988), 208

n. Laymen of either sex; the laity, which is a fine old word recommended for those who insist on using a "politically correct" sex-neutral term without sounding pompous; the lay public. [fairly common] "Your fellow magicians are not hiring you for a show, the lay people are. Appeal to them." — Walter B. Graham, How to Become a Magician for Fun and Profit (1967), 21

n. Any person (male or female) who is not a magician. [common] "It is an odd thing, but the layman always overlooks the possibility of the introduction of more than one method into the execution of a conjuring trick." — Charles Waller, Magical Nights at the Theatre (1944/1980), 43 "Many, many years ago I made it a practice to ask one and all laymen with whom I might be talking about magic, what trick had impressed them the most. Invariably it was Thurston's card throwing." — Stuart Cramer in The New Phoenix #373 (1962), 320 "Make no mistake, laymen are aware of the principle of the so-called 'luminous readers'." — Jeff Busby in Short Sheet #13 (1987), p.[10] “I often hear laymen describe tricks by professional magicians who are my friends, and whose methods I fully know. It is not unusual to hear a description that completely excludes the method used.” —Martin Gardner, How Not to Test a Psychic (1989), 9.
n. A trick (specifically a fooler) that strongly deceives a lay audience. Opposite of magician fooler. [rare]

n. The placement of playing cards on a table in accord with some predetermined (secretly coded or publicly conventional) pattern. [fairly common] The earliest trick to use this principle was the Pairs Repaired card trick based on the Mutus Dedit Nomen Cocis layout first mentioned and exposed in 1740 by Guyot. Later (by 1857) came the Q Trick. Originally gamblers cant by 1884 Will & Finck cat; 1891 Quinn; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne; 1918 Evans cat; 1945 Scarne; 1950 Maurer, for dice; 1961 K. C. Card Blue Book. Thence magicians jargon by 1935 Annemann in Jinx #8; 1937 Hugard; 1953 Elliott; 1981 Scalbert.
n. A billfold faked with a secret slit opening into its zippered compartment. [rare]
n. The Ace or Ace-packet that the other three Aces follow in the Four Ace trick. [rare]

(See also: Adams' League Deck.) n. A full (52-card) pack of marked playing cards with a baseball-themed design on the back. [archaic, formerly fairly common] Designed in the late 1910s by the S.S. Adams Company of New Jersey. The round baseballs are marked using DeLand's clock system.

n. The magician's own published account of his lecture-demonstration to an audience of colleagues. [common] Originally terse, ideosyncratic summaries of a magician's lecture-demonstration, these so-called lecture notes have tended since the 1960s to become rather well-edited and more-or-less word- for-word renderings with fairly complete details of handling and presentation. However there were a few earlier exceptions, the first being possibly Fred C. Figueroa's well-edited The Abusive Use of Sleights (New York: The Society of American Magicians, 1909). REF: J. Gary Bontjes, A Checklist of Magic Lecture Notes (1962).

n. Proper name of the glove-puppet devised and used by Jay Marshall in his ventriloquial act. Lefty is the most famous vent figure among magicians. [rare] "I love Lefty and, even though I can almost say the words with Jay, always enjoy watching it." — Phil Willmarth in The Linking Ring (Sep 1987), 48 Left-handed American magician Jay Marshall worked a regular magic and vent act with 2 wooden dummies until he joined the U.S. Army in World War II. At that time he reframed his act to use only light-weight props. His vent figure (worn on his left hand) became a regulation glove with two shoe buttons for eyes. For his first post-war job (in 1946) he adopted the white glove and "Lefty" became magical history. "A juggler named Paul Gerrits gave me the idea for using the [fingers] of the other glove for ears in 1946." One of the "Lefty" gloves is in the permanent collection of the Smithsonian Institution. REF: Severn (1979), 162-163; Marshall in Whaley questionnaire, 1989.

n. Sleight of hand; prestidigitation. [obsolescent, formerly very common] "The true art therefore of iuggling consisteth in legierdemaine; to wit, the nimble conueiance of the hand ...." — Reginal Scot, The discouerie of witchcraft (1584), Ch.22 "The true Art therefore of Jugling, consisteth in Legerdemain: that is the nimble conveyance and right dexteritie of the hand." — Sa. Rid, The Art of Iugling or Legerdemaine (1612) "Legerdemaine is an operation, whereby one may seeme to worke wonderfull, impossible, and incredible things by agilitie, nimblenesse, and slightnesse of hand." — Hocus Pocus Junior, The Anatomie of Legerdemain (1634) “On Thursday and Friday Mr. Robin gave his astonishing performances of legerdemain, or to use the good old English name, which is now fast going out date, if it is not already gone, conjuring.” — Soulby’s Ulverston Advertiser, 21 Jul 1853 This grand old word is of French origin, leger de main meaning literally "light of hand". The word entered English in the late 1400s with the spelling "lygarde-de-mayne". Laymen today apply this word to magic in general — to the delight of magicians who, of course, foster such vagueness in audience perception. Note that the word's spelling had standardized to its modern form sometime around 1650. REF: OED/2; Walker (1552). Magicians jargon (with variant spellings noted) by 1584 Scot as "legierdemaine"; 1612 Rid as "Legerdemaine"; 1634 Hocus Pocus Junior as both "Legerdemaine" & "Legerdemain"; 1658 White (3rd ed) as section titled "Experiments Performed by Legerdemain"; 1716 Neve; 1722 Dean; 1744 C.F., The Merry Medley; 1791 Lemoine in Conjuror's Magazine; 1805 Pinchbeck; 1812 Belzoni, Oxford playbill; 1815 Ingleby; 1826 Boaz; 1829 Boy’s Own Book; 1834 Leitensdorfer as "legerdermaine"; 1836 Engstrom; 1843 Crambrook cat; 1857 Magician's Own Book; 1861 Novra cat; 1873 Hartz cat; 1877 Sachs; 1896 Bertram; 1901 Evans in Magic ; 1901 Selbit; 1912 Kellar ms; 1912 Germain poster; 1923 Elliott; 1927 Tarbell; 1932 Gibson; 1949 Turner; 1952 Buckingham; 1957 Vernon in Ganson; 1966 Hutchinson; 1973 Kaye; 1976 Dalal in Mantra as the "Art of Legerdemain"; 1976 Tarr; 1979 Lamb; 1981 Ray-Mond; 1988 Waters; 1992 Randi; 1997 Waldman; 1998 L&L ca; 2002 Moskowitz in MagiCurrents; 2005 Magic Castle Newsletter.

n. Somewhat tongue-in-cheek synonym for a performer of legerdemain; a legerdmaniac. [rare] “Dai Vernon has the local legerdemainists ecstatic with his 'Jumping Jack’ trick.” — Frank Joglar [Milbourne Christopher] in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Nov 1955), 350 Standard English by 1860. REF: OED/2; RHD/2. Thence magicians jargon since around 1900 by Boston magician Bennett Springer who billed himself as the "Lyceum Legerdemainist"; 1925 Schulte in Sphinx; 1930 Mulholland in Sphinx; 1938 Harold Lloyd in Jinx #51 as "legerdemanist"; 1951 Elliott in Phoenix; 1951 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1966 Cramer; 1984 B. Robinson in LR as "this layed-back legerdemainist"; 1996 anon in LR as "the Long Island legerdemainist" referring to Bob Elliott.
n. An avid performer or student of magic; a magician. [rare]
See: Lake Guillotine. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Lake Guillotine".)
n. Contraction of levitation, which is the much more usual synonym. [fairly common, colloquial with stage illusionists]

1.n. Harry Kellar's original version of the levitation (technically only a suspension) using the Aga gooseneck. [obsolete after 1904] Much confusion exists among historians of magic because Kellar used this same title for two successive illusions, the first (1900-1904) being an Aga-type gooseneck suspension, the later (from 1904 to his retirement in 1908) being an Asrah-type wire-lift levitation. REF: J. Marshall in New Phoenix #323 (1955), 100, 101; D. Bamberg (1965/1988), 28.

n. The card-magic plot where volunteer miscalls only his previously selected card while dealing them face down, yet the magus detects the miscalled card. [rare] This effect was first suggested in 1934 by British magician Vincent Dalban. Martin Gardner subsequently evolved the Lie Speller from this. REF: Dalban, Dec 1934 letter to Annemann, in Jinx #4 (Jan 1935).

n. Variation on the standard Lie Detector card plot where in Gardner's original version the volunteer answers (freely lying or truthtelling) the magician's questions about the color, suit, and value of each card, spelling out his answers by dealing one card for each letter; yet, regardless of truth or lie, his previously selected card is always the last card dealt. [rare]

n. A shiner (see) being the most usual synonym. [very rare but not nonce, oral only] Originally the argot of card sharps by 1965 Vernon on Buffum tape as "the light comes down the sleeve"; 1984 Ortiz; 1995 Riser in MUM as "playing the light". Thence magicians jargon (but confined to a narrow circle including Dai Vernon) by 1988 Busby orally.
n. The apparatus that works the Light Bulbs Through Girl effect. [rare]
n. Stage illusion where the assistant standing in and completely filling a tall frame (the Light Bulb Cabinet) is slowly penetrated by 24 to 36 long slender illuminated electric light tubes. [rare]

n. The ability to give instant answers to apparently difficult mathematical calulations. [rare] A few gifted individuals with the ability to perform complex mathematical calculations with great speed have appeared in public performance regularly since the 2nd Century. However, most of these calculations can be simulated, and that is a trick shared by some show-offs and conjurors. Persons who specialized in this as pros include Zerah Colburn (since 1820), Vito Manglamele (since 1835), Henri Mondeux (mid-1800s), Arthur F. Griffith (c1880-1911), Romanoff (by 1909), Fred Brauns (early 1900s), and Prof. Olgo (mid 1900s). Many would also feature other memory feats. Magicians who also performed lighting calculations include Madame Konorah (1903), André Delcassan (since 1939), and Donna Delbert (by 1949). REF: Martin Gardner, Mathematical Carnival (New York: Knopf, 1975), 66-88; Robert Tocquet, The Magic of Numbers (New York: A.S. Barnes: 1957); Fred Barlow, Mental Prodigies (1951); Ellis Stanyon, ""History of Lightning Calculation", V.2 (1902), 89-90, V.3 (1902), 1-2, 11-12, 22.

n. A quick-change artist (see) being the most usual synonym. [obsolete] Originally theatrical lingo by 1889 as earliest citation in the OED/2. 535 Thence magicians jargon by 1948 Waller; 1981 Barnouw as historical.

(See also: flash paper.) n. Tissue paper made of nitrocellulose to ignite in a sudden burst, leaving no trace. [very common] Used to cover the vanish or production of a small object. This device evolved from the flash handkerchief by 1882 when it was first described in Messrs. Hamley catalog. Old-time British magician S. Gibney recalled in 1908 (Magic Circular, 286) that Bland of London sold flash paper as "Lighting Paper" in the early 1860s—possibly a false memory of the date. The publication in 1937 of Stuart Robson's Tips on Flash Paper stimulated its subsequent wide-spread use. Flash paper and the Radio Cue Prompter are the only devices I know of that were borrowed from magicians by professional gamblers—a small return for all that the magi owe to the sharps. Flash paper is truly the bookie's friend because it permits instant evanishment of the evidence (betting slips) during a police raid. Also issued to American OSS agents in WWII to make destruct-at-will notes. REF: B. Elliott in Phoenix #177 (1949), 707.

n. A quickly drawn pen-&-ink outline picture, often with reversible double-ended heads. An allied art of magic. If chalk is used, it is called a chalk talk. [very rare] Illusionist Robert Jensen included a lightning sketcher in his act in 1889. Lafayette was doing his own by 1900. In the 1940s magician Abril Lamarque performed this art. REF: Waller (1948/1980), 79; Stanyon in Magic (Jan 1901), 27.

n. The words spoken by a magician during performance; patter being the much more usual synonym; also patter lines. [rare except among magicians with a background in theater] "The usual term patter, used to denote the lines which go with the performance of a trick, is poorly chosen." — Dariel Fitzkee, Showmanship for Magicians (1943), 13 "This so-called patter that is often placed in books has done great damage. A magician should have legitimate lines; this is the term to use, lines, not patter." — Dai Vernon in Genii (Oct 1973), 417 Originally and still theatrical cant meaning the written words of an actor's part. In use as early as around 1601 in Shakespeare's Hamlet (III, ii, 3) as "I had as lief the town-crier spoke my lines." REF: OED/2, under "LINE" IIIg, where, astonishingly, the earliest citation is only 1882; Granville dict (1952), being a recent reference. Thence belatedly (by over three centuries) adopted as magicians jargon by 1931 by David Devant. Thence 1931 Farelli, 56; 1943 Fitzkee; 1947 Histed; 1952 Tannen ad in HMM as "217 M.C. lines"; 1969 Nelms, 265; 1981 Brooke #1; 1981 Busby flyer; 1985 Breese as "you needed a line which would take the heat off the effect".
n. Cardboard Connection (see) being the original and still more usual synonym.

n. Effect where metal clothes-hangers link and unlink. [rare] First reported as being invented and performed by American professional club magician Russell Prunier in early 1939, although his method is undisclosed except for the fact that he could "prepare a set right on the spot". At any event two basic later versions are known: The first method (standard coathangers plus a gimmick) was invented in the 1940s by American magician Merlin Eifert. In 1968 Eifert gave one of his gimmicks to Mike Caveney who purchased the rights in 1975 and developed a routine which he marketed in 1980 or 1981 as the "Impromptu Linking Coathangers". The second method (using a locking-key coathanger) was invented by John Stansfield of Atlanta, Georgia. He copyrighted his version in 1956, premiered it at a magic convention in Atlantic City, and self-marketed it in 1956. On Peter Biro's suggestion, Caveney introduced a "key" to adapt coathangers to his regular Linking Rings routine. In the early 1960s Connie Hayden had also made 3 sets of a locking-key-based Linking Hangers that were marketed by Richard Himber. REF: Annemann in Jinx (Feb 1939), 378; Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jun 1956), 440, 444; Mike Caveney, Linking Coathangers (1978), 2.
n. Effect where 36-inch hollow plastic hula hoops link and unlink. [rare]

n. Effect where safety pins link and unlink in chains. [common] The original version using two standard safety pins that mysteriously linked was an old children's wire puzzle that was adapted as a magic trick (by adding an unlinking move) in the early 1930s under the title Piff Paff Poof. L. Vosburgh Lyons invented the gaffed key-pin and substituted it for one of the ungaffed ones. Lyons called his trick "Slip, Snap, Spoof" and published it in 1943 in The Phoenix #47. A 3-pin (one Lyons' gaffed) routine was devised by Jerry Andrus and marketed by him in 1954 as "The Linking Pins", winning a prize as the best trick of 1955. A pet effect of Tony Slydini and Gaëtan Bloom (with an entirely new method of his own). REF: Andrus (1955), 3, 7; J. Marshall in New Phoenix (1955), 127.

n. The classic routine whose effect is that two or more solid and separate metal hoops are made to link together into a chain and then unlink; the Chinese Rings; the Chinese Linking Rings. [very common] The generally accepted legend is that this celebrated trick was a Chinese invention taught by a travelling troupe of Chinese conjurors in Dublin to the French magician, Philippe, who became the first Westerner to perform it when in 1837 he did so in Edinburgh. The truth is evidently different. In fact, European conjurors had been linking rings for over three centuries before their earliest recorded use by Chinese—or anyone else for that matter. Thus the famous Italian physician, mathematician, and gambler, Girolamo Cardano, recalled in his De Subtiltate (1550) watching street conjurors who around 1530 tossed separate rings into the air and caught them linked. It was also performed with ten rings at York, England, back around 1816 by the celebrated Indian Moslem magician, Kia Khan Khruse, who called it simply "The Solid Brass Rings" according to one of his playbills (see Dawes [1979], 99, 134), although curiously crediting it as one of his "Chinese performances". At this point, Khruse had been in England since 1815 when he first arrived (from Spain, or so he claimed) as part of Ramo Samee's "The Four Surprising Indian Jugglers" troupe fresh from Seringpatam (or so they claimed). An otherwise unknown "Mr. Usher" performed an 8-ring link in Worcester, England, in 1827 (Usher poster), advertising his act as "a representation of the Indian and Chinese Jugglers". The first troupe of authentic Chinese jugglers appeared in England around 1830 where they presented the trick using 8 rings. Next we know that English-Jewish magician Joseph Jacobs performed it in Britain in 1835. Only then, in 1837, did Philippe present it in Edinburgh after indeed studying with an unnamed lone Chinese magician in Dublin. This chronology suggests that this trick was perhaps not of Chinese origin but possibly European and even conceivably Indian. True, it has sometimes been called "The Hindoo Rings" (in the 1888 Maurer catalog and the 1909 T. Bamberg catalog) but presumably only for reasons of exotic ballyhoo rather than as the result of any search for historical truth. One late but very interesting Chinese connection with the rings is Ching Ling FOO who in 1898 or 1899 in Omaha when provoked by Leon Herrmann included the Rings in his act for the first and last time, tossing them in mid air where they linked and rolling them on the floor with reverse-English so that they linked while returning. Foo considered these feats—however remarkable—mere juggling. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1928), 41, 179; Dif #1 (1971), 102; Price (1985), 499. Following Philippe, John Henry Anderson presented the Rings in Hull on 30 Apr 1838 (Anderson playbill) — preceding his most acrimonious competitor, Barney Eagle, who performed it (with 9 rings) in Wakefield on 9 Nov 1838 (Eagle playbill). The trick was first exposed in French in 1854 by Ponsin and in English in 1857 by The Magician's Own Book. A pet effect in the hands of later innovators such as Chung Ling Soo (William Robinson with 11 rings), Leon Herrmann (15 rings), Martin Chapender (10 rings), Claudius Odin (8 rings), Chefalo (20 rings), Jack Miller (5 rings), Darriel Fitzkee (8 rings), Dai Vernon (6 rings), Al Koran (3 rings), and Richard Ross (3 rings). In the 1949 Genii-Orben Poll the Linking Rings was voted #2 out of 63 for the "Greatest Trick in Magical History". REF: Genii (Jun 1949), 301-302. “Lyle Laughlin (Carlyle) tells of the magician who explained the Linking Rings to a friend. The friend was angry. 'You don’t expect me to believe a silly explanation like that, do you?” — Fred Braue in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Mar 1947), 304

n. Stage effect where a caged woman (threatened by a lion in the same cage) is saved by the magician when he transforms himself into the lion. Not to be confused with the Lady and the Lion illusion. [obsolescent]

n. Conjuring with fluids in general. A specific example is called a liquid effect or a liquid trick. [rare] Among those few magicians who have built an entire act around liquid magic was Anverdi in the 1960s.
n. A specific example of liquid magic. [rare] "I don't like liquid tricks, but I do them." — Charlie Miller, letter to Faucett Ross, 3 Mar 1965
n. The break created and held by the pinkie-finger between two halves of a playing-card deck. [rare]
n. The psychokinetic or animation effect produced by a block of wood suddenly falling unaided off a table edge or other support. [very rare]

term: living and dead (test); Living and/or Dead (Test)
definition: n. Effect where the mentalist-magician discovers the name of the one deceased person that had been written on a billet and mixed with others, all of which gave names of living persons; the Quick or Dead trick. Compare Questions and Answer. [fairly common] Originally a trick of spirit mediums by 1907 when first exposed by David P. Abbott. Mitchell Kanter stated in 1939 (Kanter cat #1, 160) that it was originally "conceived by old 'Doctor' Schlossinger many years ago'"as a spiritualistic trick. Dai Vernon claimed (Genii, Mar 1982, p.156) that it was "introduced" to magic by Henry Hardin.
n. Illusion where the otherwise disembodied upper half of a live woman sits upon a table. [rare] This static illusion is worked by mirrors like the Sphinx illusion.

n. A puppet show featuring one or more puppeteers who show their own heads through a slit in the curtain, which are attached to small puppet bodies. [rare] Among the very few magicians who also worked this rare allied art were the Englishmen Ernest Sewell (1910s) and Clown Bertram (around the 1920s-30s). REF: Waller (1948/1980), 143, 189; Wellesley Pain, "Living Lilliputians", Strand Magazine (Feb 1903).

n. Any object concealed but available for the magician to steal for later use, particularly as a production. [very common] "With the loads in position, make your entrance." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jul 1943), 5
n. The large ball (or other large object such as a lemon or onion) used for the surprise climax load in the Cups and Balls routine. [rare]

n. The secret compartment that holds a load in an otherwise seemingly empty container; a load 542 compartment; load container. [fairly common] This chamber constitutes the fake in, as examples, the Dye Tube, Foo Can, Lota, Mirror Box, Square Circle, and some Production Cabinets.
n. A load chamber being the more usual synonym. [rare]

(See also: load chamber.) n. The secret compartment that holds a load in an otherwise seemingly empty container; a load 542 compartment; load container. [fairly common] This chamber constitutes the fake in, as examples, the Dye Tube, Foo Can, Lota, Mirror Box, Square Circle, and some Production Cabinets.

n. Dice very heavily weighted on one side to insure that one value almost always turns up. Used to force a particular number. One type is called tap dice. [fairly common] Originated with dice sharps in ancient India, Greece, and Rome, as we know from antique specimens in museums. The first detailed exposé of dice cheats (British) using loaded dice is Gilbert Walker in his A manifest detection of the most vyle and detestable vse of Diceplay (1552) where he describes "Fullams", dice whose corners are plugged with lead. The next is Charles Cotton's The Compleat Gamester (1674) where the dice are plugged with mercury. Unlike the very heavily weighted dice used by magicians to guarantee the desired value, dice cheats are content with less suspiciously crooked "loads" that assure only a slow but steady percentage advantage over the long run. REF: Scarne & Rawson, Scarne on Dice (1945); Walker (1552). The earliest reported use of loaded dice in a public performance of magic was by French magician Eugéne Verbeck in London in Feb 1885. REF: G.W. Hunter in Magic Wand (1915), 83. Originally the term "loaded dice" was introduced by honest gamblers and has been used by them, by gambling houses and casinos, by unscrupulous "sporting goods" dealers in their catalogs aimed at gullible "catalog men", and thence into Standard English. This term, "loaded dice", appears by 1781 (as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1811 Lexicon Balatronicum; 1822 Bailey; 1843 Crambrook cat; 1844 Anderson; 1855 Wyman; 1857 Green; 1865 Evans; 1873 Morris; 1877 Grandin price list; 1884 Will & Finck cat; 1911 Meyer; 1912 Quinn; 1921 Herrmann Magical Co cat; 1932 Evans Secret Blue Book cat; 1982 Williams). Meanwhile, the real sharpers cautiously avoided such a give-away term, prefering to call them "Fullams" (also spelled "fulhams", "fullums", and "fullomes") by 1552 (Walker; 1612 Rid; 1674 Cotton; 1714 Lucas; 1811 Lexicon Balatronicum). Then "percentage dice" (by 1932 Evans Secret Blue Book cat; 1945 Scarne). And, most recently, "weight" (by 1977 Prus & Sharper as "weights"; 1982 Williams; 1984 Ortiz). Sharps refer to the sure-thing heavily loaded dice adopted by magicans as "first flop dice" (by 1917 Lipman cat; 1917 Magic Novelty Co cat; 1932 Evans Secret Blue Book cat; 1945 Scarne; 1961 K.C. Card Blue Book; 1984 Ortiz) or as "dead number dice" (by 1945 Scarne; 1984 Ortiz). Thence magicians jargon as loaded dice in the narrow sense defined above by 1873 Hartz cat; 1888 Maurer cat as "a loaded die"; 1891 Martinka cat; 1896 Bertram; 1908 Stanyon ad in Magic; 1909 Hilliard; 1913 Roterberg cat #15; 1915 G.W. Hunter in Magic Wand; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1924 Heaney cat #25; 1933 Annemann; 1943 Marlo; 1966 Inzani- Henley cat #1; 1973 Alain; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1996 Hank Lee’s Book Book..
n. A secret vertical breast-pocket on the inside of the magician's coat. Used to conceal a load. [rare]
n. Any method (such as a key card, sleight, or mathematics) used by the magician to secretly identify a spectator's chosen card in the deck prior to its discovery. [common]

n. A key card (see) being the most usual synonym. [fairly common] "If a Jumbo card is inserted in a bridge deck, it makes a wonderful locator." — Al Baker in The Sphinx, Vol.31 (1932), 273 544 “Make a locator of one card by scraping its side edge with the fingernail.” — Clayton Rawson in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jul 1950), 678
n. A key card (see) being the most usual synonym. [fairly common]
a. Said of any apparatus gaffed so that it can be secretly locked up before passing to spectators, such as locking coins, the locking key ring, or a locking slate. [fairly common]
n. A combination of a shell coin and its real insert that clicks in to hold fast.

term: Locking Key Ring; locking key ring
definition: n. A key ring for the Linking Rings trick, which substitutes a spring or other closure for the usual gap in the metal hoop. [rare] "Wonder if Himber really has a locking key ring that defies detection?" — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Apr 1946), 210

n. A long card (1) being the more usual synonym. [rare] Originally, as "Longs", the argot of British card sharps by 1843 (Crambrook cat; 1844 Anderson) and American ones by 1855 (Wyman; 1875 Hartz). Thence magicians jargon by 1898 Stanyon; 1905 Leslie in Magic, 71; 1928 Thayer cat #7; 1937 Hugard; 1946 Gresham in Phoenix #115; 1958 Kanter cat #10; 1971 Tannen cat #9; 1992 Southard in Genii.
2.n. SEE: Stretching Card

n. Climax of the Salt Trick where a very large amount of salt can be poured from the magician's fist. [very rare] This effect was invented in the late 1930s by Roy Benson, using the small model Paul Fox Salt Gimmick and popularized by him. Seeing Benson's performance, Faucett Ross recommended to Fox that he design a larger Salt Gimmick. Fox did so, the gimmick being spun in aluminum by Earl Violet. Then, after WW II, repopularized by Fred Kaps using the larger model Fox gimmick. REF: Bertram (1978), 161; Lewis (1985), 137.

term: long and short pack; Long and Short Pack
definition: 1.n. A set of playing cards composed of longs and shorts (1) that the magician would use in preparing gaffed decks. [Brit.] [obsolete after 1924]

n. A playing card arched (crimped) along the middle of its length. [very rare] Originally a method used by British card sharps by 1792 when they called it "saddling" Conjuror's Magazine as "Saddling the Cards"; 1821 Ingleby; 1844 Anderson; 1855 Wyman; 1868 Green. REF: Conjuror's Magazine (1792).
n. Type of pass sleight that transposes the two halves of a deck of playing cards in their long direction. [rare]

n. A mechanical deck composed of a mix of long cards and short cards; a long and short pack (rare). [rare] Originally the argot of British card sharps by 1844 (J.H. Anderson) and American by 1855 (Wyman; 1868 Green; 1875 Hartz). Thence magicians jargon by 1898 Stanyon; 1901 West ad in Magic; 1933 Davenport cat; 1937 Annemann.
v. To replace a playing card at (or seemingly at) random in its deck. [rare]

a. Said of a playing card that seemingly has been replaced randomly in the deck. [common] "In any trick in which a card is selected by a spectator the essential feature is that he must be convinced that the selected card is lost in the deck ...." 548 — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1958), 75

n. A metal bowl in the traditional and characteristic shape of the Indian brass water vessel but faked with a load chamber; redundantly as Lota Bowl; the Hindoo Lota (obsolete). [common] Can be worked to seem, alternately, empty or full of water. This device (originally of earthenware) was invented by Indian conjurors. First reported being performed by Bengali magicians at the court of Emperor Jahangir (reigned 1605-27). Later reported around 1830s by Rev. Caunter performed at a rajah's court and in 1875 when performed in Bombay for the future King Edward VII. Borrowed thence by Western magicians. Reintroduced to modern Indian stage magic by P.C. Sorcar as the "Waters of India". REF: Siegel (1991), 160; Frost (1876), 211-212. Originally the Hindi word lota, meaning a spheroidal water bowl, usually of metal. Introduced into Standard English in 1809. REF: OED/2. Thence Western magicians jargon by 1932 Thayer cat #7S, 52; 1935 Annemann; 1939 Kanter cat 1942 Gibson in Phoenix #15; 1949 Hay; 1962 Ireland cat #17; 1979 Severn; 1980 Tannen cat #13; 1981 Ayling; 1983 Abbott cat #22; 1992 Garrett in MUM; 2002 Diamond’s Magic flyer.

n. Redundant synonym for the lota (see). [fairly common] “The Lota Bowl is one of those never-fail repeat stunts which build with each pouring.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (May 1953), 1077
n. Acronym of The Linking Ring, official publication of the International Brotherhood of Magicians (I.B.M.). [very rare] Published by the I.B.M. since 1922.

n. A paint containing a phosphor (such as zinc sulfide activated with copper) that glows in the dark. Used by magicians mainly to produce ghostly or spiritualistic effects but also to mark stage equipment and positions during a blackout. [fairly common] Patented in 1877 by W.H. Balmain but without using this term. Standard English since around 1889. REF: Webster's 10th Collegiate; OED/2. Term used by magicians by 1886 Peck & Snyder cat; 1886 Garenne; 1901 Sylvestre cat; 1903 Stanyon ad in Magic; 1919 Thayer cat #4; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1931 Douglas cat #16; 1935 Abbott cat #3; 1936 Reilly cat; 1939 Kanter cat as "Luminous Ghostlite Paint"; 1941 Chicago Magic cat #18; 1945 Wheeler cat; ; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1963 Lawston cat; 1969 Magicland cat #38; 1973 Alain; 1988 Waters; 1991 Walker.

n. Red-tinted eye glasses, enabling the performer to read red-backed playing cards marked with green ink. Compare luminous work. [rare] "Make no mistake, laymen are aware of the principle of the so-called ‘luminous readers'." — Jeff Busby in Short Sheet #13 (1987), p.[10]

n. A book test that uses a periodical. [fairly common]

1.n. Generally, any non-supernatural conjuror. Pronounced MAYJ. Plural is mages, pronounced MAYJEZ. Compare magus/magi. [very rare] From the archaic (obsolete since 1877) English "mage" (pronounced MAYJ and meaning a supernatural magician), an Anglicized form of the Latin "magus". A parallel development was the French "mage" (pronounced MAHZH) meaning a magian or magus. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1938 in the poem title of "A Ballade of the Would Be Mage" by Charlton Andrews in Jinx

n. A magician or magicians. [common] Because this old English word is a direct borrowing from Latin, the form magi properly refers only to the plural, magus being the etymologically correct singular. However, as Jeff Busby suggests, most magicians, having learned the language of magic before they learned Latin, independently coined "magi" as an obvious contraction of "magician". And a few conjurors such as Dr. A. M. Wilson who knew Latin couldn't care less. Consequently, the great majority of conjurors freely use magi as both singular and plural as well as coining the plural word magis (an unnecessarily redundant plural in Latin, but logical in English) and the rather amusing "maguses". My recommendation on usage by magicians is to observe the Latin magus/magi distinction when speaking or writing to a lay audience but to use whichever term comes most easily in addressing fellow maguses. 551 Although Hoffmann in 1876 called one trick "The Magi's Brazen Rod", his reference was clearly biblical and thus not jargon.

n. A conjuring performance; an act. [fairly common] "I would do my magic act on Cable TV, but I dont know any dirty words!" — Elwood Rabit [Cleve Haubold, aka "Van Cleve"] in The Linking Ring (May 1987), 64

n. The art of magic (see) being the most usual synonym; magical art; art magique. [fairly common] "Messrs. Braunan and Martini, a couple of fresh youngsters, are now en vaudeville in this country [the USA], doing their best to discredit the magic art by exposés." — Henry Ridgely Evans in Magic (Apr 1902), 54

1.n. Stage act where the magician, standing before a prop bar, pours any drink called for; a bar act. Usually capitalized. [very rare] Although obviously inspired by the old inexhaustible bottle and Magic Kettle effects, this modern version was created by French magician "Ryss" (Georges Gay). Billed as "Satan's Barman" he took this act to South America in 1927, playing the Casino in Buenos Aires in 1931. Ryss inspired the many copy acts. Swiss magician De Roze introduced this type of act to the USA in 1934 (a year after the repeal of Prohibition) when he appeared in the "Continental Variety" show in New York City. He was simultaneously performing it on the main stage of the Casino de Paree by December 1934 when reviewed by Annemann and Mulholland. De Roze's success bred a host of imitators, including Charles Hoffman who opened with a copy act (while De Roze was still doing his) as "The Magician Barman" in 1936 at the Astor Club. Then came Mystic Craig in 1937 with his "Mystery Bar". By 1938 Hoffman had become such a sensation that he is widely miscredited with the creation of the bar act. Also a pet act of Professeur Okati and The Great Marcel in France, Joan Brandon (by 1939), Dell O'Dell (in 1941), Val Voltane (1942), Nardini & Nadyine (1940s-60s), and Kalanag (by 1954). 554 GEN REF: Bamberg (1988), 158; Annemann in Jinx (1934), 10, and (1937), 204, 228; Price

(See also: Magic Bricks.) n. Effect where a stack of four or more numbered or lettered blocks changes order when covered and uncovered by a fitted tube; Magic Blocks. [rare]

1.n. A volume (however slim) on conjuring; a book (see); a magical book (Brit.); a conjuring book. [fairly common] "Ye dinna get magic from books." — John Ramsay, quoted in Lewis, I (1980), 34 "One good magic book is worth 100 tricks." — Jon Evans in The Linking Ring (Nov 1985), 94 "Magicians don't really like to read magic books." --- Jim Steinmeyer, Device and Illusion (1991), 9.
n. Effect where a stack of four or more numbered or lettered blocks changes order when covered and uncovered by a fitted tube; Magic Blocks. [rare]

n. The informal fellowship of magicians; magicdom. [rare] Originally Standard English by 1712 meaning a protective circle drawn around a person to fend off the supernatural powers of evil magic. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1871 A. Blitz, as book title Fifty Years in the Magic Circle; 1903 Stanyon in Magic, 37, as article title, "Thirty Years in the Magic Circle", re Carl Willmann; 1909 Collings pattering, as quoted in Magic, 60.

(See also: Circle, the.) n. Abbreviation of The Magic Circle, the most prestigious British magic club. [fairly common] The Magic Circle was founded in 1905 in London by Neil Weaver, Herbert J. Collings, and Ernest K. Adams with 23 magicians including David Devant as its first president. Its membership, which grew to 250 by 1907 and 1,500 by 1979, and was limited to males over 18 until 1991 when women were admitted. Since it began publication in 1906, the official members-only journal has been The Magic Circular. REF: Dexter (1956), 51-62; Dif #2 (1971- 74), 407-410; Lamb (1979), 96; Severn (1979), 151-152, 231-233. "In recent years the Circle has been the object of some controversy due to its refusal to admit women as members—a policy which has been a source of embarrassment to many people both within the Circle and in the larger British magic community." — T. A. Waters, The Encyclopedia of Magic and Magicians (1988), 215 201 "As Paul [Daniels] told me face to face: ‘List me six real potential T.V. star magicians within The Circle and I'll listen to you.' I am afraid I had to be silent." — Ian Adair in Trixigram (Nov 1988), 23

n. A clown-magician; a clown whose act includes conjuring. [fairly common] Among the better known magic clowns in the USA have been "Zovello" (Sam Wishner, since 556 1940s), Hal Griffin (in 1950s), "Paolo" (Paul Klingler), Ernie Kerns, and "Rebo" (Bev Bergeron, 1958-65).

n. A formal association of magicians. [fairly common] "If you want to keep your secrets, the last place to take them is a magic club." — Karl Germain, quoted in Cramer (1966), 97 "Some magic clubs have meetings where they keep minutes and waste hours." — Howard Bamman in The Linking Ring (Jan 1989), 42

n. A proprietor of a magic shop; a magical dealer (primarily Brit.). [common] “For three hundred and three score years, magic dealers have sold the paraphernalia necessary for magicians to perform their tricks.” — Jean Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jun 1955), 299 “Until just after the turn-of-the-century, magic dealers were the real keepers of the secrets, respected and looked-to by the professionals. Times have changed with the proliferation of magic shops all selling the same products.” — Jeff Busby in Thaumaturgist, No.35 (Dec 1997), 4
n. A magic shop (see) being the most usual modern synonym; a magical depot (mainly Brit.). [obsolescent after 1940s, formerly rare]
n. A magic shop (see) being the most usual modern synonym. [obsolescent after 1950s, formerly rare]

(See also: history of magic.) n. The story or chronicle of the art and craft of conjuring and conjurors; magic history. [rare] "Regarding my unmasking of Robert Houdin ... the only mistake I did make was to call it the name I did when it ought to have been 'The History of Magic.'" — Houdini, letter to Harry Leat, 20 Apr 1926 The earliest attempt at general magic history was Thomas Frost's The Lives of the Conjurors (1876, 360pp). This was followed by Sidney W. Clarke's The Annals of Conjuring (1929, 291pp); Carl Graf von Klinckowstroem’s Die Zauberkunst: Meister, Geschichte, Tricks (1954, 138pp); Milbourne Christopher's Panorama of Magic (1962, 216pp) and The Illustrated History of Magic (1973; 452pp); and Max Dif’s Histoire et évolution technique de la prestidigitation (1971-74), the largest & most nearly comprehensive history of magic. 451 Many specialized historical studies are available: David Price's Magic: A Pictorial History of Conjurers in the Theater (1985, 551pp), Brian McCullagh’s Sydney's Magic Heritage (1994, 319pp), etc, etc. These include the numerous historical biographies and autobiographies.
