1.n. Apparatus of teakettle shape that gives the effect of pouring any drink called for. [fairly common] In its several methods, merely the old Inexhaustible Bottle in new guise. First mentioned and exposed in its kettle form by P.H. Cannon in "Lessons in Magic" in Our Young Folks, Apr 1867. Performed by Chris Charlton (who falsely claimed its invention) in Leek, England, in 1904. Charlton claimed to have it shown it to David Devant. Devant, magically parodying this vogue by applying the Inexhaustible Bottle principle, inadvertently revived the kettle-shaped version as his "Obliging Kettle" in 1905 (although Devant claimed to have performed it in the provinces as early as 1902). It was later in the repertoire of Levante (by 1935 to at least 1940), Jay Palmer (by 1941 to at least 1952), and Jeffrey Atkins (1980s). REF: Sharpe (1983), 90-92; Price (1985), 358-359; Devant (1931), 87-88; Devant (1936), 119-122; Andrews (1971), 99.

n. A magic set (U.S.) or box of tricks (Brit.) being the more usual synonyms. [rare] “After he amazed ‘em, the King of Koins [Al Flosso] sold ‘em a ten-cent magic kit.” 558 — Gary Brown, The Coney Island Fakir (1997), 35

n. Earliest form of optical projector of still pictures, which were mounted on a transparent slide. [archaic, formerly common] The basic principles of the magic lantern (or zoetrope) appeared as early as 207 BC in China. In 121 BC a magician named Shao Ong staged a seance for his emperor that featured such a device, one that cast its images on a screen. REF: Robert Temple, The Genius of China: 3,000 Years of Science, Discovery, and Invention (London: Prion, 1998), 87-88. The magic lantern was slow to reach Europe. It was’t even mentioned until as late as 1420 AD in a manuscript by Giovanni da Fontana, a Venetian. It first saw print in John Bate, Mysteryes of Nature and Art (1634) and then by German Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher in the 1646 edition of his Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae [The Great Art of Light and Shadow] and detailed instructions followed in 1659 by Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens, the "father" of the science of optics. Private magic lantern shows were popular throughout Europe since the 1660s and public demonstrations became popular in the 1790s. REF: L. Mannoni, D.P. Campagnoni, & D. Robinson, Light and Movement: Incunabula of the motion picture (London: British Film Institute, 1996). The word has been Standard English since 1696, as a literal translation of the Latin laterna magica. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon (variants noted) by 1763 Dean as "Magick Lanthorn; 1820 Babcock as "Magic Lanthorn"; 1829 Boy’s Own Book; 1842 Charles Dickens Dec 3rd letter to Prof. Felton, as "magic lantern"; 1857 Magician's Own Book; 1882 Hamley cat; 1886 Peck & Snyder cat; 1988 Waters, 260; 1992 Randi; 1997 Waldman. magic for magicians; Magic for Magicians phr. Conjuring for conjurers being the most usual synonym; magician's magic. [rare] "Do not burden your audience with what is known in the profession as 'Magic for Magicians.' So called 'clever' effects, done by complicated methods, cut no ice at all and are thus so much wasted effort." — Anthony Norman, Basic Card Technique (1948), 77 "Magic for magicians happens to be a narrow segment of our art from which we personally happen to get a lot of pleasure. And why not? The main reason that most of us got interested in tricks in the first place is because we were fooled at some point in our lives by a magician." — Bruce Elliott in The Phoenix #266 (1952), 1065
See: Magi Minister. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Magi Minister".)

n. A flat-surfaced metal reflecting disk that casts whatever patterned image is on its back. [rare] The magic mirror had been invented in China by the Fifth Century AD. The scientific cause of this odd effect was long a matter of speculation until the late 1800s when it was proven by experiment that distortions on the back are minutely conveyed to the flat polished surface which then reflects this pattern. Some Japanese examples are in The Magic Circle Museum. Chinese examples have also survived. REF: Hopkins (1897), 416-421; Major C.H. Montgomery, The Japanese Magic Mirror (London: The Magic Circle, 1949); Robert Temple, The Genius of China: 3,000 Years of Science, Discovery, and Invention (London: Prion, 1998), 66-67..

n. Effect where a dummy mouse moves in lively fashion upon the hand and clothing of the magician. [rare] A popular novelty sales item with street pitchmen in the USA as early as 1874 and in Australia as recently as 1980. A pet trick of Joe Stuthard. Inspired the "Squirmal" toy of the late 1970s, which became a delightful and truly magical effect in the hands of Dick Koornwinder. REF: Hopkins (1897), 135.

n. Any dry substance that the magician sprinkles over a trick—ostensibly to make it work magically, actually as a pretext for a sleight. [rare] Specific names are woofle dust (by 1927), "Magic Sand" (in 1927 Tarbell), and "Goofer Powder" (1941 James). First described in 1584 by Prevost in using “oribus” powder in the Gypsy Thread trick as an excuse to ditch the visible cut pieces of thread in a pocket and switch them there for the secret balled-up whole thread. Then in 1793 by Decremps in his Testament de Jérôme Sharp while explaining the conventional ruse for ditching the fake knot in the Cut-and-Restored Cord trick: "Place the knot in your pocket under the pretence of taking a handkerchief or some sympathetic powder."

n. A box of assorted conjuring tricks for children; box of tricks being the more usual British synonym; a magic kit. [very common] First marketed in 1803 in Nuremberg. In Britain, Hamley's 1882 catalog listed "The Wizard's Cabinet of Magic" with ten "capital tricks" including the Ball of Worsted and the Bottle Imp. Peck & Snyder advertised a "Box of Conjuring Tricks" in 1886. The most famous were the Mysto Magic sets. The most famous in Britain were those by Ernest Sewell. REF: Hans-Günther Witt, Zauberkasten (1987). A quarterly journal devoted to the subject since 1980 is Wittus Witt's A-B-C of Magic Sets. See also Booth (1990), 167-169. "[M]agicians are always searching for methods ... that squelch the fellow who once had a magic set." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 168 "I started out in the usual way. You know, one Christmas as a kid you get a magic set and then you buy a book." — Siegfried Fischbacher, quoted in Hyla Clark (1976), 132

n. A retail store that sells magicians props, tricks, and books; a magic emporium (rare); a magic store (rare); a magic depot (U.S., obsolete), magical depot (Brit., obsolescent); a magical repository (obsolete); a conjuring depôt (obsolete). Compare dealer. [common] "There's enough apparatus in the magic shops for all the magicians in the country, but are there enough magicians in the country for all the apparatus?" — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1946), 278 "The magic store is the most secret of a magician's gimmicks." — Bruce Elliott in The Phoenix #124 (1947), 500 “Look at the average magic shop and you’ll see a collection of tricks designed to fool magicians, not entertain people.” — Robert Orben in Genii (Oct 1953) "Running a magic shop is like managing a nursery, except the babies are bigger." — Marvin Kaye, My Brother, the Druggist (New York: Crime Club/Doubleday, 1979), 95 "We've a first-rate assortment of magic; And for raising a posthumous shade With effects that are comic or tragic, There's no cheaper house in the trade." — W. S. Gilbert, The Sorcerer (1877), Act I Magic shops, particularly their back rooms, have been traditional gathering places for magicians for nearly two centuries. Originally they catered exclusively to professionals and well-to-do serious amateurs. It was not until the 1920s that many opened their doors to youths and amateurs. These shops have also provided a start toward professional performance for many magicians including such superstars as Cardini and Ali Bongo. For other magi, they remained their sole or main place of regular public performance, as with the justly celebrated Daisy White, Duke Stern, and Al Cohen.

n. A layout of numbers whose rows, columns, and diagonals add to identical totals. [fairly common] "Dr. Dr. [sic] Lyons will discuss wire puzzles and magic squares only with Dr. Gardner." — Clayton Rawson, "The Witchdoctors Club By-Laws" (1961) Although originally a form of mathematical puzzle, known to mathematicians for over 2,000 years, it has been made a magic trick by several magicians (including Heath, Meyer, Snader, Johnson, and Slaight), where the surprise effect comes from either the speed at which it is done or the fact that the total of the squares matches predicted number or a number thought of by a spectator. Standard English since around 1704. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1857 Magician's Own Book; 1931 Annemann; 1932 Heath in Sphinx; 1938 Hilliard; 1945 Jones in Bat; 1947 Kanter cat #8; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1948 Holden cat #15; 1958 Corinda; 1961 Meyer; 1972 Anderson; 1974 Dexter; 1979 Lamb; 1984 Stover in Epoptica #6; 1988 Waters; 1992 Abrams.

n. A wand being the most usual synonym; a magician's wand (Brit); a conjuring wand (obsolete). [common] "On Christmas Eve, 1885, [John Henry] Anderson laid down his magic wand, he hoped finally, in order to resume his first and best-loved occupation of an actor on the dramatic stage." — Sidney W. Clarke in The Magic Wand, V.15 (1926), 36 "Audiences expect to hear magic words and to see a magic wand, so why not use the wand in your opening mystery?" — Dawes & Setterington, The Encyclopedia of Magic (1986), 170 Originally Standard English by 1786 in its supernatural sense. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1857 Magician's Own Book; 1861 Novra cat; 1867 Stodare; 1876 Hoffmann; 1882 Hamley cat; 1896 Bertram; 1909 Downs/Hilliard; 1910 The Magic Wand periodical; 1912 Goldston; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1924 Heaney cat #25; 1937 J.G. Alexander; 1949 Tannen cat #1; 1957 Hugard; 1965 Lawston cat; 1976 Page; 1981 Ray- Mond; 1983 Ghastly Gallimaufry cat #2; 1983 Tannen cat #14; 1988 Magic City price list; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Marvello flyer; 1993 KT Magic cat; 1995 J. Gardner; 1997 Lee cat #11; 2000 Abbott flyer; 2002 Diamond's Magic flyer.
n. Effect where separate metal rings become linked in a chain when poured into or onto a container. [rare]

n. A command or incantation to ostensibly activate a supernatural force, thereby triggering a magical effect; magical mumbo-jumbo; words of art (obsolete); a conjuration (1) (obsolete). The magus may use it himself as part of his patter or he may recommend it to a volunteer assistant. Popular or once popular examples are abracadabra, allakazam, Change!, cockalorum (obsolete), Gali-Gali, Go!, hocus pocus, hiccius doctius (obsolete), jingo (obsolete), Jubeo (obsolete), mumbo jumbo (obsolete), Pass!, Pepsi Cola, Presto!, Shazam!, Sim Sala Bim, and vada (obsolete). [common] Conjurors have used magic words in their patter since at least as early as 1584 with J. Prevost in France and Reginald Scot in England . I assume they originally did so in imitation of the religious priests since antiquity. Unusual magic words are adopted by a few modern magi, such as Professor Hoffmann with "Aldeborontico/fosfico/formico", William Alstrand who used "Poogie-Poogie", and George B. Anderson who since 1954 took "Okefenokee" from the Florida swamp of that name. REF: Joglar [Christopher] in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1955), 270. "Then he utterred [sic] the magic words 'HOCUS POCUS, HI COCKALORUM CROKUS' and there was the rope all in one piece and free from knots." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jun 1950), 669 "Ask any youngster in St. Louis and the surrounding area what the magic word is—99 times out of a hundred you'll hear Pepsi Cola. It has replaced Presto, Abracadabra, and all the others." — Ernie Heldman in J. Marshall (1955), 74 "As children we saw the world of magic from a different perspective. Before we ever knew about double-lifts, or key rings, or boxes with false bottoms, I suspect that we really believed that the magic words, or spell, or wand really did the magic, and that if we had that wand or knew that spell we too could be magicians. But then we learned." — Charles J. Pecor in The Linking Ring (Feb 1997), 71
See: world of magic. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "world of magic".)

a. Of or pertaining to magic; magic being the more common adjectival synonym in America but 564 the less usual one in Britain; magicky; necromantic (obsolete). Compare magickal. [very common, particularly in Britain] "This Feat may well be called Magical, for really it is very amazing if it be well handled ...." — H. Dean, The whole Art of Legerdemain (1763 ed), 22 "Probably the most magical looking as well as the most popular of all gaffed ace assemblies is the McDonald Aces." — Darwin Ortiz, The Annotated Erdnase (1991), 201

(See also: magic art, the.) n. The art of magic (see) being the most usual synonym; magical art; art magique. [fairly common] "Messrs. Braunan and Martini, a couple of fresh youngsters, are now en vaudeville in this country [the USA], doing their best to discredit the magic art by exposés." — Henry Ridgely Evans in Magic (Apr 1902), 54
See: bartender-magician. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "bartender-magician".)
n. A magic book (1) being the standard term in the USA and the less usual one in Britain. [rare]
n. A magic dealer (see) being the more usual synonym, particularly in the USA. [fairly common, particularly in Britain]

n. A stage performance in which a series of separate tricks and illusions are tied together by an overall plot to create a playlet with magic. [rare] "Magical sketches are an excellent means of making one or two illusions go a long way." — David Devant, Secrets of My Magic (1936), 129 Devised by Maskelyne & Cooke when they premiered their "La Dame et la Gorilla" in Sep 1865 in Cheltenham as an interlude. They enlarged this in 1869 as "The Mystic Freaks of Gyges". Next they evolved their final version, Will, the Witch, and the Watchman, which they premiered in 1873 and which became a phenomenal popular success, running intermittently for three decades at the Egyptian Hall. Early imitators were Buatier de Kolta with "La Danse des Millions"and Kellar in 1906 with his "The Witch, the Sailor and the Enchanted Monkey". Later stage illusionists who have featured this format include Lafayette (in 1906 with his "The Medicine Man" 2-act playlet), David Devant, David "Fu-Manchú" Bamberg, Doug Henning, David Copperfield, and Siegfried & Roy. REF: Sam Sharpe, The Magic Play (1976); Goldston (1912), 310; Christopher (1973), 243.
adv. Having one or more characteristics of magic. [fairly common]
n. The social world of conjurors; the World of Magic; magicland; the magic circle. [fairly common]
n. A magic performance. [very rare, probably nonce]

n. A performer of natural magic; a conjurer; a deceptionist. Opposite of layman. Magician is the preferred term, while conjuror or simply performer are acceptable for stylistic variation. Popular synonyms like "wizard", "sorcerer", "professor", "wonderworker", and "necromancer" are or were used by magi mainly as publicity puffery but are now seen occasionally as jargon for the sake of sheer variety and always a bit tongue-in-cheek. [very common] "A conjuror is ... an actor playing the part of a magician." — Robert-Houdin, The Secrets of Conjuring and Magic (1868/1877 tr), 43 "A magician is an actor playing the part of a prestidigitator." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Oct 1955), 337 "In my opinion 95% of the success of a Magician depends on his ability as an actor." — T. N. Downs, ms letter to Faucett Ross, 1 Jul 1926 "If you can act you can become a magician!" — Ken Griffin, Illusion Show Know-How (1972), 1 "Few magicians and psychics are actors. They generally louse the action up." — Ted Annemann in The Jinx (1940), 544 "All magicians are a little crazy, or they wouldn't be in the business." — Michael Rubinstein, Inside Street Magic (1985), 21 "There is too much subterfuge among magicians, as it is; too much deception where there is no occasion for artifice; too much boasting, too much self-laudation, too much—to put it in plain Anglo-Saxon—downright lying. There are too many ‘wonderful' magicians in the business, too many ‘greats'.... Why this is so is not difficult to understand. The only difficulty is to read their nauseous self-advertisements." 567 — John N. Hilliard in The Sphinx (Mar 1905), 8 "The only difference between scientists and magicians is that scientists will tell you how their tricks work!" — Larry White in M-U-M (Nov 1994), 21 "I discovered at age six that almost everything in this world was phony, worked with mirrors. Since then, I've always wanted to be a magician." — Orson Welles, 1943 "The price of becoming a magician is a loss of innocence." — Charles J. Pecor in The Linking Ring (Feb 1997), 71 This word was occasionally in use in its benign non-supernatural sense by the lay public as early as 1673. Also 1834 Weeks Museum cat re an automaton conjuror. Thence, in this latter sense, magicians jargon by 1836 Engstrom; 1838 Sutton, Feb 12th London playbill, billed as "The Great Magician"; 1838 Anderson, Apr 30th Hull playbill, billed as "The Great Caledonian Magician"; 1838 Ching, Aug 30th York program; 1841 Jacobs poster; 1852 Macallister, Philadelphia playbill; 1854 "The Great Chinese Magicians", British playbill; 1857 Magician's Own Book; 1863 as a parlour magician; 1871 Cremer; 1876 Hoffmann; 1912 as a stage magician; 1913 as a comedy magician; 1924 Clarke in Magic Wand, 17; 1932 Ranson in Sphinx as a "vest pocket magician"; 1937 Holden as a "club magician"; 1950 as a vaudeville magician; 1951 E. Silverman as a "TV magician"; 1963 as a gospel magician; 1983 R. Stebbins; 1984 as a restaurant magician; 1985 Price as a "gift-show magician"; 1988 Waters; 1990 Jeffreys; 1995 J. Gardner; 2001 L&L "2002" cat as "corporate magicians".
n. Any trick (specifically a fooler) that deceives conjurors, that is, a specific instance of conjuring for conjurers. Compare layman fooler. [rare]
n. The Magician Makes Good card effect that substitutes a different patter story, one in which the magician tells of having pitted his skills against those of a card sharp. [rare]
a. Said of a trick whose method even most magicians cannot detect. The noun form is a magician fooler. [very rare, possibly nonce] 568

n. The equivoque (see), which is the most usual synonym; conjurer's choice. [fairly common] "The Magician's Choice gambit is a technique which should be learned and practiced by every magician. Basically it involves giving a spectator one or more limited choices and, by reacting instantly to these choices as if they were exactly what you wanted, guiding him to the conclusion you wish." — Phil Willmarth in The Linking Ring (Jul 1987), 65
n. A 48-card deck of playing cards faked with multiple banks of 12 cards repeated; the so-called Koran Deck. [rare]
n. Sucker by-play (business) where the conjuror pretends to blunder.

(See also: Insurance Policy.) n. Effect where the magus claims he will pay a specific sum of money if he fails to name the chosen card and shows a simulated insurance policy to cover possible failure. He miscalls the card, apparently losing; but then wins when, upon opening the policy, a giant picture of the right card appears. [common]

n. False reasoning given the audience by the conjuror; a throw-off; proof; conjurer's logic (obsolete). See also the deceitful phrase "no deception". [rare] Examples of magician's logic are: 1) "proving" a loaded production tube empty by pushing a second handkerchief through it with a wand. 2) demonstrating that "all" the billiard balls or linking rings are solid by striking some of them together.

n. Conjuring for conjurers being the more usual synonym, particularly in Britain. [rare] "I am generally not involved with 'magician's magic,' so you will find the following material to be lay-person oriented." — Gerald Edmundson in The Linking Ring (Nov 1996), 89

n. A conjuror whose appeal is mainly to other conjurors, specifically as an inventor, teacher, mentor, or good example. [rare] "Too often the magician's magician is the layman's bore." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1950), 694 "Another old saw is that a magician's magician can never make it in show business. Al [Baker] was the exception and was highly successful professionally." — David Price, Magic (1985), 416

(See also: Oil of Milk.) n. A liquid chemical that when mixed with water turns an opaque white, simulating milk. Abbreviated as OOM, its acronym. Also, less usually, called Magician's Milk. [rare] Discovered (using a petroleum product) by American magician Logan Wait around 1941, as a 651 convenient ingredient for his and Roger Montandon's Invisible Bovine trick. First marketed that same year by Montandon's Magic of Tulsa, Oklahoma. Has the obvious advantages that the "milk" did not sour and the magician need carry only a small bottle to be added to water at the place of performance. Its only disadvantages are that it is unsafe to drink and may discolor plexiglas. REF: Telephone interviews with Wait and Montandon, 23 Jun 1988; Booth (1990), 105.
n. A magic wand being the most usual synonym. [rare]

n. A tacky substance to make two objects adhere temporarily and secretly; conjurer's wax being the more usual synonym in Britain. [very common in USA] First exposed in 1584 by Reginald Scot who mentions both "greene waxe (for that is softest and therefore best)" to join coins and "red wax" on a finger-tip to pick up a coin and vanish it in a sleight. In 1844 Anderson recommended soap and pomatum. Beeswax was in use by 1876 (Hoffmann) to attach thread to a card. Diachylon (lead plaster) was first applied to cards in the mid-1800s by Austrian magician J.N. Hofzinser (d.1875) but his long-kept secret was not revealed until 1918 when published by Professor Hoffmann in his Latest Magic.

n. A female magician; a magicianess; a conjuress. Compare Magigal. [obsolescent, once fairly common] Originally borrowed from French into English meaning a supernatural sorceress. Used by Caxton in 1490, possibly as a nonce-word as his is the only citation in the OED/2 and I do not find the word in any other English-language dictionary. I did find it once in an 1895 Australian newspaper clipping, there used in its non-supernatural sense as "Jennie Anderson, magicienne, and her troupe"; but, as seen below, probably as a loan-word from magicians jargon. In any case it has long been obsolete in Standard English, although still current in French. Happily this fine old word has recently been revived, but in a non-supernatural sense, in the jargon of magicians—a very rare case of such linguistic resuscitation. However, it is not often used, as most magicians are male and the proportionately few female magicians themselves tend to use (and prefer) that conventional and ungendered word when among other professionals. When used by women magi it is largely done so as a publicity title, as with "La Magicienne, Madame Macallister" (1857), "Litzka, Harpiste-Magicienne" (c.1930), "Shan, The Lovely Magicienne and Dancer" (1951), "Paula Dolan, Dancing Magiciene [sic]" (1963), "Sandra the Magicienne" (1972), "Shelley Carroll, ‘The Magicienne'" (1979), and "Rita Jane [O'Dowd] the Magicienne" (1980s).
a. Pertaining to bizarre magick. [rare]
n. One who does magic; a magician. [very rare, probably nonce]
n. A magician who performs bizarre magick; a Mage. [rare]
v. To perform magic. [very rare, possibly nonce]

n. Having the quality of magic; magical. [rare] "For his mental routines, he [Karrell Fox] uses only ordinary-looking props, and avoids even the 572 slightest suggestion of anything ‘tricky' or ‘magicky' in his entertainingly straightforward presentation." — Bill Severn, Bill Severn's Guide to Magic as a Hobby (1979), 58-59
n. The world of magic; magicdom being the most usual synonym. [rare]

n. A magician, often somewhat facetiously. [fairly common] "If you're in the Big City check the Palace billings, more magicos appear here than at any other outlet in Manhattan." — Frank Joglar [Milbourne Christopher] in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Aug 1954), 170 Originally the Spanish word mágico, meaning a magician in both its supernatural and non-supernatural senses. Thence magicians jargon by 1834 Ching Lau Lauro, Wolverhampton handbill. Then, after a century-long gap, 1933 as title of the invitation-only magic club "Los Magicos" founded that year in southern California by Caryl S. Fleming; 1939 Señor Mardo business card as "Mágico"; 1941 Annemann in Jinx #138 as "an ex-magico"; 1945 Hayman in Conjurors' Magazine; 1948 Elliott in Phoenix #163; 1951 Arcuri letter in HMM; 1953 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1954 J. Marshall in New Phoenix #316; 1986 Desmond in LR as the "magicos of Ring 59"; 1990 Wassilak in MM as "Boston magicos". NOTE: Thence into English theatrical slang meaning magic by 1956 Bill Willard in 27 Feb Daily Variety as “moments of
n. A magician. [very rare]
See: comedy magician. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "comedy magician".)

(See also: comedy magic.) n. Conjuring performed with a comedic plot or patter; magicomedy. Compare burlesque magic. [common] "Most comedy magic is a spoof of the art, doing a trick badly or exposing it at the end." 232 — John Carney in The Linking Ring (Sep 1986), 61 "Comedy born of bewilderment is the only comedy that should be in magic." — Dai Vernon as quoted in D. Bamberg (1988), 253 "If you do comedy magic, remember that you must still have some real foolers to gain the respect of the audience." — Bev Bergeron in Severn (1979), 48

1.n. Specifically and always capitalized, Magigals International or one of its members. [fairly common] Founded in 1939 in Los Angeles as an offshoot of the Pacific Coast Association of Magicians (PCAM) as "A Magic Organization Exclusively for Women". It has grown from a local chapter 573 into a national and, finally, international organization. Basically a "ladies auxiliary", it does include a small proportion of professional and amateur women magicians and magician's assistants. Its first President was Geraldine "Gerrie" Larsen. REF: F. Ireland (1946), 190.
See: magi minister. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "magi minister".)

n. This French word for magic was occasionally used by English-speaking magi as a pretentious synonym, particularly in the phrase art magique. [obsolescent since 1928, formerly fairly common] "The problem with Al [the Only]'s 'nom de magique' is that it leaves two questions unanswered: Who is he—and what does he do?" — David Avadon in Epoptica (Nov 1985), 408
n. A magnetized coin box used together with a magnetized leather pad or, more recently, a magnetized booklet. Compare Incredi-Box. [fairly common] A Johnson Products exclusive.

n. An iron-centered genuine coin or slug that can be manipulated by magnetism, either actively or passively. Not to be confused with a magnetized coin. [fairly common] Examples are the U.S. "iron" pennies (introduced in 1943 as a wartime saver of copper), Canadian nickels (by 1950), and many palming coins. REF: Murray Sumner in Phoenix #195 (1950), 780.

(See also: snooty pups.) n. A tiny pair of plastic Scotty puppy dogs (one black, one white) mounted on oblong bases. They alternately repell or attract each other when placed nose-to-nose or nose-to-tail, [rare] Worked automatically by the magnetic bases. A highly popular low-comedy (scatological) novelty item introduced in the late 1930s. Became unavailable during World War II, as Orson Welles discovered when he tried to order a set. Spawned several variations. 851

n. Effect where a pencil (or other long object) is suspended from the palm of the hand. [rare] First reported with a rod as "Philosophy Cheated" in 1829 (The Boy’s Own Book, 165-166) and again in 1857 (Magician's Own Book, 24-25).
n. Effect where several playing cards cling to the magician's hand as if by magnetism. [rare]

n. A magician, singular. [rare] Originally a Spanish word for magician, from the Latin magus. Mago is the male form, maga the female, in that gendered language. In Mexico "mago" is the most usual word for magician. In Spain and the rest of Latin America it is "mágico". Thence the jargon of English-speaking magicians by 1983 Russo in Oct/Nov MM as "a mago by the name of ‘Davino'"; 1984 Milt Schorr in Dec MUM, 17; 1987 Mago Frank's Coloring Book. magus
n. Eastern, specifically, Indian magic. [very rare, possibly nonce]

1.n. The muse or patron goddess of magicians. Pronounced MAH-JAH. [fairly common, although somewhat in decline after the 1940s] "Once the Goddess Maja has waved her wand over some individual's head, that one is her devoted slave henceforth." — Houdini, 1919, quoted in Buffum (1977), 129 From the Sanscrit my (pronounced MY-yah) meaning originally illusion and later, by extension, deception. Still later, the Hindu goddess Maya. The word entered both English (in 1788) and German as maja (pronounced MAH-yah). In Germany it became a moderately popular girl's name in the late 1800s, as with Albert Einstein's younger sister Maja. In India as Maya it remains a popular girl's name. NOTE: Goya's famous Spanish portrait known as The Naked Maja does not depict the goddess, the Spanish word "maja" merely meaning a flashy young female. REF: L. Thomas O'Neil, Maya in Sankara: Measuring the Immeasurable (Delhi: South Asia Books, 1980), 1-39; Oxford English Dictionary, 2nd ed; Hubert Wedler, Wörterbuch der Zauberkunst (1990), 132. Interestingly, in Greek myth, the Grecian god of tricksters, Hermes (the Roman Mercury) was the illegitimate son of Apollo and the nymph Maia. REF: Lewis Hyde, Trickster Makes This World (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1998), 22, etc. Thence from theSanskrit through the German it became magicians jargon (with variants noted) by 1900 Max Berol (a German magician) in Feb Mahatma as "upholding Maga's [sic] banner in Japan"; 1919 Houdini; ca1920 Heaney cat #24 as "Maja's Wonder Drum", a Willmann prop; 1924 Conradi-Horster coined name of the new Berlin magic club "Zaubervereinigung Maja"; 1924 Roterberg palming coin as inscription, "Maja — Goddess of Magic"; 1925 Kastner, Tigris, & Cannon as name of their new Viennese magic club "Maja-Gruppe"; 1932 Savage cartoon in Sphinx; 1941 Booth; 1942 Elliott in Phoenix; 1944 Carl Wiesinger in Phoenix #60 as "if the Goddess Maja could speak"; 1946 Karson in Thompson as "clandestine meetings with the Goddess Maja"; 1947 Cramer in Phoenix #119 as "our Goddess Magi tiptoed in"; 1952 Bobo; 1982 Stevens in Berg; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wassilak in MM as "the wonders of the Goddess

term: Malini Egg Bag; Malini egg bag
definition: n. An egg bag with the secret pocket entry at a bottom inside corner. [fairly common]

term: Mango Tree Trick, The; Mango Trick
definition: n. Effect where a plant grows from a seed to a full-sized bush between successive coverings by a bowl or cone; the Growth of Flowers (3). [fairly common] One of the few authentic East Asian conjuring tricks to enter the repertoire of Western magicians. First ascribed to China in the 5th Century AD as being performed regularly at the Yung-ning-szu nunnery temple by magicians who grew melons and dates from pips. Buddhist and Taoist magicians performed this trick with mangoes, peonies, pears, etc., pretending the trick was worked by supernatural means. However, they were merely conning the audience “with their eyes confused and their pupils astray.” That is, by misdirection. Even so the trick may be of Idian origin. REF: Robert van Gulik, “The Mango Trick in China: An Essay on Taoist Magic”, Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japan, 3rd Series, Vol.3 (1954), 117-175. Then reported in India in the memoirs of Mogul Emperor Jahangir (reigned 1605-1627), giving his eyewitness account of an elaborate production by a troupe of Bengali jugglers. Also witnessed in its Indian setting and exposed by Western magicians Kellar (1886, 114-115), Baldwin (1895, 55-57), Bertram (1911), Elbiquet (1917), Carlton (1920, 179-182), Branson (1922), and Siegel (1991) Premiered in the West in 1865 in London at the Egyptian Hall by British magician "Colonel Stodare" (Joseph Stoddart). Joseph M. Hartz claimed to have done the "flower trick" in New York in 1866. M. Dockweiler claimed to have first performed his "East India Growth of Flowers" in the USA during his 1867-68 season. The earliest reported presentation of this trick in the West by authentic Indians was in 1896 when The Elite Hindoo Fakeers toured the USA. REF: Hartz, letter to the editor in Magic (Oct 1901), 5; Docweiler memoir in Mahatma (Apr 1901); Cramer (1962), for the Fakeers.
n. Abbreviation of manipulation.

v. To dexterously handle props such as cards, balls, thimbles, etc. [rare] "Goldin (perhaps because he cannot manipulate cards very well) 'gives away' the back-hand palm. Is he killing the goose that lays the Goldin eggs. Verily, it looks like it!" — Henry Ridgely Evans, column in Magic (Feb 1901), 37

1.n. A routine or entire act limited to the dexterous sleight-of-hand working with one or more types of small objects (particularly cards, coins, billiard balls, or cigarettes). Exclusive to stage acts. [common] Hence these specific terms (with year of first known usage): coin manipulation (1900) card manipulation (1901) handkerchief manipulation (1902) cigar manipulation (1902) ball manipulation (1902) billiard ball manipulation (1909) string manipulation (1914) rope manipulation (1915) thimble manipulation (1924) cigarette manipulation (1924) sponge-ball manipulation (1936) dice manipulation (1945) watch manipulation (1962) dove manipulation (1974) "Happily the mania for manipulation has abated, and the conjurer of the day is ambitious to entertain and mystify his audiences rather than to present a mere juggling act." — T. Nelson Downs & J. Northern Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909), Introductory "Skill in manipulation is no index to skill in deception." — Bill Turner, The Card Wizard (1949)
1.n. The deceptive branch of stage conjuring that depends on sleight of hand. [rare]

n. A stage magician who specializes in sleight-of-hand work with one or several particular types of object. [common] "Many prominent performers in Vaudeville call themselves 'manipulators' in preference to 581 magicians." — Henry Ridgely Evans in Magic (Feb 1901), 37 "You are the greatest manipulator of coins that ever lived." — Houdini, letter to T. N. Downs, 5 Aug 1925 "The manipulator finds the temptation strong upon him to linger lovingly over sleights, passes, and palms galore, whilst losing sight of the ultimate effect on the mind of his audience." — David Devant, Secrets of My Magic (1936), 36 "[U]nfortunately, the true manipulator tends too much towards mere displayed dexterity so that all too often there is no plot in the magical sense. One finds it hard to treat it as magic per se." — Ross Bertram, Bertram on Sleight of Hand (1983), 246 Depending on the objects manipulated, called variously a: card manipulator (by 1896) coin manipulator (by 1899) "handkerchief manipulator" (1901 Evans in Magic; 1902 Stillwell letter in Sphinx) "Paper Manipulator" (1901 Stanyon ad in Magic; 1910 Varney in Magi) "handcuff manipulator" (1904 Stanyon ad in Magic; 1909 Houdini) thimble manipulator (by 1906) "Rope Manipulator" (1915 B. Hull) cigarette manipulator (by 1924) "billiard ball manipulator" (1928 Thayer cat #7; 1941 Chicago Magic cat #18; 1973 Christopher) "dove manipulator" (1959 Owen cat #5; 1973 Tannen cat #10) "ball manipulators" (1976 Page)

n. A string-operated puppet. Compare living marionette. [rare] String-puppet shows (neurospaston) were exhibited in ancient Greece. Also in China during the Sung Dynasty (960-1127). Among the few magicians who included marionette work were 582 Alexandre Cony (1890s), Dicksonn, Arnold Crowther (in the 1920s-30s), and Wee Willie Dee (1930s-40s). The word entered Standard English around 1620 from the French meaning Little Marie. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1829 Boy’s Own Book, 151; 1905 Stanyon ad in Magic; 1924 Clarke in Magic Wand; 1934 Goldston; 1980 J. Marshall; 1985 Price, 24; 1994 Williams; 2005 Magic Castle Newsletter.
n. Any distinguishing symbol made on an object either overtly by a volunteer (initials, signature, symbol, etc.) or covertly by the magician (daub, nicked card, pricked card, etc.). [rare]

n. Playing cards (or ESP cards) whose backs (or sometimes faces or edges) have been secretly coded in any of several ways (inking, pricking, nicking, printing, etc.) to permit the magician to identify their suits or values or both; a marked deck; paper. [very common] "Marked Cards. In magic they are useful in a hundred ways. In poker you can call down 'bluffs,' raise out weak hands and always win. A little study makes you an expert, Per pack, $1.50." — Prof. Harry Houdini, Magic Made Easy (1898), Item 22 "Every magician has used Marked cards for some effect or the other." — Sam Dalal in Mantra (Jul 1975), 16 Complete decks of marked cards are called readers or reader decks in the USA and marked packs in Britain. Magicians (as did the card sharps who inspired them) distinguish several specific types of markings such as block out, bracing, daub, edge-readers, front readers, line marks, luminous readers, nail-nicking, pricked cards, and shading. REF: Guy Raymond, Marked Cards (1970); Ortiz (1984), 37-46; Litzau (1938); Dexter (1958), Ch.10. This artifice was invented by card sharps. Its first recorded use was among Venetian gamblers in 1526 as detected, remembered, and described by Gerolamo Cardano in his Liber de Ludo Aleae (ca1564). The cheat was Cardano's patrician host, Thomas Lezius, who thereby made his name in gambling history. Its use among their British brethren was first reported in 1552 by Gilbert Walker followed in 1612 by S. Rid and 1634 by Hocus Pocus Junior. Originally these cards were marked by hand. Among the earliest commercially printed marked packs were W.G. Edwards' Dioramic Cards (1908), DeLand's Dollar Deck (1910), and the Adam's League Deck (late 1910s), all three of which used DeLand's clock system. Major marked decks today include Ted Lesley's "The Working Performer's Marked Deck" (invented in 1981 and marketed since 1983) and John Cornelius's Dream Deck (marketed 583 since 1987). NOTE: See my discussion under bum-card for its often given but quite unlikely definition as a marked card. Whatever the true meaning of "bum-card", card sharps in Britain called marked cards "markt Packs" by 1674 (Cotton) and in the USA "marked packs" by 1887 (Devol). Sharpers also called them "marked cards" in both Britain (by 1753 as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1815 Ingleby) and America by 1865 (Evans, 41; 1877 Grandin pricelist; 1878 Long; 1884 Will & Finck cat; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne; 1915 Innis). But the sharpers soon tended to avoid that tell-tale term, leaving it to the general card-playing public and to magicians. Thus they began calling them "reflectors" in 1843 (Crambrook cat; 1875 Hartz). And the current (and since 1865) disguised term is "paper". REF: Guy Raymond, Marked Cards (1970). Thence, as marked cards, magicians jargon by 1859 The Boy's Own Conjuring Book; 1874 Union Purchasing Agency cat as "Marked Playing Cards"; 1877 Hoffmann; 1898 Houdini cat; 1906 Stanyon ad in Magic; 1913 Oaks cat #20; 1919 Thayer cat #4; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1924 Heaney cat #25; 1930 Orrin; 1933 Annemann; 1939 Kanter cat as "marked back cards"; 1941 Sterling cat #1; 1942 Ireland cat #10; 1950 Robbins cat #15; 1958 Dexter; 1976 Tarr; 1981 Ray- Mond; 1982 Lesley; 1984 Breese cat; 1989 Tannen cat #16 [deleted from #17]; 1990 Wedler; 1996 Hank Lee’s Book

n. One particular mechanically-operated deck of playing cards used for the Rising Cards effect. Compare Devano pack. 584 [rare] Operated by a clockwork mechanism, as a refinement of the earlier Willman deck. Hand-made, and sold by the famous Lithuanian-born British watchmaker and builder of magic apparatus, John Martin. REF: Dexter (1956), 98-100; Albo, III (1977), 3-5; 1988 Busby annotation.

n. Stage effect where the magus, bearing a lit candle, approaches his assistant who is garbed as a giant moth. She enfolds herself in her wings and the entire figure vanishes. [archaic, formerly rare]

n. A basic sleight in spongeball manipulation where two (or more) balls are squashed together and shown as one. [very rare] The use of this sleight to conceal the presence of a secret second ball while openly putting one in the palm of a volunteer was called the "Improved Sponge Ball Trick" when invented by Al Snyder in 1926. REF: Holden in Sphinx (1926), 253.
n. The general method of camouflaging an object by covering it with something that matches its surface exactly. [rare]

term: SEE UNDER: Glass of Wine/Liquid Production
definition: (See also: Ovette Master Move.) n. The card sleight that moves the face card of the cutoff upper half of the deck to the bottom while the upper half is replaced on the lower. Erroneously called the Kelly Bottom Placement. 667 [rare]
n. Effect where a burning matchstick instantly and visibly transforms into a flower when blown out. [fairly common]
n. Any pair of playing cards of same value and color such as the two black threes. [rare]
n. Abbreviation of mathematical magic (see). [rare]
n. A conjuror specializing in mathematical magic. [rare]

n. The class of conjuring tricks that is based on principles of mathematics (such as theory of numbers, set theory, probability, and topology); mathemagic. In consequence they are self- working. [rare]

n. The Sympathetic Coins (see) being the original but now less usual synonym for this effect and method. [common among coin and card men] "Magic needs another card change like it needs another performer doing ‘Matrix' in a contest." — Dan Huffman in The Linking Ring (Nov 1987), 70

See: cross-reference principle Matter through Matter phr. A penetration being the most usual synonym; Solid through Solid. [rare]. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "cross-reference principle Matter through Matter phr. A penetration being the most usual synonym; Solid through Solid. [rare]".)

n. The master of ceremonies at a magic show, usually a magician who performs a perfunctory trick or two; emcee (U.S.); compère (Brit.). [common] Prominent and popular magician-MCs have been Al Baker, Frank Lane, Werner "Dorny" Dornfield, Roy Benson, Archie Byford, John Wade, Jay Marshall, Harold Taylor, John Salisse, and Sid Lorraine. "Milbourne Christopher was a smooth, effective M.C. His quick tricks seemed designed to tie in with each act." — "Frank Joglar" [Milbourne Christopher] review in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jun 1952), 949
n. A playing card faked with moving parts to show an altered value; now usually called the Moving Pip Card. [obsolete since 1950, formerly rare]
n. Any kind of trick deck or trick card, as now most often called. Usually (but not necessarily) involves some secret movable part. [fairly common]

(See also: mechanical magic.) n. Apparatus effects worked by mechanism; mechanical effects. [rare] "Unlike most sleight-of-hand men, Don [Alan] has a knowing way with equipment and magic." — Frances Ireland in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Mar 1953), 1050 “There is nothing that downgrades magic so quickly as the sight of a teen-age ‘magician’ on television ineptly performing mechanical ‘magic’.” — Fred Braue in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Dec 1961), 47
n. Estimation (of the position of a playing card) by means of touch. Compare Natural Estimation. [rare]

n. Apparatus effects worked by mechanism; mechanical effects. [rare] "Unlike most sleight-of-hand men, Don [Alan] has a knowing way with equipment and magic." — Frances Ireland in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Mar 1953), 1050 “There is nothing that downgrades magic so quickly as the sight of a teen-age ‘magician’ on television ineptly performing mechanical ‘magic’.” — Fred Braue in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Dec 1961), 47
n. Comedy act where the magician plays the part of a medicine show pitchman. [very rare but not nonce] Among the few magicians who specialize in this type of comedy act is Doc Lovecraft.

n. A magician's assistant (traditionally female) who plays the role of a spirit medium, that is, a person with supernatural ability to receive thoughts or impressions. [common] 590 "[S]electing mediums [from the audience] has many disadvantages, the principle one being that some of the persons thus selected are apt to reveal to their friends and acquaintances, of course as a great secret, that they were never mesmerised at all, but that they simply acted and did whatever they were instructed to do." — Henri Garenne, The Art of Modern Conjuring (1886), 325-326 "Mrs. Willard is the best medium I've ever seen. She's a fast worker, and a good actress. I've never seen a so-called 'genuine' medium who could match her cabinet work." — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jul 1952), 954 (re Joy Willard, the wife of Willard the Magician) "The methods used by mediums were far more subtle than the ones used by the average magician since anything that even faintly smacked of trickery could have been fatal." — David Bamberg, Illusion Show (1965/1988), 73 Originally a term used by spiritualists to mean a person (usually female but often male) with the ability to serve as a psychic intermediary between the "spirit world" and the real world. Spiritualists cant by 1851 Rev. Mattison; 1853 Spicer as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1860 Novra handbill; 1877 Carpenter; 1891 A. Medium; 1895 Baldwin; 1901 Sylvestre cat; 1907, D. Abbott; 1935 Magnuson; 1976 Keene. Thence magicians jargon by 1875 Lynn, London playbill; 1876 Heller program; 1887 Hoffmann; 1892 Hodgson in Proceedings of the SPR; 1895 Burlingame; 1897 Caulk in Hopkins; 1898 Houdini cat; 1912 Goldston; 1922 Devant; 1924 Heaney cat #25; 1929 Larsen & Wright; 1932 Annemann; 1932 Gibson; 1934 Read; 1938 Hilliard; 1948 Tarbell; 1948 Elliott; 1956 Dexter; 1957 Furst; 1959 Corinda; 1979 Fulves; 1979 Lamb; 1981 Ruthchild; 1981 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1997 Blau ad in LR.

(See also: Dissolving Coin.) n. Effect where a metal coin covered by a cloth disappears when dropped into a glass of water; the Melting Coin. [rare] Uses a glass or clear plastic disc that is switched for the coin. A pet effect of Alfred C. Gilbert (by 1920).

n. The spectator's capacity to remember the discrete events (and their sequence) in the magician's performance. [rare] "Good misdirection, having tricked their attention, now tricks their memory as well." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 6 "Memory creates surprise at magic, because the outcome seems to contradict what the spectator remembers has gone before." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1975 ed), x "O Memory! thou fond deceiver." — Oliver Goldsmith, The Captivity (1764), Act I Cognitive psychologists distinguish between "short-term memory" that is not permanently stored in the brain and "long-term memory" that is. Short-term memories become long-term ones through either near-term vivid associations and/or rehearsal. These processes cause the brain to build new neurological links that permanently fix the memory. Even then the long-term memory's details may be incomplete or contaminated. It has been recently established that short-term memories, having been erased without any trace in the brain, cannot be "recovered" by any therapeutic means, including drugs or hypnosis. Such "recovered memories" are "false memories". REF: Elizabeth Loftus, Memory: surprising new insights into how we remember and why we forget (Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1980, 207pp). When two or more spectators have differing recollections of the same magical effect, some 591 magicians refer to the Rashomon Principle.

n. Effect where a small ink-dipped ball rolls slowly across a paper-covered board, writing the answer to any question asked by a spectator. [archaic, formerly very rare] This trick was invented (using a concealed movable magnet in the hollow board) by German mentalist Max Berol and premiered by him and his wife-partner, "Konorah the Modern Witch", in Europe sometime before 1898. William E. Robinson published the trick as "The Educated Fly" in 1898 in his Spirit Writing and Kindred Phenomena. F. D. Hewes published an improved version, titled "The Enchanted Butterfly, in Mahatma around the turn of the century. Berol brought it to the USA in 1906. David Devant revived the trick in April 1913 under the title "The A.B.C. Fly (and in patter as "the educated fly"). In 1920 Claude Conlin ("Alexander") performed it with a blackboard-writing snake as "The Goddess and the Reptile". In 1923 Eduard Bamberg retitled it "Syko" using a sculpted scarab that wrote on a blackboard. Again retitled as "Isis, the Egyptian Scarab" it became a pet effect of David Bamberg (since 1927). Later used with a rolling ball by Chang (1938). REF: Waller (1948/1980), 234; Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 154, and (1928), 42; Price (1985), 486, 521; Devant (1936), 140-141; Sharpe (1983), 137; Olson (1986), 11-14. The title is, of course, taken from the Biblical phrase, "Mene, Tekel, Upharsin", Jehovah's miraculous handwriting on the walls of Nebuchadnezzar's palace.
n. An act of mentalism. [rare]

n. A specific example of mental magic or mentalism. [fairly common] 592 “Unless the mental effect is direct and free from complicated procedure it can become one of the most boring forms of magical entertainment.” — Peter Warlock in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Apr 1956), 419

n. Effect where the mentalist-magician's three covered predictions written on the top row of a slate are found to match those later written below by a volunteer. [common] "The best selling mental effect of all time is Mental Epic." — Richard Mark, Mental Sensation (1984), 1

n. The major branch of conjuring concerned with mental effects, loosely mentalism. [common] "Mental magic is to most spectators the most mystifying magic. They see no possibility of trickery. It is to them something apart from sleight of hand and illusionary conjuring. This is because they believe that telepathy and mind reading are possible under certain circumstances and that some people have the power of foreseeing future events." — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Apr 1946), 208 "[T]he two arts are different in that mentalism seeks to create a dramatic reality of belief in the performer's ‘powers', while mental magic is designed to baffle and mystify the onlooker." — T. A. Waters, The Encyclopedia of Magic and Magicians (1988), 227 Performers noted for mental magic have included Adrian Plate, Ted Annemann, Peter Warlock, David "Dr. Faust" Hoy, and Chan Canasta.

n. A playing-card case faked to give a secret carbon-paper impression of the volunteer's writing on a selected card. [obsolescent, formerly rare] Commonly misattributed to Ralph Read (who only devised an improved version, "Ralph Read's Perfected Mental Masterpiece") and less so to Ted Annemann (who claimed invention of the original effect). REF: Abrams (1992), 73-77; Annemann in Jinx #118 [9 Nov 1940], 693.
See: Nudist Deck. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Nudist Deck".)

1.n. The major branch of magic that simulates the effects of parapsychology and the occult; loosely, mental magic; more loosely, mindreading. [common] "We regard mentalism as a highly lucrative business, and consequently do not list a lot of 'hanky-panky' effects designed to simply intrigue other performers." -- Robert A. Nelson, Nelson Enterprises Catalog Number 26 (1959), 3 "Mentalism is the art of presenting seemingly paranormal effects in an entertaining manner." — Robert Cassidy, The Art of Mentalism (1983), 3 "Mentalism is the one area of magic that seems real to a lay audience. They not only suspend their disbelief—they believe." — Phil Goldstein, The Blue Book of Mentalism (1976), 2 "It is often confused with mental magic, but the two arts are different in that mentalism seeks to create a dramatic reality of belief in the performer's ‘powers', while mental magic is designed to baffle and mystify the onlooker." — T. A. Waters, The Encyclopedia of Magic and Magicians (1988), 227 "The biggest fault to be found with mentalism as a branch of magic is that it is so very easy to do—badly!" — G. P. Sanderson, The Concealed Art of Magic (1972), 174 As the above quotations show, there is disagreement about what distinguishes mentalism from magic, much less from mental magic. Some mentalists insist that mentalism is a separate art from magic, other mentalists and most magicians accept it as a more-or-less highly specialized branch of magic. The line is drawn over subtle distinctions about three things: the types of effects presented, the style of their presentation, and the performer's claims to "powers" as opposed to "talent". Thus, according to Goldstein (1976, 2), mentalism stresses only four basic effects: clairvoyance, precognition, psychokinesis, and telepathy. Others would add to this list but all being recognized parapsychological, psychic, or occasionally, occult effects such as those associated with Bizarre Magick. In addition, mentalism is performed in an atmosphere of 594 seriousness seldom found in other branches of magic. Finally, mentalists are commonly advised to at most claim to be psychic entertainers for, if they openly claim to possess occult "powers", they invite the label of charlatan. Of course, if they do opt to pose as charlatans, they are more apt to gain fame and wealth.
