n. Convenient synonym for magician. 595 [rare] The original Merlin was the legendary wizard at King Arthur's court at Camelot. REF: Dr Norma Lorre Goodrich, Merlin (1987). First adopted as a stage name in 1906 when American magician James "Jimmy" W. Myers became "Jack Merlin". At least five other magi later took "Merlin" as stage names.
n. Stage effect where an empty umbrella-like tent collapses to disclose a woman wearing a broad- brimmed "merry widow"-type hat. [rare]

n. An Egg Bag with a semi-transparent open-work net fabric front and black-art backing with a secret load pocket; Net Egg Bag. [rare] A late variation on the venerable Egg Bag. First marketed by 1900 (and probably well before) with a net corner by the London dealership of Hiam's. By Feb 1903 Stanyon was selling a large egg bag with "net work in bottom corner", attributing it to D'Alvini who had died in 1891. By 1924 Heaney's (Catalog No.25) marketed its "The Transparent Egg Bag", with a full mesh front. So much for innovations. By 1928 Thayer's marketed its "The Productive Egg Bag" with mesh in one bottom corner (à la D'Alvini/Hiam). And as the "Mesh Egg Bag" it was popularized around 1960 by Jack Chanin with full mesh front (à la Heaney's).
a. With the simulated quality of mesmerism; hypnotic being the modern synonym. [obsolete after 1928, formerly fairly common]

n. Type of effect in which an assistant, volunteer, or confederate is placed in a simulated trance by a mentalist magician prior to their participation in some trick; hypnotism being the modern synonym. [obsolescent after 1914, formerly fairly common] 596 "... acting mesmerism is in the long run more profitable and more successful than the genuine article." — Henri Garenne, The Art of Modern Conjuring (1886), 343 Named after Austrian physician Franz Anton Mesmer (1734-1815), although invented in 1784 by his student, the Marquis de Puységur. Standard English since 1802 as a synonym for "animal magnetism". REF: OED/2; Robert Darnton, Mesmerism and the End of the Enlightenment in France (Cambridge, MA: Harvard UP, 1968); Alison Winter, Mesmerized: Powers of Mind in Victorian Britain (Chicago: U. of Chicago Press, 1999). Thence magicians jargon by 1855 Wyman; 1855 Anderson, London playbill; 1858 Eagle; 1859 Secret Out; 1877 Hoffmann; 1886 Guibal & Verbeck Jr, Liverpool herald; 1898 Houdini cat; 1909 Hilliard; 1914 Stanyon in Magic.
v. To seemingly place a person or animal in a trance; to hypnotize being the modern synonym. [obsolescent after 1911, formerly common]
(See also: Magnetized Cards.) n. Effect where several playing cards cling to the magician's hand as if by magnetism. [rare]

(See also: Anti-Gravity Glasses.) n. Effect where two tumblers placed on a cloth-covered book or board with the magician's thumb between them will remain there when the magician turns the platform upside-down; the Japanese Glass Levitation (obsolete); the Mesmerized Glasses (obsolete). [rare] An authentic Japanese trick first published by Ishii Black in The Magician (1914 or 1915) using either a paper covered fan or book. First demonstrated in the West in 1936 by Japanese magician Tenkai to the staff (William Larsen Sr, Gerald Kosky, and William Taylor) of Genii magazine, which promptly published it as the "Japanese Glass Levitation". A pet effect of Jack Gwynne since 1940 and Harry Riser in 1940s &50s. REF: Genii (Nov 1936), 11-12; Charvet (1986), 218-221.
n. Billet-reading being the more usual synonym. [rare]
1.n. In general, a transformation, which is the technical synonym, metamorphosis being used only in magicians patter and advertising. [obsolete after 1895, formerly fairly common]
n. Stage effect where a person or object placed in a cabinet slowly and visibly changes into another; the Blue Room being the later and still current synonym. [obsolete]

n. The means (sleights, forces, or gimmicks, separately or in combination) by which an effect is obtained; the modus operandi. Also sometimes called the the secret and occasionally the routine (2) in its rare secondary meaning. [very common] All magic methods must always be either hidden or dissimulated. "It is an odd thing, but the layman always overlooks the possibility of the introduction of more than one method into the execution of a conjuring trick." — Charles Waller, Magical Nights at the Theatre (1944/1980), 43 "The method should remain a mystery or the illusion is destroyed." — Lewis Ganson, Routined Manipulation, I (1950), 5 "Just tell any good magician an effect and he'll be able to figure out a method." — Joe Berg, quoted by Jay Marshall in The New Phoenix (1957), 175 "For every method, you must ‘pay the price'." — Daryl Martinez (1980), 7 "To have a variety of methods for accomplishing a particular sleight is good magic. It enables the performer to repeat moves without the spectators suspecting you had done exactly the same thing a few moments ago." — Howard Schwartzman in Green (1961), 148 598 "The methods used by mediums were far more subtle than the ones used by the average magician since anything that even faintly smacked of trickery could have been fatal." — David Bamberg, Illusion Show (1965/1988), 73

n. Ignorant and pretentious synonym for method. [rare but not rare enough] "I played with the effect and tried to come up with a methodology that would closely duplicate what I had seen." — Robert Cassidy, The Art of Mentalism (1984), 36 "Given identical methodology, there does not seem to be any ready explanation for the presentational dichotomy." — T. A. Waters, The Encyclopedia of Magic and Magicians (1987, draft) Methodology is a useful single word. Coined from "method" + "-ology", it means the science of method. It applies to the system or set of methods used in any given field of knowledge. This is its original and still current usage in Logic and the natural sciences; and it has been extended to all other branches of knowledge including magic. As the word refers to a set or system, it may not be applied to any single method. However, some pretentious illiterates in the social sciences began this unhappy misuse back in the 1950s in a transparent attempt to clothe their small thoughts in a big word. Although these emperors of scientism had no clothes, their ignorant claque bought the illusion, giving the word the status of "current usage" in a few recent dictionaries. And beyond academe, bureaucrats, ever-alert for pompous words to say nothing, were quick to adopt this sorry usage. A rare example of correct, non-jargon use by a magician is: "They [magicians] are too conscious of technique, of methodology...." (Doug Henning, interview in the San Francisco Chronicle, 19 Sep 1984, p.55). Here, by juxtaposing "methodology" with "technique", Henning clearly conceives the word as an abstract collective. We also see correct usage in the title of Ben Harris' 1985 book, Gellerism Revealed: The Psychology and Methodology Behind the Geller Effect. A marginal example where the referent is at least plural and possibly meant as a collective is "Geller's skillful methodology" (Booth [1984], 57). Misused as jargon by 1946 B. Elliott in Phoenix, 405, 645; 1976 Gill, 89, as "notable for the simplicity of its methodology"; 1981 T.A. Waters as "there is little ‘heat' on this phase of the methodology"; 1981 Ruthchild, 4, as "a more advanced methodology"; 1983 Farmer in Epoptica #3, 170, as "the methodology is that the entries in the telephone directory are fictional"; 1983 Burger, 14; 1984 Johnsson in LR as "you may not like the methodology"; 1984 Willmarth in LR as "the different methodologies used"; 1986 West in LR; 1987 Hades newsletter #94 as "fresh methodological approaches to established plots"; 1992 Altman in Genii.

n. The version of the Three-Card Monte trick that uses the Mexican Turnover sleight. [rare] Originally card sharps argot as "Mexican Three Card Monte" by 1902 Erdnase, 122. Thence magicians jargon by 1921 Gibson; 1945 Hugard in Gaultier; 1950 Fabian in Abra; 1972 Fulves as booklet title.

n. A sleight that surreptitiously exchanges a card in the hand for one on the table while seemingly using the former to flip over the latter. [common] 599 "Speaking of cards, Kaufmann, the conjurer, performs the Mexican turn-over to perfection. His three-card-monte, using the turn-over, is the most deceptive bit of sleight-of-hand in the world." — Henry Ridgely Evans, "American Notes", Magic (Oct 1903), 9 This technique originated among American card sharps as a variant sleight for the Three-Card Monte con game by 1897 (Roterberg). Although quickly adopted by magicians throughout the world, the Mexican Turnover was slow to diffuse to three-card operators outside the USA. For example, by 1914 it was still unknown in France outside magic circles. REF: Scarne (1961), 520; Gaultier (1914/1945 tr), 241. Originally coined by card sharps (specifically that of Three-Card Monte operators) as argot because of the pretended Mexican origin of that classic "short con" by 1897 Roterberg; 1902 Erdnase. Thence magicians jargon by 1897 Roterberg; 1903 Evans in Magic; 1908 Stanyon in Magic, 4; 1911 Hoffmann; 1921 Gibson; 1931 Mussey & Oursler; 1931 Cannell; 1934 Farelli; 1948 Norman; 1948 L. Carlyle in Genii, 82; 1963 Marlo in HMM; 1970 Cervon in Talisman; 1973 Alain; 1978 Müller; 1979 Lamb; 1980 Anderson; 1984 Racherbaumer; 1985 Albrecht cartoon in Epoptica #7; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1990 Booth as "Mexican turn-over"; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1991 Ortiz, 142-143; 1995 Beme in LR; 1998 L&L cat.
n. Effect where four regular-sized court cards change into the corresponding one in a minature (Playtime or Patience) deck. [rare]

n. The center deal (see) being the more usual synonym. [obsolescent, formerly rare] 600 "I can imagine a gambler going after a middle deal ... but for a magician what possible use is there for a middle deal and especially one that you can only do with certain cards." — Jean Hugard, letter to Fred Braue, 15 May 1943 Magicians jargon (variant noted) by 1940 Hugard; 1943 Buff in Phoenix; 1950 Fabian in Abra; 1955 Lyons in Ibidem; 1981 P. Harris as a "middle"; 1986 Bob Read in LR as a "middle"; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Alexander orally. NOTE: Subsequently (and consequently?) as "middle deal" the argot of gamblers by 1952 B. Elliott & J. Tuck; 1962
(See also: Wrestling Cheese, The.) n. Effect where several strong volunteers are unable to turn a large wheel of cheese on its side; the Mighty Cheese. [archaic, formerly rare]
n. Stage illusion where an assistant materializes from a pair of nested boxes previously shown empty. [rare] Featured by Horace Goldin in London in 1933.

n. Comedy effect where the magus sets aside a prediction card announcing it will equal half the value of the volunteer's chosen card; the volunteer declares "seven of Clubs" and the magus turns over a 3½ of Clubs gag-card. [fairly common]

v. To draw off simultaneously the top and bottom card during a false shuffle; milking. [rare] Originally the argot of American card sharps by 1845 Green, 122, as to "milk"; 1894 Koschitz as "milching"; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne as "milking" and "milking down"; 1931 Smith; 1961 Scarne as to "milk"; 1996 ["1997"] L&L as "Milking the Deck". Thence magicians jargon by 1934 Farelli; 1946 Hamilton in Phoenix #11; 1950 Fabian in Abra; 1962 Biddle in HMM; 1978 Müller, 12; 1997 S. Morris in LR as "draw off or 'milk' the top and bottom cards". a. Adjectivally as Milk Build. [rare] 601
(See also: DeMuth Milk Bottle.) n. Clear-glass prop shaped like an old-fashioned milk bottle filled with milk that slowly empties itself. [obsolete, formerly rare]
n. Stage illusion where the escape artist frees himself from confinement in a large, steel, water- filled container shaped like a milk can. [fairly common]

n. Effect where an electric lightbulb is plugged in and lit; the lightbulb magically goes out when milk is vanished from a cone via the Milk Pitcher; the bulb is then unscrewed and the milk poured out. [fairly common]

n. A transparent (glass or plastic) container faked with an inner shell creating a load chamber to vanish an opaque liquid such as milk; Vanishing Milk Pitcher (U.S.); Evaporated Milk (Brit.). [common] “The milk pitcher has become so popular amongst magicians that no magic show is considered by them to be complete unless it is used.” — Henry A. Colgate in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Mar 1945), 107 "Remember when the first "Magic Baby Bottle" doll's toy came out? There went the secret of the Milk Pitcher!" — Kent Cummins, "Exposures Not New", The Linking Ring (Aug 1987), 37 Based on the DeMuth Milk Bottle double-wall principle. Probably invented and certainly first marketed (by 1943) by American magician-band leader Richard Himber and once called the "Himber Milk Pitcher". Pirated by Abbott's. REF: Zolotow (1952), 106.

1.n. Card trick where spectator thinks of one playing card; is shown several boards with different sets of playing cards pictured on each; answers "yes" or "no" as to whether the chosen card is on each one; and the performer then divines the chosen card. [obsolete, formerly rare] Based on the Age Cards where by assigning a binary value to each card the performer learns 603 the thought-of card. Invented by Theodore L. DeLand in mid-1910. Rereleased in 1936 in a new version by Herman Hanson. REF: Annemann in Jinx (1936), 104.
1.n. A magician specialized in muscle-reading; a muscle-reader; a thought reader (2).
n. A topological card trick using a slit card and giving a penetration effect similar to the Sellers- Whyley Elusive Lady. [very rare]
n. A Miniature Spirit Cabinet in the form of a doll's house that produces up to 17 ghostly effects before the front is opened to show it empty. [rare]
n. Commercial name for the cheaper, lighter, and more easily manipulated version of Zombie. [rare]

n. Apparatus using a concave mirror to give a displaced 3-D image known technically as a "real image projection". [rare] An elementary prototype showing a swordsman's sword thrust back at him is illustrated on the title page of the 1664 Amsterdam edition of Porta's Magiae Naturalis. This type of optical illusion was rediscovered by accident in 1972 by American lab technician Virgil Elings. Marketed since 1977 using a 9-inch system. REF: H. Adrian Smith in Books at Brown, Vol.34 (1989), 131. 607
n. A cube-shaped production box fitted with an angled mirror to provide a concealed load chamber occupying half the volume of the box, which can be shown apparently empty. [rare]

n. A transparent drinking tumbler partitioned vertically with a two-sided mirror; a mirror tumbler. [very common] "A mirror glass is a glass with a metal partition, nickel plated and polished on both sides, placed vertically within the glass so that one half of it is reflected. The magician thinks that it looks empty —nobody else thinks so." — Louis Nikola as quoted in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Nov 1944), 81 Used to switch one object for another concealed in its invisible rear load chamber, such as the unprepared set of silks for the prepared set in the Twentieth Century Silks trick. This elegantly simple fake was invented by 1872 by Viennese magician J. N. Hofzinser who revealed its secret only to carnival magician Carl von Pospischil and perhaps a few others. English magician Joseph Michael Hartz started making them around 1890. First described (and named) in print by Hoffmann in 1903 after which it quickly became a common prop. REF: Hatch (1985), 185, 211; Hoffmann (1903), 42; Dexter (1958), 147.

n. The optical method to conceal the presence of mirrors, making them an invisible screen that conceals objects behind them. Based on the law of optical physics that “The angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence.” [fairly common] Standard devices employing mirrors include the mirror glass for small objects and the V- screen for large ones. Major illusions using mirrors include The Sphinx, the Blue Room, and Tanagra.
See: Reflected Stack. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Reflected Stack".)
n. A mirror glass (see) being the original and much more usual synonym. [rare]

n. Apparatus to produce, vanish, or exchange a literally unlimited number and size of objects, animals, or persons by providing an invisible link between backstage and a center-stage table, box, or raised cabinet. [rare]
v. Naming deliberately a wrong playing card; to miscall it. [rare] "Miscalling a card can often be used to good advantage." — Hugard & Braue, The Royal Road to Card Magic (1948), 143
n. A master of misdirection. [very rare, probably nonce]

n. The classic coin-production routine in which a seemingly endless supply of coins is plucked from thin air and dropped into a bucket or other receptacle; Aerial Mint (obsolescent); Aerial Treasury (obsolete). [common] "By nature the Miser's Dream is the greatest of all coin tricks; the man who could do it by real magic would never bother with any other feat in the whole range of conjuring." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 147 This routine was premiered under this title by T. Nelson Downs in 1895 at the Hopkins Theater in Chicago. Despite Downs' brilliant innovations, the basic trick (both effect and methods) goes back before 1852 when Robert-Houdin introduced his Shower of Money routine in London. A pet effect of, among many others, Al Flosso (1920s-70s), John Ramsay (by 1931), Harry Willard (by 1938), and Dick Williams (by 1945).
n. Effect where a borrowed pencil visibly penetrates a borrowed bank note without leaving a hole. [fairly common]

n. A genuine (it will pass every test) U.S. Treasury (or Canadian) $1 bill with its center at the corners and the corners at the center. [fairly common] This little-known information (available from the Canadian and U.S. Treasury departments) that enables the possessor to legally make these genuine but apparently misprinted bills was first recognized by Canadian magician P. Howard Lyons in 1956. First commercially marketed around 1984 by American close-up magician James Lewis (with Lyon's explicit permission, simultaneously also freely given to anyone else who might want to do so). REF: Lyons in Ibidem #7 (1956); Kaufman in Genii (Feb 1988), 549.

n. Stage illusion where the assistant (invariably female) enters a vertical cabinet whose 4 doors are closed and steel blades shoved in to divide the cabinet into 4 boxes; these are restacked in a different order and, when the doors are opened, the assistant is seen to dissected in unnatural order as well. [common] This effect of dividing a human body and reassembling it wrong was invented in Mar 1968 by American professional magician Charles "Chuck" Jones. Later versions (along with unlikely claims to invention) were by Les Smith and Bev Bergeron. This popular illusion was featured on Mark Wilson's "The Magic Land of AllaKazam" TV show in the early 1960s. Also in Doug Henning's Broadway Magic Show which opened on 28 May 1974 and was kept in his repertoir through at least 1981. The variant of the reassembly phase where the magi simply moves the door numbers on the mismatched sections into proper order was invented by Orson Welles and reengineered by Chuck Jones. REF: Jones, letter to Whaley, 28 Jul 1989; Genii (May 1969); David Seebach in New Tops (Apr 1988), 24-27.
n. Dice whose faces carry a set of non-regulation spots. A major type is tops and bottoms, which have only three sets of spots, each duplicated on its opposite side. [rare]

n. A palm reader, specifically; a fortune teller, generally. [rare] Originally (from their frequent use of palm-reading) the cant of the carnival and circus sideshows by 1928 (White re circus & carnival; 1931 Maurer re circus & carnival; 1946 Welles in Variety re carnival; 1951 Green & Laurie re vaudeville; 1977 Griffin re carnival). The fortune-teller's sideshow tent is called a "mitt joint" by 1914 (as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1927 Annemann letter to Harto; 1928 Conkle re carnival; 1931 Milburn re circus; 1939 Liebling re New York World's Fair midway; 1956 Murray re circus; 1977 Griffin) or a "mitt camp" by 1927 (RHHDAS re carnival; 1927 Gibson, Bunco Book, 24; 1935 Wolverton re carnival; 1942 Berrey & Bark dict, as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1946 Gresham; 1946 Welles in Variety re carnival; 1985 Sorrows re carnival; 2000 Franchino in LR). 615 Thence magicians jargon as mitt reader by 1977 Griffin; 1985 Price; 1992 Randi. NOTE: Also as noun "mitt reading" in 1965/1988 D.Bamberg, 91.

n. A memorized formula used as a memory aid to enable the magician to perform an otherwise complex sequence of events. Pronounced nee-MON-ik. [fairly common] Mnemonic systems (called mnemonics) are based on mathematical formulas, visual imagery coding, or word-association codes. The first visual imagery mnemonic was devised around 500 BC by Greek poet Simonides to remember the objects or persons in a room by their location. This system was elaborated in the still-popular Feinaigle System, which was devised around 1807 by the German, Gregor von Feinaigle. Magicians use them for spellers, card setups, many mathematical magic tricks, and some mentalist effects. The earliest trick-specific mnemonic is the old Mutus Dedit Nomen Cocis used for the card-layout system of that name first published in 1740 by Guyot. The most common and simplest one in magic is the word CHaSeD to remember the card-suit order of Clubs, Hearts, Spades, and Diamonds. REF: Alan Baddeley, Your Memory: A User's Guide (New York: Macmillan, 1982), 195-200; Martin Gardner, Encyclopedia of Impromptu Magic (1978), 385-392; Corinda (1958), 60. The word comes from Mnemosyne, the Greek goddess of memory. As "Mnemonika" it was in use as the cant of memory experts by 1753. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1897 Roterberg; 1902 Stanyon in Magic; 1910 Hatton & Plate; 1927 Nikola; 1935 Annemann in Jinx #10 as "Louis Nikola's system of mnemonics"; 1941 Baker; 1950 Boardé; 1955 Gardner in HMM; 1958 Corinda; 1979 Fisher; 1981 G. Grant; 1988 Waters; 1994 Earle in MUM; 1994 Gloye in LR. a. [adjectivally] [fairly common] "Cardmen who have tried the Nikola system and later switched to straight memory will agree that the mnemonic system is a hindrance rather than a help." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jun 1948), 433

n. Acronym of modus operandi. [rare] Originally British police cant by 1913 in book title of Major-General Sir Llewelyn W. Atcherley (chief constable of West Riding, Yorkshire), The Atcherley M.O. System. Note that earliest reference in the OED/2 is only 1955; 1969 "Sam" in Jackson. Thence, through writers of detective and crime fiction, into general English slang by 1956. Thence magicians jargon by 1983 Racherbaumer as "all evidence of the M.O. is destroyed"; 1984 Johnsson in LR;
n. A British brand of marked cards. [obsolete by 1979, formerly fairly common in Britain] Widely sold to British children and adult laymen from the 1950s until the 1970s.

n. Type of production cabinet with a drawn curtain front, which after being shown empty can produce two or three assistants from its secret narrow double-walled rear compartment. Compare mirror box. [fairly common]
1.n. Magic being the more recent synonym, "modern" to distinguish it from supernatural magic. [obsolescent after 1897, formerly rare]
n. An up-to-date conjuror. [rare] "Although many of the effects are old, the methods used by the modern magicians are much more sophisticated." — David Price, Magic (1985), 29 617

n. The method being the much more usual synonym; acronymed as M.O. [common] "Unfortunately the abuse of this move (the reverse palm) ruined the sleight since it cannot be done before an audience without exposing the modus operandi to at least a portion of the audience." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1943), 29 Originally Latin meaning literally "mode of operating", it passed into Standard English in 1654. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1857 Magician's Own Book; 1873 Lynn; 1876 Cremer; 1877 Hoffmann; 1899 Stanyon; 1906 Houdini in CMM; 1909 Hilliard; 1920 Lustig; 1927 Tarbell; 1944 Elliott in Phoenix; 1945 Gardner in HMM; 1945 H.R. Evans in Thompson; 1946 Hall; 1947 Bobo; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1950 Okito in Sphinx; 1950 Ganson; 1953 Branson; 1954 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1957 Maréchal; 1972 Dalal in Swami; 1973 Tannen cat #10; 1979 Wilson; 1980 Swinford in Arcane; 1980 J. Marshall; 1981 Racherbaumer in Kaufman; 1983 Cassidy; 1985 Avadon in Epoptica #7; 1986 Olson; 1987 Weibel in LR; 1987 Caveney; 1989 Lewis & Warlock; 1990 Goodsell in MUM; 1995 Earle in MUM; 1999 Dawes in Abra. Also contracted to simply "the modus" in 1974 Hanson & Zweers. NOTE: Sometimes italicized to reflect its status as a foreign loan word.
n. The Money Maker (see) being the original and still more usual synonym. [rare]

n. Ingenious apparatus that seemingly turns bill-sized slips of plain paper into paper currency; the Money Machine. [fairly common] Marketed to magicians by W. & F. Hamley's catalog in 1882 as "The Marvelous Printing Machine". Sold as a toy by a New York street vendor on Broadway sometime in the late 1800s. Used for a stage effect by James Conley in 1958. The first flat version was invented in 1954 by U.F. Grant who called it, appropriately, the Flat Model Money Maker. See also the Midas Machine for a more recent (1981) flat type. REF: Hopkins (1897), 381; Darwin (1988), 15, attributes the invention of the original roller model to the otherwise unknown "Densmore and Kessler"; Waters (1988), 234. 618
n. A paddle trick using coins, banknotes, a mirror, and rubber bands. [rare]

(See also: Coin Slide (1).) 1.n. A flat tube-like coin dropper through which a coin can be gravity-fed into the magician's hand or into an apparently impenetrable object (such as a Nest of Boxes or the Ball of Wool). A money slide (obsolete). [fairly common] Exposed in 1876 Hoffmann, 198, 207; 1877 Sachs.

n. The Over-Under Shuffle (see) being the more usual synonym. [obsolescent by 1978] Named after Monge, one of the analysts of the mathematical properties of this shuffle, doing so in Magic Wand (Dec 1954). REF: Müller (1978), 12.

n. Sucker effect where a ring attached to one dangling end cord of three that dangle from a short wood or metal stick switches to the other end when held behind the magician's back; then, when the spectators cry foul—he only turned it around—the ring is shown on the middle cord. [rare] Reportedly invented by Tom Sellers. Also reportedly first marketed by U.F. Grant. Marketed by Ken Allen in early 1955. As "Codology", a pet effect of George Kovari although with different props and method. REF: E. Dawes annotation 1988; Busby annotation 1988.
n. A full-scale (9-foot tall) guillotine. [rare]
n. Contraction of Three-Card Monte, which is the usual synonym. [common]
n. A forcing deck composed of one fair card with the rest being double-enders—fair at one end, all the same at the other. [archaic after 1945, formerly rare]

n. Magicians' versions of the old sucker's games of Three-Card Monte and the Shell Game in which the volunteer tries, always unsuccessfully, to guess which of three cards thrown face- down is, for example, the Queen of Spades, or which of three shuffled walnut shell conceals a pea, or which of three matchboxes contains a coin, and so on. [rare]

n. The version of the Chinese Sticks (see) made of bamboo. [rare] Originally (by 1925) made by American magician "Silent Mora" (Louis Jerome McCord) who devised his own special handling. A Mora-autographed set is in the Busby Collection.
n. A stage production-vanishing cabinet in the form of a cage-within-a-cage. [rare]
n. The Devil's Handkerchief (see) being the later and now more usual synonym. [obsolete after 1924, formerly fairly common]

n. A small, tightly rolled streamer of paper ribbon used as a production item. Often but not necessarily produced from the magician's mouth. So-named because they are small enough for a mouth load. Larger versions are the hat coil and the tambourine coil. [common] "The professors of legerdemain at our village fairs, pull out ribbon after ribbon from their mouth." — Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Biographia Literaria (1817) 621 First reported and explained by British magician-dealer-writer Henry Dean in 1763 (p.85) when, however, it was already "somewhat a stale Jest." In Dean's version the magician loads his mouth with one "round Bottom" (i.e., mouth coil) of lace after another, secretly tying each new one to the last and giving any color tape called for. Around 1830 a troupe of Chinese jugglers in London performed a ribbons-from-mouth production. And Chinese magician Ching Ling Foo, at his opening performance in the West in May 1899 in New York vaudeville, used a mouth coil to produce an oral pyrotechnic display. This evidence suggests possible independent Chinese invention of the mouth coil. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1928), 179; Gibson (1966), 112.

1.n. A discrete manual portion of a sleight; a manoeuvre. [common] "It will be appreciated that a small move that is over in a second often takes many paragraphs to describe." — Col. Lewis Ganson, The Dai Vernon Book of Magic (1957), 68
n. Stage effect where the magician interacts with filmed actions on a motion picture screen. [rare]

n. A playing card faked so the spots ("pips") can be changed to give it a different value; Mechanical Changing Card (obsolete). [rare] This prop was marketed as early as 1861 by Henry Novra in Britain. Around the turn into the 20th century British pub magician "Bezique" invented an examinable one, which he taught to Wilf Huggins. Houdini in 1908 asserted that it was invented by a T. Bolin of Moscow, Russia. REF: Novra, Catalogue (1861), 2; Huggins in Hugard's Magic Monthly (May 1949), 538; Houdini in Conjurers’ Monthly Magazine (Aug 1908), 367..

n. A specially gaffed billfold for the card-in-wallet trick. [rare] Using a principle found in a Harry Baron book, Tom Mullica developed this wallet in 1968 and performed it until 1975 when he first marketed it as "Tom Mullica's Miracle Card-in-Wallet".

n. A sleight that picks up simultaneously two or more playing cards from the top of the deck. If two cards, it is usually termed a double lift; if three, a triple lift; if four, a quadruple lift; and, in general, multiple lifts. [rare]
n. A set of several built-in outs for one trick that permits alternative endings to suit the audience. [rare] 623 Examples are Ralph Hull's Name-O-Card and Ultima Thule.
n. A series of sandwiches within one packet of playing cards. For example, three indifferent cards could be sandwiched between the four aces as AXAXAXA. [very rare]
n. The sleight that brings desired cards together under cover of a block of cards during the process of openly cutting the deck. [fairly common]
v. To do a turnover (1) with an unspecified number of cards acquired by a lift. [very rare but not nonce]
n. Type of effect where objects (such as billiard balls, thimbles, or candles) appear one after another in the magician's hands, seemingly out of thin air. [rare]
a. Adjectivally as the Multiplying Billiard Balls, Multiplying Money Plate, Multiplying Rabbits, Multiplying Thimbles, etc. [very common]
1.n. Spring balls (see) being the modern synonym. 624 [obsolete after 1903]

n. The comedy passe-passe bottle routine where the performer shows the extra bottle, which when it is taken away is replaced by another and yet another (up to 12) to the performer's evident confusion. [fairly common] The apparatus is a nest of bottle-shells. Originally and usually used with the Passe-Passe Bottle trick. A pet effect of Ken Brooke and Nick Lewin (since 1960s).
n. Effect where 4 lit "wax" (actually metal) candles appear successively between the fingers of the magician's hand (or 8 in two hands); Nesto Candles. [fairly common]
(See also: Multiplying Money Tray.) n. The coin tray (see) being the most usual synonym. [obsolescent]
n. Effect where a single hand-held coin becomes two. [rare] Uses a shell coin. REF: Stanyon in Magic (Sep 1912), 90.
n. The coin tray (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare]
n. The coin tray (see) being the most usual synonym. [obsolescent]
n. Effect where a hand-held pipe of tobacco become two, three, and finally four. [rare]

n. Effect where two large sponge-rubber bunnies produce many small ones; Peter Rabbit Goes to Town! (obsolescent). [common] "Most working pros will verify that there is no close-up trick that gets as much of a rise out of spectators as the multiplying rabbit routine. The charisma of these little devils is devastating to the lay public." — Rick Johnsson in The Linking Ring (Jun 1987), 87
n. The effect where a succession of 1, 2, 3, and finally, 4 thimbles appear on the finger tips of the magician's empty hand. [fairly common]

1.n. Generally, a title given various specific tricks or pieces of apparatus that give the effect of the Latin catch-phrase, multum in parvo, literally "much in little." [obsolete after 1937; once fairly common, now preempted by 2.n.]
n. The effect where the liquid in a small transparent tumbler is poured successively into a series of larger tumblers, yet filling each. [rare]

n. Any of the small (3/4" to 1") balls used in the Cups-and-Balls routine. [obsolete after 1949] Originally the Standard French word for nutmeg, which, because of its fancied resemblance to a small ball, was adopted by French conjurors by 1740 (Guyot; 1858 Robert-Houdin). REF: Robert-Houdin (1868/1877 tr), 42. Thence the jargon of English-speaking magicians by 1882 Hamley cat; 1915 Magic Wand; 1949 Hay; 1988 Waters as

n. The type of effect where the magician leads a volunteer by hand to a secret goal set by the volunteer or audience; contact mindreading; Hellstromism; Cumberlandism (obsolete); mind-reading (1)(obsolete); thought-reading (2)(obsolete). [fairly common] "Muscle reading is the art of reading a person's mind by means of clues provided by his involuntary behavior." — Martin Gardner in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jul 1955), 306 Based on the old parlor and childrens' trick known variously as the "Willing Game" and "hide the pin", it depends on the subject's unconscious muscular movements. Applied as a stage trick by American pseudo-clairvoyant John Randall Brown and first publicly performed by him in 1872. Soon given world-wide demonstration by Washington Irving Bishop (Brown's ex-assistant) since late 1877, Charles Morritt in 1878, and Stuart Cumberland (Bishop's ex-assistant) by 1883. Later famous muscle-readers have been P.H. McEwen, C. A. George Newmann (since 1895), Grossi (by 1903), Maud Lancaster, Rubini (by 1919), Joseph Dunninger, Fred Marion, Axel Hellström (by 1928), Alfred Capper, Eric Lewis (1938-48), Rolf Passel (1950s), Franz Polgar (1950s), Kreskin (by 1980s), and Lev Schneider (1980s). REF: Gardner (1978), 393-395; Price (1985), 452, 454, 481; Fitzkee (1935); Morritt in Devant (1936), 274; Jay (1986), 157, 174-199, 325-327; Truzzi in Vibrations (Dec 1983), 5-7; G. M. Stratton, “The Control of Another Person by Obscure Signs,” The Psychological Review, Vol.28 (1921), 301-314, on experiments with Rubini. Originally (around 1873) called "mind reading" to disguise the physical and visual cues upon which the performer depends. Also (around 1880) called "thought reading". The term "muscle reading" was coined by Dr. George M. Beard in 1874 after watching performances by Brown and first published by Beard in the Nov 1874 issue of the Archives of Electrology and Neurology. NOTE: The OED/2 gives a later (1879) publication by Beard as its earliest citation. Thence magicians jargon by 1889 Sid Macaire; 1892 W.E. Skinner; 1892 A. Herrmann in Cosmopolitan; 1892 Jastrow in Popular Science Monthly; 1920 Lustig; 1935 Nelson; 1939 Kanter cat; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1949 G. Anderson; 1952 Gardner; 1952 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1953 Crimmins in HMM; 1958 Corinda; 1979 Lamb; 1980 J. Marshall; 1987 Osterlind; 1988 Waters; 1991 McComb in Genii; 1992 Randi; 1994 Earle in MUM; 1997 Waldman.

n. Originally a British term synonymous with "variety theater". Only an approximate equivalent of the American vaudeville or variety, because the British version also presented revues, musicals, plays, operas, ballet, and even stage-adapted circus acts. Thence, as music-hall, the French term for their equivalent. Although the term "music hall" was coined by 1857 (OED/2), the first venue built specifically for this purpose was the Canterbury Arms Saloon (in North Lambeth, London), which had opened 17 May 1852. At its peak around 1900, there were over 500 music halls in the British Isles. REF: Eric C. Lewis, "The Late Lamented British Music Hall", The Linking Ring (Nov 1989), 55- 58, 66; D. Cheshire, Music Hall in Britain (Newton Abbott: 1974); U. Schneider, Die Londoner Music-Halls und ihre Songs, 1850-1920 (Tübingen: 1985); J. Feschotte, Histoire du music-hall (Paris: 1965); D. Cheshire & U. Schneider, British Music Hall 1840-1923: A Bibliography and Guide to Sources with a Supplement on European Music Halls (Hamden, Conn.: 1981); Dif #2

n. A commercial magic set. [common] "More American magicians were started down the road to rabbit-pulling by seeing Howard Thurston or owning a Mysto Magic set than by any other influence between 1918 and 1935." — John Booth in The Linking Ring (May 1986), 52 These sets were manufactured (in several sizes) by the Mysto Magic Company founded in 1908 by Alfred C. Gilbert and John A. Petrie in New Haven, Connecticut. Petrie dropped out in 1912 and in 1916 Gilbert, having branched out into a general toy company, changed the name to The A.C. Gilbert Company. He retired in 1952 and the last Mysto Magic set was made in 1956. In all, 85 different models were issued. Well-known magi who learned their first tricks from a Mysto Magic set include: Walter B. Gibson (in 1910), Chester Morris (1913), Orson Welles (1919), Ted Annemann (1921), Bruce Elliott (1923), Hen Fetsch, Herb Rungie, J.G. Thompson Jr, Bob Brown (around 1940), Byron Walker (1941), Johnny Thompson (around 1942), Eugene Burger (around 1942), Bill Miesel (1944), Roger Crabtree (age 8), Kent Cummins (around 1949), and Simon Aronson (around 1952). 631 REF: Richard Kaufman, "Mysto Magic Sets", Magic (Jan 1993), 32-38. The word "Mysto" (from "mys[terious" + "pres]to") was coined in the late 1890s by Eva Judson Petrie, first wife of John A. Petrie. Jargon coined in 1908 by A.C. Gilbert & J.A. Petrie. Thence 1941 Holden cat #8; 1945 Thompson; 1950 Hay; 1957 Leroy in HMM; 1966 Hutchinson; 1972 Anderson; 1983 Albrecht in Epoptica; 1985 Zollweg in Arcane #13; 1992 Bill King orally; 2000 Albrecht cartoon in Busby Xmas card. a. [adjectivally] [very rare]
n. Effect of metal bending (see) where a thick carpenter's nail slowly bends in the magician's hand. [very rare, possibly nonce]
n. The faint indentation made with a thumb or fingernail that creates a nicked card, envelope, or soft paper billet, which can be detected by touch or sight. [rare]
See: needle thru thumb. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "needle thru thumb".)

n. A finger-tip device with a stubby pencil-lead to permit surreptitious writing when wedged under the nail of the forefinger or thumb; a Swami Gimmick; a boon. Compare thumb writer; band writer. [common] This gimmick and its associated technique originated among slate mediums of the late 1800s, probably with the notorious "Dr" Henry Slade who was caught by John W. Truesdell in 1872 using it under his forefinger-nail. Truesdell published his exposé of Slade in 1883. A version was published by Stanyon in 1897; and then as a clip-on by W. E. Robinson in 1898 in his book Spirit Slate Writing (pp.52-53). Later a pet device of pseudo-psychic Bert Reese. REF: Busby (1996), 4; Truesdell (1883); Stanyon, Conjuring for Amateurs (1897), 70-71; Craige Snader Jr, The World's Smallest Magic Apparatus (1987). Thence with minor modifications by mentalist-magicians Calder, Dunninger, Sunshine, Jaks (c1929), and Mogul. 633 REF: Pierre (1975), 123-126; Harbin in Demon Telegraph #61 (1942). Magicians jargon by 1941 F.M. Chapman who probably coined it. Thence 1942 Davenport cat #61; 1943 Hugard in HMM; 1944 Thayer cat #9/5; 1944 Chapman; 1944 Elliott in Phoenix; 1945 Tarbell; 1945 Wheeler cat; 1947 Abbott cat #9; 1947 Kanter cat #8; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1949 Tannen cat #1; 1949 Braue in HMM, 511, 531; 1955 Weiner in HMM; 1961 Waters in New Phoenix #347; 1966 Inzani-Henley cat #1; 1972 Ken de Courcy in Swami; 1973 Alain; 1975 Lee cat [#1]; 1976 Goldstein; 1978 Becker; 1979 Lamb; 1982 Mason & Richardson; 1983 Cassidy; 1987 Hollywood Magic cat #16; 1987 Snader; 1988 Darwin; 1988 Waters; 1991 Chazpro ad in Genii; 1992 Patton in Genii; 1992 Minch/Fields; 1994 Hilford in MUM; 1995 Tannen cat #18; 1997 Shewan in LR; 1997 Lee cat #11; 1997 Abbott cat #25; 2003 L&L Publishing Presents #27.

n. Using a nail-writer. [rare] "But do you really think nail-writing is so easy? I don't think so, and I have used one for thirty years (my first one came from Will Goldston and was very hush-hush)." — Dr. Stanley Jaks in Abracadabra #680 (7 Feb 1959)
n. A method for producing any-card-called-for in a magical manner. [rare]

n. Effect where five cards are dealt to five persons as in the British card game of Nap (Napoleon), each then mentally choosing one card, yet the magus proceeds to name them; the Conjurer's Nap. [fairly common in Britain] First published in 1885 by Sachs (2nd ed, 143-146) as "A Game of Napoleon". Another version by Devant (1910, 82) as "The Conjurer's Nap". This effect is still popular among Britons who know of the game even though it is no longer popular. A pet effect of Lionel King, Al Koran, and Billy McComb. REF: Busby in Arcane #11 (1984), 145. Originally the cant of card players as the then popular British card game of "Napoleon" or, simply, "Nap". Thence magicians jargon by 1946 Le Dair, using an Otto the Duck; 1946 Clive; 1981 Brooke #3; 1988 Waters citing British usage; 1989 Berglas in The Trap; 1989 Warlock in Magigram; 1992 McComb orally.

n. A playing card trimmed on its sides to be slightly more or less wider than the others in its deck; a short card (but rare in this sense). Opposite of a wide card. [fairly common] Originally used by British card sharps who called it the "Breef" by 1680 Cotton; 1715 Lucas. 634 Used as a key card and now, by magicians, more often so than either the long card or the wide card.

n. Annual celebration by American magicians. It falls on October 31st, the anniversary of the death (in 1926) of Houdini and also, appropriately, of Halloween. [rare] Originally proposed in the mid-1930s by Dr. Edward Saint of Hollywood who was then acting as manager for Houdini's widow, Bess. Adopted in 1938.

n. Original term for magic in its non-supernatural sense. [obsolescent after 1903, formerly very common] Standard in Western languages as registered in the following titles of books and other documents related to conjuring: Chaucer, Fame, III, 176 (around 1384, in English) as "magickes naturel". J. Lydgate, poem "Death speaketh to Mr. John Rikil, Tregetour" (around 1425, in English) as "magike naturall". Porta, Magiae Naturalis (1558, in Latin). Scot (1584, in English) as "naturall magike". G. Harvey (1593) as "naturall and supernaturall Magique". Shakespeare, Hamlet (1602) as "naturall Magicke". F. Bacon (1605, in English) as "natural magic". Hildebrandt, Magiae Naturalis (1610, in Latin). Witgeest, Het Natuurlijk Tover-Boeck of Speel-Toneel der Konsten (1682, in Flemish). Wallbergen, Sammlung. natuerl. Zauberkuenste (1768, in German). Astley, Natural Magic (1785). A. Blitz (1815). Brewster, Letters on Natural Magic (1832). Döbler, London playbill, 1842. Rosenfeld, Leeds playbill, 1849. Anderson, Leeds playbill, 1854. Savren, Maidstone playbill, 1855. The Magician's Own Book (1857). Piesse, Chymical Natural and Physical Magic (1858). W. Frikell, London playbill, 1859. J.M. Hartz, handbill, 1864. Marion, Magie naturelle (1869, in French). Plus 1870 P. Preston; 1873 Hartz cat; 1876 Evanion, Greenwich prgram; 1877 Hoffmann; 1878 Lorento; 1886 Holden; 1897 H.R. Evans in Hopkins; 1903 Neil; 1920 Holmes; 1924 Felsman cat #18 as an “experiment in Natural Magic”; 1972 Hay; 1986 Booth; 1995 Lee cat #10, p.335.

n. The quality of making each sleight or other conjuring move simulate a normal gesture, action, or posture to avoid the spectators noticing the secret actions. [fairly common] "Perfect sleight-of-hand is deliberate, allowing the eye to follow it with apparent ease, and deceives all the more absolutely because the deception is without haste and accomplished by movements of apparent naturalness." — Frank W. Thomas, "Confessions of a Conjurer", Magic (Oct 1901), 3 "Naturalness is the mother of misdirection." — Jean G. Foley, 1924, as quoted in The Linking Ring (Aug 1987), 49 "Naturalness...is the secret of good Magic." — Harlan Tarbell (1927), Lesson 13, p.6 "Naturalness is the most powerful weapon at the disposal of the magician when he seeks to deceive. Naturalness is an anesthetic to attention." — Dariel Fitzkee, Magic by Misdirection (1945), 94 "Complete naturalness of action, speech and manner is the essence of the art." — Hugard & Braue, The Royal Road to Card Magic (1948), xvii 636 "Francis [Carlyle] is the epitome of naturalness in his sleights." — Dai Vernon, tape, 1955 "In mastering the classic palm naturalness is the important thing. If the hand that conceals the coin is not held naturally, attention is directed to it and the trick fails." — J. B. Bobo, Modern Coin Magic (1966 revision), 354

v. To tip a deck of playing cards backwards toward your body (toward your necktie) to conceal some action at the top of the deck. [rare] "Necktie this spread slightly so that the card immediately to the left of the selected card #1 will not be seen by the spectators." — Harry Riser in M-U-M (Oct 1997), 15

n. Occasional convenient or advertising synonym for magician. [obsolescent since 1930s, formerly fairly common] "The arguments of some necromancers are sound—and that's all." — George F. Schulte in The Sphinx (Jan 1934) Standard English since the 1300s, formed from the Greek nekros (corpse) plus mantis (seer), implying a person who 637 communes with the dead. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon in its non-supernatural sense by 1827 Antonio Blitz ad; 1838 Anderson, Apr 30th Hull program; 1838 Ching Lau Lauro, York playbill; 1859 J.M. Hart [sic], Shoreditch program; 1863 Kinley Schiller billing in Melbourne; 1878 Patrizio, Boston program; 1886 Kellar, Boston program; 1886 Holden; 1901 F. Thomas in Magic; 1907 Houdini in CMM; 1916 Kar-Mi flyer; 1919 H.R. Evans; 1919 Jordan; 1920 Waller; 1924 Clarke in Magic Wand; 1931 Oursler; 1942 Harad in Sphinx; 1949 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1967 Lund in Abra as “many of the name necromancers”; 1970 Necromancer, V.1, #1; 1981 Ayling as "the oriental necromancer"; 1981 Abbott cat #22.

n. Loose synonym for magic. [obsolescent since 1890s, formerly fairly common] "Sleight of hand, magic, necromancy, &c., are all terms of art applicable to the same series of performances." — The publishers, The Magician's Own Book (1857), iii "Necromancy. This word is now loosely and erroneously applied to magic in general." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1944), 92 “You’ll want this volume [Scarne on Card Tricks], be you newcomer to necromancy or old hand at card manipulating.” — Frank Joglar [Milbourne Christopher] in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Nov 1950), 724 Originally Standard English since around 1450 in the sense of the art of communicating with the dead. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1838 Sutton, Feb 12th London playbill; 1838 Anderson, May 18th Hull playbill; 1838 Ching Lau Lauro, Aug 30th York playbill; 1857 Magician's Own Book; 1863 Lynn program; 1876 Evanion, Greenwich program; 1878 Patrizio, Boston program; 1891 Burlingame; 1932 Deveen; 1939 Sellers in Jinx; 1945 Kaufman poem in Hugard Testimonial, 7; 1987 Abbott flyer as trick title "Novel Necromancy"; 1988 Waters; 1997 Ogden.

a. Advertising or convenient synonym for magical. [obsolescent, formerly common] Originally Standard English since 1574. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1838 Sutton, London playbill; 1838 Phillippe 21st Apr Edinburgh poster; 1841 Anderson, Aug Adelphi program as a "Necromantic Wand"; 1843 Crambrook cat as the "Necromantic Tent", the name of his shop in London; 1849 Rosenfeld, Leeds playbill as "necromantic entertainments"; 1852 Macallister, Philadelphia playbill; 1855 Recanati newspaper ad in Sydney, Australia, as the "Necromantic King"; 1882 as Calcutta magic club title "Friends Necromantic Association"; 1937 Hugard; 1952 Schimmel in HMM as trick title "The Necromantic Necktie"; 1965 Lawston cat; 1965 Findlay; 1974 Raven as book/prop title The Necromantic Grimoire of Augustus Rupp; 1966- 1977 as periodical title Journal of Necromantic Numismatics; 1983 Avadon in Berg as "devotees of the necromantic
n. Effect where the magus thrusts a long large needle threaded with a length of ribbon entirely through the assistant’s waist. [rare] Similar effect and same method as the old Sword thru Body trick.
n. Fakiristic effect where the magician wraps his thumb in a handkerchief and then thrusts a steel sewing needle through it without any subsequent visible damage. [rare]

n. The effect of swallowing sewing needles and a piece of thread and regurgitating them strung. Compare the Bead Trick and the Razor Blade Trick. [common] "Probably no conjuring trick ever caused a greater sensation than the needle swallowing trick, performed by a conjurer [named Matly] who was with Barnum's great show some years ago, and probably no trick is less known at the present day than this one ...." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic, V.3 (Jul 1903), 83 639 Derived directly from the Bead Trick, an original East Indian effect using beads that was introduced to the West (in England) in late 1815 or 1816 by Ramo Samee's troupe of Indian Moslem magicians and in 1819 Ramo Samee personally did the bead-stringing version in Boston. Khia Khan Khruse, as ex-member of Samee's troupe, soon substituted needles for the beads to create the subsequently famous Needle Trick. A member of the first troupe of Chinese jugglers to perform in Britain (in London around 1830) also did the trick with needles. In 1867 the Rev. Justus Doolittle reported in his The Social Life of the Chinese earlier seeing a local Chinese conjuror thread sewing needles in his mouth. Irish magician Professor Hennicke introduced the needle trick to Australia in 1875. First exposed in print in 1878 by Lorento and again in accurate detail in 1903 by Stanyon. GEN REF: Moulton (1983), 9; Khia Khan Khruse, York playbill in Dawes (1979), 134; Clarke in Magic Wand, V.17 (1928), 179, 180; Waller (1948/1980), 54. Houdini advertised (in 1898) that the Needle Trick "was taught to me by Hindoos at the [Chicago] World Fair in 1893." However, Henry Gordien, a small-time Minneapolis magician, claimed that he had sold the trick to Houdini when the latter played Minneapolis. Bert Sugar asserts that the trick was "Ovette's Original Needle Trick", invented by American circus fire- eater magician Joseph Ovette. In any case, Houdini proceeded, beginning at the Kansas City Orpheum on 10 Apr 1899 to make it one of his most celebrated effects and kept it in his act until his death in 1926. It was a pet effect of, among others, Gerald Kaufman (since 1912), Harry Usher (1915 to at least 1931), Henry Rigoletto (in 1926), Fred Keating (by 1927), Doc Nixon (from 1928), Rita del Gardi (by 1935), David Bamberg (by 1937), Melvin Eicher (by 1943), Orson Welles (in 1943), and Harold Holden (1950s). REF: Houdini (1898); Price (1985), 189; Silverman (1996), 24-25, etc; Randi & Sugar (1976), 52; Gibson & Young (1961), 53-62. Modern magi also perform it with safety razor blades (since 1929), electric light bulbs (introduced around 1942 by Peter Waring), or, coming full circle, with the original beads (in the late 1920s, as reintroduced by Carmo).

[common] "Probably no conjuring trick ever caused a greater sensation than the needle swallowing trick, performed by a conjurer [named Matly] who was with Barnum's great show some years ago, and probably no trick is less known at the present day than this one ...." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic, V.3 (Jul 1903), 83 639 Derived directly from the Bead Trick, an original East Indian effect using beads that was introduced to the West (in England) in late 1815 or 1816 by Ramo Samee's troupe of Indian Moslem magicians and in 1819 Ramo Samee personally did the bead-stringing version in Boston. In any case, Houdini proceeded, beginning at the Kansas City Orpheum on 10 Apr 1899 to make it one of his most celebrated effects and kept it in his act until his death in 1926.
