n. A type of faked deck of playing cards based on bathroom strippers. [rare] Originally the invention of card sharps. Shown by Tony Giorgio (a card player and semi-pro magician) to Larry Jennings and Bruce Cervon in 1965. Subsequently used by Jeff Busby, Ray Grismer, and at most a half-dozen other magi. Still a closely-held secret device of inner-circle cardmen. REF: Cervon, The Castle Notebooks, V.2, 62-63, entry for 8/10/65; "Mr. D" 1988 letter; Larry Jennings, interview, 23 May 1985.
n. Apparatus that permits any card called for to rise from a small houlette held in the magicians 640 hands while surrounded. [rare]
n. A set of several letter or pay packets, each fitting ("nesting") into the next larger one. [rare] First described and explained (for a card trick) in 1897 (by Roterberg, 100-106).

(See also: Mesh Egg Bag.) n. An Egg Bag with a semi-transparent open-work net fabric front and black-art backing with a secret load pocket; Net Egg Bag. [rare] A late variation on the venerable Egg Bag. First marketed by 1900 (and probably well before) with a net corner by the London dealership of Hiam's. By Feb 1903 Stanyon was selling a large egg bag with "net work in bottom corner", attributing it to D'Alvini who had died in 1891. By 1924 Heaney's (Catalog No.25) marketed its "The Transparent Egg Bag", with a full mesh front. So much for innovations. By 1928 Thayer's marketed its "The Productive Egg Bag" with mesh in one bottom corner (à la D'Alvini/Hiam). And as the "Mesh Egg Bag" it was popularized around 1960 by Jack Chanin with full mesh front (à la Heaney's).
n. The way a brand new unopened deck of cards is ordered. It is a special kind of stack.
n. Stage illusion where an assistant is strapped upright in a slim cabinet and then reappears upside down. Compare Topsy-Turvy. [archaic, formerly rare]

a. Having the quality of New Wave Magic. [new, fairly common] Originally the French term nouvelle vague (literally, new wave), which when coined in 1959 designated the cinematic movement in France that stressed improvisation, abstraction, and subjective symbolism while often using experimental camera work. As "New Wave", entered the English language in 1960, whence it soon was applied to any new movement in the arts. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1987 Coby in Dec Genii, 376; 1989 A. Stevens in Genii as "new wave magician"; 1990 Yedid ad in Genii as "New Wave Thaumatology"; 1990 D. Larsen in Genii as a "new wave illusion"; 1990 McBride in Q as "The ‘New Wave' Rising Card; 1990 Reynolds in "The Best of Magic poster as "the new wave vaudeville movement"; 1992 White in MUM as "’new wave' magicians"; 1992 Wassilak in Barnstormer as "New Wave style"; 1993 Abbott cat #24 as "New Wave Modern Cabinet"; 1995 Lee cat #10 as Bob King's "New Wave Prediction"; 1996 Busby as
n. Conjuring with newspapers. [rare] The most common example is the Torn-and-Restored Newspaper.

(See also: Torn and Restored Newspaper.) n. A Torn and Restored Paper effect as done with a newspaper; the Newspaper Tear. [common] The very large size paper sheets makes this version of the T&R Paper particularly suitable for stage production. Invented (as first noted by Jeff Busby) by British magician Hugall Benedict by 1903. Popularized by "Cortini" (Paul Korth), a German professional magician. Marketed in the USA by Brema in 1928 with his own "new and improved method". Al Baker marketed his method by 1932. Another version invented by Jean Hugard was premiered by Herman Hanson in Apr 1932 in the Thurston show in San Diego. A pet effect of Jean Hugard (1930s), Joe Karson (in 1930s using, according to Busby, an unprepared newspaper), Al Koran (in 1940s), Slydini (in 1950s), Robert Harbin, Gene Anderson, Doug Henning, Terry Seabrooke, and Nick Lewin (1990s). REF: H. Benedict in Magic (Apr 1903), 62; Holden (1937), 9; Hanson & Zweers (1974), 50. "So far as I can find, the early Magi did not perform the 'Torn and Restored Newspaper' but that, perhaps, is just as well after all." — H. Adrian Smith, "More About Hocus Pocus Junior", Tops (Oct 1941)
n. The type of book test that uses a newspaper. [rare]

n. Effect where a stack of nickels is changed into a stack of silver dimes by covering and uncovering with a brass cap. [fairly common] This variant on the old shell-operated Cap and Pence was invented by Walter B. Gibson and first made and marketed by his friend Carl Brema. By 1926 it was already being widely pirated. REF: Buffum (1981), 51-53.
n. A complete magic act or routine performed in a cabaret or nightclub. [obsolescent, formerly rare]

n. Conjuring performed in a nightclub setting; club magic being the more usual current synonym. [obsolescent, formerly rare] In the 1930s and 40s, with the decline of vaudeville, night clubs became one of the principal places where magicians could get steady employment, albeit with only short acts. Among those who made a successful transition in the 1930s from full stage to intimate club work were Cardini, Duval, Gwynne, and Carl Rosini. REF: Boston & Parrish (1947), 158-166.
n. A magician who performs in nightclubs. [obsolete, formerly rare]

term: "Box and table are dismantled to prove 'no deception'."
definition: n. Stage effect where the assistant steps inside a short cylinder, which when raised shows the assistant's feet to be invisible. [rare] The original effect was invented by Joe Karson as "No Feet—Some Feat". A pet effect of André Kole (1975) and Doug Henning (since 1982). REF: Stan Allen ad in Linking Ring (Mar 1985), 18; Waters (1988), 190, 243.
n. The Girl Without a Middle illusion being the public title. [rare, colloquial among stage illusionists]

n. Stage illusion with an ark-shaped horizontal cabinet. Large front and back flaps are opened to show it empty. The magician then produces various animals through windows and finally drops the front to reveal a female assistant. [fairly common]
n. Advanced version of contact mindreading where the mentalist omits any physical touch with the volunteer. [fairly common]
See: "Up the sleeve". (No further definition found in this dictionary for ""Up the sleeve"".)
n. A particular flourish with cards. [rare]
n. A forcing pack made on the rough-smooth principle with 26 identical rough-faced cards alternating with 26 back-roughened indifferent cards. [fairly common]

n. This special trick deck combines both the Svengali and rough-and-smooth principles, alternating 26 regular and 26 blank-both-sides cards; the Mental Photography Deck. Gives the effect where a deck of cards shown blank on all sides changes to a fully printed deck and then back to all blanks. [fairly common]

n. A pack of 52 cards with standard playing-card backs but with numbers faces, either 1-to-52 or 0-to-9 with enough duplicates to total 52 cards. Used to force numbers or among audiences who are offended by "the Devil's pasteboards". [rare]

n. Effect where a sphere, strung on a vertical cord, stops or starts in its descent at the magician's command; the Japanese Ball (obsolete). Compare cubio. [fairly common] Operated by having the cord threaded through an angled hole so that when drawn tight it stops. Of Japanese origin, although J.M. Hartz in his 1873 catalog claimed a patent and A.M. Judd in his 1879 catalog attributed the device to Robert Heller. In these original single-cord versions the ball could only descend. By 1882 some anonymous Western magus had added a second, invisible thread that by pulling could also raise the ball. A pet effect of Milbourne Christopher in 1961. REF: Hoffmann (1876), 301.
1.n. The Rising Cards (see) being the much more usual synonym. [obsolete after 1909, formerly fairly common]

(See also: Rising Pencil.) n. Effect where a lead pencil lying flat in the magician's hand rises slowly to an upright position. [fairly common] "It shouldn't be necessary to explain the method of the `rising pencil', a masterpiece in the hands of any devoted artist." — Annemann in The Jinx #118 (1940), 695 This trick originated in the 1800s with round sticks or wands (with a pin stuck in the base). Subsequently replaced by square sticks (to minimize wobble), and finally by the modern hexagonal pencil. According to Ralph Read, the improved Royal Rising version (a detachable gimmick) was invented by Nate Leipzig who showed it to Henry Hardin who promptly marketed it without authorization in his 1907 catalog. Later a pet effect of Charlie Miller. REF: Annemann in Jinx (1940), 693, 695-696.
n. A divided deck pre-set with the odd valued cards in one half and the evens in the other. (Jacks and Kings are counted as odd-valued, Queens as even.) [rare] 650
n. A special false count of the rings in the Linking Rings trick. [rare]
n. Stage effect where the magician (or assistant) seated on a chair inside a cabinet vanishes while his limbs are held from outside by volunteers. [archaic, once rare]

n. A liquid chemical that when mixed with water turns an opaque white, simulating milk. Abbreviated as OOM, its acronym. Also, less usually, called Magician's Milk. [rare] Discovered (using a petroleum product) by American magician Logan Wait around 1941, as a 651 convenient ingredient for his and Roger Montandon's Invisible Bovine trick. First marketed that same year by Montandon's Magic of Tulsa, Oklahoma. Has the obvious advantages that the "milk" did not sour and the magician need carry only a small bottle to be added to water at the place of performance. Its only disadvantages are that it is unsafe to drink and may discolor plexiglas. REF: Telephone interviews with Wait and Montandon, 23 Jun 1988; Booth (1990), 105.
n. Effect where a packet of playing cards of two different colored suits is mixed yet sorts itself out by color. [fairly common]
(See also: Okito coin box.) n. An unfaked small round metal container with fitted lid. Used to produce and vanish coins. Precision-made, usually of brass. [common]

term: Okito coin box; Okito Coin Box
definition: n. An unfaked small round metal container with fitted lid. Used to produce and vanish coins. Precision-made, usually of brass. [common]

n. A coin-box-set with one lid and three bottoms (one like the Okito Box, a second like the Boston Box, and the third with extra-narrow interior diameter. [fairly common] Co-invented by Milton Kort "in 1950 along with Walter Wilson and Ron Bauer. Conrad Hayden made them and sold them but did not advertise them. They were made for certain magi." REF: Kort letter to Whaley, 18 Jul 1989; Bobo (1966, 2nd ed), 497; Busby in Arcane #11 (1984), 138.
n. A sequence of moves that apparently shows both fronts and backs of several cards while they are tossed onto the table while, in fact, one or more surfaces are concealed. [rare]

n. Playlets using the projected shadows on wall or screen of flat puppets moved by unseen puppet-masters; Chinese shadows. Not to be confused with shadowgraphy. [rare] The "shadow play", "shadow show", or "galanty show" is a minor and now archaic allied art of magic. Of Chinese invention, reportedly for the entertainment of the T’ang Emperor Yang-kuei Fei in the 700s and certainly by the Sung Dynasty (960-1127). It was introduced by returning travellers to France (around 1735) and Italy. One Italian troupe introduced their "Italian Shadows" to England at Bartholomew Fair in 1737. It gained great popularity in 1772 when Seraphin (Dominique François) opened a shadow theater in the Palais Royale as "Les Ombres Chinoises", first in Versailles and then in Paris, bringing it to London in 1776. Thence copied by many other showmen. Among the very few Western magi who combined Chinese Shadows with their magic act were Ambroise in Paris and London in the 1770s, Philip Astley in London 1779-1790, and Gyngell in Britain in 1816-1823. REF: Paul Endel, Les Ombres Chinoises de mon Pére (Paris: 1885, 316pp); Chung-wen SHIH, The Golden Age of Chinese Drama (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1976), 10; Clarke in Magic Wand, Vol.13 (1924), 146; J.A. Camacho Barriga, Sombras Chinesas (1982, 16pp, in Portuguese); Hopkins (1897), 181-182.
n. The X-as-5 false count with playing cards. [rare]

a. Said of the method of keeping a step ahead of the spectators while the trick or series of tricks unfolds; a specific type of anticipation. As adjective, usually capitalized. [common] A one-ahead mentalist card trick (involving sighting the next card while naming and showing the previous one) was used and exposed by magicians as early as 1693 (Ozanam; 1716 Neve; 1740 Guyot; 1763 Dean; 1859 Secret Out). Subsequently applied to billet reading by spiritualist mediums in the mid-1800s. Thus, while some clever spiritualist may have independently reinvented this method, they did not invent it, as widely assumed. Italian magician Yank Hoe and his wife Omeni included one-ahead sealed-envelope billet reading in their magic act in the USA in 1891.
n. The one-ahead principle being the most usual synonym. [fairly common]

n. Method where the performer works a step behind the spectators. Opposite of one-ahead. [rare] An example: You have a billet on which you pretend to write a prediction. Fold billet, ask question, and get spectator's reply. Apparently write new answer on second billet. Fold it, query, and get reply. On third billet you write answer from second query. Again query and get reply. By pocket writing, you get answer onto fourth billet which you then switch for the dummy billet used in step one. Finally push all three written-upon billets together and hand to spectators to open, finding the predictions of their answers.
n. The method of working one-behind. Opposite of the one-ahead principle. [rare]
n. Effect where $1.35 worth of coins vanishes, leaving a single half-dollar. Same effect and method as the 21¢ Trick and $2.85 Trick except for the coins used. [fairly common]
n. Any cut of a deck of playing cards that uses only one hand; the Charlier Pass being the most common version. 655 [rare]

n. A false cut of a deck of cards held in one palm, such as the Charlier pass. [rare] The two earliest recorded uses are by German sharps, first in 1768 (Die Verrathene) and next in 1840 (Georg Grimm). REF: Volkmann & Tummers (1952), 74, 167. Among magicians, a speciality of Mulholland, Farelli, and McAthy when handing a deck to a spectator behind his back.
a. Said of a performance by a single magician, working alone (single), that is, without stage assistants; one-person. [common]

n. A booking for a single evening's performance; a one-nighter; a casual. [fairly common] “The feeling among acts at the time [1946] was, that they could live in Chicago, work in many cities for one-night stands within 500 miles, and be home at night to sleep in their own bed.” — David Charvet, Jack Gwynne (1986), 148 Originally theatrical cant since 1880. REF: OED/2; Griffin (1972). Thence magicians jargon by 1904 Evans in Magic, 97, as he "began the weary round of 'one-night stands' as they are called"; 1905 Harto form letter; 1923 Thurston, Oct 13 letter to Dante; 1927 Merlin; 1928 Leat #14; 1939 James Stewart in Jinx #57; 1945 Howe in Barnstormer; 1946 F. Marshall; 1972 Griffin; 1990 Griggs in Budget; 1996 Silverman. NOTE: Thence, from its theatrical meaning, general slang by 1937 (RHHDAS; 1963 OED/2 as its earliest citation) meaning a sexual encounter limited to a single night. NOTE: Also "two night stands" in 1923 Thurston, Sep 25th letter to Dante; and a “two-night stand” in 1997 G. Brown.

n. Contraction of one night stand, which is the most usual synonym. [rare] Originally theatrical cant since around 1920-25. REF: RHD/2nd. The OED/2, the RHHDAS, and Webster's 10th Collegiate all give 1937, an obvious error; 1972 Griffin. Thence magicians jargon by 1923 Thurston, Oct 13th letter to Dante as "a week of one nighters"; 1937 Annemann in Jinx, 216, as "one and two nighters"; 1951 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1972 Griffin; 1980 Gordon; 1987 Caveney; 656 1988 Waters, 63; 1988 Johnstone in New Tops as "two weeks of one-nighters"; 1996 Booth in LR. NOTE: Thence, from its theatrical meaning, American slang meaning a sexual encounter limited to a single night.
a. Adjectivally, said of playing cards, as in one-way backs, one-way deck, one-way principle, etc. [common]

n. A pack of playing cards with asymmetricaly patterned backs, as opposed to the more usual reversible deck; one-way backs being the less usual synonym; single enders (obsolete). [common] "For a one-way pack in a hurry, take daub on your thumb, then riffle the end of the pack several times." — Gerald Kaufman in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jul 1946), 236 "A pencil line along one narrow side of deck will immediately convert any deck to a one-way deck." — Sam Dalal in Mantra (Jul 1975), 16 Many standard commercial decks are one-way. These include the Bicycle League Back #808 (whose anomalous pattern is visible at up to 20 feet), the Bicycle Rider Back, the Bicycle Wheel Back, and the Russell Bank Note Back. Even the supposedly "reversible" Angel Back had a very slight anomaly in its scroll pattern that was exploited by the sharp-eyed T. Nelson Downs. And the Aristocrat brand has a subtle shading that makes it one-way. This principle was described as early as 1800 by Gale as applied to magicians using stripper decks. The similar principle of one-way fronts or faces was first published by 1829 in The Boy’s Own Book, p.201, as the “Ups and Downs” (and in 1857 in The Magician's Own Book, p.62, as the "Heads or Tails" trick). This was based on the fact that the court (picture) cards of the time were printed as full-length figures, unlike the modern double-headers. See also Hartz (1875, p.14, as an “Ups and Downs”). One-way backs were popularized in 1909 by Downs/Hilliard who wrongly claimed it as an "absolutely new and original" principle (p.169), Hilliard having learned it from a gambler in 657 Skagway, Alaska (Jinx, p.360). Modern masters of this principle have included Annemann (by 1931).
n. A forcing deck (1) being the usual synonym unless the user is explicitly distinguishing it from a two-way or three-way forcing deck. [fairly common]
n. Acronym of oil of milk (and, of course, "moo" spelled backwards). Pronounced UHMM. [fairly common]

(See also: Out of This World.) n. The card effect where a spectator deals a full deck face down into two piles guessing red or black suits yet one pile will be all red suits and the other all black. [common] “So far as we know, no one has yet pirated ‘Out of this World’. Everyone protects Curry on this, and that’s good.” — Fred Braue in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (May 1946), 218 "This trick, accomplished by subtlety and misdirection, may be the greatest card trick of all time." — Harry Riser in M-U-M (Jul 1990), 22

n. A card problem whose conditions are that a written prediction of a card is tabled ("open") for the spectators to see; magus then deals a deck of cards face-up from the face-down deck until stopped by a spectator; magus then deals the next card face down on the pile; the remaining cards are dealt face up showing the predicted card to be absent; it proves to be the single face- down card. [rare]

1.n. A card assembly with (4 Kings and 2 X-cards) done without covers. [obsolete] On the 1955 suggestion of the effect by Neal Elias, the method was invented by Edward Marlo in 1962 and first published at that time. REF: Marlo in New Phoenix #375 (1962), 329; Busby in Epoptica #1 (1982), 43-44.

n. The first trick in a magic act or the first act in a show; an opening. Opposite of a closer. [common] "Most mental tricks and chosen-card tricks are poor openers. Flourishes, manipulations, bare- hand productions, and sudden vanishes are natural openers." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 294 "A trick involving a number of preliminaries, such as borrowing or examining articles, or having cards chosen, is generally a bad opener." — Geoffrey Lamb, Illustrated Magic Dictionary (1979), 110 "Most All Backs routines are effective openers." — Jon Racherbaumer in The Linking Ring (Aug 1997), 105

n. An opener (see) being the more usual synonym. [fairly common] "An old showman once told me that so long as the opening was right and the finish was right, the centre didn't matter so much." — David Devant, Secrets of My Magic (1936), 72 Originally vaudeville cant. Thence magicians jargon by 1916 Thurston program; 1921 Dornfeld; 1927 Lorraine cartoon in Leat as "a good opening"; 1928 Blyth; 1938 D. Bamberg in Hilliard as "a weak opening"; 1940 Abbott cat #6 as "an unique opening"; 1941 Booth; 1943 Tarbell as "a novelty opening"; 1945 Lorraine in Thompson as a "flash opening"; 1947 Boston & Parrish; 1950 Hay as "the opening"; 1953 Christopher in HMM as "a suprise opening"; 1972 Griffin; 1977 McGill; 1982 Okal as "a strong opening"; 1986 Booth. n. [adjectivally] [rare] "Wow! — The opening effect, Glove to Dove was a winner, the dove actually flying towards Shimada." — Ian Adair in Trixigram (Apr 1988), 5

n. The performer being the more recent usual synonym. Today, the term "operator" is usually reserved for performers of Three-Card Monte or the Three-Shell Game, whether the sharps themselves or magicians are demonstrating them. [obsolescent after 1890, formerly fairly common]

n. A misleading image as visually perceived by the spectators. [common] "Most optical illusions fail to hold our attention for long because the secret of their trickery is generally transparent." — Mel Stover in Games #20 (Nov/Dec 1980), 14 Most optical illusions used by magicians depend on mirrors. These include the large-scale Sphinx, Cabinet of Proteus, and sword box stage illusions. Smaller-scale effects use the mirror glass. The early, now archaic phantasmagoria used pictures projected by the magic lantern onto a screen of smoke. Only rare use has been made of the cinema projector. A few optical illusions are delusions of direct sight, most of which depend on the principle of visual retention. Those used by magicians include: - The apparent passing of one cup through another in the Cups-and-Balls routine. Used by 1788 (Decremps & 1885 Sachs). - The Paddle Trick. 660 - The tumble ring - The Jumping Rubber Band. - Piff Paff Poof. - The Mexican Turnover sleight. - The snap change. These last six and a very few others are the only tricks that are literally "Quicker than the Eye" — or, more precisely, quicker than the brain's ability to register, because they would be perceived and detected if shown by slow-motion camera. A very few other tricks depend on optical illusion without speed: Best known to magicians are: - The Boomerang Sticks. - The geometrical vanish. GENERAL REF: Although making no reference to these specific conjuring illusions, the most detailed account of optical illusions is J. O. Robinson, The Psychology of Visual Illusion (London: Hutchinson, 1972).

n. A pneumatically or mechanically operated device giving the illusion of a small tree that visibly sprouts full-sized fruit and flowers in minutes. [rare] First exhibited by British magician Isaac Fawkes (in 1730 using apples), which suggests it may have been invented by Fawkes' famous mechanician, Christopher Pinchbeck. In 1757 British mechanician Robert Richard made an automaton orange tree with singing birds (the original model sold in 1977 at Sotheby's for £90,000). Then, in various models that also produced oranges, by Pinetti (1784), Phillippe (1845), and Robert-Houdin (which he began making in 1838 and first exhibited in 1845). Revived by Chung Ling Soo in 1906-08; and then by Houdini for his full-evening show in 1925. The Great Leon built a pneumatically growing version (1' to 4') for Orson Welles around 1941. In Oct 1994 John Gaughan exhibited his clock-work reproduction at The Magic Castle in Hollywood. REF: Sharpe (1983), see index under "Orange Tree" and p.191; Clarke in Magic Wand (1924), 144, (1925), 90; Gibson & Young (1961), 146- 149.

n. A performance by a magician done in pseudo-oriental style and usually as a silent act. [rare] "The only real advantage that big oriental acts had was that they could play any part of the civilized world, no matter what language was spoken." — David Bamberg, Illusion Show (1966/1988), 121

1.n. The performance of authentic Eastern (Islamic, Indian, Chinese, or Japanese) conjuring. [rare] "Oriental magic, until very recently, did not change at all. Even today, the street performers of the Orient each do the same predictable though clever routines." — James Randi, Conjuring (1992), 248

n. The Japanese version of paper folding. An allied art of magic. [rare] Introduced to the West by 1901 when a Glasgow dealer named Heber advertised it in a magic magazine as "Japanese Troublewit". A favorite of magicians Robert Harbin (since 1950s when he performed on British TV as "Mr. Left and Mr. Right"), Max Katz (in 1960s), Bill Madsen (in 1960s), Rick Johnsson, Bob Neale, Neal Elias, Mike Close, Michael Weber, Herman Lau, Sam Randlett, Fancy the Clown (Mrs. Sam Randlett), Martin Lewis, Shigeo Futagawa, and Prof. Yoshihide Momotani, all of whom (except the Randletts) have performed magical versions. REF: Heber ad in Magic (Jan 1901), 32; Busby in Thaumaturgist #29 (Mar 1995), 8. This Japanese word, meaning paper folding, entered Standard English in 1922 and became firmly set in 1955 at the time of the popularization of this art in the West by American amateur magician Gershon Legman. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon (with misspelling noted) by 1956 Harbin, Paper Magic; 1958 Christopher in HMM; 1962 Ireland cat #17; 1963 McArdle; 1965 Madsen in New Jinx #38; 1972 Anderson as "Oregami"; 1973 Alain; 1974 Dalal in Swami, 139; 1979 Lamb; 1982 Busby in Arcane #7; 1985 E. Lewis; 1986 Johnsson in LR; 1988 Waters; 1994 Momotani.
n. A 12-inch folding box that enlarges to produce (or folds up to vanish) an assistant. [fairly common] 662

n. A flourish being the more usual synonym. [rare] "Throwing cards ... is one of the oldest of the ornamental sleights...." — J. N. Hilliard in Downs & Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909), Ch.I This most felicitous phrase was coined as magicians jargon in French in 1868 by Robert-Houdin. Thence translated into English as English-speaking magicians jargon in 1877 by Hoffmann, 178. Thence 1909 Hilliard; 1919 Stanyon in Magic; 1934 Hugard; 1946 G. Adams in Craggs as doing "the Charlier pass as an ornamental sleight"; 1963 Vernon tape; 1988 Waters; 1996 Müller. NOTE: In 1969 Gibson wrote of "Ornamental Fans" in the above sense. Oscar
n. Original name of the Card Duck apparatus. [obsolete after 1946]

n. Any method that a magician introduces to salvage an effect if the original intended method fails; a get-out (Brit); an escape (2.n., obsolete). If a specific trick has more than one known out, it is said to have multiple outs. 663 [common] "If the performer knows enough outs, he will never fail to bring a trick to successful conclusion." — Jerry Mentzer, Magician Nitely (1974), 23 "In my experience, the 'out' has sometimes proved better than the intended effect." — Louis Histed, The Magic of Louis Histed (1947), 25 The word evolved by 1910 (RHHDAS) as a contraction of the common expression "getting out of a difficulty" (1909 Hilliard).
n. The Perfect Faro Shuffle where the top card (of the equally divided deck) is is butted so it remains on top during the weave. Opposite of an In Faro. [rare]

n. The effect where an initialed business-card of a Hindu boy climbing a rope disappears in the packet and reappears as a blank card saying "Out to Lunch" with the original initials. [fairly common] "Like that other old war horse, 'Out to Lunch,' effects with The Buddha Papers are endless and limited only by your imagination." — Brother Shadow [Carl Herron], The Papers of Gautama Siddhartha (1997)

n. The card effect where a spectator deals a full deck face down into two piles guessing red or black suits yet one pile will be all red suits and the other all black. [common] “So far as we know, no one has yet pirated ‘Out of this World’. Everyone protects Curry on this, and that’s good.” — Fred Braue in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (May 1946), 218 "This trick, accomplished by subtlety and misdirection, may be the greatest card trick of all time." — Harry Riser in M-U-M (Jul 1990), 22
n. The mirror-masked changing-room, located directly in front of the audience, for Blue Room- type stage illusions. [very rare but not nonce]

n. Method of shuffling where one hand holds the deck of cards by its short ends and drops (runs) successive batches (small packets) into the receiving hand with an up-and-down chopping motion. Compare Hindu Shuffle. [common] "The overhand shuffle is out of vogue now and has been, in faster company, for many years." — Jeff Busby in Arcane #1 (1980), 8 This was the standard way of shuffling cards until the riffle shuffle was introduced in America in the late 1800s. It remains the most usual shuffle in Britain among card players and is, after the riffle, the second most usual one in America. Originally the cant of card players by 1894 J.N. Maskelyne. Thence magicians jargon by 1920 Stanyon in Magic, 44, as "The ‘Over-Hand' or Perpendicular Shuffle"; 1935 Annemann in Jinx; 1937 Hugard; 1946 Hall; 1946 Buckley; 1949 Turner; 1950 Hay; 1950 Fabian in Abra; 1955 Ganson/Endfield; 1956 Dexter, 128; 1957 Lorayne in HMM; 1978 Müller; 1979 Lamb; 1982 Okal; 1988 Waters; 1988 Trost in New Tops; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1991 Ortiz; 1994 Racherbaumer in LR; 1998 L&L cat; 2002
v. To give the spectators too much evidence. [very rare, possibly nonce]

n. The sleight in Three-Card Monte where the upper card is released instead of the lower one. [very rare] Originally invented by Three-Card Trick operators in England by 1876 (Hoffmann), reaching their American brethren in 1891 (Quinn). Originally the argot of Monte mobs by 1933 Walsh & Scarne. Thence magicians jargon by 1955 T. Cooper in Magic Wand; 1979 Ortiz.

n. The method of shuffling (or, more precisely, merely mixing) a deck of playing cards by dealing off into the receiving hand so that the 2nd goes above the 1st, the 3rd goes below both, the 4th goes above the three, etc., until the talon is exhausted; Monge Shuffle. [rare] Because this procedure does not randomize the sequence of cards, it, like the Faro Shuffle, has been the subject of mathematical analyses by cardmen.

n. The card sleight that moves the face card of the cutoff upper half of the deck to the bottom while the upper half is replaced on the lower. Erroneously called the Kelly Bottom Placement. 667 [rare]

n. A full set of playing cards; deck being the more usual American usage. [very common, particularly in Britain] "[As] this article has been written for an American magazine, I have used, throughout, the term 'deck' instead of 'pack', its English equivalent. To be perfectly candid I think the former is the better of the two, as no confusion can possibly arise between it and the word packet." — Victor Farelli in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Aug 1946), 245 Originally the lingo of British card players since 1591 (Greene; ca1597 Harington, as earliest citation in the OED/2). The word "pack" then quickly replaced the slightly earlier "deck", which was preserved in American English. Note: American exceptions include Bailey (1822) as "a pack of playing cards". Thence magicians jargon by 1651 White; 1763 Dean; 1787 English Hussar, London program; 1801 Magony program as "a Pack of Cards"; 1829 Boy’s Own Book; 1837 Buck, London program as "a Pack of Cards"; 1838 Anderson, Hull playbill; 1838 Eagle, Wakefield playbill as "a Pack of Cards"; 1843 Crambrook cat; 1857 Magician's Own Book as a rare case of American usage; 1861 Novra cat; 1876 Hoffmann; 1886 Garenne; 1899 Little in Mahatma; 1911 Bertram; 1914 Stanyon in Magic, 80, explaining to his British readers that "'Deck' is an American term for 'Pack.'"; 1924 Clarke in Magic Wand; 1927 Merlin in book title Merlin...and a Pack of Cards as a rare case of American use; 1929 Hugard notebook; 1950 Ganson; 1956 Dexter; 1978 Müller re British usage; 1979 Lamb; 1986 Dawes & Setterington; 1990 Wedler re British usage; 1991 Edwin cat #1; 2003 Beam in LR.
n. A group of 2 to 51 (although seldom more than 6) playing cards removed from the standard modern 52-card deck. [common]
See: packet trick. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "packet trick".)

n. The general category of card tricks that use less than a full deck of playing cards, that is, a packet or small packet. [rare] The earliest version was the sharpers' Three-Card Trick, which magicians adopted by 1869 as a demonstration of gamblers' cheating methods. Next were the dazzling series of small-packet tricks, such as the Phantom Card (1907), Papel Blanco (1908), and Two Card Monte (c1909) invented, manufactured, and marketed by Theodore L. DeLand prior to World War I. The current vogue for packet tricks was effectively popularized in the late 1950s by Alex Elmsley and Dai Vernon (Twisting the Aces, etc).
n. A card conjuror who specializes in packet magic, particularly small packet magic. [very rare, possibly nonce]

term: packing box escape; packing case escape
definition: n. Effect where an escape artist frees himself from a wooden packing case; packing case escape. [fairly common]

See: packing box escape *packs flat phr. Refers to bulky apparatus that can be folded up or dismantled to make an easily transported thin package; folds flat. [fairly common]. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "packing box escape *packs flat phr. Refers to bulky apparatus that can be folded up or dismantled to make an easily transported thin package; folds flat. [fairly common]".)

n. The effect of a flat or square-sided paddle-like object showing an instantaneous change of design or color. [common] "I don't know who invented the first paddle trick, but undoubtedly he was a genius." — Billy O'Day in The Linking Ring (Sep 1986), 72 All versions use the paddle move sleight. The classic version, first exposed and fully so in 1584 by Prevost, involved pieces of paper stuck to a knife. Also partially exposed in 1584 by Reginald Scot as the Jumping Peg where a peg in a miniature paddle appears to jump from one hole to another. Variations seemingly make numbers, marks, spots, pictures, coins, or colors change. Suitable objects include dinner knives (by 1584 Prevost, 1829 The Boy’s Own Book; 1877 Sachs), pegs (1584 Scot), dice (by 1859 The Secret Out), wooden 4-sided matchsticks (by 1902 Stanyon ad in Magic; and by 1950 by Hans Kaiser in Germany), pocket knives (by Walter Jeans before 1935), business cards (in 1943 by Francis Carlyle in Phoenix #48), twin 4-sided sticks (1944 R.M. Jamison's Spot Sticks), paper matches (by 1949 Hay), pencils (by 1965 Mulholland), popsicle sticks (by 1974 Stover), and plastic cocktail sticks (by 1972 Baron). REF: Bill Palmer, The Early History of the Paddle Trick (2nd ed, 1994, 26pp) covers period 1584-1900.
n. The paddle move being the much more usual synonym despite its less specific meaning. [very rare]

n. Stage illusion where a horizontal cabinet or real palanquin (a couch) suspended above center- stage is shown empty and yet, after the curtains are closed and opened, a female assistant emerges. Compare Iasia and the Jam Illusion. [fairly common] First performed in Paris around 1885 during a revival of the opera "Les Amours du Diable" by Belgian composer Albert Grisar (1808-1869). (Grisar's 4-act comic opera had premiered in 1853 at the Opéra in Paris and was revived there in 1863.) The USA premier of the illusion was by William Ellsworth Robinson by 1899. Later a pet effect of Gustave Fasola (in 1910) and Jack Gwynne (1927-35). The method inspired Thurston's Iasia illusion of 1929. REF: Burlingame (1891), 239-241; Gibson (1966), 113, 156; Charvet (1986), 257.
See: Reflected Stack. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Reflected Stack".)

1.n. Effect where a selected egg of any species is broken to reveal a live chick that quickly grows and takes flight. [archaic] First reported and performed by Mr. Lane in 1790 when billed as "The Operation Palingenesia, or Regeneration". Next (or at least presumably the same trick judging by its title) by French conjuror Comus in London in 1795 as the "operation Paliengenesis or Regeneration". REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1924), 201, (1925), 95.

v. To remove an object (such as a playing card from a deck or a half-shell from a billiard-ball or coin) by palming; to palm being the more usual synonym. Opposite of palm on. [fairly common] Magicians jargon by 1896 Roterberg as "the 'fake' is secretly palmed off"; 1901 Thurston; 1902 Erdnase/Harto; 1902 Hardin in Evans as "palm off the shell"; 1902 Noakes in Magic as "palm off in right hand"; 1905 Hilliard in Magic as "palm off these four cards"; 1910 Stanyon; 1923 J.W. Elliott as "palmed off"; 1924 Clarke in Magic Wand as "were palmed off";1934 Hugard; 1946 Braue in HMM as "palm it off"; 1947 Hay; 1951 Ganson; 1959 Christopher in HMM as “palm off this card”; 1967 D. Bornstein in New Jinx #62 as "palm off the double backer"; 1979 Mendoza; 1980 Gibson;

(See also: palmistry (1).) 1.n. The simulated reading (1) of a volunteer's palm in a mentalist's fortunetelling act; palm reading. [rare] "PALMISTRY, n. The 947th method (according to Mimbleshaw's classification) of obtaining money by false pretences." — Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911) Originally Middle English in the 1400s and thence Standard English. REF: OED/2; Rid (1612); Hocus Pocus Junior (1634). Thence mentalist-magicians jargon by 1905 Stanyon ad in Magic; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1943 W. Larsen; 1949 G. Anderson; 1959 Nelson cat #26; 1981 Waters. Also caled "palm reading" by 1986 P. London in LR. 2.n. Sleight of hand. [obsolete by 1897, formerly rare] Rare Standard English meaning "sleight-of-hand" as applied punningly in 1711 to Gypsy pickpockets and in 1859 by Wraxall to Robert-Houdin. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1867 Stodare; 1878 Lorento; 1897 Evans in Hopkins.

n. A magician who specializes in palming. [rare] Originally the cant of gamblers, meaning one who palms, since 1671 Shadwell as cited in the OED/2 as applied to dice cheats. Thence magicians jargon by 1886 Dr. Holden; 1948 Elliott in Phoenix #167; 1951 Keating letter to Walter Winchell column signed “The Last of the Red Hot Palmers”; 1987 Bannon in LR as "non-palmers". palming g. Hiding an object in or about the hand by any sleight-of-hand method. [common] "It is because of their dexterous use of palming that the magicians of Europe and America to- day far surpass any that have gone before." — Alexander Herrmann, "Light on the Black Art", Cosmopolitan Magazine (Dec 1892) "Contrary to the opinions of most magicians I maintain that palming a card is not a difficult operation. It simply requires confidence and a proper understanding of the right method." 674 — Jean Hugard, Encyclopedia of Card Tricks (1937), 380-381 "Palming requires acting and is, therefore, not a technique for beginners." — Arturo de Ascanio, The Psychology of Palming (1982 tr), 2 "I use the word 'palming' for the sake of convenience only, being of the opinion that it ought never to have been written in a treatise on conjuring ...." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (Oct 1919), 4 This gerund was originally the cant of dice players by 1673 (R. Head as cited in the OED/2; 1674 Cotton; 1711 Lucas) as applied specifically to dice cheating (earlier dice sharps had called it "foisting"). The term palming was later extended to include card cheating by 1843 (Crambrook cat, 30; 1865 Evans, 36; 1873 Morris as "palming out"; 1876 Cremer, 94). Thence borrowed as jargon by conjurors by 1785 Denton; 1877 Hoffmann; 1899 Stanyon #1 as "palming a coin"; 1901 Chapender in Magic as "the art of palming"; 1902 Erdase/Harto; 1920 Noakes as "palming out"; 1927 Tarbell; 1931 Mussey & Oursler as "palming out"; 1937 Hugard; 1941 Vernon as "the art of palming"; 1948 Norman; 1950 Hay; 1975 Barnhart; 1980 Gibson; 1984 Racherbaumer; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1997 A-1 flyer; 1998 L&L cat. NOTE: Gambling sharps have always avoided the word palming as being indiscrete—too revealing. Curiously, magicians have not borrowed the delightful argot synonyms of the sharpers, particularly as one early synonym, "handling" (by 1803 Sporting Magazine as cited in the OED; 1815 Ingleby; 1875 Hartz) was both more accurate as well as more discrete, although magicians have used that word in a different jargon sense. More recently the sharps have called palming "holding out" (1865 Evans; 1873 Morris; 1891 Quinn; 1915 Innis; 1949 Scarne; 1982 G. Joseph). a. Adjectivally as palming coins, etc. [common]

n. Metal discs specially minted for use by coin manipulators. Seldom as singular. [common] Palming coins are used by some coinmen because they are 1) sometimes cheaper than current coinage, 2) often a more comfortable size, or because 3) the sharply milled edges give a surer hold. The first were made and sold by Martinka and Company in New York City in the late 1800s. Hamley's was also making its own by 1900. REF: Severn (1979), 184. "If the audience gets a good look at palming coins, they tend to feel defrauded." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 130 "The best palming coins are those minted by the U.S. Government. They have a finely milled edge, they ring like silver, they sell for $6.00 per dozen and the current issue has a bas relief of the late Dr. Benjamin Franklin." — Jay Marshall in The New Phoenix (1954), 1 "I never dreamed that Palming Coins would one day cost more than the real article." — Bob Dowd in The Linking Ring (Mar 1985), 68

1.n. The simulated reading (1) of a volunteer's palm in a mentalist's fortunetelling act; palm reading. [rare] "PALMISTRY, n. The 947th method (according to Mimbleshaw's classification) of obtaining money by false pretences." — Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911) Originally Middle English in the 1400s and thence Standard English. REF: OED/2; Rid (1612); Hocus Pocus Junior (1634). Thence mentalist-magicians jargon by 1905 Stanyon ad in Magic; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1943 W. Larsen; 1949 G. Anderson; 1959 Nelson cat #26; 1981 Waters. Also caled "palm reading" by 1986 P. London in LR. 2.n. Sleight of hand. [obsolete by 1897, formerly rare] Rare Standard English meaning "sleight-of-hand" as applied punningly in 1711 to Gypsy pickpockets and in 1859 by Wraxall to Robert-Houdin. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1867 Stodare; 1878 Lorento; 1897 Evans in Hopkins.
n. A handkerchief ball with two compartments, each with its own hole, thereby permitting a color change of silks as well as vanishment or production. [rare]
See: plate lifter. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "plate lifter".)
n. The cut-&-restored rope effect where a length of rope offered by the magicians is cut by a volunteer at three loops, held together by knots, and then fully restored. [rare]

1.n. Generally, a silent act; mime (1); in dumb show. [rare] "It is utterly impossible to do magic without pantomime; sleight of hand is pantomime of a difficult order. Unfortunately it is all too easy to do magic without good pantomime." — Louise Gifford in Hay, Cyclopedia of Magic (1949), 339 "PANTOMIME, n. A play in which the story is told without violence to the language. The least disagreeable form of dramatic action." — Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911) Originally theatrical cant by c1589. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1896 Bertram; 1901 Stanyon in Magic as "in pantomime"; 1938 D. Bamberg in Hilliard; 1941 Chicago Magic cat #18 as “in Pantomime”; 1943 Clark; 1943 Tarbell; 1948 Buckley; 1949 Hay; 1974 Emerson in Swami; 1981 B. Blais in Magic Dealer. Also abbreviated to “panto” in 1953 Christopher in HMM; 1997 Hudd. a. Having the quality of mime. [rare] "Don't claim that all your gags are original, pantomime comedians may not like it." — G. W. Hunter in Magic (Mar 1908), 45
n. Effect where 4 playing cards are shown, dropped into any hat, and then withdrawn as blank- faced. [archaic, formerly fairly common]

1.n. Outdoor advertising such as posters and broadsides. [rare] The outstanding lithographic firms and, in parentheses, some of the magicians they did particularly fine posters for were the Hamburg firm of Adolph Friedländer (Heller, Imro Fox, Le Roy, Thorn, Kassner, Handy-Bandy, Dante, Long Tack Sam); the Paris firm of Charles Lévy (Morton, the Isola brothers); the American lithographers Strobridge (A. Herrmann, Kellar, Thurston), Erie (Blackstone), and Otis (Carter, Germain, Raymond, George, Thurston, Nicola); and the British firm of James Upton (Chung Ling Soo). REF: Price (1985), 246, 294, 297; Sotheby's auction Catalogue of the J.B. Findlay Collection, III (1980). Originally theatrical cant since 1896 OED/2 as earliest citation; 1939 Carrington; 1985 Sorrows re carnival; 1993 Ogden re circus. Thence magicians jargon by 1926 Thurston, Oct 12th letter to Dante as "we can arrange for more paper if we need it"; 1947 Boston & Parrish; 1966 Cramer, 78, as "he had new 'paper' designed and printed"; 1982 Busby in Epoptica #1 as "some of the most gorgeous 'paper' ever posted"; 1985 Price as "a fine line of paper"; 1989 Warlock; 1989 Greget cat;
n. Effect where the escape artist frees himself from the confines of a large sealed paper bag without tearing it. [rare]
n. Effect where several wads of paper disappear one-by-one and are revealed to have collected under a hat. [rare]
n. The Flight of the Paper Balls (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare]

(See also: Afghan Bands.) n. Effect in topological magic where long loops of paper (or cloth) are cut (or torn) lengthwise to produce typically, first the expected two separate loops, then, surprisingly, two interlocked loops, and finally a single double-length loop. [common] "’You have seen the puzzle of the Paper Ring?' Mein Herr said.... ‘Yes, I know that Puzzle,' said Lady Muriel. ‘The ring has only one surface and only one edge. It's very mysterious!'" — Lewis Carroll, Sylvie and Bruno Concluded (1893) This curious and appealing trick is based on the mathematical topologists’ Möbius Strip, the three-dimensional yet one-sided surface discovered in 1858 by German mathematician- astronomer August Möbius and published by him in 1865 (although independently discovered and published in 1861 by Johann Listing). It became a popular parlor-magic trick after 1882 when first published for parlor-magic enthusiasts in Gaston Tissandier's Popular Scientific Recreations, which was the enlarged English translation of his Les récréations scientifiques (1881). First included in a professional magic act toward the end of the late 1800s by French magician-shadowist-chapeaugraphist Félicien Trewey who used it as a pet effect. Thence emerged by 1900 as the professional conjurers "Mystic Afgan [sic] Bands" in a version commercially marketed in Britain by Ellis Stanyon. Originally (and sometimes still) used with paper strips until 1920 when Carl Brema substituted cloth to save time by quick hand-tearing rather than slow scissors-cutting. In Jan 1922 Brema, on the suggestion of his associate, Philadelphia lawyer James C. Wobensmith, added the now-standard multiple-pasted twists and marketed it as "The Red Muslin Bands". This version was a pet effect of Blackstone (by 1924) and Downs (by 1926). In 1930 Stanyon published his Remarkable Evolution of the ‘Afghan Bands', his original variation that produces 2 to 5 untwisted but linked bands. By 1945 Fred Rickard introduced a further minor modification in the Wobensmith design. And Winston Freer created a rather bizarre handling. In 1977 Ed Eckl popularized (but admittedly didn't invent) the zippered cloth that he marketed as "Möby-Zip", which was later pirated by several other dealers. REF: Stanyon #4 (1900), 21; Stanyon in Magic (Nov 1903), 21; Hilliard (1938), 860; Gardner (1956), 70-77; Gibson (1927); Ed Eckl, Gardyloo (1977), 30-31; Gary Ward, "The Story of the Afghan Bands", Linking Ring (Apr 1994), 60-61. NOTE: Clarke in Magic Wand (Oct 1924), 138, wrongly claims that this trick is explained in H. Dean's book of the 1720s.

n. The art of making figures by folding single sheets of paper; troublewit; origami. Compare paper tearing. [rare] "The key folding in all paper-folding is ... the Flapping Bird. This bird was brought to the West by the Japanese prestidigitators in the 1870s or 1880s, and was first printed in 1889 in the book by Tissandier, La Science Pratique. — Gershon Legman in Robert Harbin's Paper Magic (1956) Houdini in his Houdini’s Paper Magic (1922) gives many examples, including some Japanese ones like the Flapping Bird bird and the frog. In addition to magicians Devant, Stanyon, Lorraine, and Harbin, this was a specialty of Spanish poet Unamuno (died 1936) and amateur magician Gershon Legman ("John Thursday"). REF: G. Legman in Journal of Occasional Bibliography (London: 1952) records about 150 titles.
(See also: Paper Hat Trick.) n. Type of paper tearing where colored pieces of paper are torn to make a paper hat; the Paper Hat Tear; a hat tear. [fairly common] 679

term: Paper Hat Trick; paper hat trick
definition: n. Type of paper tearing where colored pieces of paper are torn to make a paper hat; the Paper Hat Tear; a hat tear. [fairly common] 679
n. Conjuring with paper (including paper currency, newspapers, etc.). Compare paper folding and paper tearing. [rare]
n. Paper tearing (see) being the original synonym. [common]

v. Making elaborate two and three-dimensional designs from paper sheets by folding and ripping. Compare paper folding. [fairly common] An ancient pastime used by a few magicians as an entertaining adjunct to their magic act. While no sleight-of-hand is involved the sheets are faked with lightly stenciled patterns to permit fast and sure tearing. A popular version introduced in 1920 by Lyle is the Paper Hat Trick. Others are the Jacob's Ladder and the Fir Tree. "Paper Tearing to my mind has always seemed so absurdly simple as scarcely to need a description." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (Nov 1903), 20
n. Optical illusion where a straight bar appears to bend around a corner when pushed through the holes in two sides of a box. [very rare but not nonce] 680

n. Puzzle where a jumbo card assembles with 5 pieces face-up and 4 face-down. [very rare] First published by Karl Fulves in Chronicles #18 (1979), 1235-1237, where Fulves miscredits it to Japanese amateur magician Matsunobu MATSUYAMA, who denies that it was original with him. Included in the recent Klutz Puzzle Arcade (1996). REF: Matsuyama note to Whaley, 1989.

n. Conjuring with small parrots (parakeets, including budgerigars). [rare] Introduced to magic in 1945 by American magician Jack Kodell on the suggestion and with the help of George L. Boston. A pet (in both senses of the word) prop of, among others, British magus Johnny Hart. REF: Boston & Parrish (1947), 208-209.
n. The magician's visible props, particularly those used in stage as opposed to close-up work; apparatus (1). Includes all faked gear as well as unfaked. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]
n. The study of the production and perception of alleged paranormal events. [rare]

n. Effect where handkerchiefs and an umbrella are shown and the hanks are vanished to reappear tied to the umbrella's now bare ribs; the Sunshade Trick. [fairly common] This effect is worked by either of two methods. The original method used two parasols—one regular, the other pre-gaffed with duplicate hanks. The two umbrellas are then switched inside a tube. This method was introduced as "The Miraculous Umbrella" by J.H. Anderson in the early 1840s in London at the Adelphi Theatre. Also a pet effect of German magician Carl Töpfer by 1855, Clement de Lion (by 1909), and Ionia (since 1911). REF: Gibson (1966), 54; Sotheby's Catalogue of the J.B. Findlay Collection, III (1980), 94; Hilliard (1909). The second, modern method—often specifically titled the Mutilated Parasol—was invented in 1916 by Lewis Davenport and premiered that year in London in Maskelyne's Mysteries. It has a single-unit gaffed umbrella handle containing both gaffed and ungaffed ribs. 681 REF: L. Davenport in Devant (1936), 270-272; Davenport's Demon Telegraph #46 (1938).
n. A conjuror who specializes in parlor magic. [obsolescent after 1943]
n. A specific example of parlor magic. [obsolescent]

n. The alleged ability to see through opaque material. [obsolete, formerly rare] “I have never been able to decide whether Par Optic Vision or Out of This World was the most effective.” — Warren H. Corning in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (May 1947), 320

n. A semi-professional magician. [fairly common] "If Gene Anderson did not originate the term ‘part-time pro', he surely added it to the vocabulary of the modern magician and he absolutely personifies it in his own performances, preparations for performances, and in his quest to get the best from what he does." — Phil Willmarth in The Linking Ring (May 1987), 63 "Part-time professionals find themselves in stiffer competition with their full-time colleagues, owing to the part-timers greater reliance on casuals." — Robert A. Stebbins, The Magician (1984), 92

1.v. As Pass!, an imperative verb as a magic word in patter commanding Go!; passe passe (1, obsolete). [obsolescent, formerly fairly common] "Hay passe, presto vade, jubeo, by the virtue of hocus pocus, 'tis gone." — Thomas Ady, A Candle in the Dark (1655) "By the virtue of Hocus, Pocus, hay passe, prestor, be gone" — ditto
v. To secretly take (via assistant or mechanical device) a vanished object back-stage. [obsolescent, formerly rare]
1.n. Magic words of command meaning Go!; Pass (1) being the modern synonym. Pronounced PASPAS. 684

n. The transposition effect where a bottle and a waterglass exchange places; the Bottle and Glass; the Passe-Passe Trick (obsolete). Compare Passe-Passe Can. [common] This classic trick was already common by 1876 (Hoffmann as "The 'Passe-Passe' Trick"). "Although the Passe-passe bottle and glass trick is 'as old as the hills,' yet it is a splendid trick." — Harry Leat, Thoughtful Magic (1923), 49
n. The modern version of the Passe-Passe Bottle that substitutes cans for the original bottles. [very rare]
n. Specifically, the Passe-Passe Bottle trick, which is the more recent synonym after passe- passe came to be applied to a whole class of effects. 685 [obsolescent]

n. Effect where three containers of different colors receive three balls of matching color yet each is then show to hold a red, a white, and a blue ball. [rare] First described in Hatton & Plate (1910), 169-171.

n. A talking act being the more usual synonym, particularly in the USA. [fairly common] Originally vaudeville cant by 1921 Lustig. (NOTE: The earliest citation of "patter act" in the OED/2 is only 1972.) Thence magicians jargon by 1921 Lustig; 1940 Annemann in Jinx; 1943 Tarbell; 1957 Leroy in HMM; 1978 Feinman; 1983 Berg; 1984 Amy Dawes in F. Marshall; 1985 Price; 1986 Charvet; 1988 Edwin Dawes annotation; 1992 Witt in

1.n. A word-for-word script (as a suggestion for or a quotation of patter); lines. [fairly common] “The patter lines (by Sid Lorraine), which come with the instructions, are priceless.” — Al Stevenson in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jul 1941), 128
n. A conjuror who specializes in a talking act. [rare]

(See also: patter story.) n. A fully verbalized tale (often a personalized story about a gambler or mystic) superimposed on the trick; a plot (2). Compare story trick and patter line. [common] A pet form of patter with some magicians including Robert-Houdin, Hofzinser, Dr. Lynn, the early Horace Goldin, Bruce Elliott, Stewart James, and most bizarrists. "Dealers sell tricks whose sole novelty is an intricate 'patter story' to account for the outlandish properties used." 689 — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 12
See: patter theme. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "patter theme".)

n. A fully verbalized tale (often a personalized story about a gambler or mystic) superimposed on the trick; a plot (2). Compare story trick and patter line. [common] A pet form of patter with some magicians including Robert-Houdin, Hofzinser, Dr. Lynn, the early Horace Goldin, Bruce Elliott, Stewart James, and most bizarrists. "Dealers sell tricks whose sole novelty is an intricate 'patter story' to account for the outlandish properties used." 689 — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 12
n. A magician who patters. [very rare, probably nonce]

term: Paul Fox Cups; Paul Fox cups
definition: n. An art-deco set of three spun metal goblets for the Cups-and-Balls trick. [rare] 690 "If you are going to do the cups and balls and you bring a set of heavy silver plated Paul Fox cups, to my way of thinking, you are already one step ahead of the other guy with his paper cups." — John F. Mendoza, Close-up Presentation (1979), 6 Designed in 1932 by Paul Fox (Fuchs), an American professional art deco designer and magician. Fox sold or gave the first half dozen or so sets to Daley, Carlyle, Ross, Vernon, and a few others. Commercially marketed from 1959 until 1982 by Danny Dew and since 1984 by Jeff Busby Magic. These were used by the late Fred Kaps, Larry Jennings, and Mike Rogers, and currently by Michael Ammar, Piet Forton, Paul Gertner, and Scotty York. Several inferior imitations have been made and sold by unauthorized dealers, including Magic Menu (Jim Sisti & Kevin Care) as recently as 1997-98. REF: Busby files; and James P. Riser, “The Real Story of the Paul Fox Cups,” http://jamesriser.com/Cups/PF_DDHistory.html (4/13/2003).

n. A comedy effect (designed to be "worked blue") where the volunteer (victim) is shown a small cannister labled "Fresh Peas" or “Magic Peas” from which peas are poured; the victim selects one, which is returned to the can, whereupon that pea disappears and "his fresh pee" is poured in a stream of water into his open hand. [fairly common]
n. The Shell Game being the modern synonym. [obsolete after 1919]
See: Jarrett Pedestal. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Jarrett Pedestal".)

1.n. The action of a spectator, permitted by the magician, of viewing an object (such as a card-face) hidden from the magician; the Spectator Peek. Generally spectators are allowed a peek; magicians steal a glimpse.

n. A book specially made on the peek deck principle. [very rare] Of several versions, the best is reputedly Larry Becker's "Flashback", a commercially marketed item where the key words are printed in the text rather than hand-written.
n. A deck of playing cards faked to automatically reveal the card that a spectator has picked. [fairly common]
n. A card force where the spectator is allowed to peek at a playing card, seemingly having a free choice. [rare]

n. Type of shiner consisting of a tiny metal mirror that can be fixed to the hand. [fairly common] The use by Milanese card sharps of mirrors concealed in their finger-rings was first observed around 1530 by Girolamo Cardano as reported in his Liber de Ludo Aleae. REF: Cardano (1565 ms/1953 tr), 210-211. 692
n. A small wad of crumpled and balled-up paper. Compare billet, which is the folded variant. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]
n. The sleight that exchanges a piece of balled-up paper (a pellet) supplied by a volunteer for a dummy provided by the magician. Compare billet switch. [rare]

n. Synonym for billet reading. [obsolete after 1944] Originally developed by fake mediums who called them "pellet tests" by 1922 (Houdini). Magicians jargon by 1922 Houdini; 1938 Stewart Judah pamphlet; 1944 Annemann.

n. The pseudo-topological puzzle where a pencil with an attached loop of string is easily and rapidly locked through a spectator's bottonhole, yet the spectator usually finds it cannot be removed without cutting the string. [rare]
n. Effect where a round pencil is visibly pushed through the center of a borrowed coin. [rare]
v. Pencil reading being the more usual verb synonym.
See: Penetration Frame. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Penetration Frame".)
n. Variant of the old Card through Handkerchief trick where the deck is placed in its own card case before being wrapped in the hank and produced by shaking. [rare]

n. The effect of dropping one cup through another during a Cups and Balls routine. [very rare but not nonce] It is an optical and aural illusion. First described and exposed in 1788 by Decremps in his Codicille de Jérôme Sharp. Then in 1857 by Wyman in The Magician's Own Book. 7-8.
n. The effect of passing one solid object through another; Matter through Matter. For example, as in chopper effects or the Penetrating Card. Also abbreviated as penetro. [common]
n. Conjuring geared to a lay audience; commercial magic. [very rare, possibly nonce]

term: sleight of hand for laymen. And they love it."
definition: n. A metal tube (disguised as a pepper shaker) to vanish a coin thru a concealed slit-opening at the side of the flat bottom. [archaic since 1904] Although this clumsy prop enjoyed deservedly only a relatively short vogue, it very likely inspired the modern slit glass.

n. Dice altered to assure that certain faces turn up with greater frequency than others. [very rare usage among magicians but widely understood by them] Originally the argot of dice sharps by 1932 Evans Secret Blue Book cat; 1945 Scarne; 1977 Sharper in Prus; 1984 Ortiz. Thence magicians jargon by 1949 Tannen cat #1.

term: Perfect Faro Shuffle; perfect faro shuffle
definition: n. A Faro Shuffle where the two equally divided halves of the deck interleave card for card. [fairly common] "I'll show him how to do a perfect faro shuffle—perfect split and 100% interlock." — Dai Vernon, letter to Faucett Ross, 18 Jan 1956 Originally the invention of American gamblers by 1894. REF: J.N. Maskelyne, 204-205. Among the relatively few magicians who have mastered this precision sleight with sufficient assurance to use it routinely are Fred Braue (by 1940), Jeff Busby (by 1969), Bruce Cervon, Jacob Daley (1930s), Persi Diaconis, Alex Elmsley (by 1950s), Charlie Hudson, Larry Jennings, Erhard Liebenow (since 1972), Harry Lorayne, Ed Marlo, Gene Maze (by 1980), Charlie Miller, Larry Pringle, Harry Riser, Fred Robinson, Mike Skinner, Allan Slaight, Paul Swinford, Johnny Thompson, Dai Vernon (1930s), and Ronald Wohl.

n. A riffle shuffle where the two equally divided halves of the deck interleave card for card. [rare] The mathematics of this false shuffle are the same as for the perfect faro shuffle. A pet technique of Fred Black (in the 1920s), T. Nelson Downs (1920s-30s), Fred Braue (by 1940), Charlie Miller, and Jeff Busby (by 1972). REF: Busby in Epoptica #1 (1982), 41.

n. A false shuffle that alternately interleaves the two equal halves of the deck of cards thereby giving complete card control. [rare] 697 “The great appeal of the perfect shuffle to Faro dealers and magicians is its regularity. After a perfect shuffle, the dealer knows exactly what happened to each card and the same thing happens with every shuffle. Precision of this order usually indicates an underlying mathematical model, and this is certainly the case here.” — S. Brent Morris, “On the Faro Shuffle: Part Two”, The Linking Ring (Dec 1997), 59 The two main versions are the Perfect Faro Shuffle and the Perfect Riffle Shuffle depending on whether the shuffle is a faro or a riffle. Eight perfect out-shuffles (or 52 perfect in-shuffles) will recycle the entire deck to its original order.
See: scent trick, the. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "scent trick, the".)

n. Card trick where four playing cards taken from a deck are shown and then two placed in two separate pockets of a volunteer who is asked to name one card in each pocket, which the magus removes, but when the volunteer names the two remaining cards he removes them himself sees he is wrong. [very rare]
n. A comedy conjuring routine in which the magician acts constantly surprised by the magical events taking place around him or her. [rare] The classic example is Cardini's standard stage act.

(See also: Multiplying Rabbits.) n. Effect where two large sponge-rubber bunnies produce many small ones; Peter Rabbit Goes to Town! (obsolescent). [common] "Most working pros will verify that there is no close-up trick that gets as much of a rise out of spectators as the multiplying rabbit routine. The charisma of these little devils is devastating to the lay public." — Rick Johnsson in The Linking Ring (Jun 1987), 87

n. The effect where phantom figures are made to appear. [archaic after 1863, once fairly common] The Belgian optician, Étienne-Gaspard Robert, who as a showman took the name Robertson, first exhibited his "Fantasmagorie" in his native Liège in 1784. He used a magic lantern to project his eerie images onto smoke. Robertson brought his show to Paris in 1794 where it played successfully for six years. Paul de Philipsthal brought his version to London in 1801 or 1802, calling it "Phantasmagoria". REF: Clarke in Magic Wand, Vol.14 (June 1925), 98-100; Barnouw (1981), 19-21.
(See also: Phantom Tube.) n. Type of large metal or plastic dye tube fitted with an eccentric conical load chamber; Phanto Tube; Ghost Tube [Brit.]. [common in USA; not in British English]
n. A playing card whose face is printed to show a fan of two or more faces. Permits the packet effect of three (or more) cards becoming one. [fairly common]

(See also: Cigarette from Nowhere.) n. Effect where the magician mimes rolling a cigarette and placing it at his lips, yet when he takes a match from a matchbox and lights it, a real and smoking cigarette appears; the Phantom Cigarette. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]
n. A tall glass tumbler fitted with a centrally positioned vertical mirror (a la the Mirror Glass) and a hole at one side of the bottom (like a half Bottomless Glass). [very rare]
n. Type of large metal or plastic dye tube fitted with an eccentric conical load chamber; Phanto Tube; Ghost Tube [Brit.]. [common in USA; not in British English]

(See also: magnetic pencil.) n. Effect where a pencil (or other long object) is suspended from the palm of the hand. [rare] First reported with a rod as "Philosophy Cheated" in 1829 (The Boy’s Own Book, 165-166) and again in 1857 (Magician's Own Book, 24-25).
See: telephone-book test. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "telephone-book test".)

n. Effect where a volunteer initials a paper bit, which is placed on a large coin. The volunteer selects a card; and, when the paper is turned over, its face has a picture of the card. [rare] "I have always believed that the 'photographic card' is one of the greatest of all close-up tricks." — Bruce Elliott in New Phoenix (1960), 235

n. Effect where the magician places seven pairs of cards and a single card between the spread fingers of a volunteer's tabled hands, removes each pair, dividing it into two separate tabled packets whereupon the odd card apparently passes from packet to packet. [rare] Although this trick is very old and has gone by many names, it got its odd jargon-name from Imro Fox (1852-1910) who featured it at private entertainments. So-called because the volunteer is asked to place both hands upon the table and spread them as if about to play a piano. REF: Mussey (1942), 45, based on an oral report from T. Nelson Downs; Hilliard (1909), 36.
n. A Three Card Monte effect using two gaffed & one fair playing cards. [rare]
n. A load that the magician does not carry on his person (a body load) and that therefore must be picked up. [very rare but not nonce]
n. An act consisting of pickpocketing. [rare]
n. Stage effect where a long non-flexible rod (hollow or solid) is thrust horizontally through the female assistant's waist; later called Pillars of Fear and Rod thru Body. [rare]
n. Effect where two linked safety-pins visibly unlink. [obsolescent, formerly common] This is the original version of the Linking Pins.
n. Effect where the magician, wielding a long pole with a net on the end, snares a succession of live pigeons or doves out of thin air. [obsolescent, formerly rare]
1.n. Early slang term for the Cap and Pence trick. [obsolete after mid-1850s]

n. The effect of an escape from a wooden frame in which the head and hands of the escapologist are locked. [fairly common] A common dealer item by 1879 when it was called "The Mystery Pillory" and in 1882 when it was called "The Pillory Feat" in Hamley's catalog. According to Will Goldston, it was introduced by "Balabrega, the Swedish Wonder," which is quite possible as Balabrega (stagename of the Swedish-American John M. Miller) began performing professionally in 1878. Although Houdini toyed with the idea and developed plans he seemingly never performed it, although he did market plans in 1898 as the "Spirit Pillory" and the "Spanish Pillory Act." Raymond included a pillory escape in his act in Havana in 1907. REF: Hamley cat (1882); Goldston (1905), 75; Moulton (1983); Houdini (1898).

n. The Thumb Palm being the modern synonym; the pinch (obsolete). [obsolete after 1887] A type of acquitment, specifically a minor variation of the tourniquet. This sleight originated among common thieves by 1785 when it was attributed by Decremps to British coachmen in short-changing passengers. French magicians jargon as "la pincette" by 1876. Thence British magicians jargon from 1876 Hoffmann; 1886 Garenne; 1887 Hoffmann.
n. The pincette; now called the Thumb Palm. [obsolete]

n. Plagiarism or theft of a magician's invention. [rare] "Let's vary piracee With a little burglaree." — William S. Gilbert, The Pirates of Penzance (1880), Act II "It wouldn't surprise me to learn that while they were still counting the loaves and fishes some ancient magic dealer had it on the market. He probably changed it to Fishes and Loaves and claimed it for his own." — Paul Curry in letter to Jeff Busby, 21 May 1981

n. A magic performer or dealer who steals another's invention. [rare] "Your suggested fact finding committee is not a bad idea if you can figure out what to do about pirates after the committee finds the facts." — Bill Neff in letter to "Joglar" [Christopher] in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Apr 1950), 648 "I told Bruce [Elliott in 1948] that I had been screwed by more pirates than a girl stowaway on Captain Kidd's ship." — Paul Curry in letter to Jeff Busby, 2 Apr 1984

n. A gimmick consisting of a rod used to activate a trick mechanically. [archaic after 1930s] This device was applied by magicians to their tables by 1853 (Ponsin). Common in middle and late 19th Century conjuring, it is now seldom used.
n. A magician's table fitted with one or more pistons. [archaic after 1909] In use by 1853. REF: Ponsin, I (1853).

1.n. The patter in the form of a sales talk used by a magician-pitchman to sell goods. [fairly common] Originally pitchmans cant in Britain by 1861 (and probably two decades earlier) and in the USA by 1929 (and probably at least three decades earlier). REF: Confessions of a Street Conjurer (1861); Sat. Eve. Post (19 Oct 1929), 26; 1993 Ogden re circus. Thence magicians jargon by 1861 Confessions of a Street Conjurer as "The first pitch we made was near Bond Street"; 1933 Zerr in Sphinx as "at the beginning of her pitch"; 1941 R. Miller in Genii; 1948 Holden cat #15; 1954 L. Jones as booklet title The Medicine Man Pitch; 1957 Mellon in Mental-Wise as "a Horoscope Pitch"; 1958 Kanter cat #10 as a "Medicine Pitch"; 1962 F. Marshall; 1970 Boles as "the regular pitch"; 1971 Windsor ad as the "Svengali pitch"; 1981 Lees tape; 1981 B. Blais in Magic Dealer; 1981 Waters; 1988 B. Reynolds orally; 1997 G. Brown as “during the pitch”. v. To pitch; pitching [fairly common, particularly among pitchmen-magicians] Originally carnival cant by 1931 (Maurer). Thence magicians jargon by 1948 Nelson cat #22 as to “pitch ‘scopes”; 1954 J. Marshall in New Phoenix #304 as he "pitches the plate lifter"; 1970 Boles as to "pitch magic and novelty items between illusions"; 1971 T. Windsor as "how to 'pitch' balloons"; 1972 Dalal in Swami as "to pitch amulets, charms, or lucky coins"; 1981 D. Turpin in Magic Info, but recalling the 1930s; 1981 Govan as to "pitch magic"; 1983 Lees as to "pitch magic"; 1984 Koornwinder lecturing; 1997

term: Busby orally as "I pitched for him."
definition: a. [adjectivally] [rare]
n. A Throw-out Book. [rare, historical] So-called because these booklets were often pitched by a pitchman.

n. A magician who sells (pitches) magic tricks (particularly slum magic) in public places. Compare demonstrator. [fairly common] "Pitchmen offered Svengali Decks, Magic Mouses, and Whoopie Cushions." — John Booth in The Linking Ring (Aug 1997), 80 Well-known magicians who have pitched magic include: Val Andrews, in England in 1960s. Don Boles, in USA in 1960s. Ken Brooke, in Britain around 1940s. Howard Brooks, in USA. Carlton, in England, around 1900. John Cornelius, in USA in 1968. Irv Feldman, in USA in 1930s. Al Flosso, in New York City & on the road1915-19. Tony Giorgio, in USA. Henry Gordien, in New York City in 1910s. Barry Govan, in Australia since 1976. Dick Koornwinder, in Holland around 1972. Walt Lees, in England in 1970s. Jon "One-Arm Mac" McDonald, in USA in late 1920s. Michael "Mickey" MacDougall, in USA in 1933-34. Bobby Reynolds, in New York City in 1940s-50s. n. A routine in which the magician role-plays an old-fashioned pitchman in theme and patter. [rare] Inspired by a burlesque comedy pitchman act, Dave Coleman added magic to create the magical pitchman act, which he premiered as "Doc Hokum" at the 3rd Annual I.B.M. Convention in 1928, after which it has been widely imitated, including by Dr Josephus Forrestus (1930s), Tommy Windsor (1950s), Max Terhune (1950s), Lloyd Jones (1950s), Tom Palmer (1960), and Ted Carrothers (1970s-80s). REF: F. Ireland (1946), 109; Crimmins in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1954), 220.
n. A small triangular board mounted on posts at three points, one being a pencil to produce automatic writing. Compare ouija. [rare]

1.v. To hide beforehand an object to be later produced. [fairly common] Originally British thieves' slang by 1610 (OED/2). Then specifically the argot of British card cheats in referring to "markt Packs" by 1674 (Cotton as "to plant in play"; also 1714 Lucas). Thence magicians jargon by 1877 Hoffmann, 123n; 1886 Holden as "one you have ‘planted'"; 1906 Houdini in CMM; 1909 Hilliard; 1920 Holmes as "the hat is ‘planted' beforehand"; 1939 Hugard; 1945 Fitzkee as "not ‘planted'"; 1950 Jonson; 1959 Elliott as "plant them as follows"; 1960 Ganson as "have your stooge planted in the audience"; 1980 Gibson as "’plant' the envelope"; 1988 Waters. n. Any object that a confederate covertly gives the magician or otherwise interjects during the trick. [rare] Thieves argot in this sense as early as 1812. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1909 Houdini; 1931 Mussey & Oursler; 1949 Hay. a. [adjectivally] [rare]

n. The balancing and/or twirling of dinner plates, often on sticks. A former allied art of magic. [archaic, once rare] Being performed in England by British magician Signor Blitz from 1830 to 1832 when J.N. Maskelyne recalled having seen him doing it at age 6 or 7. Maskelyne made it a pet effect by at least as early as 1870. Performed by Mons. Adrean (in 1838) and the Austrians J.N. Hofzinser (died 1875) and Louis Haselmayer (by 1872). Also used by Chinese and Japanese jugglers. Indeed a troupe of Japanese jugglers imported by Amercan circus impresario Prof. Risley (Richard Risley Carlisle) brought the art to Europe and America in 1865. Later a pet effect of Max von Rhodin (since ca1909), Herbert J. Collings, and Prince Masculin (1935). First exposed (there is a gaff or two) by Neil (1903), later by Black (1914-15). REF: Blitz 1830 Hanley program in Magic (Oct 1901), 2; Neil (1903), 322-323; Ayling (1981), 32, 271-275; Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 89.

n. Stage magic is the original and always more usual synonym. However, while stage magic usually connotes performance on a full-sized theater stage, platform magic refers to any size stage down to the smallest raised platform in a nightclub or church hall. [rare]

1.n. The basic, usually implicit and unspoken, story-line underlying and outlining a magical effect; the theme being the newer but less usual synonym. [common] “A good card trick, like a good story should have a definite plot. Every action in the performance of the trick should be interwoven with that plot and should help build up the climax.” — Jean Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (May 1945), 121 "The plot is really very simple, as all good magical plots should be." — Louis Histed, The Magic of Louis Histed (1947), 60 "The plot of the trick is absolutely simple and magical: you link and unlink rings." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 281 "The feat of catching money from the air still maintains a high degree of popularity and, one presumes, it always will for the simple plot brings into magical reality the fulfilment of so many ordinary folks' wishes—money without any work!" — Peter Warlock in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1955), 365
(See also: Scrawny Chicken.) n. Comedy prop in the form of an emaciated rubber (or sometimes cloth) chicken, usually used as a production item. [rare]
n. A brass tube about 3" long that is closed by a brass stopper, which is faked to permit the contents to drop secretly into the magician's hand. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]
n. The type of leverage applied to playing cards that works the Plunger Rising Cards and a few other effects. [rare]

term: plunger rising cards; Plunger Rising Cards
definition: n. Sleight-of-hand versions of the Rising Cards where the chosen card is sandwiched between two injogged cards and levered upward by using the Plunger Principle. [rare]
n. A magicians simulated Poker dealing routine in a gambling demonstration; a Poker Demonstration. [fairly common]

(See also: pocket trick.) n. A specific feat of pocket magic; a pocket effect. [common] "The ideal pocket trick should require no preparation and difficulty of performance be reduced to a minimum, as few care to expend hours of weary practice on a trick that can only be shown to a small circle of acquaintances." — Stanley Collins in The Jinx #91 (1940), 567 713 “My favorite pocket trick is a Sponge Ball Routine. If I had to give up every other trick in my bag, this is the one I would prefer to keep.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Sep 1951), 837

n. A flat gimmick in which slips of paper can be filed in prearranged order, ready to be secretly removed from a pocket when needed; an index being the less usual synonym. When used to file playing cards it is usually termed a card index. [rare] In use by Ted Annemann by 1926 (Sphinx, May 1926). Carried to its extreme by Arthur Lloyd. REF: Annemann in Jinx (1940), 527-528, 572, and (1941), 818.
n. The general category of pocket tricks; vest-pocket magic being the later and always less usual synonym. [fairly common]

n. A specific feat of pocket magic; a pocket effect. [common] "The ideal pocket trick should require no preparation and difficulty of performance be reduced to a minimum, as few care to expend hours of weary practice on a trick that can only be shown to a small circle of acquaintances." — Stanley Collins in The Jinx #91 (1940), 567 713 “My favorite pocket trick is a Sponge Ball Routine. If I had to give up every other trick in my bag, this is the one I would prefer to keep.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Sep 1951), 837
n. A short (from 4 to 8 inch) magic wand used for close-up magic. [rare]
1.n. A miniature clipboard-like writing surface hidden in the mentalist-magician's trouser pocket used for surreptitious pocket writing.
