n. Type of body work where the magician uses his pocket as a servante, putting his hand in or past to steal or ditch an object; pocket work. [rare]
n. The one center of interest at any given moment during performance of a trick; the focus of attention. [very rare, possibly nonce]
n. A pointer card (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare] "There are twenty-two cards in the deck which are called ‘pointers,' because the majority of their spots point in one direction."

n. Any playing card whose face design is asymmetrical (one-way) because the majority of its spots (pips) point in one direction; a pointer being the less usual synonym. [rare] All standard commercial decks contain as pointers the 7 of diamonds and the ace, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9 of the other three suits as well as most jokers. This gives a minimum of 22 out of 52 cards that can be used to create a partial one-way deck. This one-way-pip principle was reported as early as 1912 by both Stanyon (in Magic) and Goldston. Independently rediscovered around 1928 by Annemann (Jinx [1935], 44).
n. Effect where the magician's brush strokes can produce colored stripes on one side of a white board and spots on the other. [rare]

a. Said of magical effects that simulate the activities of a mischievious ghost. [rare] 715 Originally entered Standard English in 1848 from the German Poltergeist meaning literally a knocking spirit or noisy ghost. REF: OED/2.

(See also: Telekinetic Timber.) n. Apparatus in form of an oblong wooden block that when placed in precarious balances eventually tips over or falls off. [rare] Inspired by Harbin's Little Tippler (1950), this self-contained prop was invented jointly by Jeff Busby (the angled 90-degree fall) and Don Albrecht (the fall off the bottle) in late 1981 when first marketed exclusively by Jeff Busby Magic, Inc, as Poltergeist Block with patter theme suggested by Max Mavin and Don Albrecht. Used by Kreskin on 2 May 1989 in his Houdini Seance at the American Museum of Magic and later in his TV magic special. Also used by Max Maven. Other more recent piracies appeared as the "Block of Foo Manchu" and "The Block".
n. The Ambitious Card effect obtained by using the Nu-Idea Deck. [fairly common] A routine invented by Ralph W. Hull using his Nu-Idea Deck and marketed by 1935. First published in Hilliard (1938).
n. Comedy effect where the magician's necktie quickly or slowly rises to a straight-out position. [fairly common]
1.n. Originally a comedy routine by Billy McComb in his marketed act "Portable Hole Collection".

n. A contortionist. [obsolete] One or more contortionists were sometimes included by magicians of the 1700s as a side-show to their entertainment. No longer considered an allied art of magic. REF: McArdle (1963). Originally Standard English between 1691 and 1830. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1725 Fawkes ad as "Posture Master"; 1736 Fawkes ad as "Posture-Master"; 1979 Dawes

n. Unofficial name of The Master Index to Magic in Print. [rare] The mammoth index of magical effects compiled by British amateur Jack Potter. The original edition appeared in his "Potter's Bar" column that appeared serially in both The Linking Ring 717 and The Budget. Published in book form by Micky Hades International in 14 volumes between 1967 and 1977, each with nearly 500 pages, totalling 100,000 cross-references to specific tricks, routines, and categories of magic published in English up to the end of 1964. Although this valuable work is a prime starting-point for researching the history of specific effects and methods, it is insufficiently incomplete and too filled with errors to be considered the final word, as several magicians believe. "One must, after all, remember that card magic has progressed rapidly since the cut-off date of the Potter index of 1964." — Jeff Busby, Short Sheet (May 1986), 2

n. Simulated paranormal ability. [rare] Originally the argot of psychics and pseudo-psychics. Thence magicians jargon by 1970 G. Nielsen in Talisman as "The Power"; 1979 Fulves as "psi power"; 1984 Busby as "Many mentalists come to believe they really have The Power."; 1988 Waters, 227, as "powers"; 1989 G. Anderson on

(See also: close-up mirror.) n. A looking-glass (usually and ideally of the 3-panel folding type) used by a close-up magician to practice moves in front of. [rare] "The best mode of judging one's success in this particular [palming] is to practice before a looking-glass." — Robert-Houdin, The Secrets of Conjuring and Magic (1868/1877 tr by Hoffmann), 48 "The only proper way to practice [sleights] is to be seated in the usual manner at a card table with a looking glass opposite; and much time and labor are saved by this plan. The correct positions and movements can be accurately secured, and the performer becomes his own critic." — S. W. Erdnase, Artifice Ruse and Subterfuge at the Card Table (1902), 24 "A few trials before the looking-glass will determine the exact amount of speed to use in riffling the cards." — J. Northern Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909), Chapter III "The beginner should practice in front of a mirror, first actually placing the card in the left hand, then imitating the natural action as near as possible ... while retaining the card in the right hand." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (Oct 1919), 4 "Practice before a mirror is a good way to learn sleight-of-hand." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Mar 1955), 260 The idea of using a mirror to practice sleight-of-hand was, as Busby pointed out, first published by French master Robert-Houdin in 1868, specifically for palming. He was followed in English 212 by Sachs (1877), 74, for the Fan Force; Hoffmann (1889), 99-100; and Stanyon (1898), 2. Erdnase's advice of 1902 was directed to both card sharps and sleight-of-hand magicians. Two years after Erdnase, American card sharp Frank Bonville also recommended the use of a mirror for practice in his The Little Secrets (1904). REF: Busby in Whaley (1991), 162-163, 402n42; Ortiz (1991), 48
(See also: Indian Prayer Chain.) n. Effect where the top ring in a foot-long chain of interlocked metal rings repeatedly tumbles to the bottom ring on command. [rare]
See: Chinese Prayer Vase. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Chinese Prayer Vase".)
a. Said of a packet or entire deck of playing cards that has been prepared by sorting into some special order, that is, stacked. Compare prepared. [fairly common]
n. The state of a set of objects (such as the cards in a deck) having been placed beforehand in some set order. [rare]

n. The effect in mentalism of knowing future events before they occur; the simulation of prior knowledge; prediction being the most usual synonym. [rare] The word was Standard English by 1611 and thence the lingo of the pseudo-scientific field of parapsychology. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1948 C. Green in HMM; 1957 Maréchal; 1960 Ganson; 1961 Gardner in HMM; 1969 Gibson; 1976 Goldstein; 1979 Lamb; 1984 Booth; 1988 Waters; 1994 Ashton in MUM.

n. The effect, particularly in mentalism, where the magician forecasts something that is about to occur; precognition; prophecy; fortune-telling. A major example is the Headline Prediction. [very common] "In theory, I do not like predictions. It has always seemed to me that the magician who includes such items in his program is underestimating the intelligence of his audience." — Victor Farelli in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Nov 1951), 864 "Predictions are always interesting." — Stuart Cramer in J. Marshall (1955), 49

n. A box (faked or unfaked) used to secretly insert a written prediction. [fairly common] A pet publicity stunt of, among many others, Joe Karston by 1936 and Orson Welles in 1956. Major collections of these chests are owned by Dr. Richard O. Mossey (1984), who lectures on their history, and Joe Stevens (1988).
a. Said of apparatus that has been loaded prior to performance. [rare]
a. Said of a familiar object (card, coin, wand, etc.) that has been physically altered to facilitate manipulation; faked. Antonym of unprepared. [very common]
1.n. Mainly British term for a stacked deck. [obsolete after 1950]

n. The overall way a trick is performed, tailoring the effect, method, apparatus, costume, plot, routining, patter, mood, etcetera to fit the audience's expectations, preconceptions, and limitations. [common] "[W]ithout proper presentation the best sleight-of-hand is nothing but a juggling feat." — Nate Leipzig in The Sphinx (Jan 1939), 300 721 "The main difference between magicians is, or should be, their presentations. The same basic trick in various hands will create a strikingly different effect." — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1955), 363 "Every performer must work out his own style of presentation of magic as in all other branches of the entertainment arts." — Greer Maréchal Jr, Magic for the Millions (1957), 19 "Presentation is really what it's all about. A minor trick well presented is infinitely superior to the most elaborate machinations which an audience can't understand or relate to." — Bill Tarr, Now You See It, Now You Don't (1976), 13
v. To set the mechanism of a piece of apparatus prior to performance or, for a close-up routine, secreting loads in the lap or up the sleeve. [rare]

n. The flourish where a hand-held deck of playing cards is fanned by simultaneously squeezing and pivoting it with the fingers of the other hand. When fanned counter-clockwise it is called a "reverse pressure fan". [fairly common] "The pressure fan has one great advantage over other methods of making the fan: it can be made with a pack in any condition, new or old." — Hugard & Braue, Expert Card Technique (1940), 166 722 "They [the cards] were so bad he couldn't even make a pressure fan." — Jay Marshall in The New Phoenix #339 (1956), 168
v. To do magic. [very rare, possibly nonce]

n. Original spelling of prestidigitator (see) [obsolete spelling after 1940s, once common] Although of honorable if miscegenous ancestry, this grand old word has been considered rather pompous by many magicians, beginning with Robert-Houdin in 1858.
n. Magic. [very rare, possibly nonce] Originally, since around 1540, Standard English meaning magic in its supernatural sense. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon in 1937 Gravatt in Jun Genii.

n. Old word for magician. [obsolete after 1895] Originally the Latin praestigiator (a worker of wonders—"prestiges") by c.50 AD (Seneca the Younger). Thence the French prestigiateur used in the 1500s (and the Italian prestigiatore, which is still the usual Italian jargon word). REF: Robert-Houdin (1868/1977 tr), 43-44, where he urged this word's revival for French magicians. Eventually a Standard English word from the early 1600s until the late 1800s. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon in 1855 Prof. Harrington ad in the Boston Bee; 1895 S. Baldwin; 1984 Dawes in MC, as historical. Presto; Presto! 1.int. A magic word that commands an effect (usually a vanish but also a production, transformation, or transposition) to occur instantly. Compare jingo (obsolete). [common, but declining in usage] "Hay passe, presto vade, jubeo, by the virtue of hocus pocus, 'tis gone." — Thomas Ady, A Candle in the Dark (1655) "Presto ..., a word used by Juglers, in their Hocus Pocus tricks." — Thomas Blount, Glossographia (1656) "Here we have a model of our up-to-date Presto Painting Works at Hey; in other words, the Hey Presto Painting Works." — William G. Stickland in Devant (1936), 256, as patter 724 From the Italian presto meaning quick or quickly. It is significant that a few Italian conjurors performed in Elizabethan and Jacobean England from the late 1500s to early 1600s. Thus Scoto (who performed for Elizabeth I) and "an Italian Jugler" (who performed for Henry, Prince of Wales, in the period 1610-12). Thence as British magicians jargon (with variants noted) by 1599 Ben Jonson as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1634 Hocus Pocus Junior as "Presto" & "Presto be gone"; 1655 Ady as “presto” & “prestor”; 1656 Blount dict; 1721 Neve; 1763 Dean; 1822 Ingleby Sen., playbill as "Presto Pass"; 1834 Ventriloquism Explained, 29, as "Presto, Presto"; 1849 Jacobs, Newcastle program as "and Presto! he is gone"; 1855 Wyman; 1857 Magician's Own Book as "Presto, Pacillo, Pass"; 1859 Secret Out; 1861 Confessions of a Street Conjurer as "Presto-quick-begone!"; 1875 Hartz as "Presto, begone!"; 1877 Sachs as "Presto, pass!"; 1882 Hamley cat; 1896 Bertram as "Hey, Presto!"; 1902 Hilliar; 1903 Evans in Magic as "Hey Presto!"; 1905 Goldston as "Hi Presto!"; 1908 Stanyon ad in Magic as "Hi-Presto"; 1909 Stanyon in Magic as "Presto!! Change!!"; 1909 Hilliard; 1920 Carrington as "Presto, pass!"; 1928 Culpitt as "Presto! Pass!"; 1928 Thayer cat #7 as "Presto!" & "Presto! Go!"; 1935 Grant; 1939 Kanter cat as "Presto!"; 1941 James; 1944 Hugard in HMM as "Hey! Presto!"; 1948 Elliott as "hey presto"; 1949 Tannen cat #1; 1949 J. Maskelyne as “”hey, presto!”; 1958 as annual Hey Presto #1 (England); 1965 Mulholland; 1975 Dalal in Mantra as "Hey Presto"; 1979 Lamb as "Hey Presto!"; 1982 Ginn; 1983 Desfor; 1988 Waters; 1993 Abbott cat #24. 2.n. Magic. [rare]

n. The punch (see) being the current synonym. [obsolescent after 1885] Originally, as "the prick", the argot of British card sharps by 1552 (Walker). Later as "pricked cards" by British sharps by 1843 (Crambrook cat; 1844 Anderson). Thence of American sharps by 1855 (Wyman; 1865 Evans; 1868 Green; 1875 Hartz; 1911 Meyer; 1933 Cameron). Also called "pricking" by American sharps by 1865 (Evans; 1894 Koschitz). Thence magicians jargon by 1843 Crambrook cat; 1844 Anderson; 1877 Hoffmann, 201; 1885 Sachs; 1897 Hercat; 1928 Thayer cat #7; 1946 Clive; 1981 Sharpe in Ayling; 1996 Müller.

n. A seemingly fair puzzle where a string or rope coiled in a figure-8 pattern upon a table can be uncoiled by the magician (using a secret move) but not by the volunteer; the garter trick (1); the endless chain. [rare] First reported by Francis Bacon (in his Silva Silvarum) in recalling one of several tricks performed around 1575 at his father's house by a conjuror. Later a common trick with Gypsies and, as a gambling scam, as "Prick in the Garter" by 1763. Thence 1843 Crambrook cat (when 725 first exposed) and as "Pricking the Garter" by 1896 (Bertram; 1912 Goldston, 32). First exposed in a magic magazine in Stanyon's Magic in 1901. Re-popularized by British magician George Blake in 1949 when he published it as "Loopy Loop". Subsequently, variations have been developed by Persi Diaconis, Fred Lowe, Phil Goldstein, Scotty York, Dennie Flynn (1975), and Neal Elias (1982). REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1924), 73; Busby in Arcane #7 (1982), 75-76; OED/2, 657, 1427. Thence magicians jargon (variant noted) by 1843 Crambrook cat as "Prick in the Garter"; 1865 Every Boy's Annual as "Prick in the Garter"; 1876 Cremer, 77; 1901 Stanyon in Magic, 6, as "Prick in the Garter"; 1912 Goldston; 1929 Waller; 1946 Schmidt in HMM, 189; 1973 Alain; 1982 Busby in Arcane #7; 1988 Waters; 1994 Racherbaumer in LR; 1997 KT Magic cat; 2000 L&L cat #13; 2001 Magic Methods cat.
n. Comedy effect where a photo showing the familiar "Pride" and "Joy" detergent cleaning product boxes are produced. [rare] Marketed by early 1970s.

1.n. Generally, any basic psychological, physiological, or physical rules that can be applied to achieve magical deception. The principles of deception; the principles of magic. [fairly common] "The fundamental principles of a sleight of hand trick, practically any trick or stage illusion for that matter, are Three Only in number, viz., Production, Disappearance and Change." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (Jun 1912), 67 "A Magician is not a Magician because he knows tricks, but because he knows Magic—the principles, the fundamentals." — Harlan Tarbell (1927), Lesson 1, p.5. "True success and satisfaction go only to those who really comprehend the underlying principles of why a trick succeeds or fails." — Greer Maréchal Jr, Magic for the Millions (1957), 16 Examples that depend on quirks of human psychology include the equivoque, Rick Johnsson's Too Perfect Principle, Phil Goldstein's Rashomon Principle, and Ascanio's (Law of) Priority Movement. Examples that depend on human physiological or sensory limitations include black art and most optical illusions. Those that depend on the laws of physics or math include mirror work and mathematical magic. While each of the four leading theoreticians of magic list certain principles, there is no consensus as to the specific items comprising a complete list. Nearly all agree that misdirection is such a principle, but even here they differ in their definition of that term.
See: Spirit Print Card Trick. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Spirit Print Card Trick".)
n. The psychological principle that the first object to move tends to capture and hold attention. [very rare]

n. Abbreviation of professional. [fairly common] 728 "'What is tragic in magic?' You ask an old pro. One who has tempted the fates. With a shake in his voice, he replies 'Don't you know? Simply a shortage of dates.'" — Harry Leat, Tragic Magic (1925), 13 Originally Standard English since 1866. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1901 S. Blake letter in Magic, 30; 1920 Carlton as a "pro"; 1970 R. Johnson; 1979 Mendoza; 1981 Brooke #1; 1983 Bauer; 1984 Zoss in New Tops; 1984 Albrecht cartoon in Epoptica; 1997 Booth in LR as "a skilled 'pro' for some years".
1.n. A trick (in its secondary sense of an effect) being the much more usual synonym. [obsolete; once fairly common particularly in Britain]
n. Any box faked so as to produce objects. One of the most widely used is the Square Circle. [common]
n. Any cylinder faked for producing objects. [fairly common]
n. A magician's wand mechanically gimmicked to produce and object such as a coin (the coin wand) or silk (the handkerchief wand). [rare]

n. Any magician who earns more than half his income by performing magic; a pro being the abbreviation; a worker (2). Opposite of an amateur. Compare semi-professional. 731 [common] "The performer, who seeks personal recognition as a true professional and is totally unaffected by his peers, looks at magic organizations and clubs as places to stay away from." — Joel Bauer, Hustle, Hustle: Making Magic Pay (1983), 27 Originally Standard English by 1811 in the sense of one who earns a livlihood from a profession. REF: OED/1. Thence magicians jargon by 1891 Burlingame; 1906 Wilson in Sphinx; 1913 Magic Circle ad in Magic; 1919 Ovette; 1921 Lustig; 1932 Mulholland; 1945 Wheeler cat; 1950 Young; 1974 Wade; 1983 R. Stebbins; 1983 Bauer; 1995

1.n. Public title appropriated by many early magicians for reasons of publicity puffery or personal conceit, just as physicien was adopted by some French conjurors in the early 1800s. Always capitalized when used as title. [obsolescent after 1926] "Don't programme yourself as 'Professor.' You are an entertainer, not a pedagogue." — J. Northern Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909) This practice began among magicians around 1783 with Pinetti. It was picked up in the early 1800s by "Professors" Felix Testot, James Taylor, J.H. Anderson, etc. It peaked during the late 1800s with its use by at least 15 major performers (notably A. Herrmann and J.M. Hartz) and at least two non-performing writers (Hoffmann and Garenne). Thenceforward the title was obsolescent, although used in the very early 1900s by F.E. Powell and Dunninger, who in 1926 was the most recent major magician to adopt it. Rarely used today and then only for comedy effect. A partial post-1850 list follows: 1851 Professor J. H. Anderson (Bristol playbill) 1852 " Gurnet, Canadian (Boston billing) 1852 " Krosso (London playbill) 1855 " Savren (Canterbury playbill) 1857 " Logrenia (London playbill) 1858 " Harrington (Boston playbill) 1858 " Kratky-Baschik (London playbill) 1870s " Hellis 1872 " A. Herrmann (London ad) 1873 " Hoffmann (as pen name) 1886 " Garenne (as pen name) 1894-98 "Houdini (Apr 16th 1894 Globe Museum playbill) 1900 " Norton (Stockport playbill) 1926 " Dunninger

n. Comedy effect where magician on noticing the end of a rope dangling from his sleeve begins to pull until it catches; then pulling from the trouser leg, finally producing a 50 foot rope with the performer's undershorts attached. [fairly common]
n. A deep pocket concealed in a tail of the magician's dress-coat. Used to ditch or, occasionally, steal an object. [obsolescent]
a. Slang abbreviation for impromptu. [very rare, possibly nonce]
n. False evidence presented by the conjuror to convince the spectators that a prop or move is 734 ungaffed; a throw-off; magician's logic; and as phrase “no deception”. [rare]

(See also: close-up case.) n. Any hand-held box (such as an attaché case or small valise) fitted with compartments in which the peripatetic close-up magician can carry all his apparatus; a prop case. [fairly common] The earliest reported example was Scottish magician Victor Farelli’s “’Body-Load’ Box”, which he’d invented and used for many years before retiring from the stage in 1939. His hinged-top 16"x10"x5" attaché case was fitted with 9 compartments holding enough props for 30 effects plus a make-up box and some toilet articles. REF: Farelli in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jul 1952), 957. The invention (probably an independent reinvention) of this convenience is attributed to Dai 210 Vernon, the much travelled Canadian close-up worker, by British magician Lewis Ganson, who recalled six years later that when Vernon first visited England in 1955, the local magi were almost as impressed to see such a handy device as they were by the magic the legendary Canadian produced from it. REF: Ganson (1961), 21. May have had its origin in the Suitcase Table, which had at least three makers by 1928. REF: Thayer cat #7 (1928), 237. "I find that a Gag Bag makes an excellent close-up case. It will hold cards, coins, etc. very nicely. There is something about having the bag you carried your props in magically changing into five different colors at the end of your act that really impresses an audience." — Rick Ross in The Linking Ring (May 1987), 72

n. A listing of the properties (props) required for a trick, routine, or act that the magician draws up beforehand as a memory aid; a property plot. [rare] Originally as "property list" by 1961 in American theatrical lingo. REF: Bowman & Ball, Theatre Language (1961); Betts (1934); Griffin (1972). Thence U.S. magicians jargon by 1937 J.G. Alexander; 1945 Fitzkee; 1954 Jaks in New Phoenix #303; 1965 Mulholland; 1972 Griffin; 1977 Malbrough; 1984 Miller in Success Book #4; 1987 Caveney.

n. A prop being the more usual synonym. Usually used in the plural as properties. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common] "I wil draw a bil of properties, such as our play wants." — Shakespeare, A Midsummer Night's Dream (c1594), I, ii, 108 "In stagecraft, the skill and personality of a performer should rise above his properties." — Charles Waller, Magical Nights at the Theatre (1948/1980), 91 "Dealers sell tricks whose sole novelty is an intricate 'patter story' to account for the outlandish properties used." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 12 Originally and still theatrical cant since around 1425; 1838 Dickens/Grimaldi. REF: OED/2; Fay (1930). Thence borrowed as magicians jargon by 1859 Secret Out; 1876 Hoffmann; 1885 Sachs; 1896 Bertram; 1901 Selbit; 1909 Stanyon in Magic as "the properties required for the trick"; 1910 Hatton & Plate; 1910 Hull; 1937 Holden; 1942 Elliott in Phoenix; 1943 Fitzkee; 1946 Jonson; 1955 Christopher in HMM; 1963 Mulholland; 1981 Abbott cat #22, p.21, as "the properties consist of ...."; 1993 KT Magic cat.

n. A prop list being the more usual synonym, particularly in the USA. [rare] Originally theatrical cant by 1910s (Harry Bouton & Co., theater instruction form dated "191_"; 1930 Fay; 1933 Godfrey, as earliest citation in the OED/2). Also as "prop plot" by 1957 (Cotes). Thence magicians jargon by 1910s Harry Bouton [Blackstone] & Co., theater instruction form open-dated "191_"; 1954 Dexter in Magic Wand; 1956 Crimmins in HMM re Dexter.
n. A prediction (see) being the much more usual synonym. [rare]
n. A quick-change act (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare, probably long obsolete except in magic dictionaries that copy from each other]

n. A quick-change artist (see) being the usual modern synonym. [obsolete] "There is a common idea to the effect that a protean artist uses a variety of ingeniously constructed suits and dresses. Such is not the case." 736 — Charles Waller, Magical Nights at the Theatre (1948/1980), 173.

(See also: Cabinet of Proteus.) n. Stage illusion where one person changes into another inside a large wooden cabinet. Self- contained, it could be worked surrounded by a committee of spectators and afterwards examined by them inside and out without revealing the secret; the Proteus Cabinet. [rare] Using the same V-mirror principle that mechanician Thomas W. Tobin had invented and sold to Col. Stodare in 1865 for the latter's Sphinx illusion, Prof. John Henry Pepper enlarged the effect and premiered it later that year at the Royal Polytechnic Institution hall, London. A later, elaborated cabinet-within-a-cabinet version is known as the Morritt Cage. Originally called simply "Proteus" (from the man in Greek myth who could take different forms) in 1865 by Pepper who himself soon renamed it The Cabinet of Proteus. Thence 1927 Gibson; 1985 Sharpe as historical; 1988 Waters as historical.
v. To give proof (misleading information). [fairly common]
n. A conjurer. [archaic] In Classical Greek, literally, "he who deals with pebbles," referring to the Cups-and-Balls trick.
n. The simulated hypothesized psychic "force" that accounts for supposed paranormal phenomena such as telepathy and psychokinesis. [rare]
a. Pertaining to the paranormal, as in psychic entertainer, etc. [common] Originally the cant of psychic researchers, having been coined on 17 Jul 1871 by Sir William Crookes. REF: OED/2.

n. A magician who specializes in mentalism or psychic entertainment. [fairly common] "Even though most ethical psychic entertainers are quick to insert a disclaimer into their programs, saying that they possess no supernatural powers, it is amusing how many members of their audiences believe they possess genuine extrasensory abilities." — Blackstone Jr & Reynolds, The Blackstone Book of Magic & Illusion (1985), 136
n. Mentalism being the more usual synonym. [rare]

n. An automaton that could spell, count, and play cards. [archaic after 1910] Conceived in 1873 by Lincolnshire farmer John Algernon Clarke (1828-1887) who sold the idea to magician-mechanic J.N. Maskelyne who then designed, built, and premiered the 22-inch high Hindu figure as "Psycho" on 13 Jan 1875 at the Egyptian Hall in London. This was the first, most popular, and most widely copied of the four automata made by Maskelyne, the others being Zoe (a drawing figure in 1877), Fanfare (a cornetist in 1878), and Labial (a euphonium player in 1878). Maskelyne's original Psycho is in the London Museum. Harry Kellar bought a pirated copy of Psycho in London in Summer 1878 which he premiered under that name in the USA later that year on Dec 9th. After his retirement Kellar gave it to Houdini. Haselmayer toured with a Psycho in 1881. It was revived at Maskelyne's in 1910. GEN REF: John Gaughan & Jim Steinmeyer, The Mystery of Psycho (1987); Sharpe (1983), 154-158; Dexter (1956), 74-74; Jenness (1967), 33, 41; Kellar (1886); Devant (1931), 195.

n. Effects of mental magic where "mental energy" alone produces physical manifestations; PK as acronym; telekinesis. Pronounced sy-ko-kih-NEE-sis. [fairly common] “Patter about psycho-kinesis [sic], the inevitable Dr. Rhine and the mysteries of thought projection.” — Al Stevenson in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jun 1959), 3 This type of effect originated with psychic pretenders (Uri Geller, etc.). Thence borrowed by magicians, although infrequently used by them. Examples of PK tricks are the gimmicked Little Tippler (1950), Poltergeist Block (1981), and Popsy Pegs. 739 The word "psychokinesis" was coined from the Greek psycho (mind) + kinesis (motion) in 1914 by Henry Holt of the Society of Psychical Research (London) and soon widely adopted by parapsychologists. REF: OED/2. Thence as magicians jargon by 1947 Braue in Nov HMM, 379; 1947 Beadles in Dec 12th Phoenix #140; 1973 Kaye; 1975 Minch; 1976 Goldstein; 1979 Severn; 1979 Lamb; 1980 P. Warlock in New Pentagram; 1981 Abbott cat #22; 1984 Booth; 1987 Coleman; 1988 Waters; 1992 Atkins in LRi; 1994 Earle in MUM; 1997 Lee cat #11 as “psycho-kinesis”.
a. Said of effects or objects exhibiting the properties of psychokinesis. [rare]

n. Type of force where the magician limits the answer or choice that the volunteer is to give by the way the question is posed. When applied to playing cards they are called the break cards. [fairly common] The largest collection of psychological forces (140) is in Ted Belante’s What’s Your E.S.P. Quotient (1982). See also Banachek, Psychological Subtleties (1999). Specific examples are: "When a woman thinks of a card it is usually a red one. A big percentage there." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Nov 1947), 370 "If you ask an average lay audience to think of a number between one and ten, the name of a flower, and a color, nine times out of ten the answers will be seven, rose, and red." — Bruce Elliott, Magic as a Hobby (1948), 199-200 "Most people call 'heads' 7 out of 10 times when a coin is flipped." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Nov 1948), 481 "... if four articles are placed in a row and someone asked to chose one, they will (unless left- handed) almost invariably chose the one second from their right." — Eric C. Lewis, A Choice of Miracles (1980), 66 "... spectators never choose the end objects in a line, or the first or last numbers in a sequence." — Arthur Carter in Magigram (Apr 1988), 518 "... if three similar objects are placed in a line and a spectator is asked to choose one of them at random, 90% of the time they will choose the centre one." — Arthur Chase in Magigram (Jun 1988), 668 "When asked to think of a number from one to fifty with two different digits, mosy people will name thirty-seven. Given a choice of numbers from one to a hundred with two different digits, both even, eighty-six is most often named." — Stephen Minch, Eddie Fields' Secret Diary (1992), 16 When it works, this is a powerful method because it seems so fair. When it fails, the magician— if he had properly rigged the trick—can then fall back on a conjurer's choice or some other anticipated out.
n. A stock reading (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare, used only by mentalists]

n. A forcing deck that combines the principles of the Peek Deck and the Svengali Deck, thereby permitting it to be fairly shuffled by the spectator before the force. [rare] The invention is reportedly claimed by American mentalist Robert Nelson. REF: Busby, 17 Aug 1988 interview.
a. With the quality of psychometry. [rare]

n. The mentalist-magicians effect of simulating an abiliity to sense information from an object. [common, particularly among mentalists] "Few people have any conception of the theory of psychometry, and one has to do quite a bit of explaining before the mystery starts." — Will Dexter in Mantra (Feb 1976), 44 The word was coined in 1842 by Dr. Joseph Rodes Buchanan, American neurologist and credulous investigator of psychic phenomena. It was adopted by spiritualists by 1901 (Sylvestre cat; 1935 Magnuson) and is widely used today by parapsychologists. NOTE: Earliest citation (credited to Buchanan) in the OED/2 is only 1854. Thence magicians jargon by 1901 Sylvestre cat; 1903 Von Bourg ad in Magic; 1935 Annemann in Jinx; 1943 Larsen; 1947 Boardé; 1949 Chislett; 1950 Christopher in HMM; 1959 Corinda; 1969 Nelms; 1975 Gibson; 1976 Goldstein; 1979 Shaxon; 1980 Raven; 1981 Waters; 1983 Cassidy; 1984 Saville & Dewey; 1987 Coleman; 1987 Webster; 1989 R. Hunter in Q; 1991 McComb in Genii; 1992 Randi; 1996 Becker ad in LR; 2005 Binarelli in LR as “Polaroid Psychometry”. a. [adjectivally]

n. A bar magician (U.S.). [very rare, possibly nonce] Very rare in both word and fact because in Britain and Ireland no pubs to my knowledge regularly employ magicians (as do a few bars in America), and only a few British street conjurers divert enough of their performance time to pubs to earn this title. 742

n. A publicity stunt (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare] "Publicity effects are not very necessary to an amateur who works only for his friends, but they are part of the professional's bread and butter." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 290

n. Tricks used by professional magicians to get free publicity by impressing credulous journalists; a bally; a publicity effect; a publicity trick (obsolete). [fairly common] Such tricks are ones worked seemingly impromptu. Examples include the Blindfold Drive, Bullet Catching, the Prediction Chest, and most challenges.
n. A publicity stunt being the most usual synonym. [obsolete after 1950]
n. The Cake in Hat (see) being the more usual synonym. [obsolescent] 743

n. A concealed gimmick to vanish a small object up the magician's sleeve or under his jacket. Opposite of a holdout (1), which produces such an object. [very common] "Happiness is a pull that never sticks!" — Sam Dalal in Swami (Mar 1974), 106 Described as early as 1857 as an "India rubber cord" attached to a coin at one end and inside the sleeve at the other. The most famous one was the Buatier pull invented in 1875 by Joseph Buatier (de Kolta) to operate his celebrated Vanishing Birdcage illusion. The De Kolta Pull was a simple thread activated by movement of the arm. Most later pulls reverted to elastic cord. Mechanically operated pulls are called reels. REF: Magician's Own Book (1857), 26; Hoffmann (1890), 196.
n. A sleight where the little finger pulls down the lower corner of a packet to enable the above cards to be taken off as an apparent single card. [rare]

term: pull out shuffle; Pull Out Shuffle
definition: n. The false shuffle where the two packets are interleaved at a sufficient diagonal to permit the original top one to be stripped out intact and replaced back on top. Compare push through shuffle. [rare] This move was first described for card sharping in 1902 by Erdnase (p.39) but with no claim to its invention. It was also being used in Chicago by "Pop" ("The Mysterious Kid") Stevens by 1919 when he taught it to Dai Vernon.
n. The push through shuffle (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare]

n. Effect where the magician slows or stops his pulse at will. [rare] 744 "[T]he simplest things, like X-Ray Eyes, and Pulse Stopping carry ten times the impact of the elaborate Vanishing Cabinets, and chrome and Plastic props that look tricky to start with!" — Sam Dalal in Swami (Dec 1972), 47 The method is a hard pad or ball secretly placed in an arm-pit, which by blocking the pressure- point there controls the flow of blood into and from that arm. A pet effect of Indian street magicians. Described as early as 1918 in The Magical Record and then by Goldston in his Tricks of the Masters (1942). REF: Ayling (1981), 39, 305.

v. To fish for information by indirect questions; pumping; fishing. [rare] Standard English since the 1600s (OED/2). Then also the argot of psychic readers by 1907 D. Abbott; 1922 Dr. X. Thence magicians jargon by 1933 Annemann as "pump for a few leads"; 1973 Kaye; 1980 Lewis #1 as "by 'pump and guess'"; 1986 Miesel; 1988 Carlisle in Magigram. n. The act of pumping for information. [very rare, possibly nonce]

n. The sleight in sleeving a coin that squirts it into the open sleeve by squeezing it between the thumb and forefinger; the Squeeze Vanish. [rare] "The action is the same as shooting a wet pumpkin seed from the fingers by squeezing it, hence the name." — Ross Bertram in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1952), 900

n. Playing cards (usually the high values) marked on the back or face by one or more tiny indentations to give a slight bump on the other side that can be felt by the dealer; pricked card(s) (obsolete). Any sharp-pointed instrument could put in the "work". [rare] Originally created as an artifice of card cheaters by 1552 (Walker) when it was called "the prick". In 1577 Northbrooke referred to the "pricking of a carde". In 1865 Gerritt M. Evans was using a sharpened fingernail to put in the work. Still used by sharpers as recently as 1961 (Scarne). Introduced to magic by 1877 (Hoffmann, 201). A pet technique of Ray Grismer, Jack McMillen, and Richard Turner. Card sharps originally called this "the prick" (1552 Walker). Later they called this to "hump" (by 1930 McGuire; 1962 Garcia); to "peg" (by 1930 McGuire; 1962 Garcia), "pegging", "pegged card" (by 1930 McGuire), to "blister" (by 1962 Garcia), and "a blister" or "a peg" (by 1983 Ortiz). Also "a punch" (by 1930 McGuire) and "to punch" (by 1962 Garcia). Thence, as "the punch", introduced to magicians jargon in 1930 by McGuire. Then 1949 Miller letter to Woodfield; 1988

n. A doll-like figure. Used by some magicians as an assistant in their magic act. Main types are the hand puppet (including the glove puppet), marionette (including the Living Marionette), and Punch and Judy. [rare] Public puppet shows were first reported in China in a document of the Han Dynasty (202 BC-AD 220). Then in the 1600s in Italy (as Polcinella), Paris in 1643 by the brothers "Brioche" (Pierre & François Dattelin), and London in 1662 (as Punchinello). Powell was the most famous English puppeteer in 1710. Since 1864 magician Robert Heller included both marionettes (Heller's Wood Minstrels) and Punch & Judy puppeteers as interludes in many of his shows. One of the few magicians who was also himself a puppeteer was Arnold Crowther in the 1920s- 30s. REF: Chung-wen SHIH, The Golden Age of Chinese Drama (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1978), 9-10; George Speaight, The History of the English Puppet Theatre (1955); Clarke in Magic Wand (1924), 141; Marshall Wynnychuk, Puppetry for Magicians (1962, 32pp). The word entered Standard English by 1538 through the Middle French poupette meaning little doll. Thence magicians jargon by 1900 Triplett, 16, as “Animated Puppets”; 1934 Goldston; 1958 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1976 Gill; 1980 J. Marshall; 2001 Diamond's Magic flyer as a "white bunny puppet". a. [adjectivally] [rare]
n. The allied art of magic where hand-puppets are manipulated from back-stage. A principal form 747 is Punch and Judy. [rare]
n. Special sleight to work the Purse Game. [very rare]
n. The false count that deals off the deck two or more cards as one. [rare]

n. The false shuffle where the two packets are interleaved at a sufficient diagonal to permit the entire original top packet to be pushed completely through the other and replaced on top again; the pull through shuffle. Compare pull out shuffle. [rare] "For all practical purposes the push through shuffle is infinitely superior to the pull out—it is sure and cannot miss." — Dai Vernon, Revelations (1984), 208 This move was first described for card sharping in 1861 by Robert-Houdin. Next exposed in 1865 by Gerritt M. Evans (p.37) as a then standard false shuffle called the "intricate shuffle". And then in 1902 by Erdnase (p.39). Used to profitable perfection in 1919 by "Pop" ("The Mysterious Kid") Stevens in Chicago. REF: Busby in Whaley (1991), 182. Thence among magicians it was mastered in the 1920s by Dai Vernon (who learned it from gambler Pop Stevens) and Jack Merlin; and in the 1930s by Dr. Jacob Daley and Leslie Brown (in Britain).

v. To stack a portion of a deck of cards during a false shuffle; to run up. [obsolete, formerly very rare] Originally card sharps argot by 1865 Evans, 20, as American argot; 1876 Cremer, 90, as British argot; 1891 Quinn as American argot; 1894 Maskelyne as American argot "to put up" cards. Thence magicians jargon by 1909 Hilliard as to "put up cards".

v. Stacking a portion of a deck during a false shuffle; running up; to put up (obsolete). [obsolete, formerly very rare] Originally card sharps argot by 1876 Cremer, 86, as "putting up cards"; 1894 Maskelyne as "'putting up' hands for the dupe". 749 Thence magicians jargon by 1909 Hilliard as "'putting up' cards".

n. Any ungaffed device or verbal problem designed to test ingenuity. [fairly common] "A puzzle is a problem in which the answer must be given to make it effective. A trick is any puzzle or diversion which is still effective even though the answer or secret is never revealed." — Walter B. Gibson, quoted in The Jinx #71 (1939), 484 “The difference between a trick and a puzzle, by common acceptance is that after a trick is performed the audience doesn’t know how it was accomplished, but once a puzzle is done the audience is aware of the method and can repeat it.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (May 1954), 137 "The essence of a puzzle's fascination is that its solution involves the process of bringing order out of chaos, and thus gives the solver the `ego-kick' that comes with a realization of his mental powers and abilities, and his joy in the act of re-creation." — Gerald L. Kaufman, The Book of Modern Puzzles (2nd ed, 1954) "Most optical illusions fail to hold our attention for long because the secret of their trickery is generally transparent. But the remarkable constructions known as `geometrical vanishes' are so confounding that they continue to delight, amaze, and cause people to question their own sense of sight after the mechanics of the puzzles have been explained." — Mel Stover in Games #20 (Nov/Dec 1980), 14 "Magic is entertaining, unsolved puzzles are annoying." — Bill Okal, A New Look at Some Classic Close-Up (1988), 17 "Dr. Dr. [sic] Lyons will discuss wire puzzles and magic squares only with Dr. Gardner." — Clayton Rawson, "The Witchdoctors Club By-Laws" (1961) Some puzzles are magic-oriented in that they either have a secret solution (like the Key and Ring or Pencil and Loop) or produce weird and almost inexplicable results (like geometrical vanishes). Other puzzles that can be given a magical presentation include the tumble ring. The world's leading puzzle collector is Jerry Slocum, an American who as of 1996 had over 20,000 puzzles and had supplied the material for several books on the subject. Magician-writer Martin Gardner has been the leading authority on mathematical puzzles. REF: Jeff Busby in Thaumaturgist, No.33 (Feb 1997), 7; Jerry Slocum & Jack Botermans, Puzzles Old & New: How to Make and Solve Them (Seattle: U of Washington Press, 1986); Donald Michie, "Puzzle-learning versus Game-learning in Studies of Behaviour," in I. J. Good (editor), The Scientist Speculates (London: Heinemann, 1962), 90-100.
a. Adjectivally as abbreviation of the Question and Answer trick. [rare]
n. Esoteric remark shared by the tight inner circle of American magicians around Charlie Miller and Dai Vernon. (I am not yet free to define this term further.) [very rare, oral only]
See: Lippincott Coin Box. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Lippincott Coin Box".)
n. Advertising title used by or applied to some early top-billing magiciennes; female counterpart of the male King. [obsolete, formerly fairly common]

n. The mentalism, specifically telepathic, effect where spectators write questions on papers that are put away (in a receptacle in plain view or in the mentalist's pocket), yet the medium gives relevant answers. [rare] Originally a technique of psychic readers. Invented and first performed in New Orleans in the early 1870s by Samri S. Baldwin by cleverly adapting the ancient fortune-tellers' scam to a modern theatrical format. Baldwin called his two-person question-and-answer act "Somnomancy." This type of act was quickly copied (or further adapted) by numerous other psychics including Anna Eva Fay. It soon led to development of the Living and Dead Test. While several different methods are used by performers of the question-and-answer act, this is the trick to which some psychics adapted the magicians' thumb tip to work the billet switch. REF: Price (1985), 448-451; Boardé (1947), 79; Hay (1950), 281. Magicians jargon by 1928 Thayer cat #7 as "Questions and Answers"; 1947 Boardé; 1950 Hay; 1959 Corinda.

n. An act involving quick changes; a protean act (obsolete). [rare] "The quick-change act, whether given by itself or as an adjunct to a magical performance, is always a good card with the public when well played." — Will Goldston, Exclusive Magical Secrets (1912), 371
n. The Living and Dead Test (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare]

n. The famous effect where a bunny is produced from an empty hat. [common] "The production of ... rabbits from a hat is always very startling." — Edwin Sachs, Sleight of Hand [1877], 183 "Here it is — magic's most famous and best-loved trick! Magicians know many methods for producing a rabbit from a hat." — Will Dexter, 101 Magic Secrets (1957) "The production of a rabbit from a top hat is sometimes used to symbolize magic, although it is not an old trick, a good one, or one frequently performed." — Geoffrey Lamb, Illustrated Magic Dictionary (1979), 120 “That's the first time you ever saw a rabbit take a magician out of a hat.” — Orson Welles in movie Follow the Boys (1944) This trick was performed (perhaps for the first time) by French conjuror Louis Comte in 1814 but did not enter the standard magical repertoire until the late 1830s. Previously, pigeons had been the preferred animal-from-hat. Anderson was performing it in Britain by 1838 with various "beasts". A Barnardo Eagle poster of 1841 shows him pulling rabbits and birds from a hat. First exposed in 1836 by A.B. Engstrom. Marketed as early as 1843 by Crambrook catalog (p.15) in London. Also exposed in print in 1876 by Hoffmann and again in 1886 by Garenne. An ever- popular trick but now rarely performed because few magicians bother to carry a live rabbit even if they have the necessary audacity to do this trick. REF: Edwin Dawes article in Magic Circular (Apr & May 1987).
n. A trap-table with an oval spring-hinged double-flap opening to vanish a bunny or bird; a Dove Trap (archaic). [archaic after 1924, formerly rare]
n. A changing tray to vanish a bunny (and usually exchange it for something else, such as candy). [rare]
n. Comedy apparatus that rolls out a flattened bunny. [fairly common]

n. A concealed radio receiver used by a magician to overhear signals from an assistant during a mind-reading act. This device was introduced to magic in 1913 by David Devant in his the Yogi's Star mind- reading trick. Selbit used it in 1919 at a faked séance that fooled Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. Professional card cheats apparently did not get around to adopting the Radio Cue Prompter until 1949 when one card mob was detected using it by magician John Scarne. REF: Christopher (1973), 264-265. This term was coined as card sharps argot by 1961 K.C. Card Co. Blue Book.

term: Rag, a Bone, and a Hank of Hair, A
definition: n. The Vampire Illusion (see) being the most usual modern synonym. [obsolescent]

n. Paintings made by attaching bits of colored cloth to an easel. A once popular allied art of magic. [formerly fairly common, now rare] A popular art by the end of the 1900s. No less than Nate Leipzig began his celebrated stage career around 1902 performing rag pictures under the stagename of "Nate Berol". Also a pet effect of the Duval Brothers (by 1924), Caro Miller (1930s-40s), Dante (in 1941), Willard Smith (1950s), Edgar Benyon (until 1968), and Amy Dawes (since 1967). Much less popular today.
n. The first trick pack of playing-cards designed specifically for card fanning. Different patterns appear each time the deck is fanned. [rare]

n. The principle based on the fact that under certain circumstances two or more spectators can be led to perceive the same effect in different ways. [rare] One example is that when two spectators are each shown two playing cards (a force card and an indifferent card), each assumes the indifferent card is the one selected by the other spectator. Another is the Smith Myth.

n. A set of three small metal bars, one containing a metal slug that rattles to-and-fro when shaken; Demon Bars (obsolete). [fairly common] "It's quite usual to see an inexperienced performer show, say, the Three Card Trick, the Rattle Bars, and the Walnut Shell Trick, one after the other. Because the methods of working are different, he regards each as a different trick—but not so the spectator." — Will Dexter, Famous Magic Secrets [1956], 21 Probably invented (and certainly first manufactured and marketed) by Carl Brema as "The Demon's Bars" in 1925 in The Sphinx & "The Devil Bars" in The Osirian. I find no supporting evidence for Mussey & Oursler's speculation (in 1931) that the rattle bars were invented by con artists as a variation on the shell game. A pet effect of "One-Arm" McDonald around 1930. A later variant is the Wandering Lipsticks.

n. A shallow wooden box with sliding lid and false bottom, which permits the magician to steal a small object (such as a marked coin or ring). [common] First described in 1854 by Ponsin (II, 26). Modern variants include the Rattle Bars in 1925 (Carl Brema) and the "Rattle Ball" by 1963 (Tannen cat #4; 1987 Supreme cat; 1995 Tannen cat #18). Impromptu versions use three matchboxes and a coin (or marble) or three pill-boxes and a pill.
n. The later, more visible version of the Needle Trick that uses double-edged safety-razor blades. [fairly common]

n. A folding or telescoping stick used by pseudo-psychics to secretly touch or control distant objects in the dark. [rare] Lengthens from a short and easily concealed 4-to-17 inches up to 3-to-11 feet. Invented by spiritualists and commonly used by them.

1.v. To visually identify the secret symbols on marked cards, which are, therefore, also called readers. [fairly common] "When you have the 'key' you can read this deck from the back at a distance of fifteen feet." — Max Holden, Catalog #8 (1941), 30 Originally the argot of card sharps by 1865 (Evans, 41, as "The player, as he deals the cards, will of course read and remember his adversary's hand...."; 1902 Erdnase, 16, as "Each card is marked at both ends, so as to be read in any position."; 1904 Bonville; 1977 Sharper in Prus, as "You seldom have time to read paper at a stag."). After this term became too widely known among the suckers, some sharps introduced the argot-verb "kill" by 1933 (J.J. Cameron; 1938 Hilliard). Thence magicians jargon by 1903 Stanyon ad in Magic, 14, as "Any pack of cards read from their backs; for the first time in magic history."; 1924 Felsman cat #18 as “You can ‘read’ any card from the back”; 1928 Thayer cat #7 as "can be read at a distance of 15 feet"; 1938 Hilliard; 1939 Kanter cat as "easily read for both suit and value"; 1942 Goldston; 1947 Marlo; 1948 Manning in HMM; 1956 Dexter as "the magician can ‘read' their values without seeing their faces"; 1957 Maréchal; 1975 Dalal in Mantra as "the cards can be read from a great distance"; 1987 Busby in Short Sheet #13 as "you cannot ‘read' the cards without the gimmick". w. As noun.
n. Readers being the more usual synonym. [rare]

n. A complete deck of marked cards; a reader deck (U.S.); paper(3) (U.S.); a marked deck (U.S.); a marked pack (Brit.). [common] Originally "readers" was the argot of American card sharps and professional gamblers by 1890 (Quinn; 1894 Koschitz; 1902 Erdnase; 1911 Meyer; 1961 Scarne; 1973 Lampkin; 1981 R.M. Allen). Adopted as argot by British card sharps by 1894 (J.N. Maskelyne, which is the earliest citation in the OED/2). But the sharps on both sides of the Atlantic soon dropped that word when it became to widely known, although honest professional gamblers and catalog-men still call them that. Among American sharps the earlier and still preferred alternate term is "paper" by 1865 (Evans, 41; 1984 Ortiz). Thence magicians jargon by 1908 Stanyon ad in Magic, 94; 1909 P. Abbott ad in Magic Mirror; 1913 Oaks cat #20; 1931 Douglas cat #16; 1937 Hugard; 1942 as edge-readers; 1947 Abbott cat #9; 1949 Tannen cat #1; 1951 Baker; 1956 Dexter; 1958 as front readers; 1984 Warlock in LR as "a deck of long distance 'readers'"; 1988 Waters; 1988 Grismer; 1989 Tannen cat #16; 1998 Busby.

1.n. Simulation of a fortuneteller's act of perceiving a client's past, present, and/or future; a read (3.n.). [common, particularly among mentalists] Originally the argot of psychics by 1901 Sylvestre cat; 1907 D. Abbott; 1921 Alexander; 1935 Magnuson. Thence mentalist-magicians jargon by 1935 Annemann in Jinx #9 as "a single reading"; 1939 F. Ross Jan 25th letter to P. Fox; 1940 Mahendra; 1943 Larsen; 1947 Kanter cat #8; 1947 Boardé as "a reading"; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1948 Tarbell; 1952 Zolotow; 1956 Mellon in Mental-Wise; 1969 Nelms; 1974 Minch; 1976 Goldstein; 1977 Hyman in Zetetic as a “character reading”; 1980 Gibson; 1978 Becker as "the ‘reading' of the cards"; 1981 Waters; 1981 Ruthchild as a "psychic reading"; 1983 Cassidy as "audience reading"; 1984 Saville & Dewey; 1988 Busby annotation as a "canned reading"; 1997 Tannen flyer; 2000 Franchino in LR as “psychic readings”. v. To simulate the above; to read (3.v.). [very rare]

n. The nearly perfect simulation of a supernatural effect. [fairly common] "When the magic seems to happen with no sleight-of-hand or suspicious moves being apparent then that's 'Real Magic'." — Horace Bennett, Alternate Handlings (1983), 21 "In doing magic, you must make yourself believe that you are performing real magic in order to make it actually seem so." — Dunninger, Dunninger's Secrets (1974), 9 "Cardini was on the stage. I cannot tell you about any sequences, because it was real magic." — Rhadamanthus Jr in The Jinx (1941), 789 "In David [Roth]'s hands, it's pure 'Real Magic'." — Harry Lorayne in The Apocalypse (Mar 1981) "The popular magician Doug Henning, for example, is a true master of suspending disbelief. With Henning, tricks come alive and turn into real magic." — Ben Harris, Gellerism Revealed (1985), 12

n. A sleight that keeps a playing card toward the base of the palm below the fingers pinched between the base of the thumb and outer side of the hand. This leaves the fingers entirely free, unlike the deep palm (Gambler's Palm) where only the upper joints are free. Not to be confused with the back palm. [rare] "I consider this perhaps the greatest step forward in card work that I've ever made; and if it should be original with me, I've certainly got something worthwhile." — Fred Braue, notebooks, 10 Aug 1935 "This is truly the most perfect sleight that I have ever witnessed." — Charlie Miller, letter to Jean Hugard, undated [c.Jan 1939]
n. Effect where the performer interacts with a phonograph record, which provides all or part of the patter and may even supply a card prediction. [rare]

n. A shuffle that keeps blocks of red and black cards separated, such as the four Clubs, Hearts, Diamonds, and Spades. [rare] Probably invented by Laurie L. Ireland (using an overhand shuffle). In any case, first published anonymously in Seven Circles in Sep 1931 and then by Ireland in New Card and Coin Manipulation (1935). A classic example is Curry's "Out of this World" trick. Modern cardmen use a riffle shuffle. REF: Martin Gardner in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jun-Sep 1950).
n. The classic palm being the more usual (and more elegant) synonym. [obsolescent, formerly rare]

n. An oral technique to ditch or steal small objects. It is not true vomiting, as the object goes only as far as the middle or lower oesophagus and not down into the stomach. [rare] 765 Originally an artifice of carnival freak-show performers. Houdini claimed that, while working with the Welsh Brothers Circus in 1895, he learned the technique from an old member of the San Kitchy Akimoto Japanese jugglers' troupe by practicing with a small peeled potato on a string. Subsequently he used this technique to defeat body-searches for concealed gimmicks in his challenge handcuff act. Japanese magicians use it to vanish and produce ivory balls. And in the 1920s and early 30s American vaudeville was treated to the Arabian regurgititator, Hadji-Ali, who swallowed and brought up nuts as well as spray kerosine to stoke a fire followed by a stream of water to extinguish it. By the 1950s Sorcar was regurgitating a goat's tongue for his infamous tongue cutting routine. REF: Edwin A. Dawes, “Hard Acts to Swallow: Regurgitation as a form of entertainment through the ages”, Gullet, I (1991), 105-112.
v. A put-back move of a previously undisclosed playing card into its packet. [rare]
v. To make a second load after the first has been stolen and produced. [rare]

n. Effect where magus takes a playing card from a deck of one color, has it marked and is inserted into a differently colored deck, which is then turned face up. Spectator then choses any visible card, which turns out to the marked card, thereby demonstrating two minds working as one. [rare] Probably invented by American mentalist Ted Annemann.
n. Effect where the number of banknotes in a packet stays the same no matter how many or how often some are removed. [fairly common]
n. A reputation-maker (see) being the newer and somewhat more usual synonym. [fairly common]
v. To rearrange or re-prepare apparatus or a card setup secretly (on-stage or beforehand); to set again; resetting. [fairly common]

n. A house magician at a posh restaurant or club. [rare] Examples in the 1980s included Finn Jon at the Crazy Horse Saloon in Paris, Michael Skinner at the Golden Nugget in Las Vegas, Jimmy Grippo at Caesar's Palace, Ray Mertz at the Forks Hotel in Buffalo, Jef Eaton at the Zoo in Milwaukee, and, of course, Dai Vernon at the Magic Castle in Hollywood. Examples in the 1990s include Curtis Kam at Waikiki's Hale Koa Hotel in Hawaii, Michael Skinner still at Vegas' Golden Nugget, & Al James at Schulien's in Chicago.. 768
See: restaurant magic. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "restaurant magic".)
n. A restaurant magician being the more usual synonym. [rare]
n. The climax of a trick where a selected object (such as a playing card) is displayed by the magician. [fairly common]
1.n. Any sleight that turns a playing card or cards face up in a deck, making it a reversed card (1.n.). [rare] This sleight was described by 1877 (Sachs).
n. Card effect where the four aces scatter from one packet to four following an Ace Assembly. [rare]

n. A card fan made by rotating the deck counterclockwise from right to left. [rare] So fanned, the deck appears to be consist of all blanks (except for the face card). When a true blank card is the face card, it can be used in a Nudist Deck routine. Dunninger was evidently the first to use the Reverse Fan to expose but one card on the bottom of the deck, thereby using it as a mentalist's force. Also a pet method for forcing by Orson Welles. REF: Elliott in Phoenix #103 (5 Apr 1946), 414.

n. The in-the-hands unweaving procedure done by alternately upjogging and downjogging cards and then stripping out one projecting packet. [rare] First described in 1915 by S. Victor Innis as an open procedure used by card sharps to secretly prepare the deck. Miscredited to Ed Marlo by some magicians.
n. A deck of playing cards with a symmetrical back pattern. Opposite of a one-way deck. [very rare but not nonce]
n. A mechanical deck that allows you to show any card named to be reversed in its deck. [archaic]
n. An E.S.P. Deck (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare]

n. Patter spoken in rhyme. [rare] As seen from the following examples, rhymed patter was in use in England by 1634. English magician Oswald Williams was famous for performing his tricks to limericks in the early 1900s. 773 A pet style of J. Warren Keane (1930s), Dell O'Dell (1930s-50s), and Johnny Thompson (1980s). "Any member who uses rhymed patter will be tarred, feathered, ridden out of town on a rail and presented with a Bon Voyage gift consisting of Dell O'Dell. — Clayton Rawson, "The Witchdoctors Club By-Laws" (1961) "Thus by activitie have I learn'd to do, out of one little ball for to make two." — Hocus Pocus Junior, The Anatomie of Legerdemain (1634), [13] "The first Trick that e'er I learn'd to do, Was, out of one Ball to make them into two: Ah! Since it cannot better be, Out of these two, I'll divide them into three, Which is call'd the first Trick of Dexterity." — Henry Dean, The Whole Art of Legerdemain (London: 6th ed, 1763), 9
n. Walking through a Ribbon (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare]

n. Effect where one bowl is filled with rice, then covered by a second bowl, which when raised shows twice as much rice. The effect ends when the rice turns to water; the Chinese Rice Bowls. [common] This trick is Indian in origin, although often called The Chinese Rice Bowls and explicitly credited to China by Goldston (1942, p.12), probably because it was a pet effect of "Chung Ling Soo" (William E. Robinson). That original version used one unfaked bowl and one faked in 774 Lota Bowl fashion.

n. Effect where a stack of large wooden checkers are covered by a tube, an orange is covered by a matching tube, rice is poured into a vase, and all three change places. [fairly common] A popular stage trick since the early 1900s. A pet effect of James Hamilton and Peter Reveen (1980s).

1.n. The card manipulation that thumbs back a corner or end of a deck and then releases it so that the cards spring forward quickly, one after another; a ruffle (obsolete). [fairly common] Originally the cant of American card players by 1894 (J.N. Maskelyne, 137, which is also the earliest citation in the OED/2). Thence magicians jargon by 1902 Neil, 87, as "make a riffle"; 1909 Hilliard as "the riffle"; 1912 Goldston; 1923 Elliott; 1946 Buckley; 1948 Norman; 1949 Lamb; 1950 Hay, 43, as "the ‘step' riffle"; 1959 Katz in HMM; 1960 Ganson/Vernon;

n. The forcing of a card by riffling the deck before the spectator's eyes and delaying momentarily at the force card. Compare Ultima Thule, which is a fan force. [fairly common] The momentary hesitation may be achieved either dextrously by a simple break in the even tempo of the riffle or automatically by use of a short card. Jack Merlin called this force "very old" when he wrote in 1927-28. He was right, it having been first described in 1853 by Ponsin and subsequently in 1902 by Erdnase (p.166). A later variation by fanning is the Ultima Thule force.

n. A shift done under cover of riffling the deck. [rare] Jean Hugard learned this sleight in the 1910s. First published in the mid-1940s in France. A specialty of Derek Dingle and Ken Krenzel. REF: Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1947), 302.
n. The standard playing-card shuffle that springs (riffles) the ends or sides of the two separated packets of a deck into each other; the riffle (2). [very common]
a. Said of a sidejog where the card protrudes from the right-hand side of the deck. [very rare, possibly nonce]

v. To switch; ringing (obsolete). [rare] Originally (by 1753) as a verb "to ring" in the argot of British gambling sharps who took it from the popular expression "ringing the changes," which originally referred to bell-ringing. American card sharpers also used to "ring in" by 1857 Green who spelled it "wring"; 1865 Evans as "to ring in"; 1873 Morris as "rung in"; 1876 Cremer; 1891 Quinn; 1894 Koschitz; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne as "ring in"; 1961 Scarne as "ring in". REF: See also RHHDAS and OED/1. Thence magicians jargon by 1876 Hoffmann, 157; 1897 Stanyon; 1909 Hilliard; 1944 Gibson in Phoenix #63 as to "ring in"; 1950 Hay as "can be wrung in"; 1950 Rawson in HMM as “the half deck which you have just rang in”; 1975 Pierre as "rung in"; 1977 Kaye as "ring in a substitute, unprepared deck"; 1985 Willmarth in LR as to "ring in"; 1987 Johnsson in LR; 1988 Waters as to "ring in" and "ring out"; 1998 Gloye in LR as “ring in”. n. A switch or substitution [obsolete after 1909]
See: Grind-A-Ring. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Grind-A-Ring".)

n. Effect where a borrowed finger ring vanishes from the magicians hand to reappears on one of the loops of a key case. [rare] “... perhaps the strongest trick you can do with a finger ring is the often troublesome Ring Flight, a finicky little gimmick that can turn on you when you least expect it. Horror stories abound 778 wherein priceless little trinkets are sent careening about in darkened restaurants, losing gems and gaining scratches.” — David Acer in The Linking Ring (Apr 1998), 108
n. Effect where a ring is vanished and reappears strung on the center of a rope. Compare Ring on Stick. [rare] A pet effect of Charlie Miller and Jim Ryan.

n. Effect where a small metal ring penetrates a long stick or cane held at both ends by volunteers; the Ring on Wand. [fairly common] Versions of this classic trick were reported and exposed in 1693 by French writer Ozanam and in 1716 by British magical writer Neve. Consequently, its common attribution (Hay 1950) to Indian conjurors as the originators and introducers to Western magic is probably false. First reported in India by Branson (1922) who eyewitnessed it there using a bamboo stick. In either case the trick was popular among Western magi by 1876 (Hoffmann, 230; 1877 Sachs) and was featured by Charles Bertram at the end of the 1800s. Later a pet effect of Giovanni.

n. The Linking Rings being the formal and more usual synonym. [fairly common] “The greatest stage performance with the rings that I have ever seen was that done by Chung Ling Soo.” — Jean Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Mar 1948), 399

n. Classic effect where one or more playing cards mysteriously ascend from a vertical deck; the Card Rise; The Aerial Cards; The Obedient Cards (obsolete); The Ascending Cards (obsolete). [very common] "The Rising Cards, to me, is about the most impressive card trick in existence." — Will Dexter in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Sep 1954), 183 "My earliest recollection of magic is that of being hidden under our dining table, pulling the thread which worked the rising cards for my elder brother." — Jean Hugard, Houdini's "Unmasking": Fact vs. Fiction (1957), 21-22

n. Effect where a lead pencil lying flat in the magician's hand rises slowly to an upright position. [fairly common] "It shouldn't be necessary to explain the method of the `rising pencil', a masterpiece in the hands of any devoted artist." — Annemann in The Jinx #118 (1940), 695 This trick originated in the 1800s with round sticks or wands (with a pin stuck in the base). Subsequently replaced by square sticks (to minimize wobble), and finally by the modern hexagonal pencil. According to Ralph Read, the improved Royal Rising version (a detachable gimmick) was invented by Nate Leipzig who showed it to Henry Hardin who promptly marketed it without authorization in his 1907 catalog. Later a pet effect of Charlie Miller. REF: Annemann in Jinx (1940), 693, 695-696.

n. Effect where a rod (wand, pencil, or pen) held by the thumb and fingers vertically at the top slides slowly up to its base. [rare] This standard pocket trick was invented by Dr James W. Elliott (died 1920). Hence Waters' crediting the effect to Amac is wrong unless referring to the mere substitution of a pencil for a wand. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (Mar 1928), 35; Waters (1988), 7.
n. Piercing a Woman (see) being the original title of this Howard Thurston stage illusion. [rare]
See: magician’s rope Rope-A-Rama. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "magician’s rope Rope-A-Rama".)
n. Effect where four short pieces of rope visibly become one long rope when drawn thru the magicians hand. [obsolete, once fairly common]

n. Any fastener to secretly attach the ends of two ropes. [fairly common] Originally an artifice of escape artists to permit a quick release from rope bindings. Houdini's device of screw-threaded tapped-tube inserts to disconnect (and later, reconnect) rope ends by a half-turn during a spirit cabinet act was first exposed in 1912 by Will Goldston with Houdini's permission. REF: Goldston (1912), 285; Gibson (1930), 37. When around 1920 Dr. Harlan Tarbell substituted rope for string, thereby stimulating the Cut-and-Restored Rope routine craze, he borrowed the invention of the escapologists to provide the secret disconnection and reconnection. His modification of the old Cut-and- Restored String artifice of a wax or rubber cement join was required by the heavier ropes which could not be sufficiently strongly held together during the necessary naturalistic handling required. Initially, Tarbell used snap fasteners. Then, by 1930, engineer-magician Joseffy suggested the screw fastener, which Tarbell proceeded to design and adopt, calling it (since 1930) the Caesar Gimmick, presumably because of the pun on "seize" suggested by Tarbell's manufacturer, Frank Caesar, a Chicago dealer. Both the screw and snap types are also called the Tarbell Gimmick in mistaken honor of their non-inventor. In 1943 or 1944 Mystic Craig invented the magnetic fastener. REF: Hilliard (1938), 786-787; B. Elliott in Phoenix #1945, 351.

n. Any technique for tying up a performer with long cord in such a way as to give him easy release. Specific examples include the Davenport Tie, Jacoby Rope Tie, and Kellar Rope Tie. [fairly common] While a thumb-tie had been used as early as 1785 by Italian magician Pinetti, a true long-rope body-tie did not come until later. The first version was perhaps that developed by the Davenport Brothers while still young boys, taking it to the professional stage in 1855 as part of their spectacular spiritualistic act. This success quickly spawned numerous copy acts, both as pseudo-spirtualism and as exposés. For example, in 1865 J.N. Maskelyne and G.A. Cooke, having accidentally glimpsed the Davenports untied in their cabinet, evolved their own rope release. The elder of the Nemo Brothers (who performed in England) later claimed he had been taught their rope tie long before by Ramo Samee. In 1871 Osbonaki of Satsuma's Royal Japanese Troupe was billed in Boston as the "Davenport Brothers Rope Tying Exposer", having volunteers tie him with a 60-foot rope. Harry Kellar, while employed as an assistant to the Davenports around 1872, worked out his own rope tie. German magus Jacoby-Harms developed his by 1885. REF: Christopher (1975), 9-10; Clarke in Magic Wand (Mar 1927), 44, 47. Originally (?) the argot of spirit mediums by 1901 Sylvestre cat.
(See also: Flower in Buttonhole.) n. Effect where a flower instantly appears in the bottonhole of the magician's jacket. [rare]

term: Ross Bertram cups; Ross Bertram Cups
definition: n. A specially designed set of three metal tumblers for the Cups-and-Balls trick. [rare]

n. A prepared card whose face is treated with a sticky substance (roughing fluid, etc.) to make it adhere to the back of the next card. Opposite of slick card. [rare] Earliest recorded use of this technique was by the mid-19th Century Viennese magician Hofzinser (who used solid diachylon), but did not become more widely used until Hoffmann published the secret in 1918.
a. Adjectivally as Rough and Smooth Deck, rough-and-smooth principle, etc; abbreviated as R&S. [fairly common]
v. Making a rough card. Opposite of slicking. [rare]

n. A chemical solution that when applied to playing cards causes them to adhere to one another, thereby showing two cards as one. [common] "You thought it was roughing fluid—and it turned out to be lacquer!!!" — Sam Dalal in Swami (Feb 1974), 101 Basis of the Brain Wave Deck and certain other so-called mechanical decks. The original formula involved diachylon (lead plaster) dissolved in carbon tetrachloride. Later, Canada Balsam was substituted; and, today, wood resin or gum arabic in either carbon tetrachloride or ether.

n. Nickname of the informal gathering of Chicago-area magicians at a succession of local restaurants. The regulars over the years have included Earl Adcock, Bert Allerton, Russell Barnhart, Joe Berg, Sam Berland, Arthur Buckley, Dorny, Jack Kodell, Ed Marlo, Jim Ryan, Chick Schoke, Matt Schulien, and Russ Walsh. [rare] Founded in 1929. Originally at the Nanking Restaurant, it moved to De Lazon's, and finally to Kofield's. REF: Berg (1983), 17, 32; Boston & Parrish (1946); Charvet (1986), 126-126; Gordon (1980), 51.

n. A catch-phrase, bit of business, or trick that becomes comical by repetition throughout an act; a continuity gag (Brit.); a repeater (2). [fairly common] The lota is a favorite device for this purpose, the magician returning to it again and again to produce water between other tricks. The Six-Card Repeat is also used. And, in the 1980s, Steve Spill uses a dummy goose and David Copperfield used real ducks for such business. Famous repeated tag-lines or catch phrases, some also used for misdirection, include Al Flosso’s “From the mystic isle of Malagoola.” REF: Braue in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jan 1949), 501, gives other examples.

See: salt trick salt trick; Salt Trick, The w. Effect where common table salt transposes between the magician’s hands; the Salt Pour. Compare the salt vanish. [fairly common]. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "salt trick salt trick; Salt Trick, The w. Effect where common table salt transposes between the magician’s hands; the Salt Pour. Compare the salt vanish. [fairly common]".)

n. Potassium nitrate in its dry crystalline form, which is easily ignited by a spark. [very rare] Used in magic, possibly for the first time, in Joe Berg’s ‘Ever-Ready’ Lit Cigarette Production. REF: Avadon in Berg (1983), 116.

n. Acronym of the Society of American Magicians. Properly pronounced by its letters “Ess-Ay-Em”, never as “Sam”. [fairly common] Founded in 1902 by Dr W. Golden Mortimer and Dr Saram R. Ellison in the famous backroom of Francis J. Martinka’s magic shop. REF: H.R. Evans in Magic (Oct 1903), 9; Severn (1979), 228-229; Hanson & Zweers (1974), 65.
a. A playing card specially printed with identical “faces” front and back; acronymed as SBS. [rare] A single SBS card was included in the Fa-Ko deck. REF: Jones (1973), 4-5.
n. The illusion where an assistant is completely confined in a box that is then sawn through at its midpoint. Compare Sawing a Woman in Half. [rare]

n. The ever-popular stage illusion of apparently cutting through a human confined in a long box with head and feet protruding to make two seemingly separate halves; the Sawing. Compare Sawing Through a Woman. [fairly common] Inspired by Selbit's Sawing Through a Woman of 1920, which was a mere penetration effect, Horace Goldin invented this more spectacular variation where the assistant is shown separated after being sawn through. Goldin premiered his invention on 3 Jun 1921 at the annual banquet of the Society of American Magicians at the McAlpine Hotel in New York City. For this performance only, a man was used. When Goldin publicly premiered this act next month at the Palace Theatre on Broadway, he wisely placed a woman, Miss Irene Vanderbilt, in this "perilous" role and billed it as "A Woman Sawn in Half". Goldin's version soon became a pet effect of innumerable magicians including Servais Le Roy, The Great Leon (1921 with his own one-lady/fake feet method), Jack Gwynne (1922), Raymond (from 1926), Thurston (by 1929), Dante, Orson Welles (1943), and Kent Cummins. Exposed by 1929 (Gibson) and in innumerable public newspapers and magazines. REF: Lewis & Warlock (1989), 138; Caveney (1987), 78-80; Christopher (1973), 266-268; D. Bamberg (1965/1988), 86-87; Charvet (1986), 14-16.
n. A mentalist working with a horoscope. 797 [very rare except among mentalist-magicians] Originally carnival cant by 1942. REF: Ruth Mulvey, "Pitchman's Cant," American Speech (Apr 1942).
n. Comedy prop in the form of an emaciated rubber (or sometimes cloth) chicken, usually used as a production item. [rare]

n. A mentalist-magician's simulation of a spirit-medium's "sitting". Pronounced SAY-ahns. [fairly common] If conducted in semi-darkness it is called a dark séance, if under bright illumination a light séance. Compare full-light séance. Originally (from the French word meaning a sitting) the argot of spirit mediums by 1845 Warburton as cited in the OED/2; 1860 H. Novra handbill; 1891 A. Medium; 1895 F. Baldwin in S. Baldwin; 1907 D. Abbott; 1922 Dr. X; 1976 Keene. Thence magicians jargon by 1886 Garenne as "during the séance"; 1900 B. Powell in Magic as "Dark and Light Séances"; 1932 Gibson; 1934/1977 D. Abbott; 1937 Musson; 1939 Kanter cat as "cabinet seances"; 1948 Hugard in HMM as "a spirit seance"; 1951 Scarne; 1960 Corinda; 1981 Waters; 1983 Cassidy; 1986 Burger; 1990 Wedler; 1990 Wassilak cartoon in MUM; 1997 Brother Shadow (Carl Herron). a. [adjectivally] [rare] 798

n. Effect in mentalism where performer reads messages in closed envelopes; the envelope test. [rare] "One of the standard tests in the field of 'mental magic' has long been the reading of messages placed in sealed envelopes." — George G. Kaplan, The Fine Art of Magic (1948), 211. Done by the one-ahead method, the first envelope to be read being either that of a stooge or made transparent with alcohol.

1.n. The act of second dealing. Almost always a plural, referring to its repeated use. [fairly common] “Walter [I. Scott] can deal seconds, tell you he’s doing it and yet no matter how closely you watch, you cannot detect him.” — Al Baker in Broadway Magic News (Jul 1932), 1 Originally card-sharps argot by 1822 Bailey (p.137) as "slip the [top] card, and take out a second"; 1865 Evans as "playing the 'second'" (p.32) and "deals a second" (p.42); 1894 J.N. Maskelyne; 1930 McGuire as "deal a perfect second"; 1931 Smith; 1933 Cameron as "dealing seconds"; 1944 MacDougall; 1951 OED/2 as "to deal seconds" as its earliest citation; 1977 Sharper in Prus as "dealing seconds"; 1982 Hayano. Thence magicians jargon by 1898 J.W. Elliott in Mar Mahatma; 1902 Neil as "Dealing Seconds"; 1909 Hilliard as "deal seconds"; 1927 Merlin as "deal a few seconds"; 1930 Holden in Jul Sphinx as "seeing Scott do seconds"; 1933 Goldston as "dealing seconds"; 1937 Hugard as "deal seconds"; 1946 Buckley as "dealing seconds"; 1949 Boyar; 1949 LePaul as "dealing seconds"; 1969 A. Sharpe as "dealing seconds"; 1975 Barnhart as "dealing seconds"; 1983 Hayden as "deal four ‘real' seconds if you want to"; 1988 Grismer as "dealing seconds"; 1991 Busby in Whaley as "deal a Second"; 1991 Ortiz as "dealing seconds"; 1997 A-1 flyer as "Dealing Seconds". 2.n. The second deal being the usual synonym. Usually as singular. [rare] "Most seconds can be detected by the difference in noise." — Charlie Miller, letter to Faucett Ross, 14 Nov 1931 “I’ll meet you at the dueling grounds with Milton Chase card swords or nothing. As for seconds, I chose Charlie Miller’s.” — Bill Larsen’s reply to Joglar’s challenge in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Apr 1951), 778 Originally (?) the argot of American card sharps by 1977 (Sharper in Prus, as "If the people are sharp, the first thing you eliminate are seconds and bottoms, because the mechanic's grip will give you away.") Thence (?) magicians jargon by 1931 Miller, letter to Ross; 1932 Baker in Broadway Magic News as “100% at seconds”’ 1960 Marlo; 1969 Racherbaumer in Hierophant #1 noting its vogue-word use among the Chicago inner-circle cardmen; 1981 P. Harris; 1984 M. Nash orally.

n. The false deal that deals the second card down from the top. [common] 799 "For many years I have considered the second deal to be one of the most useful sleights in card magic and yet one that is little used by conjurers, presumeably because of its reputation of being extremely difficult." — P.
