H. Lyons in Ibidem, No.34/35 (Aug 1969), 3 This sleight was invented by professional card sharps. First exposed in 1822 in the American Robert Bailey's autobiography (where he refers to its use in 1812 when he invented the Faro Box to thwart this practice by Faro dealers). Then in 1840 in Georg Grimm's Neuestes Spielbuch. Also mentioned by Crambrook (1843), Green (1850), Robert-Houdin (1858), Evans (1865), again Green (1868), and Sachs (1877). REF: Bailey (1822), 137-138, 161; Busby in Whaley (1991), 188; Ortiz (1991), 78-83. In 1882 Professor Hoffmann's first detailed instructions in English introduced this sleight into the repertory of magicians. Originally card sharps argot by 1882 Hoffmann; 1930 McGuire as "Scott's second-deal". Thence magicians jargon by 1898 J.W. Elliott in Mahatma; 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 127; 1929 Gibson; 1931 Annemann in Sphinx; 1937 Hugard; 1948 Fitzkee/Buckley; 1950 Hay; 1956 Dexter; 1960 Marlo; 1962 Braue in HMM; 1975 Barnhart; 1979 Lamb; 1981 Walton; 1988 Grismer; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1991 Munari; 1994 Racherbaumer in LR; 1997 A-1 flyer; 1998 L&L cat. NOTE also "envelope second deals" in 1942 (Gibson in Phoenix #17) as an old technique for switching envelopes. v. To second deal; second dealing; to deal seconds (1). [fairly common] As verb, originally (?) the argot of card sharps by 1944 MacDougall. Thence (?) magicians jargon by 1909 Hilliard; 1920 Stanyon in Magic as "second deal the cards"; 1939 Art Lyle in Jinx; 1943 Hugard in HMM; 1946 Zovello in HMM; 1949 Elliott in Phoenix #168; 1950 Fabian in Abra; 1955 Ganson in Endfield; 1956 Dexter; 1962 Braue in HMM; 1975 Warlock in Mantra; 1975 Barnhart; 1980 Anderson; 1982 Busby in

n. The effect of seeing an object or knowing a fact without use of normal sensory perception; telepathy; extrasensory perception; ESP. Compare blindfold effects. [obsolescent, formerly common] "[S]econd sight is and always has been a matter of well-drilled phrases or signals, prearranged rotation of articles, well-built apparatus or well-trained confederates, but never a feat of actual thought-transferrence." — Houdini, The Unmasking of Robert-Houdin (1909), 208 Used by magicians in mind-reading acts. Psychics and late 19th Century magicians called it clairvoyance. Modern magi as well as pseudo-psychics also call it telepathy. As the method was reported in 1584 by Scot (a simple verbal code as was also being practiced by Breslaw in 1781) and the term was adapted by J.H. Anderson by 1838, Robert- Houdin's claims to have invented the effect and coined the term in 1846 are disproved. In any case, Robert-Houdin premiered his version (initially using a verbal code) on 12 Feb 1846 in Paris. Among the several later performers who worked exclusively second sight acts were Albany (since 1886), The Steens, the Lorenz Svengali Trio, The Zomahs, and The Trees. Originally Standard English since 1616 in its occult sense as cited in the OED/2; 1901 Sylvestre cat; 1921 Alexander. Thence first adopted as magicians jargon by 1838 by John Henry Anderson, Apr 30th Hull playbill as "The Magician will Display the Wonderful Power of SECOND SIGHT!" Thence 1848 C. Herrmann, Apr 20th London poster; 1848 Robert- Houdin, Aug 19th London poster; 1851 Heller program; 1855 Wyman; 1855 Kirbye; 1858 Kratky-Baschik, London program; 1861 Novra cat as "that pretended faculty called second sight"; 1875 Lynn, London playbill; 1877 Hoffmann; 1884 Hermon; 1886 Peck & Snyder cat; 1895 Burlingame #1; 1898 Houdini cat; 1901 Stanyon in Magic; 1924 Heaney cat #25; 1934 Read; 1939 H.A.Smith in Tops; 1943 Welles, Hollywood playbill; 1947 Buckley & Cook; 1955 Hugard in HMM; 1965 Curry as obsolete; 1977 Fulves as obsolete; 1979 Lamb; 1980 Tannen cat #13; 1985 Price as historical. Also in French magicians jargon as "seconde vue" in 1848 Robert-Houdin, May 24th London poster; 1849 Gandon;

term: second sight act; Second Sight Act
definition: n. A complete performance of second sight. [obsolescent after 1968, formerly rare]

n. The hidden means used to create an effect; the method being the more usual synonym. [common] "All the best tricks have simple secrets." — Will Goldston, Exclusive Magical Secrets (1912), 55 801 “No trick exchanged after the secret has once become known.” — Thayer Magic Mfg. Co., Catalogue, No.7 (1928) "The success of a trick does not depend on the cleverness of its secret. It depends on the cleverness of its performer." — Bill Turner, The Card Wizard (1949), 15 "The secrets of the mind, the REAL secrets of magic, cannot be exposed." — Dariel Fitzkee, Magic by Misdirection (1945), 35 "Magic's virtue is in its secrets — that makes it unique in the arts." — Karl Germain, quoted in Cramer (1966), 69 "It is only conjuring of the parlour-magic and trap-door illusion kind, that depends more on the secret than on ability, which palls when the novelty has gone." — S. H. Sharpe in Devant (1936), 13 "The sooner conjurers realise that locked books and secret codes will never prevent the secrets of tricks being found out and broadcast, the better." — S. H. Sharpe in Devant (1936), 21 "It has been my experience that more secrets have been revealed by the poor performance of amateurs, who squawk at exposures." — Fulton Oursler in The Linking Ring (Jan 1941), 830 "Magicians have a saying: 'If you want to keep a secret, publish it in a magical magazine.'" — Will Dexter, Famous Magic Secrets [1956], 114

n. Obscure information about physical facts that enables certain tricks to work with either sleights, prearrangement, or apparatus; arcana being the less usual but surely better suited synonym. [rare]

term: Seeing with the Fingertips; Seeing with the Finger Tips
definition: n. The version of eyeless vision where the fingers simulate the "seeing", a term that modern 802 parapsychologists call "dermo-optical perception" to make it sound scientific. [rare] REF: Martin Gardner, Science: Good, Bad and Bogus (1981).
n. The Girl without a Middle (see) being the British original and still more usual title for this stage illusion. [rare]
1.n. Originally a miniature spirit cabinet routine that includes the passing of a solid ring onto a cord within the cabinet. See also Astro Ball Cabinet. [fairly common]
(See also: chosen card.) n. The playing card selected from a deck by a volunteer; the selected card. [common]

a. Said of any trick whose apparatus includes all parts necessary for working the effect. [common] "Secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster." — Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol (1843), Stave One 803

n. Effect where the magician levitates himself without the aid of external apparatus. [rare] The classic version is the Balducci Levitation. Used for many years by David Roth. "Self-levitation has taken the magic world by storm. Ever since David Blaine levitated himself on national television, magicians the world around have discovered that their lives are not complete unless they can float!" — Hank Lee's Magic Factory ad in The Linking Ring (Aug 1997), 15
n. A semi-professional magician; a semi-professional. [rare]
See: Serpent Handkerchief. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Serpent Handkerchief".)

n. A shelf or open receptacle hidden behind the magician's table. Pronounced sur-VAHNT, although often mispronounced ser-VAN-tee by English-speaking magi. [common] Used for loads and steals. Special types include the bag servante, body servante, card servante, chair servante, necktie servante, shelf servant = table servante, and vest servante. According to Robert-Houdin (writing in 1868), famous French conjuror Comus (d.1807) invented the servante (by 1765 when he first played London) by simply attaching the then conventional gibecière to the back of his table, a practice soon widely adopted by other magicians. French magicians, taking the Standard French word servant that meant a side-table, introduced it as jargon by 1868 (Robert-Houdin). Thence the jargon of English-speaking magicians by 1859 Secret Out as "servant"; 1877 Hoffmann; 1882 Hamley cat; 1888 Maurer cat as "servant"; 1896 Roterberg; 1897 as a card servante; 1899 as a chair servante; 1900 Selbit ad in Magic as a "Belt Servante"; 1901 West ad in Magic as a "Belt Servant"; 1903 as a table servante; 1903 as a vest servante; 1903 as a bag servante; 1906 as a body servante; 1906 Stanyon ad in Magic as a "Cannon Ball Servante"; 1907 a shelf servante; 1910 Hatton & Plate; 1919 Stanyon in Magic as a "Ball Servante"; 1922 Houdini; 1927 Orrin; 1939 Kanter cat; 1950 Hay; 1953 Slydini; 1972 Griffin; 1977 Delvin; 1979 Lamb; 1980 Tannen cat #13; 1984 Bamman in LR prematurely as obsolete; 1986 Hades cat #2 as a "lap servante"; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1990 as a necktie servante; 1991 Wassilak cartoon in MUM; 1992 Avadon in Genii; 1994 Busby in Thauma; 1997 Abbott cat #25. v.t. To dispose of as by placing in a servante or by pocketing. [obsolete, formerly very rare]
n. A private meeting of two or more magicians to demonstrate tricks and moves to each other; a bull fight (obsolete). [common, particularly among card magicians] 806

n. Prearranged playing cards; a deck or packet of cards of which the entire set or only a section has been stacked in predetermined order of suits and/or values; a stacked deck; a prearranged deck/pack; a rosary. Compare system and cold deck. [common] This technique was first described as used in conjuring tricks by Guyot in 1770 (?); copied in 1774 by Hooper and by Ponsin in 1854. Card players in general call this a "stacked deck", magicians do so only rarely. Professional card sharps specifically call it a "cold deck" (by 1857) or "cooler" (by 1915). Writing in 1877 Hoffmann explicitly noted that English-speaking magicians had no jargon-word for it. Became common jargon by 1931 Mussey & Oursler, 115; 1931 Annemann, 11; 1940 Gardner; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1944 St. John in Cornish Pixie; 1944 Kaplan in HMM; 1950 Hay; 1957 Maréchal; 1973 Emerson in Swami; 1979 Lamb; 1980 Adair; 1984 Cervon; 1988 Waters; 1995 Riser in MUM as "any set-up will suffice"; 1997 Racherbaumer in LR. v. To make a setup but, as verb, always as two words, set up. [rare]

n. Effect where the magician unerringly locates the one key from among seven that will open a padlock. [fairly common] "Since it was first proposed by Kolar, and popularized by Ted Annemann, the Seven Keys to Baldpate effect has been an audience pleaser." — Jeff Busby in Short Sheet #10 (1986), 8 American magician-escapist J.J. Kolar invented the effect (and the initial method using a switch of a key). First published in 1931 by Theodore Annemann in his The Book Without a Name (pp 54-57). A pet effect of Robert Harbin. Inspired the different (no-switch) methods of John Snyder Jr's "Psy-Key Lock" (by 1936), Abbott’s “Master Lock Mystery” (by 1940, using magnetism), Stuart Judah’s “Keys of Judah” (1955), and Carl Wolf's Lock of Gibraltar (c1957) & Key-R-Rect (c1963). Hen Fetsch’s method (by 1959) switches the locks! REF: Abrams (1992), 116; Busby in Epoptica #6 (1984), 383.

1.n. A screen or diversion; cover; more generally, misdirection being the original and still more usual synonym. [new, still rare] "Its better to have too much shade than too little." — Frank Simon (1983), 16 Originally, as verb, the argot of American card sharps by 1943 (Maurer); thence as noun by 1961 (Woodfield as "what's the shade?"; 1977 Sharper in Prus as "use a sucker for shade"; 1977 Martin Gardner in Humanist; 1981 Vernon in Genii; 1984 Vernon; 1984 Ortiz). Also American pickpockets argot by 1955 (Maurer). Introduced to magicians jargon by Dai Vernon by 1965 (in Vernon-Buffum tape). Thence 1981 Busby cat as "uses a movement of the deck as ‘shade' for the secret action"; 1982 Lorayne; 1985 Jennings lecturing as "you've got all this shade to cover it"; 1985 David Grippenwald orally as "it's got plenty of shade"; 1988 Waters; 1990 Patton in Genii as
n. Marking cards by delicately filling-in selected white areas of the back pattern with a dilute solution of ink the same color as the backs. [very rare]
See: shadowgraphy. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "shadowgraphy".)

n. Illusion where a square cabinet with translucent paper panels is shown empty, a lightbulb lowered through the top, the front panel closed, gradually the silhouette of a human figure appears, and the assistant breaks out through the panel; the Shadow Cabinet. [fairly common]
n. A hand shadow (see). [rare] “Many magicians through the years have featured shadowgraphs as part of their entertainment.” — John J. Crimmins Jr in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Oct 1959), 56

1.n. Title of a priest of the Ural-Altaic peoples of Northern Eurasia who uses magic (both natural and supernatural). Pronounced SHAM-en, SHAY-men, and shah-MAHN. [very rare] From the Siberian Tungusic shaman, the word entering Standard English in 1698. REF: OED/2.

n. A magic word. [rare] Originally coined in Feb 1940 by, presumably, the cartoon writer, Bill Parker, as the magic word that enables young Billy Batson to become transformed into super-hero Captain Marvel. The word received wider exposure — particularly to adults — in 1941 in the 12-chapter movie serial "The Adventures of Captain Marvel" and then again in the 1960s when used in the American TV series "The Andy Griffith Show" and "Gomer Pyle". REF: Les Daniels, Comix: A History of Comic Books in America (1971), 14; Raymond William Stedman, The Serials (1971), 126; OED/2. Thence magicians jargon (variant noted) by 1978 Sterling cat as "SHAZZAM!"; 1981 Abbott cat #22; 1986 Hades cat
(See also: table servante.) n. A servante that attaches to a table out of sight at its back, that is, on the performer's side; a shelf servante. [obsolescent, formerly rare]

1.n. Fake apparatus in the form of a hollow or half-dummy. Used to simulate a complete object such as a ball, bottle, candle, cigar, coin (the shell coin), die, or wand (the shell wand). Compare half-shell. [very common]

n. A faked coin hollowed out on one side to contain a real coin that is shaved in diameter. See also shell half and expanded shell. [fairly common] Used to change one coin to another of different size, to multiply one coin to two, or to make two become one.
n. The Three-Shell Game (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare] Originally the argot of gambling cheats by 1890 as earliest citation in the OED/2.

n. The pass (2) being the most usual synonym for this sleight that transposes the halves of a packet of cards, enabling the magus to cancel the previous cut (in the case of a false cut) or to bring a chosen card to wherever it is wanted. One variant is the slip. [fairly common] "The shift has yet to be invented that can be executed by a movement appearing as coincident card-table routine; or that can be executed with the hands held stationary and not show that some manoeuver has taken place, however cleverly it may be performed." — Erdnase, The Expert at the Card Table (1902), 96 "EIGHT HOUR SHIFT PUZZLES DAI VERNON" — Charlie Miller, fake newspaper headline at San Francisco World's Fair, 1939 Originally American card sharps argot, certainly by 1902 Erdnase; 1933 Cameron; 1944 MacDougall; 1949 Scarne. Thence the jargon of American magicians by 1898 (Stebbins; 1902 Erdnase/Harto; 1909 Hilliard; 1920 Stanyon in Magic, 44; 1927 Tarbell; 1955 Vernon letter of Oct 3rd to Miller; 1978 Müller; 1979 Lamb re American usage; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1991 Ortiz; 1994 Racherbaumer in LR) and in England since 1910

n. A small concealed gimmick with a shiny surface (such as a mirror or button of polished metal) used to glimpse by reflection a supposedly hidden object such as the face of a card whose back is turned toward the magician; a glim; light; reflector. See peek mirror for a particular type. [fairly common] This device originated with card cheats using mirrors concealed in their finger rings in Milan, Italy, by 1530 as first reported by Girolamo Cardano in his Liber de Ludo Aleae (ca1564 ms/1953 tr, 210-211). And then again in England in 1635 by Hocus Pocus Junior (added in his 814 2nd edition). Magicians used a drop of liquid (water or beer) on the table to glimpse cards held directly above it as first explained in 1651 by White and then 1763 Dean, 6th ed, p.78; and 1859 Secret Out. Originally this word was argot among American card sharps by 1891 Quinn; 1894 Koschitz; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne; 1911 Meyer; 1917 Lipman cat; 1924 Henderson; 1927 Gibson; 1931 Smith; 1933 Cameron; 1939 MacDougall; 1949 Scarne; 1961 K.C. Card Blue Book; 1962 Garcia; 1973 Lampkin; 1977 Dalal in Mantra; 1995 Riser in MUM. Thence magicians jargon by 1938 Annemann as a "card shiner"; 1940 Hugard; 1941 Horowitz in Jinx; 1942 Mussey; 1951 Farelli in HMM, 813; 1955 Walsh in New Phoenix, 108; 1958 Corinda; 1959 Owen cat #5 as "a pipe with shiner"; 1969 Gibson; 1969 A. Sharpe; 1978 Tannen cat #12; 1979 Cyprian; 1981 Ray-Mond; 1983 Hayden; 1988 Waters; 1993 Edmonds in LR; 1994 Munari ad in LR.

n. Removing a man's shirt without apparently unbuttoning it or from under his jacket. Compare vest turning. [rare] First reported performed by Italian conjuror Giuseppi Pinetti. He made it a popular trick and the only one in his repertoire whose method he himself exposed in 1784. The 1792 edition of Breslaw's Last Legacy attributes this trick to Philip Breslaw (who died in 1783), but this may only be a steal from Pinetti. Also described in The New Conjuror's Museum, and Magical Magazine, I (1803). The method was being sold in 1843 by Crambrook for a shilling. Also exposed in 1904 by Stanyon in Magic (p.72). A pet effect of Dr. L.E. Duncanson (1920s), Ted Annemann (1930s), Ovette (1930s), Johnny Aladdin (1950s), and today of Walter "Zaney" Blaney, Dominque, and Ricki Dunn. Widely exposed in early Boy Scout manuals. Only incompetants use the stooge and prepared shirt method.
See: Hunter Puzzle Knot. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Hunter Puzzle Knot".)

n. Stage effect where an arrow (or bullet) from a bow (or gun) passes through an unharmed assistant to hit a bull's-eye target behind her. The trajectory (and penetration) being indicated by a ribbon. [fairly common] Premiered by Billy "Chung Ling Soo" Robinson" in England in early 1907 using an arrow-firing muzzle-loading musket. He then premiered it in Australia on 27 Feb 1909. Marketed as early as 1909 through the T. Bamberg catalog with the bow-&-arrow effect. First exposed in 1912 by Goldston. A pet effect of Shungopavi (sometime before 1913 using the bow-and-arrow version), François De Villiers (in 1911), Frederick Eugene Powell (in introducing the P&L rifle version in 1929), Thurston (in 1931), Murray (in 1933), Dante (1936-41), Francisco (1940s using a male assistant), and Kalanag (1956). REF: Zelka in Conjurers’ Monthly Magazine (Apr 1907), 261; Stanyon in Magic (Dec 1908), 20; Waller (1980), 151; Goldston (1912), 463.

n. A short card being the more usual synonym. [fairly common] Originally, as "Shorts", the argot of card sharps by 1843 Crambrook cat; 1852 Anderson; 1855 Wyman; 1875 Hartz. Thence magicians jargon by 1898 Stanyon; 1901 West ad in Magic; 1905 Leslie in Magic; 1923 C. Williams in Magic Wand; 1930 Orrin as "a 'short'"; 1933 Davenport cat; 1935 Annemann in Jinx; 1936 Thayer cat #8; 1937 Hugard; 1937 Annemann; 1946 Clive; 1946 Gresham in Phoenix #115; 1947 Histed; 1947 Braue in HMM as “using a short to control”; 1948 Elliott in Phoenix #143 as "ring the short in"; 1958 Kanter cat #10; 1984 Goshman lecturing as "a short".

n. A playing card that has been trimmed at the ends (or, occasionally, at the sides), making it shorter (or narrower) than the others in the deck; a short. When cut narrow, it may be called either a narrow card or incongruously, a short card. Opposite of a long card. Compare with cornered card (1). [common] "And if you think a short card is simple, check back a number of years and discover that Vernon was fooling the best in the business with applications of the principle long before magicians recognized its value." — Annemann in The Jinx #53 (1939), 378 "The long or wide card had a long innings but has finally been superseded by the short card which serves the same purpose in a much subtler way." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Mar 1946), 201 Used as a key card, because it can be felt when the magician riffles the end of the deck. Generally preferred by American magicians over the long card because it is less noticeable and cheaper and easier to manufacture. British and Continental conjurors, however, tend to favor the long card, at least until 1950. New York cardman Sam Horowitz mastered the short card in 1922 or 1923. Originally, as "Shorts", the argot of British card sharps by 1843 (see entry under short). Thence, as short card, adapted into magicians jargon by 1876 Hoffmann; 1905 Leslie in Magic; 1909 Hull instruction page; 1926 Gibson; 1927 Vernon; 1930 Orrin; 1927 Tarbell; 1934 Farelli; 1935 Deleport in Trixter Monthly; 1945 Morris in HMM; 1948 Norman; 1948 Kaplan; 1950 Hay; 1955 Christopher in HMM; 1967 Baron; 1976 Goldstein in Mantra; 1976 Severn; 1979 Lamb; 1980 Adair; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1992 Wassilak in Genii; 1998 L&L cat. a. [adjectivally] [very rare but not nonce]
n. A quick, deliberate display (flash, 2) of the face of a playing card. [very rare but not nonce]

n. The Miser's Dream coin production routine, being a later and now most usual synonym. [obsolete after 1950] This routine was already old when Robert-Houdin performed it in London in 1852 (Robert- Houdin, London poster). It was first exposed in 1867 by Stodare (also 1876 Hoffmann).

(See also: Shower of Sweets.) n. Effect where many pieces of candy are produced from a borrowed handkerchief. [obsolescent, formerly common, particularly in British usage] “A perfect Christmas trick and one that is very rarely performed is the Shower of Sweets from a borrowed handkerchief.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Nov 1951), 867 This trick may well be of Chinese origin, a member of a troupe of Chinese jugglers (advertised as being from Pekin) having presented it in London around 1830 as a shower of nuts from an empty handerkerchief. Then performed with candy ("sweets" in British English) as early as 1838 by George Sutton in London's Strand Theatre. The simple prop was marketed as early as 1843 by Crambrook in London. First explained in 1857 (Wyman in Magician's Own Book, 16- 17; then 1868 Robert-Houdin; 1876 Hoffmann, 251-254). Once quite popular as a give-away treat for adults and children, this pleasant trick is seldom performed today. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand, V.17 (1928), 179; Ayling (1981), 360-361.
n. Effect where an impressive volume of plumes are produced from a handkerchief. [archaic, formerly rare]

n. Effect where many pieces of candy are produced from a borrowed handkerchief. [obsolescent, formerly common, particularly in British usage] “A perfect Christmas trick and one that is very rarely performed is the Shower of Sweets from a borrowed handkerchief.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Nov 1951), 867 This trick may well be of Chinese origin, a member of a troupe of Chinese jugglers (advertised as being from Pekin) having presented it in London around 1830 as a shower of nuts from an empty handerkerchief. Then performed with candy ("sweets" in British English) as early as 1838 by George Sutton in London's Strand Theatre. The simple prop was marketed as early as 1843 by Crambrook in London. First explained in 1857 (Wyman in Magician's Own Book, 16- 17; then 1868 Robert-Houdin; 1876 Hoffmann, 251-254). Once quite popular as a give-away treat for adults and children, this pleasant trick is seldom performed today. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand, V.17 (1928), 179; Ayling (1981), 360-361.

n. The qualities of a showman, specifically the combination of promotional and presentational ability. [common] "Showmanship is that intangible necessity that takes an act out of the ordinary and pushes it up the ladder of success." — Dunninger "The greatest factor in Houdini's success was his showmanship." — Walter B. Gibson, Houdini's Escapes (1930), 8 "Anyone who's done a levitation knows that eighty percent of it is showmanship." — Franz Harary, interview in The Linking Ring (Nov 1984), 98 Originally the cant of (or Standard English referring to) carnival-type exhibitors by 1859 Sala as cited in the OED/2; 1910 Julian Wylie in The Wizard; 1934 in the Merriam-Webster New International Dictionary 2nd ed; 1967 Boles. Thence magicians jargon by 1903 Stanyon in Magic; 1907 Keene; 1909 C. Williams in Magic Mirror; 1912 Goldston as "the quality of showmanship"; 1919 Ovette; 1923 Leat; 1930 Lustig; 1931 Booth; 1931 Mussey & Oursler; 1936 Weber; 1937 Holden as "clean cut showmanship"; 1943 Fitzkee; 1946 Maurice; 1948 Buckley; 1953 Robbins; 1956 Dexter; 1957 Maréchal; 1960 Christopher in HMM; 1961 Posgate; 1969 Nelms; 1977 McGill; 1979 Lamb; 1984 S.P. Smith in LR; 1986 Howard; 1990 Wedler; 1994 Wassilak cartoon in MUM.
n. Stage illusion where a cluster of spikes in a frame is pushed without bodily harm thru an assistant prone in a box on a table. [rare] 818

v. To more-or-less randomly mix the playing cards in a deck or packet. [very common] Originally the lingo of card players since at least as early as 1570. REF: OED/2; Hugard in HMM (Aug 1950), 695. Thence magicians jargon by 1584 Scot as "shuffle the cards"; 1612 Rid as "shuffle the Cards" & "shuffle them often"; 1763 Dean as "shuffle them often" & "let a stander-by shuffle"; 1829 Boy’s Own Book as “shuffle them well”; 1838 Anderson, Hull playbill as "they may be shuffled by the different parties";1857 Magician's Own Book; 1909 Hilliard; 1930 Holden in Sphinx; 1946 Zovello in HMM; 1978 Gross; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler. n. The art of mixing playing cards; shuffling. Depending on the particular method used, known variously as the faro shuffle, Hindu shuffle, overhand shuffle, etc. [very common] Originally the lingo of card players since 1651. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1829 Boy’s Own Book, 203, as “a momentary shuffle”; 1859 as a false shuffle; 1877 as the dovetail shuffle; 1902 as the stock shuffle; 1909 as the riffle shuffle; 1920 as the overhand shuffle; 1930 Holden in Sphinx; 1934 as the Hindu shuffle; 1937 as the push through shuffle; 1938 as the Greek shuffle; 1940 as the faro shuffle; 1959 as the Zarrow shuffle; 1972 as the Shank Shuffle; 1976 as the Klondike shuffle; 1978 Müller; 1978 Gross; 1979 Lamb; 1998 L&L cat. a. [adjectivally] [rare] "Shuffle work credited to magicians was used by card cheats well before magical card workers became aware of it." — Jeff Busby in Thaumaturgist, No.33 (Feb 1997), 3

n. A pseudo-psychic who believes in his or her own powers. Or a spectator who gulliblly accepts paranormal phenomena as real, the perfect mark for the pseudo-psychic. 819 [rare] "A 'shut-eye' is a fortuneteller who goes for his own lies, a faker who fools himself." — Orson Welles, Orson Welles' Eversharp Almanac (1945), Episode 6 Originally the cant of pseudo-psychics by 1935 Magnuson; 1976 Keene, 23. Thence magicians jargon by 1935 Magnuson; 1945 Welles orally; 1990 Piatt price list as "designed for the ‘shut eye' in mind"; 2001Busby in eBay ad as a "shuteye".

term: Si Stebbins System; Si Stebbins Set-up
definition: 1.n. The popular card setup where the entire 52-card deck is prearranged by both suits and values — the suit order being the common CHaSeD one and the value order such that each card is three higher than the previous one (for example: 6, 9, Q, 2, 5, etc); the Thurston system (Brit.). [common] “The ‘Si Stebbins’ set-up is part and parcel of standard card magic. Odd, though he sold the system which bears his name he used another set-up when he entertained with cards himself.” — Frank Joglar [Milbourne Christopher] in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Dec 1950), 730 There are two setups associated with Si Stebbins, a long-held secret that led to much confusion on the part of Clinton Burgess (in Elliott [1923], 56n) and Jean Hugard (in Card Manipulations #5 [1936], 146). In fact, while Stebbins used another and better system for himself (see 2.n., below), he taught this inferior one. This was invented and published by Stebbins in 1898 in a cheap brochure. In 1900 he met Howard Thurston and personally explained this inferior system. Thurston, while correctly attributing its invention to Stebbins, popularized it in 1901. REF: Stebbins (1935), 3; Stebbins (1898); Thurston (1901).

n. Effect where the magician releases his chained and padlocked wrists; the Siberian Transport Chain (obsolete). [fairly common] Professor Herwinn (William Humpage, 1861-1946) claimed its invention, probably rightly so. However, according to T.A. Waters, this effect was invented by British magician P.T. Selbit using an unfaked chain and lock, the release depending on the way the volunteer follows instructions in fettering the escapist. But it is not mentioned among Selbit's effects in his 1989 bio by Lewis & Warlock. According to Gary Darwin it was invented by Boston magic dealer W.D. LeRoy, but I suspect this was only because he may have marketed it. REF: Waters (1988), 66; Darwin (1988), 19. The term probably arises from a semantic confusion between Houdini's regular chain escapes and his celebrated escape on 11 May 1903 in Moscow from a "Siberian Transport Cell" in which he was merely shackled.

(See also: Siberian Chain Escape.) n. Effect where the magician releases his chained and padlocked wrists; the Siberian Transport Chain (obsolete). [fairly common] Professor Herwinn (William Humpage, 1861-1946) claimed its invention, probably rightly so. However, according to T.A. Waters, this effect was invented by British magician P.T. Selbit using an unfaked chain and lock, the release depending on the way the volunteer follows instructions in fettering the escapist. But it is not mentioned among Selbit's effects in his 1989 bio by Lewis & Warlock. According to Gary Darwin it was invented by Boston magic dealer W.D. LeRoy, but I suspect this was only because he may have marketed it. REF: Waters (1988), 66; Darwin (1988), 19. The term probably arises from a semantic confusion between Houdini's regular chain escapes and his celebrated escape on 11 May 1903 in Moscow from a "Siberian Transport Cell" in which he was merely shackled.

n. Spiritualistic materialization effect where a spirit emerges horizontally from the magician's side in a cloud of vapor, turns upright, steps forward, and speaks to the audience. [archaic since 1907]

n. A conjuror who performs in a circus or carnival sideshow. [rare] Some magicians were strictly circus sideshow magicians. These included John Schiedler in the late 1800s and Daniel P. Mannix in the 1930s. A few subsequently famous magicians spent part of their apprenticeship doing sideshow magic. These included Roltare (1890s), Alex P. Davis (1890s), Houdini (1895), Joe Ovette (around 1900), Linga Singh (by 1905), Harry Willard (around 1911), Al Flosso (1915-39), Fetaque Sanders, Faucett Ross, Billy O'Day (in 1938), Johnny Platt, Micky Hades (1940s), James Randi (around 1945), "Chandu" (Karol J. Michalski, early 1950s), Ricki Dunn (in 1950s), and Tom Ogden (1973).
n. A sleight that palms off one or more cards from the side of the deck; the side-slip. [fairly common]

n. Strippers trimmed to bulge slightly outward along the sides. Opposite of end strippers. [rare] Originally American card sharps argot by 1891 Quinn; 1932 Evans Secret Blue Book. Sharps also called them "humps" by 1890 Quinn; 1894 Koschitz; 1932 Evans Secret Blue Book; 1961 K.C. Card Blue Book; 1961 Scarne. Thence, as side strippers, magicians jargon by 1936 Holden cat #5; 1937 Hugard; 1939 Kanter cat; 1944 Fitzkee; 1960 Haines cat; 1972 Hay; 1984 Willmarth in LR; 1990 Wedler; 1994 Munari ad in LR.
n. The Monte effect with four jumbo cards where the spectators cannot keep track of the ace while it is repeatedly mixed among three blank-faced cards. [fairly common]
See: eyeless vision. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "eyeless vision".)

n. An entire performance or segment during which the performer uses no patter; a dumb act. Relies on pantomime (1), usually with musical accompanyment. Compare dumb show. Opposite of a talking act. [common] "If you can't boost do a silent act." — D. J. "La Vellma" Lustig (1920), 30 "There is a very great difference between a silent act of magic and a magic act in pantomine." — Arthur H. Buckley, Principles and Deceptions (1948), 37 The silent act originated in the circus and carnival where it was common, presumably because of the prevailing hubbub. It was introduced to the vaudeville stage by Houdini in Apr 1899 when he brought his escape act from the carnival to the Orpheum Theatre in Omaha. Next, with a strictly magic act, was Horace Goldin in 1900. Then Adelaide Herrmann with her "A Night in Japan" act, which was staged by 1902. Theo Bamberg used this mode for his "Okito" act from its outset, which was by 1902; and Silent Mora adopted this style in 1904. The generally acknowledged master of the silent performance was Cardini who adopted it in 1927, continuing until his retirement in 1966. Cardini's great public success stimulated a silent vogue that has 825 continued to the present with such major practitioners as Marvin "Mr. Electric" Roy, Johnny Hart, Norm Nielsen, Flip, Sam Angelico, Scott Cervine, and Teller of Penn & Teller. REF: Laurie (1953); Price (1985), 88, 421.

1.n. Specifically, a piece of very thin, highly compressible fabric such as a fine handkerchief or scarf or flag. [very common] Originally made of genuine Chinese or French silk, although inferior nylon or nylon-silk mixes have been marketed since World War II.
n. A small box or cabinet (cabby) with hinged drop-down doors, front-and-back, one of which is fitted with a secret load chamber to vanish handkerchiefs (silks); a silk cabinet. [fairly common]

n. See following quote. [rare] "I was totally baffled in later years [1930s?] by Jack Spalding's Silk Through Cane. Twisting a 24" silk into a role-like rope, he dropped it over a cane held horizontally by a spectator. Taking the ends of the silk, he visibly pulled it right up through the cane. Then went back down again for a visible penetration. Then he looped the silk over the cane, and holding both ends of the silk in one hand, pulled it once again right through the cane! This was detailed in an early Sphinx and later in Reel Magic by Albenice. It has since been used and taught by several magicians without credit to Jack Spalding." — Stuart Cramer in The Linking Ring (Jul 1995), 59
n. The Color-Changing Silks (see) being the most usual synonym; the dyeing silks. 827 [rare]
n. Effect where two silks of same color are shown tied together; a silk of different color is brought forth and it almost instantly appears tied between the previous pair. [rare]

n. Conjuring with thin cloth. [fairly common] The cotton cambric handkerchief was used in occasional individual tricks as early as 1584 (Scot, in describing the Coin Handkerchief). The silk handkerchief, with its special quality of extreme compressibility, was not adopted as magical apparatus until the mid-1800s. Its first recorded use was by Robert-Houdin in connection with his "The Vanishing Handkerchief," for which, incidentally, he invented the first pull (using elastic). A full-scale silk routine was introduced by Buatier de Kolta and first written up extensively in Hoffmann's Later Magic (1903) after which silk magic routines became a common part of magicians' acts. REF: Rice, I (1948), 2-3. Magicians introduced knotting and unknotting silks in performance by 1900; and these knot tricks were soon being published, the first booklet devoted exclusively to the subject being Ellis Stanyon's New Handkerchief Tricks (1900). Then in the early 1930s Louis Gerber of Cincinnati, Ohio, introduced a silk act based on an interconnected routine of knotting/unknotting silks. In 1937 Harold R. Rice bought Gerber's 16-knot routine and published it as Naughty Silks. By 1941 Rice had routined enough new knot effects to publish his More Naughty Silks, which was a 30-minute routine with 60 such effects with only a single silk. REF: Rice, III (1962), 1218.

n. Magicians thread being the more usual synonym. A popular misnomer, as the high-grade sewing thread was actually made of cotton. [obsolete after 1949, formerly fairly common] "The favorite method of causing cards to rise is by the use of 'the conjurer's faithful friend,' the black silk thread." — J. Northern Hilliard in Downs & Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909) Thence magicians jargon (variants noted) by 1857 Magician's Own Book as "black silk thread"; 1876 Hoffmann; 1903 Stanyon in Magic as "black silk thread"; 1908 D. Abbott as "invisible black silk thread"; 1916 Collins; 1928 Thayer cat #7 as "Black Silk Thread"; 1931 Douglas cat #16 as "black silk thread"; 1939 Kanter cat; 1941 Holden cat #8 as "Black Silk
n. An apparatus version of Twentieth Century Silks. [rare]
n. Effect where a silver coin held in a volunteer's hand is transformed into a silver nugget in the magician's hand with the volunteer left holding a transparent coin. [fairly common]
n. Stage illusion where innumerable small but solid objects are produced from a metal top hat resting on a small skeleton stand. [archaic, formerly rare]

n. A magic word. [rare] Dante, before age six when his parents emigrated from Denmark to the USA, learned from his mother the jingle "Sim Sala Dim, Sala Du, Sala Dim" in a Danish childrens song. Around 1927 he began using these as magic words on stage. When performing back in Copenhagen in 1930, someone suggested their use as an advertising slogan but someone else complained that "Dim" would not look good in English. Hence Sim-Sala-Bim was agreed to, soon appearing in Dante's ads and spoken as his opening greeting-cum-benediction. In 1931, Dante's son, Alvin Jansen, composed his "Sim-Sala-Bim" fox-trot theme music. Dante's uniquely personal phrase was pirated by German Nazi magician Helmut "Kalanag" Schreiber when in 1940 he had Leo Leux compose a march under that title to words by Schreiber. Then, beginning in 1947, he used Sim-Sala-Bim as his show title, as magic words, and Leux's march. Also adopted as magic word by Richiardi Jr by 1966 and Granville "Faust" Taylor by 1969. Silvan adopted "Sim Sala Bim" as title of his 1972, 1973, & 1978 Italian TV specials. GENERAL REFS: Price (1985), 283-284; Moi-Yo Miller, lecturing, 27 Jan 1985; Furst (1957); Christopher (1973), 402; Hokuspokus Zauberkunst (1993), 69-71; Lee Jacobs ad in Linking Ring (Aug 1997), 2.

n. A single act (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare] "He [Pauline] is said to have been paid the highest salary of any 'single' in vaudeville." — David Price, Magic (1985), 479 Originally U.S. theatrical lingo by 1923. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1947 Boston & Parrish as "Jarrow ... was another fine single"; 1952 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM as “doing a single”; 1957 A. Leroy in HMM; 1974 Hanson & Zweers as "On this circuit Herman worked as a single."; 1986 F. Marshall in LR; 1992 Randi; 1994 Bluemle in MUM; 1997 Booth in LR as "working as a single". NOTE: Also called "solo" as in "she worked solo" in 1984 F. Marshall.

n. An act with only one performer, working alone; a single. If two performers work together, it is called a double act. [fairly common] Originally vaudeville cant by 1937. REF: 1937 [Robert Reinhart] in Variety; 1952 Granville dict., which is the earliest citation in the OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1937 [Reinhart] in Variety; 1961 Gibson & Young as "a ‘single' act"; 1974 Hanson & Zweers; 1976 Gill; 1985 Price; 1985 Reynolds/Blackstone Jr; 1986 Olson; 1986 Charvet.
n. A buckle that separates only one playing card from the others. [rare]
n. A one-way deck being the more usual synonym. [obsolete, formerly rare] 831
n. The pointer cards in a one-way deck. [obsolete, formerly rare]
n. A dove pan whose lid is fitted with only one load chamber. Compare Double-load Dove Pan. [very rare]

n. A member of the audience at a séance. [rare] Originally the argot of psychics by 1887. REF: Hodgson & Davey in Proceedings of the Society for Psychical Research (1887); Sylvestre cat (1901); Stanyon in Magic (1904), 56; Webster's New International Dictionary of the English Language (1909 ed); OED/2 where earliest citation is only 1909; Keene (1976), 10. Thence magicians jargon by 1900 Triplett; 1901 Sylvestre cat; 1907 Houdini in CMM; 1928 Thayer cat #7; 1928 Annemann in Sphinx; 1930 S. James in Sphinx; 1940 Dunninger in Jinx #74; 1948 Nelson cat #22; 1949 Christopher in HMM; 1969 Nelms; 1983 Cassidy; 1987 Busby in Epoptica #8.

n. Card trick where several cards are repeatedly false-counted as six openly discarding some each time until only six remain. [common] "Ken [Griffin] doesn't particularly enjoy doing the Six Card Repeat. Magicians groan when they see it but a lay audience is always entertained by it. So it stays in our show." — Roberta Griffin, Illusion Show Know-How (1972), 2 The original version (with 18 cards) was invented by American magician Tommy Tucker and premiered in 1936. A pet effect of Sid Lorraine (late 1930s), Baffles Brush (late 1930s when he simplified it by introducing pockets on several cards), Blackstone (in 1947) and Clarke Crandall. It inspired Tom Bowyer's famous Repeat Bill Trick. Dai Vernon's version secretly adds as well as openly discards cards. REF: Lorraine 20 Jun 1988 letter to Whaley; Lewis, I (1980), 179.
n. A con game that lends itself to magicians demonstrations of gambling cheating. [rare]

n. A simulated human digit, hollow and flesh-colored, added to the magician's hand as an inconspicuous extra middle finger; false finger (fairly common); extra finger (obsolescent); hollow finger (obsolete); Slik Silk. [common] Being hollow, it is used for the production of silks. This device was first described in 1896 for this purpose by both Charles Bertram and August Roterberg. Maurice Garland was using it by 1903 when reported in Hoffmann’s Later Magic. Gary Darwin attributes its invention to Charles Morritt. REF: Magic Wand (1934), 149; Bertram (1896), 238-239: Darwin (1988), 19. "The customer at one of our display stands at a convention trying to insert the 'Sixth Finger' onto his middle finger — "It's rubbish" he stated, "It couldn't possibly fit anyone's finger". When I showed him that it was supposed to fit in-between the fingers and not to be worn, he didn't believe this." — Ian Adair in Trixigram (May 1988), 16 "After the handerkerchief is produced, false finger and handkerchief can both be handed out for examination." — Al Baker in The Sphinx (1930), 272
See: purse frame. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "purse frame".)

n. Effect where the spectator's chosen card is revealed as the only one left in the jaws of a tiny simulated human skull dangling by a cord from the spectator's fingers after it has dropped the rest of the deck. [obsolescent]

n. Apparatus for vanishes, productions, or transformations masked by slats (vertical or horizonal) alternating with gaps that can be momentarily closed by other hidden but moveable slats, including mirrors. 833 [rare] May be large enough for stage illusions (such as Thayer's X-Ray Double Box illusion by 1928) or small enough for vanishing playing cards (such as the Slat Jumbo Card Frame and Berg's Sucker Sliding Card Frame).
n. A hand-held school slate that may be either unprepared or gaffed. Used by pseudo-spiritualists for the slate test and by mentalists for a slate trick. [very common]

n. The type of spirit effect where hand-writing mysteriously appears on hand-held blank school slates. [fairly common] This production effect uses any one of three methods: fake slates, switched slates, or surreptitious writing on the slate. Slate tests were invented by psychics in 1851 and made popular among them by the American fraud, "Dr." Henry Slade, the "Slate Medium", who had developed improved methods. Prosecuted in London, Slade's slate test was effectively exposed in court on 10 Oct 1876 by J.N. Maskelyne. REF: Jeff Busby, Dominque Duvivier's Einstein's Blackboards (1996), 4. Capitalizing on the sensational publicity, Maskelyne introduced "Slade's Slate Writing" in his magic act at Egyptian Hall that November. Other magi were quick to copy: thus Samri S. Baldwin (by Jan 1877), Baldwin's former assistant Eugéne Verbeck (by 1885), Adolph Fernau Guibal, Kellar (by 1888), and Houdini (in 1925 as an exposé). Kate Fox added slate-writing to her spiritualistic stage act in 1888. Still performed by mentalist-magicians (such as the late 834 Robert Parrish) but very seldom by psychics because this method of cheating has become too widely known. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 91, 143, 144; Jenness (1967), 37. Originally the lingo of psychic mediums by 1896 Burlingame; 1898 Robinson; 1921 Alexander. Thence (variants noted) magicians jargon by 1896 Burlingame; 1899 Little in Mahatma as a “slate writing test”; 1902 anon [H.R. Evans?] in Magic, 78; 1919 Ovette; 1920 Lustig; 1929 Gibson; 1935 Annemann; 1936 Thayer cat #8 as a "Spirit Slate Test"; 1939 Kanter cat; 1945 Robbins cat #10; 1950 Hay; 1963 Tannen cat #4; 1968 Furst; 1979 Fulves; 1982 Hay 4th ed; 1996 Busby orally.
n. Any bit of mental or pseudo-spiritualistic magic that uses a school slate. [fairly common]

n. Performing a slate test. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common among mentalists] "It is rather singular, but it is true, that the most difficult audience to fool is a crowd of boys, while a company of learned investigators of the phenomena of spirit rappings and slate writings would be perhaps the easiest." — Frank W. Thomas, "The Confessions of a Conjurer", Saturday Evening Post (13 Oct 1900). Originally the argot of spiritualists by 1885 Century Magazine as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1888 Kellar; 1888 Cumberland; 1891 A. Medium; 1897 Evans; 1898 Robinson; 1901 Sylvestre cat; 1907 D. Abbott; 1921 Alexander; 1935 Blau flyer; 1940 Abbott cat #6. Thence (with variant noted) mentalist-magicians jargon by 1888 Kellar program; 1892 Hodgson in Proceedings of the SPR; 1898 Houdini cat; 1898 Robinson; 1924 Anneman [sic] in Sphinx; 1928 Thayer cat #7; 1929 Nixon as "slate work"; 1933 D. Abbott; 1939 Kanter cat; 1943 Larsen; 1956 Christopher in HMM.

v. To dispose by sleight-of-hand of an object up the magician's jacket sleeve; sleeving. [fairly common] "Contrary to common belief, it is much easier to sleeve a heavy coin than a light one." — George Starke, "Sleeving as an Art", Hugard's Magic Monthly (Mar 1945), 105 "Jarrow says that when you can sleeve buckshot on a tin roof and not hear anything—then you can sleeve properly." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (May 1946), 218 Used to either vanish or ditch a small object.
See: "Up the Sleeve". (No further definition found in this dictionary for ""Up the Sleeve"".)

n. Sleight of hand that uses the magician's jacket sleeve to dispose of objects. [rare] "A good sleeve-worker has the uncanny skill of a juggler and the precision of a marksman." — Will Dexter, Famous Magic Secrets (1956), 130

n. Effect where a chosen card is discovered by the magician kicking the deck with his foot. [rare] Invention credited to one otherwise unidentified Milton (Herbert Milton?) by Hugard by 1937. Sold initially by Stewart Jules by 1940. The literal master of sleight of foot was Carl Herman Unthan, a turn-of-the-century German vaudeville star who, born without arms, could perform a two-footed Pass, Second Deal, and Waterfall flourish with a deck of playing cards. This clever phrase was coined by German-American magician Imro Fox by 1902 (possibly by 1890) as a bit of comedy business where, pretending to catch his foot in a carpet would remark, "That's sleight of foot." REF: Stanyon in Magic (May 1902), 57. 837

n. The secret manipulation of objects in the hands to produce an effect; prestidigitation; legerdemain; finger flinging; fingerwork; hand magic; dexterity of hand (obsolete). [very common] "Lookers on feel most delight That least perceive a juggler's sleight, And still the less they understand, The more they admire his sleight-of-hand." — Samuel Butler, Hudibras (1663-78) “Women are like tricks by sleight of hand, Which, to admire, we should not understand.” — William Congreve, Love for Love (1695), Act IV, scene iii "Perfect sleight-of-hand is deliberate, allowing the eye to follow it with apparent ease, and deceives all the more absolutely because the deception is without haste and accomplished by movements of apparent naturalness." — Frank W. Thomas, "Confessions of a Conjurer", Saturday Evening Post (31 Oct 1900) "The ideal conjuring performance is a happy combination of apparatus and sleight of hand." — Downs & Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909) ""My forte is strictly sleight-of-hand, leaning on the comedy side. I leave the boxes and the rabbits to the guy who can juggle two heavy suitcases. My show packs in a cigar box. ... When I run, I don't want to be bothered with any suitcases." — Art Lyle in Thompson, My Best (1945), 364 "Sleight-of-hand is a secret action by the hands designed to conceal exactly what is taking place." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Oct 1955), 337 The technique was first exposed (as opposed to mere mention in passing) in 1584 by Reginald Scot. The term came into use around 1400 in its Standard English general meaning of manual dexterity and by around 1605 was applied specifically to conjuring. Thence as magicians jargon (with the variant spelling as "slight" noted) by 1634 Hocus Pocus Junior, [p.2], as "slightnesse of hand"; 1635 Hocus Pocus Junior, 2nd ed [not in 1st], 56, as "slight of hand"; 1655 Ady as "slight of hand"; 1716 Neve as "slight of hand"; 1731 Fawkes obit as "dexterous Performance by Slight of Hand"; 1763 Dean as "Slight of Hand"; 1785 Denton as "Slight of Hand"; 1818 Francis as "Slight of Hand"; 1839 Adrien Sr, Jul 29th Boston playbill as "Slight of hand"; 1857 Wyman in Magician's Own Book; 1861 Novra cat as "sleight of hand"; 1876 Hoffmann; 1876 Cremer; 1877 Sachs as book title; 1899 Stanyon #1; 1901 Evans in Magic; 1927 Tarbell; 1950 Hay; 1952 Buckingham; 1976 Tarr; 1977 McGill; 1978 Gross; 1979 Lamb; 1980 Adair; 1981 Ray-Mond as "slight of hand"; 1984 Miller in Genii; 1988 Waters; 1992 Randi; 1995 J. Gardner; 1997 Waldman. a. Hyphenated as in sleight-of-hand artist or sleight-of-hand man. [fairly common]

term: sleight-of-hand man; sleight of hand man
definition: n. A sleight-of-hand artist being the most usual synonym.. [rare] "Gad, the old man would disinherit me if he knew I spent my time with second dealers and sleight of hand men." — Frank Joglar [Milbourne Christopher] in Hugard's Magic Monthly (May 1951), 793 "Unlike most sleight-of-hand men, Don [Alan] has a knowing way with equipment and mechanical magic." — Frances Ireland in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Mar 1953), 1050
n. Psychological misdirection. [rare] "The sleight-of-hand is reduced to bare minimum and the spectators are fooled by sleight-of- mind." — Clayton Rawson in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Feb 1950), 634
a. Free of sleights. [rare]
n. A sleight-of-hand artist. [rare]

n. Any playing card (but usually an ace) whose face is treated to make it a slick card, that is, more slippery than the other cards in the deck. [rare] Used by magicians as a key card. Originally an artifice of card sharps. First exposed by Max Holden in The Sphinx (Mar 1924). Originally the argot of card sharps by 1917 Lipman cat; 1921 Herrmann cat; 1924 Henderson; 1932 Evan's Secret Blue Book; 1933 Cameron; 1939 MacDougall; 1959 Hunt & Co cat; 1973 Lampkin as a "slick ace deck". Sharpers also called it the "eel" by 1933 J.J. Cameron. Thence magicians jargon by 1933 Drummond [i.e., Annemann], Climax Card Routine; 1936 Gravatt; 1936 Ross, Aug 4th letter to Miller; 1940 Hugard in Merlin; 1943 Baker in Phoenix #54; 1949 Turner; 1952 Abbott cat #13; 1998 Busby

n. A slick card (see) being the most usual synonym. [obsolete after 1948, formerly very rare] Originally card sharps argot since 1674, as described above under entry slick card. Thence magicians jargon by 1935 Hilliard; 1948 Norman.

v. Making a slick card. Opposite of roughing. [obsolete, formerly rare] Originally the argot of card sharps by 1674 Cotton; 1938 Litzau. Thence magicians jargon by 1938 Litzau; 1946 Hall; 1948 Norman.
n. A thick chemical compound that when applied to playing cards makes a slick card or so-called slick ace. [obsolete by 1958, formerly rare]

1.n. The glide being the more usual synonym. [obsolete after 1911, formerly rare] From the French prestidigitators term glisser la carte ["slide {or glide} the card"], which was their jargon by 1876 (Hoffmann). Thence, by simple translation, English-speaking magicians jargon by 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 168; 1902 Stanyon in Magic,
n. The die box sucker-effect with a half dollar that vanishes to be reproduced elsewhere. [rare]

term: Sliding Die Box; sliding die box
definition: n. The die box being the later and now more usual synonym. [fairly common]

A simulated human digit, hollow and flesh-colored, added to the magician's hand as an inconspicuous extra middle finger; false finger (fairly common); extra finger (obsolescent); hollow finger (obsolete); Slik Silk. v. To move a card (by a variant of the shift) to the bottom or middle of the deck. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common] Used by magicians today only for forcing. Originally British card sharps argot as verb by 1844 Anderson as "to slip the card". Thence magicians jargon as verb by 1859 Secret Out; 1875 Hartz as to "slip a card"; 1876 Hoffmann as "to ‘slip' a card"; 1927 Merlin as "to slip the cut"; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler. n. The card sleight, specifically a variant of the shift, that moves any card (usually the top one) to the bottom or middle of the deck. [fairly common] Magicians jargon as noun by 1865 Taylor; 1876 Hoffmann; 1913 Elbiquet; 1927 Merlin; 1932 Carmier in Sphinx; 1956
n. A playing card or business card with a deliberate cut in it. [very rare, possibly nonce]
n. A tumbler of clear glass gimmicked with a narrow horizontal slot at the side and level with the base through which a coin may be slipped. [rare]

n. An intentionally bumbling series of running cuts that appears to mix the blocks alternately face- up and face-down yet all cards face the same way and in their original order. [fairly common] “The onlookers, who were veterans in the art of conjuring, immediately recognized this activity as the well-known ‘slop-shuffle.’” 843 —Ray Hyman, The Nature of Psychological Inquiry (1964), 34
n. The four ace effect where the Aces arrive one by one (rather than all at once) in the "leader" packet. [fairly common]

n. Effect where any card is taken with the right hand, put into the left (backs of hands facing spectators), card folded down into left hand, and both hands slowly separated, turned around and fingers parted to show that the card has vanished. Then, with a snap of the fingers, the card instantly reappears in the fingers. [rare]

n. A packet of cards of known identities kept together while shuffling or cutting a deck; a block. [rare] Originally the argot of American card sharps by 1931 Smith as "running slugs"; 1984 Ortiz; 1988 Williams in Epoptica #11; 1992 Giorgio in Genii. Thence magicians jargon by 1984 J. Thompson orally; 1984 Busby orally as "running a slug"; 1988 Waters, 36, but typoed as "slue"; 1996 ["1997"] L&L cat.

n. Shoddy magical apparatus or cheap tricks sold at exorbitant mark-ups, usually at temporary stands at fairs, conventions, and street corners or at joke-shop novelty counters. [rare] The archetypal items of slum magic are the Svengali Deck and the Paddle Trick. Less usual ones include Crazy Cube. Originally American criminal argot by 1909 meaning cheap jewellery; 1924 Henderson. Thence also, since around 1920, 844 American carnival lingo meaning cheap merchandise sold or given as prizes. REF: Tillotson (1909), 88, 95; OED/2; Wentworth & Flexner (1975 ed); Gibson (1927); Maurer (1931); Gresham (1953); Scarne (1961); Ortiz (1984); Sorrows (1985). Thence magicians jargon by 1936 W.A. Johnson ad in LR as "magic slum"; 1980 J. Marshall; 1983 Marvin Burger interview in San Francisco Examiner; 1988 Lorraine orally; 1997 G. Brown, 35, as “selling slum”. a. [adjectivally] [fairly common] "Beware of slum dealers who copy some of our own small effects which we put on the market." — Carl Brema, advertisement, around 1919

n. A non-toxic super-absorbent polymer powder that solidifies any liquid such and water or milk in which it is mixed. [new, fairly common] "It was more fun than putting Slush Powder in your gold fish tank." — Seth John Ossinsky & Jim Beck in The Linking Ring (Jun 1995), 162 Originally used in magic to create the Milk to Silk trick. Thence used for several effects.
n. Branch of conjuring using little props such as cards, coins, eggs, paper, ropes, thimbles, and silks. [fairly common]
n. A group of 2 to, say, 6 playing cards handled as a separate batch. [rare]

n. Any card trick (specifically a packet trick) that uses only a few (2 to, say, 6) cards from the deck. [fairly common] 845 Although currently once again in vogue, tricks with small packets date back at least to Hofzinser in the mid-1800s. Classic examples are Three-Card Monte and DeLand's Two-Card Monte.

n. Effect in card magic where two volunteers are made to select the same card from a packet by a mathematical process. [rare] "Thirty-five years ago a young man walked into my store and became my best book customer from then on. His knowledge of magic is prodigeous, and yet in all those years, I do not think I ever saw him do a trick. His name is Fred Smith. He told me a trick he dreamed up, and I named it the Smith Myth. I included it as a bonus in The Five O' Fetsch." — Gene Gordon, Magical Legacy (1980), 173
n. A throw-off; a red herring that creates a false line of logic rather than merely confuses. [very rare] "You need smoke to take the heat off." — Jeff Busby, orally, 1984

term: Smoke from (the) Fingertips; Smoke from Finger Tips
definition: n. Effect where the magician produces smoke from his empty hands by merely snapping his fingers. [rare] Achieved by application of two different chemicals pastes, one on the thumb and the other on the forefinger, which when rubbed together produce volumes of smoke.

1.n. The effect where smoke is generated inside an upside-down tumbler (or other sealed container) or two tumblers placed rim-to-rim. [rare] The method of this standard effect of chemical magic involves secretly mixing ammonia with hydrochloric ("muriatic") acid. Described in a magic book as early as 1872 in Cremer's Hanky Panky under the title "How to Introduce Cigar Smoke into an Air-tight Vase". A pet effect of 847 Chung Ling Soo.

n. Effect where the magician pantomimes filling his clenched fist with tobacco, lighting it, and then — using his extended thumb like a pipestem — really smoking it; the Smoke Trick(4). [fairly common] The effect was conceived by English-American movie comedian Stan Laurel in June 1938. A practical stage method was invented by American magician Ade Duval by mid-1940 when he was already famous for his "Rhapsody in Silk" routine — a title, incidentally, suggested to him by Paul Fox. Duval had almost certainly been inspired by seeing Laurel & Hardy's Blockheads (released Aug 1938) where Laurel gives this complete effect of stoking his fist with invisible tobacco and then actually smoking it through his thumb. (David Price categorically but wrongly attributes Duval's inspiration to the earlier L&H film Way Out West [Apr 1937] where, by camera trickery, Laurel merely makes his thumb a torch and proceeds to light a real pipe.) Both effects were original with Laurel, who improvised them (neither were in the scripts) while filming on the set, the first from observing a crew member unsuccessfully trying to light a cigarette. Duval was working on the trick when he arrived in Australia in 1939 for what would prove a most successful tour that was extended well into 1941. In Melbourne in 1940 he befriended Charles Waller who learned about the Smoking Thumb trick, presumably directly from Duval. Waller's close friend and local magician-dealer, Dr. Richard Rowe, somehow acquired this trick — very probably because he invented or helped develop the trick's highly practical gimmick. In any case, soon after leaving Australia in early 1941, Duval premiered the trick, which proved an instant success. Magicians were unable to figure it out (and I am not at liberty to disclose it). However, American professional Frank Lane learned somehow (probably from Duval) of Dr. Rowe's connection. In response to an enquiry from Lane, Rowe sold him the trick on 1 Aug 1941. Lane started to advertise it, but was induced by angry friends of Duval to withdraw it after a single ad. Duval continued to feature the Smoking Thumb until his retirement in 1951. In 1957 Lenz & Andrews marketed their "Strato Smoke" apparatus thru Tannen's (ad in Mar HMM, 552). A pet effect of Billy McComb (in 1949) and Fred Kaps (until 1980)—but both using inferior gimmicks of their own devising—Finn Jon (1980s), and Don "Guli-Guli" Fernandes (1990s). 848 REF: Waller (1948/1980), 240; Rowe, "1-7-41" letter to Lane; Lane, undated letter to F. Csuri; Busby interview 16 Mar 1985; Price (1985), 358; Randy Skretvedt Laurel and Hardy (Beverly Hills: Moonstone Press, 1987), 324, 345.

n. Effect where an artificial serpent rises from a basket, the chosen card clutched in its jaws. [fairly common] Introduced (and probably invented) by American magician Russell Swann by 1939, using apparatus made by Earl Violet. Marketed by British magician-dealer Jack Hughes. June 849 Cochrane and Billy McComb won the British Ring Shield in 1949 with an act that featured this trick. Abbott's marketed a clockwork-activated version in the USA. A pet effect of Russell Swann and Prince Mendes (1950s). REF: Busby orally 1989 (re Violet's letters); Lever (1981), 70; P. Abbott (1960), 23.

n. Occasional allied art of South Asian magicians where a live snake is placed in a catatonic state. [rare] "... apart from their skill as snake charmers, in the basket trick, and one or two other illusions, the ability of the entire fraternity of Indian jugglers is beneath contempt." — Harry Kellar, A Magician's Tour (1886), 114 "A snake may be struck just behind the head or even pinched with the performer's fingers which will result in a temporary paralysis so that it becomes quite rigid and resembles a stick, doubtless known to Aaron and the magicians of Ancient Egypt." — Will Ayling, Oriental Conjuring and Magic (1981), 119 The above quote regarding Aaron's Rod-to-Snake effect rings with circumstantial truth. The Old Testament records that Egyptian priest-magicians of the 13th Century BC did this trick until Aaron produced a larger snake that swallowed theirs. Magician Robert Heller often saw modern Egyptian street magicians perform this feat in Cairo in 1873 and understood its hypnotic cause. This same Rod-to-Snake trick was reported by Roman Catholic missionaries as worked by Aztec priests of Mexico in the 15th & 16th centuries. REF: Ayling (1981), 117-122; Evans in Hopkins (1897), 1; Clark in Magic Wand, V.16 (1927), 206; Carrington (1909), 39-41. Standard English by 1897 (Mark Twain as earliest citation in the OED/2). Thence magicians jargon by 1909 Carrington; 1919 Stanyon in Magic; 1931 Mussey & Oursler; 1949 J. Maskelyne;
n. Effect where the operator can catch a hook on a rubber band inside a red cylinder, but a volunteer can't. [common]

n. A novelty practical-joke item made from any of several finely ground substances that induce violent sneezing in humans. [rare] Veratria is a powdered vegetable alkaloid discovered in 1819 that was commonly known by 1876 to induce violent sneezing. However veratria is also a very dangerous poison, even tiny quantities (1-16th grain) being capable of causing death. REF: OED/2; Magic (Mar 1906), 45, & (Aug 1906), 83; In 1904 Swedish-American practical-joker Soren S. Adams invented his own relatively safe formula and marketed it, thereby launching the famous S.S. Adams Company. REF: Zolotow (1952).

n. A tiny pair of plastic Scotty puppy dogs (one black, one white) mounted on oblong bases. They alternately repell or attract each other when placed nose-to-nose or nose-to-tail, [rare] Worked automatically by the magnetic bases. A highly popular low-comedy (scatological) novelty item introduced in the late 1930s. Became unavailable during World War II, as Orson Welles discovered when he tried to order a set. Spawned several variations. 851

term: Snowstorm in China; Snow Storm in China
definition: n. Effect where torn bits of paper in water are formed into a sodden mass yet, when fanned, become instantly dry and flutter from the fingers like snow-flakes; Wintertime in China. [fairly common] First reported in Japanese conjuring books of the 1700s according to Christopher (1962, p.121). Performed in London in 1885 by Italian magician Yank Hoe (Clarke in Magic Wand [Mar 1928], 43). First exposed in 1910 by both Devant (pp.36-38, as "A New Drying Machine") and Hatton & Plate (p.223). Presented in Australia in 1913 by the magicienne with the "Japanese Village" troupe. Again exposed in 1914-15 by Ishi Black and in 1927 by Tarbell (Lesson 4, p.8), the latter calling it "Wintertime in China". Writing in 1922, Branson (pp.7-8) mentions having seen Chinese conjurors doing it. Used by Dai Vernon in his "Harlequin Act" in New York City in 1938 and carried over to his "Dai Yen" and "Dr. Chung" Chinese acts of the early 1940s. Later a pet trick of Fred Keating (in 1952), Stewart Judah (by 1955), Abb Dickson (by 1982), Peter Samelson (in 1984), and Sitta (1980s).
a. Said of a natural, unobtrusive and therefore unnoticed movement, as opposed to a "hard" one. [rare]
n. Effect where soiled handkerchiefs need merely be placed in a cardboard laundry-soap box to be produced clean. The production box may then be torn up and shown empty. [fairly common]

See: verbal code spongeball; sponge ball w. A sphere made of porous, compressible material. [very common] “In 1928, the late G.W. Hunter showed me the first set of sponge balls ever seen in London.” w. Victor Farelli in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Dec 1951), 875 Sponge rubber was invented in 1886. Adapted to magic by Jesse L. Lybarger and first published for a spongeball manipulation routine in 1926. These first balls were hand-carved by magicians from sponge-rubber blocks, although a few magi preferred to use natural sponge. More recently, both materials were superseded by flexible polyurethane foam, also hand-cut. Then New York magician-dealer Al Stevenson devised a secret process for making nearly perfect spheres from the polyeurothane foam. After Stevenson’s death, Albert Goshman improved the process and virtually monopolized the manufacture and sale of the item, indeed being mainly responsible for the current popularity of sponge-balls as a leading prop. REF: Page & Goshman (1985), 53; Avadon in Berg (1983), 66-67.. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "verbal code spongeball; sponge ball w. n. Effect where a filled whiskey shot-glass on the magician's palm instantly vanishes when covered and compressed by the other hand. [fairly common] The vanish is worked by a particularly clever sleeve-pull, a rubber ball just big enough to be jammed into the mouth of the glass. Invented by American amateur magician & dentist Doc Zola of Saginaw, Michigan. First marketed in Dec 1933 by Australian-American magician Percy Abbott by his brand new magic manufacturing firm in the USA. Known as "The Trick that built the Abbott Magic Company." First exposed in 1936 by Blackstone in the Sunday Buffalo Courier-Express. A pet effect of Tommy Cooper. REF: Behnke (1974); Annemann in Jinx (1936), 148.

n. Effect where when two large black cubes, with a yellow cube between, are pushed together, the yellow cube slowly and visibly squeezes into nothing. [rare]

n. Trade name of the first playing cards with their indexes in diagonally opposite corners. [obsolescent, formerly rare] Prior to 1873 all playing cards required viewing the entire face to learn its value. Then, in 1873, Andrew Dougherty's company introduced its "Triplicate" ("Trips") cards that placed miniature reproductions of the full faces in diagonally opposite corners. Then in or soon before 1876, "Squeezers" were introduced by the New York Consolidated Playing Card Company. Since 1877 when the two rivals jointly released their "Bulldog Squeezers" (showing two chained bulldogs named "Trip" & "Squeezer" snarling at each other) this type of deck quickly dominated the world market. REF: Busby in Whaley (1991), 158-159; OED/2, p.1873. Thence magicians jargon (from the "squeezing" used to view the corners) by 1904 Stanyon ad in Aug Magic, 106; 1939 872 Kanter cat as "'Squeezer' Cards"; 1941 Holden cat #8 as "Angel Back Squeezer Cards"; 1982 Albrecht cartoon in Epoptica #1 as "squeezer angels"; 1988 Waters; 1988 Busby in Thauma #5 as "Bulldog Squeezers"; 1996 Ward in LR.
n. Effect where a circle cut in a folded-in-half sheet of newspaper becomes a square when unfolded. [fairly common]

n. Effect where two chosen cards are replaced in the deck, which is wrapped in paper (and sometimes bound with a rubber band). Then, when the magus or spectator stabs the packet through the side with a knife, the chosen cards are found to lie aside both sides of the blade; the Card Stab (1). [rare] A pet effect Nate Leipzig (by 1928), Leon L. LeCount (by 1945), etc.
