n. Effect where a piece of crumpled paper slowly and visibly changes into an egg while being 879 bounced on an oriental fan; the Egg on Fan (U.S.). [rare] The method consists of the switch of the paper for a crumpled hollow egg skin that slowly resumes its natural shape (followed, sometimes, by a switch for a real egg that can be broken). Reportedly of Japanese origin, although I know of no specific performances. In any case, adopted (or invented) by British magician Max Sterling for his "The Magic of Japan" act that premiered at Maskelyne's Home of Mystery in London in Nov 1905. Later a pet trick of Carmo (by 1914, having learned it from Sterling). The trick then went out of popularity until the early- 1930s when revived by Tommy Martin (by 1935). Then a pet effect of Orson Welles (in 1944, having been taught by Edgar Bergen), Maldo, Harold "Three Tricks" Taylor (since 1960s), Jeff Busby (having seen Edgar Bergen do it), Peter Samelson (in 1984), and Jonathan Neal Brown. REF: F. Ireland (1946); Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 150; Ayling (1981), 29, 238-240; Magical World (1911), 181; Busby in Thaumaturgist #37 (1999), 7-8.

n. An egg bag faked with an external yet virtually invisible pocket. [rare] Conceived by Detroit magic dealer Harold Sterling, by simply turning a 1942-model plaid Tarbell Egg Bag inside out and working it that way. This design was introduced in performance and print and subsequently used by Edward Marlo, Ross Bertram, Frank Shields, Jeff Busby, Chuck Smith, and, most recently, David Ben. REF: Busby in Epoptica (1982), 54- 55; Sterling cat #2 (1945), 43, where Sterling claims "originated in 1925" by him.

n. The handkerchief ball (see) being the most usual synonym. [fairly common] Named after American magician George Stillwell who, after reading the chapter on "Tricks with Handkerchiefs" in Ellis Stanyon's Conjuring for Amateurs (1897), became the first professional magician to develop an all-silk production act. By 1902 he was presenting his act, billed as the "Handkerchief Manipulator." His was, rightly so, the most famous handkerchief act of his time. Although Stillwell used a handkerchief ball in his act, he was—contrary to later writers—not its inventor, as the hank ball had been advertised as early as 1895. REF: Stillwell, Aug 30th letter in Sphinx. 880

n. Giving rehearsed answers or standardized general statements about the person receiving a reading(1); a canned reading; psychological reading; stock spiel; or spiel. Compare cold reading. [rare] Used by mentalists either as a supplementary filler during a cold reading or when they have no specific information about the sitter other than such visible attributes as sex, race, age, etc.

n. A stock reading (see) being the most usual synonym. [rare, used only by mentalists] Originally the argot of pseudo-psychic readers by 1935 Magnuson. Thence mentalists jargon by 1977 Hyman in Zetetic; 1987 Kowalski in Epoptica #10 as "a stock spiel can be trouble"; 1988 Busby annotation. 881 stocking g. Arranging (by false shuffling) a stock of playing cards after they have been culled. Compare stacking. [rare] Originally card sharps argot by 1822 Bailey, 67, as "a stocking and slipping of cards"; 1857 Green; 1865 Evans; 1873 Morris; 1876 Cremer, 97; 1877 Grandin pricelist as "for stocking cards"; 1887 F. Francis as earliest citation in both the OED/2 & the RHHDAS; 1891 Quinn; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne; 1902 Erdnase; 1944 MacDougall as in "stocking the cards". Thence magicians jargon in 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 127; 1909 Hilliard as "complete the stocking of the aces"; 1911 Hoffmann; 1969 Gibson; 1991 Busby in Whaley.
1.n. A hollow egg-shaped container with a hole in the side; hollow egg. Made of plastic or even a real blown egg. [fairly common] Used to transform a silk into an egg.
n. Stage illusion where two female assistants are produced from a palanquin previously shown empty; the Jam Illusion. [rare]

n. A performer who swallows pebbles. 882 [archaic, formerly rare] Stone eating is an old trick, known as early as 1006 AD in Prague. A famous stone-eater was the Italian, Francesco Battalia, who performed in London in 1641. Sometimes formerly seen as an allied art of magic. REF: Christopher (1962), 10; Jay (1986), 277-284.

n. A secret assistant of the magician posing as an audience member; a confederate; a plant (2.n.). [common] "Dunninger on television with 'no paid stooges' — but Billy Rose to the occasion." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Nov 1948), 481 "Apart from artistic pride and ethical considerations, it is a dangerous business for magicians to use a stooge in perpetrating a hoax on the public. Sooner or later the stooge will boast of the part he played in the deception." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Aug 1955), 322 "The show [Kalanag's] is loaded with stooges. There were so many of them—I counted seven I was sure of—that I was beginning to believe maybe the guy does carry a company of eighty— sixty of them confederates." — Robert Lund in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Sep 1957), 65 "Neff is proud of the fact that since the beginning of his career he has avoided using ‘stooges' or volunteers from the audience who have been rehearsed. He feels that a spontaneous reaction is so important and therefore he 'cues' the boys during the progress of the effect and the entire show benefits from the added effort he puts forth." — Arnold Furst, Great Magic Shows (1968) "In our opinion, a STOOGE is the most versatile and effective magical prop ever devised." — Sam Dalal in Swami (May 1973), 65 Originally American vaudeville or theatrical slang by 1913, referring to a comedian's assistant. REF: Mathew's Dictionary of Americanisms; OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1939 Orville Meyer in Jinx; 1942 Elliott in Phoenix; 1945 Flosso in Sphinx; 1945 Wheeler cat; 1946 Ripley; 1949 Stuthard; 1949 Hay; 1950 Joseph; 1956 Dexter; 1958 Leroy in HMM; 1958 Corinda; 1960 Ganson; 1962 Larsen in Genii; 1976 Goldstein; 1978 Hudson; 1979 Lamb; 1981 Becker; 1983 Cassidy; 1987 Willmarth in LR; 1988 Mickey Maven as "no stooges are employed"; 1990 Ellis in Australian Magic Monthly; 1991 Ortiz; 1992 883 Dorian in letter to Whaley; 1996 Gloye in LR. v.i. To act as a stooge; stooging. [rare]
n. The use of stooges. [very rare, possibly nonce]

n. Type of card trick the effect of which is that the spectator selects a card and the magician deals cards off a deck until the spectator says "stop" at any arbitrary point. The chosen card, needless to say, is produced right at that point. [fairly common] The original Stop Trick was used and described in 1868 by Robert-Houdin. A pet effect of Frederick Bancroft (by 1897) and Nate Leipzig (by 1909). REF: Hugard (1937), 321; Max Katz in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1956), 505.
n. Magic accompanied by fully verbalized tales. [rare]
See: Strait Jacket Escape for preferred spelling. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Strait Jacket Escape for preferred spelling".)

n. Mainline conjuring (as opposed to mentalism or other specialties including comedy magic) performed in a serious manner. [fairly common] "His peers differed in their opinions of his ability to do straight stage magic." — Kenneth Silverman, Houdini!!! (1996), 390-391
n. A stranger card (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare]

1.n. A playing card from one deck secretly added as a duplicate to a regular deck; a stranger. [fairly common] The stranger doubles for the forced chosen card during the discovery phase of the trick. It may 886 be of a different back-pattern or color from the regular deck, which is usually borrowed.
n. Effect where different colored balls stacked in a transparent tube change places, vanish into a box, and reappear. [fairly common]
n. Effect where a soda straw can be cut in half without cutting a string that had been previously strung through it. [rare]

n. A street magician (U.S.); a Hanky-omer (Brit., obsolete?). [fairly common] "I am known as a Hanky-omer, that means a Street Conjuror in the Posh phrase." — Dick "Twister" Turpin in Magic Info (1981), 343 Standard English by 1861 (The Times, Jan 10th, as "street-conjuror"). Magicians jargon by 1920 Carlton; 1943 Huggins; 1949 J. Maskelyne; 1980 Lewis #1; 1981 O. Griffiths; 1983 J. Haviland; 1989 Howard in Q; Haviland in Abra.

n. Conjuring performed in open, public places. [fairly common] Conjurors have performed in urban streets since at least as early as Greek and Roman antiquity. In medieval Europe, all magicians worked the streets, although a very favored few of them won 887 more-or-less temporary access to the courts of kings for their entertainments. Among these were John Rikil who served Henry V around 1420, Brandon who performed for Henry VIII between 1521 and 1535, and Thomas Stanley who did so for Mary I in 1554. Even after the mid-1700s when Katterfelto, Philadelphia, Falconi, and Pinetti brought magic into the theater, most European conjurors continued to work in the open in public streets and at fairs. The rising popularity of amateur conjuring in private parlors in the early 1800s and of vaudeville and carnival magic in the late 1800s, left the streets to the minority of magicians. The "Zouave" worked Parisian streets in the late 1800s as did Claudius Odin at the turn of the century. In the USA Henry Gordien was working New York City's Lower East Side in the late 1910s. In Britain, notable streets magicians were Carlton (circa 1895), Solly Mack (c1900), Tom Reid (c1900), Wilf Huggins (c1907), Billy Payne (1920s), Percy Press (1920s-30s), Dick "Twister" Turpin (1930s), Horace Spencer (1930s), Professor Goff (1930s), Ronald "N'Gai" Marleigh-Ludlow (late 1930s), and Charlie Edwards (1920s-40s). Edwards was the last British street magician around the mid-century mark when magic moved off the public thoroughfares in Britain, Europe, and America, a move coinciding with and supposedly caused by the mass introduction of television. Following a 20-year gap, the current revival of the art of street magic saw the pioneers Philippe Petit in Paris (around 1966), Jeff Sheridan in New York City (from 1967), Alfie (1970s), Jerry Salazar in San Francisco, Harry Anderson in San Francisco (in 1970s), and Mal Cross in New York (1970s). More recent performers in New York include Max Howard (1980-81), Billy McQueen, Carl Melish, and Michael Rubinstein. Others throughout America include Gerry Hart. John Lenahan worked the streets of the USA and Europe in the early 1980s. Jim Haviland worked Britain in the late 1980s. Allain "Diabolo" Porthaud has worked the island of St. Martin since 1983. GENERAL REF: Claflin, Street Magic (1977).

See: expanded shell stretching 1.g Generally, any effect where an object or person undergoes unnatural elongation such as Stretching a Rope and Stretching a Woman. [fairly common]. term: Stretching a Rope; stretching a rope
definition: n. The effect of making a rope seem to lengthen (from, say, 3 to 9 feet or even 13 feet) by being pulled in the magician's hands. Opposite effect of the later Idiot Rope. [fairly common]

term: Stretching a Woman; stretching a woman
definition: n. The Elastic Lady being the most usual synonym; the Stretching (2). [rare]
n. A force where only one item is offered the volunteer. Compare ranging force. [rare]
n. A sleight for obtaining a second deal. [rare]

n. A stripper deck (see) being the more usual synonym; Slippers (Brit.). [fairly common] Originally the common argot of American card sharps by 1822 Bailey, 141, as "they cut the cards, what the sharpers call the strippers, so that you cannot win a paralee"; 1843 J.H. Green as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1857 Green; 1865 Evans; 1873 Morris; 1877 Grandin pricelist; 1884 Will & Finck cat; 1894 Koschitz; 1902 Erdnase; 1904 Bonville; 1911 Meyer; 1912 Quinn; 1924 Henderson; 1930 McGuire; 1933 Cameron; 1949 Scarne; 1973 Lampkin; 1984 Ortiz. Thence introduced in 1894 by J.N. Maskelyne to his fellow magicians among whom it caught on quickly, becoming their jargon by 1897 Roterberg; 1900 Triplett; 1905 Keane; 1909 Hilliard; 1910 Naldrett in Magical World; 1914 DeLand cat; 1919 Stanyon ad in Magic; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1927 Vernon; 1927 Gibson; 1928 Leat & Jonson; 1931 Douglas cat #16; 1932 Thayer cat #7S; 1937 Hugard; 1939 Kanter cat; 1950 Hay; 1952 Farelli in HMM; 1971 Tannen cat #9; 1981 G. Grant; 1981 Govan; 1992 Jay Marshall in letter to Whaley. NOTE: Although some magicians make the obvious pun between this cardmans jargon-word and burlesque-show slang for a striptease artist, that later coinage of "stripper" did not occur in print (in Variety) until 1930 in the USA. REF: OED/2, which also traces "strip teaser" to 1930 and "striptease" to 1936; Green & Laurie dict (1951 ed). stripping g. Removing playing cards from their deck by pulling; to strip out. [rare] Originally the argot of card sharps by 1873 Morris; 1939 MacDougall as "stripping the deck"; 1973 Lampkin. Thence magicians jargon by 1987 Bannon in LR as "stripping them out of the deck"; 1988 Busby annotation; 1997 S. Morris in LR as "stripping out the desired cards".

1.a. Said of any effect or routine that is particularly impressive, startling, or baffling. Opposite of weak, although magicians seldom use that adjective. [common] "The Card Through the Handkerchief is one of the classics of card magic. Performed correctly, it is as strong an effect as you could wish for." — Blackstone Jr & Reynolds, The Blackstone Book of Magic & Illusion (1985), 185 "An effect strong enough for David Copperfield to perform on his last Network TV Special!" — Hollywood Magic, Catalog No.18 (1993), 27
n. Stage illusion where an assistant, padlocked to a board in a cabinet, vanishes and appears freed elsewhere. [obsolescent, once fairly common]

(See also: Suitcase Table.) n. A carrying-case specifically designed for magicians, which can be converted into a table for performance and carries their props; Su-Table. [fairly common] In early 1907 Stanyon's in London advertised a "'Box' Table", a folding carrying case that opened into a table but without the capacity to include small props. Later that year it was announced that Horace Goldin had patented a similar prop, which Ted Marks planned to introduce in the USA, although Joseph Hayman reported that such a device had been used by comedy musical teams for years. In 1919 or 1920 the Heaney Magic Company in the USA advertised a "Table Turns to Trunk", actually a standard hand-held suitcase and probably of 896 German make. In 1928 marketed by Thayer's as "Table to Suit Case". Richard Himber marketed his version in 1946. Later manufactured by both American semi-pro prop maker Merv Taylor and Gene DeVoe and, currently, by several others. REF: Joseph Hayman in Conjurers’ Monthly Magazine (1907), 384; Stanyon ad in Magic (Mar 1907), 46; Heaney cat #24 (ca1919), 74; Thayer cat #7 (1928), 237; Owen Magic Supreme, Catalog 9 (1976), 29, misattributing invention to Taylor.
n. Slangy abbreviation of Substitution Trunk (1). [common, particularly in speaking] "The sub-trunk is probably the best illusion on earth." — Jonathan Pendragon in Genii (Dec 1989), 372
n. Secret replacement of one object by another; a switch.

1.n. Stage illusion where a shackled and bagged assistant is locked in a large case yet in seconds exchanges places with the magician; the sub trunk; Metamorphosis (2). Compare the Brooks Trunk. [common] "Without much doubt, the greatest substitution effect in the entire repertoire of magic is The Substitution Trunk Trick." — Dariel Fitzkee, The Trick Brain (1944), 108 Based on J.N. Maskelyne's Box Trick, which had been used only for escapes, Houdini bought a second-hand faked trunk from a down-and-out magician in 1892 or 1893 and introduced the substitution element in his act in 1893, billing it as "Metamorphosis". Using as assistants initially his partner Jack Hayman, then with brother Theodore, and, finally, his new wife Beatrice and, with revivals, until his death in 1926. Subsequently in the stage acts of a great many magi, notably Owen Clark (by 1903), Raymond (in 1904), Nicola, Fred Keating (in 1927), David Bamberg (since 1929), Edgar Benyon (until 1968), George Goebel (in 1982), Sheets & Spill (in 1983), and The Pendragons (1980s-90s) who do perhaps the fastest version on record. In 1949 Leon Mandrake became the first to include a Costume Change in a Sub Trunk routine, followed most recently by Fielding West. REF: Silverman (1996); Gresham (1959), Chapters 2-3; Christopher (1969), 18-19; Gibson & 893 Young (1961), 1-7; Linking Ring (Apr 1994), 79.

n. A small but significant element in handling. [common] "In magic, as we all know, old principles are continually being clothed with new subtleties, eventually metamorphosing into what can essentially be considered original marvels of mystery." — Arthur Kraft & Frederick L. Kraft, MagnetiCoins (1971), 5

a. Said of any effect where the magician leads the spectators to believe they have detected the method and then works a double bluff to surprise them even more. [very common] "This is a trick of the kind so prettily described by conjurors as a 'Sucker'." — Charles Waller (1929), 163 Originally American slang since 1838 meaning a greenhorn, someone figuratively still sucking at the teat. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1905 as a sucker trick; 1914 as the Sucker Die Box; 1920 Holmes as "the ‘sucker' feature"; 1921 A.P. Blaeser in Dornfeld as "The Sucker Card Box"; 1924 as sucker effect; 1924 as sucker gag; 1936 Hugard as "a sucker vanish"; 1945 Wheeler cat as "the ‘sucker' byplay"; 1947 Fleischman & Gunther as "sucker stuff"; 1953 Elliott as "a sucker explanation"; 1959 Nelson cat #26 as “a sucker climax”; 1961 Ganson as a "sucker climax"; 1976 Owen cat #9 as "Sucker Cigarette Box"; 1978 Gross as "the ‘sucker' explanation"; 1980 Tannen cat #13 as "sucker finish"; 1995 Busby orally as "a sucker card trick". v. To work a sucker effect on the audience. [very rare, possibly nonce]
See: silk-to-egg. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "silk-to-egg".)
n. A sucker effect being the slightly more usual synonym. [fairly common]
n. A feint (see). [rare]

n. Effect during a silk-through-the-hand dyeing when a "tell-tale" tag of silk protrudes from the magicians fist, apparently unnoticed by him during his "explanation" of the trick, which then, of course, concludes as a sucker gag. [rare] Performed professionally by British magician Leslie Guest at the 1st IBM Convention in 1926 when, Sid Lorraine, asking permission to use it, was told by Guest that "It isn't my trick—I don't whose it is." A pet effect of Lorraine who was performing it in Britain in 1928-29. First published by American dealer Frank Lane as "A Comedy Handkerchief Routine" in 1935 in his booklet (co-authored with U.F. Grant), They're Off (pp.13-15). Pirated and marketed immediately after World War II by a British amateur. A pet effect of Eric Lewis until it simply became too popular in Britain, particularly with Billy McComb and Ken Brooke. It enjoyed a revival in the USA, notably with Dai Vernon. REF: Lorraine 20 Jun 1988 letter to Whaley; Lewis, I (1980), 70, and II (1980), 33. 895
n. Effect where where a card is made to behave like the die in the sucker version of the sliding Die Box. [rare]
n. A sucker effect being the most usual synonym. [fairly common] "Well, a sucker trick can be a lot of fun if you handle it with some degree of tact." — Sammy Smith in M-U-M (Sep 1997), 26

n. The technique (verbal or physical) of misdirection in which something is implied to be something it is not. [rare] Professor Hoffmann (1910 article) wrote that "the true secret of the magician's power lies specially in suggestion, a term of much wider significance" than misdirection. "Psychology is used to sharpen another weapon in the close-up man's armoury—suggestion." — Will Dexter, Famous Magic Secrets [1956], 24

n. A carrying-case specifically designed for magicians, which can be converted into a table for performance and carries their props; Su-Table. [fairly common] In early 1907 Stanyon's in London advertised a "'Box' Table", a folding carrying case that opened into a table but without the capacity to include small props. Later that year it was announced that Horace Goldin had patented a similar prop, which Ted Marks planned to introduce in the USA, although Joseph Hayman reported that such a device had been used by comedy musical teams for years. In 1919 or 1920 the Heaney Magic Company in the USA advertised a "Table Turns to Trunk", actually a standard hand-held suitcase and probably of 896 German make. In 1928 marketed by Thayer's as "Table to Suit Case". Richard Himber marketed his version in 1946. Later manufactured by both American semi-pro prop maker Merv Taylor and Gene DeVoe and, currently, by several others. REF: Joseph Hayman in Conjurers’ Monthly Magazine (1907), 384; Stanyon ad in Magic (Mar 1907), 46; Heaney cat #24 (ca1919), 74; Thayer cat #7 (1928), 237; Owen Magic Supreme, Catalog 9 (1976), 29, misattributing invention to Taylor.

1.n. Effect where two handkerchiefs or two sheets of tissue paper (a white one, usually borrowed, and a red one) have their centers cut out into round holes and are restored with their centers transposed. [fairly common] Originally with handkerchiefs, later replaced by tissue paper. This classic effect was a pet of Russell Swann who revived it in the early 1930s.
n. The Parasol (see) being its most usual title. [very rare]
n. The suspension (not strictly a levitation) where an assistant (female) reclining on a board floats in mid-air after both supports are removed. [fairly common] 897

n. Apparatus effect where 10 cards (or only 5 in the smaller and cheaper "Supersonic Card Prediction Jr" version) are displayed on a horizontal bar with backs to audience, magus makes written prediction of card that will be selected, and it is when volunteer choses a number from 1 to 10 and the magus counts over to the card at that point on the bar. [rare]

term: Sure Shot Dice Box; Sure-Shot Dice Box
definition: n. A dice box (2) that permits controlled rotation of two dice. For a more tightly controlled version see Eli's Die Box. [fairly common]

a. Said of a trick that is sufficiently angle-proof that it may be safely performed with the spectators on all sides of the magician. [common] "Some magic can be done when you are surrounded, and it falls in the highest category of magic." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (1950), 36 "A move is not good magic unless one can do it surrounded." — John Booth in The Linking Ring (Dec 1987), 61 “The illusion [Compacted] was originally designed for the female magician ‘Jade’ to be used surrounded in a circus.” — James Dimmare in M-U-M (Jul 1998), 28

n. The effect of an object floating in mid-air without any logical means of support; the Aerial Suspension. Contrasted with levitation. [common] A crude type of human suspension reputedly originated in India, however the earliest documented performance there was not until 1828 or 1829. Subsequently, in 1832, Sheshal, "The Brahmin of the Air", also performed this feat in Madras. But the effect and same method had already, in 1826(?), been performed in Europe by a British magician who billed himself as a Chinese, "Ching Lau Lauro" or "M. Ching". Later it became a pet effect of Robert-Houdin (from 1847), Compars Herrmann (from 1848), Anderson (from 1849), Prof "The Fakir of Oolu" Sylvester (from 1865), Charles DeVere (from 1869), Cora de Lamond (in 1872), Winston Freer, James J. DeVoll (in 1940), and, most recently, of Scott Cervine (1984). The main versions seen in modern platform magic are the Broom Suspension and the Sword Suspension. REF: Frost (1881); Anderson (1976). The word suspension was coined in its magical sense in late 1847 in Paris by Robert-Houdin for his celebrated "La Suspension Éthéréenne" illusion, which used a significantly more sophisticated mechanical support. Thence introduced as jargon among English-speaking magicians in 1848 by Compars Herrmann, May 3rd London playbill as "Suspension Éthéréenne". Thence 1848 by Robert-Houdin, London poster; Herrmann, Aug 21st London program as "Suspension by Ether"; 1848 Anderson, Dec 26th London poster as "Suspension Chloroforeene"; 1876 Hoffmann as "the aërial suspension"; 1956 Dexter; 1972 Griffin; 1973 Kaye; 1976 Armstrong; 1980 J. Marshall; 1986 Blackstone Jr & Reynolds; 1987 Abbott cat #23; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1992 Randi; 1997 Waldman; 2000 Abbott flyer. "suspension of disbelief, the" phr. Catch-phrase denoting the need of the audience to enter into the fiction created by the performer. 899 [rare] "Mentalism is the one area of magic that seems real to a lay audience. They not only suspend their disbelief—they believe." — Phil Goldstein, The Blue Book of Mentalism (1976), 2 "The skilled mentalist uses the same psychological principles to manipulate the minds of his audience that a good magician does, but there is one big difference. He does not ask for the 'willing suspension of disbelief' as a magician does. For many in that audience, real belief, or the strong susceptibility to it, has taken care of that." — Blackstone Jr & Reynolds, The Blackstone Book of Magic & Illusion (1985), 136 "In the overall, the successful magician need only have the audience suspend its disbelief." — Rich Bloch in Cassidy, The Art of Mentalism (2nd ed,1984), 1 "Suspension of disbelief is something that every magician must achieve in order to entertain and mystify his audience successfully. If he can't achieve this state then he is just exhibiting tricks." — Ben Harris, Gellerism Revealed (1985), 12 "He had that extraordinary talent which made people believe — or at least made them suspend their disbelief." — John Gardner, Confessor (1995), 164 This popular catch-phrase originated in the sentence in Samuel Taylor Coleridge's Biographia Literaria (1817), Ch.14: "... that willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith." Coleridge’s original application to readers of literature soon became widely applied to theatrical audiences. Thence magicians jargon by 1969 Nelms, 19; 1984 Cassidy, 3; 1995 J. Gardner; 1997 Pecor in LR; 1998 Tudor in LR.

n. A mechanical deck of playing cards comprising 26 ordinary cards, all different, alternating with 26 short cards, all of the same suit and value; Svengalis; the self-forcing pack; the Long and Short Pack (2). [very common] Originally intended for forcing a card, but soon adopted to other magical purposes. The principle was known as early as 1584 when it was applied to the flick book, which Sam Sharpe asserts was the basis of the long-and-short card Svengali Deck. Whatever its inspiration, the Svengali Deck was invented by Burling Hull, patented by him in 1909, and marketed by him in 1910. Pirated by W.D. LeRoy who apparently renamed it Svengali, adopting the name of the fictitious evil hypnotist in George du Maurier's then current best-selling novel, Trilby (1894). REF: Sharpe (1937), 19; Fulves (1983); Hull (1910, ad); Hanson & Zweers (1974), 66; Stanyon in Magic (Apr 1914), 65. An improved version was invented by Ralph Hull and marketed as the Mirage Deck in 1934. REF: Hay (1950), 217.

n. A Svengali deck. [fairly common] "I can think of no better purchase for the beginner in magic than the 'Svengali'." — Val Andrews in Roy & Andrews, Illusions (1985), 120 "Avoid familiar trick packs like Svengali." — Ed Marlo in J. Marshall, TV, Magic and You (1955), 82

1.n. A convenient synonym for or title of a magician or mentalist. [rare] Originally the Hindi word swami (from the Sanscrit svamin) meaning a master, lord, or prince and used as a respectful term of address. Entered Standard English in 1773. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1939 "Swami Brahma" as one mentalist's stage name; 1945 Swami Magician's Magazine, V.1, #1; 1954 Francis Carlyle, Boston Magicale billing as "The Swami Ribber"; 1972 Swami magazine, V.1, #1. 2.n. Contraction of Swami Gimmick. [rare]

n. A nail writer or thumb writer being the more usual synonyms; simply a Swami (2). [fairly common] This, the original type of nail writer, was invented by pseudo-psychics. Introduced to magicians in 1921 by "C. Alexander" (Claude Conlin Sr). 901 Magicians jargon by 1943 Vivian St. John in Phoenix #37; 1946 Clive; 1947 Gen ad; 1948 Norman; 1951 Dexter in Gen; 1958 Corinda; 1966 Inzani-Henley cat #1; 1973 Alain; 1977 MacMillan cat; 1977 Brooke tape; 1977 Cassidy; 1977 Kaye; 1979 Lamb; 1982 Mason & Richardson; 1986 Supreme cat; 1987 Snader; 1988 Waters; 1988 Kennaugh in Magigram; 1990 Wedler; 1990 Davis in Vibrations; 1995 Tannen cat #18; 1997 Goodsell in MUM; 1997 Lee cat #11; 1997 Abbott cat #25; 1998 Lesley in MUM.
n. Any holdout device that delivers and retracts a nailwriter (Swami Gimmick). [rare]
See: Potsherd Trick. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Potsherd Trick".)

n. The small device that Punch and Judy workers place in their mouths to produce the characteristic sound of Punch's voice to distinguish it from the other characters in the show. [rare] Introduced by Italian marionette workers who called it a "pivetta". Thence to French puppet workers who called it a "sifflet de la pratique". In England it was called a "squeaker" by 1699, a "swatchel" (from "Mr. Swatchel", an alias of Mr. Punch himself) by 1790, and thence finally "swazzle" by 1942. REF: George Speaight, Punch & Judy: A History (1970), 20, 47, 69, 121-122; OED/2.
n. A sideways shift executed from a deck held crosswise. [rare]

n. Type of effect where, paradoxically, an effect is made to seem to have occured when, in fact, nothing did or that is so obviously self-working as to be absurd. [rare] Swindles include, generally, the use of confederates and, specifically, the Piano Trick.
n. Opposite of switch-out.
n. A changing wallet (see) being the more usual synonym; a switching wallet. [rare]

n. The method of cutting a deck of cards in the right hand by swinging the upper portion to the left and forward through a semi-circle, dropping it onto the left hand, and completing the cut by placing the remaining portion on top of it. [rare]

term: Sword thru Body; Sword through the Body
definition: n. Effect where a sword is thrust through the waist of the victim who remains unharmed. Compare Sword thru Neck. [rare] Uses both the effect and method of the old Bridle trick of string-thru-nose first exposed in 1584 by Scot. Writing in 1858, Robert-Houdin exposed the method used by a French street performer: the stiff sword passed sideways from hip-to-hip through a leather scabbard placed between the thin man's tucked-in real belly and a fake cardboard one. Also performed front-to-back with a flexible blade guided by a metal tube by Joseph Buatier [de Kolta] in London at the Egyptian Hall at his premier there on 10 May 1875. Buatier's method was first exposed in 1897. A featured effect of Carter (in 1927) and Doug Henning (in 1987). REF: Robert-Houdin (1858/1859 tr), Ch.22; Hopkins (1897), 152-153.
1.n. A small cube-shaped sword cabinet fitted to the assistant's head; the dagger chest. [rare]

n. Effect that a sword penetrates a stock encircling the neck of a volunteer. [common] Based on Joseph Buatier's 1875 method and effect of the Sword though the Body. A pet effect of Tom Ogden. 905 The "Neck Spiker" (using a single gimmicked spike) was marketed by Menge by 1958. Bob Ellis had also marketed his "Double Neck Spiker" (with two criss-crossed spikes) by that same year. REF: Kanter's Catalog of Magic #10 (1958), 223.

n. Stage effect where an assistant, supine upon three upright swords, remains suspended at the neck after the two swords at the back and ankles are removed. [fairly common] Based, of course, on Robert-Houdin's Suspension. The earliest account of the sword version, possibly fictitious, was published in 1877 by the notorious founder of theosophy, Madame Blavatsky. She claims it was a common trick of Hindu jugglers in India. Otherwise invented (or, at least, reinvented in the West) by F. D. Hewes ("The White Yogi") who had never been to the Orient. Hewes used a rigid body-harness fitted to a socket in the key sword. He and his brother premiered it in 1899. The trick has been a perennial favorite ever since, including performance by Calcutta street magician Azuri Yahya (around 1920), Jack Gwynne (in 1955), Gogia Pasha, Doug Henning (in 1976); Michel de la Vega (early 1980s), and The Mystery Magician video-tape (in 1986). REF: H.P. Blavatsky, Isis Unveiled (1877), 75; Ayling (1981), 125-126; Sharpe in Armstrong (1976), 251, 254.

n. A performer who engages in sword-swallowing as an occasionally allied art of magic. [rare] "It is ironic that, while many circus and sideshow acts which employ various gaffs (strong man, ‘torture' act, sharpshooter) are thought to be genuine demonstrations of skill, the genuine feats of sword swallowers are thought to be accomplished by faked swords that 'fold up'." — T. A. Waters, The Encyclopedia of Magic and Magicians (1988), 324 Standard English by 1827. REF: OED/2.

n. The act of swallowing swords or other long and sharp objects, which may be faked or not. An allied art of magic. [rare] The art of sword-swallowing probably goes back to ancient Egypt and Greece. It was quite popular in the Roman Empire — being reported by Plutarch (c.100 AD) and Apuleius (c.150 AD) among others. The art continued through mediaeval times. It is not until the early 1500s, in a report by Spanish writer Ludovicus Vives, however, that we get a clear statement of sword- swallowers who routinely combined this with other magic tricks. The first named performer who combined sleight-of-hand and sword-swallowing was William Bradshaw who worked the Bartholomew Fair in 1690. Italian conjurer Highman Palatine included knife swallowing in his act in London in 1763. Sword-swallowing was also practiced by Amerindian medicine-men by the 1600s, and by Indians in the early 1800s, Ramo Samee including swallowing a 2-foot sword in his magic act in the USA in 1819 and London in 1822. In 1876 Kellar added sword-swallower "Ling Look" (the Hungarian David Guter) to his act. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1924), 24, 27, 906 28, 73, 93, 129, 132, (1925), 34, (1927), 206, 208; Hopkins (1897), 156-161; Jay (1986), 285- 293; Richard Cohen, By the Sword (New York: Random House, 2002), 282-284. Standard English by 1873. REF: OED/2.
n. Effect where the magician's packet of 13 clubs (openly arranged in sequence) invisibly sort themselves to match the sequence of the 13 shuffled clubs from a volunteer's deck. [rare]
n. Invisible ink (see) being the more usual synonym. [obsolete] Originally Standard English by 1721. REF: OED/2.

n. Effect where three cards are chosen by volunteers from a deck with the word of a common object on each; then, when three borrowed objects are placed on these cards, they are found to match. [rare] Uses a set-up and a subtle force based on Stewart James' principle of synonymy. Invented by mentalist Ed Mellon in 1956 and first advertised by him as "Synonymental" in his magazine Mental-Wise. It quickly became Mellon's all-time best-seller.

n. The method of forcing that uses the ambiguity between certain words and objects. [rare] Particularly bold but seldom used. Reportedly first applied to magic in the 1930s in a trick by Stewart James. It is the basis of mentalist Ed Mellon's famous Synonymental trick, which he published in 1957. Originally Standard English since 1586, meaning the discrimination between synonyms. REF: OED/2. Thence coined as magicians jargon in 1957 by Ed Mellon in Mental-Wise, 2. Thence 1963 Tannen cat #4; 1972 Hull as the "Synonymy Force"; 1977 Kaye, 184; 1983 Busby orally; 1995 Tannen cat #18.
n. A playing-card setup (see) being the most usual synonym. [fairly common]

n. Illusion where the magician, manacled and chained flat on a table with a heavy, spiked board above him, must escape—under cover of a curtain—in a specified number of seconds before the spikes fall to impale him. [fairly common] This recently popular torture-escape illusion was invented in 1954 by American magician André Kole and performed exclusively by him until 1974 when he licensed it to a select few that included Doug Henning and David Copperfield (1987-88). It was based on Walter Cerretta Jean's "The Death of Cora" illusion built by him by 1898 but never performed because it was not fail-safe. Cora was first published by Goldston in 1927. Lester Lake developed a workable version in Shredder. REF: Waters (1988), 327; Warlock (1986), 17-20.

v. To engage in table hopping, which is the more usual synonym. [rare] Originally Standard English since 1942 meaning to move about in a restaurant or nightclub from table to table to chat with friends. REF: Webster's 10th Collegiate. Thence magicians jargon by 1979 Kaye in his My Brother, the Druggist novel; 1980 Kardyro in New Tops; 1984 Al The
n. The art of the table hopper; to table hop; table magic (2). Compare walk-around. [fairly common]

n. Effect where a small table levitates when the mentalist-magician places his hand or hands on the top; the Floating Table. Compare table tipping. [rare] Originally a trick of fraudulent spiritualistic mediums. Adapted to magical performance (using nail-head and finger-ring) by Alexander Herrmann and premiered by him. J.N. Maskelyne briefly added it in 1873 to his first season at the Egyptian Hall. Presented by Joseph Buatier in 1875 at Egyptian Hall. First exposed in 1897 (Hopkins, 519). REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1927), 90, 97. Originally the argot of pseudo-spiritualistic mediums by 1883 as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1895 Baldwin; 1898 Robinson; 1922 Dr. X. Thence magicians jargon by 1900 Stanyon; 1905 Goldston; 1905 Leslie ad in Magic as "Ring for Table Lifting"; 1912 Stanyon in Magic, 31; 1913 Roterberg cat #15; 1920 Carrington; 1931 Douglas cat #16; 1943 Elliott in Phoenix #36; 1958 Gibson; 1959 Corinda; 1965 Lawston cat; 1984 Cyro in Magic Info; 1987 Supreme cat; 1988 Waters.

1.n. Generally, the sub-class of close-up magic performed at table anywhere (usually seated, occasionally standing); table-work; Compare stand-up magic. [fairly common] Ideally, uses only those props normally available at a dinner table (napkins, knives, sugar lumps, saltshakers, goblets, etc), but often supplemented by pocket tricks.

n. Effect where tapping or knocking sounds emanate from a wooden table in coded response to questions put by the mentalist-magician or audience members. [archaic, formerly rare] "Table rapping, in a small circle, can be convincing and awesome." — Will Dexter in Mantra (May 1976), 53
n. A servante that attaches to a table out of sight at its back, that is, on the performer's side; a shelf servante. [obsolescent, formerly rare]
n. The ribbon spread (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare] Reportedly first published in l'Illusioniste (Paris) prior to World War I.

n. Table tipping (see) being the slightly more usual synonym. [rare] Originally spiritualists cant by 1903 (as earliest citation in the OED/2). Thence magicians jargon by 1927 Goldston; 1958 Gibson; 1988 Waters, 326.

n. The type of spirit effect where small tables appear to move by themselves; table-turning being the less usual synonym; table tilting; table turning (obsolete). Compare table lifting and table rapping. [rare] An instant popular craze among Americans by January 1853 that quickly spread during the rest of the year throughout Europe and Britain. Although a few scientists suspected the movement was caused by unconscious muscle power, it was not until mid-year that British physicist Michael Faraday ran and published experiments that proved this to be the case. Such are the limits of human memory that it again became a popular fad in the late 1960s marked by equal credulity in its paranormal motive power. REF: Christopher (1970), 115-123; Michael Faraday, "Experimental Investigation of Table- moving", The Athenaeum (Jul 1853), 801-803. Although this effect was borrowed by magicians from psychics, each uses different methods— gimmicks and muscle fatigue, respectively. Originally spiritualists cant by 1854 [Bornson], The Rappers; 1855 Smedley as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1866 Barnum; 1888 Cumberland; 1891 A. Medium; 1898 Robinson. Spiritualists also called it "table turning" by 1853 (Anonymous) and "table tilting" by 1903 (OED/2). Thence magicians jargon by 1943 Larsen; 1945 Wheeler cat; 1949 Hay; 1980 Randi; 1997 Busby in Thauma #33. NOTE: Parapsychologists, with the pomposity typical of credulous scientism, have been dignifying this cheap trick by calling it "typtology" since before 1926. REF: L.C. Wimberly, "Spook English", American Speech (Mar 1926).

(See also: table magic.) 1.n. Generally, the sub-class of close-up magic performed at table anywhere (usually seated, occasionally standing); table-work; Compare stand-up magic. [fairly common] Ideally, uses only those props normally available at a dinner table (napkins, knives, sugar lumps, saltshakers, goblets, etc), but often supplemented by pocket tricks.

(See also: table magic.) 1.n. Generally, the sub-class of close-up magic performed at table anywhere (usually seated, occasionally standing); table-work; Compare stand-up magic. [fairly common] Ideally, uses only those props normally available at a dinner table (napkins, knives, sugar lumps, saltshakers, goblets, etc), but often supplemented by pocket tricks.
n. A magician specialized in table magic. [rare]
a. Said either of an object that has been placed on a table or of cards that are shuffled on a table rather than entirely in the hands; table as adjective. [fairly common]
n. The removal of a card from a deck or packet other than the one apparently removed, such as while dealing seconds or bottoms. Also applied to coins. [rare]

a. A hollow, square, or oblong container that can be completely dismantled to "prove" it empty. Compare Tear-Apart Vanish. [rare] In use as early as 1923 when S.S. Henry employed it for a dove vanish. REF: Price (1985), 424.

n. The telltale sound of an object such as the clink of a coin, snap of a dealt card, chime of a watch, cackle of dice, pop of a thimble, or crinkle of stiff paper. Usually dissimulated, sometimes simulated. [rare]

n. An entire performance or segment throughout which the performer uses patter; a patter act (particularly in Britain). Opposite of a silent act. [fairly common] Originally vaudeville cant by 1898. REF: Boston Post (29 Mar 1898) re show at the Boston Palace that included Houdini; Laurie (1953). Thence magicians jargon by 1907 Hicks in CMM, 54, re Van Hoven as “a clever talking and magical act”; 1923 Dusenberry; 1943 Tarbell; 1947 Hay; 1948 Buckley; 1950 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1955 J. Marshall; 1984 Ammar; 1985 Vernon orally; 1989 G. Johnson in LR as "I do a talking act"; 1990 Booth; 1992 Witt in ABC of Faxic; 1998 Warlock in LR. Also as a "talking show" 1965/1988 Bamberg.

n. A free-standing wooden Buddha that answers questions in a muted human voice; the Whispering Buddha. [rare] Built by Carl Owen of Thayer's magic shop in Los Angeles on the suggestion of Claude Conlin in March 1919 by Thayer's as a follow-on to Thayer's Talking Vase of 1917. Both devices operated on the induction-coil principle that Conlin had pirated from David P. Abbott's Talking Teakettle of 1909. Owen made a total of 17 Talking Buddhas, which Thayer's sold not only to such professionals as mentalist-lawyer William Larsen Sr but also to such celebrities as banker A.P. Giannini and movie actress Marion Davies as toys for the rich. REF: Buffum (1977), 99-100; Alexander (1921), 23-24.

n. A human hand made up to look like a face and used as a ventriloquist's figure. The performer's thumb and forefinger form the lips and mouth. Compare hand puppet. [rare] Edwin Dawes once asserted that the "Talking Hand is of ancient origin" but traced its earliest pictorial representation only to a Hogarth print of 1755 and its first staging to English ventriloquist Albert Smith at Egyptian Hall in 1852. REF: Dawes (1979), 151-152.
n. Stage effect where a large open-front box is brought in on a wheelbarrow and shown to contain a lion's head that floats in space and talks and sings. [archaic]

n. Effect where a skull (real or dummy) answers questions by clicking its jaws or nodding. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common] Greek writer Lucian (AD 117-c180) exposed the humanoid-headed live snake of Alexander the Paphlagonian (a contemporary charlatan), which answered questions in a human voice speaking faintly through its opening and closing jaws. The real serpent's head was tucked under Alexander's arm; the fake head cradled in that arm; the jaws moved by horsehair; and the voice piped to the fake head through tubing from a concealed assistant. REF: Christopher (1973), 13. Then, by 1885 (Sachs, but not earlier edition), as a magicians trick, although posing as an anti-spiritualistic demonstration. In fact, it was so effective that some spiritualistic mediums adopted it, being advertised in the 1901 Sylvestre catalog as the "Spirit Skull of Althotas." These early versions all operated by an off-stage thread-puller. David P. Abbott (with the technical assistance of electrical engineer Charles W. Robbins) invented a particularly effective version that added an electromagnet to the old thread hook-up. He sold some 25 of these, including one to Kellar (in 1915) and another that he traded to HAN Ping-ch'ien (also in 1915). By 1908 Joseffy had invented the first entirely self-contained version, one that moved solely by clockwork, Joseffy simply timing his questions. REF: Chislett (1949), 47; D. Abbott (1934/1977), 11, 24, 35-37, 43-45; Cramer (1966), 85; D. Abbott (1908), 6-9. Originally called "The Animated Skull" in 1885 (Sachs). Jargon as the Talking Skull by 1895 Burlingame; 1898 Houdini cat; 1902 Stanyon in Magic; 1918 The Sphinx; 1921 Goldston; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1924 Heaney cat #25; 1927 Gibson; 1930 Ervin in Sphinx; 1939 Douglas cat; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1944 Larsen; 1945 Sterling cat #2; 1945 Wheeler cat; 1947 Kanter cat #8; 1947 Hay; 1949 Chislett; 1949 Tannen cat #1; 1950 Christopher in HMM; 1973 Alain; 1979 Lamb; 1984 Bamman in LR as obsolete; 1988 Waters; 1991 Walker; 1993 Ewing as historical; 1999 Abbott flyer.

n. A free-standing papier-maché kettle-shaped object that would answer (intelligently and in a human voice) questions put to it by a spectator when the latter placed its spout to his or her ear. 917 [archaic, formerly rare] Based on the wireless induction microphone principle discovered in 1885 by Edison. The first version (or so Joseph F. Rinn later recalled) was a teakettle used by medium R.W. Flint in the 1880s. A clumsy, heavy, sealed papier-maché kettle was built by William Meyers of Chicago but was unsuccessful because its mechanism was too obvious. Perfected in 1907 by wealthy Omaha amateur magician David P. Abbott. His papier-maché "kettle" had an induction coil concealed around the sides that did double-duty as a diaphram- speaker. Activated by electromagnetic induction and operated by an off-stage female assistant who listened in to questions with a microphone concealed in the performance room and answered over a speaker-system that activated the kettle's induction coil. Abbott supplied kettles to Kellar (in 1915), HAN Ping-chien (in 1915 or 1916), Hereward Carrington, Dr. Saram Ellison, and Thomas Chislett (in 1924). REF: D. Abbott (1934/1977), 9, 11, 38-43, 48-50; Rinn (1950), 10; Chislett (1949), 59; T. Bamberg (1952), 86; Alexander (1921), 24. Houdini fully and unconscionably exposed this trick in the Oct 1922 issue of Popular Radio Magazine. REF: Silverman (1996), 285 Revived by 1940 as a pet trick by Sonia Zaranoff and again in 1947 by Robert Nelson.

n. A free-standing papier-maché vase that would answer questions in a muted human voice. [archaic] Operated on the induction-coil principle of the Talking Teakettle that had been perfected in 1909 by David P. Abbott. This concept was pirated by Claude Conlin Sr ("Alexander") and merely adapted to a vase-shaped object (as well as to the Conlin-Thayer wooden Talking Buddha). Conlin's device was built by Carl Owen of Thayer's magic shop in Los Angeles and marketed as the "Voice from the Great Beyond" by Thayer's in Nov 1917, three years before the first commercial radio station began broadcasting in the USA. REF: Buffum (1977), 93, 98-99; Alexander (1921), 24.

n. The undealt portion of a deck of playing cards; the stock. [fairly common] Originally, in this sense, the lingo of card players since 1830. REF: OED/2 under "stock" as well as "talon". Thence the jargon of cardmen-magicians by 1947 Braue in HMM, 370; 1954 Vernon Sep 14th letter to Miller; 1955 V. St. John in Magic Wand; 1980 The Talon #1, magazine; 1984 Busby in Arcane #12; 1986 Willmarth in LR; 1988 Waters; 1989 McCarthy in Genii; 1990 Wedler; 1992 Riser in MUM; 1998 Racherbaumer in MUM.

n. A tambourine coil being the more usual synonym. [very rare] 918 "Tambo", as a contraction of tambourine, was originally (by 1848) minstrel-show cant, designating the black-faced endman who played the tambourines opposite "Bones" who played the bones. REF: OED/2; Waller (1948/1980), 84, 134.
n. The frames used to make a tambourine for the Tambourine Trick; Tambourine Rings. Not to be confused with Tambo Coils. [rare]

n. Old production effect where a vast pile of paper ribbon (tambourine coils) emerges from a tambourine. Now called the Drum Illusion. [obsolete, formerly fairly common] First explained in 1896 by both Roterberg (The Modern Magician, 95-99) and Burlingame (II, 28).
n. Tambo Rings being the more usual synonym. Not to be confused with tambourine coils. [rare]

n. Sideshow illusion where several tiny human figures performed upon a minature stage. [archaic] Human actors backstage are projected in a reduced image by a concave-mirror and lens arrangement. Invented by German illusionist Alexander Fürst in the late 1800s. Later patented by the Frenchman Sollé and exhibited in Paris in 1914. The apparatus was first made and marketed in 1914 by Carl Willmann of Hamburg. David "Fu-Manchú" Bamberg, who saw this effect presented at the old Kratky-Baschik magic theater in Vienna in 1924 called it "the most perfect optical illusion ever conceived." Kratky-Baschik's original apparatus was donated by Dr Hellmuth Teumer to the Kollmann Museum in Leipzig where it was destroyed by fire after a WW II Allied air raid. REF: Zmeck (1978), 345; Sharpe (1985), 161, crediting Sollé as the inventor; Heaney Magic Co., Catalog No.24 (ca1920), 87; Bamberg (1988), 103. 919 A scaled-down version (a living head in a glass bottle) was being performed by minor British music-hall illusionist Henry Phillips in the 1860s or 70s. REF: Clarke in The Magic Wand (Mar 1927), 193. The full-scale version played Coney Island after World War I for two years (including 1922) at the “Tanagra Theatre”. The apparatus was brought from Germany by one Blumenfeld, an optician employed by the Zeiss Optical Works. REF: Arthur Leroy in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Sep 1957), 47; Dunninger (1965), 69.

n. A holder made of perforated metal used to contain a smoldering load of pre-lit cigarettes. [once fairly common, now rare] In use for a single lit cigarette as early as 1929 but then called simply a "Cigarette Holder" (Gibson, 1929).

n. A dancing magician who performs one or more magic tricks while doing a tap-dance. [very rare, possibly nonce] "Miss Revelle commenced her act with a tap-dance routine, Lighted Cigarette production, catching the cigarettes as she danced." — Tony Taylor, Spotlight on 101 Great Magic Acts (1964), 64 "Tommy [Smothers] created this character, a tap-dancing magician, and I provided all the magic for it." — Blackstone Jr in Jeffreys (1988), 34 The first of this absurdly funny but happily rare breed was the little-known Renee Revelle by 1946 when she played the Beacon Theatre in Vancouver, Canada. The second and most recent was Tommy Smothers who acted this role in Brian De Palma's first movie, Get to Know Your Rabbit, in 1970 (although not released until 1972). Later in 1970 Smothers replayed this same role at Caesar's Palace in Las Vegas for 5 or 6 weeks with Blackstone Jr on stage in a comic battle of magicians. REF: Taylor (1964), 64; Jeffreys (1988), 34-35; Laurent Bozereau, The De Palma Cut (New York: Dembner Books, 1988), 29-30.

n. Type of loaded dice faked with internal mercury-filled channels, which when tapped ("for good luck") shifts the load to favor certain numbers. [archaic?] Reported in the USA as early as 1865 by Gerritt M. Evans. Originally invented by dice sharps for the game of Craps but, because they are necessarily and therefore suspiciously opaque, virtually obsolete. Also their unreliability holds little attraction for magicians. Indeed, Busby remarks "I have never heard of a magician who used them". Certainly anyone who heeds Scarne's advice on these miserable devices wouldn't! REF: Evans (1865); Scarne (1945); Busby 1988 annotation. Originally, as "Tapping Dice" or "Tappers", dice sharps argot by 1945 Scarne. As "Tapper Dice" by 1995 Rosenberger. Thence as tap dice magicians jargon by 1988 Waters.

n. The egg bag faked with a horizontal pocket one-third of the way up from the inside. Compare Sterling Egg Bag and Albini Egg Bag. [rare] This variant of the egg bag was invented by Dr. Harlan Tarbell and first published by him in 1927 in the Tarbell Course (Lesson 24, pp 6-7).

(See also: Rope Gimmick, which was the original and still most usual term..) n. Any fastener to secretly attach the ends of two ropes. [fairly common] Originally an artifice of escape artists to permit a quick release from rope bindings. Houdini's device of screw-threaded tapped-tube inserts to disconnect (and later, reconnect) rope ends by a half-turn during a spirit cabinet act was first exposed in 1912 by Will Goldston with Houdini's permission. REF: Goldston (1912), 285; Gibson (1930), 37. When around 1920 Dr. Harlan Tarbell substituted rope for string, thereby stimulating the Cut-and-Restored Rope routine craze, he borrowed the invention of the escapologists to provide the secret disconnection and reconnection. His modification of the old Cut-and- Restored String artifice of a wax or rubber cement join was required by the heavier ropes which could not be sufficiently strongly held together during the necessary naturalistic handling required. Initially, Tarbell used snap fasteners. Then, by 1930, engineer-magician Joseffy suggested the screw fastener, which Tarbell proceeded to design and adopt, calling it (since 1930) the Caesar Gimmick, presumably because of the pun on "seize" suggested by Tarbell's manufacturer, Frank Caesar, a Chicago dealer. Both the screw and snap types are also called the Tarbell Gimmick in mistaken honor of their non-inventor. In 1943 or 1944 Mystic Craig invented the magnetic fastener. REF: Hilliard (1938), 786-787; B. Elliott in Phoenix #1945, 351.
n. The cut-and-restored rope effect that uses the Rope Gimmick. [rare]

n. A deck of pictorial playing cards used for fortune-telling. Pronounced TAR-oh 921 [fairly common, particularly among mentalists] Created during the early 1400s by the aristocracy in northern in Italy by adding 22 new picture cards to the then standard deck of playing cards for a new trick-taking card game. This game and its special deck soon spread through France, Switzerland, & Germany. In the late 1700s the deck was first assigned occult significance and given false Egyptian (= Gypsy) origins by Antoine Court de Gebelin, a Protestant pastor and Freemason. As Tarot, the word entered Standard English in 1598 from the Middle French, tarots, which itself came from the Italian tarocchi. REF: Ronald Decker, Thierry Depaulis, & Michael Dummett, A Wicked Pack of Cards: The origins of the occult Tarot (London: Duckworth, 1996); OED/2; Jim Magus, Turn of a Friendly Card (1985, 40pp). Thence magicians jargon by 1945 Wheeler cat as "Tarot cards"; 1946 Gresham in Phoenix #115; 1948 Nelson cat #22 as “Tarot Cards”; 1948 Larsen; 1950 Messenger in Coven as "Tarot Cards"; 1958 Kanter cat #10 as "Tarot Fortune Telling Cards"; 1969 Nelms as the "tarots" and "tarot cards"; 1976 Raven; 1981 Waters; 1981 Lee cat #4; 1984 Saville & Dewey; 1986 Hades cat #2 as "Tarot Cards"; 1997 Lee cat #11 as "Tarot Cards".

n. Stage effect where a very large wooden cube (a typical box for shipping tea) is shown empty; four small chests of tea are emptied into the large one, which is then opened to reveal a female assistant and no tea. [rare]

n. Effect where livestock (such as a rabbit or two doves) are vanished from a box when the top, bottom, and sides are removed one-by-one and their newspaper-covered sides punched through by the magician's fist. Compare take-apart box, which has solid wood rather than paper. [fairly common] First marketed in the USA by Abbott's. A pet effect of Kalanag (in 1950s).

term: Tearing a Deck/Pack of Cards (in Two/in Half)
definition: n. Ripping a complete deck of 52 playing cards crosswise. Merely a flourish unless used in the Torn Card trick. "Contrary to belief, the tearing of a deck does NOT require strength at all. Merely a bit of leverage properly used does the trick for the weakest of people." — Annemann in The Jinx #66 (1939), 460 A pet trick of Alexander Herrmann (by 1887) and Harry Kellar. Exposed by Hilliard in 1909 (as "To Tear a Pack of Cards"). Later a pet effect of Claude Golden, Will Dexter, and John Mulholland (in 1941), but these cardmen used it as part of the Torn Card trick. The same technique can be used to tear a 500-page telephone directory in half. REF: Stanyon in Magic (Jun 1920), 68; Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jun 1946), 225. 922

n. Effect where beans or other small objects placed in the performer's mouth drop visibly and audibly from his eyes onto a plate. [rare] Originally a carnival and side-show trick. Introduced to magic in 1922 by American magus E. J. "Ernie" Moore with whom it became a pet effect in his vaudeville act. He also made a short film of this effect to run as a trailer at his theaters. REF: Price (1985), 271.

n. Psychokinesis (see) being the more usual synonym. [fairly common] Originally the cant of psychic researchers by 1890, having been then recently coined by A. Aksakof. REF: OED/2; L.C. Wimberly, "Spook English," American Speech (Mar 1926). Thence the jargon of mentalist-magicians by 1923 Newman in Sphinx; 1951 Hugard in HMM; 1959 Corinda; 1965 F. Greenfield in New Jinx #35 as trick title; 1975 Minch; 1976 Dalal in Mantra; 1981 Abbott cat #22; 1985 Warlock in LR; 1986 Golden Gate Magic ad in LR; 1986 Magicians' World Newsletter; 1988 Waters, 271; 1988 Select Magic cat; 1988 Magic Shop Hot Sheet; 1990 Wedler; 2003 Durant in LR. Also acronymed as "TK" in 1975 Minch.

n. Apparatus in form of an oblong wooden block that when placed in precarious balances eventually tips over or falls off. [rare] Inspired by Harbin's Little Tippler (1950), this self-contained prop was invented jointly by Jeff Busby (the angled 90-degree fall) and Don Albrecht (the fall off the bottle) in late 1981 when first marketed exclusively by Jeff Busby Magic, Inc, as Poltergeist Block with patter theme suggested by Max Mavin and Don Albrecht. Used by Kreskin on 2 May 1989 in his Houdini Seance at the American Museum of Magic and later in his TV magic special. Also used by Max Maven. Other more recent piracies appeared as the "Block of Foo Manchu" and "The Block".

n. A magician playing the role of a telepath. [rare] Originally the lingo of psychics by 1894. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1916 F. Thayer in Jul Magical Bulletin; 1939 Annemann; 1945 Newmann in Thompson; 1947 Rawson in HMM; 1984 Booth; 1985 Price.

n. The effect in mind-reading of paranormal communication between two minds; thought transference. [common] 924 “Even telepathy seems to me a striking case of the subjection of the intellect by the will-to- believe.” —Prof. G. Stanley Hall in Amy Tanner, Studies in Spiritism (1910), xxxi "Dunninger puts over a perfect illusion of telepathy, not only for the radio audience, but for the Studio audience as well." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Nov 1943), 23 "If any layman realizes that 'telepathy' and 'question reading' are mere tricks, he immediately loses interest. It does not, in fact, have any entertainment value." — David Price, Magic (1985), 439 The word telepathy was coined from its Greek roots (tele + pathy, meaning literally "distant feeling") in 1882 by British psychic researcher and classical scholar Frederick W.H. Myers. REF: OED/2.

(See also: Telephone Trick.) n. Effect where a volunteer chooses a card, calls a telephone number provided by the mentalist, and hears the person who answers name that card; telephone test. [fairly common] This ever-popular trick requires a code and a confederate at the answering end of the phone.

n. Effect where a volunteer chooses a card, calls a telephone number provided by the mentalist, and hears the person who answers name that card; telephone test. [fairly common] This ever-popular trick requires a code and a confederate at the answering end of the phone.

n. Effect where an object or person is instantly moved from one place to another; a transposition being the more usual synonym. [rare] This word was coined (from the Greek tele ["far"] + Latin porto ["carry"]) in 1931 by Charles Hoy Fort (1874-1932) in Lo! to categorize one of the "wild talents" that he devoted the last 26 years of his life researching. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1969 Nelms; 1969 Fulves; 1974 Shiels in Peninsular West; 1979 Kaye in My Brother, the Druggist novel; 1987 Busby in Short Sheet #13; 1990 Wedler; 1996 Silverman. NOTE: Also as verb to "teleport" in 1969 Fulves. a. [adjectivally] [very rare]

n. Conjuring performed before the TV camera. [rare] "Television magic is easy once you learn to control its limited field of vision." — Ben Harris, Gellerism Revealed (1985), 21 Pioneering performances of magic on TV include the following. First was Allan Hale on 9 Jan 1931 in a broadcast from a London studio of the Vanishing Cigarette, T&R Card, and Pase- Passe Cards. Johnnie Giordmaine on closed-circuit at Eaton's department store in Canada on 28 Aug 1933. Next on broadcast TV was Fred Culpitt on the premier BBC experimental show in 1936, followed by Gali-Gali with close-up in New York on 15 Sep 1939, Jay Marshall on Dumont TV in New York in 1940, Dr & Mrs Aaron Weiss with escapism in New York on 31 Oct 1946, Milbourne Christopher on WCBS-TV in New York in Feb 1947, and Frank Garcia in New York in 1948. 926 By 1948 there were only 8 thousand TV sets in America but the industry then exploded to 2.5 million sets in 1949, 4 million in 1950, and 31 million in 1955. Subsequently TV has become the most important showcase for magic. The longest-running weekly TV magic show was Dick Williams’ “Magicland”, which was seen 1966-1989 for nearly 1,200 wekly shows. REF: Magic Wand (Mar 1931 & Oct-Nov 1936); Annemann in Jinx (1939), 436; J. Marshall (1955), 3, 105, 111-113; Booth (1990), 18-63; Christopher (1973), 405, 409, 426-430; B. Harris (1985), 21-22; Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jan 1947), 288. The two best presentational books are Marshall (1955) and Williams (1994).

n. Any unintended discrepancy in a trick that could tip the method used to a careful spectator. [rare] Originally the argot of card sharps by 1982 Hayano; 1984 Ortiz, derived from the old noun “tell-tale”; 1987 David Mamet’s movie House of Games. Thence magicians jargon by 1987 Busby in Short Sheet as "but the ‘tell' is still there"; 1991 Ortiz as "attempts to eliminate this tell"; 1997 Racherbaumer in LR as "a ‘tell' (as poker players are want [sic] to say)".
n. Trick pack of playing cards that enables the magus to name the card peeked in a deck that has been shuffled, bound in a rubber-band, and tossed out to the spectator. [rare]

(See also: Temple of Benares.) n. Stage illusion where the assistant enters a small, ornate box (decorated as an oriental temple) that is closed and impaled with several swords; the box is opened to show the assistant has vanished; the box is again closed; the swords withdrawn; and the assistant emerges unharmed. [fairly common]

n. Stage illusion where the assistant enters a small, ornate box (decorated as an oriental temple) that is closed and impaled with several swords; the box is opened to show the assistant has vanished; the box is again closed; the swords withdrawn; and the assistant emerges unharmed. n. A four-panelled screen (each panel 9x12-inches) cleverly hinged so they can always be convincingly shown as three. Used to produce small items. [common] "All those who can't do a decent Half Pass by March 30 will be sentenced to perform Grant's Temple Screen between strippers in a filthy nightclub in Oklahoma City for the rest of eternity." — Richard Kaufman in Genii (Dec 1987), 398

n. The pace (and its variations) at which the magician does a trick, routine, or act. Compare timing and temps. [rare] "The tempo of his [Chang's] show was slower than that of some of the other big shows of today. As the reader will gather, this fact counts with me as a recommendation." — Charles Waller, Magical Nights at the Theatre (1948/1980), 233

n. On the off-beat, which is the later and still current synonym; the timely moment for a sleight or other action to occur unnoticed; the timing (1). [rare] "The French use the term 'temps' (time) to denote a time or favorable moment for executing a sleight or secret movement, just as we now use, 'timing'." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jun 1952), 952

n. A refined version of the thumb tie. [fairly common] 928 Introduced to Western audiences by Japanese magician "Ten-Ichi" (Shokyuku HATTORI) in 1901 during his first tour of American vaudeville. In London, on his last tour in 1905, Ten-Ichi taught his method to Carl Rosini who made it a pet effect. A pet effect of Maki KITAMI (in 1986). n. The sleight that conceals a face-up card in one hand under a palmed card dropped from the other hand. [rare]

n. A trick in mental magic but falsely implying possible failure because it pretends to depend on the vagaries of paranormal mental abilities; experiment. [common] Developed by fraudulent psychic mediums in the mid-1800s, because they needed the excuse of possible failure in those occasional circumstances where they felt they had to abort a trick for fear of being exposed. Major examples are the billet test, blindfold test, book test, living and dead test, and slate test. Originally the argot of spirit mediums by 1880 Vere; 1891 A. Medium; 1901 Sylvestre cat; 1907 D. Abbott; 1952 Zolotow. Thence magicians jargon by 1895 Burlingame; 1896 as a slate test; 1897 Caulk in Hopkins as "rope tests"; 1903 as a ballot test; 1922 as a living and dead test; 1924 Heaney cat #25; 1925 Zancig in Osirian; 1926 as a book test; 1929 Gibson; 1931 as a magazine test; 1932 as a newspaper test; 1932 as a telephone-book test; 1933 Annemann; 1935 as a blindfold test; 1935 as a telephone test; 1938 Ross, Nov 30th letter to Fox; 1944 as a billet test; 1947 Buckley & Cook; 1974 Dunninger; 1979 Fulves; 1982 R. Dorian in Sperber; 1993 Mann flyer; 1996 Kreskin pattering on TV.

n. Circumstances where the method of a trick is seemingly vulnerable to detection. [fairly common] "Except under test conditions no one can blindfold your eyes so as to prevent your being able to see!" — William Larsen Sr (1944) Usually used in connection with psychic tricks but sometimes in a challenge.
See: "how it's done". (No further definition found in this dictionary for ""how it's done"".)

1.n. Sideshow illusion where the living head and bust of the female assistant is suspended in mid-air. [archaic] Being static, this illusion is usually presented as a sideshow exhibit. Invented by British illusionist Dr. H.S. Lynn. Seen by Lewis Carroll at the Aquarium, Brighton, on 20 Sep 1884. Also staged at the Folies-Bergère in Paris. REF: Sharpe (1985), 37; Hopkins (1897), 63; Stanyon in Magic (Sep 1901), 102.

n. The performance of simulated miracles; thaumaturgics (obsolete). [obsolescent after 1943, formerly rare] From the Greek thauma ["wonder"] + ergon ["work"]. Standard English from around 1727 when, however, its meaning was literal. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon by 1868 M. Dockweiler, recalling in the Apr 1901 Mahatma, a trick title from his 1867-68 program; 1938 Annemann in Jinx #51 as "trod the trail of thaumaturgy"; 1943 Welles playbill; 1992 Randi.

n. The plot (1) being the more usual synonym. [rare] “For my money one of the best plots on which to hang a sequence of magical effects is the perverse magic theme.” — Clayton Rawson in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jul 1950), 678

n. Amusement parks whose buildings and settings are built around a central motif such as fairyland or wild west. Although the term "theme park" was not coined until 1960, the institution began earlier in the USA (near Los Angeles) with Disneyland in 1955. It quickly spread to Italy (early 1960s?), West Germany (1966), Belgium (late 1960s), Puerto Rico (1967), France (1987), and other countries. Popular American ones that feature magicians among their other entertainers are Knott's Berry Farm, Marriott's Great America, Busch Gardens, Dogpatch USA, and the soon-to-open Maharishi Vedaland Theme Park in India (designed by Doug Henning). Typically performers play 6 shows per day, 6 days per week. REF: Doug Anderson, Straight Talk about Theme Park Magic (1984).
n. Effect where stabbing the shadow of an object causes the object to be destroyed. [archaic, once fairly common]
n. The set of general principles that explains what makes the art of conjuring deceptive. Compare the principles of magic. [rare]

n. A playing card of extra thickness used as a key card; a double card (2). Not to be confused with a wide card. [fairly common] Originally an artifice of card sharps by 1843 (Crambrook cat as the "Old Gentleman"; 1858 Green). Thence adopted by magicians by 1914 (Stanyon in Magic; and 1926 Gibson/Thurston).
n. A routine or complete act of thimble manipulation; the thimbles (2). [rare]
n. The sleight-of-hand routine using sewing thimbles; thimble magic; the thimbles (2). [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]
