definition: n. The modern shallow-box version of Sawing a Woman in Half. [fairly common] Originally designed in 1924 by American illusion designer Guy Jarrett as a 12" high and 16" wide box with a trap out the back but never built. Independently reinvented by Turkish magician Zati Sungur in 1932, traded by him to Tihanyi who took it to Owen Magic in California where Carl Owen and John Daniel evolved the still-current trapless 13" x 24" stage version. Harry Willard built his own version of tin around 1938. REF: Steinmeyer in Jarrett (1981), 59-60; And (1978), 54-55; Buffum (1977), 159-160; R.W. Read in LR (Jan 1988), 42.
n. Mental magic version of the Stop Trick where the spectator merely thinks the word "stop" while the performer deals the cards and the selected card is found at that place. [rare]

n. The magician's demonstration of the old con-game where the 24 aces through sixes of a deck are laid out in 6 rows (one for each value) and the two players alternate in turning up cards until one has totalled 31 pips and won or the other has exceeded that number and lost. Not to be confused with the old French casino card game of trente et un, which was also sometimes known in English as Thirty-One. [fairly common] Reportedly introduced to America by the Englishman, Charles James Fox ("Dr. Bennett"), for his amusement and, no doubt, profit, sometime in the early 1800s. The reference is possibly to the famous English Liberal politician, Charles James Fox (1749-1806), who was indeed an avid gambler and active supporter of the American colonies. The game is also called "Nim" since 1901. REF: Wyman in The Magician's Own Book (1857), 71; Green (1868), 48; Stanyon in Magic (1913), 29, 53-54; Barnhart (1983), 66; OED/2. Originally the argot of con-men by 1857 Wyman in Magician's Own Book; 1868 Green. Thence magicians jargon (variants noted) by 1857 Wyman in Magician's Own Book; 1910 Devant, 53; 1913 Stanyon in Magic; 1931 P. Abbott; 1945 Wheeler cat as "The Game of 31"; 1947 Abbott cat #9 as "The Game of 31"; 1948 Kaplan; 1969 Lowe lecture notes; 1972 Anderson; 1975 Trost; 1981 Supreme cat #30; 1982 Toto; 1985 Neale; 1988 Waters as the "Game of Thirty-One"; 1996 ["1997"] L&L cat.
n. A windlass (reel) with a very long (30 to 40 foot) strand of thread. 936 [archaic]
1.n. A mindreader (see). [rare]

n. Any strand of fine hair, cotton thread, nylon, or plastic monofiliment used secretly to transmit the motive power for many tricks; so-called silk thread. See also invisible thread [very common] "I sincerely pity those sorcerers whose supernatural power hangs on a thread." — Robert-Houdin, Memoirs (1858/1859 tr), Ch.15 "The educated man, his eyes dimmed by the knowledge of many wonders, overlooks the fine black thread which pulls the spirit hand, and says: 'Wonderful!'" — Frank W. Thomas, "The Confessions of a Conjurer", Saturday Evening Post (31 Oct 1900) First exposed in 1584 by Prevost in France where a human hair was used to make a ring jump into a drinking glass. And later that same year by Reginald Scot in England where a long black hair was used to make a coin jump out of a pot and dance on the table. Next in 1612 by S. Rid, where "a long black haire of a womans head" is used to pull a coin across a table. REF: Baker (1951), 9-11.

n. Magicians' demonstration of the card sharps' "short con" where the dealer ("tosser") bets the spectator ("sucker") that he cannot keep track of one of three cards as they are repeatedly tossed ("thrown") upon the table in more-or-less dazzling but seemingly fair manner. The Three-Card Trick is the British synonym; Effo the Elephant is a kid-show version; Two Card Monte is a version with only two playing cards. [common in U.S. usage, very rare in British] "His [Kaufmann's] three-card-monte, using the turn-over, is the most deceptive bit of sleight-of- hand in the world." — Henry Ridgely Evans, "American Notes", Magic (Oct 1903), 9 "We thoroughly agree with Erdnase that no card feat will give as good returns for the practice expended as the grand old pastime of three card monte." — Dai Vernon, Revelations (1984), 121 Henri Decremps, writing in 1786, describes a primitive four-card version as played by French sharpers of the time. This con game evidently developed its elegant modern three-card form in Mexico whence it reached New Orleans by 1837 when one Mr. Phillips was fined and the game outlawed, not to return until the outbreak of the Mexican-American War in 1846. George Devol (writing in 1887) recalled and described a game he operated on the Mississippi around 1853. It was reported in 1857 by Green as a popular game in New Orleans coffee houses. Quinn (writing in 1890) recalled losing a game in Kansas in 1860. It was also being played on the streets of Paris by 1861 (Taylor) and in Scotland by 1865 (Taylor). First adopted and adapted by magicians as a demonstration of gambling tricks in 1876 by Professor Hoffmann. In 1908 American card-magic inventor-dealer Theodore DeLand introduced the first gaffed-card version in his "Pickitout" trick, followed by his Two Card Monte. Monte workers have evolved ten quite different methods to induce the sucker to pick the wrong card. Often two or three of these methods would be alternated during play. In chronological order of reported invention these were (with non-USA locations specified): 1. Sheer razzle-dazzle confusion by 1868 (Evans, in Dick & Fitzgerald revised edition only). I suspect this is a false explanation by D&F's ill-informed editor. 2. Crimping/uncrimping (the bent corner) by 1872 (Toulmin in Britain; 1876 Hoffmann in Britain; 1887 Devol; 1890 Grannan; 1891 Quinn; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne in Britain; 1896 Kid Royal; 1896 Bertram in Britain; 1902 Erdnase; 1903 Carter; 1905 Johnson; 1910 Kid Canfield; 1911 Meyer; 1911 Adams in Australia; 1914 Gaultier in France; 1927 Merlin; 1933 Goldston in Britain; 1933 Walsh & Scarne; 1955 Ganson/Endfield; 1984 Ortiz). 3. Marking/unmarking by 1872 (Toulmin in Britain; 1877 Henry Hoyt diary; 1877 Devol; 1891 Quinn; 1911 Adams in Australia; 1933 Walsh & Scarne; 1955 Ganson/Endfield). 4. Underthrowing/overthrowing by 1876 (Hoffmann in Britain; 1891 Quinn; 1894 J.N. Maskelyne in Britain; 1896 Bertram in Britain; 1902 Erdnase; 1903 Carter; 1911 Adams in Australia; 1914 Gaultier in France; 1927 Merlin; 1933 Walsh & Scarne; 1955 Ganson/Endfield in Britain; 1984 939 Ortiz). 5. Second dealing by 1876 (Cremer in Britain). 6. A misspotted card by 1886 (Garenne in Britain; 1903 Carter, noting its almost exclusive use in the USA, rarely—if ever—in Britain; 1911 Meyer; 1914 DeLand cat). 7. Holding and then throwing one-by-one all three cards from one hand by 1891 (Quinn; 1896 Bertram in Britain where the target card was a short; 1905 Johnston). 8. Affixing/detaching a bit of spit-dampened paper by 1894 (J.N. Maskelyne in Britain; 1949 W.R. Woodfield Jan 9th letter to Audley Walsh, with San Francisco blacks; 1949 Walsh May 5th letter to Woodfield, with New York subway gangs). 9. The Mexican Turnover change by 1897 (Roterberg; 1902 Erdnase; 1933 Walsh & Scarne; 1984 Ortiz). 10. The "Flip" change by 1933 (Walsh & Scarne). 11. Using a Short Card for one of the indifferent cards by 1948 (Phoenix #143). The term "Three-Card Monte" was standard argot among American card sharps since 1854 as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1865 G.M. Evans, 65; 1873 Morris; 1876 Cremer, 180, citing non-British usage; 1877 Grandin pricelist; 1878 Long; 1887 Devol; 1891 Quinn; 1902 Erdnase; 1905 Johnson; 1909 Irwin; 1911 Meyer. Thence magicians jargon (variant noted) by 1897 Roterberg; 1900 Triplett, 20, as “The Three Card Monte Trick”; 1903 Carter; 1903 H.R. Evans in Magic; 1914 DeLand cat; 1924 Heaney cat #25; 1927 Merlin; 1928 Thayer cat #7; 1929 Gibson; 1933 Scarne & Walsh; 1939 Kanter cat; 1951 Grant; 1956 Ganson/Endfield; 1964 Judah; 1967 Tarr; 1979 Ortiz; 1980 Tannen cat #13; 1981 Abbott cat #22; 1988 Waters; 1989 Sheets in Q; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1991 Ortiz; 1992 Randi; 1994 Yedid flyer; 1997 A-1 flyer; 1997 Abbott cat #25; 2000 L&L cat #13; 2001 Magic
n. Illusion where three figures are produced in succession from a cabinet that had been previously shown empty. [rare]

n. The mini-version of the Cups and Balls trick that substitutes three "walnut" shells (real or plastic) and a "pea" (a sponge-rubber pellet); the Shell Game; Thimble Rig; Pea and Thimbles (obsolete). Shown by magicians only as a demonstration of the old "sucker's game" of that name. [fairly common] Early British "blacklegs" used either a real pea, small ball, or a piece of red brick. Magicians usually used an india-rubber pellet by 1902 (Mahatma; 1912 Stanyon in Magic) and later a sponge-rubber one, although a few conjurors preferred natural sponge. Based quite likely on the ancient Cups-and-Balls, this sharpers scam probably developed in England where it was first reported in 1716 by English poet and dramatist John Gay in his Trivia: or, The Art of Walking the Streets of London. Gay called it the "Thimble's Cheats" and describes it as played with "three Thimbles and a little Ball." Villany Unmask'd, an anonymously written book published in London in 1752 describes the game being played with thimbles and a button. The use of a pea with the three thimbles is reported in 1825 in Hone's Every Day Book. The game was introduced to magicians in 1843 in the world's earliest known magic catalog, W.H.M. Crambrook's, where it was called "Thimbles and Pea." REF: OED/2; Dawes (1979), 47; Read (1938), 5-7; Scarne (1961), 516-518; Toole Stott, II (1972), 106, 116. NOTE the mistranslation of "jeu des gobeletz" [the Cups & Balls] as "thimble rig" in the Penguin Books edition of Rabelais's Pantagruel (1532). This "game" eventually migrated to America. Green (writing in 1844) recalls the educational experience of being the dupe in a game of the "thimbles" played with a round natural sponge or paper pellet in Mr. Shibbley's ten-pin bowling alley in Cincinatti in 1829 when the then callow 16-year old vagabond was taken for all his savings. A Mississippi River gambler named Dr. Bennett claimed to have invented the game (Green, 1868); but this was untrue as it had been in existence almost a half-century before the septuagenarian Bennett's birth. In any case, the game was always and on both sides of the Atlantic considered declassé, even among other gambling cheats. Play was largely confined to fairs, race-tracks, amusement centers, and other mass sporting locales. Around 1890 some clever American sharper substituted walnut shells. Since then the public has called this con "The Three-Shell Game," "The Shell Game," or "The Pea and Shell Game." But the operators have long known it simply as "the nuts" (Scarne 1961; Ortiz 1984) and recently as "the blocks" by 1984 (Ortiz). Still later some other ingenious American grifter 941 substituted bottle caps for the walnut shells and a mashed pellet of bread dough for the "pea"; and this is its most usual form seen today. In Britain, this game was called by sharpers the "thimble rig" by 1825 (Hone as cited in the OED/2), "thimblerigging" by 1839 (Thackeray as cited in the OED/2), and the "Thimbles" by 1876 (Cremer). In America, sharpers called it variously "The Game of Thimbles," "Thimbles," "Little Joker," or "Best Two in Three," all by 1868 (Green); "thimble-rigging" in 1873 (Morris), and "Thimble Rig" by 1911 (Meyer). In America the operator was called a "thimbler" by 1844 (Green) and a "thimble-rigger" by 1868 (Green; 1873 Morris; 1911 Meyer). The term Shell Game originated in the argot of American gambling cheats by 1890 as earliest citation in the OED/2; 1891 Quinn; 1910 Kid Canfield; 1911 Meyer. Thence as Three-Shell Game magicians jargon by 1902 Mahatma; 1928 Thayer cat #7; 1931 Douglas cat #16; 1934 Chanin; 1935 Abbott cat #3; 1936 Holden cat #5; 1938 Read; 1938 Osborne; 1942 Ireland cat #10; 1945 Sterling cat #2; 1945 Wheeler cat; 1949 Tannen cat #1 as "3 Shell Game"; 1951 Scarne; 1959 Joseph; 1966 Inzani-Henley cat #1; 1976 Tarr; 1986 Hades cat #2; 1990 Select Magic price list; 1993 KT Magic cat; 1995 Tannen cat #18; 1996 Vernet ad in Witt; 1997 Lee cat #11; 1997 Abbott cat #25; 1999 Diamond’s Magic flyer; 2003 Vernet Internet cat.

definition: n. Stage effect where an assistant enters one of two barrels set together and separated by a thick metal disk with a 2-inch hole and emerges from the other. [rare]

Thence magicians jargon by 1933 Walsh & Scarne; 1950 Hay; 1955 T. Cooper in Magic Wand as "the 'Throw'"; 1955 Ganson/Endfield; 1964 Judah; 1981 Walton; 1986 Dawes & Setterington; 1991 Busby in Whaley; 1991 Ortiz. v. To deal (toss) Three-Card Monte. [rare] Card sharps argot by 1891 Quinn; 1902 Erdnase; 1982 Turpin in Magic Info recalling the 1930s. Sharps also called this "throwing" in 1891 Quinn. Thence magicians jargon by 1903 Carter; 1933 Walsh & Scarne; 1940 Charlton in Jinx #107; 1956 Endfield in Ganson/Endfield; 1981 Walton as to "Monte throw". 2.v. To toss a specific group of playing cards from the bottom to the top of the deck during an overhand shuffle. [rare] Originally card sharps argot by 1902 Erdnase, 27. Thence magicians jargon by 1902 Erdnase/Harto, 194, as "run seven and throw balance on top"; 1987 Waters; 1988
1.n. SEE: Throw-Out Coil
n. Playing card specially printed with the magician's picture, greeting, or advertising, usually made extra-thick (heavy) for card-scaling to the audience. 943 [rare]
n. The sleight that makes a silent enumeration of a desired number of playing cards while riffling the edge of the deck with the thumb. [fairly common]

1.n. The sleight that holds objects (such as coins or a billiard-ball half-shell) between the flexed first and second joints of the thumb; thumb palm (2.n., obsolete). [very rare] 944 An unnatural position for the thumb, but it does free the fingers.

1.n. The sleight that conceals a small object (usually a coin, thimble, ball, or cigarette) upright (instead of horizontally) between the base of the thumb and the first finger; the Italian palm (obsolete); the Frikell palm (obsolete); the pincette (obsolete); the pinch (obsolete). [common] This sleight was first published in 1854 by Ponsin.

1.n. The palming sleight that uses an injogged card to lever up the top card into the palm of the other hand. [obsolescent]

1.v. To disclose a secret method, either inadvertently during performance or by deliberate explanation; tipping; to expose. [common] “Personally, I get upset when I see someone ‘butcher’ what should be a beautiful classic of magic. Is it any wonder why so many ‘heavies’ won’t ‘tip’ their best stuff.” w. Daryl Martinez, Daryl (1980), 2 “With edge work you don’t want to appear to be looking at the deck, otherwise you’ll tip what you’re using.” w. Jeff Busby, The Secret of the Palmettos (1998), 52 Underworld contraction by 1948 of the popular slang phrase to “tip-off,” which itself had been coined by 1929. REF: Wentworth & Flexner (1975 ed); Ortiz (1984).

n. The concept that any method that has been stripped of all but one discrepancy (weak point) is more vulnerable to detection than a method that has more. [rare] "This simply means that an effect can be so perfect that it allows of only one possible solution. Under such circumstances, there is a danger that astute spectators will jump to a rather obvious conclusion." — Ellison Poland in Rick Johnsson, Practical Impossibilities (1976), xv This most interesting but controversial concept was first articulated by American magician Rick Johnsson in 1970 as "an extension of some thoughts Leo Behnke and I kicked around in the late fifties." While Johnsson applies it specifically to the theory of magic, it is equally applicable to the general theory of deception. In my view, Johnsson's Too Perfect principle holds true only for those (all too frequent) cases where the one remaining discrepancy cannot be adequately camouflaged. REF: Poland in Johnsson (1976), xv; Johnsson, "Come a Little Closer", Linking Ring (Nov & Dec 1984); Jim Buffaloe in Linking Ring (Dec 1987), 81.

n. A sleight that palms the top card of a deck. More often used than the bottom palm, its antonym. [fairly common] The term originated as American card sharps argot by 1902 (Erdnase, 83). Thence (through Erdnase) introduced to magicians jargon in 1911 Hoffmann in Magic Wand; 1950 Hay; 1961 Green; 1976 Tarr; 1978 Müller; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1991 Ortiz; 1992 Racherbaumer in LR; 1992 Burt ad in Genii; 1997

n. The pocket work sleight of poking any small palmed object (card, etc) into the upper far corner of a vertically cut trouser pocket, which may then be pulled out to show it apparently empty, as the "dead corner" is not exposed. Compare double pocket. [fairly common]

n. A special type of body servante in the form of a detachable cloth pocket that can be pinned under the magician's clothing at unsuspected places; a poacher's pocket. [common] Used mainly for ditching but also, occasionally, for stealing. Originally, as a "poacher's pocket" used by British poachers to hide their illicitly trapped or shot game. This artifice was later adopted by pickpockets and shoplifters to evade initial suspicion and, if pressed, a conventional search. Finally adapted to magic in 1919 by British magician Harold Comden as a card vanisher. Used with good effect by a very few magicians such as George Davenport, Topper Martyn, Patrick Page, Fred Kaps, and Bob Fitch; but it did not become widely known much less appreciated and used until after publication in 1983 of Michael Ammar's comprehensive manual, Ammar himself having discovered Topit in 1978 or 79. REF: Busby in Epoptica #4 (1983), 217-218; Farelli in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1953), 63; Fitch (1980).
n. Conjuring with playing cards whose plane has been secretly altered by folding or cutting. [rare]
n. Topological magic with playing cards. [rare]
n. Any specific effect or method in topological magic. [very rare]
n. Effect where a wooden matchstick run head-first through a slender tube emerges reversed. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common]
n. The Torn and Restored Card (see) trick being the modern synonym. [obsolete]
n. The effect where a banknote is cut and restored. [rare] A pet effect of Johnny Paul.

n. The effect where a playing card is ripped into several parts yet later found whole; the Torn Card Trick. [rare] By the late 1790s this trick was being performed (but by burning the card) by Gregory at London's Bartholomew Fair. Before around 1888 the effect was commonly worked by a mechanical flap-card, one corner of which folds back out of sight. This was succeeded by the methods using other types of fake cards and/or sleights.
n. Effect where a cigarette is shredded by hand and later shown whole. [rare]

n. A Torn and Restored Paper effect as done with a newspaper; the Newspaper Tear. [common] The very large size paper sheets makes this version of the T&R Paper particularly suitable for stage production. Invented (as first noted by Jeff Busby) by British magician Hugall Benedict by 1903. Popularized by "Cortini" (Paul Korth), a German professional magician. Marketed in the USA by Brema in 1928 with his own "new and improved method". Al Baker marketed his method by 1932. Another version invented by Jean Hugard was premiered by Herman Hanson in Apr 1932 in the Thurston show in San Diego. A pet effect of Jean Hugard (1930s), Joe Karson (in 1930s using, according to Busby, an unprepared newspaper), Al Koran (in 1940s), Slydini (in 1950s), Robert Harbin, Gene Anderson, Doug Henning, Terry Seabrooke, and Nick Lewin (1990s). REF: H. Benedict in Magic (Apr 1903), 62; Holden (1937), 9; Hanson & Zweers (1974), 50. "So far as I can find, the early Magi did not perform the 'Torn and Restored Newspaper' but that, perhaps, is just as well after all." — H. Adrian Smith, "More About Hocus Pocus Junior", Tops (Oct 1941)

n. Effect where a small piece of paper is ripped to pieces and later shown intact; paper tearing(1); a paper tear. [fairly common] Popularized by Chinese magician Ching Ling FOO after he came to the USA in 1898. Also a pet effect of Chinese magician HAN Ping-chien during his USA tour in 1914-15, at which time (1915) he taught it to Omaha amateur David P. Abbott in exchange for Abbott's Talking Teakettle and Talking Skull. Later a pet effect of T. Nelson Downs (in 1926). REF: W.B. Graham in D. Abbott (1977), 11.
See: De Grisy, Edmond. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "De Grisy, Edmond".)

n. Effects of gore, pain, or dismemberment. [rare] "This effect [The Chinese Strangulation Rack] is gruesome but they liked it. Take Sawing, for example, or any of those burning, shooting, tearing illusions. ... The sleights and artistic magic, they don't lose their hair over. They like to see someone in pain." — David Bamberg in The Sphinx (Feb 1928), 471 Prime examples are the Buzz-Saw Illusion, Decapitation, Guillotine, Finger Chopper, Human Pincushion, Needle thru Arm, Sawing a Woman in Two, and Tongue Cutting. English magician P. T. Selbit was the most prolific inventor of such effects. They form the veritable blood-and-bones of the French Grand Guignol and are a frequent theme in Bizarre Magick.
n. The throw (in Three-Card Monte) being the more usual synonym.

n. Mental card effect where magus takes a deck, puts a heavy rubber band around its middle and tosses it to any spectator, telling that person to lift up at any point in the deck and peek that card, remember it, and toss the deck to another audience member. That person then does the same. After the third spectator has peeked into the bound deck, the magus names three cards and the three persons agree that he called theirs. Compare Telomatic Deck. [rare]

n. Effect where magicians writes prediction of two playing cards and places them on the table; then two spectators freely choose two cards from a ribbon-spread face-up deck and place them on table; the cards match the predictions. [rare] "So you can do 'Touch' with pure sleight-of-hand. You won't approach the natural moves possible with Paul Curry's special pack." — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Mar 1958), 114

n. The French drop (see) being the newer and more usual synonym. [obsolescent, formerly common] Originally the Standard French word le tourniquet, meaning to turn. Thence French magicians jargon by 1868 Robert-Houdin. Thence English-speaking magicians jargon by 1876 Hoffmann; 1899 Stanyon #1; 1927 Orrin; 1937 Clark; 1941 Tarbell; 1949 Hay; 1951 Ganson; 1979 Lamb; 1980 J. Marshall; 1988 Waters. a. [adjectivally] [obsolete, formerly very rare, possibly nonce]
n. Later version of the Himber Ring consisting of a plain wedding band. [rare]
a. Acronym of torn and restored. [fairly common]

1.n. Generally, the effect where one object changes into another object or changes a characteristic. [fairly common] Small-scale transformations (as with playing cards) are usually called color-changes. The method is called a switch.
n. A quick-change artist, specifically one who transforms himself into an assistant or vice-versa. [obsolete, formerly very rare]
n. A playing card faked with two layers to show one value under subdued lighting and another value under stronger lighting. [rare]

n. A see-through force bag. [rare] Somewhat of a misnomer, as the transparency feature makes it impossible to "change" one type of object into a visually different one unless all the objects are packaged alike. However, the transparency makes this device much more convincing for forcing than the old opaque change bag.
n. Slangy abbreviation of transposition. Used only in titles of tricks such as Treasury Transpo. [fairly common]

n. The effect of an object vanishing at one location and reappearing in another; a transpo. [common] "With any transposition trick, it is crucial that the spectators understand what is where before the transposition or there is no effect when things change places." — Phil Willmarth in The Linking Ring (Sep 1986), 87 965 All transposition effects combine two separate methods: a vanish of something followed by its production.

n. A concealed flap or door in the magician's stage floor (a stage trap), backing scene, table (a trap table), or box; a trapdoor. Traps are used to either produce or vanish objects. Specialized types include the elevator trap, rabbit trap, star trap, wrist trap, and the trapdoor. [very common] The trap originated in Italian Baroque theaters with their mechanical stage fitted with elaborate devices to enhance illusion in opera and drama. The oldest surviving Baroque stage—fitted with movable traps—is the Drottningholm Court Theatre in Sweden, which was built in 1766. Those conjurors who first got off the streets and onto the stage in the 1700s adapted this useful idea and fitted traps to their tables. Use of a table trap in conjuring was first described in 1784 by Decremps in exposing a contemporary trick by Pinetti. Originally (and still) theatrical lingo from at least as early as 1800 OED/2; 1838 Dickens/Grimaldi. Thence magicians borrowed both the device and its word as jargon by 1785 Denton; 1815 Ingleby; 1829 Boy’s Own Book; 1876 Cremer; 1879 Judd cat as "trappe"; 1896 Bertram; 1898 N.M. Hopkins; 1901 Stanyon in Magic as "The rabbit ... disappears through trap in chair."; 1909 Houdini as a "table trap"; 1912 Goldston; 1923 Leat; 1923 J.W. Elliott; 1924 Felsman cat #18 as a “Ball or Orange Trap” & “black art traps”; 1928 Thayer cat #7 as "floor traps"; 1972 Griffin; 1973 Alain; 1980 J. Marshall; 1983 Sharpe, 116; 1988 Waters; 1989 Blanchard in MC; 1991 KT Magic cat #3; 1993 Gloye in LR; 1998 Dimmare in MUM as a “full-length body trap”; 2006 Bergeron in LR as “a stage trap”. w. [adjectivally] [fairly common]
n. Any hinged flap-type trap. [rare]
n. A topological card trick. [rare]

n. A magician's table fitted with one or more traps. [archaic] Use of a table trap in conjuring was first described in 1784 by Decremps in exposing a contemporary trick by Pinetti. These passed out of common use around World War I, being superceded by the Black Art Table.

n. A sleight in billiard ball manipulation where a ball, resting on top of the fist of the lower hand, is seemingly swept off by the upper hand while actually dropping into the lower; trap pass. [very rare] First described in 1876 by Hoffmann (pp.405-407) but using an egg. So named because the lower hand opens to act like a magician's table trap. Jargon coined in 1910 by Burling Hull. Thence 1978 Gross.

n. Effect where four selected and signed cards are randomly buried in the deck and shuffled yet instantly disappear from the deck to reappear in four different pockets of the magician. [fairly common] "Dai Vernon's 'Travellers' effect ... is surely a classic. It is not often seen, however, probably because it is very difficult to accomplish." — John Bannon in The Linking Ring (Jun 1987), 62

term: SEE UNDER: Cards up the Sleeve
definition: n. Effect where a lady's leg-garter vanishes from a case or tray and appears on an assistant's leg; the Garter Trick (2). [very rare]
n. An oblong octagonal metal changing tray that vanishes or produces coins; the coin tray. [archaic after 1891]

n. An assistant (usually female) in a stage act whose primary duties are to fetch and remove apparatus, usually on a tray. Compare box-jumper. [obsolete, formerly very rare but not nonce] American magicians jargon by 1929 (as recalled by Hanson in Zweers [1974], 44).

n. Effect where two banknotes, one signed by a volunteer and both padlocked together between two clear plastic plates, change places. [rare] Based on the Out to Lunch principle. REF: Kaye (1977), 81-82.
n. Shadowgraphy being the most usual synonym. [obsolete, once very rare]

1.n. An effect plus its method. Used by magicians in this sense only when communicating among themselves. [very common] "The first Trick that e'er I learn'd to do, Was, out of one Ball to make them into two." — H. Dean, The Whole Art of Legerdemain (6th edition, 1763), 9 "All the best tricks have simple secrets—when you know them." — Will Goldston, Exclusive Magical Secrets (1912), 55 “No trick exchanged after the secret has once become known.” — Thayer Magic Mfg. Co., Catalogue, No.7 (1928) "If you want to hide a good trick, put it in print." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1946), 210 "A knowledge of conjuring tricks makes a boy more alert to the trickery of the world he will have to cope with in maturity." — Karl Germain [died 1959], quoted in Cramer (1966), 3 "The tricks are not important. You are important." — Albert Goshman, lecturing, 3 Nov 1984
n. A gimmicked playing card; a faked card (obsolescent); a fake card (obsolescent); a false card (obsolete). [fairly common]

n. Loosely, any set of faked playing cards; mechanical deck; prepared cards. [common] "Quite recently I purchased no less than six trick packs of cards, presumably all different if the several specifications were honest. These six packs were offered by so many different advertisers, and ... under as many different names. ... I found the whole six packs practically identical, ... the only difference in any case being a slight difference in the arrangement of ‘long' and ‘short' cards throughout the pack." — Ellis Stanyon in Magic (Feb 1911), 36 “To those who scorn a trick deck, who think that it is ‘cheating’ in the magic sense, just a few words: Jean Hugard ... once told me that in magic it is the effect that counts.... How the effect is accomplished is of little consequence. After all, if one uses a short card, or a crimp, or bridge, does not the deck become a ‘trick’ deck?” — Al Stevenson in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jan 1961), 81 "A lay audience can't always appreciate the art of magic. People think I have a trick deck or something. But there's no way I could do the things I do with a trick deck of cards." — Derek Dingle, interview in Clark (1976), 45

n. Convenient synonym for magician but usually tongue-in-cheek or disparagingly. [fairly common] "Too many performers still make an entrance as a stout magician, and exit looking like a starved trickster." — Annemann in The Jinx #26 (1936), 162 “An enterprising club can have its pick of a dozen or more top tricksters who will lecture on their special phase of sorcery and demonstrate their techniques.” — “Frank Joglar” [Milbourne Christopher] in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (May 1950), 660 "The trickster's chief aim is to deceive his audience about the way his tricks are done." — Henning Nelms, Magic and Showmanship (1969), 19 Originally Standard English by 1711 meaning a prankster. REF: OED/2. Thence magicians jargon (variant noted) by 1902 Margery ad in Magic billing himself as "Trickiest Trickster in Tricks"; 1909 Stanyon ad in Magic; 1915 Impromptu Trixter V.1, #1; 1935 U. F. Grant's Trixter Monthly, V.1, #1; 1940 Haskell billing as the "Deluxe Trickster"; 1941 Holden cat #8; 1949 Turner as a "card trickster"; 1950 Lorraine in HMM as “to throw the average trixter off the scent”; 1957 Crimmins in HMM as a "card trickster"; 1975 Dalal in Mantra; 1976 Eldin as book title The Trickster's Handbook; 1978 Gross as "the card trickster's patter"; 1985 Price as "second-sight tricksters"; 1987 Abbott cat #23 as "the talking trickster"; 1988 Waters; 1988 Adair in Supreme Newsletter as "TV tricksters"; 1992 Randi; 1997 Gloye in LR.
n. Comedy effect same as Tipsy Turvy Bottles with added kicker climax where the magician's bottle turns up-side down. 972 [rare]
n. A plastic water glass faked to make it easily disappear. [rare]
n. A pack of playing cards that combines the Svengali and stripper gaffs. [rare]
n. A buckle with three adjacent cards. [very rare]
See: Three-Way Forcing Deck. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Three-Way Forcing Deck".)

n. A multiple lift that picks up three cards together; a triple. [fairly common] "Allerton rarely missed by more than one. When he did, a double—or triple—lift would pull him out." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Apr 1959), 124
n. The classic mentalism effect where a prediction evolves in three stages. [rare]
n. The card turnover (1) sleight that reverses three cards as one in the deck by turning over the triplet, which had been acquired by a triple lift. [rare]

n. Effect where, after half of a deck of playing cards is turned face-up and riffle shuffled into the face-down portion, all cards are face-down except for the previously selected one. [fairly common]
n. Slangy spelling of tricks. [fairly common]

n. The folding of paper to make various figures; an entertainment—really a sort of dextrous flourish— used by some conjurors as an allied art to supplement their feats of magic; paper folding. [common] "Experts at second dealing, etc. take a dim view of paper tear tricks and will give you an inferiority complex if you listen to them. I have not scorned paper tricks, and Troublewit, the leader of them all, has been performed by me on every big TV show that exists." — Jay Marshall, TV, Magic and You (1955), 34 This is the European equivalent of the Japanese origami. First mentioned (according to Andrew Pinard) in J. M., Sports and Pastimes (1676) as a children’s pastime. Possibly of French invention, being called there Le Papier de Père Mathieu, it was in the repertoire of French magicians by 1693 when described by Ozanam who noted 33 designs. First reported in England in the 1722 edition of Dean's The Whole Art of Legerdemain where it is called "Trouble-Wit." Prominent later magician-performers include J. N. Hofzinser (by Jan 1857), Madame Cora 975 (by 1872 when she introduced it to the Australian stage), David Devant (in 1896), Adrian Plate, Félicien Trewey, Ellis Stanyon, Jean Caroly, Edgar Benyon (until 1968), Robert Harbin, Frank Herman (by 1942), Jay Marshall (by 1942), Sid Lorraine, Milbourne Christopher (since 1952), and Shari Lewis. REF: Clarke in Magic Wand (1924), 138; Waller (1948/1980), 49.
n. The Okito Glass (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare]

See: Kuma Tubes Tumble Rings f. A chain made of 30 (or fewer) interlocked steel rings that when the top ring is released from the suspended chain will appear to tumble down from ring to ring until it ends by linking itself to the 977 bottom ring. [very rare but not nonce] Originally an optical-illusion puzzle but can be performed as a magic trick. Martin Gardner was able to trace it back initially to a British book published in 1932, R. M. Abraham’s Winter Nights Entertainments but believes it “undoubtedly much older.” True, as Gardner later found a much earlier reference to The English Mechanic and World of Science (23 Nov 1888), 251, where it is called “the Magic Chain” and described as “A curious little thing ... occasionally offered for sale in the streets.” REF: Martin Gardner, The Unexpected Hanging and Other Mathematical Diversions (Chicago: U of Chicago Press, 1991), 147, 154-155, 249.. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Kuma Tubes Tumble Rings f. A chain made of 30 (or fewer) interlocked steel rings that when the top ring is released from the suspended chain will appear to tumble down from ring to ring until it ends by linking itself to the 977 bottom ring. [very rare but not nonce] Originally an optical-illusion puzzle but can be performed as a magic trick. Martin Gardner was able to trace it back initially to a British book published in 1932, R. M. Abraham’s Winter Nights Entertainments but believes it “undoubtedly much older.” True, as Gardner later found a much earlier reference to The English Mechanic and World of Science (23 Nov 1888), 251, where it is called “the Magic Chain” and described as “A curious little thing ... occasionally offered for sale in the streets.” REF: Martin Gardner, The Unexpected Hanging and Other Mathematical Diversions (Chicago: U of Chicago Press, 1991), 147, 154-155, 249.".)
n. Effect where ornate short swords penetrate a balloon in a tube without bursting it. [fairly common]

1.n. A card sleight that vertically rotates two or more cards (previously acquired by a lift) to bring them back-to-back with the rest in the deck. [rare] If two cards are so reversed, it is called a double-turnover (1); if three, a Triple Turnover; and generally, if more than two, a Multiple Turnover.
n. The flipover box (see) being the most usual synonym. [obsolete, formerly rare]

(See also: Curry Turnover Change.) n. A sleight that exchanges one playing card for another while turning it from a face-up to a face- down position; the Turnover Change. [fairly common] "Paul Curry's Turnover Change ... is one of the finest and most deceptive of all good card changes and not too hard to master." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Feb 1946), 196
n. A cut of the deck (a shift) done while the deck is turned face up or face down; the Herrmann pass. [fairly common] First exposed in 1897 (Roterberg, 10) as the Herrmann pass.

term: TV Card Frame; T.V. Card Frame
definition: See: Television Card Frame. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Television Card Frame".)

(See also: television magic.) n. Conjuring performed before the TV camera. [rare] "Television magic is easy once you learn to control its limited field of vision." — Ben Harris, Gellerism Revealed (1985), 21 Pioneering performances of magic on TV include the following. First was Allan Hale on 9 Jan 1931 in a broadcast from a London studio of the Vanishing Cigarette, T&R Card, and Pase- Passe Cards. Johnnie Giordmaine on closed-circuit at Eaton's department store in Canada on 28 Aug 1933. Next on broadcast TV was Fred Culpitt on the premier BBC experimental show in 1936, followed by Gali-Gali with close-up in New York on 15 Sep 1939, Jay Marshall on Dumont TV in New York in 1940, Dr & Mrs Aaron Weiss with escapism in New York on 31 Oct 1946, Milbourne Christopher on WCBS-TV in New York in Feb 1947, and Frank Garcia in New York in 1948. 926 By 1948 there were only 8 thousand TV sets in America but the industry then exploded to 2.5 million sets in 1949, 4 million in 1950, and 31 million in 1955. Subsequently TV has become the most important showcase for magic. The longest-running weekly TV magic show was Dick Williams’ “Magicland”, which was seen 1966-1989 for nearly 1,200 wekly shows. REF: Magic Wand (Mar 1931 & Oct-Nov 1936); Annemann in Jinx (1939), 436; J. Marshall (1955), 3, 105, 111-113; Booth (1990), 18-63; Christopher (1973), 405, 409, 426-430; B. Harris (1985), 21-22; Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Jan 1947), 288. The two best presentational books are Marshall (1955) and Williams (1994).

n. A trade name for the Svengali Deck. [obsolete after c.1980, formerly common] "His fascination with card and close-up magic began when a high school buddy fooled him with some 'TV Magic Cards' — the Mysto Magic Set of the '70s." — Phil Willmarth in The Linking Ring (Jun 1987), 59 Marketed by Marshall Brodien under this title from around 1971 on. Tony Clark learned his first magic in 1972 from a set.
n. Twentieth-Century Silks (see) being the less prosaic and now more usual synonym. [fairly common]
1.n. Cards Across (see) being the most usual current synonym.
n. Acronym for The World's Greatest Magician, the adopted title of world-famous but notoriously egocentric Indian magician P.C. Sorcar (1913-1971). [obsolescent]
(See also: double dove production.) n. The dove production where the magus produces simultaneously two doves, one from each bare hand; twin dove production. [rare]
n. The four-ace trick that uses the Elmsley Count, specifically where the aces turn up singly in a face down packet. 981 [fairly common]
n. Impromptu effect where the magician's hand flat on a table rotates thru more than a 360-degree angle. [new, rare]

n. Method of keeping two steps ahead of the spectators during the unfolding of a trick; like the one ahead but at an additional remove. [very rare] "In the nail bending sequence, you are Two-Ahead, loading the bent nail into the cabinet for the sixth effect, as you're in the middle of the fourth." — Jeff Busby, Sefalaljia--Automated (1995)
n. A Monte effect with two playing cards. [fairly common]

n. Effect where $2.85 worth of coins (2 silver dollars, a half dollar, and a dime) vanish from the magicians hand, leaving a single silver dollar. Same effect and method as the 21¢ Trick and the $1.35 Trick except for the coins used. [fairly common]
n. Any code used to pass information between the mentalist and the medium in a mindreading act. [rare]

n. A type of force where the force-card appears as the only clearly visible one while the deck is fanned before the spectator's eyes; the thought force being the less usual synonym. Pronounced UL-ti-ma THOOL-ee. Compare riffle force. [rare] This is a later variant of the riffle force that used a hesitation while riffling the deck. The original fanning version was first published in 1868 by Robert-Houdin as "The Card Thought Of" and thence in 1876 by Hoffmann (p.111) and 1886 by Edwin Sachs as "Divination of Thought". It was a pet force of Jack Merlin (by 1928), Fred Braue (since 1939), and a few other inner- circle magi until 1940 when more widely published as "Ultima Thule" in Hugard & Braue's Expert Card Technique, although Braue was not then free to disclose some of the experts' more subtle handlings. Popularized as "Mental Fan Force" by Derek Dingle. REF: Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Apr 1959), 124.
n. The sleight that opens up a billet like a tiny umbrella by pushing the thumb into the fold. [rare]

See: Parasol Trick *"Un tour de Maître Gonin" [French] Standard French catch-phrase meaning any artful or cunning device. Literally, "a trick of Master Gonin", so-called from the earliest French conjuror known by name, Gonin, who flourished in the early 1500s, and two later namesakes who performed in Paris through the 1600s. 985 REF: Dif #1 (1971), 109-110; Clarke in Magic Wand (1924), 40.. (No further definition found in this dictionary for "Parasol Trick *"Un tour de Maître Gonin" [French] Standard French catch-phrase meaning any artful or cunning device. Literally, "a trick of Master Gonin", so-called from the earliest French conjuror known by name, Gonin, who flourished in the early 1500s, and two later namesakes who performed in Paris through the 1600s. 985 REF: Dif #1 (1971), 109-110; Clarke in Magic Wand (1924), 40.".)

n. Effect where spectator chooses and is given two suits from a riffle-shuffled full deck, both spectator and magus alternate in dealing single cards to make 26 pairs (one face up, the other face down), and then on examining them the spectator finds that each pair is a pair matching in color and value. [rare] This classic card trick was co-invented in 1947 by Bascom Jones and Fred Shields and marketed by them. REF: Magic Castle Walls of Fame (1988), 469.
n. Effect where 4 handkerchiefs tied to a length of tape visibly untie themselves in whatever sequence the audience specifies. [rare]
1.a. Said, literally, of a physical screen (cover) provided by positioning the magician's hands, body, or props between his secret move and the spectator's angles of vision. [fairly common]

n. The informal interpersonal network of the most avid magicians who diffuse among themselves the latest effects and methods by word-of-mouth and private letter, often years before publication or public performance. Compare the inner circle. Opposite of aboveground. [fairly common] "Characteristically, it is the unpublished material, merely spoken of or held covetously by a chosen few, that houses the truly great secrets of the noble art." — Ricky Jay, Cards as Weapons (1977), 25

1.n. Effect, usually performed as a publicity stunt, where the escape artist frees himself from constraint (handcuffs, sealed box, etc) while submerged in a river or bay. [rare] Houdini made his first underwater escape in Dresden, Germany in September 1900 by jumping into the Elbe River while manacled. Around 1907 Popular Mechanics reported an amateur escapologist who excaped from a submerged barrel. On 7 Jul 1912 Houdini made his first escape from a sealed packing-box dumped into New York's East River. The underwater escape was also a pet publicity stunt of Harry Blackstone who under his orignal name of Harry Bouton had invented a metal box with a secret sliding panel to do publicity stunts. (Blackstone Jr claimed that his father may have preceeded Houdini in the underwater box escape but gives no date, the published photos obviously only dating sometime in or after 1918 when Blackstone took that stagename. And he is documented as doing the stunt as late as 1922.) REF: Annemann in Jinx (1939), 468; Blackstone Jr (1985), 54-59; Christopher (1973), 372-373. 987
n. The Professor's Nightmare being the more usual synonym. [very rare]
a. Not faked; natural; ordinary; ungaffed; unprepared. Opposite of faked. [fairly common]
a. Not gaffed; ungimmicked; unprepared; unfaked; gaffless. Opposite of gaffed. [rare]
a. Free of any gimmick; ungaffed; unprepared. Opposite of gimmicked. [fairly common]
v. To ditch, which is the more usual synonym. Opposite of to load. [rare]

(See also: Untying Silk.) n. Effect where the magician knots a handkerchief, dangles it from his fingers where it visibly unties itself from bottom to top; the Untying Handkerchief. Compare the Serpent Silk. 989 [rare] The original version (using a thread) was invented by Al Baker. He taught it to Adrian Plate (died 1919) who taught it to Max Holden. It was later published by Percy Naldrett. Later still, G. W. Hunter invented another version. The version that uses a hand-held reel (invented in 1939 by Albenice) is called the Serpent Silk. REF: Holden in Sphinx (1927).

n. Effect where the magician knots a handkerchief, dangles it from his fingers where it visibly unties itself from bottom to top; the Untying Handkerchief. Compare the Serpent Silk. 989 [rare] The original version (using a thread) was invented by Al Baker. He taught it to Adrian Plate (died 1919) who taught it to Max Holden. It was later published by Percy Naldrett. Later still, G. W. Hunter invented another version. The version that uses a hand-held reel (invented in 1939 by Albenice) is called the Serpent Silk. REF: Holden in Sphinx (1927).

v. To take off a packet of cards from the top of the deck and place it on the bottom while cutting or shuffling. Opposite of undercut. [rare] Originally the argot of American card sharps by 1902 Erdnase, 27. Thence magicians jargon by 1920 Stanyon in Magic; 1928 Leat & Jonson; 1946 Zovello in HMM; 1949 Hay; 1956 Dexter.

n. Any apparatus, particularly a fake or gimmick, that can be used for more than one specific trick; a utility item; a utility prop. [fairly common] Examples are the thumb tip, coin box, lota, mirror glass, dye tube, pulls, reels, the Himber Wallet, and Topit. These are distinguished from such non-utility devices as the Key Ring, Chop Cup, or the gimmicks provided with Chesbro's Coin in Lighter or Fox's Long Pour, which are designed for one specific trick only.

n. Two mirrors that meet at a 90-degree angle. When placed behind a symmetrical environment, mirrored-side out with the angled juncture pointing toward the spectators, it is invisible. Used to conceal a load or make a vanish of any object placed behind it. [very rare] This optical device was invented in the early 1860s by Thomas W. Tobin, a mechanician and Secretary of the Royal Polytechnic Institution in London. There, in 1865, in collaboration with Professor John Henry Pepper, a magician who lectured at the Polytechnic, they developed, patented, and premiered their "Proteus" (later called the "Cabinet of Proteus"), one of the most popular optical illusions of the time. Subsequently it became the method for the Sphinx and many other clever illusions such as the Temple of Buddha.

v. A magic word used to vanish an object; Go!. [obsolete after 1700s] "Hay passe, presto vade, jubeo, by the virtue of hocus pocus, 'tis gone." — Thomas Ady, A Candle in the Dark (1655) Originally the Latin vade meaning to go or vanish and the source of the English verb fade. REF: OED/2.

n. Stage effect where, upon a raised platform, the magus constructs a female manikin from such bits and scraps as a tripod, cloth, wig, and mask; and, upon applying make-up to the face, it comes to life as a real woman; Rag, a Bone, and a Hank of Hair (obsolescent); Creo (obsolete). [fairly common]
n. Effect where a wooden block, impaled by a wooden stake, in a square tube visibly penetrates the stake to fall out. [fairly common]
n. Abbreviation of vanish and vanishing. Used mainly in trick titles. [rare]

n. The effect of an object disappearing; a disappearance being the less usual synonym. Opposite of a production. [common] "A vanish is more surprising and effective than a production." — Faucett Ross, letter to Charlie Miller, 7 May 1956 "There are two types of vanishes, the visible vanish and the covered vanish, where the vanish takes place under a cloth or within a box or other container." — Blackstone Jr, The Blackstone Book of Magic & Illusion (1985), 121
1.n. Effect where a round alarm clock disappears when suspended from a hook; the Flight of Time (1). [very rare]

term: Vanishing Coin in (a) Glass of Water
definition: (See also: Dissolving Coin.) n. Effect where a metal coin covered by a cloth disappears when dropped into a glass of water; the Melting Coin. [rare] Uses a glass or clear plastic disc that is switched for the coin. A pet effect of Alfred C. Gilbert (by 1920).

n. An electric lamp with shade that on command vanishes from one table and reappears on another. [obsolete, formerly rare] A crude, non-mechanical version was presented by Goldin at London’s Palace Theatre in July 1901. Kellar planned to add it to his act in late 1902. Adopted by Fred Harcourt in late 1902 when he premiered it in Australia. REF: Stanyon in Magic (Sep 1901), 99; Evans in Magic (Oct 1902), 4; Kudarz in Magic (Feb 1903), 42; Hornmann letter in Conjurers’ Monthly Magazine (Mar 1908), 205-206; Willmann letter in Conjurers’ Monthly Magazine (Aug 1908), 373. The first fully mechanical model was the Conradi Vanishing Lamp, of which a copy made in 1904 is in the Proust Collection. Houdini featured another copy in his full-evening show of 1925-26. This had been built at Conradi-Horster’s shop in Hamburg and was kept in its oft- needed repair by Carl Brema. REF: Proust ad in The Linking Ring (May 1997), 33; Bamberg (1988), 65.

1.n. The effect where the magician’s wand instantly disappears. [common] The method, the collapsible shell wand, was invented as a practical joke in 1887 by twelve- year-old Theo Bamberg (“Okito”) while assisting his father David Tobias Bamberg. The father directed his son to devise a trick using the shell wand, and young Bamberg quickly created the still standard routine. A pet effect of Edward Reno. In 1960 Russ Walsh marketed his Vanishing Wand based on his Vanishing Cane principle. REF: Tarbell, V (1948), 353.

term: Vent; vent. [the period is now obsolete]
definition: 1.n. A ventriloquist, as slangy abbreviation. [fairly common] “Like a diabolical vent, Fulves holds a Marlo dummy by its heels and throws his voice to say bitchy things ….” — Jon Racherbaumer, Sticks & Stones, No.12 (1977), 2 Originally vaudeville cant by 1893. REF: Ganthony (1893) as quoted by the OED/2; Lustig (1921); Granville dict (1952). There is no effect in magic more startling than a really good visible vanish.” — Blackstone Jr, The Blackstone Book of Magic & Illusion (1985), 121 Prime examples are the Vanishing Birdcage and the Vanishing Cane.. 1.n. Any billfold (usually gaffed) used in a magic effect such as the Card to Wallet. [common] 1013 “I am a wallet Nut! I particularly enjoy tricks with wallets — I must have a dozen that I have been performing over the years — unfortunately it takes a dozen different wallets to do the dozen different effects!” — Art Emerson in Mantra (May 1975), 7 Major gaffed types include Berg’s Super Wallet (1932), Dick Washington’s so-called LePaul Wallet (1940s-50s), the Balducci Wallet (1958), the Himber Wallet (1963), the Jennings Wallet (1965), the Mullica Wallet (1968), and the Horwitz Wallet (by 1984). Others include the Bendix Bombshell and Chuck Leach’s Eclipse Wallet.
2.n. Any trick with a gaffed billfold. [very rare, possibly nonce]

n. Popular practical-joke item designed to give a flatulent sound when an unsuspecting person sits on it. White in LR. Wide card — A playing card that is a bit broader than the others in its deck; a broad card (obsolete); a long card, which is the more usual term although incongruous as it covers cards that may be longer as well as others that are wider. [obsolescent, formerly fairly common] “The long or wide card had a long innings but has finally been superseded by the short card which serves the same purpose in a much subtler way.” — Jean Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Mar 1946), 201 Used as a key card, as its presence can be felt at the side of the deck. This type of faked card was evidently introduced by British card cheats—probably with their bum-cards by 1552 (Walker) and certainly so by 1674 (Cotton) when they called it, again incongruously, “the Breef”. Also called “briefs” by American card sharps by 1865 Evans and 1894 Koschitz. The wide card was used by French conjurors by 1769 (Guyot). Magicians jargon as wide card by 1774 Hooper; 1861 Novra cat; 1875 Hartz; 1914 Stanyon in Magic; 1924 Felsman cat #18 as “Wide and Narrow Packs”; 1933 Davenport cat; 1938 Hilliard; 1948 Norman; 1948 Kaplan; 1949 Turner; 1950 Jonson; 1957 Radner; 1973 Alain; 1979 Severn; 1980 Adair; 1983 Berg; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wedler; 1996 Müller. . Also called a broad card (obsolete) by 1876 Heather; 1877 Sachs. Wielder of the wand phr. A magician; a wand wielder. [rare] 1023

1.n. The venerable effect where a colorless liquid is transformed into a red one; Water into Wine (obsolete). [fairly common] First exposed by Thomas Hill in 1581 using dried and powdered lees, which secretly added to a glass of water give both the color and taste of wine—a very “small” wine ‘tis true and non- alcoholic to boot but one that could be drunk as “proof”. A non-chemical method to give this effect was first disclosed by Guyot (1740). The usual modern method (exposed by Stanyon in 1904) where crystals of potassium permanganate are added to water, simulates the color only and is unsafe to drink.

n. A finger-ring in the shape of two chicken wishbones joined at the tips and worn with the two resulting “V”s pointing toward the back of the hand and the palm, respectively. Useful as a card or coin holdout or in stealing a card. [rare] A traditional finger-ring design in parts of West Africa, South India, and China. The first magician to wear it was Nate Leipzig (d.1939). He inspired John Booth to have one made for himself. Jack Chanin was advertising this as the “Magicians Only Ring” in 1945. Booth introduced it to Soviet magicians in 1965 through Arutian Akopian. Recently adopted by American skiers. REF: Booth (1986), 178-182.

1.n. Occasional convenient synonym for a magician; the Wiz. Usually uncapitalized. [common] “You’ll find a number of such youthful wizards among the members of the London Society of Magicians. Before they’re out of their teens they have developed an uncanny ability for sleight of hand, and by the time they’re ten years older they’re reputable entertainers making useful guineas by performing in public.” — Will Dexter, Famous Magic Secrets [1956], 48 “A male magician is a wizard and a female magician is a witch.” — anonymous misogynist member of The Magic Circle justifying its exclusion of women, as quoted in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (1948), 452

Grant’s Temple Screen for a smaller later version with better method. [archaic, formerly rare] Reportedly marketed as early as 1907 in the S. LeRoy catalog. Used by W.W. Durbin by 1910.. 1.n. A magician, specifically in reference to the specialized props used by him, such as cards, coins, doves, etc. [common] Originally the argot of gambling sharps by 1896 Bertram as a “worker of the broads”; 1933 Walsh & Scarne as a “monte worker”; 1962 Garcia as a “paper worker”; 1984 Ortiz as a “glim worker”. Thence magicians jargon by 1904 Lester ad in Magic as “trunk workers”; 1907 Keene as a “sleight-of-hand worker”; 1928 Thayer cat #7 as a “billiard ball worker”; 1930 Holden in Sphinx as “sleight of hand workers”; 1935 Abbott cat #3 as a “cigarette worker”; 1939 Kanter cat as “blindfold workers”; 1940 Abbott cat #6 as a “coin worker”; 1940 as a thimble worker; 1941 Holden cat #8 as “mental workers”; 1942 Ireland cat #10 as a “silk worker”; 1946 Karson as “Zombie workers”, referring to the prop and not the performers’ disposition; 1950 Elliott in Phoenix #197 as “psychic workers”; 1952 Fabian in Abra as a “cigarette worker”; 1956 Dexter as a “sleeve-worker”; 1963 Ganson/Vernon as an “Egg Bag worker”; 1966 as a dove worker; 1979 Harbin as a “ring worker” re the Linking Rings; 1981 Waters as a “scope worker” referring to a horoscope; 1984 S. Wells in LR as a “sponge ball worker”; 1984 Ammar as a “Topit worker”; 1991 Bergeron in Genii as a “bird worker”; 1998 Busby as a “cigarette worker”. 2.n. A professional magician, usually with reference to his place of employment, such as a club worker or restaurant worker. [fairly common] “Michael Close is always a formidable ‘worker’ and chooses only the strongest commercial magic for his repertoire.” — Dan Garrett in M-U-M (Oct 1996), 20
n. Effect where several strong volunteers are unable to turn a large wheel of cheese on its side; the Mighty Cheese. [archaic, formerly rare]

n. The sleight that conceals a coin or ball at the sleightly flexed juncture of the hand and forearm. [obsolete after 1945, formerly very rare] This sleight, always rare and apparently no longer used, was a favorite of T. Nelson Downs. REF: Hilliard (1909).
n. Any of several methods by which the magician may tie his wrists together that allows for a quick 1033 release. Similar to the more familiar thumb tie. [rare]

n. A trap in a table top that opens by pressure from the magician's wrist and closes by its spring- hinge. [archaic after 1924, formerly fairly common] Marketed by at least as early as around 1858 by Henry Novra (catalog, p.17, as a "Mechanical Trap").
n. Commercial name for the square circle as marketed in Britain by Davenport's since 1938. [rare]
n. An indifferent card (see) being the earlier and still more usual synonym. [fairly common]

term: X-ing the Cut; X-ing the Deck
definition: (See also: Crossing the Cut.) n. The cut force (see) being the more usual synonym. [rare]

n. A large cabinet with open slats in which an assistant appears. Compare the X-Ray Double Box. [very rare] First marketed by Thayer's by 1925. X-rays were discovered, named, and (contrary to usual scientific practice) immediately publicised in 1895 by German physicist Wilhelm Konrad Röntgen. The term entered Standard English next year. REF: OED/2.

n. One particular playing card divination. [very rare] Both the effect and its special deck were invented by "Henry Hardin" (E. A. Parsons) and first marketed by him around 1893 as the "Superb Card Trick". It was retitled soon after the term "X- ray" entered Standard English in 1896. REF: Sphinx, VII (1908); OED/2.

n. A pack of playing cards faked with a cut-through window-slot over one corner index of each card (except the top and bottom ones). Not to be confused with the Peek Deck. [fairly common] "This, in the opinion of the author [Downs], is the most perfect method of reading cards ever invented." — Hilliard in Downs & Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909), Ch.7

n. Variant of the Eyeless Vision effect where the mentalist sees through solid objects. [fairly common] "[T]he simplest things, like X-Ray Eyes, and Pulse Stopping carry ten times the impact of the elaborate Vanishing Cabinets, and chrome and Plastic props that look tricky to start with!" — Sam Dalal in Swami (Dec 1972), 47 Originally a fake effect of pseudo-psychics, particularly the 19-year old Spaniard, Joaquin Maria Argamasilla, who came to the USA in 1924 and was exposed that May by Houdini. Quickly adopted by magicians, Houdini using it in his psychic exposé act later that year. A celebrated and featured effect of Kuda "The Man With the X-Ray Eyes" Bux (1938-47), P.C. Sorcar (by 1950), Edgar Benyon (to 1968), and Jon Marshall (early 1980s billed as "The Man With the X- Ray Eyes"). REF: Houdini, Houdini Exposes the Tricks Used by the Boston Medium Margery...Also a Complete Exposure of Argamasilla (New York: Adams Press, 1924); Christopher (1969), 184- 185. Originally the argot of pseudo-psychics, probably coined in 1924 as the billing for Argamasilla, "The Spaniard with the X-Ray Eyes." NOTE: The earliest citation in the OED/2 is only 1939. Thence magicians jargon by 1924 Anneman [sic] in Sphinx as "working the X-Ray Eyes"; 1931 Booth; 1937 Chicago Magic cat #17; 1943 Fitzkee; 1943 Welles, program, as "The Girl [Rita Hayworth] with the X-Ray Eyes"; 1952 Gardner in HMM; 1956 Dexter; 1956 Joglar [Christopher] in HMM; 1957 Keel; 1972 Griffin; 1978 Warner's Magic Factory in Feinman; 1986 Dawes & Setterington; 1988 Waters; 1988 Supreme ad in Magigram.
n. Effect where a continuous stream of table salt pours from an empty salt shaker-cap, whether screwed onto an empty shaker or by itself. [rare]

n. The series of inexpensive magic books bound in yellow-colored card-board published in Britain by Pearson & Co. from 1904 to 1930. [obsolescent, colloquial] "I found out later it was the professional magicians who had books 'The Yellow Perils'. And the reason? They contained so many top secrets that the magicians of the day feared their publication would wreck the profession." — Jack Delvin, Magic of the Masters (1977), 8 Authors—most quite well known—in this series of some dozen books included Arthur Ainsley, Will Blyth, David Devant, C. Lang Neil, C. Ivor Smith, Bert Douglas, Will Goldston, Louis Nikola, and L. Widdop. So-called because their yellow binding, cheapness, and rather good quality posed a threat of wide public exposure that seemed analogous to the "Yellow Peril", the then current (since 1898) catch-phrase for the widely perceived threat to Western civilization of the so-called Yellow Races of East Asia. REF: Webster's 10th Collegiate.
n. Acronym for (your) favorite method. [rare]
n. Stage effect where a large lit chimney lamp on a table is vanished beneath a silk to reappear instantly on another table. [archaic]
n. Stage mind-reading effect where the assistant, isolated on a glass platform accurately identifies borrowed objects in a locked basket suspended in mid-air. [archaic by 1928]

n. Magic in the "yuppie" style. [very rare, possibly nonce] "There's a whole new genre of books being published which I can only define as ‘yuppie close- up—material from young upwardly-mobile prestidigitators." — Jeff Busby in Short Sheet #13 (1987)

(See also: Divided Lady.) n. Stage illusion where the assistant is manacled while standing in a cabinet, the doors closed, wide blades pushed through on either side to divide the two parts of the cabinet and the lady, which are then separated; then the process is reversed until the assistant is revealed in her original position. [rare]

n. ESP Deck (see) being the later and more usual synonym. [rare] Originally the cant of parapsychologists when coined as "Zener cards" (after their inventor, Dr. Karl E. Zener [1903- 1961]) in 1930 by Dr. Rhine. By 1936, after Zener left his research program, Rhine substituted a square for Zener's original rectangle and renamed them "E.S.P. cards". Rhine's fellow parapsychologists adopted both terms for the modified deck but soon came to prefer the latter, as do magicians. NOTE: The earliest citation in the OED/2 is only to 1934. Thence magicians jargon (variants noted) by 1949 Warlock in Phoenix #180; 1974 Dexter; 1976 Gill as "Zenner cards"; 1978 Müller; 1979 Fulves as "Zenner cards", prematurely declaring the term obsolete; 1983 Punx in Vibrations as "Zenner Cards"; 1989 Goldstein in LR as "Zener symbol cards"; 1994 Racherbaumer in LR.; 2002 Willmarth in LR as a "Zenner (ESP) deck". NOTE: Sometimes misspelled "Zenna" and "Zenner". Current British mentalist Peter Estyn Jones uses the stage name "Peter Zenner", but he took it from another source. 1041 NOTE: Gave its name in 1980 to "Zennerism", a trick by David Britland using ESP cards.
n. Effect where spectators select five cards from a 25-card packet, shuffle them back in, display the whole packet on a card easel, whereupon the magus picks out the chosen cards. [rare]
n. The Cards Across-type effect where each of two volunteers count off 15 cards and seals them in an envelope, yet 3 selected cards pass from one envelope to the other. [fairly common]

n. Effect where a playing card in a frame has its middle pushed out to one side. [rare] Danny Korem was marketing this effect by 1978 (and reportedly advertising it in Genii). Sometime later Gaëtan Bloom (marketed by 1978) and Bernard Bilis did it without a frame. Another version was invented by Stephen Mathews (marketed in 1986). A frame version was also marketed by Supreme Magic. REF: Tannen ad in Linking Ring (Mar 1986); Busby 1988 annotation.
n. Effect where an ordinary cigarette placed in a see-thru plastic case undergoes the Zig-Zag effect when the center of the case is slid to one side yet withdrawn restored. [fairly common]

(See also: fanning powder.) n. Zinc stearate, finely powdered, for dusting on playing cards to insure an even slickness when 354 fanned or otherwise manipulated; marketed under the tradename Fan-Ez. Also used in the Dry Hand trick. [common] Introduced to magicians in the early or mid 1930s by American ex-cop and gambling dealer- magician Audley Walsh using what was then a secret formula and marketed by him as "Fan-Ez". See Soo-Zee for the special box invented by Ken Allen in the 1950s to apply fanning powder quickly and evenly. REF: Art Johnston in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Sep 1955), 315.

n. Effect where three spectators peek at cards in a shuffled and spread deck; performer gives deck a quick shuffle and is immediately able to remove the secretly selected cards from his pocket. [rare]

n. Outlandish comedy prop made of a real banana with a zippered rubberized skin. Often used as a running gag as the magi takes successive bites, zipping it up again each time. [fairly common] Perhaps originally a comedians' prop, having been used by comedian Harpo Marx and comedy magician Harry Cecil (in the 1930s) among others. 1043 REF: Ireland Catalog No.17 (1962), 141.

(See also: Amputation.) n. Effect where the mid-part of a volunteer's fore-arm is seen to have vanished after after being placed in a horizontal box and cut through by two steel blades. [rare]
