(See also: Clock Dial.) n. Effect where the dial moves on a clock-face without apparent mechanism, stopping at a pre- selected number; the Cabalistic Clock (obsolete); Obedient Clock (obsolete). [rare] This effect was performed as early as 1777 by Breslaw when he called it the "Magic Clock". Also performed in 1806 by De Philipsthal (program) and in 1816 by Gyngell Sr (poster). These original models were animated by concealed thread pulled from offstage, as exposed as early as 1791 by Eckartshausen. On 3 Jul 1845 French clockmaker-magician Robert-Houdin premiered his "La Pendule Cabalistique". As we now know from an original in the possession of French magic dealer Jean Caroly, this model (or, at least, a later modification by Robert- Houdin) was activated by electricity. Hofzinser invented a version controlled by a movable weight. Later a pet effect of Robert Heller (1851), De Biere, Fred Keating (1930), and Cecil Lyle. Seldom performed today. REF: Sharpe (1983), 159, 166-172; Frost (1876), 130; Houdini (1908); Sardina (1950), 57-58; Fischer (1942/1985 tr), 165-166.
See: card trick.
(See also: fan.) n. An arc of hand-held playing cards; a card fan. [common]
See: fanning.
See: card man.
(See also: card easel.) n. A rack (easel) with a ledge or compartments to display an array of playing cards upright to the spectators; a card stand. May be gaffed or not. [rare]

(See also: Dove Pan.) n. A smaller (2½ to 5 inch deep and 8 to 10 inch diameter) version of the Duck Pan; the Chafing Dish (obsolescent). [common] Used to produce a live dove or similarly sized object from the load chamber in its suspiciously commodious lid. If fitted with only one load chamber, it may be termed a Single-load Dove Pan; if with two, a Double-load Dove Pan. Marketed by 1888 by Otto Maurer who called it a "Pigeon Pan".

(See also: Rice Bowls.) n. Effect where one bowl is filled with rice, then covered by a second bowl, which when raised shows twice as much rice. The effect ends when the rice turns to water; the Chinese Rice Bowls. [common] This trick is Indian in origin, although often called The Chinese Rice Bowls and explicitly credited to China by Goldston (1942, p.12), probably because it was a pet effect of "Chung Ling Soo" (William E. Robinson). That original version used one unfaked bowl and one faked in 774 Lota Bowl fashion.

(See also: Click Pass.) n. A coin sleight that retains coins in one hand while seeming to drop them into the open palm of the other; the Downs click pass and the Clink Pass being less usual synonyms. [fairly common] This sleight was invented by T. Nelson Downs and first described by him in 1900 (Hilliar/Downs). The deception is caused by the loud clinking sound made, as if the coins had really fallen into the other hand. Used in working several coin-passe tricks including Coins to Glass and Coins through the Table.
(See also: club act.) n. Conjuring performed in a cabaret or club; club magic; club show; cabaret act [Brit.]; cabaret magic [mainly Brit.]. [fairly common]

(See also: coin stand.) n. A rack (easel) to display coins to the spectators; a coin easel (obsolete). Usually gaffed. [rare] “Magicians who use tables should have their tricks built in the table top. ... Built in coin stands would have no suspiciously thick bases.” — Milbourne Christopher in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jul 1947), 332

(See also: coin wand.) n. A wand mechanically faked to produce a folding coin from its tip by activation of a stud; a money wand (obsolete).. [common] Used in performance as early as 12 Mar 1872 by American magicienne Madame Cora de Lamond at the Masonic Hall, Dunedin, New Zealand. First described and marketed in 1873 in the Hartz catalog (p.70). First exposed in 1876 by Hoffmann (p.203) when called the "Half- crown Wand" (also 1885 Sachs 2nd ed). Later models can be loaded with as many as five folding coins. REF: F. Marshall (1984), 12-13.

(See also: Funnel.) n. A metal funnel faked with a double-wall whose inner compartment can hold a secret load of liquid to be discharged at the magician's whim; the Magic Funnel being a later and still less usual synonym; the Comedy Funnel. One particular routine is called the Human Pump. [fairly common] First described and explained in 1584 by Prevost in France. Next in 1634 by Hocus Pocus Junior in England. Then in 1655 by Thomas Ady in his A Candle in the Dark, in 1740 by Guyot, and 1763 by Dean. Obviously a popular trick, it was also reported being performed in 1825 by an anonymous conjuror at Bartholomew Fair. REF: Prevost (1584/1998 tr), 161-166; Clarke in Magic Wand, Vol.13 (1924/25), 92, 94-95, 137; Frost (1876), 103-104. 398

(See also: Bang Gun.) n. A toy pistol that when triggered deploys from its barrel a flag with the word "BANG!"; a Comedy Gun being the original but now less usual synonym. [common] “As for the 'Bang Gun’, it is so unlike any real weapon ever seen on land or sea that its use is only justified before an audience composed of children who are just able to read words of four letters.” — Jean Hugard in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (Jun 1945), 124 "Any member caught using a Bang Gun in public for any purpose will be expelled forthwith." — Clayton Rawson, "The Witchdoctors Club By-Laws," 1961 "[A] Bang Gun ... is not funny unless you can read." — Henry Hay, The Amateur Magician's Handbook (4th ed, 1982), 327 Marketed in Britain by Harry Leat in 1932 and perhaps invented by him. Marketed in the USA by Holden's by 1936, by Kanter's (as the "Silent Gun with a Big 'Bang'"), and by Abbott's (as the "Comedy Gun") by 1940. Rereleased in 1956 by Harold Sterling. A pet prop of Carl Ballantine. In 1943 Orson Welles conceived of and premiered the Bang Rifle. REF: Leat in Leat's Leaflets #27 (1932); Holden's Catalog #5 (1936); F. Marshall in New Phoenix (1957), 178; Tommy Hanlon Jr interview with Whaley, 12 Dec 1991, re Welles.

(See also: magic book.) 1.n. A volume (however slim) on conjuring; a book (see); a magical book (Brit.); a conjuring book. [fairly common] "Ye dinna get magic from books." — John Ramsay, quoted in Lewis, I (1980), 34 "One good magic book is worth 100 tricks." — Jon Evans in The Linking Ring (Nov 1985), 94 "Magicians don't really like to read magic books." --- Jim Steinmeyer, Device and Illusion (1991), 9.

(See also: Crazy Cube.) n. Effect where the magi divines the uppermost number on a die placed inside two boxes; Dice Wonder. [rare] A classic slum-magic pocket trick made magical in the hands of Dutch magician Flip in the 1980s.
See: Dr..
See: Dry Hand.
See: Spotter.
(See also: trick card.) n. A gimmicked playing card; a faked card (obsolescent); a fake card (obsolescent); a false card (obsolete). [fairly common]

(See also: flash handkerchief.) n. A cotton or linen fabric kerchief converted chemically into nitrocellulose (gun-cotton) so it can be ignited in a sudden burst, leaving no trace. [archaic, formerly rare]

See: Goldfish Bowls fishing g. Pumping being the somewhat more usual synonym. [fairly common] "Curiously, with this trick spectators don't realize you're fishing." — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Apr 1959), 124 Originally the argot of psychic mediums by 1907 D. Abbott; 1924 Houdini; 1926 Wimberly glossary. Thence jargon among mentalist-magicians by 1934 Read; 1947 Boardé; 1969 Nelms; 1972 Anderson; 1974 Grismer in Genii; 1976 Goldstein as "the art of fishing"; 1979 Beam & Morris as "fishing for the card"; 1981 Racherbaumer in MUM as "requires ‘fishing' techniques"; 1986 Hades cat #2; 1986 Miesel as "a little ‘fishing' should narrow it down to the correct card"; 1988 Waters; 1988 Johnsson in LR; 1989 Leveridge price list as "without any ‘fishing' for clues"; 1997 Lee cat #11 as “no fishing”. NOTE: Also verb as "to ‘fish'" in 1965/1988 D. Bamberg, 86. And as adjective "a ‘fishing' sequence" in 1997 Craven in.
(See also: Aerial Fishing.) n. Effect where fish are caught in mid-air by rod-and-reel; fish-catching. [fairly common]
See: flick book.
See: Floating Lightbulb.

(See also: Flyto.) n. Stage effect where the magician's assistant is transposed from one cage suspended above the stage to another. Pronounced FLY-TWO. Also The Flying Visit (obsolete). [fairly common]
See: packs flat.
(See also: force book.) n. A bound volume faked by special printing for use in mind-reading book tests; a forcing book. [fairly common]
(See also: force card.) n. The playing card that the magician induces a volunteer to accept; originally a forced card (obsolete); a forcing card (obsolete). [common]
See: take a break.
See: Thirty-One.
(See also: jumbo coin.) n. An oversized coin, 2 or 3 inches in diameter. [rare]
See: Auto Tires Illusion.
See: Demon Wonder Box Gizmo Glass c. A self-contained stemmed wine goblet that visibly fills up with or empties any liquid. [rare] Released by Abbott’s in 1947..

(See also: handcuff escape.) n. The effect of a release from manacles; the handcuff trick. The cuffs may be faked or not. [fairly common] "Perhaps other 'dressed-up' stunts that Houdini performed onstage stayed with his audiences longer. But the handcuff escape and the jail escape were the bread and butter of his act." — Randi & Sugar, Houdini: His Life and Art (1976), 168 The handcuff escape had been performed as early as 1700 by La Tude in France and by Samri "The White Mahatma" Baldwin in 1871 in New Orleans. However, it was not until development of formidable modern-type cuffs between the 1860s and 1880s that it became a regular act with escape artists. This began in the 1890s with Joe Godfrey (an Australian in the USA) who was soon followed by Louis Paul, Zamora, and Houdini (from 1899 to 1908). REF: Gibson & Young (1961), 8-23; Waller (1980), 159-160. 437

(See also: hat trick.) n. Any trick or routine where one or more objects are produced from a hat; a hat production; the Inexhaustible Hat (obsolete). [common] The earliest version reported was the Cake Baked in Hat as performed by French sleight-of- 443 hand man Delisle in 1749. The Rabbit from Hat trick was introduced by French magician Louis Comte in 1813 but did not become common until the 1840s. The Inexhaustible Hat was introduced by French magician Comus in the early 1800s (and pushed to the limit in the late 1800s by J. M. Hartz in his Devil of a Hat). The Cannon-Ball Trick (from hat) was introduced by 1857.
See: Twister.
See: egg bag.

(See also: lota.) n. A metal bowl in the traditional and characteristic shape of the Indian brass water vessel but faked with a load chamber; redundantly as Lota Bowl; the Hindoo Lota (obsolete). [common] Can be worked to seem, alternately, empty or full of water. This device (originally of earthenware) was invented by Indian conjurors. First reported being performed by Bengali magicians at the court of Emperor Jahangir (reigned 1605-27). Later reported around 1830s by Rev. Caunter performed at a rajah's court and in 1875 when performed in Bombay for the future King Edward VII. Borrowed thence by Western magicians. Reintroduced to modern Indian stage magic by P.C. Sorcar as the "Waters of India". REF: Siegel (1991), 160; Frost (1876), 211-212. Originally the Hindi word lota, meaning a spheroidal water bowl, usually of metal. Introduced into Standard English in 1809. REF: OED/2. Thence Western magicians jargon by 1932 Thayer cat #7S, 52; 1935 Annemann; 1939 Kanter cat 1942 Gibson in Phoenix #15; 1949 Hay; 1962 Ireland cat #17; 1979 Severn; 1980 Tannen cat #13; 1981 Ayling; 1983 Abbott cat #22; 1992 Garrett in MUM; 2002 Diamond’s Magic flyer.

(See also: hooked coin.) n. A large coin with a pin soldered to it to attach to clothing fabric; a hook coin; a hoo coin being the obsolete but best disguised synonym. [fairly common] "Nudist magicians shouldn't use the hooked coin." — Clarke Crandall in The Talisman (19 Jun 1970), 70 Used to steal or ditch the coin. First described in 1900 by Hilliar (p.174). A pet device of Bill Spooner.
See: I.B.M..
See: Jubeo.
(See also: Stolen Jam.) n. Stage illusion where two female assistants are produced from a palanquin previously shown empty; the Jam Illusion. [rare]

(See also: Jap Box.) n. A square-frame container with a removable bottom and one or two false hinged sides; Japanese Handkerchief Box (obsolete); Japanese Inexhaustible Box (obsolete); a hank box (obsolete). If it has one false side, it is called a "Single Load Jap Box", if two, a "Double Load Jap Box". [fairly common] "Maybe I am getting cranky on account of my arthritis, but it annoyed me to see a great big Jap Box used to vanish a single handkerchief." — Rhadamanthus Jr in The Jinx (1941), 789 Used for productions, particularly of silks. Designed to simulate the traditional Japanese rice boxes. REF: Glenn Gravatt, Jap Box Tricks (1937). Originally termed the Japanese Inexhaustible Box by 1876 (Hoffmann; 1891 Burlingame; 1903 Stanyon ad in Magic). Then as the Japanese Handkerchief Box in 1913 (Roterberg cat #15; 1919 Thayer cat #4; 1920 Holmes; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1937 Gravatt; 1941 Chicago Magic cat #18). Also, bizarrely, as the "Egyptian Handkerchief Casket" in 1915 (B. Hull) and the "Egyptian handkerchief box" in 1937 (Gravatt). Finally, contracted as standardized jargon to Jap Box by 1911 H.A. Robinson ad in Magic, 19; 1913 Roterberg cat #15; 1919 Thayer cat #4; 1920 Holmes; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1937 Gravatt; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1949 Hay; 1952 Christopher in HMM; 1957 Furst; 1962 Rice #3; 1964 T. Garrett in Psycho-Gizmo; 1965 Lawston cat; 1969 T. Palmer; 1973 Tannen cat #10; 1977 Tricks Co cat #2; 1979 Lamb; 1982 Tenyo cat; 1988 Darwin; 1989 UST Magic cat; 1992 Willmarth in LR; 1994 Tilford ad in MUM; 1997 Abbott cat #25.

(See also: Jap Box.) n. A square-frame container with a removable bottom and one or two false hinged sides; Japanese Handkerchief Box (obsolete); Japanese Inexhaustible Box (obsolete); a hank box (obsolete). If it has one false side, it is called a "Single Load Jap Box", if two, a "Double Load Jap Box". [fairly common] "Maybe I am getting cranky on account of my arthritis, but it annoyed me to see a great big Jap Box used to vanish a single handkerchief." — Rhadamanthus Jr in The Jinx (1941), 789 Used for productions, particularly of silks. Designed to simulate the traditional Japanese rice boxes. REF: Glenn Gravatt, Jap Box Tricks (1937). Originally termed the Japanese Inexhaustible Box by 1876 (Hoffmann; 1891 Burlingame; 1903 Stanyon ad in Magic). Then as the Japanese Handkerchief Box in 1913 (Roterberg cat #15; 1919 Thayer cat #4; 1920 Holmes; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1937 Gravatt; 1941 Chicago Magic cat #18). Also, bizarrely, as the "Egyptian Handkerchief Casket" in 1915 (B. Hull) and the "Egyptian handkerchief box" in 1937 (Gravatt). Finally, contracted as standardized jargon to Jap Box by 1911 H.A. Robinson ad in Magic, 19; 1913 Roterberg cat #15; 1919 Thayer cat #4; 1920 Holmes; 1924 Felsman cat #18; 1937 Gravatt; 1940 Abbott cat #6; 1949 Hay; 1952 Christopher in HMM; 1957 Furst; 1962 Rice #3; 1964 T. Garrett in Psycho-Gizmo; 1965 Lawston cat; 1969 T. Palmer; 1973 Tannen cat #10; 1977 Tricks Co cat #2; 1979 Lamb; 1982 Tenyo cat; 1988 Darwin; 1989 UST Magic cat; 1992 Willmarth in LR; 1994 Tilford ad in MUM; 1997 Abbott cat #25.
See: Coins through Table.

(See also: Shadow Box.) n. Illusion where a square cabinet with translucent paper panels is shown empty, a lightbulb lowered through the top, the front panel closed, gradually the silhouette of a human figure appears, and the assistant breaks out through the panel; the Shadow Cabinet. [fairly common]

(See also: Beam Shot.) n. Effect where a flashlight in a bag or handkerchief lights when the spectator holds it over the only pile of cards whose top card is the previously selected card; Laser Beam. [rare]
See: Pairs Repaired.

(See also: Castle, the.) n. Nickname of the Magic Castle in Hollywood. [fairly common] Opened on 2 Jan 1963 by William Jr and Milton Larsen in a turreted Gothic Victorian mansion in the Hollywood Hills. Serves as a lavish private club for its (in 1988) nearly 5,500 members, including over 2,500 magicians. 175
See: MDA.

(See also: Funnel.) n. A metal funnel faked with a double-wall whose inner compartment can hold a secret load of liquid to be discharged at the magician's whim; the Magic Funnel being a later and still less usual synonym; the Comedy Funnel. One particular routine is called the Human Pump. [fairly common] First described and explained in 1584 by Prevost in France. Next in 1634 by Hocus Pocus Junior in England. Then in 1655 by Thomas Ady in his A Candle in the Dark, in 1740 by Guyot, and 1763 by Dean. Obviously a popular trick, it was also reported being performed in 1825 by an anonymous conjuror at Bartholomew Fair. REF: Prevost (1584/1998 tr), 161-166; Clarke in Magic Wand, Vol.13 (1924/25), 92, 94-95, 137; Frost (1876), 103-104. 398

(See also: King Tut.) n. Effect where the magus can place a tiny plastic mummy-like figure in its case but, when a volunteer tries, it jumps out. [rare] The method for this popular pocket trick is magnetism. Variants of the King Tut-Ankh-Amun in his sarcophagus theme include the West German “Pedro”, a dog that won’t stay in its bed, a nude woman in her bathtub, etc., etc.
See: Spirit Nut.
See: pass (5).

(See also: magic shop.) n. A retail store that sells magicians props, tricks, and books; a magic emporium (rare); a magic store (rare); a magic depot (U.S., obsolete), magical depot (Brit., obsolescent); a magical repository (obsolete); a conjuring depôt (obsolete). Compare dealer. [common] "There's enough apparatus in the magic shops for all the magicians in the country, but are there enough magicians in the country for all the apparatus?" — Fred Braue in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Dec 1946), 278 "The magic store is the most secret of a magician's gimmicks." — Bruce Elliott in The Phoenix #124 (1947), 500 “Look at the average magic shop and you’ll see a collection of tricks designed to fool magicians, not entertain people.” — Robert Orben in Genii (Oct 1953) "Running a magic shop is like managing a nursery, except the babies are bigger." — Marvin Kaye, My Brother, the Druggist (New York: Crime Club/Doubleday, 1979), 95 "We've a first-rate assortment of magic; And for raising a posthumous shade With effects that are comic or tragic, There's no cheaper house in the trade." — W. S. Gilbert, The Sorcerer (1877), Act I Magic shops, particularly their back rooms, have been traditional gathering places for magicians for nearly two centuries. Originally they catered exclusively to professionals and well-to-do serious amateurs. It was not until the 1920s that many opened their doors to youths and amateurs. These shops have also provided a start toward professional performance for many magicians including such superstars as Cardini and Ali Bongo. For other magi, they remained their sole or main place of regular public performance, as with the justly celebrated Daisy White, Duke Stern, and Al Cohen.

(See also: Maja.) 1.n. The muse or patron goddess of magicians. Pronounced MAH-JAH. [fairly common, although somewhat in decline after the 1940s] "Once the Goddess Maja has waved her wand over some individual's head, that one is her devoted slave henceforth." — Houdini, 1919, quoted in Buffum (1977), 129 From the Sanscrit my (pronounced MY-yah) meaning originally illusion and later, by extension, deception. Still later, the Hindu goddess Maya. The word entered both English (in 1788) and German as maja (pronounced MAH-yah). In Germany it became a moderately popular girl's name in the late 1800s, as with Albert Einstein's younger sister Maja. In India as Maya it remains a popular girl's name. NOTE: Goya's famous Spanish portrait known as The Naked Maja does not depict the goddess, the Spanish word "maja" merely meaning a flashy young female. REF: L. Thomas O'Neil, Maya in Sankara: Measuring the Immeasurable (Delhi: South Asia Books, 1980), 1-39; Oxford English Dictionary, 2nd ed; Hubert Wedler, Wörterbuch der Zauberkunst (1990), 132. Interestingly, in Greek myth, the Grecian god of tricksters, Hermes (the Roman Mercury) was the illegitimate son of Apollo and the nymph Maia. REF: Lewis Hyde, Trickster Makes This World (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1998), 22, etc. Thence from theSanskrit through the German it became magicians jargon (with variants noted) by 1900 Max Berol (a German magician) in Feb Mahatma as "upholding Maga's [sic] banner in Japan"; 1919 Houdini; ca1920 Heaney cat #24 as "Maja's Wonder Drum", a Willmann prop; 1924 Conradi-Horster coined name of the new Berlin magic club "Zaubervereinigung Maja"; 1924 Roterberg palming coin as inscription, "Maja — Goddess of Magic"; 1925 Kastner, Tigris, & Cannon as name of their new Viennese magic club "Maja-Gruppe"; 1932 Savage cartoon in Sphinx; 1941 Booth; 1942 Elliott in Phoenix; 1944 Carl Wiesinger in Phoenix #60 as "if the Goddess Maja could speak"; 1946 Karson in Thompson as "clandestine meetings with the Goddess Maja"; 1947 Cramer in Phoenix #119 as "our Goddess Magi tiptoed in"; 1952 Bobo; 1982 Stevens in Berg; 1988 Waters; 1990 Wassilak in MM as "the wonders of the Goddess

(See also: telepathy.) n. The effect in mind-reading of paranormal communication between two minds; thought transference. [common] 924 “Even telepathy seems to me a striking case of the subjection of the intellect by the will-to- believe.” —Prof. G. Stanley Hall in Amy Tanner, Studies in Spiritism (1910), xxxi "Dunninger puts over a perfect illusion of telepathy, not only for the radio audience, but for the Studio audience as well." — Jean Hugard in Hugard's Magic Monthly (Nov 1943), 23 "If any layman realizes that 'telepathy' and 'question reading' are mere tricks, he immediately loses interest. It does not, in fact, have any entertainment value." — David Price, Magic (1985), 439 The word telepathy was coined from its Greek roots (tele + pathy, meaning literally "distant feeling") in 1882 by British psychic researcher and classical scholar Frederick W.H. Myers. REF: OED/2.
See: Milko.
(See also: Amputation.) n. Effect where the mid-part of a volunteer's fore-arm is seen to have vanished after after being placed in a horizontal box and cut through by two steel blades. [rare]

(See also: coin wand.) n. A wand mechanically faked to produce a folding coin from its tip by activation of a stud; a money wand (obsolete).. [common] Used in performance as early as 12 Mar 1872 by American magicienne Madame Cora de Lamond at the Masonic Hall, Dunedin, New Zealand. First described and marketed in 1873 in the Hartz catalog (p.70). First exposed in 1876 by Hoffmann (p.203) when called the "Half- crown Wand" (also 1885 Sachs 2nd ed). Later models can be loaded with as many as five folding coins. REF: F. Marshall (1984), 12-13.
(See also: OOM.) n. Acronym of oil of milk (and, of course, "moo" spelled backwards). Pronounced UHMM. [fairly common]
See: the Bridle.
(See also: one-man.) a. Said of a performance by a single magician, working alone (single), that is, without stage assistants; one-person. [common]

(See also: inventor.) 1.n. A magician who devises entirely new principles in magic. [rare] "Don't tell every one you meet that you are the inventor of the back hand palm—because you are not." — J. Northern Hilliard in Downs & Hilliard, The Art of Magic (1909) "There are perhaps a dozen true magician-inventors in the world and all the others used these men's ideas and sometimes improved them." — David Bamberg, Illusion Show (1965/1988), 121 492 "The ingenious inventors were those who were able to dream of wonderful impossibilities, solve them with simplicities (it had to be practical), and wind up with something that had all the elements of theatre. Selbit, LeRoy, Fasola, DeKolta, Morritt, Maskelyne, Yettmah, and Jarrett were all people like that."

(See also: pass.) 1.v. As Pass!, an imperative verb as a magic word in patter commanding Go!; passe passe (1, obsolete). [obsolescent, formerly fairly common] "Hay passe, presto vade, jubeo, by the virtue of hocus pocus, 'tis gone." — Thomas Ady, A Candle in the Dark (1655) "By the virtue of Hocus, Pocus, hay passe, prestor, be gone" — ditto

(See also: Insurance Policy.) n. Effect where the magus claims he will pay a specific sum of money if he fails to name the chosen card and shows a simulated insurance policy to cover possible failure. He miscalls the card, apparently losing; but then wins when, upon opening the policy, a giant picture of the right card appears. [common]

(See also: Topit.) n. A special type of body servante in the form of a detachable cloth pocket that can be pinned under the magician's clothing at unsuspected places; a poacher's pocket. [common] Used mainly for ditching but also, occasionally, for stealing. Originally, as a "poacher's pocket" used by British poachers to hide their illicitly trapped or shot game. This artifice was later adopted by pickpockets and shoplifters to evade initial suspicion and, if pressed, a conventional search. Finally adapted to magic in 1919 by British magician Harold Comden as a card vanisher. Used with good effect by a very few magicians such as George Davenport, Topper Martyn, Patrick Page, Fred Kaps, and Bob Fitch; but it did not become widely known much less appreciated and used until after publication in 1983 of Michael Ammar's comprehensive manual, Ammar himself having discovered Topit in 1978 or 79. REF: Busby in Epoptica #4 (1983), 217-218; Farelli in Hugard's Magic Monthly (1953), 63; Fitch (1980).
(See also: pocketing.) n. Type of body work where the magician uses his pocket as a servante, putting his hand in or past to steal or ditch an object; pocket work. [rare]
See: Swazzle.
(See also: Snapper.) n. Effect where the operator can catch a hook on a rubber band inside a red cylinder, but a volunteer can't. [common]

See: Ring on Stick ringing g. To ring, in its gerundive form; switching. [obsolescent, formerly rare] American card sharps used this word in the expression "ringing in" and "ringing in cold decks" by 1857 Green, but spelled "wringing"; 1865 Evans as "ringing in"; 1873 Morris; 1890 Quinn. Thence magicians jargon by 1876 Hoffmann, 158; 1886 Garenne; 1944 Larsen as "the ringing in of a stacked deck"; 779 1962 Ireland cat #17 as "wringing [sic] in other colors"; 1985 Johnsson in LR as "the `ringing in' is automatic"..
(See also: spring blind.) n. A spring-wound shade (like a window roller-blind) to instantly and visually reveal or conceal an object; a roller blind. [rare]

(See also: Shadow Box.) n. Illusion where a square cabinet with translucent paper panels is shown empty, a lightbulb lowered through the top, the front panel closed, gradually the silhouette of a human figure appears, and the assistant breaks out through the panel; the Shadow Cabinet. [fairly common]

(See also: Silk Cabby.) n. A small box or cabinet (cabby) with hinged drop-down doors, front-and-back, one of which is fitted with a secret load chamber to vanish handkerchiefs (silks); a silk cabinet. [fairly common]
See: sleight..

(See also: S.A.M..) n. Acronym of the Society of American Magicians. Properly pronounced by its letters “Ess-Ay-Em”, never as “Sam”. [fairly common] Founded in 1902 by Dr W. Golden Mortimer and Dr Saram R. Ellison in the famous backroom of Francis J. Martinka’s magic shop. REF: H.R. Evans in Magic (Oct 1903), 9; Severn (1979), 228-229; Hanson & Zweers (1974), 65.
See: Handkerchiefs and Soup Plate.
See: Cabala.
(See also: Switch Wallet.) n. A changing wallet (see) being the more usual synonym; a switching wallet. [rare]
See: table hopper.

(See also: trap table.) n. A magician's table fitted with one or more traps. [archaic] Use of a table trap in conjuring was first described in 1784 by Decremps in exposing a contemporary trick by Pinetti. These passed out of common use around World War I, being superceded by the Black Art Table.
(See also: Doll House.) n. The stage illusion where a large dollhouse, shown empty, disgorges the magician's female assistant. [common]

(See also: trap vanish.) n. A sleight in billiard ball manipulation where a ball, resting on top of the fist of the lower hand, is seemingly swept off by the upper hand while actually dropping into the lower; trap pass. [very rare] First described in 1876 by Hoffmann (pp.405-407) but using an egg. So named because the lower hand opens to act like a magician's table trap. Jargon coined in 1910 by Burling Hull. Thence 1978 Gross.

(See also: trickster.) n. Convenient synonym for magician but usually tongue-in-cheek or disparagingly. [fairly common] "Too many performers still make an entrance as a stout magician, and exit looking like a starved trickster." — Annemann in The Jinx #26 (1936), 162 “An enterprising club can have its pick of a dozen or more top tricksters who will lecture on their special phase of sorcery and demonstrate their techniques.” — “Frank Joglar” [Milbourne Christopher] in Hugard’s Magic Monthly (May 1950), 660 "The trickster's chief aim is to deceive his audience about the way his tricks are done." — Henning Nelms, Magic and Showmanship (1969), 19 Originally Standard English by 1711 meaning a prankster.
